en: May Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us;
may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us.
Homage to Brahman!
Homage to you, O Vāyu!
You alone are the perceptible Brahman.
I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman;
I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Satya.
May that protect me;
may it protect its speaker;
may it protect me.
May it protect the speaker.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together;
may we work together with vigor.
May it be well-studied by us; may we not hate one another.
Om! Peace! Peace! Peace! He who is the bull of the meters, whose form is the universe—he was born from the immortal meters.
May that lord Indra endow me with wisdom.
May I become a sustainer of immortality among the gods. May my body be full of insight.
My tongue is most sweet; from my two ears I have heard much.
You are the treasury of sacred knowledge, covered by wisdom.
What has been heard, protect it. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
I am the shaker of the tree; my fame is like the ridge of a mountain. With my purifier held aloft, I am my own immortal nectar, like a prize-winning steed.
"Obeisance to Draviṇa, the radiant;
obeisance to Sumedhas, anointed with immortality"—
this is the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku.

Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, while performing sacrifices. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise [you] with hymns of praise.
May we attain the life-span ordained by the gods. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being;
may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
The Whole is full; this is full. From the full, the full is drawn out. When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!

May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, as well as strength and all my senses, be nourished. May I never deny Brahman; may Brahman never deny me. May there be no denial, may there be no denial for me. May those virtues which reside in the self and are established in the Upaniṣads be in me; may they be in me.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
May my speech be established in my mind;
may my mind be established in my speech.
Be manifest and radiant.
Be the axle-pin of my Veda;
do not let what I have heard fall away from me through this study.
I join together the days and nights;
I shall speak the Right;
I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me;
may it protect its speaker;
may it protect me.
May it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace! May you also direct our mind toward what is auspicious.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.

I seek refuge in that God who illumines the self through the intellect, whom the seeker of liberation approaches for protection— he who ordained Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sutras.
The First Chapter. Composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma Sūtras.
The first quarter of the first chapter.
The venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara-Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
This Śārīrakamīmāṃsā was printed by Sonurnishrunker Sumerivvala for Śrī Vāṇīvilāsa Mudrāyantrālaya.
The commentary on the Sūtra.
Composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.

When it is established that the object and the subject—the spheres of the notions of "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "I" (*asmat*), which possess the contradictory natures of darkness and light respectively—cannot exist as each other, then it follows all the more that their respective attributes cannot exist as each other. Therefore, it is logical that there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the object and its attributes—which fall within the sphere of the notion of "you"—upon the subject, which consists of consciousness and falls within the sphere of the notion of "I"; and conversely, there is a superimposition of the subject and its attributes upon the object. It is proper that this [mutual] superimposition be considered false.

Nevertheless, by superimposing the nature of one upon the other and the attributes of one upon the other through mutual non-discrimination—having coupled the real and the unreal, which are absolutely distinct as attribute and substrate due to false knowledge—there arises this natural worldly practice: "I am this" and "this is mine."
He asks: "What is this so-called superimposition (adhyāsa)? It is replied: "It is the appearance, in the form of a memory, of something previously perceived elsewhere.
Some describe it as "the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another."
Some, however, maintain that where there is a superimposition of one thing upon another, it is an error based on the failure to grasp their distinction.
Others, on the other hand, describe it as the mere conceptualization of contrary attributes belonging to that very object upon which the superimposition occurs.
In every case, however, it does not deviate from the nature of the appearance of the attributes of one thing in another.
And thus there is experience in the world: for mother-of-pearl appears like silver, and the single moon appears as if it had a second.

But how can there be a superimposition of objects and their attributes upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is not an object? For everyone superimposes one object upon another object that is situated directly before them; yet you maintain that the inner self, being devoid of the notion of "thou" (*yuṣmat-pratyaya*), is not an object. It is said in reply: this [inner self] is not absolutely a non-object, because it is the object of the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*), and because the inner self is well-known through its immediate presence (*aparokṣatva*).
Nor is there this rule that an object must be superimposed only upon another object standing directly before one;
for even in the case of the sky, which is not perceptible, the ignorant superimpose such things as a surface or impurity. Thus ends the first chapter.
Thus, even with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), which is non-different from it, there is the superimposition of the non-self (anātma-adhyāsa).
The wise consider this superimposition (*adhyāsa*), characterized in this manner, to be ignorance (*avidyā*).
They call the ascertainment of the true nature of a thing through the discrimination of that [superimposition] knowledge (*vidyā*).
This being so, that upon which something is superimposed is not affected even in the slightest degree by any defect or quality produced by that [superimposition].

Taking for granted this very mutual superimposition of the Self and the non-Self, which is called ignorance (*avidyā*), all worldly transactions involving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) proceed; likewise, all scriptures—whether concerned with injunctions, prohibitions, or liberation—are based upon it. But how can the means of knowledge, such as perception, and the scriptures have as their object one who possesses ignorance? It is said in reply: because the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is impossible for one who is devoid of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, senses, and so forth, the operation of the means of knowledge is impossible.
Indeed, without employing the senses, the practical activity of perception and the rest cannot occur.
Furthermore, the functioning of the sense organs is not possible without a substratum;
nor does anyone act with a body whose self-nature is not presided over [by consciousness].
And in the absence of all this, the status of being a knower cannot be established for a Self that is unattached.
Furthermore, there is no operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) without a cognizer (pramātṛ).
Therefore, the means of valid cognition such as perception, as well as the scriptures, have as their object only that which is characterized by ignorance (avidyā).
This is because they are not distinct from [the means of cognition used by] cattle and other animals.

For just as cattle and other animals, when there is a connection of their ears and other senses with sounds and other objects, turn away from those cognitions of sound and so forth that are disagreeable and move toward those that are agreeable;

just as, upon perceiving a person standing before them with a raised staff in hand, they begin to flee, thinking, "He wishes to kill me," but upon perceiving someone with green grass in his hand, they move toward him.

In the same way, men whose minds are developed, upon perceiving those with cruel looks who are reviling them and raising swords in their hands—provided they are powerful—turn away from them; conversely, they advance toward those who are the opposite.

Therefore, the linguistic usage regarding means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is common to men and animals alike. And it is well known that the usage of perception and so forth among animals is preceded by a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*).

From the observation of that commonality, it is determined that even for persons possessing intellectual cultivation, their practical activity based on perception and other means is identical at that time.

As for scriptural practice, although one who acts with deliberation is not entitled [to perform rites] without knowing his connection to the next world, nevertheless, the true nature of the Self—which is to be known through the Vedānta, which transcends hunger and other such states, which is free from distinctions such as Brahmin or Kṣatriya, and which is beyond saṃsāra—is not required for entitlement, because it is of no use there and would indeed be contradictory to the requirements of entitlement.
Furthermore, a scripture that functions prior to such knowledge of the Self as it truly is does not transcend having ignorance as its domain.

For instance, scriptural injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" proceed by relying on the superimposition of specific attributes such as caste, stage of life, age, and condition upon the Self.
We have already stated that superimposition (adhyāsa) is the cognition of something in what is not that thing.
For example, my son, when one's wife or others are incomplete or complete, one superimposes external attributes upon the self, thinking, "I myself am incomplete" or "I am complete";

likewise, one superimposes the attributes of the body, thinking, "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am fair," "I stand," "I walk," and "I sit"; and likewise, one superimposes the attributes of the senses, thinking, "I am mute," "I am blind," and so forth. (First Chapter)

"I am impotent, deaf, blind"— in this way, one superimposes the attributes of the internal organ, such as desire, volition, doubt, and determination, upon the inner self. Likewise, having superimposed that which is the object of the notion of "I" upon the inner self— the witness of all its own fluctuations— one superimposes that inner self, the witness of all, upon the internal organ and so forth by way of the reverse process.
Thus, this beginningless and endless natural superimposition (adhyāsa), consisting of false cognition, which impels one toward the state of being an agent and an enjoyer, is evident to all the world.
For the sake of abandoning this cause of evil and for the attainment of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, all the Vedāntas are commenced.
And how this is the purport of all the Vedāntas, we shall demonstrate in this Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā.
This is the first aphorism of the Vedānta-mīmāṃsā-śāstra, which is intended to be expounded: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman."

In this context, the word *atha* (then) is understood in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*); it does not signify the commencement of a new topic (*adhikāra*), because the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is not itself something to be commenced; nor does it signify auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), because auspiciousness cannot be syntactically connected with the meaning of the sentence, which is the desire to know.
The word *atha* is indeed employed for another purpose; for, by its direct denotation (*śruti*), it serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*),
and because dependence on what was previously mentioned is not distinct from immediate succession (*ānantarya*) in its result.

And since it has the sense of "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*), just as the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) invariably requires the prior study of the Veda, so too must that which the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) invariably requires be stated.
However, the immediate succession following the study of one's own Vedic portion (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is common to both.
But is there not a distinction here in the Sūtra-bhāṣya regarding the immediate succession following the comprehension of ritual action (*karmāvabodha*)?
No;
for even prior to the inquiry into Dharma, the inquiry into Brahman is possible for one who has already studied the Vedānta.

And just as there is a rule of immediate succession regarding the cutting out of the heart and other organs because the sequence is intended to be significant, so too is no such sequence intended here.

Because there is no evidence for a relationship of subordinate and principal, or for a relationship of a qualified person and a qualification, between the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman;
and because of the difference in their fruits and objects of inquiry:
the knowledge of Dharma has prosperity as its fruit, and that depends upon ritual performance.
However, the knowledge of Brahman has liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) as its fruit and does not depend on any other performance;
furthermore, Dharma, which is to be investigated, is something yet to be brought into being (*bhavya*) and does not exist at the time of its cognition, because it is dependent upon human activity.
In this case, however, Brahman—which is to be investigated—is an already existing reality (*bhūta*), and since it exists eternally, it is not dependent upon human activity.
And because there is a difference in the operation of the injunctions:
for the injunction that is the defining characteristic of dharma informs a person only by enjoining him with respect to its own object;
the injunction regarding Brahman, however, merely informs the person.

Since awakening is produced by an injunction, a person is not enjoined to bring about awakening—just as one is not enjoined to bring about the cognition of an object through the contact of the sense-organ with that object.
Therefore, something must be stated immediately prior to which the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is taught.

It is said: [the requirements are] the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, the perfection of the means such as tranquility and self-control (*śama-dama-ādi*), and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*).
For when these [means] exist, it is possible to desire to know and to know Brahman both prior to and after the inquiry into Dharma; not otherwise.
Therefore, by the word "atha" (then), the immediate succession to the attainment of the aforementioned means is taught. [Sūtra 1.1.1] First Chapter.
The word "ataḥ" (hence) signifies a reason.

For the Veda itself demonstrates that the means to the highest good, such as the Agnihotra and other rites, yield impermanent results, in passages such as: "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"; and likewise, it demonstrates that from the knowledge of Brahman alone the supreme human goal is attained, in passages such as: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."
Therefore, immediately after the attainment of the aforementioned means, the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken.
The desire to know Brahman is *brahmajijñāsā*.
And Brahman has the definition that will be stated [later]: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed].
For this very reason, one should not suspect that the word "Brahman" has any other meaning, such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

The word "brahmaṇaḥ" is used in the sense of the object (karma-ṣaṣṭhī), not as a residual relation (śeṣa); for the desire to know (jijñāsā) requires an object of inquiry, and no other object of inquiry has been specified.

Now, one might argue that even if the residual genitive were accepted, it would not contradict Brahman being the object of the desire to know, since a general relationship necessarily implies a specific one.
Even so, for one who discards the directly perceived objecthood of Brahman and instead postulates an indirect objecthood by way of a commonality, the effort would be in vain.

If it is argued that it is not in vain because it serves to propose an inquiry into everything resting upon Brahman, we say no; for when the primary subject is embraced, those things required by it are also necessarily implied.

For Brahman is the primary object because it is that which is most desired to be attained through knowledge. When that primary object of inquiry has been embraced, those things without which Brahman cannot be inquired into are already implied by that very act; thus, they need not be formulated as separate aphorisms.
This is just as when it is said, "The king is going," the going of the king along with his retinue is thereby stated. (Śabara-bhāṣya on Sūtra 1.1.1)
And because of the conformity with scripture.
Scriptures such as, "From which indeed these beings are born," and so forth, explicitly show that Brahman is the object of the desire to know, stating, "Desire to know That; That is Brahman.
And this [status of being the object] is supported by the Sūtra only if the genitive case is understood in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Therefore, in the phrase "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*).
The desire to know is *jijñāsā*. Knowledge culminating in realization is the object of the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix *san*, because desire has its fruit as its object.
For Brahman is that which is intended to be understood by means of the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Indeed, the realization of Brahman is the supreme human goal, because it eradicates the evils such as ignorance—the seed of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence.
Therefore, Brahman ought to be investigated.
Furthermore, that Brahman must be either well-known or unknown.
If it is well-known, it need not be an object of inquiry;
if, on the other hand, it is unknown, it cannot possibly be an object of inquiry.
It is said: there indeed exists Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, omniscient, and endowed with all powers.

For when the word *brahman* is etymologically analyzed, meanings such as eternal purity and so forth are understood, since these follow from the meaning of the verbal root *bṛṃhati* (to grow or expand).
Furthermore, the existence of Brahman is established because it is the Self of all.
For everyone indeed perceives the existence of the self; one does not think, "I am not.
If the well-known existence of the self did not occur, then everyone in the world would perceive, "I am not.
And the self is Brahman.

If, then, Brahman is already well-known in the world as the Self, it follows once again that it is already known and therefore not a fit object for inquiry; no, for [the inquiry concerns] its specific nature. (First Adhyāya)
This is because of conflicting views.
Ordinary people and the Lokāyatikas maintain that the self is merely the body characterized by consciousness.
Others hold that the sense organs themselves are conscious and constitute the self.
Others say it is the mind (*manas*);
some say it is mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) and momentary;
others say it is emptiness (*śūnya*).
Others maintain that there exists a transmigrating being, distinct from the body and so forth, who is both agent and enjoyer;
some hold that he is merely the enjoyer and not the agent;
and some assert that there exists a Lord (Īśvara) distinct from him, who is omniscient and omnipotent.
Others maintain that the self is the enjoyer.
Thus, many are in disagreement, relying upon arguments and statements, as well as fallacious arguments and fallacious statements.
In this regard, one who accepts something without inquiry may be obstructed from the supreme good and may incur misfortune.

Therefore, under the guise of introducing the inquiry into Brahman, the investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) of the Vedānta texts—aided by reasoning that does not contradict them—is now commenced for the purpose of attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
It has been stated that Brahman is to be sought after.
But what is the defining characteristic of that Brahman? To this, the venerable author of the Sūtras replies: "From which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world]."
"Janmādi" (having birth, etc. is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound;
thus, "birth, subsistence, and dissolution" is the meaning of the compound.
Furthermore, the status of birth as the "first" (ādi) depends both on the order of mention in the scripture (*śruti*) and on the actual nature of things (*vastuvṛtta*).

The section concerning "origination and so forth" (janmādyadhikaraṇa) in the Śruti. First, regarding the locus [of the inquiry], it is the scriptural passage: "From which indeed these beings are born," because in this sentence the sequence of origination, subsistence, and dissolution is observed.
Furthermore, according to the actual nature of things, subsistence and dissolution are possible only for a substrate that has acquired its existence through origination.
The word "asya" (of this) is a designation by means of the pronoun *idam* for the subject (*dharmin*) brought to mind through perception and other means.
The genitive case indicates the relationship between the subject and its attributes, such as birth and so forth.
The word "yataḥ" (from which) is a designation of the cause.

The completion of the sentence is: "That from which the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of this world—which is differentiated by name and form, joined with many agents and enjoyers, the locus of actions, results, places, times, and specific causes, and whose structure is inconceivable even by the mind—proceeds from a cause that is omniscient and omnipotent, is Brahman.
Although there are other modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*), they are included within these three; thus, only birth, subsistence, and destruction are mentioned here.

However, if one were to take the [stages] enumerated by Yāska— namely "is born," "exists," and so forth— it might be suspected that since these are possible only during the period of the world's maintenance (*sthiti*), the origination, maintenance, and destruction of the world from its primal cause would not be included. To prevent such a suspicion, those [stages] are taken wherein the origination of Brahman from its cause, as well as its maintenance and dissolution therein, are comprised.

Furthermore, it is not possible to conceive of the origin and so forth of the world—characterized as described above—as proceeding from anything other than the Lord (Īśvara) who possesses those same characteristics; that is, not from the insentient *pradhāna*, nor from atoms (*aṇu*), nor from non-existence (*abhāva*), nor from a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*).
Nor can it arise from inherent nature (*svabhāva*), because specific place, time, and causes are here accepted as the basis for its production.
Proponents of the doctrine of God as the cause consider this very inference to be the proof for the existence of a Lord distinct from the transmigrating souls.
First Chapter. [Objection: But has not that very same thing been presented here as well in the Sūtra on "origination and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*)? [Reply: No.
Because the aphorisms (*sūtras*) have the purpose of stringing together the flowers that are the Vedānta passages;
for it is indeed the Vedānta passages that are cited by the aphorisms and subjected to inquiry.
Indeed, the realization of Brahman is accomplished through the determination resulting from the inquiry into the meaning of those passages, and not through other means of knowledge such as inference.

However, when Vedāntic statements exist that proclaim the cause of the world’s origin and so forth, inference—provided it does not contradict those Vedāntic statements—is not excluded as a means of valid knowledge for grasping their meaning; for the Śruti itself accepts reasoning as an auxiliary aid.

To illustrate: the Śruti says, "He is to be heard and reflected upon," and "Just as a learned and intelligent man would reach Gandhāra itself, even so does a person who has a teacher know [the Self]"—thus it demonstrates its own reliance on the assistance of human intellect.

In the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), scripture (*śruti*) and the other means of knowledge do not function as authorities in the same way as they do in the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). Rather, in this context, scripture and the rest, as well as experience (*anubhava*) and the others, serve as authorities according to their respective applicability; for the knowledge of Brahman culminates in direct experience and has an already existing reality as its object. Indeed, in the case of that which is to be accomplished (*kartavya*), there is no dependence upon experience, and thus scripture and the other means would alone possess authority, since that which is to be accomplished derives its existence from human action.

Worldly and Vedic action can be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise—just as one goes by horse, on foot, or otherwise, or does not go at all. Likewise: "In the Atirātra sacrifice, one takes the Ṣoḍaśin cup; in the Atirātra, one does not take the Ṣoḍaśin cup"; "One offers after sunrise; one offers before sunrise."
In this context, injunctions and prohibitions, as well as options, general rules, and exceptions, would be meaningful in the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya;
however, a real entity (*vastu*) is not subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpyate*) such that it "is thus" or "is not thus," or "exists" or "does not exist.
Conceptual constructions, rather, depend upon the intellect of the person.
The knowledge of the true nature of a thing does not depend upon human intellect;
rather, it depends solely upon the thing itself.
For, regarding a single post, there does not arise the knowledge of reality in the form, "Is this a post, or is it something else, such as a person?"
In that regard, "it is a person or something else" is false knowledge;
"it is indeed a post" is true knowledge, because it depends upon the actual state of things.
Thus, the validity of cognitions concerning existing entities depends upon those entities themselves.
This being the case, even the knowledge of Brahman is dependent solely upon the thing itself (*vastutantra*), because its object is an already existing reality (*bhūtavastu*).

[Objection: But if Brahman has an already existing reality as its object, it would necessarily fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); thus, the investigation of Vedāntic passages would result in being purposeless.
[Reply: No.
Because a relation [of the effect] is apprehended through the fact that the senses have no Brahman as their object.
By their very nature, the senses have effects as their objects, not Brahman as their object.
For if Brahman were an object of the senses, it would be apprehended as "this effect is related to Brahman."
However, when the mere effect is apprehended, it is impossible to determine whether it is connected with Brahman or connected with something else.
Therefore, the Sūtra on "origination and so forth" (janmādi) is not intended for the presentation of an inference; rather, it is for the purpose of pointing out a Vedānta passage.
But what is that Vedānta passage which the Sūtra here intends to indicate?
"Having begun with, 'Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa, saying:
"Venerable sir, teach me Brahman," [the text] says: "That from which indeed these beings are born..."
That by which living beings are born and live, and into which they enter when they depart— this is the first chapter.
"Seek to understand that;
that is Brahman.
And the definitive statement concerning it is: "Verily, from Bliss alone indeed these beings are born."
"By bliss they are born;
by bliss they live; into bliss they enter and merge.
Other passages of this kind, which concern the cause whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, and whose essence is omniscience, should also be cited.
By demonstrating that Brahman is the cause of the world, it was suggested that Brahman is omniscient; confirming this very point, [the Sūtra] says: "Because [Brahman] is the source of the Śāstra."

Brahman is the source— that is, the cause— the instrument for the great scripture consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth, which is augmented by many branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), which illuminates all objects like a lamp, and which is almost omniscient. For such a scripture, characterized as the Ṛgveda and so forth, and endowed with the qualities of an omniscient being, there can be no origin from anyone other than an omniscient being.

Whatever treatise of extensive meaning originates from a particular person—just as grammar and other sciences originate from Pāṇini and others for the sake of even a single portion of what is to be known—it is well known in the world that he possesses a knowledge far superior to that [treatise].

What need is there to say more? From that Great Being, from whom arises—without effort, as a mere sport and like the breath of a person—the source known as the Rigveda and so forth, which is divided into many branches, which is the cause of the distinctions among gods, animals, humans, castes, and stages of life, and which is a mine of all knowledge—as stated in such scriptural passages as, "This Rigveda is the breath of this Great Being"—that Great Being possesses unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence.

Alternatively, the meaning is that the scripture (*śāstra*)— namely the *Ṛgveda* and so forth as previously described— is the source (*yoni*), the cause, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for attaining the true nature of this Brahman.
The intention is that Brahman, the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, is understood solely through the means of valid knowledge that is scripture,
as exemplified in the previous sūtra by the passage beginning, "From which indeed these beings are born."

For what purpose is this sūtra, since by the previous sūtra alone—which cited such a scripture as an example—the fact that Brahman has scripture as its source (*śāstrayonitva*) was already demonstrated?

It is replied: In that [previous] case, because scripture was not explicitly mentioned by the words of the sūtra itself, one might suspect that the sūtra "from which [arise] birth, etc. (*janmādi-sūtra*) merely put forward an inference (*anumāna*).
To remove that suspicion, this sūtra was composed: "Because [Brahman] has scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

But how can it be said that Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition, when it has been demonstrated that scripture is intent upon action, according to the principle: "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their purpose are useless"?
Therefore, the Vedāntas would be useless because they do not have action as their purpose;

or else, they would be subordinate to injunctions for action by way of revealing the agent, the deity, and so forth, or they would have as their purpose the injunction of other actions such as meditation (*upāsanā*).

For it is not possible to establish the nature of an already established entity; because such an established entity is the object of perception and other means of knowledge, and because there would be no human purpose in establishing it, as it is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted.

For this very reason, so that passages such as "He wept" (so'rodīt) would not be rendered meaningless, their meaningfulness was established by the principle that "because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they serve the purpose of praising the injunctions.

Furthermore, the utility of mantras such as "For the sake of food, thee" (iṣe tvā) was established through their connection to ritual action by virtue of their denoting the action itself and its means.
Therefore, nowhere has the meaningfulness of Vedic sentences been observed or logically justified apart from a connection to an injunction.

Furthermore, an injunction (*vidhi*) is not possible with respect to the established nature of an existing entity (*vastu-svarūpa*), because an injunction has action as its object. Therefore, the Vedānta texts are subordinate to injunctions of action by way of revealing the nature of the agent, deity, and so forth required for that action. Now, if it is argued that this cannot be accepted for fear of contradicting the context (*prakaraṇa*), even then they must be understood as being concerned with actions such as meditation (*upāsanā*) mentioned within their own sentences. Thus, since Brahman is not the source of the scripture (*śāstra-yonitva*), this being the position reached, it is said: "But that [Brahman is known] from the harmony [of the texts]. (Sūtra 1.1.4)
The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the prima facie view.

That Brahman—omniscient, omnipotent, and the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world—is understood through the Vedānta scriptures. How so? Through systematic coordination (samanvaya). Because of systematic coordination.

For in all the Vedāntas, the section concerning the meaning of sentences (*vākyādhikaraṇa*) is consistently followed as demonstrating this very subject matter with intentional significance. Such passages include: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1); "One only, without a second" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1); "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1); "This is that Brahman, without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.5.19); "This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of everything" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.5.7); and "Brahman, the immortal, is this [world] before us" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.10.4), and so forth.

Furthermore, when the definitive concordance (*samanvaya*) of the words contained therein with respect to the nature of Brahman is understood, it is not reasonable to postulate another meaning, as that would entail the abandonment of what is heard in scripture (*śrutahāni*) and the assumption of what is not heard (*aśrutakalpanā*).

Nor is it determined that those [passages] are intent on propounding the nature of an agent, a deity, or similar entities, because of scriptural texts such as "Then by what means, and whom, would he see? which negate action, its factors, and their results.

Moreover, even though Brahman is an established reality, it is not an object of perception and other such means of knowledge, since the identity of Brahman and the Self expressed in "That thou art" cannot be understood without the scripture.
As for the objection that instruction would be purposeless because [the Self] is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, this is not a fault;
for the human goal is accomplished precisely through the realization of Brahman as the Self—which is itself free from rejection and acceptance—since this leads to the abandonment of all afflictions.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction even if a text primarily intended to propound a deity or similar object serves the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*) contained within its own words.

But in that way, it is not possible for Brahman to be subordinate to an injunction for meditation, because in the state of oneness—being devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—the sublation of the cognition of duality consisting of action, factors of action, and so forth, is logically established.

For there is no possibility of the re-emergence of the cognition of duality once it has been destroyed by the cognition of the oneness of Brahman, such that Brahman could be presented as subordinate to an injunction for meditation.

Even though elsewhere the validity of Vedic statements has not been observed without contact with an injunction (*vidhi*), nevertheless, because the knowledge of the Self culminates in its own fruit, it is impossible to deny the authority of the scripture concerning that subject.
Nor is the authority of the scripture something to be apprehended through inference, such that it would require an illustrative example observed elsewhere.
Therefore, [the authority of the Upanishads] is established. (Brahma Sūtra, First Chapter)
The authority of the Veda as established by scripture.

On this point, others object: even if Brahman has the scripture as its means of valid knowledge, nevertheless, Brahman is presented by the scripture solely as the object of an injunction for realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*).

Just as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *āhavanīya* fire, and so forth—though not known from ordinary experience—are presented by the scripture as subordinate elements of injunctions, so it is here.
Why is this so? Because the scripture has as its purpose the instigation to action (*pravṛtti*) and the cessation from action (*nivṛtti*).
For thus it is stated by those who know the purport of the treatise: "Its purpose is indeed seen to be the comprehension of action";

"An injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that impels one toward action"; "The knowledge of that [Dharma] is instruction (*upadeśa*"); "The collection of words that have attained that state [of being parts of an injunction] is for the sake of action"; and "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those passages which do not have that as their purpose are useless.
Therefore, a treatise is meaningful only insofar as it impels a person toward a particular object and turns him away from another particular object.
And other [passages] are employed as being supplementary to that;
by analogy with them, the Vedāntas would likewise possess purposefulness in that same way.

And if they are subordinate to injunctions, it is logical that just as the Agnihotra and other means are enjoined for one who desires heaven and so forth, so too the knowledge of Brahman is enjoined for one who desires immortality.

But has it not been stated here that there is a difference in the objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*): in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, dharma—which is yet to be produced (*bhavya*)—is the object of inquiry, whereas here, Brahman—which is already existent (*bhūta*) and eternally accomplished—is the object of inquiry?
In that case, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman ought to be distinct from the fruit of the knowledge of dharma, which depends upon ritual performance.
It cannot be so; for Brahman is presented only as being prompted by injunctions regarding what is to be done (*kāryavidhi*).

"Verily, the Self (ātman) is to be seen; that Self which is free from sin, free from old age, free from death, free from grief, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolve is true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand. "One should meditate on the Self alone. "One should meditate on the Self as the world. "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Since such injunctions exist, when the inquiry arises—"Who is this Self? What is that Brahman?"—all the Vedānta texts serve to define its nature, stating: "Brahman is eternal, omniscient, omnipresent, eternally satisfied, and by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free; Brahman is consciousness and bliss," and so forth.
And through the worship of that [Brahman], liberation—which is an unseen result—will be the fruit, as seen in the scriptures.

However, if there were no entry into an injunction of duty (*kartavyavidhi*) and the texts merely stated a bare fact (*vastumātra*), then because taking up or abandoning would be impossible, the Vedānta passages would be entirely purposeless, like sentences such as "The earth has seven islands" or "That king is going.
Now, even when stating a bare fact, purposefulness is observed in cases such as "This is a rope, not a snake," where the fear produced by delusion is removed.
Similarly here as well, there would be purposefulness through the statement of the reality of the non-transmigrating Self, which serves to remove the delusion of being a transmigrator.

This might be so, if the delusion of being a transmigrator were removed by the mere hearing of the nature of Brahman, just as the delusion of a snake is removed by the mere hearing of the true nature of the rope;
however, it is not so removed.

Even for one who has heard the Brahman, there is the observation of transmigratory attributes such as pleasure and pain as before; furthermore, there is the observation of injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) subsequent to hearing, in the passage: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon.
Therefore, Brahman must be accepted as having the scripture as its authority solely by virtue of being the object of an injunction for realization.
First Chapter: Visū. Here it is replied: No;
because of the difference between the fruits of ritual action and the knowledge of Brahman.

Action—whether physical, vocal, or mental—which is established by the *śruti* and *smṛti* and is designated as "dharma," is the subject of the inquiry formulated in the aphorism: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*).
For even "adharma," such as violence and the like, is to be investigated for the sake of avoidance, since it is characterized by prohibitive injunctions (*pratiṣedha-codanā*).

Regarding these two, dharma and adharma, which are defined by injunction and are beneficial or harmful, their fruits are pleasure and pain; these are directly perceived, experienced through the body, speech, and mind alone, produced by the contact of the senses with their objects, and are well known among all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary plants.
Beginning from the human state up to those embodied beings ending with Brahmā, a gradation of happiness is traditionally heard.
From that, a gradation of its cause—dharma—is also understood.
From the gradation of dharma follows a gradation of qualification.
Furthermore, a gradation of qualification based on factors such as desire, capability, and learning is well known.

Accordingly, it is understood from scripture—specifically from the passage "having dwelt there as long as their works endure"—that those who perform sacrifices and other rites proceed by the northern path due to excellence in knowledge and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereas those who possess only the means of sacrifice, public works, and charity proceed by the southern path through the sequence of smoke and so forth; moreover, within that [southern path], both a gradation of pleasure and a gradation of its means are understood from the scriptures.

Likewise, it is understood that even the slightest fragment of pleasure found among beings from humans down to the stationary (sthāvara) is achievable only through dharma characterized by injunctions, as it exists in varying degrees of intensity.

Similarly, because a gradation of suffering is observed among embodied beings in higher and lower realms, a corresponding gradation is inferred in its cause—adharma—as well as in the prohibitions characterizing it and in those who practice it.

Thus, for those possessed of defects such as ignorance, there exists the impermanent form of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of a gradation of pleasure and pain preceded by the assumption of bodies caused by the varying degrees of merit and demerit; this is well-established through Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning.
And so the Śruti text, "For one who possesses a body, there is no cessation of the pleasant and the unpleasant," reiterates the nature of transmigratory existence as it has been described.

From the prohibition of the touch of the pleasant and the unpleasant in the passage, "Verily, the bodyless state is not touched by the pleasant or the unpleasant," it is understood that the state of bodilessness known as liberation—which would otherwise be the effect of dharma characterized by Vedic injunction—is here prohibited.
For if it were the effect of dharma, the prohibition of the touch of the pleasant and the unpleasant would be untenable.
If it is argued that bodilessness itself is the effect of dharma, we say no.

Because this [state] is its very nature—according to such scriptural passages as: "The wise man does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self which dwells within bodies that are themselves unstable; for this Person is without breath, without mind, pure, and indeed unattached"—it is established that the bodiless state called liberation, being distinct from the fruits of actions to be performed, is eternal.

In this regard, something might be "transformative-eternal" (*pariṇāminitya*), such that even while it undergoes modification, the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not sublated— as, for example, the earth and so forth for those who maintain the eternity of the world, or as the *guṇas* for the Sāṃkhyas. But this [Self] is absolute, immutably eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*), all-pervading like space, devoid of all modification, eternally satisfied, partless, self-luminous by nature, and that wherein merit and demerit, along with their effects and the three periods of time, do not occur.

This very state of bodilessness, known as liberation, is established by such scriptural passages as: "Other than dharma, other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, other than the past and the future," and so forth. (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.4)
Therefore, that is Brahman, for which this inquiry has been commenced.

If that [Brahman] were taught as a subsidiary to something to be performed (*kartavya*), and if liberation (*mokṣa*) were admitted to be something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by means of that performance, it would necessarily be non-eternal.
This being the case, it would follow that liberation is merely some superior degree among the aforementioned fruits of action, which exist in varying degrees and are themselves non-eternal.
Furthermore, liberation is accepted as eternal by all proponents of liberation;
therefore, it is not logical to teach Brahman as something subordinate to an action to be performed.

Moreover, scriptural passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "And his actions perish when He, the high and the low, is seen," "Knowing the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing from anywhere," "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness," "He knew Himself alone, thinking 'I am Brahman,' therefore He became all that is," and "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness?"—all these, by showing that liberation occurs immediately after the knowledge of Brahman, preclude any other intervening effect.

Likewise, the passage "The seer Vāmadeva perceived this very [Self]: 'I was Manu and the Sun'" should be cited to exclude any other action to be performed between the vision of Brahman and the state of being the Self of all; just as in the expression "standing, he sings," it is understood that there is no other action by that agent between the acts of standing and singing.

[Nārada said: "For you are our father, since you carry us across to the further shore of ignorance; for I have indeed heard from those like your holiness that the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow."

"Thus, O Blessed One, I grieve; may the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of this grief. And likewise, "To him whose impurities were washed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra showed the further shore of darkness. Such scriptural passages demonstrate that the fruit of the knowledge of the Self is solely the cessation of the obstacles to liberation.

Similarly, there is the aphorism composed by the Teacher (Bādarāyaṇa) and supported by reasoning: "Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the removal of the one immediately preceding it, resulting in liberation."
Furthermore, the removal of false knowledge arises from the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self.

This realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is not of the nature of a mental identification (*saṃpad*), such as: "The mind is indeed infinite; the Viśvedevas are infinite; by that [realization], he conquers an infinite world.

Nor is it of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), such as the practice of viewing the mind, the sun, and so forth as Brahman, as in: "One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman" and "The sun is Brahman—this is the instruction."

Nor is [the knowledge of identity] caused by connection with a specific ritual action, as in the cases of "Air indeed is the absorber" (*vāyurvāva saṃvarga*) or "Breath indeed is the absorber" (*prāṇo vāva saṃvarga*).
Nor does it have the nature of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) that is a subordinate part of a ritual, like the act of looking at the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*).

For if the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self were accepted as having the form of a metaphorical identification (*saṃpad*) or the like, the syntactic coherence of words in such sentences as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), and "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), which aim to establish the reality of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, would be undermined.
Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder," which declare the cessation of ignorance as the fruit [of knowledge], would be contradicted;

likewise, statements regarding the attainment of that state, such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," would not be consistently applicable if [the knowledge] were merely of the nature of a mental identification (saṃpad) or the like.
Therefore, the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is not of the nature of a mental identification or similar means.
Therefore, this is the first chapter.
Knowledge of Brahman is not dependent upon human activity;
rather, like the knowledge of an object that is the domain of means of valid cognition such as perception, it is dependent solely upon the thing itself.
For such a Brahman and its knowledge, it is impossible by any reasoning to conceive of an entry into the realm of effects (*kārya*).

Nor can Brahman enter into the realm of effects by being the object of the act of knowing (*vidi-kriyā*), because its status as the object of the act of knowing is denied in the passages: "It is indeed other than the known and above the unknown" (*anyad eva tad viditād atho aviditāt*) and "By what should one know Him by whom all this is known? (*yenedaṃ sarvaṃ vijānāti taṃ kena vijānīyāt*).

Likewise, there is also a negation of Brahman being the object of the act of worship: having presented Brahman as being beyond the scope of the senses in the passage, "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed," it continues, "Know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship.
If it is argued that since Brahman is not an object [of cognition], its status as having the scripture as its source (*śāstrayonitva*) is untenable, we say no;
for the scripture has as its purpose the cessation of the distinctions imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).

For the scripture does not intend to teach Brahman as an object limited by its own measurement. Rather, by teaching it as the inner self (pratyagātman) beyond the reach of the objective domain, it removes the distinctions of the known, the knower, and the act of knowing, which are all constructed by ignorance. Thus says the scripture: "He for whom it is not known—that one has known it; he who thinks he knows it—does not know it."

"It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know"; "one should not see the seer of seeing, nor hear the hearer of hearing, nor think the thinker of thinking, nor cognize the cognizer of cognition"—and so forth.

Therefore, since [the scriptures] establish the nature of the eternally liberated Self by removing the state of being a transmigrator imagined through ignorance, there is no defect of impermanence regarding liberation.
On the other hand, for one for whom liberation is something to be produced, it is logical that it must depend upon some action—whether mental, vocal, or physical.

Likewise, if liberation were a modification (*vikārya*), then in those two positions, liberation would necessarily be impermanent. For in the world, neither a modification such as curd nor a product such as a jar is ever seen to be eternal.

Nor is there a dependence on action even for the sake of attainment, because liberation, being the very nature of one's own self, is not something to be attained; and even if it were distinct from one's own nature, Brahman could not be attained, since, like space, its nature is eternally attained by all due to its omnipresence. Furthermore, liberation is not something to be refined (saṃskārya), such that it would require an action.

For what is called "conditioning" (saṃskāra) must occur either by the imparting of qualities to that which is to be conditioned, or by the removal of defects. It cannot occur through the imparting of qualities, because liberation is the very nature of Brahman, to which no excellence can be added.
Nor can it occur through the removal of defects, because liberation is the eternally pure nature of Brahman.

If it is argued that liberation, though being an inherent attribute of the self, remains concealed and is manifested when the self is refined by action—just as the quality of luminosity is manifested in a mirror when it is refined by the act of polishing—it is not so;
for it is impossible for the self to be the locus of action.
Action cannot come into existence without modifying that which serves as its locus.
If the self were to undergo modification through an action residing within itself, the consequence would be that the self is impermanent;
furthermore, statements such as "this is said to be unchangeable" would be contradicted,
and that is undesirable.
Therefore, an action having itself as its locus is not possible for the Self;
nor is the Self refined by an action having another thing as its locus, because such an action does not have the Self as its object. [End of] Chapter One of the *Dārśanika-sūtra*.

It is observed that the embodied self (*dehī*) is being purified by actions such as bathing, sipping water, and wearing the sacrificial thread which have the body as their locus; however, this is not so, because it is only the Self—conceived through ignorance as being a composite of the body and other factors—that is being purified.
For it is directly perceived that bathing, sipping water, and so forth, are inherent in the body.
It is logical that by that [purification] which has the body as its locus, some entity—which is indeed conjoined with that [body] and grasped as the Self through ignorance—is refined.

Just as the fruit of health belongs to the one who identifies with the body through the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu) resulting from medical treatment directed at the body, so too it is that in whom the cognition "I am pure" or "I am refined" arises—due to bathing, sipping water, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and so forth—that is refined;
and that [entity] is precisely the one conjoined with the body.
By that very same agent, which is the object of the notion of "I" and the one who causes cognition, all actions are accomplished;

and he alone enjoys their fruit, according to the Vedic mantra: "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other looks on without eating," and also: "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the body, the senses, and the mind, is the enjoyer.
Likewise: "The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings."

"The overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, absolute, and devoid of qualities"—and "He has pervaded that which is bright, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, pure, and unpierced by evil"—these two mantras demonstrate that Brahman is incapable of receiving any added excellence and is eternally pure.
Furthermore, liberation is the state of being Brahman.
Therefore, liberation is not something to be refined by purificatory rites either.
Therefore, no one can point out any other door for the entry of ritual action toward liberation than this one shown in the Sūtra and its Commentary (Bhāṣya).
Consequently, apart from knowledge alone, even the slightest trace of the entry of ritual action is not possible here.
[Objection: But is it not the case that what is called "knowledge" is a mental action? [Reply: No.
Because of their difference in nature.

For that which is called "action" (*kriyā*) is that which is enjoined independently of the actual nature of the object and is dependent upon the mental activity of the person, as in such passages as: "To whichever deity the oblation has been taken, one should meditate upon her with the mind while about to utter the *vaṣaṭ*," and "One should meditate upon the twilight with the mind.
Although meditation (*dhyāna*) and reflection (*cintana*) are mental, they can nevertheless be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise by a person, because they are dependent on the person.
Knowledge, however, is produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And a means of valid cognition has as its object a thing exactly as it is.
Therefore, knowledge cannot be made, unmade, or otherwise made.
That [knowledge] depends solely on the object itself;
it does not depend on scriptural injunction (*codanā*), nor does it depend on the person.
Therefore, even though knowledge is mental in nature, there is a great distinction [between it and other mental acts].
And just as in the passage, "Man indeed, O Gautama, is fire; woman indeed, O Gautama, is fire," the cognition of fire regarding a woman and a man is mental;
yet because it is produced solely by scriptural injunction (*codanā*), it is merely an action and dependent upon the person.
However, the cognition of fire regarding fire that is already well-known in the world is not dependent on scriptural injunction.
Nor is it dependent on a person;

rather, since it depends solely on the object that is its perceptual domain, this is indeed knowledge and not an action— this is to be understood in the same way regarding all objects of the means of valid cognition.

This being the case, even knowledge whose object is the Self as Brahman, which is exactly as it is (*yathābhūta*), is not dependent on an injunction (*codanā*). Although optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like are heard in relation to that subject, they become blunted because their object is one that cannot be enjoined, just as the sharpness of a razor applied to a stone and the like; this is because its object is a reality that is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired.

What, then, is the purpose of those statements that bear the semblance of injunctions, such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, is to be heard"? We reply: they are for the purpose of turning one away from the objects of natural worldly activity.

For a person who proceeds with an outward orientation, thinking "May what is desired be mine, may what is undesired not be mine," does not attain the ultimate human goal therein; therefore, the [scriptural] texts such as "The Self, indeed, should be seen" turn that seeker of the ultimate human goal away from the sphere of activity of the natural aggregate of the body and organs, and direct him toward the current of the inner Self.

For one who has set out in search of the Self, the true nature of the Self—which is neither to be rejected nor to be accepted—is taught by such passages as: "All this is what this Self is," "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he know? "By what, my dear, should one know the knower? and "This Self is Brahman.
As for the claim that knowledge of the Self, which consists primarily of non-action, serves neither for rejection nor for acceptance, that is indeed admitted to be so.
Indeed, this is our ornament: that when the realization of Brahman as the Self occurs, all duties cease and one achieves the state of having accomplished all that was to be done.

Thus says the Śruti: "If a person should know the Self, thinking 'I am this,' desiring what, or for the sake of what, would he suffer along with the body? And the Smṛti says: "Having said this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has fulfilled his purpose."
Therefore, in that commentary on the Sūtras, Brahman is presented as being subordinate to the injunction for spiritual realization.

As for what some say—that there is no portion of the Veda which speaks of a mere entity (vastu) apart from injunctions regarding engagement (pravṛtti), withdrawal (nivṛtti), and their subsidiaries—that is not so;

because the person taught in the Upaniṣads is not subsidiary to anything else. That person who is understood through the Upaniṣads alone—the non-transmigrating one whose nature is Brahman, distinct from the four kinds of substances such as those to be produced and so forth, situated in his own context, and not subsidiary to anything else—it cannot be said that he does not exist or that he is not known.
"This very Self is 'not this, not this,'" because of the use of the word "Self" (ātman), and because the Self cannot be denied—for he who would deny it is himself that very Self.
An objection may be raised: "It is untenable to say that the Self is known only from the Upanishads, since the Self is the object of the notion of 'I'"; [we reply:
no, for that has already been answered by the fact that [the Self] is the witness of that notion.

For indeed, apart from the agent who is the object of the notion of "I," that witness—who dwells in all beings, who is equal, one, immutably eternal, the Person, and the Self of all—is not apprehended by anyone either in the section on ritual injunctions or in the systems of logic.

Therefore, he cannot be denied by anyone, nor can he be reduced to being a mere subordinate element of an injunction. Furthermore, because he is the very Self of all, he is neither to be rejected nor to be accepted.
For the entire collection of perishable modifications perishes only up to the limit of the Person.
For the Self (puruṣa) is indestructible because of the absence of any cause for destruction;
and it is immutably eternal because of the absence of any cause for modification;
therefore, its very nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free.

Therefore, the specific qualification "pertaining to the Upaniṣads" applied to the Person in such passages as, "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal; I ask you about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads," is appropriate only if the Person is revealed by the Upaniṣads. Consequently, the assertion that there is no portion of the Veda concerned with an already existing reality (bhūtavastu) is mere temerity.

Furthermore, as for the enumeration by those who know the purport of the scriptures, beginning with "For its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of ritual action," that must be understood as referring to the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions, since they concern the inquiry into dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*).

Moreover, for those who accept the absolute principle that "since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their purpose are useless," there follows the undesirable consequence of the uselessness of all teachings concerning existing entities (*bhūta*).

If an existent entity is taught apart from engagement or withdrawal, only by way of being subservient to something to be accomplished (*bhavya*), then what is the reason for saying that an absolutely immutable and eternal existent is not taught?
For an existent thing (*bhūta*) being taught does not itself become an action (*kriyā*).

If it is argued that even though an existent thing is not an action, the teaching of an existent thing has action as its sole purpose because it serves as a means (*sādhana*) for action—this is no fault;
for even while having action as its purpose, the object possessing the power to accomplish that action is indeed what is taught.
Its purpose, however, is to have action as its goal;
yet by this much, it does not follow that the reality is not taught.

If you ask, "Even if it were taught, what would that have to do with you?", it is replied: the teaching of the reality of the Self, which has not been previously understood, must likewise be of that same nature [as having action as its goal].

By the realization of that [Brahman], the cessation of false knowledge—the cause of saṃsāra—is effected as the purpose; thus, its purposefulness is no different from the instruction regarding things that are means for action. Moreover, cessation is taught in such injunctions as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," and that [cessation] is not an action.
Nor is it a means for action.
If the teaching of things that do not have action as their purpose were useless, then it would follow that the teachings on cessation—such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed"—would be purposeless;
and that is undesirable.

Nor can it be maintained that the negative particle (*nañ*)—due to its association with the meaning of "killing" as established by its own nature—is capable of implying a state where no action is undertaken, apart from the indifference consisting in the cessation of the act of killing.
For this is the very nature of the negative particle: that it makes known the non-existence of that which is connected to it.
And the cognition of non-existence is the cause of indifference.
And that [prohibition] subsides of its own accord, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.

Therefore, we consider that in injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," the meaning of the prohibition is simply indifference resulting from the cessation of an engaged action; this applies except in cases such as the vows of Prajāpati.

Consequently, the statement regarding the pointlessness [of the Vedas] should be understood as referring to those arthavādas which consist of narratives and the like that do not contribute to human goals.

As for the argument that "a mere statement of an existing fact (*vastumātra*), if not entered into as part of an injunction to act, would be purposeless—like the statement 'the earth consists of seven islands' (*saptadvīpā vasumatī*)"—that has been refuted; for even when stating a mere fact, such as "this is a rope, this is not a snake," a purpose is clearly observed.

Now, it was argued that since one who has heard of Brahman is still seen to be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) just as before, the teaching does not possess purposefulness in the same way as the statement regarding the nature of the rope.

To this it is replied: It is impossible to show that one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self remains subject to transmigratory existence as before, because such a state contradicts the realization of Brahman as the Self produced by the authority of the Veda.

For while it is observed that one who identifies with the body and so forth possesses suffering, fear, and the like, it cannot be imagined that the very same person, upon attaining the realization of Brahman as the Self through the authority of the Veda and thereby ceasing that identification, would still possess that same suffering, fear, and so forth caused by false knowledge. (Brahmasūtra 1.1.4)

For it is not the case that because suffering caused by the seizure of wealth is seen in a wealthy householder who possesses pride in his wealth, that same suffering caused by the seizure of wealth must also occur for that very person when he has become a renunciant and is devoid of pride in wealth. Nor is it the case that because pleasure caused by the pride of possessing earrings is seen in one wearing earrings, that same pleasure caused by the pride of possessing earrings must also occur for that very person when he is separated from the earrings and devoid of the pride of possessing them.
This has been stated by the Śruti: "Verily, while one is bodiless, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant touches him."
If it is argued that the state of being bodiless occurs only when the body has fallen [after death] and not while one is alive, we say no;
for the state of having a body is caused by false knowledge.
Indeed, apart from the false knowledge characterized by the identification of the Self with the body, it is impossible to conceive of any other cause for the state of having a body.
We have already stated that bodilessness is eternal because it is not caused by karma.

If it is argued that embodiment is caused by dharma and adharma produced by that [self], we say no; for the connection with a body is unestablished, and thus the production of dharma and adharma by the self is unestablished, since it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence between the connection with a body and the production of dharma and adharma by that [connection].
This conception of beginninglessness is merely a blind tradition, because agency is untenable for the Self due to the absence of any inherence of action in it.
If it is argued that agency is observed in kings and others by virtue of mere proximity [to their subordinates], we say no;
for their agency is established through their relationship with servants acquired by means of bestowing wealth and other such means.

But it is not possible to postulate any basis for a relationship of owner and owned between the self and the body and so forth, as one might postulate for the giving of wealth and the like. Rather, false identification (*mithyābhimāna*) is the perceptible cause of that connection. By this, the status of being a sacrificer (*yajamānatva*) of the self is also explained.

If it is argued that for the Self, which is distinct from the body and so forth, the ego-identification (*ahaṃ-abhimāna*) with its own body and such is metaphorical (*gauṇa*) and not false (*mithyā*), we say no; for the distinction between the metaphorical and the primary is well-established only for those whose difference between entities is already known.

For when a difference between entities is well-known—as, for example, when a specific form possessing a mane and so forth is established as the primary referent of the word and concept "lion" through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and another person is established as being endowed with lion-like qualities such as cruelty and valor—then, for that person, the word and concept "lion" applied to that man become metaphorical.
This is not the case for one who does not perceive a distinction between things.
For such a person, the application of another word and cognition to something else occurs solely on the basis of error (*bhrānti*), and not figuratively (*gauṇa*).

Just as in dim darkness, when the specific details are not grasped, the word and cognition "this is a post" have the post as their object; or just as in the case of mother-of-pearl, the certain word and cognition "this is silver" arise suddenly; so too, in the aggregate of the body and so forth, how can the word and cognition "I," which arise without metaphorical transfer due to the failure to distinguish between the Self and the non-Self, be said to be figurative?
Even for learned men who distinguish between the Self and the non-Self, the word and the cognition remain undiscriminated, like those of shepherds and their flocks.

Therefore, for those who maintain the existence of a Self distinct from the body and so forth, the notion of "I" with respect to the body and such is purely false, not figurative. Consequently, since being embodied is caused by false cognition, it is established that even for the wise person while living, there is bodilessness.
And likewise, there is a scriptural passage concerning the knower of Brahman: "Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so does this body lie;
then this bodiless, immortal life-breath is indeed Brahman, it is light itself" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7).

And also: "Though possessing eyes, he is as if without eyes; though possessing ears, he is as if without ears; though possessing speech, he is as if without speech; though possessing a mind, he is as if without a mind; though possessing breath, he is as if without breath. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.13–14).

Smṛti as well—in passages such as "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady?"—by describing the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady, demonstrates that the knower has no connection with any worldly activity.
Therefore, for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self, there is no state of transmigratory existence as before.
Conversely, whoever still possesses a state of transmigratory existence as before has not realized the identity of Brahman and the Self; thus, the position is faultless.

Furthermore, as for the argument that because reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are seen to follow hearing (*śravaṇa*), Brahman must be subordinate to an injunction and not culminate in its own nature—that is not so;
for reflection and meditative absorption, like hearing, have the purpose of realization.
For if Brahman, once realized, were employed elsewhere, then it would indeed be subordinate to an injunction.
But that is not the case, because reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), like hearing (*śravaṇa*), also have comprehension as their purpose.

Therefore, it is not possible for Brahman to be established by the authority of scripture merely as the object of an injunction for realization; thus it is established that Brahman is an independent object of scriptural authority, being known through the concordance of the Vedānta texts.
And this being so, the commencement of a separate treatise concerning that subject in the words "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) is justified.

For if the treatise were solely intent upon the method of practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*), then since [the inquiry] would have already been commenced by the words "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), a separate scripture would not need to be begun;

and even if it were to be begun, it should have been commenced thus: "Now, therefore, the desire to know the remaining Dharma" (*athātaḥ pariśiṣṭa-dharmajijñāsā*), just as in the case of the aphorism: "Now, therefore, the desire to know that which pertains to the sacrifice and that which pertains to the person" (*athātaḥ kratvartha-puruṣārthayor jijñāsā*).

However, since the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*) was not previously promised, the commencement of this scripture for that purpose—namely, "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*)—is appropriate.
Therefore, all injunctions and all other means of valid knowledge terminate precisely in the realization "I am Brahman.

For when the non-dual Self—which is neither to be rejected nor to be accepted—is realized, the means of valid knowledge can no longer function, as they would be rendered objectless and devoid of a knower.
Furthermore: "Since the secondary and false selves do not exist, through the sublation of the son, the body, and so forth..."
If one has the realization, "I am indeed Brahman, the Self," how could there be any duty?
Prior to the realization of the Self that is to be sought, the Self possesses the status of a knower;
once sought, it is the knower itself that becomes free from evil, defects, and the like.
"Just as the notion of the body being the self is assumed to be a means of valid knowledge,
so too is this worldly [means of knowledge] considered valid until the certainty regarding the Self is attained.

Thus, it has been stated that the Vedānta texts— which have the realization of Brahman as the Self as their purpose and are coherent in their intent toward Brahman as the Self— culminate in Brahman even without entering into the sphere of ritual action.
It has been stated that Brahman is omniscient, omnipotent, and the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world.

However, the Sāṃkhyas and others, believing that an established entity can only be known through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), infer other causes such as *pradhāna* and interpret the Vedānta texts solely with that intent.
Indeed, in all Vedānta passages concerning creation, they seek to establish the cause by means of inference from the effect.

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the conjunctions of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* are to be inferred eternally. However, the followers of Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣikas), from these very same statements, infer God to be the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the atoms (*aṇu*) to be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
In this manner, other logicians as well, relying on fallacious statements and fallacious arguments, arise here as proponents of prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣavādins*).

In that regard, the Teacher—who is proficient in words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—in order to demonstrate that the Vedānta texts have as their purport the realization of Brahman as the Self, sets forth and refutes the understandings based on those fallacious statements and fallacious arguments by treating them as prima facie positions.

In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain that the Pradhāna—consisting of the three guṇas, insentient and independent—is the cause of the world, say: those Vedāntic passages which you have stated demonstrate that the omniscient and omnipotent Brahman is the cause of the world can also be applied to the theory of the Pradhāna as the cause.
For the quality of omnipotence is indeed possible for the Pradhāna with respect to its own transformations;
likewise, omniscience is also possible [for it].
How so? That which you consider to be knowledge is a quality of *sattva*, according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "knowledge is born from *sattva*.
And by means of that knowledge, which is a quality of *sattva*, persons possessing bodies and organs are well known as omniscient yogis;
for omniscience is well established when there is the unsurpassed excellence of *sattva*.
