It is not possible to attribute either omniscience or limited knowledge to the isolated *puruṣa*, who is devoid of activity and consists of mere consciousness alone.

However, because the *pradhāna* consists of the three *guṇas*, the *sattva* quality—which is the cause of all knowledge—exists even in its state as *pradhāna*. Thus, omniscience is figuratively attributed to the *pradhāna*, which is actually insentient, within the Vedāntic texts. Furthermore, you too, by asserting that Brahman is omniscient, must necessarily accept that omniscience exists only through the possession of the capacity for all knowledge.
For Brahman does not exist as constantly performing the act of knowing all objects.
To explain: if knowledge were eternal, Brahman’s sovereignty with respect to the act of knowing would be lost;

if, on the other hand, that [knowledge] were non-eternal, then upon the cessation of the act of knowing, Brahman too would cease [to know]. Therefore, omniscience results precisely from its possession of the power for all knowledge.
Moreover, you maintain that prior to creation, Brahman is devoid of all causal instruments;
yet it is not possible for knowledge to arise in anyone in the absence of the body, sense organs, and other means of cognition.

Furthermore, while it is plausible for Pradhāna—being multiform—to be the cause due to the possibility of its transformation, like clay and so forth, this is not possible for Brahman, which is uncomposite and unitary. Such being the position reached, this Sūtra is commenced: "On account of seeing (īkṣati), [Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture (aśabda)."
The Cause: The insentient *pradhāna* postulated by the Sāṃkhya cannot be accepted as the cause of the world in the Vedāntas,
for it is not based on scripture (*aśabda*).
How can the wordless [Brahman] possess the quality of seeing? Because the cause is heard to be a seer.

How so? For thus it is heard: beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," it continues, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It emitted heat.

Therein, having determined that the world—which is denoted by the word "this" and is differentiated by name and form—was of the nature of Being prior to its origination, the text shows that very Being, denoted by the word "Sat," which is the subject under discussion, is the creator of fire and the other elements preceded by the act of seeing.
Likewise, in another place: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone;
there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)

"He thought, 'Let me now create the worlds,' and he created these worlds"—thus [the text] declares that creation was preceded by reflection. And in another place, having introduced the Puruṣa consisting of sixteen parts, it says, "He reflected; He created Prāṇa."

Furthermore, in the phrase "on account of seeing" (īkṣateḥ), the intention is to indicate the meaning of the verbal root, as in the case of "sacrificing" (yajateḥ), and not merely the citation of the root itself.
Consequently, passages such as, "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge;
from him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food," which likewise refer to the omniscient Lord as the cause, should also be cited.
As for what was said—that the Pradhāna will be omniscient through knowledge as a quality of Sattva—that is not tenable.
For in the state of Pradhāna, because the qualities (guṇas) are in equilibrium, knowledge as a quality of Sattva is not possible.
[Objection: But was it not said that it will be omniscient by virtue of possessing the power for all knowledge?
That too is not tenable.

If, while the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) persists, the Pradhāna were called "all-knowing" by relying on the power of knowledge inherent in Sattva, then one might as well call it "knowing only a little" by relying on the power that obstructs knowledge inherent in Rajas and Tamas.
Furthermore, the modification of Sattva is not denoted by the verb "to know" unless it has a witness (sākṣin).
Furthermore, the insentient *pradhāna* cannot possess the status of a witness;

therefore, the omniscience of the *pradhāna* is untenable. As for yogis, however, because they are sentient, their omniscience—caused by the preeminence of the quality of *sattva*—is logical; thus, [the *pradhāna*] is not a valid example.

Furthermore, if the power of seeing were attributed to the *pradhāna* only by reason of its being an instrument—just as a lump of iron possesses the power of burning only because it is an instrument of fire—then it would be logical to conclude that the cause of the world is primarily that omniscient Brahman which is the instrumental cause of the *pradhāna*'s power of seeing. As for the argument that even for Brahman, primary omniscience is not tenable because, if knowledge and action are eternal, independence with respect to the act of knowing is impossible; [The response follows: This is not so. Just as in the case of the sun, whose light is eternal, we speak of its "shining" and "warming" through the manifestation of rays, so too, although the knowledge of Brahman is eternal, its omniscience is established by the manifestation of objects of knowledge through the agency of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the term "creator" (*kartṛ*) is applied to Brahman in the sense of being the presiding cause (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), just as a carpenter is called the "maker" of a chariot. Thus, the status of Brahman as the cause of the world is well-established.
To this it is replied: First, you must explain how there could be a loss of omniscience if knowledge and action were eternal.
For it is a contradiction to say that one who possesses eternal knowledge capable of illuminating all objects is not omniscient.
Indeed, if knowledge were non-eternal, one might know at some times and not know at others, and thus there would be a lack of omniscience.
This fault does not exist in the case of the eternity of knowledge.
If it is argued that the designation of independence regarding the object of knowledge is untenable if knowledge is eternal, we say no;
for even in the case of the sun, whose heat and light are continuous, we observe the designation of independence in such expressions as "it burns" and "it illuminates."

[Objection: Surely, when there is a conjunction between the sun and that which is to be burned or illuminated, the designation "it burns" or "it illuminates" would be appropriate; however, since Brahman has no conjunction with objects of knowledge prior to creation, the illustration is dissimilar.
[Reply: No.

Just as the designation of agency is seen in the expression "the sun shines" even though there is no [external] object of action, so too the designation of agency for Brahman in the statement "it thought" (*tadaikṣata*) is possible even though there is no object of knowledge; thus there is no inconsistency.
Moreover, if an object of action were required, the scriptural texts concerning Brahman's being the agent would be all the more appropriate.
But what was that action prior to creation, which did not exist before? Chapter One, Section One.
We maintain that name and form—which are unmanifest yet intended to be manifested, and which are indefinable as being either identical to or different from Brahman—are the objects of God’s knowledge.

For if those learned in the Yoga scriptures assert that even for yogins there exists direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of objects past and future through the grace of that [Lord], what need is there to mention that this eternally established Lord possesses eternal knowledge whose objects are the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world?
Furthermore, as for the objection that prior to creation it is impossible for Brahman to be a perceiver without a connection to a body and so forth—that criticism does not apply here.
Since Brahman’s nature as knowledge is eternal—just like the light of the sun—it is illogical for it to require the means of knowledge.
Furthermore, the arising of knowledge might depend on a body and other such factors for a transmigrating being who possesses ignorance and the like;
but this cannot be the case for the Lord, who is devoid of any cause that could obstruct His knowledge.

And these two mantras demonstrate that the Lord is independent of a body and the like, and possesses unobstructed knowledge: "No effect or instrument is found for Him; neither equal nor superior to Him is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are innate.
[And: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes and hears without ears."

"He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of him; he is the one to be adored, the great Puruṣa. But [an objection is raised]: "Surely there is no transmigrating soul other than the Lord who is devoid of causes obstructing knowledge, according to such scriptural texts as, 'There is no other seer than He; there is no other knower than He.

In that case, why is this said—that the arising of knowledge in the transmigrating soul depends upon the body and so forth, but not so for the Lord? To this it is replied: True, there is no transmigrating soul other than the Lord.

Nevertheless, the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the aggregate of the body and so forth is indeed admitted for the Self, just as the connection with limiting adjuncts such as a jar, a water-pot, or a mountain cave is admitted for space (*ākāśa*).

And based on that [connection], there is the worldly linguistic usage of words and cognitions, such as "the hole of a jar" or "the hole of a water-pot," even though these are not distinct from space itself. Furthermore, based on that [connection], the false notion of a distinction within space—such as "the space of a jar" and so forth—is observed.

Similarly, here too, there exists the false cognition of a distinction between the Lord and the transmigrating soul, produced by the non-discrimination of the connection with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the aggregate of the body and so forth.

And it is observed that even for one who is in reality the Self, there arises through a series of preceding false cognitions alone an attachment to the non-Self—the aggregate of the body and so forth—as being the Self. This being the case, the status of being a transmigrator is established, and for such a transmigrator, the state of being a seer in dependence upon the body and other factors is logically consistent.

As for the argument that, because the *pradhāna* consists of multiple constituents, it can logically function as a cause—just like clay and other materials—whereas Brahman, being non-composite, cannot, that has already been refuted by the fact that the *pradhāna* is not based on scripture (*aśabda*).

Furthermore, we shall elaborate later (in the sūtra beginning with "Not so, because of the difference in nature") how, even by means of reasoning, the causality of Brahman alone can be established, and not that of the *pradhāna* or others.

Here [the opponent] says: What was stated—that the non-intelligent *pradhāna* cannot be the cause of the world because of the scriptural mention of "seeing" (*īkṣitṛtva*)—is otherwise possible as well;
for we observe metaphorical usage regarding the intelligent even when applied to the non-intelligent.

Just as, observing that the bank of a river is about to fall, one says "the bank wishes to fall" (*pipatiṣati*), such metaphorical usage regarding the intelligent is seen even in the case of the non-intelligent bank; in the same way, metaphorical usage regarding the intelligent may apply to the non-intelligent *pradhāna* when creation is imminent. Chapter One.
The movement will be as follows: "Then It thought" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

Just as in the world some conscious being, having bathed and eaten, thinks in the afternoon, "I shall go to the village by chariot," and thereafter proceeds accordingly with regularity, so too does the Pradhāna proceed with regularity in the form of Mahat and the rest;
therefore, it is figuratively described as if it were conscious.

But for what reason is the primary sense of "seeing" set aside and a figurative one assumed? Because we observe that even in the case of insentient fire and water, there is a figurative use of the term as if they were sentient, in such passages as "That heat saw" and "Those waters saw.
Therefore, it is understood that even the seeing whose agent is the Existent (Sat) is figurative, since the statement occurs in a context abounding in figurative usage.
This being the position reached, the following Sūtra is commenced: "If it be said that [the seeing] is figurative, no, because of the word 'Self'."
As for the claim that the insentient *pradhāna*—which is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*)—possesses a figurative power of seeing, just as water and fire do, that is incorrect.
Why? Because of the word "Self" (*ātman*).

Having begun with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and having stated the creation of fire, water, and food [earth] through the passages, "It thought" and "It created fire," the text refers back to that same subject, the "Being" which had thought, and designating those elements of fire, water, and food by the term "deities," says: "This very deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*) and differentiate names and forms.'"
In that case, if the Pradhāna were imagined to have looked on by means of the functions of the Guṇas, then it alone—being the subject under discussion—would be referred to by the words "this deity.
However, the deity would not then denote the individual soul (jīva) by the word "Self" (ātman).
For the so-called jīva is indeed conscious, the ruler of the body, and the sustainer of the vital breaths, as is well known from both common usage and etymological derivation.
How could that [jīva] be the self (ātman) of the insentient pradhāna?
For "self" indeed means one's own nature (svarūpa).
It is not possible for the sentient jīva to be the nature of the insentient pradhāna.
But if Brahman, as the conscious and primary seer, is accepted, then the application of the word "Self" (ātman) to it with reference to the individual soul (jīva) becomes appropriate.

Thus, in the passage, "That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That thou art, Śvetaketu"—having taught the subtle Being under discussion as the Self by using the word "Self" in the phrase "That is the Self," he then teaches it as the Self of the conscious Śvetaketu in the words "That thou art."

However, water and fire must be insentient because they are objects [of perception], and because they are mentioned as being merely instruments in the process of the differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth; furthermore, there is no reason for them to have a primary sense [of "seeing"] as the word *ātman* does. Therefore, it is appropriate that their "seeing" is figurative. Even in their case, however, the capacity to see depends entirely upon being presided over by the Existent (*sat*). As for the Existent, it has already been stated that its "seeing" is not figurative on account of the word *ātman*.
Now, it might be argued that the word "self" (ātman) is applied even to the insentient *pradhāna* because it accomplishes all the purposes of the self;
just as the word "self" is used for a servant who carries out all the king's purposes, as in the expression, "Bhadrasena is my very self.

For the *pradhāna* assists the self (*ātman*), which is the *puruṣa*, by effecting its enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), just as a servant serves a king by engaging in treaties, warfare, and so forth.

Alternatively, the single word *ātman* may refer to both consciousness (*cetana*) and the unconscious (*acetana*), as seen in such usages as ‘the self consisting of the elements’ (*bhūtātmā*) and ‘the self consisting of the senses’ (*indriyātmā*); just as the single word *jyotis* (light) refers to both a sacrifice and a flame.

In this regard, from where does it follow that the word "Self" (ātman) is not used in a secondary sense because of the act of "seeing" (īkṣati)? To this, he recites the answer: "Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon That."

The non-intelligent *pradhāna* cannot be the referent of the word "Self"; for, having taken up the previously mentioned *sac-chabda* (Being) as "That is the Self," and having taught the realization of that [Self] to the conscious Śvetaketu who was to be instructed—saying, "That thou art, O Śvetaketu"—the scripture teaches liberation by saying, "The man who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body, then he shall be merged. Thus, because of this teaching of liberation, the *pradhāna* is not the intended meaning.

For if the insentient *pradhāna* were denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*) and were made to understand—while being a sentient seeker of liberation—that "you are that" (*tat asi*), meaning "you are insentient," then the scripture would be teaching a falsehood for the person's detriment and would thus lack authority.
However, it is not proper to consider this faultless scripture to be non-authoritative.

If the authoritative scripture were to teach that the non-conscious, non-self is the Self to one who is ignorant but desirous of liberation, he—out of faith—would not abandon his view of that [non-self] as the Self, following the maxim of the blind man and the bull's tail, nor would he realize the Self distinct from it;
and this being the case, he would be deprived of the goal of human existence or would incur misfortune.

Therefore, just as one teaches the means such as the *agnihotra* exactly as they are to one who desires heaven and the like, so too it is logical that for one who desires liberation, the Self is taught exactly as it is in the words, "That is the Self; That art thou, O Śvetaketu. This being the case, the teaching of liberation for one whose intention is truthful is justified by the analogy of grasping and releasing the heated axe.

Otherwise, if the teaching of the reality of the Self were not primary, this would be a mere meditative identification (*saṃpat*) with an impermanent result, like the instruction, "One should know: 'I am the hymn (*uktha*).'"
In that case, the instruction regarding liberation would be untenable.
Therefore, the word "Self" (ātman) cannot be used figuratively with respect to the minute atom (aṇiman).

However, in the case of a servant, because the distinction between master and servant is perceptible, the use of the word "Self" in the sense "Bhadrasena is my self" is appropriate as a figurative expression.

Furthermore, even if the word "drauṇi" is observed in some instances [to denote a non-spiritual object], it is not on this basis alone that the assumption of a secondary (gauṇī) sense is justified for an object whose meaning is established by verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇaka), as that would lead to a lack of confidence in all cases.
As for the argument that the word "ātman" is common to both sentient and insentient things—just as the word "jyotis" applies to both a sacrifice and a flame—that is not so;
for it is improper to assume multiple meanings [for a single term].

Therefore, the word *ātman* primarily denotes only that which is conscious; it is applied to the elements and so forth through a metaphorical attribution of consciousness, as in the expressions "the self of the elements" (*bhūtātmā*) and "the self of the senses" (*indriyātmā*).

Even though the word *ātman* is common to both [the conscious and the unconscious], its application to one or the other cannot be determined without some determining factor, such as the context or a qualifying term.
And here, there is no reason whatsoever that determines it to be the unconscious.
But the subject under discussion is the Self along with its seer, and the conscious Śvetaketu is present;
for we have already stated that it is impossible for the conscious Śvetaketu to have an unconscious self.
Therefore, it is certain that the word "Self" here refers to a conscious being.

The word *jyotis* (light) is conventionally established in common usage as referring only to fire; however, its application to the sacrifice (*ṛtu*) is based on a similarity to fire imagined through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Thus, this is not a valid example.

Alternatively, one may explain the word *ātman* in the preceding sūtra itself by dispelling all doubts regarding its figurative or common meanings, and then explain the subsequent sūtra as an independent reason for refuting the Pradhāna as the cause: "Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to That."
Therefore, the non-intelligent Pradhāna cannot be denoted by the word "Sat."
And for what further reason is the Pradhāna not denoted by the word "Being"? Because there is no statement regarding its being something to be abandoned.
If that which is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) were indeed the non-Self (anātman), then [the Upanishad] would have taught here, "That is the Self; you are That.

Fearing that one might become intent upon that [non-Self] due to hearing such an instruction while remaining ignorant of the Self, the scripture—desiring to point out the primary Self—would declare that [the non-Self] is to be abandoned.

Just as one wishing to show the star Arundhatī first causes [a person] to grasp a nearby, gross, non-primary star, saying "This is Arundhatī," and then, having set that aside, subsequently causes them to grasp the actual Arundhatī; so too does the scripture.
In that case, one would have to say, "This Self is not that";
yet he did not speak thus.
For it is seen that the conclusion of the sixth chapter rests solely upon the realization of the Self as pure Being (sanmātra).
The word "ca" (and) is intended to demonstrate an additional point regarding the contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*).
Even though there is the statement that [the world] is to be abandoned (*heyatva*), a contradiction with the proposition would still result.

For it was proposed that "by the knowledge of the Cause, everything becomes known," as in: "Or did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3).
"How indeed, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about?

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—even so, my dear, does that instruction come about. Since this is heard at the beginning of the passage, it cannot be the case that when the Pradhāna—which is denoted by the word *sat* and is the cause of the class of objects of enjoyment—is known (whether as something to be abandoned or not), the class of enjoyers becomes known; for the class of enjoyers is not a modification of the Pradhāna.
Therefore, the Pradhāna is not denoted by the word "I."
And for what further reason is the Pradhāna not denoted by the word "Being"? Because of its own scriptural study.
With reference to that very cause denoted by the word "Being," it is heard [in scripture]: "When a person here sleeps—this is what is called sleep—then, my dear, he has become united with Being;
he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ); therefore they say of him, 'he sleeps' (svapiti)."
"He has gone to his own (svam apīto bhavati). This scriptural passage etymologically explains the name "he sleeps" (svapiti), which is well known in the world as applied to a person.
Here, by the word "own" (sva), the Self (ātman) is meant.
He becomes merged in that which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) under discussion; the meaning is that he has gone into it (*apigata*).
It is well known that the root *i* preceded by *api* has the sense of merging, as seen in the usage of "origin and dissolution" (*prabhavāpyayau*) for birth and destruction.

When the individual soul (*jīva*), through its connection with specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the movements of the mind, perceives the objects of the senses, it assumes those particular forms and remains awake.
Perceiving dreams characterized by those latent impressions (vāsanās), the mind becomes that which is denoted by the word "mind" (manas).

When those two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) cease in the state of deep sleep, due to the absence of distinctions created by the adjuncts, it is as if merged into its own self; thus it is said, "For he becomes one with his own self.
Just as the etymology of the word "heart" (hṛdaya) has been shown by the Śruti: "This very Self is in the heart; this is its etymological derivation: 'He who is in the heart' (hṛdi ayam)."
Therefore, it is "dear" (hṛdyam).

Or rather, just as the Śruti shows the basis for the application of the words *aśanāya* and *udanya* in the passages, "The waters alone lead away that which has been eaten" and "The fire alone leads away that which has been drunk," so too, by means of the etymological explanation of the name *svapiti*, it demonstrates this meaning: "He has gone into his own Self, which is denoted by the word *Sat*."
Furthermore, a conscious self could not take an unconscious primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as its own essential nature.
If, on the other hand, primordial matter itself were denoted by the word "self" because it belongs to the self, even so, the contradiction would arise that "the conscious goes into the unconscious.
Moreover, another scriptural passage—"Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing without nor within"—shows the merging of the conscious [self] into the conscious during the state of deep sleep.

Therefore, that in which the dissolution of all conscious beings occurs must be that conscious entity denoted by the word "Being" (sat), which is the cause of the world; it cannot be the unconscious primordial matter (pradhāna).
And for what further reason is the Pradhāna not the cause of the world? Because of the uniformity of the course [of all things].

If, as in the systems of the logicians, there were a divergence in the Vedānta texts regarding the understanding of the cause— such that in some places conscious Brahman is the cause of the world, in others the unconscious Pradhāna, and in yet others something else entirely— then, at times, one might have interpreted scriptural passages such as "He who perceives" (īkṣati) in accordance with the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause. But this is not the case.

For the understanding that the conscious principle is the cause is indeed the same in all the Vedāntas. Thus, they all demonstrate the causality of the Self (ātman): "Just as when a fire is burning, sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self all vital breaths (prāṇas) proceed each to its respective station, from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds"; "From that very Self, ether was produced"; "All this is indeed from the Self alone"; and "From the Self this vital breath is born. Furthermore, we have already stated that the word *ātman* denotes the conscious being.

This is a reason for the authority [of the Vedānta]: that the Vedānta texts have a uniform direction (*samānagati*) regarding an intelligent cause, just as the eye and other senses have a uniform direction regarding form and other objects.
Therefore, due to this uniformity of direction, Brahman, which is omniscient, is the cause of the world.
And for what further reason is Brahman, the omniscient, the cause of the world? Because it is so stated in the Śruti.

Moreover, it is heard in its own words that the omniscient Lord is the cause of the world; for in the *Mantropaniṣad* of the *Vaitathyas*, referring to the omniscient Lord, it says: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs, and there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him" (Svetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9).
Therefore, it is established that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world, and not the non-intelligent *pradhāna* or anything else.

Beginning with the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" and ending with "And because it is so heard," the Vedāntic passages cited by these sūtras have been demonstrated, through the application of reasoning, to establish the meaning that the omniscient and omnipotent Lord is the cause of the world's birth, subsistence, and dissolution.
Furthermore, by presenting the uniformity of their purport (*gatisāmānya*), it has been explained that all Vedāntas teach a conscious being as the cause.

Therefore, what is the motivation for the subsequent portion of the text? It is said: Brahman is indeed understood to be twofold—qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the distinctions of modifications of name and form, and its opposite, which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts.

As it is said: "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūman*);
but where one sees something else, hears something else, understands something else—that is the finite (*alpa*)."

"That which is the Plenum (bhūman) is immortal; that which is small is mortal. "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made names, sits calling them forth. "Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, stainless—the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. "Not this, not this. "Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long. And: "One state is deficient, the other is complete. In these and thousands of other ways, the Vedāntic texts demonstrate the twofold nature of Brahman according to the distinction between the spheres of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), as seen in the commentary on the Sūtras.
In that state of ignorance, all worldly activity regarding Brahman—characterized by the relationship between the object of worship and the worshiper, and so forth—takes place.

Among these, some meditations on Brahman are for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), some are for the sake of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*), and some are for the sake of the success of ritual actions (*karmasamṛddhi*).
Their distinction arises from the difference in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*).

Although the one supreme Self, the Lord, is indeed to be meditated upon as distinguished by various specific qualities, nevertheless, the fruits differ according to the particular qualities meditated upon;

for there is the Śruti: "In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become," and also: "As a person acts and behaves in this world, so does he become after departing from here. And from Smṛti: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end..."
"O son of Kuntī, he always goes to that very [state], being permeated by the nature of that.

Although the one Self is hidden within all beings, both moving and stationary, nevertheless, due to the gradations of the specific limiting adjuncts of the mind (*cittopādhiviśeṣatāratamya*), a gradation is heard in scripture regarding the progressively manifested Self—even though the Self is eternally unchanging and uniform—by way of specific powers of sovereignty (*aiśvaryaśaktiviśeṣaiḥ*), as in the passage: "He who knows His Self as more fully manifested. This is also stated in the Smṛti: "Whatever being is possessed of majesty, or is glorious, or even powerful..."
"Know that each of those has arisen from a portion of my splendor"—in this way, wherever there is an excellence of majesty, that very one is enjoined as the Lord to be meditated upon.
Likewise, here too, he will state that the golden person within the solar orb is indeed the Supreme Being, on account of the mark of being free from all evil.
This same principle is to be understood in other cases such as "The ether [is Brahman], because of its marks."

Thus ends the first chapter on immediate liberation. Although the cause—knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñāna*)—is taught by means of specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it must be determined through a careful examination of the purport of the sentences, as it is subject to doubt regarding whether it refers to the higher or the lower Brahman when its connection with a specific adjunct is not intended to be expressed; as for instance in this very work [the *Brahma-sūtra*]: "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition" (1.1.12). In this way, although Brahman is one, it is taught in the Vedāntas both as an object of meditation and as an object of knowledge, according to its association with required limiting adjuncts or its state where such associations have been discarded. To demonstrate this, the subsequent portion of the text is commenced.

And as for that refutation of a non-conscious cause which was stated on the grounds of "the commonality of destiny," that too is further elaborated by one who, while explaining other passages concerning Brahman, negates any cause contrary to Brahman: "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition."

In the Taittirīyaka, following the sequence of recitation, after the [sheaths] consisting of food, vital breath, mind, and cognition, it is stated: "Different from this one consisting of cognition is another inner self, consisting of bliss.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt:

Is the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) used here to denote the Supreme Brahman itself, which was introduced as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," or is it something other than Brahman, like the [sheaths] consisting of food and so forth?

What, then, is the initial position? The one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) must be a secondary self (*amukhya ātmā*) that is something other than Brahman. Why? Because it falls within the series of secondary selves beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*).
Even so, it might be argued that because it is the innermost of all, the one consisting of bliss is indeed the primary Self.
It cannot be so, because of the mention of its connection with limbs such as "the beloved" and because of the scriptural statement regarding its having a body.
If the Self were the primary [Self], there would be no contact with the beloved and so forth;
however, here it is heard in scripture: "The beloved itself is its head," and so on.
Furthermore, its corporeality is heard in the scripture: "Of that [former], this indeed is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), which belongs to the former.
This means that of the former—the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya)—this very one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the embodied self.
And for one who exists as embodied, contact with pleasure and pain cannot be warded off.

Therefore, when it has been argued that the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the transmigrating soul, this is said in reply: "The one consisting of bliss [is the Supreme Self] because of repetition.
The self consisting of bliss must be the Supreme Self alone.
Why? Because of repetition.
For the word "bliss" (ānanda) is indeed repeated many times with reference to the Supreme Self alone.

Having introduced the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), and having stated its nature as essence (rasa) in the words "He is indeed essence," it is further said: "For only by perceiving this essence does one become blissful;
for who indeed could inhale, and who could exhale?"

"If this bliss did not exist in space (ākāśa), this [Self] would not cause bliss. "This is the inquiry into bliss. "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss. "Knowing the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing from anywhere.
And also: "He understood that bliss is Brahman."
Moreover, in another scriptural passage, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*), the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is seen applied to Brahman itself.
Thus, because the word "bliss" is repeatedly applied to Brahman, it is understood that the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman.

As for the argument that the *ānandamaya* is also non-primary because it falls within a series of non-primary selves beginning with the *annamaya*, that is not a fault, because the *ānandamaya* is the innermost of all.

Indeed, the scripture, desiring to teach the primary Self itself while following the common understanding of the world, takes the body composed of food—which is not the Self but is well-known as the Self among the extremely deluded—just like a statue cast from molten copper poured into a mold; it then causes [the student] to grasp each subsequent non-Self as the Self, being similar to each preceding one, in order of increasing interiority. Having thus proceeded for the sake of ease of comprehension, it finally taught the primary Self, which is the innermost of all, consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). This is most appropriate.
Just as when the Arundhatī star is being shown, although many stars that are not the principal one are pointed out, that which is finally indicated is indeed the principal Arundhatī;
so too here, because the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the innermost of all, it possesses the status of the principal Self.
As for what you say—that the attribution of having the head and other limbs to the principal Self is untenable—that [attribution] is produced by the immediately preceding limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
There is no fault in this, for [the Self] is not possessed of intrinsic nature;
moreover, the fact that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) has a body is shown through the succession of bodies beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*),
and not because it possesses a body directly like a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*).
Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is indeed the supreme Self.
If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word "Self"] because of the word being a term for a modification, we say no, because of its abundance.
The Supreme Self must be the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya);

why? Because of the word denoting a modification (vikāra). For this other word "ānandamaya" is understood from its etymological root as a term denoting a modification, since the suffix *mayaṭ* has the meaning of "consisting of a modification."
If it be argued that, like the words *annamaya* and so forth, this word *ānandamaya* also refers exclusively to a modification (*vikāra*), we say no;
for the suffix *mayaṭ* is also recorded in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).

Indeed, according to the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of what is being discussed as its primary constituent" (*tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed even to denote abundance.
Just as the expression "a sacrifice consisting of food" (*annamaya yajña*) denotes one in which food abounds, so too Brahman, which abounds in bliss, is called "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

Furthermore, the abundance of bliss in Brahman is established by the determination that the bliss of Brahman is unsurpassed, after it has been stated that bliss increases a hundredfold at each successive stage beginning from the human level.
Therefore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance.
And because there is a designation of that as its cause.
For this reason as well, the suffix *mayaṭ* has the sense of abundance (*prācurya*);
because the Śruti declares that Brahman is the cause of bliss, stating, "For he alone causes bliss" (*eṣa hyevānandayāti*), which means "he causes [others] to be blissful.
For it is well known that one who causes others to be blissful is possessed of abundant bliss.

Just as in the world, when someone causes others to attain the status of a wealthy person, it is understood that he himself possesses abundant wealth; so it is here. Therefore, since the suffix *mayaṭ* can also signify abundance, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the Supreme Self.
And it is sung as being merely according to the description of the mother.
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the supreme Self;
because [the scripture says], "He who knows Brahman attains [the Supreme]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). Chapter One.

Beginning with the word "Supreme," that very Brahman which was introduced in the mantra, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and determined by the qualifiers of being Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite; from which, through the sequence starting with space, all beings—both stationary and moving—were born; which, having created the beings, entered into them and abides in the cave as the innermost of all; and for the sake of whose realization the series of "Another inner Self, another inner Self" was commenced—that same Brahman described in the words of that mantra is here sung as "Another inner Self, consisting of bliss."
Furthermore, it is logical that the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa have a single meaning, as there is no contradiction;
otherwise, there would be the abandonment of the subject matter at hand and the introduction of something not under discussion.
Moreover, unlike the cases of the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth, no other inner self is designated beyond the one "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
And this very Vāruṇī lore of Bhārgava culminates in this: "He understood that bliss is Brahman.
Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed the supreme Self.
Not the other, because it is not possible [otherwise].

For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the supreme Self alone, not the other; "the other" means the transmigrating individual soul (jīva) distinct from the Lord. The individual soul is not denoted by the term "consisting of bliss."
Why? Because it is untenable.
For, with reference to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is heard in scripture: "He desired:
'May I be many, may I procreate.'"
He performed austerity.
Having performed austerity,
he created all this.

Regarding the phrase "whatever this is," therein [is meant] the prior volition (abhidhyāna) before the production of the body and so forth; the non-difference of the creator from the modifications being created; and the creation of all modifications—none of which is possible apart from the Supreme Self.
And because there is a designation of difference.
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is not a transmigrating being:

because, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss, the text designates the individual soul and the one consisting of bliss as distinct by stating, "He is indeed essence (rasa); for only by attaining essence does one become blissful."
Indeed, that which has already been attained cannot be something yet to be attained.

How then are the Śruti and Smṛti passages such as "The Self is to be sought" and "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self" to be understood, given that it has been stated that what is already attained cannot be something yet to be attained? Certainly; nevertheless, even though the Self remains with its essential nature unimpaired, we observe in common worldly experience a false conviction of "Selfhood" in non-Selfs such as the body and so forth, caused by the failure to realize its true nature.

Therefore, the designation of distinctions such as "the Self of the self that has become the body and so forth is not sought but is to be sought," "not attained but is to be attained," "not heard but is to be heard," "not thought about but is to be thought about," and "not known but is to be known" becomes logically consistent.
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality, any seer or hearer other than the omniscient Supreme Lord is indeed denied by such statements as, "There is no other seer but He.
But the Supreme Lord is distinct from the embodied agent and enjoyer called the *vijñānātman*, who is constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Just as from a magician who holds a shield and sword and ascends into the sky by means of a rope, that very magician—who is the ultimate reality—is distinct from [the one] standing on the ground;
or just as the space not delimited by limiting adjuncts is distinct from the space within a jar which is delimited by such adjuncts. (First Chapter)

And it is with reference to such a distinction between the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) that it was stated: "Not the other, because of impossibility; and because of the designation of difference."
And because of direct perception, there is no dependence on inference.

Furthermore, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because of the mention of the quality of desiring—"He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—the non-intelligent *pradhāna* imagined by the Sāṃkhyas, whether as the one consisting of bliss or as the cause, must not be accepted.

Although the *pradhāna* has already been refuted on the grounds that "because of seeing [the Self], it is not the one taught in scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*), it is refuted once more here incidentally by relying on the scriptural statement of desiring mentioned in the preceding sūtra, for the purpose of elaborating upon the uniformity of the teaching (*gatisāmānya*).
And in this [state], he teaches its union with that.

For this reason as well, the term *ānandamaya* does not refer to the *pradhāna* or to the individual soul (*jīva*); because with reference to this very Self under discussion as the *ānandamaya*, the scripture teaches its union for this awakened individual soul. "Union with that" (*tadyoga*) means being joined with that [Self], which is the attainment of its state—that is, liberation. The scripture teaches this union: "For when he finds fearless support in this invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and baseless [Self], then he becomes free from fear."
"For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear comes upon him.

What is meant by this is stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: when one perceives even a slight difference in this Self consisting of bliss—a difference characterized by non-identity—then one does not turn away from the fear of saṃsāra.
But when one abides uninterruptedly in this "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) through identity, then one turns away from the fear of saṃsāra.
And that is possible only if the Supreme Self is accepted, not if the Pradhāna is accepted.
Therefore, it is established that the "consisting of bliss" is the Supreme Self.

Regarding the inclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*), this must be stated here: "Now, this person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*); different from this one consisting of the essence of food is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*); different from that is another inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*); different from that is another inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). Since there is thus a continuous series of the suffix *mayaṭ* used in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), how can it be that, all of a sudden, in the case of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) alone, the suffix *mayaṭ* is taken to mean abundance (*prācurya*) and to have Brahman as its object, according to the maxim of the "half-old woman"?
If it is argued that this is because of the context of Brahman introduced by the words of the mantra, we say no.
In that case, it would follow that even those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the rest are Brahman.
To this he replies: It is appropriate that those consisting of food and so forth are not Brahman, because after each of them, another inner self is described;
however, after the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), no other inner self is mentioned.

Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something not under discussion.

To this it is replied: although, unlike in the case of the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others, the phrase "another inner self" is not heard after the one consisting of bliss, nevertheless, the one consisting of bliss is not Brahman;
"The southern wing is joy (*pramoda*), the northern wing is delight (*ānanda*), the self (*ātman*) is bliss (*ānanda*), and Brahman is the tail, the support.
In this context, that which was introduced here as Brahman in the wording of the mantra—"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—is what is referred to here as "Brahman is the tail, the support.

It is precisely with the desire to make that [Brahman] known that the five sheaths (*kośa*), beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), are postulated.
In that case, how can there be the charge of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something irrelevant?

[Objection: But surely Brahman is mentioned as a limb of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) in the passage, "Brahman is the tail, the support," just as in the cases of those consisting of food and so forth, where it says, "This is the tail, the support," and so on.
Under such circumstances, how can it be understood that Brahman is the primary subject itself? [Reply: We say: because it is the subject under discussion.

[Objection: Surely, even if Brahman is understood as being a constituent part (*avayava*) of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), its status as the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*) is not lost, because that which consists of bliss is Brahman itself. [Reply:

To this it is said: if that were so, there would be an inconsistency in holding that the very same Brahman is the "self consisting of bliss" as the whole (*avayavin*), while that same Brahman is also the "tail, the support" as a part (*avayava*).

However, if one must choose between the two, it is more reasonable to accept the designation of Brahman precisely in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," because of its direct connection with the word "Brahman."
"O Ānanda, it is not so, because of the absence of connection with the word *brahman* [in the phrase 'made of maya'].
Furthermore, after stating "Brahman is the tail, the support," this is said: "On this there is also this verse:
'He becomes non-existent indeed...'"
"If one knows 'Brahman is non-existent,' and if one knows 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing."

And since this verse—without having drawn back the *ānandamaya*—declares the merits and defects of the existence and non-existence of Brahman alone, it is understood that in the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support," Brahman itself is the primary subject, and not the *ānandamaya* self.

Furthermore, the doubt regarding its existence or non-existence is appropriate [only for Brahman], because the *ānandamaya* characterized by joy, delight, and so forth, is well-known to all the world.

But how is it that Brahman, being the primary subject itself, is designated as the "tail" (puccha) of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), as in the statement, "Brahman is the tail, the support"? This is not a fault.

"Tail" is used in the sense of being like a tail; what is intended here is that the bliss of Brahman is the support, the ultimate resort, and the single abode for all worldly kinds of bliss, and not that it is a literal limb or part.
For another scriptural passage states: "Other beings live on only a minute portion of this very bliss."

Moreover, if that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) were Brahman, Brahman would have to be accepted as possessing attributes (*saviśeṣa*), because it would have pleasure and so forth as its limbs.

However, Brahman without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) is heard of in the remainder of the passage, since it is described as being beyond the reach of speech and mind: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to attain it."
"Having known the bliss of Brahman,
one fears nothing from anywhere.
Moreover, when it is said that [Brahman] abounds in bliss, the smallness of suffering is also implied.
In common worldly usage, abundance (prācurya) is dependent upon the existence of its counterpart in the form of scarcity.

This being the case, the scriptural passage concerning the *bhūman*—Brahman—"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else, that is the *bhūman*"—would be contradicted, as it would imply the non-existence of anything distinct from that Brahman.
Furthermore, because of the differences in what is dear (*priya*) and so forth for each individual body, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) must be distinct [in each instance].

Brahman, however, does not differ with each individual body, because of the scriptural declaration of its infinity in such passages as, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and from another scriptural text: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings. Furthermore, no repetition of the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is heard [in the context of Brahman].
For in every case, it is the mere meaning of the nominal stem that is repeated:
"He is indeed rasa; for only by obtaining rasa does one become blissful.
For who indeed could inhale, and who could exhale?"

"If this bliss did not exist in space," "This is the inquiry into bliss," "He who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere," and "He understood that bliss is Brahman"—these [texts] [support this].

Furthermore, if it were certain that the term *ānandamaya* has Brahman as its referent, then one might assume a repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the *ānandamaya* in the subsequent uses of the mere word "bliss" (*ānanda*); however, we have already stated that the *ānandamaya* is not Brahman, on account of reasons such as having "pleasure for its head."

Therefore, since in another scriptural passage—“Brahman is consciousness and bliss” (vijñānamānandaṃ brahma)—the nominal stem *ānanda* is seen to be used for Brahman, and since there is the usage regarding Brahman in the text, “If this bliss did not exist in this space,” it should be understood that this is not a repetition of the term *ānandamaya*.
As for this repetition of the word *ānandamaya*, which ends in the suffix *mayaṭ*—in the passage, “He reaches this self consisting of bliss”—that does not have Brahman as its object;
for it falls within a series of non-self entities such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, which are modifications and are themselves to be transcended.

[Objection: But surely, if the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which is to be reached, were not Brahman—just like those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth—then the attainment of Brahman could not be specified as the fruit for the knower. [Reply:

This is not a fault, because by the very mention of reaching the one consisting of bliss, the fruit consisting in the attainment of Brahman—which serves as the tail and foundation—is indeed specified; this is because it is further elaborated upon in the Sūtra-bhāṣya with the words, "Now there is also this verse," and "From whence words turn back," and so on.

As for the scriptural passage cited—"He [it] desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—which occurs in proximity to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), that passage, being connected with the Brahman mentioned in the immediately preceding phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," does not establish the status of the one consisting of bliss as Brahman.

Furthermore, because the subsequent text beginning with "He is indeed essence" (*raso vai saḥ*) is dependent upon that [preceding Brahman], it does not have the one consisting of bliss as its subject.
[Objection: But surely, the masculine designation "He desired" (*so'kāmayata*) would be inappropriate if applied to Brahman.

This is not a fault, because in the passage, "From this very Self (ātman), space was produced," Brahman is the subject under discussion even by means of the masculine word *ātman*. As for the Bhārgavi-Vāruṇī knowledge—"Brahman is bliss"—in that case, since the suffix *mayaṭ* is not heard and the state of having pleasure as its head and so forth is not mentioned, it is appropriate that bliss itself is Brahman. Therefore, without relying on even the slightest distinction, such qualities as having pleasure as its head cannot belong to Brahman by its own nature alone.
Moreover, it is not Brahman with attributes that is intended to be taught here, because of the scriptural statement regarding its transcendence of the sphere of speech and mind.

Therefore, as in the case of the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and the others, the suffix -maya in the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) must be understood in the sense of a modification, not in the sense of abundance.

The sūtras, however, are to be explained as follows: regarding the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support," is Brahman intended here as a limb of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), or is it intended as the primary subject itself? Since the word "tail" suggests it is a limb, that being the prima facie view, it is replied: because of the repetition [of the word "Brahman"], in the statement "the self consists of bliss," Brahman is taught as the primary subject itself in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support."

Because of repetition, for in this concluding section, "But he becomes non-existent indeed," Brahman alone is what is being repeated. As for the objection that it is not so because of the word denoting a modification—that is, the word "tail" (puccha) is intended as a word denoting a limb—and therefore Brahman cannot be the primary subject because of this word for a limb: the refutation of that must now be stated. "Not so, because of abundance" (prācuryāt). The word "modification" is intended here as a word for a limb; as for the claim that Brahman is not the primary subject because of the word "tail" denoting a limb, its rebuttal is to be explained.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because the term "member" (avayava) is applicable due to abundance;
"abundance" means a preponderance, and the meaning is that the statement occurs in a context where members predominate.

For, although the members beginning with the head and ending with the tail have been mentioned for those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, [the text] mentions other members such as the head and so on for that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and then says, "Brahman is the tail, the support," by way of a preponderance of members, not with the intention of [Brahman] being a literal member.
For this reason, by the word "through repetition" (*abhyāsāt*), the primacy of Brahman has been established.

Furthermore, because of the designation of it as the cause: for Brahman is designated as the cause of the entire aggregate of effects, including that which consists of bliss, in the passage, "It created all this, whatever there is.
And it is not logical that Brahman, being the cause, should be a constituent part (*avayava*) of its own effect—the one consisting of bliss—in a primary sense.
Other sūtras as well should be understood as establishing, according to their respective contexts, that very Brahman which was indicated by the words of the question.
[The person] within [the sun and the eye is Brahman], because of the teaching of its attributes.

In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, in the section concerning the "Inner" (*antara-adhikaraṇa*), this is recorded in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to the very tips of his nails; as a lotus flower is reddish-yellow like a monkey's bottom, so are his eyes; 'Ud' is his name—he has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils. This refers to the divine realm (*adhidaivata*). Then, regarding the self (*adhyātma*), it says:
"Now, that person who is seen within the eye," and so forth.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is it some transmigrating soul who has attained excellence through the power of superior knowledge and action that is heard of as the object of meditation in the solar orb and in the eye; or is it the eternally established Supreme Lord?
What, then, is the initial position? That it is a transmigrating soul. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of its possessing form.

First, with regard to the person in the sun, a form such as "having a golden beard" and so forth has been cited; that very same form is obtained by extension for the person in the eye as well, through the statement: "The form of this one is the very same as the form of that one.
And yet, it is not appropriate for the Supreme Lord to possess a form, according to the scriptural text: "Without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying."

Furthermore, because a substratum is mentioned in the passages, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye," for the Supreme Lord—who is without substratum, established in His own glory, and all-pervading—a substratum would not be taught.
For there are two scriptural texts: "In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own glory," and "He is omnipresent and eternal like space."
The first chapter of the Aiśvarya-sūtra:

Regarding the limitation of sovereignty, the Śruti states, "He is the lord of those worlds that are beyond this one and of the desires of the gods," thus defining the limitation of sovereignty for the person in the sun;
and, "He is the lord of those worlds that are below this one and of the desires of men," thus defining it for the person in the eye.
Furthermore, it is not fitting for the Supreme Lord to possess a sovereignty characterized by limitations;

for there is an unrestricted scriptural declaration: "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded.
Therefore, when it is thus argued that the Supreme Lord is not within the eye or the sun, we reply: "The one within [is the Supreme Lord], because of the teaching of His attributes."
The person who is heard of in the passages, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye," is indeed the Supreme Lord, not a transmigrating soul.
Why? Because of the teaching of His attributes;
for the attributes of that Supreme Lord are taught here.

For example, having caused [the name] "His name is Ut" to be heard, [the text] etymologically explains the name of that person in the sun as "He has risen above (udita) all evils," by means of the departure of all evil.
And it extends that very etymological explanation of the name to the person in the eye as well, stating, "Whatever is his name, that is his name.
Furthermore, the departure of all evil is heard in scripture only with respect to the Supreme Self, in such passages as, "This Self is free from evil... and so forth.

Likewise, in the passage concerning the person in the eye, [the text] determines that he consists of the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, the *uktha*, and the *yajus*: "That itself is the *ṛc*, that is the *sāman*, that is the *uktha*, that is the *yajus*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.1). And this is possible for the Supreme Lord, because, being the cause of all, it is logical that He is the self of all.

Having sequentially described the *ṛc* and *sāman* as consisting of earth and fire with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*), and as consisting of speech and breath with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), the text says: "His two songs are the *ṛc* and the *sāman*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8), referring to the deities.
Likewise, with respect to the internal self, it says, "Whatever are its joints, those are the joints.
And that is possible only if it is the Self of all.

Furthermore, the passage, "Now, those who sing on the lute, they sing of this very one; therefore, they are winners of wealth," shows that even in worldly songs, it is this very one that is being sung about.

And that [sovereignty] is possible only through the possession by the Supreme Lord, as seen in the Bhagavad Gītā: "Whatever being is possessed of glory, beauty, or power, know that to have sprung from a fragment of my splendor.
Furthermore, the unimpeded lordship over the desires of the world, as it is heard [in scripture], leads one to understand the Supreme Lord.

As for what was said—that the scriptural mention of possessing a form such as golden hair and beard is not possible in the case of the Supreme Lord—we reply: even the Supreme Lord may, by the power of His will, assume a form consisting of *māyā* for the sake of favoring his devotees (*sādhaka*), according to the traditional teaching: "This is indeed *māyā* created by me, O Nārada, that you see me endowed with the qualities of all beings; you ought not to know me in this way.
Furthermore, where the Supreme Lord is taught in His form devoid of all distinctions, there the scripture says: "Without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying," and so forth.

However, because He is the cause of all things, the Supreme Lord is also designated as the object of worship by means of certain qualities of transformation, such as in the passage: "He whose work is all, whose desires are all, whose fragrance is all, whose taste is all," and so forth.
Likewise, the description of having golden hair and beard will also be applicable.

As for the argument that He cannot be the Supreme Lord because of the mention of a support, it is said in reply: even for one who is established in His own majesty, the teaching of a specific support is intended for the sake of meditation. (First Chapter).
There will be no such fault; for since Brahman is all-pervading like space, its existence within everything is logically established.

Furthermore, even the scriptural mention of limitations on its sovereignty is intended solely for the purpose of meditation, with reference to the distinction between the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata).
Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught as being within the eye and the sun.
And [the Self] is different [from the body] because of the designation of difference.

Furthermore, there exists a Lord who is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), distinct from the individual souls (jīvas) that identify with the bodies of the sun and so forth; for another scriptural passage makes a distinction between them: "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun, who controls the sun from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

For in that passage, the Inner Controller is clearly pointed out as being distinct from the sun, the knower, and the conscious self (vijñānātman), by the statement: "He who is within the sun, whom the sun does not know.
That very same Being must also be the Person within the sun here, because of the identity of the scriptural description.
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is taught here.
It is space, because of its characteristic marks.

Regarding this, they cite the following: "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he replied. "For indeed, all these beings arise from space alone; they rest in space, and they merge into space. Space is indeed greater than these; space is the supreme resort. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the Supreme Brahman denoted by the word "space" (ākāśa), or is it the elemental space (bhūtākāśa)?
Whence arises this doubt? Because its usage is observed in both senses.
First, the word *ākāśa* is well-established in common parlance and in the Veda as referring to a particular element (the ether).

Yet it is also seen used occasionally for Brahman, where Brahman is determined either by the force of the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) or by the hearing of attributes not shared [by anything else]—as in such passages as, "If this *ākāśa* were not bliss," and "Verily, *ākāśa* is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman. Thus, and so forth.
Therefore, there is a doubt.
What, then, is appropriate here? That it is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
Why? Because that [ether] enters the intellect more quickly through its more commonly established usage.

Furthermore, this word "ether" (ākāśa) cannot be understood as having a common meaning for both [the element and Brahman], because that would entail the fallacy of multiple meanings for a single term.
Therefore, the word "ether" must be used in a figurative sense with respect to Brahman;
for Brahman resembles the ether in many respects, such as all-pervasiveness and so forth.
Furthermore, when the primary meaning is possible, a secondary sense ought not to be accepted;
and here, the acceptance of the primary ether alone is indeed possible.
But [it may be argued that] the subsequent portion of the passage, "For all these beings, verily, arise from ether alone," and so forth, would not be appropriate if the elemental ether were intended.

This is not a fault, for even the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) can logically be established as a cause through the sequence of air and so forth. Indeed, it is known from scripture: "From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire," and so on.
Furthermore, both its greatness (*jyāyastva*) and its being the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇatva*) are possible for the elemental ether in relation to the other elements.

Therefore, when it is argued that the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), we reply: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks. It is appropriate here that the word "ether" refers to Brahman.
Why? Because of its characteristic mark (*liṅga*).
For this is a characteristic mark of the supreme Brahman: "All these beings, indeed, arise from Ākāśa alone.
For it is the established rule in the Vedāntas that the origin of beings is from the supreme Brahman.
But has it not been shown that even the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) is a cause through the sequence beginning with air?
True, it has been shown;

nevertheless, because the root cause, Brahman, would not be accepted [as such], the restrictive phrase "from ether alone" (ākāśād eva) and the qualification of the elements as "all" (sarvāṇi) would not be consistent.

Likewise, "they merge into ākāśa" is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Brahman; and "for ākāśa is indeed greater than these, ākāśa is the ultimate resort," refers to greatness and being the ultimate resort.
For absolute greatness is taught of the Supreme Self alone in the passage, "greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds.
Similarly, being the ultimate resort is also more appropriately applicable to the Supreme Self, as it is the supreme cause.
And scripture says: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss; it is the gift, the supreme goal of the giver.

Moreover, having censured Śālāvatya’s position on the ground of its defect of finitude, Jaivali, desiring to state something infinite, adopted the ether (ākāśa); and having identified that ether with the Udgītha, he concludes: "This is the Udgītha, higher than the high; this is the infinite."
Moreover, that infinity is a characteristic mark of Brahman.

As for what was further stated—that although the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) is understood more immediately by the force of common usage, it is nevertheless understood from the context of that specific passage—we reply: it is not accepted because we perceive qualities of Brahman in the remaining parts of the text.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (ākāśa) has been shown to refer to Brahman in such passages as, "Ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form."

Likewise, the use of words synonymous with "ether" (ākāśa) is observed in reference to Brahman, as in: "In the imperishable syllable, in the highest ether (vyoman), upon which the gods have taken their seats"; "This is that Vidyā of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa, established in the highest ether"; and "Om, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman, Kha is the ancient one," and so forth.
Even when the word "ether" occurs at the beginning of a passage, its determination to have Brahman as its object is appropriate on account of the concluding portion of the passage.
For the word "fire" (agni), though occurring at the beginning of the sentence in the expression "Agni studies the Anuvāka," is seen to refer to a young student.
Therefore, it is established that the word "ether" refers to Brahman.
In the commentary on the Sūtra, it is stated: "For this very reason, [the word 'prāṇa' refers to] breath."

Beginning with the words, "O Prastotṛ, that deity which is connected with the Prastāva in the Udgītha," the scripture continues: "Which is that deity? 'Prāṇa,' he said; for indeed, all these beings merge into Prāṇa alone, and from Prāṇa they emerge. This very deity, Prāṇa, is connected with the Prastāva. In this regard, the doubt and its resolution are to be understood in the same manner as before.
For in such passages as, "The mind, my dear, is fastened to the vital breath (prāṇa);

the vital breath, indeed, is fastened to the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2), the word *prāṇa* is seen to refer to Brahman; yet, in both common usage and the Veda, it is more well-known as denoting a modification of air.
Therefore, a doubt arises as to which of these two is appropriately taken up here by the word *prāṇa*.

What, then, is appropriate here? It is appropriate to take the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a modification of air, as the subject; for we have already stated that the word "breath" is more commonly established in that sense. But is it not the case that, as before, it is appropriate here too to understand Brahman alone on account of its characteristic marks?
For here too, in the supplementary passage, the entering and emerging of the elements is understood as an action belonging to the Supreme Lord.
[Objection: No, because the entering and emerging of the elements is seen even in the case of the primary vital breath (prāṇa).

For it is thus recorded in scripture: "When a person sleeps, then speech enters into the vital breath, the eye into the vital breath, the ear into the vital breath, and the mind into the vital breath; when he awakes, they are born again from the vital breath alone."

This is directly perceived: at the time of sleep, while the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains unimpaired, the functions of the sense organs (*indriya*) are dissolved, and at the time of awakening, they appear once again.

Furthermore, because the elements (*bhūta*) have the senses as their essence, the subsequent passage—which speaks of the dissolution and emergence of the elements into the primary vital breath—is not contradictory.
Moreover, the Sun and Food, who are the deities of the *udgītha* and *pratihāra*, are mentioned immediately after the vital breath, who is the deity of the *prastāva*.
Furthermore, those two do not possess the nature of Brahman;

and because of that commonality, the vital breath (prāṇa) also does not have the nature of Brahman. This being the position reached, the author of the Sūtras says: "For this very reason, the vital breath [is Brahman]. This refers to the phrase "on account of its characteristic marks" (talliṅgāt), which was indicated in the preceding Sūtra.
For this very reason, on account of those marks, even the word "prāṇa" must refer to the supreme Brahman.
For the connection of prāṇa with the marks of Brahman is also heard in scripture: "All these beings indeed enter into prāṇa alone, and from prāṇa they emerge.
The origination and dissolution of all beings, which are stated to be caused by prāṇa, lead to the understanding that prāṇa is Brahman.

But was it not already stated that even when the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) is accepted as the subject, the observation of "entering" and "emerging" is not contradictory, because this is seen in the cases of sleep and waking?
To this it is replied: in the cases of sleep and waking, what is observed is the entering and emerging of the sense organs alone, resting upon the vital breath, and not of all beings;
whereas here, according to the scriptural text, "All these beings indeed," it refers to all beings together with their senses, their bodies, and as entered by the individual soul (jīva).
Even when the mention of "beings" (*bhūta*) is understood as referring to the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), even then there is no contradiction in its being a characteristic mark of Brahman.

Now, it might be argued that we hear of the dissolution of the sense organs along with their objects into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during sleep, and of their emergence from the vital breath during waking: "When one is asleep and sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very vital breath; then speech goes together with all names into him," and so forth.
Even in that case, on account of those characteristic marks, the word *prāṇa* refers to Brahman alone.
As for the further argument that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not Brahman because of its proximity to food and the sun—that is incorrect;
for when, by the force of the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), it is perceived that the word *prāṇa* has Brahman as its referent, mere proximity is of no consequence.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the word *prāṇa* is more commonly established in the sense of the fivefold vital function, that must be countered in the same manner as the word *ākāśa*.
Therefore, it is established that the vital breath (prāṇa), as the deity of the introductory section (prastāva), is Brahman.

In this context, some cite the passages "the breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*) and "for the mind, my dear, has food as its fuel" (*annaṃ hi somya manaḥ*). That, however, is not correct; *Upadeśasāhasrī*, First Chapter. (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on Śaṅkara’s *Upadeśasāhasrī*. The first line identifies the chapter, while the second presents an opponent's objection regarding the nature of the self, citing specific Upaniṣadic verses.)
Because of the difference in words and the context, doubt is untenable.

Just as in the expression "the father of the father," it is understood that the one designated by the nominative case ("the father") is distinct from the one designated by the genitive case ("of the father"); similarly, because of the difference in words in the phrase "the breath of breath," it is determined that the "breath of breath" is other than the well-known breath.
For there can be no designation of difference by saying "that very thing is that.
Furthermore, when something is mentioned within a particular context—even under another name—it is understood that it is that very subject of the context which is being designated.
