Just as in the section concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the word "jyotis" in the phrase "One should sacrifice with the Jyotis every spring" refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, so too, in the context of the Supreme Brahman, how could the word "prāṇa" heard in the passage "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to prāṇa" be understood to refer merely to a modification of air?
Therefore, since this is not an object of doubt, this example is not appropriate;
however, regarding the Prāṇa as the deity of the Prastāva, the doubt, the prima facie argument, and the final conclusion have already been established.
[The Brahman is] light, because of the mention of its feet.

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad declares as follows: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the back of all, on the back of everything, in the highest worlds than which there are no higher—this very light is the one within the heart, namely, this light which is here within the person.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the word "light" (jyotis) used here to denote physical light such as that of the sun and so forth, or does it refer to the Supreme Self?
It has already been stated that even though the word "breath" (prāṇa) refers to something else, its subject matter is Brahman because of its characteristic marks (liṅga).
Here, however, it is deliberated whether those very characteristic marks exist or do not exist.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the word "light" (jyotis) refers only to the sun and so forth.
Why? Because of common usage.
For these two words, "darkness" and "light," are well known to have mutually opposed referents.
Darkness is said to be that which obstructs the functioning of the eye, such as the gloom of night and so forth.
The light that assists this very [self] is the sun and so forth.
Likewise, this scriptural statement, "it shines," is well known to refer to the sun and other such luminaries.
For Brahman, which is devoid of form and other qualities, cannot properly be said to "shine" in the primary sense.
And because of the scriptural mention of a boundary:

for it is not fitting that heaven should be the boundary of Brahman, which is the seed of all things moving and stationary and the Self of all; however, heaven could be the boundary of light as an effect that is limited.
And there is the Brāhmaṇa passage: "The light beyond heaven.
Now, an objection may be raised: since even a light that is an effect is perceived everywhere, its being bounded by heaven is inconsistent;
let it then be the unevolved (atrivṛtkṛta) fire that is first-born.
No, because there is no purpose for fire that has not been made tripartite.
If it is argued that its very purpose is to be an object of meditation (*upāsya*), we say no;

for we observe that the sun and other such objects are made objects of meditation precisely because they are prompted by some other purpose, and because the Vedic revelation states without qualification: "Of these, I shall make each one threefold."
Furthermore, it is not well-known that even non-tripartite fire has heaven as its boundary.
Let it be, then, that only tripartite fire is denoted by the word "light" (jyotis).
But was it not stated that light such as fire is perceived even below heaven?
This is not a fault;
for even though light is understood to be present everywhere, its restriction to a specific location— by the phrase "beyond the heaven"— for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory.
However, the postulation of specific spatial divisions for Brahman, which is itself without parts (niṣpradeśa), is not tenable;
furthermore, the scriptural mention of a multiplicity of locations in the passage, "In worlds that are beyond all, the highest of the high," is far more appropriate in the case of the effected light.
Moreover, in the passage, "This indeed is that light which is within this person," the supreme light is seen being superimposed upon the light within the body.
Furthermore, superimpositions arise based on similarity— as in the passage, "Its head is *bhūḥ*, for there is one head, and this syllable is one. However,
it is well known that the light within the belly is not Brahman,
because of the scriptural statement, "This is its sight," and "This is its hearing," which indicates that it is characterized by heat and sound.

This is because of the scriptural statement, "One should meditate upon this as both the seen and the heard," and because of the mention of a minor fruit in the passage, "He who knows this becomes beautiful and famous"; for meditation on Brahman is intended for a great fruit.
Furthermore, there is no other mark of Brahman in its own sentence than that which pertains to light, as in the case of the vital breath and the ether.
Nor is Brahman indicated even in the preceding sentence, because of the mention of a meter: "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this being.
Even if, somehow, Brahman were indicated in the preceding sentence, there is nevertheless no recognition of it here.
For in that [other passage], heaven is heard of as the locus in the phrase "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven";
here, however, in the phrase "The light beyond heaven," heaven is mentioned as a boundary.
Therefore, since the light here must be understood as the elemental light—this being the position reached—we reply: the light here must be understood as Brahman.
Why? Because of the mention of "feet" (caraṇa), meaning because of the designation of "quarters" (pāda).

For in the preceding passage, Brahman was indicated as four-footed by this mantra: "Such is its greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that. All beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven."

In that context, that very Brahman which was indicated as having four quarters—of which three quarters are immortal and connected with heaven—is recognized here as being indicated by virtue of the connection [between the two passages].

To set that aside and imagine the light to be the elemental (prākṛta) light would result in the fallacies of abandoning the subject under discussion (prakṛtahāna) and introducing something not under discussion (aprakṛtaprakriyā).
Furthermore, the continuity of Brahman is not found only in the passage concerning light.

For even in the subsequent Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, Brahman will continue to be the subject; therefore, here too, by the word "light" (jyotis), Brahman is to be understood. As for the objection that the two words "is entered" (apyate) and "light" (jyotis) are well-known in the sense of the effected light, this is not a fault;

because when Brahman is understood through the context, these two words do not act as qualifiers [of the effect], since their usage is possible even with respect to Brahman as indicated by the shining effected light, as seen in the Vedic mantra:
"By whose splendor the sun shines."

Alternatively, this word "light" (jyotis) does not refer exclusively to that light which assists the function of the eye, because its usage is observed elsewhere as well, such as in the passages, "By speech alone he shines at the end," and "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering].
Therefore, whatever illuminates anything is designated by the word "light.
This being the case, the application of the word "light" to Brahman is also appropriate, since Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is the cause of the illumination of the entire universe.
From the Upanishadic texts such as: "Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined," and "The gods worship that immortal light of lights," and so forth.

As for what was said—that the limitation by heaven (the sky) is not possible for the omnipresent Brahman—it is replied here: even though Brahman is omnipresent, the appropriation of a specific location for the sake of meditation is not contradictory.
But has it not been stated that the postulation of specific locations for Brahman, which is without parts (niṣpradeśa), is untenable?
This is not a fault, because even though Brahman is without parts, the postulation of specific locations is tenable due to its connection with specific limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
For instance, meditations on Brahman connected to specific locations are heard in scripture, such as "in the sun," "in the eye," and "in the heart."
By this, the multiplicity of supports expressed in the phrase "on all sides" (*viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*) has been established.

As for the argument that because it is superimposed upon the light within the body—which is inferred from heat and sound—that light must be a product of action even though it is beyond the heavens, that too is incorrect;
for it is possible for the supreme Brahman itself to serve as a symbol (*pratīka*) of the corporeal light, just as it serves as a symbol for names and so forth.
As for the statement, "One should meditate [on it] as seen and heard," the quality of being seen and heard will apply by way of the symbol (*pratīka*).
Furthermore, the argument that it cannot be Brahman because of the mention of limited fruits is untenable;
for there is no rule or reason that Brahman must be resorted to for such a fruit, but not for another.

For where the supreme Brahman, divested of all connection with particular attributes, is taught as the Self, there it is understood that the fruit is of a single uniform nature, namely liberation. But where Brahman is taught in connection with specific qualities or specific symbols (*pratīka*), there various fruits pertaining to the sphere of transmigratory existence—both high and low—are observed in such scriptural passages as, "He who knows this becomes an eater of food, a giver of wealth, and finds wealth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Although there is no mark indicating that the light is Brahman within its own sentence, nevertheless, what is seen in the preceding sentence must be accepted.
This was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "The light [is Brahman], because of the mention of the feet."

But how can the word "light" (jyotis) be displaced from its own context by the proximity of Brahman occurring in another sentence? This is not a fault; for since the pronoun "that" (yat), which is read earlier in the phrase "Now, that light which is beyond this heaven," refers back to the Brahman specified in the preceding sentence through its inherent power of denotation, it is established by the force of the context that the word "light" also has Brahman as its object.
Therefore, in this instance, "light" should be understood as Brahman.

If it be argued that [the Self is not the object of meditation] because of the mention of the meters, we say no; for there is a declaration of the fixing of the mind [upon the Self], and thus scripture shows.

Now, as for what was stated regarding the previous passage—that Brahman is not denoted there because the metre named Gāyatrī is denoted in the words, "Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here"—that must be refuted.
But how can it be said that Brahman is not denoted because of the mention of a metre? For in the verse, "Such is its greatness," Brahman is shown to possess four quarters.

This is not so. In the first chapter [of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*], beginning with "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and having explained that very Gāyatrī through its divisions of beings, earth, body, heart, speech, and breath, the mantra is cited—namely, "This is that four-footed, sixfold Gāyatrī; of this it is said in a Ṛg-verse: 'Such is his greatness'"—referring to that very Gāyatrī whose form has been thus explained. How could this mantra, cited in reference to that Gāyatrī, suddenly denote Brahman as being four-footed?
As for the word "Brahman" occurring there in the phrase "That which is indeed Brahman," that too refers only to the meter because the meter is the subject under discussion.
For in the passage, "He who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman thus," they explain it as "the secret doctrine of the Veda.
Therefore, if it is argued that Brahman is not the subject under discussion because the meter is being denoted, this is not a valid objection.

Likewise, because of the restriction of the fixing of the mind (*cetorpaṇa-nigada*), by means of the meter named *Gāyatrī*, the fixing of the mind—that is, the concentration of consciousness—upon the Brahman that underlies it is declared by this Brāhmaṇa passage: "The *Gāyatrī* indeed is all this.
For it is not possible for the mere arrangement of syllables that constitutes the *Gāyatrī* to possess the nature of being the self of all.

Therefore, that which is indicated here as the cause of the world—the Brahman underlying the modification known as *Gāyatrī*—is what is called "all this," just as in the statement: "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
Furthermore, we shall explain in the section "Non-difference from that, on account of the words concerning origin and so forth" (*Brahmasūtra* 2.1.14) that the effect is not distinct from its cause.

Likewise, elsewhere too, meditation upon Brahman through the medium of its modifications is observed: "For the Bahvṛcas meditate upon this very one in the Great Hymn (*uktha*), the Adhvaryus in the fire-altar (*agni*), and the Chandogas in the Mahāvrata.
Therefore, even though the meters are mentioned, Brahman with four feet is indeed indicated in the preceding passage.
That very same [Brahman] is referred to in the *jyotiḥ* passage as well, for the purpose of enjoining another form of meditation (according to the Sūtra-bhāṣya).
Another teacher says:
Brahman is directly denoted by the word *gāyatrī*, on account of the commonality of number.

Just as the Gāyatrī has four feet with six syllables each, so too Brahman is four-footed. Furthermore, elsewhere a word denoting a meter is seen to be applied to another object due to a similarity in number; for example, having begun with "These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the Kṛta," the text says, "This is that Virāj, the endless."
In this view, since it is Brahman itself that is denoted, there is no designation of a *chandas* (meter).
In any case, Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding sentence.
And because the designation of the stages beginning with "sustenance" (bhṛti) is thus appropriate.
For this reason also, it must be accepted that Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding passage;
because the Śruti designates the elements and so forth as its feet.
For, having pointed out the beings, the earth, the body, and the heart, it says: "This is that Gāyatrī, which has four feet and is sixfold."
For if Brahman were not the basis, it would not be possible for the elements and so forth to constitute the "feet" of mere Vedic meter (*chandas*).
Moreover, if Brahman were not the basis, this *ṛc*—"Such is His greatness"—would not be applicable.

For by its own natural sense, this *ṛc* denotes Brahman, since the quality of being the self of all is established in the words: "One foot of Him are all beings; three feet of Him are the immortal in heaven."
This very verse is also recited in the *Puruṣasūkta* as having Brahman as its ultimate subject;
and Smṛti likewise demonstrates that Brahman possesses such a nature, stating: "I pervade this entire universe, standing with but a single fraction [of Myself]. (Gītā 10.42)
Furthermore, there is the designation, "That which is indeed that Brahman.
This being so, the primary meaning [of the term] is justified.

Moreover, the scriptural mention of "these five persons of Brahman" (*brahmapuruṣa*) in reference to the apertures of the heart is possible only if the intended sense is their connection with Brahman.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding passage;
that very same Brahman is referred to in the *jyotis* passage as being recognized through its connection with the word "that" (*tat*).
If it be argued that this is not so because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case.
As for this which was stated regarding the *apūrva*: in the passage "Its three quarters are the immortal in heaven," the sky (*dyauḥ*) is taught as a substratum by means of the locative case;
whereas here, in the passage "Now, that which is beyond the sky," it is taught as a limit by means of the ablative case.
Therefore, because of this difference in instruction, there is no recognition of that [same thing] here; thus, that objection must be refuted.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because there is no contradiction in either case.
In both types of instruction—whether ending in the locative case or the ablative case—recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not contradicted.

Just as in common experience a hawk, though connected with the top of a tree, is seen to be designated in two ways—as "the hawk on the treetop" and "the hawk beyond the treetop"—so too Brahman, which is truly in heaven, is designated as "beyond heaven."

Another says: Just as in the world a hawk, even though not actually connected with the top of a tree, is seen to be designated in two ways—as "the hawk on the top of the tree" and "the hawk beyond the top of the tree"—so too, although the existent Brahman is beyond heaven, it is taught as being "in heaven.
Therefore, there is a recognition here of the Brahman previously mentioned.
Thus, it is established that the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the word "light."
Likewise, the vital breath [is Brahman], because of its accompanying presence.

In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, there is the narrative of Indra and Pratardana, beginning with the words: "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra by means of his battle and manliness," and so forth. In that [text], it is heard: "He said: 'I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self (prajñātmā). Worship me as life and immortality. This constitutes the topic under discussion. In that [text], it is heard: "He said: 'I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self. Worship me as life and immortality.'"
Likewise, later on it is said: "Now, indeed, it is *prāṇa* alone, as the conscious self (*prajñātman*), which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to stand up.
Similarly: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker. And at the end: "This very *prāṇa* is the conscious self, blissful, undecaying, and immortal," and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: what is denoted here by the word "prāṇa"—is it mere air, or the self of a deity, or the individual soul (jīva), or the supreme Brahman?
But was it not already explained under the sūtra "For this very reason, prāṇa" that the word prāṇa has Brahman as its referent;
and here too, there are marks of Brahman, such as "blissful, undecaying, immortal," and so forth?
How, then, can doubt arise here? We reply: because of the observation of multiple characteristics (*liṅga*).
For not only the characteristic of Brahman is perceived here; there are indeed characteristics of other [entities] as well, such as: "Know me alone" (1.4.10).
"'Bring rice!'—this is a characteristic mark of Indra as the deity.

"'Having taken hold of this body, he causes it to rise'—this is a characteristic mark of the vital breath (prāṇa). "'One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker,' and so forth—this is a characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva)."
Therefore, a doubt has arisen.
Since it is well known that "prāṇa" refers to air, this being the prima facie view, it is stated here that the word *prāṇa* must be understood as Brahman.
Why? Because of the consistency [of the context] (*tathānugamāt*).
For, when the sentence is examined from beginning to end, the syntactical connection of its words is found to be intent upon the exposition of Brahman.

To begin with, at the outset, when Indra said to Pratardana, "Choose a boon," Pratardana proposed the boon that is the supreme human goal: "You yourself choose for me that boon which you consider most beneficial for a human being.
How could the *prāṇa* (vital breath), which is thus taught to him as the most beneficial, not be the Supreme Self?

For there is no attainment of the highest good other than through the knowledge of the Supreme Self, according to such scriptural passages as: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. Likewise, [the passage] beginning with, "He who knows Me—his world is not destroyed by any deed, neither by theft nor by the killing of an embryo," is consistent only with the acceptance of Brahman. Indeed, the destruction of all karma through the knowledge of Brahman is well-established in such scriptural texts as: "And his karmas are extinguished when He, the higher and the lower, is seen."
Furthermore, the state of being the self of intelligence (*prajñātmatva*) is possible only in the case of Brahman;
for it is not possible for air, which is insentient, to be the self of intelligence.
Likewise, in the concluding passage as well, qualities such as bliss, being undecaying, and being immortal—as in "bliss, undecaying, immortal"—do not properly apply to anything other than Brahman.
"He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action; for he alone causes him to perform good action whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds.
And he alone causes him to perform evil action whom he wishes to lead down from these worlds"—and "He is the lord of the world, He is the protector of the world, He is the ruler of the world.
All this can be consistently understood if the Supreme Brahman is accepted, but not if the vital breath (prāṇa) is taken in its primary sense.
Therefore, the vital breath is Brahman.

If it be argued that [the Self taught here] is not the Supreme Self because of the instruction regarding the speaker's own self, we say no; for in this passage there is an abundance of references to the connection with the Inner Self.
What was stated—that "breath is Brahman"—is now challenged: the word "breath" does not refer to the Supreme Brahman.
Why? Because there is an instruction regarding the Self of the speaker.

For the speaker, a certain specific embodied deity named Indra, taught his own Self to Pratardana, beginning with "Know me alone," and proceeding with the expression of egoity, "I am breath, the conscious self."

How could that very vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is taught as being the self of the speaker, be Brahman? For the quality of being a speaker is not possible for Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as "without speech, without mind" (*avāk anas*). Likewise, Indra praised himself by means of attributes connected with a physical body—which are impossible in the case of Brahman—through such statements as: "I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ; I delivered the Arunmukhas and the Atis to the jackals. [End of First Chapter] *Prāṇa-sandarbha* [First Adhyāya] (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly, so the translation reflects the partial nature of the source.)
And it is appropriate that you [are the breath] because of Indra's possession of strength;
for it is known from scripture that "breath indeed is strength," and Indra is well known as the deity of strength.
Whatever nature of wooliness there may be, they say that it is indeed the work of Indra.
Furthermore, the state of being the self of wisdom is possible for the divine self because its knowledge is unimpeded;
for they say that the deity possesses unimpeded knowledge.
And since the teaching regarding the Self of the deity is thus determined, statements such as "being most beneficial" and so forth must be applied to that very subject (the deity) as far as possible.

Therefore, having raised the objection that Prāṇa is not Brahman because of the instruction concerning the Self of the speaker Indra, it is answered: "For there is an abundance of connection with the inner Self in this [chapter].
"Connection with the inner Self" means connection with the individual self (*pratyagātman*); "its abundance" means its prevalence, which is perceived in this chapter.

The statement, "As long as the vital breath (prāṇa) dwells in this body, so long is there life," shows that the power to bestow and withdraw life belongs solely to the vital breath, which is the inner self (pratyagātman) and the conscious self (prajñātman), and not to any external deity.
Likewise, the statement, "In the existence of the vital breaths lies the highest good," shows that the vital breath is the support of the senses within the body itself.
Similarly, it says, "The vital breath alone, being the conscious self, having grasped this body, causes it to rise."

Having begun with, "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," and then saying, "Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed on the spokes and the spokes are fixed on the nave, even so these elements of being (bhūtamātrā) are fixed on the elements of cognition (prajñāmātrā), and the elements of cognition are fixed on the vital breath (prāṇa); this very vital breath is the self of cognition (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal," [the text] concludes by identifying the inner Self (pratyagātman) alone as the axle and hub of the activity of the objects and senses. Furthermore, the concluding statement, "One should know that as my Self," is appropriate if the inner Self is accepted, but not if something external (parācīna) is accepted.
And there is another scriptural passage: "This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all.
Therefore, because of the abundance of references to the inner self (adhyātma), this is indeed an instruction on Brahman, not an instruction on the self of a deity.
How then is there an instruction regarding the Self by the speaker? [The answer is: "But the instruction is according to the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva."

The deity named Indra, perceiving his own self as the Supreme Self through the vision of the seers—according to the scriptures—in the form "I am indeed the Supreme Brahman," taught: "Know me alone. This is just as the seer Vāmadeva, seeing that very reality, realized: "I was Manu and I was the Sun"; for the Śruti declares: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became that."

As for what was further stated—that after saying "Know me alone," Indra praised his own self with the attributes of his physical body, such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son and so forth—that must be refuted.

To this it is replied: first of all, the mention of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son and the other deeds is not introduced for the purpose of praising Indra as the object to be known, in the sense that "Since I am one who has performed such deeds, therefore know me.
How then? It is for the purpose of praising the knowledge [of him].

For this reason, after citing violent acts such as those against the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the text connects them with a praise of knowledge through such passages as: "Not even a single hair of mine was harmed therein; and for one who knows me, his world is not harmed by any action whatsoever. What is meant by this is: since not even a hair of mine—who have become Brahman—is harmed despite having performed such cruel deeds, so too for anyone else who knows me, their world is not harmed by any action at all.
But that which is to be known is Brahman itself, as will be stated in the passage, "I am the breath, the conscious self. Therefore, this is a statement concerning Brahman.

If it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] because of the indicative marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; because of the threefoldness of meditation, and because that [threefoldness] is possible here due to its being based on [Brahman].

Even though, due to the observation of an abundance of internal connections, this is not an instruction concerning the outward-facing self of the deity, nevertheless, it cannot be a statement about Brahman.
Why? Because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the marks of the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa).
First, a clear mark of the individual soul is found in this passage: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," and so forth.

For here, the status of being the object of knowledge is predicated of the individual soul (jīva), who is the presiding overseer of the body and the organs, as he is active through the instruments such as speech and the rest.

Likewise, there is also a characteristic mark of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa): "Now, indeed, it is the prāṇa itself, the conscious self, which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise.
And the sustaining of the body is a property of the chief vital breath.

In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), after introducing the vital breaths beginning with speech, it is heard [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]: "The chief vital breath said to them: 'Do not fall into delusion; I alone, having divided myself fivefold and entered this body (*bāṇa*), support and maintain it.

For those, however, who read "having taken hold of this body" (*imaṃ śarīraṃ parigṛhya*), the passage must be explained as meaning that [the chief vital breath] supports the body by taking hold of this living self (*jīva*) or the aggregate of the senses.
Furthermore, the state of being the conscious self (*prajñātmatva*) is appropriate for the living self (*jīva*) because of its nature as consciousness.

Even in the case of the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the designation of it as "intelligence"] is indeed appropriate because it depends upon other vital breaths that are the instruments of intelligence.

Thus, when both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the principal vital breath are accepted, the designation of non-difference through their coexistence, as well as the designation of difference by way of their distinct natures, are both justified. This is shown in such passages as: "That which is the vital breath is intelligence; that which is intelligence is the vital breath," and "For these two dwell together in this body and depart together."

But if it were the Brahman that was being grasped, how and why would there be any difference? Therefore, if it be argued that here either the individual soul (jīva) or the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), or both, are intended and not Brahman, this is not so; because of the threefold nature of the meditation.
For if that were the case, a threefold meditation would result—namely, meditation on the individual soul, meditation on the chief vital breath, and meditation on Brahman.
Nor is it proper to accept this [interpretation] within a single sentence;
for the unity of a passage is understood through its opening and its conclusion.

Having begun with "Know me alone," and having stated, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self; meditate upon me as life and immortality," one observes at the end that the opening and the conclusion are of a single form: "This very Prāṇa is the conscious self, bliss, undecaying, and immortal."
In that case, it is appropriate to assume a unity of meaning.

Furthermore, the characteristic marks of Brahman cannot be interpreted as referring to something else, because [the text speaks] of the ten elemental constituents (*bhūtamātrā*). Chapter One. First Section. First Sūtra.
Furthermore, since it is impossible to enjoin the portions of wisdom apart from Brahman,

and because even in other passages the word "prāṇa" is applied to Brahman due to the presence of Brahmanic characteristics (liṅga), and because here too there is a connection with Brahmanic characteristics such as the presentation of what is most beneficial, it is understood that this is indeed an instruction on Brahman. As for the characteristic of the principal vital air (mukhya-prāṇa) that was shown— namely, "having taken hold of this body, he causes it to rise"— that is incorrect.

Since even the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) is dependent upon the Supreme Self, it can be figuratively attributed to the Supreme Self, as the Śruti declares: "No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna);

rather, they live by something else upon which these two depend. Furthermore, as for the indication of the individual soul (jīva) shown in such passages as, "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," that too does not preclude the position that [the object of knowledge] is Brahman.
For the individual soul (*jīva*) is not absolutely different from Brahman, according to such scriptural texts as "That thou art" and "I am Brahman.

However, by relying on the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*), that which is Brahman itself is called the "individual soul," the agent, and the enjoyer.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in the teaching—beginning with "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker"—which aims at turning one toward the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in order to show its true nature as Brahman by abandoning those distinctions created by limiting adjuncts.

Furthermore, another scriptural passage— “That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed, know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here”— and others like it, show that the Self, even while engaged in activities such as speaking, is indeed Brahman. As for the objection raised— that the perception of a distinction between the vital breath (prāṇa) and the conscious self (prajñātman), as stated in the passage “For these two dwell together in this body and together they depart,” is untenable for one who maintains the doctrine of Brahman— that is no fault.

Since the distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and are the respective substrates of the two powers of knowledge and action, is logically established;

yet the inner self, when conditioned by these two adjuncts, remains non-different in its essential nature—therefore, their identification in the statement "The vital breath itself is the conscious self" is not contradictory.

Or rather, there is this other meaning of the sūtra: "Or else, because of the threefoldness of meditation, and because [the characteristics] are dependent [on Brahman], and because they are connected with it here" (BS 1.1.31): even in a passage concerning Brahman, the indicative marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital air (*mukhyaprāṇa*) are not contradictory.
How so? Because of the threefoldness of meditation.

Here, a threefold meditation on Brahman is intended: by means of the attributes of the vital air, by means of the attributes of intelligence (*prajñā*), and by means of its own [Brahman’s] attributes.

In that context, the attributes of *prāṇa* are stated: "Worship *āyus* as the immortal," "Life-breath (*prāṇa*) is *āyus*," "Having taken hold of this body, it makes it rise up," and "Therefore, one should worship this very thing as the *uktha*.

Then, having begun with, "Now we shall explain how all beings become one in this consciousness (*prajñā*)," the text continues: "Speech alone is one limb of this [consciousness] which it did not fail; beyond it, the objective element (*bhūtamātrā*) is disposed accordingly. Having mounted speech by means of consciousness, one obtains all names through speech," and so forth; these are the attributes of *prajñā*.

Now, these ten elements of being (bhūtamātrā) correspond to wisdom (prajñā), and the ten elements of wisdom (prajñāmātrā) correspond to being. If there were no elements of being, there would be no elements of wisdom; if there were no elements of wisdom, there would be no elements of being.
For form would not be established from either one alone;
it is not that they are separate.
Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes, and the spokes are fixed upon the hub—this is the first chapter.

"Father, even so these elements of being (bhūtamātrā) are deposited in the elements of intelligence (prajñāmātrā), and the elements of intelligence are deposited in breath; this very breath is the intelligent self (prajñātman)"—such is the attribute of Brahman.
Therefore, this single meditation on Brahman itself is intended to be threefold, by means of its two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and its own inherent nature.
Elsewhere as well, in passages such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body," meditation on Brahman through the attributes of its limiting adjuncts is accepted.

In this case as well, that [interpretation] is appropriate, because the unity of meaning is understood from the opening and the conclusion of the passage, and because the marks of Brahman—namely, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the conscious self (*prajñātman*), and Brahman itself—are perceived.
Therefore, it is established that this is indeed a statement concerning Brahman.

Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa-Parivrājaka-Ācārya). Composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.
First Chapter, Second Quarter. Om. Second Quarter.

In the first quarter [of the *Brahma-sūtras*], it was stated in the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this" that Brahman is the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world, including space and the rest.
Of that Brahman, who is the cause of the entire world, attributes such as omnipresence, eternity, omniscience, omnipotence, and being the self of all have indeed been stated.

Furthermore, by demonstrating the reasons for certain words well-known in other senses to refer to Brahman, several passages containing ambiguous marks of Brahman were determined to have Brahman as their subject.

Furthermore, other passages containing indistinct marks of Brahman are subject to doubt as to whether they set forth the supreme Brahman or some other entity. To resolve this, the second and third sections (pādas) are commenced with the following: "On account of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere."

The following is taught [in scripture]: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, as it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; one should meditate upon It with a calm mind. Now, man is indeed composed of his resolve (*ṛtu*);

as is his resolve in this world, so does he become after departing from here. Therefore, let him form a resolve: 'Consisting of mind, having breath for its body,' and so forth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1–4).

Here, a doubt arises: is the embodied self (*śārīra ātman*) taught as the object of meditation by means of attributes such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), or rather the supreme Brahman? What, then, is the initial position? That it is the embodied self.
Why? Because its connection with the mind and other faculties is well known for that [self] which is the lord of the body and the organs, but not for the supreme Brahman.

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "For he is without breath, without mind, pure. But an objection is raised: since Brahman has already been presented by its own name in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," how can the embodied self (śārīra ātman) be suspected here as the object of meditation? This is not a fault.
This statement does not have as its primary purpose the injunction for the meditation on Brahman;

what then? It has as its primary purpose the injunction for tranquility (śama), because it says: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and by which it breathes; one should meditate [on it] being tranquil."

This is what is meant: since all this collection of modifications is Brahman alone—because it is born from that, dissolved into that, and breathes in that—passions and the like are not possible when there is the single self-nature of everything; therefore, "one should meditate as tranquil.
Furthermore, if the sentence were intent on enjoining tranquility (*śama*), it would not be possible to enjoin meditation on Brahman by means of this very statement.
Rather, meditation is enjoined by the passage, "He should form a resolve" (*sa ṛtuṃ kurvīta*).
The term "meditation" (dhyāna) here means the mental resolve regarding the seasons.
And as its object, there is heard the characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva): "consisting of mind, having breath for its body.
Therefore, we say that this meditation has the individual soul as its object.

Even such scriptural passages as "He becomes a person possessing a self, having all odors, and having all tastes; he attains sovereignty over all ceremonies, and all desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2) are appropriately understood as referring to the individual soul (jīva) in its various successive states. Furthermore, the qualities of having the heart as its abode and being minute in size—as in "This is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice or a grain of barley"—are possible only for the individual soul, which is as small as the tip of an awl, and not for the unlimited Brahman.
But surely, even such passages as "greater than the earth" and so forth cannot be applicable to that which is limited.

To this we reply: first of all, both minuteness and greatness cannot be attributed to a single thing because of their mutual contradiction; and if one must be accepted, then, because it is mentioned first in the text, it is proper to accept minuteness.
The superiority [of the soul] will, however, be in relation to the state of Brahman.

And since it has been determined that the subject matter is the individual soul (jīva), the mention of Brahman at the end—"This is Brahman"—is also solely concerned with the individual soul, as its purpose is to refer back to what has been introduced.

Therefore, when it is thus argued that the individual soul is the object of meditation by virtue of attributes such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya), we reply: it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is to be meditated upon here by means of attributes such as "consisting of mind."
Why? Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere.

That which is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the referent of the word "Brahman"—the cause of the world—and which is heard here at the beginning of the passage in the words "All this, indeed, is Brahman," is appropriately taught as qualified by the attributes of consisting of mind and so forth.
This being the case, there will be neither the abandonment of the subject under discussion nor the introduction of something not under discussion.
But was it not stated that at the beginning of the passage, Brahman was mentioned with the intention of enjoining tranquility (*śama*), and not with its own intended meaning?

To this it is replied: although Brahman was indeed mentioned with the intention of enjoining tranquility, nevertheless, when "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and other qualities are being taught, that same Brahman remains proximate; the individual soul (*jīva*), however, is neither proximate nor is it denoted by its own specific term—this constitutes the difference.
And because the intended qualities are appropriate [in that case].
"Those [words] intended to be spoken are *vivakṣitāḥ*.

Although in the case of the impersonal Veda, because there is no speaker, the sense of "intention" (*icchārtha*) is not possible, nevertheless it is figuratively attributed by means of its result, which is the act of inclusion (*upādāna*).
Even in common worldly usage, that which is expressed by words and is to be accepted is said to be "intended," while that which is not to be accepted is said to be "not intended."
Similarly, in the Veda as well, that which is stated as something to be adopted is intended (*vivakṣita*), while the other is unintended (*avivakṣita*).
Adoption and non-adoption, moreover, are understood from the intention (*tātparya*) or lack of intention of the Vedic statement.

Thus, in this context, those qualities intended for meditation—taught as things to be adopted such as "having true resolve" (*satya-saṃkalpa*) and so forth—are appropriate in the case of the Supreme Brahman.
For the quality of having true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatva) is possible only for the Supreme Self, because its power is unimpeded in the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

And as a quality of the Supreme Self, it is heard in the passage, "The Self which is free from evil," where it says, "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true," and also "whose self is space" (ākāśātmā).
The meaning of "ākāśātmā" is that his self is like space.
Brahman shares a similarity with space through attributes such as all-pervasiveness;
this very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "greater than the earth.
Furthermore, even if it is explained that "space is its self," that too is possible, since Brahman—the cause of the entire universe and the self of all—has space as its self.
For this very reason, [the text says] "possessing all actions" (*sarvakarmā*) and so forth.
Thus, in the first chapter of the Sūtra,
the qualities intended here as objects of meditation are applicable to Brahman.
As for what was stated— that the marks of the individual soul (jīva), such as "consisting of mind" and "having vital breath as its body," are not applicable to Brahman—
we reply that even those are applicable to Brahman.
For, because Brahman is the Self of all, qualities related to the individual soul, such as consisting of mind and so forth, become related to Brahman as well.
And thus there are Śruti and Smṛti passages concerning Brahman: "Thou art the male, thou art the youth, or even the maiden;
thou, as an old man, totterest along with a staff; thou art born, facing every direction";
and "That [Brahman] has hands and feet everywhere, it has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides."
And [the scripture says]: "Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands encompassing all.

Furthermore, the scriptural text "For it is without breath, without mind, pure" has as its object the pure Brahman; however, this [other] scriptural text, "Consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body," has as its object the qualified Brahman—this is the distinction.
Therefore, because the intended qualities are logically consistent, it is concluded that the Supreme Brahman alone is taught here as the object of meditation.
You are a woman; because you are not subject to rebirth, you are not the embodied self.
By the preceding sūtra, the appropriateness of the qualities intended for Brahman was stated;
by this [sūtra], their inappropriateness in the embodied soul (śārīra) is stated.
The word "tu" (but/however) serves the purpose of emphasis.
By the reasoning already stated, [the Self] possesses qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*);
however, the embodied individual soul (*jīva*) does not possess these qualities.

For this reason, qualities of such a kind as "one whose resolve is true" (*satyasaṃkalpa*), "whose self is space" (*ākāśātmā*), "without speech" (*avākī*), "without regard" (*anādara*), and "greater than the earth" (*jyāyān pṛthivyāḥ*)—as found in the Sūtra-Bhāṣya—are not compatible with the embodied soul in their literal sense.
The term "embodied" (śārīra) means that which exists within the body.
Now, one might object: does not the Lord also exist within the body?
True, He does exist within the body.
But [the Self] does not exist only in the body,
because its all-pervasiveness is heard in such scriptural passages as, "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space," and "All-pervading and eternal like space.
The individual soul (jīva), however, exists only in the body, because it has no functioning outside the body, which is the locus of its experience.
And because of the designation of the action and the agent.
For this reason as well, the embodied soul is not the possessor of qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya);
because there is a designation of object and agent: "Having departed from here, I shall attain him.
By the word "him" (etam), the text designates the Self under discussion—possessing qualities such as consisting of mind—as the object, that is, as the goal to be attained.
"I shall attain" refers to the embodied one (the disciple) as the agent and the attainer.
"I shall attain" means "I shall reach.
Furthermore, when a distinct destination exists, it is not logical to designate a single entity as both the object and the agent.
Likewise, the relationship between the object of worship and the worshiper is also based solely on difference;
therefore, for this reason as well, the embodied soul is not the one characterized by "consisting of mind" and so forth.
Because of the distinction in the sound.

For this reason as well, the one characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (manomaya) is other than the embodied soul; for in another scriptural passage within the same context, there is a supplementary statement: "Just as rice, or barley, or millet, or the grain of millet—so is this person within the heart golden. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6)
The word denoting the embodied self (śārīra-ātman) is the locative form "antarātmann";

therefore, the distinct word "puruṣa" ending in the nominative case, qualified by attributes such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya), is the designator of the Self as characterized by those qualities.
Therefore, the distinction between those two is understood.
And because of the Smṛti.

Furthermore, Smṛti shows the distinction between the embodied self (śārīra) and the supreme Self (paramātman) in such passages as: "The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine.

Here, one asks: who is this so-called embodied self, distinct from the supreme Self, who is denied [as the creator] in passages such as "But because of impossibility, it is not the embodied self"? For Śruti, in passages of this kind—"There is no other seer than He; there is no other hearer than Him"—precludes any self other than the supreme Self.
Likewise, Smṛti also contains such passages as: "And know Me, O Bhārata, as the Knower of the Field in all fields."

To this it is replied: This is indeed true. The Supreme Self alone, when delimited by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is metaphorically designated as the "embodied one" (*śārīra*) by the ignorant.
Just as space, though unlimited, appears to be limited due to the influence of limiting adjuncts such as jars or water-pots, so it is here.

And with respect to that [delimited state], the conventional usage of distinctions such as "action" and "agent" is not contradicted, prior to the realization of the oneness of the Self through the instruction "That thou art. This is because [the distinction] persists until the grasp of the unity of the Self is attained through the study of the scriptures. [Notes on locations: Kaṅkatiśi-saṃsthāna Sāranātha, Vārāṇasī; *Sūtra-bhāṣya*.
But once the oneness of the Self is grasped, there would indeed be a complete cessation of all worldly transactions such as bondage and liberation.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of meditation] because of its having a small abode and because of its being designated as such, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, just like space.

It has been argued that because the "dwelling" (*oka*)—meaning the small nest or abode—is defined as "this is my Self within the heart," and because the Self is designated by its own term as being "smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley," it is the embodied soul (*jīva*), limited in size like the point of an awl, that is taught here, and not the omnipresent Supreme Self (*paramātman*); this must now be refuted.
To this we reply: this is not a fault.
For first of all, the designation of omnipresence for that which occupies a limited space is in no way tenable.
However, because that which is omnipresent exists in all places, even the designation of it as being in a limited space is possible from a certain point of view;

for example, although one is the lord of the entire earth, one may nevertheless be designated as the "lord of Ayodhyā. But by what point of view is the Lord, though omnipresent, designated as having a small abode and as being minute?
We say that it is because He is to be perceived in this way:
thus, the Lord, endowed with a multitude of qualities such as subtlety and so forth, is taught there in the lotus of the heart as one to be perceived— that is, to be seen—
just as Hari is [perceived] in the Śālagrāma stone.
In that regard, his cognitive consciousness (*buddhi-vijñāna*) is the grasper;
even though the Lord (*īśvara*) is omnipresent, he becomes gracious when worshipped therein.
And this should be viewed as being like space.
Just as the all-pervading ether is designated as "smaller than the eye of a needle" and so forth in relation to such things, so too is Brahman. Thus,
having discerned this, the smallness of abode and the minuteness of Brahman are relative to that [comparison], not ultimate.

In this regard, the objection that—because Brahman has the heart as its abode and because hearts differ in every body—the Brahman would likewise be subject to defects such as multiplicity, having parts, and non-eternality (just as we observe in the case of Śuka and others who have different abodes)—is also thereby refuted.
If it be argued that this refers to the attainment of the state of enjoyment, we say no, because of the difference in nature.

If it be argued that, because Brahman is all-pervading like space and is connected to the hearts of all living beings, and because it is not distinct from the embodied soul in its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpa*), the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth would necessarily follow as being non-distinct [from Brahman];
and because of their oneness, there is indeed no transmigrating soul other than the supreme Self, according to such scriptural texts as "There is no other knower but He" (*nānyo'to'sti vijñātā*);
therefore, the experience of enjoyment would accrue to the supreme Brahman itself—if this is said, we reply: No.
On account of the difference in nature.

First of all, the consequence of Brahman experiencing enjoyment—simply because it is connected to the hearts of all living beings and because its nature is consciousness—does not apply to Brahman as it does to the embodied soul, because of this difference in nature.
For there exists a distinction between the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord.
One is the agent and enjoyer, possessing the means of dharma and adharma as well as pleasure, pain, and so forth;
the other is the opposite of that, characterized by qualities such as being free from sin.
Because of this distinction between these two, there is experience for one, but not for the other.

Furthermore, if the connection with an effect were admitted to exist by mere proximity, without depending on the inherent power of the thing itself, then it would follow that even space and other such entities could undergo burning and so forth. These same objections and their refutations apply equally to those who maintain that the Self is all-pervading and manifold.

As for the argument that because Brahman is one and there is no other Self, the experience of the embodied soul (the *jīva*) entails the experience of Brahman—we reply: first, this "beloved of the gods" must be asked how he has determined that there is no other Self.

If you argue that this is known from such scriptural texts as "That thou art," "I am Brahman," and "There is no other knower than this," then the scriptural meaning must be understood exactly as the scripture teaches; one cannot adopt a "half-old-woman" approach (accepting part while rejecting another) regarding it. Furthermore, the scripture—in the passage "That thou art"—teaches that Brahman, characterized by attributes such as being free from sin, is the Self of the embodied soul. This very teaching precludes the status of being an experiencer for the embodied soul itself. How, then, could there be the contingency of Brahman experiencing through the experience of that [soul]?
Now, if the identity of the embodied soul with Brahman is not grasped, then the experience of the embodied soul is caused by false knowledge;
it does not, however, affect Brahman, whose nature is the ultimate reality.

For when the sky is conceptualized by the ignorant as having a surface or being soiled and the like, the sky does not, in ultimate reality, become characterized by that surface, dirtiness, or anything else.
To this he replies: "No, on account of the difference" (vaiśeṣyāt).
Even though there is non-difference, it does not follow that Brahman must experience the enjoyment [of pleasure and pain] through the body's enjoyment, because of the difference.
For there is indeed a distinction between false knowledge and right knowledge.
Experience is constructed by false knowledge, whereas oneness is seen through right knowledge.
Furthermore, the reality perceived through right knowledge is not touched by experience constructed by false knowledge.
Therefore, not even a trace of experience can be attributed to the Lord.

"The Self [is meant], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving. (Sūtra 1.2.12) In the *Kaṭhavallī* Upaniṣad, the following is recited as a *pratīka*: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who indeed knows where He is? (KaṭhU 1.2.25).
In this passage, no eater is explicitly indicated by the mention of boiled rice and its condiment; rather, the instrument [of eating] is mentioned.

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether fire is the eater, or the individual soul (jīva), or perhaps the supreme self (paramātman), because there is no specific determination among these three—fire, the individual soul, and the supreme self—as they are all found mentioned in questions and statements within this text.
What, then, is the initial position? That fire is the eater.
Why? Because of both scriptural authority and common renown, as in "Fire is the eater of food.
Or rather, the individual soul (jīva) might be the eater, because of the observation [in scripture]: "One of them eats the sweet fruit."
It is not the Supreme Self, because of the scriptural vision that "the other, not eating, looks on. This being the position reached, we reply: the eater here must be the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving.
For here, the moving and the unmoving—the stationary and the mobile—is understood as food, with death serving as the condiment.
And for such a primordial being, no one other than the Supreme Self can possibly be the devourer in its entirety.
However, it is logical that the Supreme Self, while withdrawing the entire collection of modifications, devours everything.
[Objection: But here, the mention of "the moving and the unmoving" is not perceived.

How can the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving (the entire world) be taken as a reason [for the conclusion] as if it were already established? This is not a fault, because here the entire multitude of living beings is understood to have food as their nourishment (*adyatva*) with death as their condiment (*mṛtyūpasecana*); furthermore, since Brahmins and Kṣatriyas are the most prominent, it is appropriate for them to be cited as representative examples.

As for the objection that even the Supreme Self cannot be an eater, because the Sūtra-bhāṣya states in the [third] chapter that "the other, not eating, looks on," we reply: this scriptural observation is a prohibition against the enjoyment of the fruits of karma, because such enjoyment is what is immediately relevant in that context.
This does not prohibit the withdrawal of modifications, because Brahman is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the cause of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
Therefore, the Supreme Self alone must be the "eater" (attā) here.
And because of the context.
For this reason as well, the Supreme Self alone must be the "Eater" here;
because this context belongs to the Supreme Self, beginning with the passage, "The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and it is logical to accept that which is under discussion.
And the statement, "Who indeed knows where he is? indicates that being difficult to discern is a characteristic mark of the Supreme Self.
For they have entered the cave, because of the perception of that [Self].

In the Kaṭhavallīs themselves it is recited: "The two who drink the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest upper realm—the knowers of Brahman call them shadow and light; so too those who have entered the cave, the five who maintain the sacred fires, and those who have kindled the three fire-sticks. This is the section [of the commentary].
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) indicated here, or rather the individual soul and the supreme self (*paramātman*)?
If it were the intellect and the individual soul, then the individual soul would be established as distinct from the aggregate of causes and effects (the body) in which the intellect predominates;
and that [distinction] is indeed what must be established here [in the verse]: "Regarding this man who has died, there is a doubt: some say 'he exists,' and others say 'he does not exist.'"

"Teach me this knowledge"— since [Naciketas] was thus asked, "This is the third of the boons granted by you," it follows that the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) are distinguished; consequently, the Supreme Self, who is distinct from the individual soul, is established as the subject of instruction.

That too must be established here, because [the Lord] was asked: "Apart from dharma, apart from adharma, apart from this [world of] what has been done and what has not been done, apart from what has been and what is to be—that which you see, tell me that.
To this, the objector says: neither of these two positions is possible.
Why? Because "drinking the *ṛta*" is indeed the enjoyment of the fruits of action, as indicated by the scriptural mark "in the world of good deeds.
And that is possible for the conscious Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), not for the insentient intellect (*buddhi*).
By means of the dual number in the word "the two drinking," the Śruti shows that the drinking belongs to two.
Therefore, the position that [the two] are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is not possible.
For this very reason, the position that they are the knower of the field and the supreme self (*paramātman*) is also not possible;
because even in the case of the conscious supreme self, the drinking of the *ṛta* is impossible, as stated in the mantra-text: "The other, not eating, looks on."

To this it is replied: this is not a fault; for we observe that even when "those with umbrellas are going," the term "umbrella-bearer" is applied metaphorically to many who do not possess umbrellas because of the presence of even a single person with an umbrella.
In the same way, even when only one is drinking, two may be called "the drinkers."
Alternatively, the individual soul (jīva) drinks,
while the Lord (īśvara) causes it to drink;
yet even while causing [another] to drink, He is said to "drink," since we observe that the status of being a "cook" is commonly attributed even to one who causes another to cook.
Furthermore, it is possible that the term refers to the apprehension of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*);
for we observe the usage of agency attributed to an instrument in such expressions as "the fuel cooks.
Moreover, within the context of the internal self (*adhyātma*), no other two beings are possible who could be described as "drinking the [subtle] essence."
Therefore, there arises the doubt: are these two the intellect and the individual soul, or rather the individual soul and the supreme self?
According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), what is initially established? That they are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Why? Because of the qualification "having entered the cave" (*guhāṃ praviṣṭau*).
Whether the "cave" refers to the body or to the heart, in either case it is logical that the intellect and the knower of the field have entered the cave.
Furthermore, when it is possible [to interpret it otherwise], it is not reasonable to assume that the all-pervading Brahman has a specific location.
Moreover, the phrase "in the world of good deeds" shows that it does not transcend the sphere of karma.
The Supreme Self, however, does not abide within the sphere of either good or evil deeds, according to the scriptural text: "He increases not by action, nor does He become less."
Furthermore, the designation "shadow and light" is appropriate as a reference to the conscious and the unconscious, because they are mutually distinct like shadow and light.

Therefore, when it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) must be meant here, we reply: the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) are what are meant here.
Why? Because both of them are conscious and share the same essential nature.
Furthermore, when a number is heard, it is observed in common worldly usage that the cognition applies only to things of a similar nature.
When it is said, "A second for this cow must be sought," it is a second cow that is sought, not a horse or a human being.
Thus, here, since the individual soul has been determined by the mark of drinking the *ṛta*, when a second is sought, only the Supreme Self, which is of a similar conscious nature, is understood.
Now, was it not said that because the Self is seen to be hidden in the cave, the Supreme Self (paramātman) should not be understood [there]?
To this we reply: it is precisely because of the observation of its being hidden in the cave that the Supreme Self should be understood.
For the state of being hidden in the cave belongs to the Supreme Self alone, as is repeatedly stated in the Śruti and Smṛti. Thus ends the first chapter.

In such passages as "It is seen hidden in the cave, dwelling in the depths, the ancient one," "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven," and "Seek the Self that has entered the cave," the teaching of a specific location for the purpose of perceiving Brahman—even though Brahman is omnipresent—is not contradictory; this has already been stated. Furthermore, the fact that [the soul] resides in the world of meritorious deeds is not incompatible with both [Brahman and the soul], just as the term "possessor of an umbrella" applies to a single person who is accompanied by someone holding an umbrella.
The expression "shadow and light" is also not contradictory;
for transmigratoriness and non-transmigratoriness are mutually distinct like shadow and light, since transmigratoriness is produced by ignorance while non-transmigratoriness is ultimate.
Therefore, the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) are the two who have entered the cave.
And from what [source] are the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) understood? From the qualifying attributes.
Furthermore, this qualification applies only to the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).

By means of the subsequent passage beginning with "Know the self as the rider, and the body indeed as the chariot," the text employs the metaphor of the rider and the chariot to conceive of the individual self as the rider—the one who travels through both saṃsāra and liberation.
Then, with the words "He reaches the end of the journey, that highest step of Viṣṇu," it conceives of the supreme self as the goal to be reached.

Likewise, in the preceding passage as well— "Having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that ancient God, who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave, and dwelling in the abyss— the wise man casts off both joy and sorrow"— these two alone are distinguished by the relationship of the knower and the object of knowledge.
Moreover, this is a clear manifestation of the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, the specific mention of the speakers in the phrase "the knowers of Brahman say" is appropriate only if the Supreme Self is intended.
Therefore, in this context, both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) must be spoken of.
This same reasoning applies to passages such as "Two birds, inseparable companions... and so forth.
For even there, because the context concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), the two birds belonging to the primordial nature (*prākṛta*) are not being spoken of.
By the indicative mark of eating in the phrase "One of them eats the sweet fruit," the one is the individual soul (*vijñānātman*);
by the marks of non-eating and sentience in the phrase "The other looks on without eating," the other is the supreme self (*paramātman*).

And in the immediately following mantra, those two very entities are distinguished by way of the relationship between the seer and the seen: "On the same tree, the person is immersed; deluded, he grieves through his lack of lordship.
But when he sees the other, the Lord, being adored, and His glory, he becomes free from sorrow."

Another [teacher] says: This verse, "Two birds... (dvā suparṇā), does not support the final conclusion of this section, because it is explained otherwise in the Paiṅgi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa: "'Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit'—this is the *sattva*; 'the other looks on without eating'—the wise one looks on without eating; these two are the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*.
As for the claim that the word *sattva* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the word *kṣetrajña* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), that is not so;
for the words *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* are well-known to refer respectively to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the embodied self (*śārīra*).

And because it has been explained in that very same place: "That is this *sattva* by which one sees a dream; now, he who is this embodied witness is the *kṣetrajña*; these two, *sattva* and *kṣetrajña*, [are distinct]. Nor does this section admit of being the position of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). End of the first chapter.
For here, the embodied *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is not intended to be described as possessed of the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as agency and enjoyership.
How then? It is intended as having the nature of Brahman, consisting solely of the essence of pure consciousness, transcending all attributes of transmigratory existence;

this is because of the scriptural statements, "The other, not eating, looks on" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.6) and "The other, not eating, perceives as the Knower," as well as from such Śruti and Smṛti passages as "That thou art" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7) and "Know Me also as the *kṣetrajña*" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 13.2).

Furthermore, the observation of the withdrawal of knowledge (*vidyopasaṃhāra*) is only thus intelligible, as in: "These two are the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*; indeed, nothing at all defiles one who knows this," and so forth. But how, on this view, can there be the statement that the insentient *sattva* is the enjoyer, namely: "One of them eats the sweet fruit—the *sattva*"? It is replied: this scripture did not set out with the intention of declaring that the insentient *sattva* is the enjoyer. What then? It was intended to declare that the sentient *kṣetrajña* is non-enjoying and that its true nature is Brahman.
For that purpose, one superimposes the state of being an enjoyer upon the *sattva*, which is subject to modifications such as pleasure and pain.
Indeed, this agency and enjoyment are conceived through the failure to distinguish between the mutual natures of the *sattva* and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).
In ultimate reality, however, neither is possible for either of them: because the *sattva* is insentient, and because the Knower of the Field is changeless.
Furthermore, because the nature of the being is established by ignorance (*avidyā*), agency and the like are absolutely impossible [for the Self].

Thus, the Śruti—beginning with "Where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another"—shows that the conventional usage of agency and so forth pertains solely to the domain of ignorance, just like the worldly dealings with elephants and other things seen in a dream.

And by stating "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? and so forth, it precludes the conventional usage of agency and the like for the one possessed of discrimination.
Because of the intermediate state prior to rebirth.
"In the space within the eye, this person who is seen—this is the Self," he said; "this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman.
"And even if one pours clarified butter or water into this [eye], it flows away along the eyelashes," so it is heard in the scripture. This is the section (*adhikaraṇa*).

In this regard, a doubt arises: is this being referred to as the reflection residing in the eye, or the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānātman*), or the self of the deity who is the presiding controller of the sense organ, or the Lord (*īśvara*)?

What, then, is the initial position? That it is the shadow-self, the counterpart of the person. Why? Because its visibility is well-known, and because the teaching occurs in the form of a familiar statement: "This person who is seen in the eye."
Or rather, it is logical that this is a designation for the conscious self (vijñānātman);
for when one sees a form with the eye, that [self] is present in the eye.
Furthermore, the word "self" (ātman) is appropriate in this view.

Or rather, the person within the sun is perceived as the one who favors the eye, according to the scripture: "By means of his rays, he is established in this [eye]"; furthermore, qualities such as immortality and so forth can somehow be possible even in the case of a deity.

It is not the Lord (Īśvara), because of the mention of a specific location. This being the position reached, we reply: the Supreme Lord alone is the person taught here as being within the eye. Why? Because of the appropriateness (upapatti).
For it is indeed possible that the qualities born of *guṇa* belong to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is being taught here.
First of all, the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) applies to the Supreme Lord in its primary sense, according to the Vedic revelation: "That is the Self; thou art That."
Furthermore, immortality and fearlessness are repeatedly mentioned in connection with that [eye].
Likewise, this location in the eye is consistent with the Supreme Lord;
for the Supreme Lord is untainted by all defects, as is heard from scriptural passages such as "having shaken off all evil" (*apahatapāpmā*).

Likewise, the location of the eye is taught as beneficial for all ointments, according to the Śruti: "Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water into this [eye], it goes only to the two eyelids.
Furthermore, the teaching of qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (saṃyadvāma) is appropriate only with respect to that [eye].
"They call him the Conductor of Blessings," and so forth.
For it is said: "Into him indeed all blessings converge," and "He alone is the leader of blessings, for he leads all blessings;
he alone is the leader of lights, for he shines in all worlds. Therefore, on account of this reasoning, the Inner One is the Supreme Lord.
And because of the designation of place and so forth.

But how, it may be asked, can the eye be the dwelling place of Brahman, which is all-pervading like space? To this it is replied: this objection would indeed be valid if this were the only dwelling place specified for Him.
For there are other dwelling places as well—earth and so forth—which are specified for Him in such passages as, "He who dwells in the earth," and so on.
Among those, the eye is also specified in the passage, "He who dwells in the eye."

By including the phrase "on account of the designation of place and so forth," the author shows that it is not only a single place that is improperly attributed to Brahman; rather, even such things as name and form—which are inappropriate for Brahman, which is devoid of name and form—are seen being designated in various places, such as "His name is 'Ut'" and "He has a golden beard," and so on. It has already been stated that although Brahman is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), it is nevertheless taught in various contexts as possessing qualities (saguṇa) by means of qualities belonging to name and form, for the purpose of meditation.
It has already been stated that even for Brahman, who is omnipresent, a specific location for the purpose of perception is not contradictory, just as Viṣṇu is perceived specifically at Sālagrāma.
And because of the very designation of a distinct excellence of happiness, "Ca Ca."
Moreover, one should not dispute here whether Brahman is denoted in this passage or not;
for its being Brahman is established simply by the mention of that which is characterized by bliss.

Indeed, it is that very Brahman characterized by bliss which was introduced at the beginning of the passage as "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," and that same [Brahman] is what is denoted here.

Because it is logical that the subject under discussion should be accepted [as the one to whom the instruction is given], and because of the promise to declare only the goal in the words, "But the teacher will tell you the way.

But how is it understood from the beginning of the passage that Brahman qualified by bliss is what is being known? It is said: having heard these words of the fires, "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," Upakosala said, "I understand that Prāṇa is Brahman, but I do not understand Ka and Kha.
To this, the reply was: "That which is indeed Ka is Kha; that which is Kha is Ka."

In this context, the word *kha* is established in common usage as denoting the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*). If the word *ka*, which signifies bliss (*sukha*), were not employed as its qualifier, then it would follow that the word *brahman* is applied to the mere elemental ether with the intention of treating it as a mere symbol (*pratīka*), just as it is applied to names and so forth.
Likewise, since the word *kaṃ* is well known to denote worldly pleasure produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects, if the word *khaṃ* were not employed as its qualifier,
there would be the misconception that worldly pleasure is Brahman. However, when the two words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* qualify one another, they lead to the understanding of Brahman as consisting of bliss.

In that context, if the second word "Brahman" were not employed, and it were merely said, "Kaṃ khaṃ brahma," then because the word "kaṃ" would be used solely as an adjective, happiness (sukha) as a quality would become the object of meditation.
To prevent this, both words "kaṃ" and "khaṃ" have the word "brahman" as their head-word, resulting in "Kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma.
