For it is indeed desired that even a quality such as happiness be meditated upon by way of its possessor.
Thus, at the beginning of the discourse, Brahman characterized by bliss was taught.

Furthermore, each of the fires—the Gārhapatya and the others—having taught its own respective majesty, conclude by saying, "This, my dear, is our knowledge and the knowledge of the Self," thereby making it known that Brahman was indicated previously.
Moreover, the promise, "But the teacher will tell you the way," precludes the intention to speak of any other matter than the path itself.

"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this"—thus, by declaring that the person residing in the eye is not afflicted by evil when known, the text shows that this person in the eye is Brahman.

Therefore, having stated that the very Brahman under discussion resides in the eye and possesses qualities such as being the "center of blessings" (saṃyadvāma), the text begins with the words, "This person who is seen in the eye, he is the Self," in order to describe the path of the knower of That, beginning with light (arcis).
And because the scripture describes the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads.

Furthermore, the Person residing in the eye is the Supreme Lord, because the destination known as the "Path of the Gods" (devayāna) is well-known in the Śruti for one who has heard the Upaniṣads—that is, for the knower of Brahman who possesses the realization of the secret doctrine—as follows: "Then, having sought the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, they conquer the Sun by the northern route.

This indeed is the abode of the vital breaths; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is the supreme goal; from this they do not return. And in the Smṛti as well: "Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice..."

Regarding this, it is said: "Those people who know Brahman go to Brahman when they depart. This very [path] is seen here being described for those who know the Person in the eye. Having begun with, "Now, whether they perform meritorious deeds or not, they all pass into the light," it continues: "From the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning; there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman. Those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool."
Therefore, by means of the well-known path pertaining to the knower of Brahman, the fact that the one situated in the eye is Brahman is determined.
First Chapter:
On account of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other.

As for what was further stated—that it might be the self consisting of shadow, the self consisting of consciousness, or the self consisting of a deity who resides in the eye—it is said in reply: none of these others, such as the self consisting of shadow, deserves to be grasped here. Why? Because they are not stable. For it is not possible for the self consisting of shadow to have a permanent residence in the eye.
For whenever a certain person approaches the eye, the reflection of that person is seen in the eye;
when he has departed, it is no longer seen.
And the Śruti passage, "This person who is in the eye," by virtue of its proximity, teaches that the person visible in one's own eye is to be meditated upon.
Nor is it reasonable to assume that one worships by placing some person who casts a shadow near one's eye at the time of meditation;
for the scripture, stating "He perishes following the destruction of this very body," shows that even the shadow-self is unstable. Furthermore, [such an assumption] is impossible.
In that [case], there is no perception of qualities such as immortality in the shadow-self.
Likewise, since the individual self (vijñānātman) is connected to the entire body and its organs in common, it cannot be said to reside in the eye alone.
However, although Brahman is all-pervading, its connection with specific locations such as the heart is observed for the purpose of apprehension.
Furthermore, even in the case of the individual self (*vijñānātman*), there is an impossibility of attributes such as immortality.

Although the individual self is indeed non-different from the supreme Self, nevertheless, because mortality and fear have been superimposed upon it by ignorance, desire, and action, immortality and fearlessness are not tenable in its case.
Likewise, qualities such as being the "center of blessings" (*saṃyadvāmatva*) are entirely untenable in this [individual self] due to its lack of sovereignty.

Even if the deity were to reside in the eye—on the basis of the scriptural text, "By its rays, this [deity] is established in this"—nevertheless, its being the Self (ātmatva) is not possible, because it possesses an outward-turned nature (parāgrūpatvāt).
Furthermore, immortality and other such qualities are also impossible, because its birth and dissolution are heard of in scripture.
Even the immortality of the gods is relative, depending on their persistence for a long period of time.
Even sovereignty is dependent upon the Supreme Lord and is not inherent;
for the Vedic mantra declares: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows, out of fear the sun rises; out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on."
Therefore, this one residing in the eye must be understood to be the Supreme Lord alone.

And in this view, the expression "is seen" should be explained as referring to the wise person who relies on the scriptures and so forth; it is mentioned as if it were well-known for the purpose of generating interest.
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) [is Brahman], because His attributes are designated with respect to the deities and so forth.

Beginning with the passage, "He who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within," it is heard [in the scripture]: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the Immortal," and so forth.
Here, someone dwelling within—who is a controller—is heard of as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) with respect to the deities, the worlds, the Vedas, the sacrifice, the elements, and the self.

Regarding this, a doubt arises from the appearance of an unfamiliar designation: Is he some deity whose self is the presiding principle over the elements, or some yogi who has attained powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), or perhaps something else entirely?
What, then, first suggests itself? Since the designation is unknown, the bearer of that designation must also be something unknown, namely, some other entity altogether.
Alternatively, it is impossible to maintain that there exists any other entity whatsoever whose nature has not been defined.
Furthermore, the term "inner controller" (*antaryāmin*) is applied by virtue of the act of controlling from within; thus, it is not entirely unknown.
Therefore, some deity presiding over the earth and other elements must be the inner controller.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "He whose abode is earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind," and so forth.
Since he possesses a body and organs, it is logical that the deity—who dwells within earth and the other elements—should be their controller;
or else, some perfected yogi might possess the power of control by entering into all things.
But the Supreme Self is not perceived [therein], because He is devoid of body and organs;

such being the position reached, this is said in reply: that which is heard of as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) with respect to the divine realm and so forth must be the Supreme Self alone, and none other.
Why? Because of the declaration of His attributes (taddharmavyapadeśāt).
For indeed, the attributes of that Supreme Self are seen to be indicated here.

To begin with, the attribute of being the controller is appropriate for the Supreme Self, since it abides within and governs the entire aggregate of modifications—earth and the rest—which is divided according to the distinctions of the divine realm and so forth;
this is because, given its status as the cause of all modifications, all powers are logically established in it.
"In this passage, 'This is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3), the attributes of being the Self and being immortal apply primarily to the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, by stating 'whom the earth does not know,' the text shows that the inner ruler is distinct from the individual self of the deity,
for the deity of the earth would indeed recognize itself as 'I am the earth.'"
Likewise, designations such as "unseen" and "unheard" are appropriate for the Supreme Self because it is devoid of form and other such qualities.
As for the objection that it is not possible for the Supreme Self—which lacks body and organs—to be a controller, this is not a fault;
for He possesses body and organs precisely through the very body and organs of those whom He controls.
Nor does the fault of infinite regress arise from the idea that there must be another controller for him, because there is no difference [between them].
For it is only when a difference exists that the fault of infinite regress can occur.
Therefore, the Supreme Self alone is the inner controller.
And it is not based on Smṛti, because there is no mention of its specific characteristics.

It might be argued that properties such as being unseen and so forth are also possible for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) imagined by the Sāṃkhya tradition, since they accept it as being devoid of form and other such qualities. For they remember in their tradition: "It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Furthermore, its status as a controller is also possible, because it is the cause of all transformations (*vikāra*).
Therefore, the Pradhāna should be the referent of the word "Antaryāmin.

Although the Pradhāna was already refuted in the sūtra "Not the one devoid of scriptural authority, because of seeing" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*), it is raised again here on the grounds that designations such as "not being seen" and so forth could possibly apply to it.
To this, the following reply is given: "Nor can the Pradhāna, which belongs to Smṛti, be the referent of the word 'Antaryāmin'."
Why? Because its attributes are not predicated [of it].

Even though the designation of being a "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth might be possible for the Pradhāna, nevertheless the designation of being a "seer" and so forth is not possible for the Pradhāna, because they admit that the Pradhāna is insentient (*acetana*).
For the supplementary portion of the passage here states: "The unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower.
Furthermore, the nature of being the Self is not possible for the Pradhāna.
If the Pradhāna is not accepted as the Inner Ruler because qualities such as selfhood and being a seer are impossible for it, then let the embodied soul (śārīra) be the Inner Ruler.
For the embodied soul, being conscious, is a seer, a hearer, a thinker, and a knower; and it is the Self because of its inwardness;
and it is immortal, since the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit is possible for it.
Furthermore, attributes such as being unseen and so forth are well-established in the case of the embodied self (śārīra),

because there is a contradiction in the agent of actions such as seeing being the object of those very actions, and because of scriptural texts such as, "One cannot see the seer of seeing. Moreover, it is the nature of that self to inwardly rule the aggregate of the body and the organs, owing to its being the experiencer.

Therefore, in response to the claim that the embodied soul is the inner ruler (antaryāmī), the author reads the following: "And the embodied soul [is not the inner ruler], for both [recensions] indeed teach him as distinct."
The word "no" (neti) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
Furthermore, the embodied self (śārīra) cannot be the inner ruler (antaryāmī).

Why? Because although qualities such as being a seer (draṣṭṛtva) and so forth are possible for it, nevertheless, due to its limitation by adjuncts (upādhi)—like the space within a jar—it is not capable of abiding within and ruling over the earth and other elements in their entirety.

Moreover, both branches—the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas—indeed record this embodied self (śārīra) as distinct from the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin), as their respective substratum and object of control, just like the earth and other elements. The Kāṇvas read: "He who dwells in consciousness" (vijñāne tiṣṭhan);
the Mādhyandinas read: "He who dwells in the self" (ya ātmani tiṣṭhan).
In this reading, "He who dwells in the self," the word "self" (ātman) denotes the embodied self.
Even in this reading, "He who dwells in consciousness," the word *vijñāna* refers to the embodied self (*śārīra*), for the embodied self is composed of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
Therefore, it is established that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is the Lord, distinct from the embodied self.

But how can two seers be possible within a single body—one being this Lord, the Inner Controller, and the other being this other, the embodied self? What, then, is the inconsistency here? It would contradict scriptural statements such as, "There is no other seer than He."
For here, indeed, it denies any other Self than the internal ruler (antaryāmin) who is the seer, hearer, thinker, and knower.
If it is argued that this statement is for the purpose of denying another controller, we say no;
because there is no possibility of another controller and because the scripture speaks without distinction.

To this it is replied: This designation of a difference between the embodied self (*śārīra*) and the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) is caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body and organs presented by ignorance (*avidyā*); it is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
For there is only one inner self (*pratyagātman*); two inner selves are not possible.

However, for that which is one alone, the conventional usage of difference is produced by limiting adjuncts, just as [one speaks of] the "space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*) and the "great space" (*mahākāśa*).

Consequently, all of this—the scriptural texts concerning the distinction between the knower and the known, the means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest, the experience of transmigratory existence, and the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions—is rendered consistent.
Thus, the Śruti says: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another"; this demonstrates that all worldly activity pertains to the realm of ignorance (avidyā).
"But where for him everything has become the Self alone—by what means could he see whom? Thus, with regard to the sphere of knowledge, [the scripture] precludes all worldly transaction.
That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes.

"Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained—[that] which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtler than the subtle, imperishable; that which is the source of beings—into that the wise perceive [it as] the substratum. Thus it is heard in scripture.

In this regard, a doubt arises: Is this source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), or the embodied soul (*śārīra*), or rather the Supreme Lord?
In this context, it is logical that the Pradhāna is the non-intelligent source of beings (bhūtayoni), because only non-intelligent things are presented there as examples:
"As a spider emits and retracts [its thread], as herbs arise from the earth,
and as hair and body-hair grow from a living man, so does the universe arise here from the Imperishable."
[Objection: Surely the spider and the person are presented here as examples of conscious beings.
[Reply: We say no.

For it is not the case that consciousness alone possesses the nature of being the source of the thread or the source of hair and body-hair. It is well known—in the Sūtra-bhāṣya—that the unconscious body of the spider, presided over by consciousness, is the source of the thread, and the body of the person is the source of the hair and body-hair.

Furthermore, although the description of "not being seen" and so forth was possible in the previous [passage], the Pradhāna was not accepted because the description of "being a seer" and so forth was impossible there.
In this case, however, the attributes such as "not being seen" are possible in the Pradhāna;
nor is any contradictory attribute mentioned here.

[Objection: But surely this supplementary statement, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," is not possible in the case of the insentient *pradhāna*; how then can the *pradhāna* be asserted as the source of beings?

[Reply: To this it is said: Having first taught the source of beings as possessing the qualities of invisibility and so forth by means of the word "syllable" (*akṣara*) in the passages, "By which that syllable is attained" and "That which is invisible," the text will later teach again, "Higher than the high imperishable.
Therein, he who is heard as being higher than the imperishable will be the one who is all-knowing and all-perceiving.
However, it is *pradhāna* alone that is designated by the term "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*) as the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*).

But when the word "source" (*yoni*) signifies a cause (*nimitta*), then the embodied soul (*śārīra*) might also be the source of beings, because the multitude of beings is produced through merit and demerit.
This being the position reached, it is replied: this source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so forth, must be the Supreme Lord alone, and none other.
How is this understood? From the teaching of attributes.
For here, an attribute of the Supreme Lord is seen being stated: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving.
Indeed, neither the non-intelligent *pradhāna* nor the embodied soul (*śārīra*), whose vision is limited by adjuncts (*upādhi*), can possess omniscience. Thus ends the first chapter.

Or rather, omniscience is possible [in that sense]. But was it not already stated that this omniscience and all-knowingness belong only to the one higher than the source of beings (bhūtayoni), which is designated by the word "syllable" (akṣara), and not to the source of beings itself?
To this it is replied: it is not so possible.

For this reason, having first pointed out the source of beings under discussion—the "Imperishable" (akṣara)—as the material cause of that which is born, in the words, "From the Imperishable, the universe arises here," the text subsequently points out the "All-knowing One" (sarvajña) likewise as the material cause of that which is born, saying: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge; from Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food.

Therefore, because it is recognized through the identity of description, it is understood that the attributes of being all-knowing and all-perceiving are predicated of the very same "Imperishable" source of beings under discussion.
Even in the passage "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*), no one other than the Imperishable—the source of beings under discussion—is being designated as higher.

How is this understood? Because it has been promised that the very Imperishable which is the source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, is what must be explained in the words: "He who knows the true Person, the Imperishable—he has truly declared that knowledge of Brahman.
If so, how then is it designated as "higher than the high Imperishable"? We shall explain that in the subsequent Sūtra.
Moreover, two kinds of knowledge are stated here as things to be known, namely "the lower and the higher.
Having there described the lower knowledge characterized by the Ṛgveda and so forth, the text says: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained," and so on.
In this context, the Imperishable is heard of as the object of the higher knowledge.

If, however, something other than the Supreme Lord were postulated as the Imperishable (akṣara) possessing qualities such as invisibility and so forth—as in the Sūtra-bhāṣya—this would not be the higher knowledge (parā vidyā).
For this distinction between higher and lower knowledge is established on the basis of their respective fruits: worldly prosperity and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
Furthermore, no one accepts that knowledge of the Pradhāna results in the supreme good.
Furthermore, three sciences would have to be admitted on your view, because the supreme Self—the Imperishable Source—is being propounded there.
However, only two sciences to be known are specified here.

Moreover, the expectation of knowing everything through the knowledge of one thing—as expressed in the words, "O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known?"—is only possible if Brahman, which consists of all things, is intended; it is not possible if the Pradhāna, which is merely insentient, or the individual enjoyer, who is distinct from the objects of enjoyment, were meant.

Moreover, having introduced *brahmavidyā* as the primary subject in the passage, "He taught that *brahmavidyā*, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son," the text shows that it is indeed *brahmavidyā* by demonstrating, through the division into higher and lower, that the higher knowledge (*parā vidyā*) leads to the realization of the Imperishable (*akṣara*).
Furthermore, the designation "*brahmavidyā*" would be contradicted if the Imperishable to be realized through it were not Brahman.

Furthermore, the lower knowledge characterized by the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, which consists of ritual action (*karmavidyā*), is introduced at the commencement of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) for the purpose of praising that higher knowledge, as seen in such censuring statements as: "For these are rafts, unstable, having the form of sacrifice; the eighteen [Vedic branches] in which the inferior ritual is taught—those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good, they return again to old age and death. Having thus censured the lower knowledge, the text shows that one who has desisted from it gains the qualification for the higher knowledge: "Having examined the worlds gained through actions... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1). Chapter One.
"A Brahmin, having become weary of [the world], should realize that there is nothing uncreated through what is created;
for the sake of realizing That, he should approach a Guru alone—who is learned (śrotriya) and established in Brahman—with fuel in hand.

As for the argument that because non-intelligent things such as earth are employed as examples, the source of beings (bhūtayoni) must also be non-intelligent by way of the thing illustrated (dārṣṭāntika), that is incorrect.
For there is no rule that an absolute similarity must exist between the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and the subject of illustration (dārṣṭāntika);

moreover, since gross entities such as earth and so forth have been employed as examples, it is not accepted that the source of beings (bhūtayoni), which is the subject of illustration, is itself gross.
Therefore, the source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so on, is none other than the Supreme Lord.
And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is neither of the other two.
For this reason as well, the Supreme Lord alone is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), and not the other two—the embodied soul (*śārīra*) or primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
Why? Because of the designation of distinctive attributes and difference.
For the text distinguishes the source of beings under discussion from the embodied soul by way of its dissimilarity: "For the divine, formless Puruṣa is both within and without, indeed unborn."
"For [Brahman] is without breath, without mind, pure" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).

Indeed, these specific attributes such as being "divine" and so forth are not possible for the embodied soul (śārīra), who—possessing the conceit of limitation by name and form presented by ignorance—superimposes those qualities upon itself.
Therefore, it is the Person of the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣada-puruṣa) who is spoken of here directly.
Likewise, the text designates the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) as distinct even from the *pradhāna*, stating: "Higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*).

The "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) is the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which consists of the causal power of the seeds of name and form—the subtle elements of beings resting upon the Lord and serving as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). By designating it as distinct—referring to that which is changeless and higher than everything that is a modification, saying "higher than the high Imperishable"—the text shows that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is intended here, not some independent principle called *pradhāna* for the sake of which a designation of distinction would be stated.

What then? If even the *pradhāna*, when postulated, could be conceived as the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) denoted by terms such as "the Undeveloped" (*avyākṛta*) without contradicting scripture, then let it be so postulated.
Therefore, it is established here that the Supreme Lord is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) on account of the designation of difference.
And for what further reason is the Supreme Lord the source of beings? Because of the presentation of His form.

Moreover, immediately after the passage "higher than the Imperishable is the High," we observe that following the description of the creation of the principles beginning with Prāṇa and ending with Earth, the form of that very source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) consisting of all modifications is presented: "Fire is his head, the sun and moon his eyes, the quarters his ears, the revealed Vedas his speech, the wind his breath, the universe his heart, and from his feet came the earth; for he is the inner self of all beings."
And that [description] is appropriate for the Supreme Lord alone, because He is the cause of all modifications;

for this presentation of form is not possible for the embodied soul, whose majesty is limited to its body, nor for the Pradhāna, because it is impossible for either to be the inner self of all beings.
Therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), and not the other two.

But how is it understood that this presentation of forms refers to the source of beings? It is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and from the fact that there is a reference back to what has been previously introduced.
For, having introduced the source of beings with the words "From him is born breath" and "He is the inner self of all beings," the statement [in question] must indeed concern the source of beings.

Just as the statement, "Study under this teacher; he has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas," refers specifically to the teacher, so it is here. But how can a form consisting of a body be possible for the Source of Beings, which possesses qualities such as invisibility? This is stated with the intention of expressing its being the Self of all, and not with the intention of attributing a physical body; thus there is no fault, just as in the passage, "I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food," and so forth. Others, however, think that this is not a presentation of the form of the Source of Beings, because it is presented as something being born.

For previously, in the passage beginning with "From this is born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the senses; ether, air, light, water, and the earth which supports all," he pointed out the entire collection of principles from the vital breath down to the earth as being born. And later on as well, in the passage beginning with "Therefore, fire is its fuel, the sun [its smoke]" and ending with "and from this come all herbs and juices," he will likewise point them out precisely as being born.

How could the form of the source of all beings (*bhūtayoni*) be introduced here in the middle, quite unexpectedly? Furthermore, its being the self of all will be mentioned after the completion of the account of creation, in the passage beginning, "The Person alone is this whole world, action," and so forth.

Moreover, we observe that the birth and other states of Prajāpati, whose body is the three worlds, are pointed out in both Śruti and Smṛti: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; as soon as born, he was the sole lord of beings."

"He supported this earth and this heaven; to what god shall we offer worship with oblation?"—the phrase "he evolved" (samavartata) means "he was born. Likewise: "He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called the Puruṣa;
the first creator of beings, Brahmā, evolved in the beginning.
Even for the *vikāra-puruṣa* (the Puruṣa as a product), it is possible to be the inner self of all beings, because he abides within all beings in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
In this view, the presentation of all forms in passages such as "The Person alone is all this, [consisting of] action" should be explained as a means for the realization of the Supreme Lord.
Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the distinction of a common term.

Having commenced with the questions, "What is the Self? What is Brahman? and "You are currently studying this very Vaiśvānara Self; tell that to us," and having taught the connection of heaven, sun, wind, ether, water, and earth with qualities such as "excellent splendor" (*sutejas*) and so forth by means of individual meditations, and having instructed—by censuring those partial meditations—that these [elements] constitute the head and other parts of Vaiśvānara, it is recorded in the scripture: "But he who meditates on him as limited to the span of a thumb... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1). Chapter One.
"One who meditates upon Vaiśvānara as the Self, as the great abode, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.

Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head is indeed *sutejas* (the brilliantly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is *vāyu* (wind), the trunk is *pṛthagvartmātmā* (the self of diverse paths), the abdomen is *bahula* (vast), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), the feet are the earth, the chest is the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the body hair is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the heart is the *gārhapatya* fire, the mind is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire," and so forth.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the term *vaiśvānara* intended to teach the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), or the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), or the deity presiding over it, or the embodied soul (*śārīra*), or perhaps the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)? What, then, is the cause of this doubt? It is because the word *vaiśvānara* is used as a common designation for the digestive fire, the elemental fire, and the deity, while the word *ātman* is used for both the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord. Consequently, a doubt arises as to which [of these] is to be accepted as appropriate and which is to be rejected.

What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That it is the digestive fire. Why? Because its specific application is observed in certain passages, such as: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is that which is within man, by which this food is digested, which is eaten," and so forth.

It may be merely the fire element, since its usage is observed even in that general sense, as in "The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner for the entire world" (*viśvasmā agniṃ bhuvanāya devā vaiśvānaraṃ ketumahāmakṛṇvan*). Or it may be the deity whose body is fire, because its usage is also observed in that sense, as in the scriptural passage: "May we be in the good favor of Vaiśvānara; for he is the king, the glory of the worlds" (*vaiśvānarasya sumatau syāma rājā hi kaṃ bhuvanānāmabhiśrī*), wherein the deity is possible as one endowed with sovereignty and other such attributes.

If it is argued that, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Self" (*ātman*), and because the word "Self" alone is used at the beginning in the passage "What is our Self? What is Brahman?", the word "Man" (*nara*) should be understood as "Self," and thus Vaiśvānara is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*);
for he, as the enjoyer, is in close proximity to Vaiśvānara, and the qualification "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*) is possible in his case since he is limited by adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that Vaiśvānara is not the Lord (*īśvara*).
In the commentary on the Sūtra, why is this stated? [It is because] Vaiśvānara must be the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of a distinction among common terms;
"distinction among common terms" means a specific qualification of two terms that are otherwise common to more than one referent.

Although both these terms, *ātman* and *vaiśvānara*, are common to more than one [subject]—the term *vaiśvānara* being common to three, and the term *ātman* to two—nevertheless, a distinction is observed by which their reference to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is accepted, as seen in the passage: "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *sutejas*" and so forth.

For here it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone, characterized by having a head and so on, is presented in a different state as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) for the purpose of meditation, because He is the cause.

For since the cause possesses states corresponding to all the states found in its effects, it is logical that it should have the worlds and so forth as its constituent parts. Furthermore, the fruit described in the passage, "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves," which has all the worlds and so forth as its locus, is possible only if the Supreme Cause is accepted. Furthermore, there is the scriptural statement regarding the burning away of all evil for those who know it: "They are burned away"; and there is the introduction with the words "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? using the terms "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman. These concluding marks of Brahman lead to the Supreme Lord alone.
Therefore, Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Lord.
That which is being remembered would be an inference.
For this reason also, the Supreme Lord alone is Vaiśvānara;

because such a form consisting of the three worlds—namely, "Fire is his mouth, the sky is his head"—is recorded in Smṛti as belonging to the Supreme Lord alone: "Salutation to Him, the Soul of the worlds, whose mouth is fire, whose head is the sky, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the sun, and whose ears are the quarters."

The meaning is that this remembered form, by inferring the underlying Vedic scripture (*śruti*), serves as an inferential mark (*liṅga*)—that is, an indicator—that this word *vaiśvānara* has the Supreme Lord as its referent.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason; the meaning is: since this is an indicator, for that reason also, Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Self.

Although this is a praise—"Salutation to Him, the Self of the worlds"—nevertheless, even such praise cannot properly occur in this form unless there exists an underlying Vedic statement (*vedavākya*).

"One whose head the wise declare to be the earth, whose navel is indeed the sky, whose two eyes are the moon and the sun, whose ears are the quarters, and whose feet are the ground—know him to be the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings. Smṛti passages of this kind should also be cited here.

In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, [it is stated]: "If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of meditation] because of its being mentioned along with sound and other qualities, and because it is established within [the body], we say no; for there is instruction regarding such a vision, because [otherwise] it would be impossible, and they also read this as a 'Person' (*puruṣa*)."
To this, [the opponent] replies: Vaiśvānara cannot be the Supreme Lord.
Why? Because of the word and other reasons, and because of his abiding within.
First, as for the word: the term "Vaiśvānara" cannot apply to the Supreme Lord, because it is conventionally established in another sense.

Likewise, there is the word "fire" in the passage, "This is that Agni Vaiśvānara"; by the word "and so forth," there is the conceptualization of the threefold fire, such as "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire," and so on; and by the passage beginning with, "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as an oblation," there is the mention of the state of being the locus for the offering of breath.
For these reasons, Vaiśvānara should be understood as the digestive fire within the stomach.
Likewise, its abiding "within the person" is also heard in scripture: "He knows it as abiding within the person. And that is possible in the case of the digestive fire.

As for what was said—that Vaiśvānara must be the Supreme Self because of specific indications such as "The head itself is Sutejas"—to this we reply: on what basis is this determination made, that when specific indications appear in both ways, one should resort only to those indicating the Supreme Lord and not to those indicating the gastric fire?
Alternatively, this designation may refer to the elemental fire which exists both internally and externally.

For even in his case, a connection with the worlds and so forth is understood from the wording of the mantra, as in: "He who by his light spread over this earth and heaven, the two worlds, and the intermediate space" (RV 10.88.3), and so on. Alternatively, because of the deity’s possession of sovereign power, he may have the heavenly world and other realms as his limbs, being [conceived of] as having such a body.
Therefore, Vaiśvānara is not the Supreme Lord.
To this it is replied: "Not so, because of the teaching of the contemplation [of Him] as such.

It is not proper to reject the Supreme Lord on the grounds of sound and other such reasons. Why? Because there is a teaching of the contemplation [of Him] as such, without abandoning His nature as the gastric fire.

For here, the vision of the Supreme Lord is taught with respect to the Vaiśvānara fire within the belly, just as in such passages as, "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman. Alternatively, the Supreme Lord, having the internal fire as His limiting adjunct (upādhi), is taught here as the object to be seen, just as in such passages as, "Consisting of mind, having breath for its body, and light for its form. If the Supreme Lord were not intended here and only the mere internal fire were intended, then specific attributes such as "The head itself is the excellent luster" would be impossible.
However, we shall explain in the subsequent sūtra how this distinction cannot be established even by relying on the fire that has become a deity.
Furthermore, if only the gastric fire were intended, it would possess merely its location within the person,
but not the nature of being a person.
Moreover, the Vājasaneyins study this very person [as Vaiśvānara]: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is the person; he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara as such—the person established within the person.
For the Supreme Lord, however, both his being a person and his being established within the person are appropriate, because he is the Self of all.

As for those who read the portion of the Sūtra as "puruṣavidham api cainam adhīyate" (and they study him also as person-shaped), for them the meaning is this: if one were to adopt the mere digestive fire, there would be only the state of being established within the person.

But it does not mean "having the form of a person" (puruṣavidhatva); for the Vājasaneyins also study this as having the form of a person, saying: "He who knows him as having the form of a person, as abiding within the person.

And this "having the form of a person" refers to what is taken from the cosmic context (adhidaivata), beginning with the head and ending with being established on the earth, as well as what is well-known from the individual context (adhyātma), beginning with the head and ending with being established on the chin.
For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being.

As for the further argument that—because the Vedic mantras show a connection with the heavenly world and so forth even for the elemental fire—the conceptualization of its parts, such as "the sun indeed is his head" (*sūrya eva sutejāḥ*), must pertain to that very fire, or else to a deity whose body it is due to the possession of sovereign power—that too must be refuted.
To this, it is said: for the very reasons already stated, Vaiśvānara is not a deity.
Likewise, the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) is also not Vaiśvānara;

for it is not possible to conceive of the elemental fire—which consists merely of heat and light—as having heaven as its head and so forth, because one modification cannot possibly have another modification as its self.

Similarly, although the deity possesses lordly power (*aiśvarya*), the conception of her having heaven as her head and so forth is not possible, because she is not the ultimate cause and because her sovereignty is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
And the impossibility of the word "Self" [applying] to any of these positions remains established. First Chapter:
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even directly.

It was previously stated that the Supreme Lord is to be meditated upon either as having the gastric fire as His symbol (*pratīka*) or as having the gastric fire as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), in accordance with the mention of His being "established within" and other such attributes.

Now, however, the teacher Jaimini considers that there is no contradiction whatsoever in accepting the meditation on the Supreme Lord directly, even without resorting to the conception of a symbol or an adjunct.

[Objection: But if the gastric fire is not accepted, would not the statement regarding its being "established within," as well as the reasons such as the word [of scripture] and so forth, be contradicted?
To this it is replied: First of all, the statement regarding being "established within" does not contradict [the context].

For here, the phrase "he knows him who is man-like and established within the person" is not spoken with reference to the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), because that is neither the subject under discussion nor has it been mentioned.

How then? It is said, "he knows him who is man-like and established within the person," with reference to that "man-likeness" which was previously attributed to the parts of the person from the head down to the chin.

Just as one sees a branch established upon a tree, so it is here; or rather, with reference to that which is the mere witness-form of the aforementioned Supreme Self—which possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being "man-like" both with respect to the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaivata*)—it is said: "He knows [Him] who is man-like and established within the person."

And when it is determined—by virtue of considering the preceding and following passages—that the Supreme Self is being accepted, then the word *vaiśvānara* will apply to that very object through some etymological derivation (*yoga*), such as "He is both the All (*viśva*) and Man (*nara*)," or "He is the Man of the All," or "The All are the Men within Him. Thus, the Supreme Self is *viśvānara* because He is the Self of all; and *vaiśvānara* is simply *viśvānara* with the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) having no other meaning, as in the cases of *rākṣasa*, *vāyasa*, and so forth.
Furthermore, the word *agni* will also refer exclusively to the Supreme Self by resorting to derivations such as "the leader" (*agraṇī*).
The conceptualization of [the fires] such as the Gārhapatya and their status as the locus for the oblations of breath are also appropriate for the Supreme Self, because it is the Self of all.

But how, then, is the scriptural statement regarding [the Self] being "the size of a thumb" compatible with its being the Supreme Lord? He begins to explain that: "On account of manifestation," says Āśmarathya.
Even for the Supreme Lord, who is beyond all measure, there may be a state of being "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) for the purpose of manifestation.
Indeed, it is said that the Supreme Lord manifests Himself as having the dimension of a span for the sake of His worshippers;
or rather, He is manifested specifically in particular locations, such as the heart and other points of perception.
Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya maintains that even with regard to the Supreme Lord, the scriptural mention of being "the size of a span" is appropriate on account of His manifestation.
The beginning of the recollection, and so forth.
Or rather, this [Self] is remembered by the mind as established within the heart, which is the size of a span;
therefore, it is called "span-sized" (*prādeśamātra*).
Just as barley grains measured by a *prastha* measure are called "a *prastha*," so it is in this case.

And although, in the case of barley grains, their own inherent measure is manifested through its connection with a *prastha* measure— as explained in the first chapter— and whereas here there is no measure belonging to the Supreme Lord that could be manifested through a connection with the heart, nevertheless, it is said that some recollection may serve as a basis for the scriptural mention of "measuring a span" (*prādeśamātra*) in whatever way possible.

Or rather, although this [Supreme Lord] is not of the measure of a span, He is to be meditated upon as being of the measure of a span, so that the scriptural statement regarding His being "of the measure of a span" may have purpose.
Thus, the teacher Bādari maintains that the scriptural mention of the Supreme Lord as being "of the measure of a span" is based on the occasion of such meditation.
Jaimini [holds that the fruit arises] from the attainment [of the knowledge], for thus the scripture shows.
Or rather, the scriptural mention of being "the size of a span" (prādeśamātra) may be intended as a metaphorical identification (saṃpatti).

Why? Because the Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa, in a similar context, while identifying the limbs of Vaiśvānara—the Self of the three worlds—extending from heaven down to the earth with the parts of the body from the head down to the chin, shows that the Supreme Lord is metaphorically identified as being "the size of a span. It says: "The gods, indeed, were well-informed and attained [this knowledge] as one who is the size of a span. But I shall explain these to you in such a way that I will effect this very identification of him as being the size of a span."
Pointing to the head, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Pre-eminent. Pointing to the eyes, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the One of Excellent Splendor.
Pointing to the nostrils, he said: "This is Vaiśvānara as the Self of Diverse Armor."
Pointing to the principal ether, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Abundant.
Pointing to the principal waters, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Wealth.
Pointing to the chin, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Foundation."
The term *cubuka* refers to the lower part of the face, that is, the chin.

Although in the Vājasaneyaka the sky is recorded as having the quality of being "the highest support" (*atiṣṭhātva*) and the sun as having the quality of "splendor" (*sutejastva*), whereas in the Chāndogya the sky is recorded as having the quality of "splendor" and the sun as having the quality of "multiformity" (*viśvarūpatva*),

nevertheless, nothing is lost by this difference, because the scriptural statement regarding the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*) is common to both, and because all the recensional branches (*śākhā*) must be understood in agreement.
The teacher Jaimini considers the scriptural statement regarding the span of a thumb's breadth to be more appropriate as a sign of prosperity.
And they enjoin him in this [state].
The Koṇcas cite this very one as the Supreme Lord in the space between the crown of the head and the chin, saying: "That which is the infinite, unmanifest Self—it is established in Avimukta.
"In what is that Avimukta established?
"It is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī."

"What indeed is Varaṇā and what is Nāsī? In this regard, it is explained: "Because she wards off (*vārayati*) all evils committed by the senses, she is Varaṇā; because she destroys (*nāśayati*) all evils committed by the senses, she is Nāsī. Having thus etymologically defined Varaṇā and Nāsī, they further ask: "And what is her location?
That which is the junction of the eyebrows and the nose—that is the junction of the heavenly world and the beyond. This is the first chapter.
Thus it is. Therefore, the scriptural statement that the Supreme Lord is "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) is logically established;
the statement regarding Him being "immeasurable" (abhivimāna) has the intention of referring to His nature as the inner self (pratyagātman).
It is called *abhivimāna* because it is measured (perceived) by all living beings as their own inner self (*pratyagātman*);
or, it is *abhivimāna* because it has gone inward (*abhigata*) due to being the inner self, and is a measure (*vimāna*) due to its freedom from measurement;
or, it is *abhivimāna* because it measures out the entire universe, owing to its being the cause.
Therefore, it is established that Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Lord.

Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the Commentary on the Sūtras of the Investigation of the Body (Śārīrakamīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya), composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (Paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
Composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.

The abode of earth and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word.

This is heard [in scripture]: "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all the vital breaths—know Him alone as the one Self; let go of other words. He is the bridge to immortality.
This is the reason here.

Since this passage mentions the "extent" (otatva) of light and so forth, it is understood that there is some "abode" (āyatana); regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether this abode might be the supreme Brahman or something else entirely.
On this point, the prima facie view is that the abode must be something other [than Brahman].
Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "This is the bridge of immortality."

For in the world, a bridge is known to have a further shore; however, it is impossible to admit that the supreme Brahman has a further shore, because of the scriptural revelation that it is "endless and shoreless.
Furthermore, if another entity were accepted as the abode, the *pradhāna* well-known from Smṛti would have to be accepted, since its status as the cause makes its being an abode logically consistent.

Or [the "thread" might be] the air well-known from scripture, because of the scriptural mention of its nature as a thread: "Air, O Gautama, is indeed that thread; by air, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world and the other world, and all beings, are strung together" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1). Or it might be the embodied soul (the individual self), because it is logical for it to be the substratum with respect to the phenomenal world which is the object of experience. Such being the position, the Sūtra says: "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. Heaven and earth are "dyu-bhuvau"; that which has heaven and earth as its beginning is "dyu-bhv-ādi."

In this sentence, that which consists of heaven, earth, the intermediate space, the mind, and the vital breaths—the world thus described as being woven upon something else—its substrate must be the Supreme Brahman.
Why? Because of its own word; that is to say, because of the word "Self" (ātman).
For the word "Self" occurs here in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self."

Furthermore, the word "Self" (ātman) is appropriately applicable when understood as the Supreme Self (paramātman), and not when understood in any other sense. In some places, Brahman is heard of as the abode by its own name: "O dear one, all these creatures have Being (sat) as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support.

And here too, Brahman is celebrated by its own name both before and after [this passage]: "The Person alone is all this—the work, austerity, Brahman, and the supreme immortal," and "Brahman indeed is this immortal in front; Brahman behind, Brahman to the south and to the north."

In this regard, however, because there is the scriptural teaching that "all this has the nature of having That as its abode" (*tattvāyatana-vad-bhāva-śravaṇāt*), and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "All is Brahman," a doubt may arise that the Self is manifold in nature—just as a tree consists of branches, trunk, and root—such that the Self is of various flavors and diverse. "Salutation"—this is what is meant:

it is not a manifold Self characterized by the expansion of effects that is to be known; rather, dissolving the expansion of effects created by ignorance through knowledge, know that very one Self, which is the sole substratum and of a single essence.

Just as when it is said, "Bring that on which Devadatta sits," one brings only the seat and not Devadatta, in the same way, it is the Self of a single essence, which serves as the substratum, that is taught as the object to be known. Furthermore, a condemnation is heard in scripture regarding one who falsely identifies with modifications: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity."

The grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "All is Brahman" is for the purpose of dissolving the phenomenal world (prapañca), not for the purpose of establishing a manifold nature; for we hear of its being of a single essence in such passages as: "Just as a lump of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of consciousness.
Therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Brahman.

As for what was said—that because of the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (*setu*) and because it is logical for a bridge to have a further shore, there must be something other than Brahman that serves as the abode of heaven, earth, and so on—it is replied here: by the scriptural mention of a "bridge," only the quality of being a support (*vidhāraṇatva*) is intended, not having a further shore and so forth.
For just because a bridge made of clay or wood is seen in the world, it does not follow that the bridge here must also be made of clay or wood.

Furthermore, the meaning of the word "bridge" is simply the quality of supporting; it does not imply having a further shore and so forth, since the word *setu* is derived from the root *ṣiñ*, which has the sense of binding.

Another says: That knowledge of the Self which is celebrated in the passage, "Know Him alone as the one Self," and that relinquishing of speech expressed in, "Relinquish other words"—these two are here proclaimed by the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (*setu*) because they are the means to immortality, as in the text, "This is the bridge to immortality.
It does not, however, refer to the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Therefore, the argument that because of the mention of a "bridge," the abode of heaven, earth, etc., must be something other than Brahman, is incorrect.
Because of the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated.
For this reason as well, Brahman alone, which is beyond this world, is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; because its being approachable by the liberated is seen to be designated here.
"Approachable by the liberated" (muktopasṛpya) means that which is to be approached by those who are liberated.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the notion of "I am" (*ahamasmīti*) with respect to the body and other things that are not the Self; from that arises attachment (*rāga*) toward their worship and so forth, and aversion (*dveṣa*) toward their humiliation and so forth; and from the perception of their destruction arise fear and delusion (*moha*). Thus, this multitude of evils with its endless divisions is directly perceived by all of us as a continuous stream. By contrast, there is a designation concerning the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, stating that this [Self] is to be approached and attained by those who are freed from defects such as ignorance, attachment, and aversion. How so? "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder."

Having stated, "And his actions are extinguished when He is seen, who is both the high and the low," the text further declares, "Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. Moreover, that Brahman is the goal to be reached by the liberated is well-known in the scriptures, as in such passages as: "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."
However, it is well known that the Pradhāna and other such principles do not possess the quality of being approached by liberated conscious beings (*cinmuktopasṛpyatva*).

Furthermore, here in this text, the state of being that which is to be known through the relinquishing of speech is predicated of the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self; cast off other words; He is the bridge to immortality."
Moreover, this is seen regarding Brahman in another scriptural passage: "A wise Brāhmaṇa, having understood that very [Self], should practice wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech.
For this reason also, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the supreme Brahman.
There is no inference from this because of the absence of desire for it.
Just as a specific reason (*vaiśe�gika hetu*) was stated to establish Brahman, there is no such specific reason to establish another entity; thus he says:
"The *pradhāna* imagined by the Sāṃkhya tradition is not to be understood here as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, because it is not denoted by that word.
Why? Because it is not designated by that term.
The word *tacchabda* means a word that expresses that [insentient] *pradhāna*; *atacchabda* means a word that does not express that.
For there is no word here that expresses an insentient *pradhāna*, by which an insentient *pradhāna* might be understood as either the cause or the abode.
There exists, however, a word here that expresses its opposite, the sentient, such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and so forth.
For this very reason, air also is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth in this context.
And [the word] "prāṇabhṛt" [is also used].

Although the individual living being (*prāṇabhṛt*), who is the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), possesses both selfhood and consciousness, nevertheless, since knowledge limited by adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot possibly possess omniscience and other such qualities, this very term [“that”] indicates that the living being is not to be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Furthermore, for the non-omnipresent living being limited by adjuncts, even the status of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is not properly possible.
The separate formulation of the sūtra is for the sake of what follows.
And for what further reason should the individual living being not be accepted as the abode of that which begins with "being"? Because of the designation of difference.

Furthermore, a distinction is expressed here: "Know Him alone as the one Self," which indicates the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower. In this context, since the individual soul (prāṇabhṛt) is the seeker of liberation, it is the knower;
by process of elimination, it is understood that Brahman, denoted by the word "Self," is the object of knowledge—the abode of heaven and so forth—and not the individual soul.
And for what reason should the living being not be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth? Because of the context.

Moreover, this context concerns the Supreme Self, because of the requirement for the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one, as expressed in the passage: "O Venerable Sir, when what is known does all this become known?
For when the Supreme Self, which is the self of all, is known, all this becomes known; this would not be the case if only the individual living being (prāṇabhṛt) were meant.
And for what further reason should the individual living being not be accepted as the abode of "Being" (bhūman) and so forth? [From the] First Chapter:
And on account of abiding and eating.
No; for with reference to the "two abodes" (the body and the self), in the verse "Two birds, inseparable companions," the staying and eating are indicated:
"One of them eats the sweet fruit" refers to the consumption of the fruits of action, while "The other looks on without eating" refers to abiding in a state of indifference.
And by those two terms, "abiding" (sthiti) and "moving" (gati), the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (kṣetrajña) are understood therein.
If the Lord is intended as the abode of earth and so forth, then the separate mention of that aforementioned Lord from the individual soul is appropriate;
otherwise, the mention of something not under discussion would be accidental and disconnected.
[Objection: But would it not follow that for you as well, the separate mention of the *kṣetrajña* from the Lord would be entirely arbitrary?
[Reply: No, because he is not intended to be expressed [as the primary subject].

For the *kṣetrajña*, being connected to limiting adjuncts such as the intellect in each body by virtue of being an agent and an enjoyer, is already well-known from worldly experience; he is not intended to be expressed by the Śruti with its primary purport.
Since the Lord (Īśvara) is not well-known from worldly experience, He will be shown through the explicit intent of the Śruti; it is not reasonable for His word to be arbitrary.

This has also been demonstrated in the statement "the two selves have entered the cave" (*guhāṃ praviṣṭāvātmānau*), where it is shown that in the Ṛgvedic verse "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*), the Lord and the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) are intended.

Even when, according to the interpretation provided by the Paiṅgi Upaniṣad, the qualities (*sattva*) and the individual soul are said to be denoted in this verse, there is still no contradiction whatsoever.

How so? Here, the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*), which is perceived in each body through its identification with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the quality of being a sentient being—just like the apertures in a jar and the like—is denied [as the abode] on the grounds that it cannot be the abode of "Being" (*bhū*) and so forth.
However, that which is indicated as distinct from all bodies by means of its freedom from limiting adjuncts is the Supreme Self alone.

Just as the apertures in jars and the like, when indicated apart from their limiting adjuncts such as the jars themselves, are nothing other than the great space (*mahākāśa*), so too, since it is impossible for the individual soul to be anything other than the Supreme, the denial [of its being the abode] is not tenable.
Therefore, the negation of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth applies only to those who identify with limiting adjuncts such as the individual self (*mātra*).
Consequently, the Supreme Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
This very point is established by the sūtra itself: "Because of the mention of its attributes, [Brahman is that which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth]."
For this [verse], "In whom the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space," is recited in the midst of that very passage concerning the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*);
it is, however, introduced again for the sake of further elaboration.
The Infinite [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith.
The instrument [of knowledge].
They recite this: "But the Infinite (bhūman) indeed is what one should desire to understand; 'Venerable sir, I desire to understand the Infinite.
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite."
"Now, where one sees something else, hears something else, or cognizes something else—that is the finite," and so forth.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: could the *bhūman* (the Infinite) be the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or rather the Supreme Self?
Why the doubt? Because, first of all, the term *bhūman* denotes abundance.

Because of the traditional grammatical rule, "There is elision of the suffix *bahuc* and [the substitution of] *bhū* for *bahu*," it is remembered that the word *bhūman* ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). When there arises a specific desire to know what the nature of that abundance (*bahutva*) is, it appears from the proximity of the Sūtra— "Prāṇa, indeed, is greater than hope"— that *prāṇa* is *bhūman*.
Likewise, from the introduction of the context—“For I have heard from those like your reverence that one who knows the Self overcomes grief;
I, O Blessed One, am grieving; may your reverence carry me across to the further shore of grief”—it also appears that the *bhūman* is the Supreme Self.
In this regard, there arises a doubt as to which [interpretation] should be accepted as correct and which should be rejected.
What, then, is the conclusion reached? That the vital breath (prāṇa) is the "fullness" (bhūman). Why? Because we observe a succession of questions and answers regarding what is "more" (bhūyaḥ).
For instance: "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than name? and "Speech, indeed, is greater than name."

Likewise, there is a continuous flow of questions and answers regarding what is greater than speech, beginning with "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than speech? and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech," extending from name up to the vital breath (prāṇa).

However, no such question or answer is seen regarding anything greater than the vital breath, such as "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than the vital breath? or "Such-and-such, indeed, is greater than the vital breath."

Having explained in detail that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed greater than everything beginning with name and ending with hope—starting with "The vital breath, verily, is greater than hope"—and having authorized the status of one who perceives the vital breath as an "exceeding speaker" by saying, "One should say, 'I am an exceeding speaker,' and not deny it," [the text] then draws upon this state of being an exceeding speaker—which is the vow of the vital breath—in the passage, "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker who exceeds by means of the Truth. By thus introducing the "Fullness" (*bhūman*) through a succession beginning with Truth while not abandoning the vital breath, it is understood that [the text] considers the vital breath itself to be the Fullness.

But how, when the *prāṇa* is being explained as the *bhūman*, can the statement "where one sees nothing else," which is intended as a definition of the *bhūman*, be explained? It is said in reply: because in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), when the organs have been swallowed by the *prāṇa*, the cessation of activities such as seeing is observed, this definition—"where one sees nothing else"—is possible for the *prāṇa* as well.

And thus the Śruti, having described the state of deep sleep as the cessation of the activity of all the organs through the passage beginning with "he does not hear, he does not see," and then stating that "in this city, the one consisting of breath alone remains awake" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12), shows that the state of deep sleep has the breath as its primary element by declaring the waking of the fivefold breath within that very state.
Furthermore, that which is heard in scripture regarding the blissfulness of the Infinite—"That which is the Infinite is bliss"—is also not contradictory.
Because it is heard that bliss exists specifically in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) in the passage: "In this state, O Deva, he does not see dreams, and then there is bliss in this body";

and because the statement, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman), that is the Immortal," is also not contradictory with respect to the vital breath (prāṇa), since there is the scriptural text: "The vital breath, indeed, is the Immortal."

But how is it appropriate that this section begins with the desire to know the Self—expressed in the statement, "The knower of the Self overcomes grief"—for one who considers the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to be the plenitude (*bhūman*)? We reply: it is because the vital breath itself is intended here as the Self.

For instance, [the text] makes the vital breath the Self of all, saying, "The vital breath is indeed the father, the vital breath is the mother, the vital breath is the brother, the vital breath is the sister, the vital breath is the teacher, the vital breath is the Brahmin," and further, "Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub, so everything is fixed in this vital breath."
And because of the illustrations of being the self of all and of the nave of a wheel,
the state of being "much" (bhūman) in its expansive nature belongs to Prāṇa.
Therefore, it follows that Prāṇa is Bhūman.
Therefore, this is said: here, the Supreme Self alone must be the Bhūman, not the vital breath (prāṇa).
Why? Because of the teaching regarding that which is beyond the state of serene repose (saṃprasāda). "Serene repose" refers to the state of deep sleep.

Because of the etymological derivation that "in this one is perfectly serene" (*samyak prasīdati*), and because it is mentioned alongside the states of dreaming and waking in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, the term "perfect serenity" (*saṃprasāda*) here refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since it is the breath that remains awake during that state of perfect serenity.
The meaning is that [the Self] is taught as being superior to the vital breath.
If the vital breath (*prāṇa*) were indeed the "much" (*bhūman*), then it would have been taught immediately after that [name]; this would have been consistent.

For it is not the case that after [teaching] "name," one teaches "the much is name"; rather, something other than name, namely speech (*vāk*), is taught as distinct from name in the words, "Speech, verily, is more than name."
Likewise, in each instance, that which is taught as superior to speech and the other organs is indeed something different from them;
similarly, the "Plenum" (bhūman) taught as superior to the vital breath (prāṇa) must be something distinct from the vital breath.
But is it not the case that here there is no question, such as: "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than the vital breath?"?

Nor is there a reply stating, "There is indeed something greater than breath"; how then can it be said that the Bhūman is taught as being superior to breath? For we observe that the quality of being an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond), which is carried over in the subsequent passage, refers specifically to the sphere of breath: "But he indeed is an ativādin who speaks beyond by means of the True. Therefore, there is no teaching of anything superior to breath. To this, it is replied in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: First of all, it cannot be said that this is merely a carrying over of the quality of being an ativādin as pertaining to breath alone, because of the specific qualification: "He who speaks beyond by means of the True."
But surely this specific statement also must concern the vital breath (prāṇa) alone;
how so? Just as when it is said, "He is an Agnihotrin who speaks the truth," one does not become an Agnihotrin by speaking the truth;
by what then? Only by the Agnihotra sacrifice itself.

That speaking of truth, however, is stated as a specific qualification for the Agnihotrin; likewise, when it is said, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of truth," transcendental speech does not consist in the mere speaking of truth;
rather, by what? Precisely by the previously mentioned knowledge of Prāṇa.
We say that it is not the case that "speaking the truth" is intended as a special qualification for those who know the vital breath (prāṇa);
for that would entail abandoning the meaning of the scripture.
For by the scripture itself, speaking beyond [others] is understood here through the speaking of truth, in the words: "He who speaks beyond by means of truth—he truly speaks beyond."
There is no explicit mention of the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa) here; however, it might be connected by virtue of the context.
In that case, the direct scriptural statement (śruti) would have to be set aside in deference to the context.

Furthermore, the word "but" (*tu*) would not be appropriate for the purpose of excluding the subject under discussion [if it were merely a restatement], as in the passage, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally" (*eṣa tu vā ativadati*).
And the initiation of a new effort in the statement, "But truth alone must be sought to be known" (*satyaṃ tveva vijijñāsitavyam*), indicates the intention to speak of a different matter.

Therefore, this should be viewed as analogous to how, when the praise of a single Veda is the topic at hand, one says, "But he is a great Brāhmaṇa who studies the four Vedas," thereby praising the four-Veda scholar as something distinct from those who know only one Veda.
Nor is there a rule that a desire to express another meaning must necessarily take the form of a question and answer;
for the desire to express another meaning arises from the impossibility of a connection with the subject matter at hand.

In that context, having heard the instruction up to the point of "the end of life," Sanatkumāra himself further instructs Nārada, who had become silent, as follows: "That which is called 'speaking beyond' by means of the knowledge of the vital breath—which pertains to the unreal realm of modifications—is in fact not speaking beyond at all. But he indeed speaks beyond who speaks beyond by means of the Truth. In this passage, "Truth" (satya) refers to the Supreme Brahman, because it is of the nature of ultimate reality;
for another scriptural text states: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

To Nārada, who had been thus instructed and who approached him saying, "Venerable Sir, may I speak beyond the truth?", the teacher instructs him on the *bhūman* (the Infinite) through a succession of means beginning with knowledge.
It is understood that what was promised there as something to be spoken of as being superior to *prāṇa*—namely, the *satya* (Truth)—is precisely what is here called the *bhūman*.
Therefore, since there is an instruction on the *bhūman* as being superior to *prāṇa*, it follows that the *bhūman* must be the Supreme Self, distinct from *prāṇa*.
In this way, the commencement of this section for the purpose of investigating the Self will be justified.
Furthermore, the claim that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is intended here as the Self is also untenable;
for the vital breath does not possess the nature of the Self in its primary sense.
Furthermore, the cessation of sorrow does not exist apart from the knowledge of the Supreme Self, according to another Vedic text: "There is no other path for going.

And having begun with, "May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow," it concludes: "To him, whose impurities were washed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra showed the further shore of darkness.
Here, "darkness" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of sorrow and the like.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the instruction—even at the risk of one's life—it would not be said that the vital breath (prāṇa) is dependent on anything else;
for the Brāhmaṇa text states, "From the Self comes the vital breath.
And it will be shown that at the end of the section, the intention is to speak of the Supreme Self.
If it be argued that the "Bhūman" (the Infinite) is merely the vital breath (*prāṇa*), we say no;
for from the passage, "In what, O Venerable Sir, is he established? In his own greatness," up until the conclusion of the section, it is the Bhūman alone that is carried forward.
Furthermore, the nature of being "Bhūman"—which consists in vastness—is all the more appropriate for the Supreme Self, as it is the cause of all things.
And because of the logical consistency of the doctrine.

Moreover, those things which are designated as "plurality" (bhūman) are subsumed within the Supreme Self; for the text, "He does not see another, he does not hear another, he does not cognize another—that is plurality," makes known the absence of activities such as seeing and so forth in the state of plurality.

And this absence of activities such as seeing is understood to apply to the Supreme Self from other scriptural passages, such as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? and so on.

Furthermore, that absence of activities such as seeing which was mentioned regarding the state of deep sleep was stated with the intention of expressing the non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) of the Self alone, not with the intention of describing the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because this occurs within the context of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Moreover, the bliss (*sukha*) that was mentioned in that state was also stated with the intention of expressing that the Self itself is of the nature of bliss;
for it says: "This is his supreme bliss; other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss."

Here too, by rejecting conventional happiness with the words, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman) is bliss; there is no bliss in the small; the Plenum alone is bliss," [the text] shows that Brahman alone is the Plenum and the Bliss. Furthermore, the immortality mentioned in the passage, "That which is the Plenum is immortal," leads one to understand the Supreme Cause.

Because modifications are relative to immortality, and because of another scriptural passage stating, "Other than this, everything is perishable" (*ato 'nyad ārtam*), so it is that these attributes— truthfulness, being established in one's own glory, omnipresence, and being the self of all— which are heard in scripture, are appropriate only in the Supreme Self and not elsewhere. Therefore,
it is established that the *bhūman* (the Infinite) is the Supreme Self.
The Imperishable in the expanse of the sky.
