[The text continues: "In what, then, is the ether woven, warp and woof? He said: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare that this is indeed that Imperishable (akṣara), which is neither gross nor subtle," and so forth; thus the Imperishable is heard of in the scripture.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is the word "akṣara" used here to denote a phoneme (varṇa), or does it refer to the Supreme Lord?

In this regard, since the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) is well-known in common usage as referring to a syllable—as seen in such expressions as "the collection of akṣaras"—and since it is improper to override established usage; and furthermore, because in other scriptural passages such as "Oṃkāra alone is all this," even a syllable is determined to be the Self of all by virtue of being an object of meditation; thus, the conclusion reached is that the word "akṣara" refers to a syllable. To this, it is replied: The Supreme Self alone is denoted by the word "akṣara. Why? Because of its supporting everything up to the ether—that is, because it sustains the entire aggregate of effects beginning with the earth and ending with space.

For in that [passage], after stating that the entire collection of modifications beginning with earth—which are distributed across the three periods of time—is woven like warp and woof in space alone, as in "In space, indeed, all this is woven to and fro," and then introducing the Imperishable (akṣara) by means of the question, "In what, then, is space woven to and fro?", it concludes: "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, space is woven to and fro.
And this support of everything up to the ether is not possible for anything other than Brahman.
As for the statement, "The syllable Om is indeed all this," that too should be understood as being for the purpose of praise, because it is a means for the realization of Brahman.
That which does not perish (akṣara) and which pervades (aśnute) is the supreme Brahman itself, by virtue of its eternity and omnipresence.

[Objection: This might be so. If the support of everything up to the sky is admitted on the grounds that an effect is dependent upon a cause, then this is also possible for the proponent of Primordial Matter (pradhāna) as the cause. How, then, can the support of everything up to the sky lead to the realization of Brahman? To this, the author reads the answer: "And that [support] is because of the command. (Sūtra 1.3.10)
And that support of the sky's limits is the work of the Supreme Lord alone. Why? Because of His command.
For a command is heard here in such passages as: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart," and so forth.
And governance is the work of the Supreme Lord; governance does not belong to that which is insentient.
For there is no governance over objects such as jars on the part of insentient causes such as clay and the like. (First Chapter)
And because of the exclusion of other states.

Furthermore, because of the exclusion of any other entity (*anyabhāvavyāvṛtti*), Brahman alone is denoted by the word "Akṣara"; the supporting of everything up to the sky (*ambarāntadhṛti*) is its specific function, and not that of anything else.

What is this "exclusion of any other entity"? The existence of another is "other-existence" (*anyabhāva*); the exclusion from that is "exclusion of other-existence" (*anyabhāvavyāvṛtti*); [it is] because of that.

This is what is meant: since another entity than Brahman might here be suspected as being denoted by the word "akṣara," the scripture excludes that [other] akṣara which sustains everything up to the ether by stating its essential nature: "Now, this akṣara, O Gārgī, is unseen but the seer, unheard but the hearer, unthought but the thinker, unknown but the knower.
While the designation of being "unseen" and so forth is possible even for the Pradhāna, the designation of being the "seer" and so forth is not possible for it, because it is insentient.

Likewise, because of the negation of any distinction between selves in such passages as, "There is no seer other than this, there is no hearer other than this, there is no thinker other than this, there is no knower other than this," even the embodied self (śārīra) when possessed of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) cannot be denoted by the term "Lord" (īśvara).
Furthermore, because the possession of limiting adjuncts is negated in the passage, "It is without eyes, without ears, without speech,
without mind," for there can be no such thing as an embodied self that is devoid of limiting adjuncts.
Therefore, it is certain that the supreme Brahman alone is the Imperishable (akṣara).
Sūtra 1.3.13: He [is Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing.

Having introduced the subject with the words, "O Satyakāma, this syllable *oṃ* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the wise man, by means of this very support, attains one or the other," it is further heard [in the scripture]: "But he who meditates on the highest Person (*paraṃ puruṣam*) by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures (*trimātra*)... [and] "He is the object of the act of seeing" (*īkṣatikarma*).
Now, in this passage, is the higher Brahman taught as the object of meditation, or rather the lower?
Because it is stated that "by this very path one follows either the higher or the lower," a doubt arises. In this regard, the initial position is that this [Brahman] is the lower Brahman.

Why? Because it is said that the fruit for the knower of that [Brahman] is spatially limited, as expressed in the passages: "He becomes united with the heat in the sun" and "He is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman."
For it is not logical that one who knows the supreme Brahman should obtain a fruit limited by space, since the supreme Brahman is omnipresent.
But [one might object]: if the lower Brahman is accepted, the qualification "the other person" would be inappropriate.
This is not a fault, because the superiority of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established in relation to the body (piṇḍa);
such being the position reached, the following is stated in reply.
It is the Supreme Brahman alone that is taught here as the object to be manifested.
Why? Because of the designation of the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*);
"seeing" (*īkṣati*) means perceiving.
That which is pervaded by seeing is the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarma*);

there is a designation of this person to be meditated upon as the object of seeing in the remainder of the passage: "He sees the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings.
In that context, even an unreal thing can be the object of the act of meditation (*abhidhyāti*), because even that which is imagined through the mind is the object of the act of meditating.

However, in the world, it is observed that the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*) is indeed an existing entity; therefore, it is understood that this Supreme Self alone, which is the object of perfect vision, is designated here as the object of the act of seeing. This is established by the first chapter [of the *Brahmasūtra*]. And it is that very same [Self] who is recognized here as the one to be meditated upon by means of the two words "Supreme Person" (*parapuruṣa*).

[Objection: But has not the "highest person" (para-puruṣa) been mentioned in connection with meditation (abhidhyāna), whereas the "one higher than the highest" (parāt-para) is mentioned in connection with seeing (īkṣaṇa)?
How then can one be recognized as the other in the other context? To this it is replied: First of all, the two words "person" (puruṣa) are common to both cases.
Furthermore, in this instance, the "highest person" under discussion—which was to be meditated upon—is not being referred to by the term "mass of living beings" (jīva-ghana).
By this [phrase], it would follow that this Puruṣa who is to be seen as "higher than the high" must be something other [than the Self].
What, then, is meant by "the mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*)? It is said: *ghana* means a solid form; thus, a "mass characterized by life" is a *jīvaghana*.

Just like a lump of salt, that state of being a fragmentary individual (*khilyabhāva*) in the form of a living being belonging to the Supreme Self—which is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and which is "beyond" the objects and the senses—is here called the *jīvaghana*.

Another says: "He is led by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8). That world of Brahman, which was indicated in the immediately preceding passage and which is superior to all other worlds, is here called the "mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*). For, since a collection of all individual souls (*jīvas*)—who are surrounded by their instruments—is found in Hiraṇyagarbha, the resident of the world of Brahman who is the self of all instruments, the world of Brahman becomes the "mass of living beings.
Therefore, that Person who is beyond it—the Supreme Self, who is the object of the act of seeing—it is understood that He alone is also the object of the act of meditative reflection (*abhidhyāna*).
Furthermore, the qualification "the Supreme Person" (paraṃ puruṣam) is appropriate only if the Supreme Self (paramātman) is understood;

for the Supreme Person is indeed the Supreme Self, because there is nothing else whatsoever beyond Him, as another Vedic text states: "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal."

Furthermore, by distinguishing between the higher and the lower Brahman in the passage, "That which is Brahman is the syllable Om," and subsequently stating that the supreme Person is to be meditated upon by means of the syllable Om, the text leads us to understand that the supreme Person is indeed the highest Brahman.

Moreover, the statement regarding the fruit of liberation from evil—"Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he freed from evil"—indicates that the Supreme Self is the object of meditation here.

Now, as for what was said—that for one who meditates upon the Supreme Self, a fruit limited by space is not appropriate—it is considered as follows: for one who meditates upon the Supreme Self with the three-measured *oṃkāra* as a support, the fruit is the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), and through that, the gradual arising of perfect knowledge; thus, this will be intended as liberation by stages (*kramamukti*), and there is no fault.
The small one [is Brahman], on account of the subsequent [scriptural passages].

Now, the following passage is recited: "Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether (ākāśa). That which is inside that [ether] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. With regard to this, a doubt arises as to whether this ether heard of as being within the small lotus of the heart is the elemental ether, or the individual self (vijñānātman), or the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Whence arises this doubt? From the two words "ether" (ākāśa) and "city of Brahman" (brahmapura).
For this word "ether" is seen to be used both for the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) and for the supreme Brahman.
In that case, the doubt is whether the small (dahara) space must be the elemental ether itself, or whether it is the supreme Brahman.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "the city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*): does this refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), as in "as large as this space here [is], so large is that space within the heart; that is the city named Brahman," where the body is the city of that which is called Brahman? Or is it the city of the Supreme Brahman itself, such that it is the "city of Brahman"?
In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether the small space (*daharākāśa*) belongs to either the individual soul or the Supreme Brahman, who is the lord of the city.
In this regard, since the word "ether" (ākāśa) is conventionally established in the sense of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), it follows that the "small" (dahara) ether is indeed the elemental ether;
and its smallness is relative to the small abode [of the heart].

Furthermore, the relationship of comparison between the standard of comparison and the object compared—expressed in the phrase "this ether within the heart is as large as that"—is based on the distinction between the external and the internal.
Furthermore, heaven, earth, and so forth are contained within it, because space is one in its nature as the element of ether (*ākāśa*).
Alternatively, it might be concluded that the "small" (*dahara*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), on account of the term "city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*);
for this body, which is the city of the soul, is called the "city of Brahman" because it has been acquired by the soul through its own karma.
And by this [analogy], its designation by the word "Brahman" is established;
for the Supreme Brahman has no relationship with the body in the form of a master-and-possessor relation.
In that regard, it is observed that the owner of a city dwells in a portion of that city, just as a king [dwells in his capital].
Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) is conditioned by the mind (manas),
and since the mind is generally established in the heart, this abiding within the heart must belong to the soul alone;
its smallness (daharatva) also becomes intelligible for that very reason, as it is compared to the point of an awl.

The comparison with space and so forth will be intended to express non-difference from Brahman; moreover, it is not the small space that is heard of as being "to be sought" or "to be understood," because it is mentioned as a qualification of that which is within it, in the words, "that which is within it."
To this we reply: the Supreme Lord alone must be the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) here, not the elemental ether nor the individual soul (*jīva*).
Why? Because of the subsequent reasons found in the remainder of the passage.

For instance, regarding the small ether (daharākāśa) which was stated to be that which is to be sought after, there occurs a response preceded by an objection, beginning with "If they should say to him... and continuing, "What is there that is to be sought after, or what is to be understood? [The response] is as follows: "He should say: As vast as this external ether is, so vast is this ether within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it," and so forth.

In this context, by negating the smallness of the ether—which had attained smallness through its being contained within the lotus—by means of a comparison with the well-known [external] ether, it is understood that the status of the small ether as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is being negated.

Although the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the elemental ether, nevertheless, a comparison of that very thing with itself is not possible; thus, the suspicion that it refers to the elemental ether is removed.

Now, it was argued that even for a single ether, the relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison is possible through an imagined distinction between an external and an internal part.
This is not possible;
for this recourse to an imagined distinction is a desperate resort.

Moreover, even if one were to describe the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison by imagining a distinction, it would be untenable for the internal space to possess the same magnitude as external space, because the internal space is limited.
But surely, even for the Supreme Lord, a size equal to that of the ether is not tenable, because of another scriptural passage stating, "He is greater than the ether.
This is not a fault;
for [the present passage] serves to remove the smallness that would otherwise result from the context of being enclosed within the lotus. Chapter One.
Because the sentence is intent upon [the nature of] Brahman, it does not have the purpose of teaching [the existence of] space;
for if it were to teach both, the sentence would be split.
Furthermore, the containment of heaven, earth, and so forth within a single part of space that is merely imagined as being encircled by lotuses is not logically tenable.

"This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"—thus, both the nature of being the Self and qualities such as freedom from evil are not possible in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
Although the word "Self" can apply to the individual soul (*jīva*), nevertheless, for other reasons, even the suspicion that it refers to the *jīva* is removed.

For it is impossible to remove the smallness of the *jīva*—which is limited by its adjuncts (*upādhi*) and compared to the point of an awl—from the fact that it is contained within the lotus of the heart.
If it is argued that the omnipresence and other attributes of the individual soul (jīva) are intended to be predicated [of Brahman] with the desire to express its non-difference from Brahman;
then it is more logical that the omnipresence and other attributes of that very Brahman—by whose nature the soul's omnipresence and so forth are intended—are directly predicated [of itself].

As for the improper argument that, because the city is characterized by the soul in the phrase "the city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*), this city must belong to the soul alone as its master—just as a king is the master of a city—the soul must therefore reside in only one part of the city.

To this we reply: this "city of Brahman" (brahmapura) refers to the very city of that Supreme Brahman—namely, its real body—because the word "Brahman" has its primary meaning in reference to Him. Furthermore, He too has a connection with this city, because He is the locus of perception, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as: "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest mass of living beings," and "This Person dwells in the city within all cities. Thus, it is the Supreme Brahman who is intended here.
Or rather, according to the Sūtrabhāṣya, it is precisely within this city of the living self (jīvapura) that Brahman is perceived as being present, just as Viṣṇu is present in the Śālagrāma stone.

Having stated that actions have finite fruits—by saying, "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes"—the text then declares the infinite fruitfulness of the knowledge of the space within the heart under discussion: "But those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. This indicates its nature as the Supreme Self. As for what was said—that the small space (dahara-ākāśa) is taught as the object to be sought and understood because it is mentioned as a qualification of something else—that is not so.

To this we reply: if space were not stated as that which is to be sought after, then the demonstration of the nature of space—beginning with "As large as this space is, so large is this space within the heart"—would be untenable.

"But surely this [small ether] is taught only for the purpose of showing the existence of a reality residing within; for after raising the objection, 'If they should say: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace, and within it is a small ether; what is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand?"'—it is shown, at the time of the refutation, by beginning with the analogy of the ether, that heaven, earth, and so forth are contained within it.
This is not so;
for if that were the case, then that which is contained within—the heaven, earth, and so forth—would have been stated as that which is to be sought after and understood.

In that case, the remainder of the sentence would not be consistent. For, having drawn forth from the context the ether (ākāśa) which is the substratum for the resting of heaven, earth, and so on—as seen in the passage, "In this [ether] all desires are contained; this is the Self, free from evil"—the remainder of the sentence shows, by means of the word "and" (ca) signifying a conjunction, that both the Self which is the substratum of the desires and the desires themselves residing therein are what must be known: "But those who depart from here after having discovered the Self and these true desires... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6). Thus, the remainder of the sentence demonstrates this.

Therefore, it is understood that even at the beginning of the passage, it is the small ether itself—having the lotus of the heart as its locus—that is described as the object to be known, together with the earth and other elements contained within it, and with the true desires.
And on account of the reasons stated, it remains established that this is the Supreme Lord.
For it is so seen from both movement and sound, as well as from the inferential mark.
It has been stated that the small one within the lotus of the heart is the Supreme Lord because of subsequent reasons;
those very same subsequent reasons are now being elaborated upon.
For this reason as well, the small one is indeed the Supreme Lord.

Because in the supplementary passage of that day, the words "going" and "world" indicate the Supreme Lord alone, as it says: "All these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it.

Therein, having designated the previously mentioned small space (*dahara*) by the term "world of Brahman," the "going" toward that object—which is predicated of the individual souls denoted by the word "creatures"—leads to the conclusion that the small space is Brahman.

For thus, the daily departure of living beings toward Brahman during the state of deep sleep is observed in another scriptural passage, such as: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the True" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1). Even in common worldly usage, they say of one who is in a profound, sound sleep: "He has become Brahman," or "He has attained the state of Brahman.

Likewise, the term "Brahma-world" (brahmaloka), when applied here to the small [ether], removes any suspicion that it refers to the ether consisting of the individual soul (jīva) and leads to the understanding that this [small ether] is Brahman.

But would not the word "brahmaloka" also imply the world of Kamalāsana (Brahmā)? It would so imply it if it were derived through the function of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) as "the world of Brahmā.

However, when derived through the function of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that "brahmaloka" means "the world which is itself Brahman," it will lead one to understand the Supreme Brahman alone.
And this very daily journey to the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) is the indicative mark for accepting the word "brahmaloka" as functioning through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
For it is not possible to assume that these creatures go day after day to the effected world of Brahman known as Satyaloka.
And because its greatness is perceived in this [earth] through the word "ghṛta."
And for the reason of being the supporter, this "small" (dahara) one is indeed the Supreme Lord.

How so? Having introduced the subject with "In this, there is a small inner space," and having described the containment of everything within it by means of the analogy of space, and having applied the word "Self" (ātman) to that very same entity and taught its association with qualities such as freedom from sin, the text points back to that very same subject without departing from the context: "Now, that Self is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded.
In that passage, because of its grammatical coordination with the word "Self," "support" (vidhṛti) refers to the supporter.
The suffix *ktic* is used here in the active sense (*kartari*), according to grammatical tradition.

Just as in the world a dam (*setu*) is a supporter of the flow of water so that the excellence of the fields may not be confounded, even so this Self is the dam— the supporter— of these worlds, which are divided by distinctions such as the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth, as well as of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), for the sake of non-confusion, that is, for the sake of non-mixture.
Thus, in this present context, the text shows the greatness characterized by the supporting of the small [space].
And this greatness belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, as is known from another scriptural passage: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand supported," and so forth.

Likewise, in another certain statement regarding the Supreme Lord, it is heard: "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded."
Thus, for the reason of its being supported, this small space (dahara) is indeed the Supreme Lord.
And because of common renown.
For this reason as well, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is referred to by the words "the small [space] within this [heart], the ether" (daharo 'sminnantarākāśaḥ);

because the word "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known to denote the Supreme Lord, as seen in such scriptural usages as "He is indeed called Ākāśa, the sustainer of name and form" and "All these beings, verily, arise from the ether alone. However, the word "ether" is never observed to be used in reference to the individual soul (jīva).

However, it has been stated that the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), despite the well-known application of the term "ether" to it, must not be accepted [as the subject of the comparison], because of the impossibility of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, and so forth.
If it is argued that "he" refers to the other [the individual soul] because of its mention elsewhere, we say no, because of impossibility.

In the Sūtra-bhāṣya, it is argued that if, on the strength of the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the "small" one (*dahara*) were accepted as the Supreme Lord, then there exists for the other—the individual soul (*jīva*)—as well, a reference in its supplementary passage: "Now, he who, having risen from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form—he is the Self," so he said.

For here, because the word *saṃprasāda* is seen in another Vedic text to refer to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it is capable of bringing to mind the individual soul who possesses that state, and not any other entity.

Likewise, the emergence of the individual soul (jīva), which has the body as its support, from the body is possible, just as the emergence of air and other elements, which have space as their support, from space;

and just as in the world, although the word "space" (ākāśa) does not refer to the Supreme Lord, it is accepted as referring to the Supreme Lord in passages such as "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form," because of its association with the attributes of the Supreme Lord, so too will it be in reference to the individual soul.

If it be argued that, because of the reference to the "other" [the individual soul], it is that very soul which is spoken of in the passage, "The small [space] within this [heart] is the ether," this cannot be so;
why? Because of impossibility.
For the individual soul, being characterized by the conceit of limitation through adjuncts such as the intellect, could not be compared with the ether.
Furthermore, for one who does not identify with the attributes of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are not possible.
This has been explained in detail in the first *sūtra*;
however, it is brought up again here to dispel the suspicion that [the Self] might be something additional.
And he will state further on: "And the reference is for another purpose."
Thus ends the first chapter.
But [the Self] whose true nature has become manifest [is liberated], if [it is said to be] "from the north."

The suspicion that the individual soul (jīva) might be [the object of the teaching], which arose from the reference to the other [the eye], has been refuted on the grounds of impossibility. Now, however, a renewed suspicion regarding the individual soul is raised—like the rising again of one who was dead through the sprinkling of nectar—from the subsequent statement of Prajāpati. For there, having first promised that the Self, characterized by qualities such as being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpman*), is what must be sought and understood, he says, "This person who is seen in the eye, this is the Self," thereby pointing to the individual soul, the seer residing in the eye, as the Self.

Having repeatedly referred back to that very same subject with the words, "I shall explain this further to you," the text explains that it is the individual soul (jīva) itself in its various states, saying, "He who moves about in sleep being honored—this is the Self," and "When he is thus asleep, composed, serene, and knows no dream—this is the Self.
Furthermore, it shows that this very soul possesses qualities such as freedom from sin, stating, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."

Having observed the defect in the state of deep sleep—that "he indeed does not thus know himself at this time, thinking 'I am this,' nor these beings"—and having begun with the words, "I shall explain this very same [Self] to you further, and nothing other than this," the text, after first censuring the connection with the body, shows that the individual soul itself, having risen from the body, is the Supreme Person, stating: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form; he is the Supreme Person."
Therefore, there is indeed the possibility of the attributes of the Supreme Lord existing in the individual soul (jīva).
If someone should object that, for this reason, the phrase "the small ether within this" refers to the individual soul alone, we would say to him:
"But [it is] the one whose true nature has become manifest."
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view;

the meaning is that even from the subsequent passage, no suspicion regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) can arise here. Why? Because even there, it is the individual soul whose true nature has become manifest that is intended to be expressed.
"One whose true nature has become manifest" (āvirbhūtasvarūpa) means that his essential form has become manifest;
the term "jīva" (living being) is used here by way of referring to what was previously the case.

This is what is meant: having first pointed out the seer characterized by the eye with the words "He who is in the eye," and having then distinguished him from the body as the self through the *Udaraśarāva* Brāhmaṇa, the text repeatedly draws that very same seer forward as the subject to be explained with the words "But him alone, my dear... By means of the sequence of presenting the states of dream and deep sleep, it explains this individual soul (*jīva*) in its true nature as the Supreme Brahman—the ultimate reality—by saying, "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form"; it does not explain him in his state as an individual soul.
That supreme light which is heard of as that which is to be attained is the Supreme Brahman;
and it possesses attributes such as being free from sin and so forth.

That alone is the ultimate real nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), according to scriptural texts such as "That thou art," and not the other [nature] which is imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

For as long as one does not realize the Self—which is of the nature of immutable, eternal consciousness—as "I am Brahman," thereby dispelling the ignorance characterized by duality (such as the notion of a person in a post), so long does the state of being a *jīva* persist for the living soul.

However, when one is awakened by the Śruti, having been drawn away from the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect, [it declares]: "You are not the aggregate of body, senses, life-breaths, nor the intellect, nor even a transmigrating being; rather, you are that which is the Truth, the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness—*tat tvam asi* (That thou art)."

Then, having awakened to the Self whose nature is immutable and eternal, and rising up from this identification with the body and so forth, he becomes that very Self which is immutable and eternal; for according to such scriptural texts as, "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," that alone is his ultimate reality, by means of which, having risen from the body, he manifests in his own true form.

But how is it possible for its own form to be produced by itself in that which is eternally immutable? In the case of gold and the like, however, whose own forms are obscured by contact with other substances and whose specific characteristics are unmanifest, there may be a manifestation of their own form through purification by means of alkaline salts and so forth;
likewise, in the case of stars and the like, whose light is obscured during the day, there may be a manifestation of their own form at night when they are separated from the obscuring factor.
But no suppression of the soul's eternal light of consciousness by anything is possible, because it is non-contacting like space, and because that would contradict what is observed;
for seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing constitute the very nature of the individual soul (jīva),
and that nature is seen to be eternally perfected even when the soul has not yet emerged from the body.
For every living being conducts its worldly affairs by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing; otherwise, such conduct would be impossible.
If that [conduct] were to occur only after one has emerged from the body, then the observed conduct prior to that emergence would be contradicted.
Therefore, what is the nature of this "emergence from the body," and what is the nature of this "manifestation in one's own form"?

To this it is replied: Prior to the arising of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-vijñāna*), the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is the light of vision and so forth—becomes, as it were, non-discriminated from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations.
Just as the natural transparency and whiteness of a pure crystal appear, prior to the apprehension of discrimination, as if non-discriminated from limiting adjuncts such as red or blue;

yet, through the apprehension of discrimination produced by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the crystal is said to "emerge" in its own form of transparency and whiteness subsequent to that [apprehension], even though it was already exactly so before.

Likewise, for the individual soul (*jīva*) which exists as non-different from limiting adjuncts such as the body, its "rising up from the body" is the discriminative knowledge produced by scripture; and the "manifestation in its own nature," which is the fruit of that discriminative knowledge, is the realization of the nature of the absolute Self.

Similarly, it is through mere discrimination or non-discrimination that the Self possesses or lacks a body, as evidenced by the Vedic mantra: "The bodiless within bodies," and by the Smṛti: "Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, it neither acts nor is tainted," which records the absence of any distinction between being embodied and being bodiless.
Therefore, due to the absence of discriminative knowledge, its true nature remains unmanifest; yet, through discriminative knowledge, it is said that its true nature becomes manifest.
However, such things as manifestation and non-manifestation of the true nature itself are not possible, precisely because it is the very essence (svarūpa).
Thus, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is caused solely by false knowledge (mithyājñāna), and not by any real difference in substance.
Because there is no distinction in their being unattached like space.

And why should this be understood in this way? Because, having taught, "This person who is seen in the eye," it further teaches, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1) Chapter One.

If the seer who is well-known in the eye and is perceived as the seer were different from Brahman—which is characterized by immortality and fearlessness—then there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the immortal and fearless Brahman.
Nor is this reflected self (*praticchāyātmā*) indicated by the description "in the eye," for that would entail the consequence of Prajāpati being a speaker of falsehood.

Likewise, in the second section as well, in the passage "He who moves about being honored in a dream," the one indicated is not different from the seer, the person in the eye, mentioned in the first section; for the opening statement is, "I shall explain this very same [self] to you further."
Furthermore, one who has awakened declares the very thing seen in the dream, saying, "I saw an elephant in my dream today; I do not see it now.
Yet he recognizes that very same seer, saying, "I, who saw the dream, am the very same I who now see the waking state.

Similarly, in the third stage [of deep sleep], the text says, "Indeed, at this time he knows himself thus: 'I am this,' but he does not know these beings," thereby showing only the absence of specific cognition during the state of deep sleep, but not denying the knower.
As for the statement there, "He has gone to utter destruction," that too is intended to mean the destruction of specific cognitions, not the destruction of the cognizer;
for another scriptural passage states, "For there is no loss of the knower's knowledge, because of its imperishability."

Likewise, in the fourth section as well, having begun with "I shall explain this very same thing to you further, and not anything other than this," and then, through an elaborate exposition beginning with "O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal," [the text] rejects the connection with limiting adjuncts such as the body and shows that the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the term *saṃprasāda*, "attains its own true form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*), thereby demonstrating its attainment of the nature of Brahman; thus, it does not show the individual soul to be something other than the supreme Brahman, whose nature is immortal and fearless.

However, some, considering it improper to refer back to the individual soul (*jīva*) when the intention is to speak of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), interpret the passage as follows: "I shall explain further that very Self, characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin, which was indicated at the beginning of the section, saying 'this very one to you'. For them, the use of the pronoun *etam* ("this very one"), which relies on what is immediately proximate, would be set aside, and the force of the word *bhūyas* ("further") would be contradicted.
Because that which has been expressed by one synonym is not being expressed by another synonym;

furthermore, if Prajāpati were to explain something other than what was promised in the statement "But this very thing I shall explain to you," prior to the fourth section, he would incur the charge of being a deceiver.

Therefore, by the dissolution of that non-ultimate individual form—which is presented by ignorance, defiled by defects such as agency, enjoyership, passion, and hatred, and joined with manifold evils—one attains through knowledge the true nature of the Supreme Lord, which is the opposite of that [individual form] and characterized by qualities such as being free from sin, just as one perceives the rope and so forth upon the dissolution of the [illusory] snake and so forth.
However, other disputants, as well as some among our own followers, maintain that the individual form is indeed ultimate.

This *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra] has been commenced for the purpose of refuting all those views which, being opposed to right vision (*samyagdarśana*), maintain a plurality of selves; [it teaches that] there is only one Supreme Lord, the eternally immutable essence of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), who, through ignorance (*avidyā*) or illusion (*māyā*), appears as manifold—like a magician—and that there is no other essence of consciousness.

As for the fact that the Sūtrakāra, having raised the doubt regarding the individual soul (jīva) within the context of the statements concerning the Supreme Lord, refutes it with the words "Not so, on account of impossibility" (na asaṃbhavāt) and so forth—the intention there is this: in the one, immutable, eternal, unattached Supreme Self, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, the individual form of the soul—which is the opposite of that—is superimposed, like the appearance of a surface or a stain upon the sky.

[The Sūtrakāra] thus confirms the distinctness of the Supreme Self from the individual soul, thinking: "I shall remove that [superimposition] by means of passages intended to establish the oneness of the Self, supported by reasoning, and by refutations of dualism."
However, the text does not intend to establish that the individual soul (jīva) is something other than the Supreme;
rather, it merely restates the distinction between souls as well-known in the world and imagined through ignorance (avidyā).
For it is thought that in this way, the injunctions regarding ritual action, which proceed by restating the soul's natural status as agent and enjoyer, are not contradicted.

However, the scripture demonstrates that the very goal to be established is the identity of the self with the body of the Śāstra, through such passages as: "But the instruction is by means of the vision of the Śāstra, like that of Vāmadeva.
Furthermore, we have already described the resolution of the contradiction regarding the injunctions for ritual action based on the distinction between the enlightened and the unenlightened.
And, Nanda, the act of grasping is for the sake of another.

Now, as for this reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) shown in the supplementary portion of the passage concerning the "small" (*dahara*), beginning with "He who is this serene being" (*ya eṣa saṃprasādaḥ*) and so forth—if that were explained as referring to the Supreme Lord within the small space—it would follow that the passage is purposeless, since it would neither be an instruction for the meditation on the individual soul nor an instruction regarding the specific subject under discussion. Therefore, the author says: this reference to the individual soul has another purpose; it does not terminate in the essential nature of the individual soul.
What then? It terminates in the essential nature of the Supreme Lord. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya)

How so? The individual soul (jīva), denoted by the word "serenity" (saṃprasāda), having become the presiding lord over the cage of the body and senses during the activities of the waking state, and having experienced dreams constructed from the impressions (vāsanā) of those [activities] while moving through the channels (nāḍīs), becomes weary and, desiring a refuge, rises above the identification with both forms of the body. Then, in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), having attained the supreme Brahman—the supreme light denoted by the word "ether" (ākāśa)—and having abandoned the possession of specific cognitions, it manifests in its own true nature.

That supreme light which is to be attained by him, and by whose own nature he emerges manifest—that very Self, characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth, is the object of meditation; thus, this reference to the individual soul (jīva) is also consistent for those who maintain that the Supreme Lord is the subject of the discourse.
If it is argued that this is because of limited scriptural knowledge, that has already been answered.

As for what was said—that the smallness of the ether heard in the scriptural passage, "In this [city] is a small inner ether," is not possible in the case of the Supreme Lord, whereas smallness is appropriate for the individual soul (jīva) which is compared to the point of an awl—an answer to that must be stated. For the answer has already been given: relative smallness is indeed possible even in the case of the Supreme Lord, as stated in the sūtra: "If it be objected that [the Lord is] not [the subject here] because of his having a small abode and because of the designation of that [smallness], we say no, because he is to be meditated upon in such a way, and because [the comparison] is like the ether. (Brahma Sūtra 1.2.7).
He indicates that this very same solution is to be applied here as well.
Moreover, this smallness has been refuted by the Scripture itself, which compares it with the well-known space: "As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart."
First Chapter:
And because of the imitation of that [the sun].
They declare in the scripture: "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. This concludes the section.

In this regard, when there arises a doubt as to whether that which "shines after which all things shine, and by whose light all this is illumined" is some element of light (*tejodhātu*) or the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*), the initial position is that it is an element of light.
Why? Because of the denial of the shining of luminous bodies such as the sun and others.
For it is well known that things of the nature of light, such as the moon and the stars, do not shine during the day while the sun—which is itself of the nature of light—is shining.

Likewise, since all this— including the moon and the stars— does not shine when together with the sun, it is understood that the sun must be some entity whose very nature is light. Furthermore, the phenomenon of being outshone (anubhāna) is only possible for that which possesses the nature of light, because we observe imitation among things of a similar nature,
as in the expression, "he follows him who is walking."
Therefore, when it has been argued that "the element of fire (tejodhātu) must be something [else]," we reply: this Self must indeed be the Intelligent One (prājña).
Why? Because of imitation (anukṛti);
imitation means following after.
This "shining after" expressed in the passage, "Everything shines after Him alone as He shines," is possible only if the Prājña (the Supreme Self) is accepted;
for they declare the Prājña Self to be "of the nature of light and of true resolve.
On the other hand, it is well known that the sun and other luminaries shine after some element of light.
And because the fiery elements, such as the sun and others, are equal [in nature], there is no dependence on another fiery element which they might follow by shining;
for a lamp does not shine after another lamp.
As for what was said—that imitation is observed among things of a similar nature—this is not an absolute rule.
For even among things that possess distinct natures, imitation is observed;
just as a red-hot iron ball, which imitates fire, burns after the burning fire, or as earthly dust follows the blowing wind.
By the word "anukṛte" (in imitation), the author has indicated "anubhāna" (resonance).
And the phrase "of that" (tasya) indicates the fourth quarter of this verse:
"By its light all this shines. Furthermore, the manifestation of the sun and other luminaries being described as caused by that [light] points to the Self as the Prājña.
For they declare the Prājña Self in the passage: "The gods worship Him as the light of lights, as life, as immortality."
Furthermore, it is unestablished and contradictory to claim that the light of the sun and other luminaries shines by means of another light,
for one light is obstructed by another light.
Alternatively, this shining caused by that [Brahman] is not said to belong only to the sun and others enumerated in the verse.

What then? Because of the non-specific scriptural statement "all this," the manifestation of this entire collection of names, forms, actions, agents, and results is caused by the existence of the light of Brahman; just as the manifestation of the entire collection of forms is caused by the existence of the sun's light, so it is here.
Furthermore, by employing the word "there" in the passage "the sun does not shine there," the text shows that it refers to the subject under discussion.

And Brahman is the subject under discussion, as indicated by the passage, "In whom the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space are woven" (Muṇḍaka 2.2.5); and immediately thereafter, "In the supreme golden sheath, the stainless, partless Brahman... (Muṇḍaka 2.2.6).
"That is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know.
To the question, "How is it the light of lights?", this [verse] arises: "The sun does not shine there.

As for what was also said—that the negation of the shining of luminous bodies such as the sun is appropriate only if there is another luminous element, just as the sun [is the source] of others—[that is refuted by the following].
In that case, however, it has been established that no other element of fire is possible. Furthermore, the negation of their manifestation is appropriate even with respect to Brahman;
for whatever is perceived is perceived solely by means of the light of Brahman.

But Brahman is not perceived by means of another light, because its very nature is self-luminosity, such that the sun and other luminaries would shine within it; for Brahman reveals everything else, but Brahman is not revealed by anything else, according to such scriptural passages as, "By his own light he sits," and "He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped."
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti.
Moreover, this very nature of the wise Self is recorded in the Bhagavad Gītā: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines That;
that is My supreme abode, reaching which they do not return.
And: "The splendor residing in the sun which illumines the entire world..."
And also: "Know that which is in the moon and that which is in fire to be Mine."
"He is known from scripture alone. (Sūtra-bhāṣya) It is heard in the Śruti: "The person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self";
likewise: "The person the size of a thumb is like a smokeless light;
he is the lord of what has been and what is to be; he is the same today and the same tomorrow—this indeed is that."
In this regard, there arises a doubt: as for this person (puruṣa) the size of a thumb who is mentioned as the agent, is he the individual self (vijñānātman) or the supreme self (paramātman)?
On this point, the initial position is that it must be the individual self because of the instruction regarding its limited size.
For it is not possible for the Supreme Self, which is infinite in length and breadth, to possess the size of a thumb;
however, because the individual self (vijñānātman) possesses limiting adjuncts (upādhi), its being thumb-sized is possible through a certain figurative conception.
And from Smṛti: "Then [he saw] one bound by a noose, fallen under control, emerging from the body of Satyavat..."
Regarding the statement, "Yama forcibly drew out the person the size of a thumb," it is certainly not possible for the Supreme Lord to be drawn out by Yama by force;
therefore, in that context, the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) of thumb-size is established.
When this [prima facie] position has been reached, the following is stated: this person measured as thumb-sized must indeed be the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of the words, "the ruler of what has been and what is to be.
For no one other than the Supreme Lord possesses unbounded sovereignty over the past and the future.
Furthermore, the phrase "this indeed is that" connects here the subject under discussion with that which was previously asked about.
"This indeed is that," meaning that which was asked as "Brahman";

for it was Brahman that was asked here in the passage: "Tell me that Brahman which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, and other than what has been and what is to be."

"From the word itself"—that is, from the scriptural statement of the name alone, it is understood that the Supreme Lord is the one denoted by the term "Īśāna. But how can there be an instruction regarding the size of the omnipresent Supreme Self? To this we reply: "But [the measurement is] with reference to the heart, because [the scripture] has humans as its intended audience."

Even though the Supreme Self is omnipresent, this measurement of being "the size of a thumb" is stated with reference to its abiding within the heart; it is like the space, which is said to be "the size of a joint of a bamboo" with reference to that specific location.
For it is not possible for the Supreme Self, which is beyond all measure, to be literally the size of a thumb.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that no other being than the Supreme Self can be understood here on account of terms such as "Īśāna" (the Ruler) and others.

Now, an objection is raised: since the hearts differ according to each individual living being, the size of the thumb cannot be established even with reference to them. To this, the answer is given: "Because the qualification belongs to human beings.
For although the scripture applies without distinction, it actually confers eligibility upon human beings alone.

Because of their capacity, because of their desire, because they are not excluded, and because of the scriptural injunctions regarding initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth—this has been explained in the section on qualification (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the body of human beings has a fixed dimension;
and by virtue of proportionality, their heart also has a fixed dimension, measuring exactly one thumb-breadth.

Therefore, because the scripture has humans as its qualified audience, it is appropriate that the Supreme Self is described as being the size of a thumb, with reference to its abiding within the human heart.

As for the argument that, on account of the teaching regarding its limited size and because of Smṛti, this one the size of a thumb must be understood as a transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) alone—that is answered by the point that, just as in passages such as "That is the Self, That art thou," this teaching of Brahman-hood is imparted concerning the transmigrating soul itself while it remains the size of a thumb. Thus it is said in the Sūtra-bhāṣya.

For the operation of the Vedānta texts is indeed twofold: in some places it is intent upon defining the nature of the supreme Self (paramātman); in others, it is intent upon teaching the identity of the individual self (vijñānātman) with the supreme Self.
Here, the identity of the individual self with the supreme Self is being taught.
No one possesses the size of a thumb.
He will clarify this very point further: "The person the size of a thumb is the inner self, eternally seated in the hearts of men.
One should draw him forth from one's own body with fortitude, as one extracts a stalk from a reed."
"One should know that as pure, immortal consciousness."
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] even beyond that [the path of knowledge exists], because it is possible.
It has been stated that the scriptural mention of [the self] being "the size of a thumb" is with reference to the human heart, because the scripture has humans as its qualified audience;
in connection with that, this is now said:
Certainly, the scripture does have humans as its qualified audience.

However, there is no restriction here in this inquiry into the knowledge of Brahman that it applies to humans alone. The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the scripture qualifies those who are above those humans, namely the gods and others as well.
Why? Because it is possible.
For the grounds for eligibility, such as desire and so forth, are indeed possible even for them;
among these, desire directed toward liberation is possible even for gods and others, arising from considerations such as the impermanence of the splendors belonging to the realm of transformations.

Likewise, their capacity [for action] is also possible, because it is understood from mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), epics, purāṇas, and common worldly usage that they possess embodied forms;
nor is there any prohibition against them;
nor can their eligibility for rites be set aside by the scriptural injunction regarding initiation (upanayana). Thus ends the first chapter.
Because study is for the purpose of learning the Veda, and because those [sages] possessed the Veda through their own intuitive revelation;

moreover, it shows that they undertook student-life (*brahmacarya*) and so forth for the sake of acquiring knowledge: "For a hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student with Prajāpati," and "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa."
"Teach me, O Blessed One, the Brahman," and so forth. Furthermore,

as for the reason given for the lack of qualification for ritual acts— that "it is not for the gods, because there is no other deity [to be worshipped by them]," and "not for the seers, because there is no lineage of seers"—
that does not apply to the case of knowledge (*vidyā*).

There is no specific task for the rivers to perform by Indra’s command while they are being authorized for the sciences (vidyās); nor is there any such requirement for Bhṛgu and others on account of their belonging to the same gotras as Bhṛgu and so forth.

Therefore, by whom can the eligibility of the gods and others for the sciences be prevented? Even if the gods and others are eligible, the scriptural statement regarding the "thumb-sized" (aṅguṣṭhamātra) person would not be contradicted, as it refers to the thumb of the individual [god] himself.
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various [results].

This might be so: if the qualification of gods and others for the sciences were asserted by accepting that they possess bodies and so forth, then—because of their corporeality—their presence in person would have to be accepted as a constituent part of the ritual, just as in the case of the officiating priests and others.
And in that case, there would be a contradiction regarding the ritual;
for the status of Indra and others as constituents of the sacrifice through their personal presence is not observed.
If it is argued that this is not possible because it is impossible for a single Indra to be present in his own form simultaneously at many sacrifices, we reply: there is no such contradiction.
Why? Because of the assumption of multiple forms.
It is possible for a single divine being to assume multiple forms simultaneously.

How is this understood? From scriptural revelation (*darśana*). For instance, having introduced the question "How many gods are there? with the answer "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three," and then, in response to the inquiry "Which are they?", the Śruti declares: "These are merely their powers; there are indeed only thirty-three gods. Thus, the scripture demonstrates that each individual divine self possesses multiple forms simultaneously.

Likewise, by means of the sequence of subsuming the thirty-three gods within the six, and so on, the text—by asking "Which one is the single god? and answering "Prāṇa"—demonstrates that the gods have the singular form of Prāṇa, thereby showing that this very same single Prāṇa possesses multiple forms simultaneously.
Similarly, Smṛti also states: "O bull among the Bharatas, having attained power, a yogin may indeed create many bodies for himself and traverse the earth with them all."

"He may obtain sense-objects by some [powers] and perform severe austerity by others; and he may again contract them, just as the sun contracts its multitude of rays"—this kind of passage shows that even for yogins who have attained powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness), there is the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies; how much more so, then, for the gods who are perfected from birth? And because the assumption of multiple forms is possible, a single deity, having divided itself into many forms, simultaneously becomes a subordinate part (*aṅga*) in many sacrifices.

And it is logical that [the Lord] is not seen by others due to His possession of powers such as invisibility (*antardhāna*). There is another explanation for the sūtra-phrase "because various attainments are observed" (*anekapratipatter darśanāt*): even among those possessing bodies, various modes of attainment are observed in injunctions concerning subordinate status (*aṅgabhāva*).

In some cases, even a single embodied entity does not simultaneously enter into the state of being a constituent part in multiple places, just as a single Brahmin is not fed simultaneously by many people who are feeding him; and in other cases, even a single embodied entity does enter into the state of being a constituent part in multiple places simultaneously, just as a single Brahmin is saluted simultaneously by many people who are saluting him.

Similarly here, since a sacrifice consists of the act of relinquishing [an offering] after having designated [a recipient], many people may simultaneously relinquish their respective substances while designating a single embodied deity; thus, even though the gods possess bodies, nothing whatsoever is contradicted regarding their ritual action.
If it be argued that [the world] is sound, we say no; because it originates from this [Brahman], as established by both perception and inference.
Granted that no contradiction regarding action might arise if one were to admit that gods and others possess bodies;
however, a contradiction would indeed arise in the case of the Word (śabda).
How so? For it was established that the authority of the Veda rests upon its independence, by relying on the innate connection between the word and its meaning.

Now, if it is argued that a deity possessing a body, even if admitted, might—by virtue of its sovereign power—consume sacrificial offerings connected to multiple rites simultaneously, nevertheless, due to its possession of a body, it would be subject to birth and death like ourselves and others. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the established authority of Vedic words, since this occurs while the eternal relationship between the eternal word and its eternal meaning is being perceived. If this is said, we reply: this contradiction also does not exist. Why? Because of the "origination" [of the world] from that, as stated in the Sūtra and its commentary.
For it is precisely from the Vedic word that the world originates.

In the passage, "From whom the origin, etc., of this world [proceeds]," it was determined that the world has its origin in Brahman; how then can it be said here that it has its origin in the Word (Śabda)? Moreover, even if the origin of this [world] from the Vedic word were admitted, how would the contradiction regarding the Word be resolved by that much? For these entities—the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, and Maruts—are indeed non-eternal, because they possess the quality of having an origin.

And if that [the world] were eternal, by what could the non-eternality of the Vedic words denoting it, such as "Vasu" and so forth, be prevented? For it is well known in the world that when a son is born to Devadatta, the name Yajñadatta is given to him;

therefore, if it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction regarding the word, we say no, because we observe the eternity of the relationship between the meaning and words such as "cow" (go) and others.
For it is not the case that because individual instances such as cows and the like are subject to origination, their generic forms (ākṛti) must also be subject to origination.
Indeed, it is only the individual instances of substances, qualities, and actions that originate, not their generic forms.

Furthermore, the relationship of words is with generic forms, not with individual instances, because it is impossible to grasp the relationship [of a word] to individual instances due to their infinity.

Even though individual instances arise, because the generic forms (*ākṛti*) are eternal, no contradiction is observed in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*). Likewise, it should be understood that even if the arising of individual instances such as the gods is admitted, no contradiction exists in the case of words such as "Vasu," because their generic forms are eternal. Furthermore, the specific generic form of the gods and others—possessing embodied bodies—is established from the *mantras*, *arthavādas*, and other sources. *First Adhyāya*
This is to be understood from the context.
Alternatively, words such as "Indra" and so forth are based on their connection with specific positions, just like the word "general" (senāpati) and others.
Consequently, whoever occupies a particular position is designated by the corresponding term such as "Indra," and thus no fault arises.
And this "origination from speech" is not stated with the intention of [speech] being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), as is the case with [the world's] origination from Brahman.

How then? It is said that "there is origination from it" because, while the eternal word exists in the form of the signifier (*vācaka*) and possesses an eternal connection with its object, there is the production of individual objects (*arthavyakti*) capable of being engaged with through verbal usage.
But how is it understood that the world originates from the word? By means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

For direct revelation (śruti) is immediate perception, because it is independent with respect to its authority; whereas tradition (smṛti) is inference, because it is dependent with respect to its authority;
for both of them show that creation is preceded by the Word.

"‘Eta’—with this Prajāpati created the gods; ‘asu’—with this, human beings; ‘indavaḥ’—with this, the ancestors; ‘tiraḥ pavitram’—with this, the cups (grahas); ‘āśavaḥ’—with this, the hymn (stotra); ‘viśvāni’—with this, the recitation (śastra); and ‘abhi saubhaga’—with this, other creatures," so says the Śruti.

Likewise, elsewhere as well, in passages such as "He [Brahman] united with Speech through the mind," creation preceded by sound is heard here and there. Smṛti also states: "The beginningless and endless, eternal Speech was emitted by the Self-existent One."

"In the beginning, [there was] the divine Veda-made [speech], from which all activities proceed"; this "emission" (utsarga) of speech must also be understood as consisting in the initiation of the tradition, since no other kind of emission is possible for that which is without beginning or end; likewise: "[It is the source] of the names and forms of beings, and of the setting in motion of actions. (Sūtra-bhāṣya).
"In the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned [the world] from the very words of the Veda";
and also: "But he, in the beginning, fashioned separately for all beings their names and their actions, as well as their distinct conditions, from the very words of the Veda."
Moreover, it is evident to all of us that when one intends to perform a certain action, one first recollects the word expressive of that action and only thereafter performs the action;
likewise, it is understood that for Prajāpati, the creator, the Vedic words appeared in his mind prior to creation, and subsequently he created the objects corresponding to them.
Thus, the Śruti—"He uttered 'Bhūḥ', he created the earth"—and similar passages show that the worlds such as Bhūḥ were created from the very words like 'Bhūḥ' which had appeared in his mind.
Furthermore, with reference to what kind of sound is this "origination from sound" being stated? He says: "The *sphoṭa*.

For, on the view that [sound consists of] phonemes (*varṇa*), because they arise and perish, it would be untenable to say that the manifestation of gods and other beings originates from eternal sounds;
moreover, phonemes arise and perish, since they are perceived differently and yet again with each utterance.

For instance, even when a particular person is not visible, he is specifically identified merely by hearing the sound of his recitation, such that one determines: "This is Devadatta who is studying," or "This is Yajñadatta who is studying.
Furthermore, this perception of difference regarding the phonemes is not a false cognition, because there is no subverting cognition to contradict it.
Moreover, it is not logical that the comprehension of meaning should arise from the phonemes alone.
For each individual phoneme cannot convey the meaning, because of the possibility of deviation;
nor is there a cognition of a collection of phonemes, because phonemes occur in a temporal sequence.

If it should be argued that the final phoneme, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, will cause the meaning to be understood, that is not so;

for a word causes the understanding of an object only when it is itself perceived, depending as it does upon the prior apprehension of the relationship [between the word and its meaning], just like smoke and other such signs.
However, there is no perception of the final phoneme as being accompanied by the mental impressions produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, because those impressions are imperceptible.

If it is argued that the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, will cause the meaning to be understood, this is not so; for even the recollection, which is the effect of those impressions, occurs sequentially.
Therefore, the *sphoṭa* alone is the word.

And that [word], when the seed of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the cognition of each individual phoneme reaches its full maturation through the cognition of the final phoneme, suddenly manifests to the cognizer as the object of a single cognition.
Nor is this single cognition a memory whose objects are the phonemes, because since the phonemes are many, it is impossible for them to be the object of a single cognition.
Furthermore, because it is recognized (*pratyabhijñāyamāna*) at every utterance, it is eternal; for the cognition of difference has the phonemes as its object.
Therefore, from that eternal *sphoṭa*, which is of the nature of sound and is the signifier, the world—which consists of actions, factors of action, and results—arises as the signified.
"But it is the phonemes themselves that constitute the word," says the venerable Upavarṣa.
Now, it was argued that phonemes are subject to arising and perishing;
that is not so, because of the recognition that "these are those very same [phonemes]."

If it is argued that recognition occurs due to similarity, as in the case of [growing] hair and so forth, we say no; for it is impossible for recognition to be sublated by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that recognition is caused by the generic form (*ākṛti*), we say no.
Because there is recognition of the individual [letter].

For if, at each pronunciation, distinct individual manifestations of the phonemes were perceived—just as distinct individuals such as cows are perceived—then that recognition would have to be based on a generic form (*ākṛti*);
but this is not the case.
For it is indeed the individual phonemes themselves that are recognized at each utterance;
for the cognition is "the word 'cow' has been uttered twice," and not "two words 'cow' have been uttered."

Now, it was argued that phonemes are indeed perceived as distinct due to differences in their utterance, since a distinction is perceived merely from hearing the sounds of study by Devadatta and Yajñadatta; to this, it is replied: when there is a certain recognition regarding the phonemes, then—given that phonemes are manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions (of the air)—this diverse cognition regarding the phonemes is caused by the diversity of the manifestors, not by the nature of the phonemes themselves. Furthermore, even by one who maintains that phonemes are individuals, universals (ākṛtis) of phonemes must be postulated for the sake of establishing recognition.

And in those cases, one must admit that the cognition of difference is caused by external adjuncts (*paropādhika*); therefore, it is simpler to assume that the cognition of difference resides only in the individual phonetic manifestations (*varṇavyakti*) while the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is based on their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
And this very recognition is the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) of the cognition of difference regarding the phonemes.

For how could a single *ga*-sound, while being uttered by many people at the same time, simultaneously possess multiple forms—namely, as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), nasalized (*sānunāsika*), and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*)?
Alternatively, there is no fault [in our position] if this perception of difference is caused by the sound (*dhvani*) and not by the phoneme (*varṇa*).

But what is this thing called "sound" (*dhvani*)? It is that which enters the path of hearing for one listening from a distance who does not yet perceive the distinction between the phonemes. Chapter One.
And as one draws near [to the sound], one perceives distinctions among the phonemes (varṇa) such as sharpness, softness, and so forth;

the specific qualities such as the acute accent (udātta) and others are based on those [distinctions], not based on the intrinsic nature of the phonemes themselves, because phonemes are recognized as identical in every utterance.
This being the case, these cognitions of acute (*udātta*) and other accents will indeed have a real objective basis (*sālambana*).

Otherwise, since phonemes (*varṇa*) are recognized as being without distinction, the specific qualities such as acuteness would have to be imagined as produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*).

However, because conjunctions and disjunctions are not themselves perceptible, their dependent distinctions cannot be determined in relation to the phonemes. Therefore, these cognitions of acute and other accents would necessarily be without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
Moreover, one should not insist that there is a difference in phonemes—which are recognized as being the same—on account of distinctions such as high pitch (*udātta*) and so forth;
for it is impossible for one thing to be differentiated by the differentiation of another thing that itself remains undifferentiated.
Indeed, people do not consider a genus to be different because of the difference between individual instances.
Since the comprehension of meaning is possible from the phonemes themselves, the postulation of *sphoṭa* is purposeless.

If it is argued: "I do not postulate a *sphoṭa*; rather, I perceive it directly, because it manifests instantaneously in a cognition in which impressions have been deposited by the apprehension of each individual phoneme," we say: no, for even this cognition has the phonemes as its object.
This single cognition which occurs after the apprehension of each individual phoneme has all the phonemes as its object, not some other entity.
How is this known? Because even in this cognition, the phonemes such as *ga* persist, whereas phonemes such as *da* do not.

For if the sphoṭa, as an entity distinct from the *ga*-phoneme and others, were the object of this cognition, then just as the *da*-phonemes and so forth would be excluded from it, the *ga*-phonemes and others likewise would be excluded from this cognition.
But that is not the case;
therefore, this single cognition is merely a memory whose object is the phonemes.

Now, it was argued that because phonemes are manifold, they cannot logically be the object of a single cognition; to that we reply: it is possible for even a plurality to be the object of a single cognition, as is seen in cases such as "a row," "a forest," "an army," "ten," "a hundred," and "a thousand."

As for the cognition that "this word 'gauḥ' (cow) is one," that is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), based on the delimitation of a single meaning among many phonemes (*varṇa*), just like the cognitions of a forest, an army, and so forth.

Here he says: if the phonemes themselves, by appearing collectively as the object of a single cognition, were the word (*pada*), then there would be no apprehension of specific words in cases such as *jārā*, *rājā*, *kaḥ*, and *pika*;
for those very same phonemes appear identically in each of these instances.

To this we reply: even though there is a simultaneous recollection of all the phonemes, just as ants ascend to the cognition of a "line" only by following a specific order, so too will the phonemes ascend to the cognition of a "word" only by following a specific order.
Thus, although the phonemes themselves remain unchanged, the apprehension of distinct words produced by the distinction of their order is not contradictory.

In the linguistic usage of elders, these phonemes (*varṇas*), being assisted by their sequential order and having acquired a relationship with specific meanings, appear in exactly the same form in one's own usage within a cognition that reflects upon them as a whole immediately after the apprehension of each individual phoneme; thus, they will cause those respective meanings to be understood without error. For the proponents of phonemes (*varṇavādins*), this is a simpler hypothesis. However, for the proponents of the *sphoṭa*, there is both the loss of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved; for these phonemes, while being apprehended in sequence, [are said to manifest the word-sound]. (First Chapter)
The view that the phonemes manifest the sphoṭa, and that the sphoṭa in turn manifests the meaning, would be a more cumbersome hypothesis.

Moreover, even if it were the case that different phonemes arise with each utterance, nevertheless, since one must necessarily admit the existence of universals of phonemes as the objective basis for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the process of conveying meaning which has been established for the individual phonemes must be transferred to those universals.
Consequently, there is no contradiction in the view that the manifestation of individual entities such as gods proceeds from eternal words.
And for this very reason, there is eternality.

Since it has been established that the Veda is eternal because no author is remembered, an objection was raised regarding its contradiction with the admission that individual beings such as gods originate [from it]. This was resolved by the statement, "Because [the world] originates from that. Now, he further strengthens that very established eternity of the Veda with the words, "And for this very reason, there is eternality.
