For this very reason—because the world, consisting of gods and others of fixed forms, originates from the words of the Veda—the eternality of the Vedic words must also be understood.

And likewise, a Vedic mantra states: "By means of sacrifice, they found the path of speech; they discovered it entered among the seers. This shows that speech was already present and was subsequently discovered. Furthermore, Vedavyāsa records this very same fact: "At the end of the age, the great seers, authorized by the Self-existent One himself, recovered through austerity the Vedas along with the Itihāsas which had disappeared."

"And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even though there is a recurrence [of creation], on account of the observation [of such recurrence] and of tradition. (Sūtra-bhāṣya) Now, it might be argued: if the individual manifestations of gods and so forth were to arise and cease in a continuous series, just like the manifestations of animals and so forth, then—due to the non-interruption of the practical usage consisting of the designator, the designated, and the designation—the contradiction regarding the word would be resolved by the permanence of the relationship [between word and meaning]. But when, as the declarations of Śruti and Smṛti state, the entire triple world, having abandoned its names and forms, dissolves without residue and a new one comes into being, how then can there be no contradiction?
In this regard, it is stated: "Because names and forms are the same.
Even then, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra must first be accepted;
for the Teacher will establish the beginninglessness of saṃsāra in the passage: "And it is both logical and observed."

And just as in beginningless *saṃsāra*, despite hearing of dissolution and origination like sleep and waking, there is no contradiction in worldly activity because the subsequent waking is like the previous waking; so too should it be understood regarding the origination and dissolution of different cosmic cycles (*kalpa*).

Furthermore, the dissolution and origination [of the world] are heard of in relation to sleep and waking: "When, sleeping, he sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this very breath (prāṇa). Then speech merges into it along with all names; the eye merges into it along with all forms; the ear merges into it along with all sounds; the mind merges into it along with all thoughts. When he awakes, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from this Self all the vital breaths (prāṇas) emerge, each to its own abode; from the breaths the gods, and from the gods the worlds."

It might be argued as follows: [the case of] deep sleep is not contradictory because the continuity of the activities of other persons is not interrupted, and because for one who has awakened from deep sleep, it is possible to reconnect with the activities of the previous waking state;

however, in the case of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there is a disparity because all worldly activity is cut off, and just as with the activities of another birth, it is impossible to reconnect with the activities of a previous cosmic cycle (*kalpa*).

This is not a fault. Even though the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) destroys all worldly activity, it is possible for lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others to reconnect with the activities of a previous *kalpa* through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Although ordinary living beings are not seen to reconnect with the activities of a previous birth, nevertheless, the case of these lords must not be treated like that of ordinary beings.

For, although there is no difference in their status as living beings, it is observed that among those ranging from humans down to plants, the obstruction of knowledge, power, and so forth becomes increasingly greater at each successive stage.

Likewise, among those beginning with humans and ending with Hiraṇyagarbha, the manifestation of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth becomes increasingly greater as one moves higher; thus, the supreme sovereignty heard of in the Śruti, Smṛti, and traditional discourses regarding those who appear at the beginning of every kalpa cannot be denied.

Therefore, for the Lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others—who have performed preeminent knowledge and action throughout past kalpas, who appear at the beginning of the present kalpa, and who are favored by the Supreme Lord—it is possible to connect with the worldly transactions of a previous kalpa, just like one waking from sleep. Thus says the Śruti: "I, seeking liberation, take refuge in that God who alone creates Brahmā in the beginning and imparts the Vedas to him; He is the Light of the Self's intellect."

And Śaunaka and others record in their Sūtra-bhāṣya: "The *dāśataya* hymns were seen by seers beginning with Madhucchandas. Likewise, for each Veda, the seers of the sections (*kāṇḍarṣi*) and so forth are recorded in tradition. Scripture also shows that the performance of rites must be preceded by knowledge of the seers: "He who, not knowing the seer, the metre, the deity, and the Brāhmaṇa of a mantra, performs a sacrifice or teaches it, strikes against a pillar or falls into a pit," and having begun thus, it concludes: "Therefore, one should know these [four] regarding every mantra."
Dharma is prescribed for the attainment of happiness by living beings, and adharma is prohibited for the avoidance of suffering.

Furthermore, attachment and aversion have as their objects visible and traditionally revealed (ānuśravika) pleasure and pain, not objects of a different nature. Therefore, each successive creation, being produced as the fruit of dharma and adharma, is produced as one that resembles the preceding creation.
And there is a Smṛti [text] which says: "Whatever actions those beings performed in a previous creation, those very same they take up again and again when being created."

"For the violent and the non-violent, the mild and the cruel, the righteous and the unrighteous, the truthful and the false—they enter into that by which they are permeated; therefore, that which is pleasing to each becomes theirs.
Furthermore, even as this world dissolves, it dissolves only with its power remaining.

And it arises solely from a causal potency (*śakti*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being causeless. Furthermore, it is not possible to postulate potencies that possess multiple forms.

Therefore, in this beginningless cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), the regularity of the continuous streams of worlds such as the earth and others, the continuous streams of groups of living beings characterized as gods, animals, and humans,

and the fixed arrangement of the fruits of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) must be understood as being like the necessity of the relationship between the sense organs and their objects;

for it is impossible to imagine that the worldly process— beginning with the connection between sense organs and their objects— could be different in every dissolution (*pratisarga*), as if there were a sixth sense organ and its corresponding object.

And for this reason—because all world-ages (*kalpa*) possess identical linguistic conventions and because the Lords (*īśvara*) are capable of reconnecting with the conventions of other ages—the individual entities (*viśeṣa*) manifest at each new creation with exactly the same names and forms.

Since they possess identical names and forms, even when the cyclic recurrence of the world characterized by great creation and great dissolution is admitted, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the authority of the Word (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) and other means of knowledge.
Scripture and tradition both demonstrate this identity of names and forms: "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon just as before."

"Both heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and then the sky"—the meaning is that just as the world, beginning with the sun and moon, was fashioned in the previous kalpa, so too did the Supreme Lord fashion it in this kalpa.
Likewise: "Agni, indeed, desired."

"May I be an eater of food among the gods"—thus [thinking], he offered this cake on eight potsherds to Agni and the Kṛttikās. In this injunction for the *nakṣatreṣṭi* sacrifice, one should cite such scriptural passages which demonstrate the identity of name and form between the Agni who performed the offering and the Agni to whom the offering was made. Smṛti also states: "The names of the ṛṣis and those visions found in the Vedas..."

At the end of the night, the Unborn One bestows upon those very beings the same [conditions] they were born with; just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear again and again in their cycle,
so too do those same states of being reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas.

Just as those who possessed [certain] conceits in the past were [designated] by their names and forms, so too are the present gods [to be understood]; for the gods of the past are [known] by their past forms and names—such passages of this kind are to be observed.
Jaimini [holds that there is] no entitlement [to the knowledge of Brahman] for those such as the Madhukas, because of the impossibility [of their performing the required rituals].

The proposition that even gods and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is here being reconsidered. The teacher Jaimini considers that gods and others lack such qualification;
why? Because it is impossible in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and others.

For if qualification were admitted for the knowledge of Brahman, then, since there is no distinction in their being forms of knowledge, qualification would have to be admitted for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations as well.
But this is not possible;
how so? In the passage, "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," human beings would have to meditate upon the sun by superimposing the nature of honey upon it.

For if the gods and others were admitted to be worshippers, how could Āditya worship another Āditya? Furthermore, after enumerating the five nectars (amṛtas), beginning with the red [color], which depend upon Āditya, and teaching that the five groups of gods—the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas—subsist respectively upon those respective nectars, the text shows the attainment of the greatness of the Vasus and others for those who know the nectars subsisted upon by the Vasus and so forth, through such passages as: "He who thus knows this nectar becomes one of the Vasus themselves and, with Agni as his mouth, being satisfied by seeing this very nectar... and so on.

Furthermore, whom else among the Vasus and others could the Vasus and their peers—who subsist on nectar—possibly recognize as such? Or what other majesty of the Vasus and others could they possibly desire to attain? Likewise, in meditations upon the self of the deities, such as "Fire is one foot, wind is one foot, the sun is one foot, the quarters are one foot" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.2), and "Wind, indeed, is the absorber," and "The sun is Brahman—this is the instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), it is not possible for those very deities themselves to have the qualification [for such meditation].

Likewise, even in those meditations connected with sages, such as "These two, Gautama and Bharadvāja—this one is indeed Gautama, this one is Bharadvāja," and so forth, it is not possible for those very sages themselves to have the qualification [to perform them].
Furthermore, why is there no qualification for the gods and others? Because [the deities] exist within the luminaries.

That which is this circle of light, revolving through day and night, illuminates the world; it is to this that words denoting deities, such as "Āditya" (the Sun) and others, are applied, both because of common worldly usage and because of the established sense of the complementary passages [of the Vedas].

Furthermore, it is impossible to conceive of this circle of light as having a connection with a body consisting of a heart and so forth, or with consciousness, desire, and the like, since it is understood to be insentient, like clay and other such material objects.
By this, Agni and the others have been explained.

It might be argued that this fault does not apply because the fact that gods and others possess bodies and so forth is understood from mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), histories (itihāsas), purāṇas, and common worldly usage. To this we reply:
"No. First of all, there is no such thing as "worldly usage" that exists as an independent means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
An object is said to be "well-known from the world" only when it is already established by means of valid cognitions such as perception and the like, whose objects are non-erroneous.
Furthermore, none of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception and the rest, applies here.
Since even the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are of human origin, they require another basis for their authority.

Moreover, the explanatory passages (arthavādas), being intended for the purpose of praise within a single syntactical unit with an injunction, do not independently establish the existence of the embodied forms and other attributes of the gods and so forth.

Furthermore, they declare that even mantras, though enjoined by the Śruti and other means and integrated into ritual performance for the purpose of denotation, are not a source of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding any factual matter;
therefore, there is no eligibility for gods and others [to perform Vedic rites].
But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] that there is indeed an existence [of the soul after death], for it exists.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view.

The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, maintains that there is eligibility for gods and others as well. Although eligibility is impossible in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations which involve a mixture of deities and so forth, nevertheless, it is possible in the case of pure Brahma-vidyā; for eligibility depends upon factors such as desire, capability, and the absence of prohibitions.
Nor should the qualification be set aside even in cases where it is possible, merely because it is impossible in some instances.
For among humans as well, it is not the case that all—such as Brāhmaṇas and others—are qualified for all [sacrifices] like the Rājasūya;
the same principle that applies there will apply here as well.

Furthermore, with reference to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is scriptural evidence (*liṅgadarśana*) indicating the eligibility of the gods, such as: "Of the gods, whoever awakened to that, he indeed became that; likewise among the seers (*ṛṣis*), and likewise among men" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.2); "They said: 'Come, let us search for that Self, by searching for which one obtains all worlds and all desires'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1);
and "Indra, indeed, went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the Asuras," and so forth.
There is also Smṛti evidence, such as the dialogue between the Gandharva and Yājñavalkya, and others.

As for what was also stated, "And because [the deities] exist in the light," we reply: even those words denoting deities such as Āditya and others, which have the light and so forth as their object, designate specific divine selves endowed with consciousness and possessed of lordly power (aiśvarya) and other attributes, because they are treated as such in the mantras, arthavādas, and other texts.
By virtue of their possession of lordly power, the deities have the capacity to abide in the form of the light and so forth, and to assume various bodies at will.
For it is heard in the *Subrahmaṇyā* explanatory passage: "Medhātithi’s ram"—namely, "Indra, having become a ram, carried off Medhātithi, the descendant of Kaṇva.
And it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The Sun, having become a man, approached Kuntī.
Furthermore, even in the case of clay and other such materials, conscious presiding deities are admitted.
This is because we observe such statements as "the earth spoke" and "the waters spoke.
Furthermore, the insentience of the elemental substrates (bhūtadhātu), such as light and so forth, even when they exist in forms like the sun and others, is accepted;
however, it has been stated that the presiding deities (devatātmānaḥ) are sentient, based on their activity in the context of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavāda), and so on.

Regarding what was stated—that because the Mantras and Arthavādas have other purposes, they lack the capacity to reveal the corporeal form and other attributes of the deities—we reply: for it is perception and non-perception that are the causes for establishing existence and non-existence, not whether something has another purpose or not.
For instance, even one who has set out for another purpose perceives and acknowledges that grass, leaves, and so forth, which have fallen on the path, truly exist.
To this it is said: the comparison is unequal.
For in that case, there exists a perceptual cognition directed toward objects such as grass and leaves, by means of which their existence is established;

here, however, since the explanatory passage (arthavāda) forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction for the sake of praise, it is impossible to determine a separate cognitive activity directed toward a historical fact.
For when a great sentence conveys a meaning, there is no separate conveyance of meaning by an intermediate sentence;

just as in the sentence containing the negative particle, "One should not drink liquor" (*na surāṃ pibet*), because of the connection of three words, only the single meaning of the prohibition of drinking liquor is understood, and not also an injunction to drink liquor resulting from the connection of the two words "one should drink liquor" (*surāṃ pibet*). To this it is replied: the illustration is unequal.
It is appropriate that, in the prohibition of drinking liquor, there is no apprehension of an intermediate sentence-meaning because the syntactical connection of the words is unitary;

however, in the case of an injunction and its explanatory passage (arthavāda), the words situated in the arthavāda first attain a separate syntactical connection concerning a historical event, and subsequently, by virtue of the requirement for purposefulness (kaimarthyavaśena), they freely serve as eulogies of the injunction.

For just as in the injunction "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," there is a connection between the words "to Vāyu" (*vāyavya*) and so forth—which reside within the injunctive statement—and the injunction itself, it is not the case for these words occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own portion; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity. For it does not occur that "Vāyu should sacrifice," nor "the swiftest deity should sacrifice," and so on.
By proclaiming the nature of the wind (*vāyu*), however, they establish an intermediate connection and thus praise the injunction that "this ritual has such-and-such a deity.
Therefore,

when an intermediate sentence-meaning falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) proceeds by way of restating (*anuvāda*) that [already known] fact.

Where there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there it is a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*). But where neither of those two [contradiction or lack of other means] exists, should one assume it is a figurative statement due to the absence of another means of valid cognition, or rather, because of the non-contradiction with another means of valid cognition, should it be taken as a statement of an existing fact (*vidyamānārthavāda*)? Those who rely on perception must resort to it as a statement of an existing fact, not as a figurative restatement. By this, the mantra is also explained.
Moreover, the essential nature of Indra and the other deities is required by the injunctions themselves which enjoin oblations to those deities;
for it is impossible to conceive of Indra and the others in the mind if they are devoid of a specific form,
and it is impossible to offer an oblation to a particular deity unless that deity has been mentally represented.
And it is declared: "One should meditate upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken up when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Nor is it possible for the mere word to be the actual nature of the object, because of the difference between the word and its meaning.
Therefore, it is not proper to reject the nature of Indra and the other deities as it is understood from mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) by means of the authority of the word alone.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas as well, being rooted in mantras and arthavādas, are capable of establishing the corporeal form of deities and so forth by means of the method already explained;
they may also be rooted in perception and other means of knowledge,
for that which is imperceptible to us was indeed perceptible to those of ancient times.
Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛtis that Vyāsa and others engaged in direct dealings with gods and other beings.
He who should say that the ancients lacked the capacity to deal with gods and others—just as people today do not—would be denying the manifold variety of the world;

he would be saying that there was never at any other time a universal sovereign Kṣatriya, just as there is none now, and thereby he would obstruct the injunctions for the Rājasūya and other sacrifices.

Moreover, he would be asserting that even at other times, as now, the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) were largely unsettled; consequently, he would render the scripture (*śāstra*) which establishes those regulations purposeless.
Therefore, by virtue of the excellence of their merit (*dharmotkarṣa*), the ancients conversed directly with gods and others.
Furthermore, they record in their tradition: "Through the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), there is communion with the desired deity," and so forth.
Furthermore, yoga—which is recorded in tradition as having the attainment of powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) as its fruit—cannot be rejected on the basis of mere audacity;

for scripture proclaims the greatness of yoga: "When the fivefold quality of yoga has arisen from earth, water, fire, air, and ether, and is fully operative, there is neither disease, nor old age, nor death for him who has attained a body made of the fire of yoga."
It is not appropriate to compare the power of the sages—who were seers of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas—with our own power. Therefore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas possess a foundation.
Furthermore, when it is possible [to find a basis], it is not right to determine that worldly renown is without foundation.
Therefore, it is established that the understanding of gods and others as possessing embodied forms is derived from the mantras and other sources.
Consequently, since the presence of desire for liberation and other such qualifications is possible, the eligibility of gods and others for the knowledge of Brahman is also established.
Furthermore, the scriptural accounts of gradual liberation are likewise rendered consistent with this view.
For it is indicated by the hearing of that disrespect toward Śuka and by his rushing toward him.
First Chapter.

Just as, having set aside the restriction that human beings alone are qualified [for Vedic study], it was stated that gods and others also possess qualification for the knowledge [of Brahman], so too this section is commenced to remove the following doubt: might there not likewise be a qualification for a Śūdra by setting aside the restriction that only the twice-born are qualified? This is the purpose of the present section.
In this regard, it is first established that even a Śūdra may have the qualification [for knowledge];

for both the desire [to know] and the capacity [to practice] are possible in him, and because no prohibition is heard such as "therefore a Śūdra is unfit for sacrifice," there is likewise no prohibition stating "a Śūdra is unfit for knowledge.
Furthermore, the reason for his lack of qualification for ritual acts—namely, his lack of sacred fires (anagnitva)—does not serve as a disqualification for his qualification for knowledge.
For knowledge cannot be understood by one who is devoid of the Āhavanīya and other sacrificial fires.
Moreover, there exists a scriptural indicative mark (*liṅga*) that supports the eligibility of Śūdras;

for in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the text refers to Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, who was desirous of hearing, using the word "Śūdra": "Come, O Śūdra! Let this [knowledge] be yours alone, together with the cattle."
Furthermore, Vidura and others, though born from a Śūdra womb, are recorded in tradition as being endowed with distinguished knowledge.

Therefore, when it is argued that a Śūdra is entitled to the study of knowledge (vidyā), we reply: there is no entitlement for a Śūdra because of the absence of Vedic study. For only one who has studied the Veda and understood its meaning is entitled to engage with the contents of the Veda.
Furthermore, there is no study of the Veda for a Śūdra,

because the study of the Veda is preceded by the initiation ceremony (upanayana), and that initiation ceremony pertains only to the three [higher] castes. As for the desire for knowledge, that cannot be a cause for entitlement in the absence of the capacity [to perform the rites].

Furthermore, mere worldly capacity is not the sole cause for eligibility (*adhikāra*), because in the case of a scriptural subject matter, scriptural capacity is required; and scriptural capacity has already been excluded by the refutation [of the possibility] of Vedic study [for Śūdras].

As for the statement, "A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice," that indicates his lack of entitlement even to knowledge (*vidyā*), because it is based on a logical principle (*nyāya*); and since that logical principle is common [to both cases].
Furthermore, as for the fact that you consider the hearing of the word "Śūdra" in the Saṃvarga-vidyā to be an indicative mark (liṅga), it is not an indicative mark;
for there is an absence of logical justification (nyāya).
Indeed, the observation of an indicative mark becomes illuminative only when it is supported by logical reasoning.
And there is no logical justification for this;
at best, this word "Śūdra" might authorize a Śūdra only for that single Saṃvarga-vidyā, because it occurs in that specific context, but not for all meditations.
However, because it occurs within an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or illustrative passage), this [text] is not capable of authorizing a Śūdra in any case whatsoever.
Moreover, it is possible to apply this word "Śūdra" to the subject under discussion;

how so? It is explained as follows: from this speech of the swan, "O Janaka, why do you speak of him, who is such a person, as if he were Raikva with the cart?", a fever arose in Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa upon hearing his own lack of respect.

It is understood that the seer Raikva indicated her by this word "Śūdra" in order to demonstrate his own lack of direct knowledge [of her identity], since a Śūdra by birth has no entitlement [to such instruction].
But how, it may be asked, is the grief that arose indicated by the word "Śūdra"? It is said: he is called "Śūdra" because of running (√dru) toward that grief;
for he ran toward the grief, or was run toward by the grief, or ran toward Raikva with grief—thus he is "Śūdra."
Because the meaning derived from the etymological components is possible, whereas the conventional meaning is impossible;
and this very meaning is indeed observed in this narrative.
Sūtra 1.3.35:
And because his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from a subsequent indicative mark [in the form of] Caitraratha.
For this reason as well, Jānaśruti was not a Śūdra by birth;

for his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from the examination of the context and from the indicative mark (liṅga) found in the subsequent mention of him alongside Caitraratha Abhipratārin, who was a Kṣatriya. Indeed, in the subsequent supplementary portion of the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the Kṣatriya Caitraratha Abhipratārin is mentioned: "Then a student of sacred knowledge saw Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni while they were being served by a cook."
And the status of being the priest of Caitrarathi Abhipratārin is to be understood as resulting from his connection with the Kāpeyas;
for the connection of Citraratha with the Kāpeyas is known from the text, "The Kāpeyas indeed officiated at the sacrifice for Citraratha.
And generally, those of the same lineage serve as priests for those of the same lineage.

Furthermore, from the statement, "And from him was born one named Caiprarathi, a lord of the Kṣatras," his status as a Kṣatriya is to be understood through the comprehension of his being a *kṣatrapati*.
Thus, Jānaśruti’s mention alongside that Kṣatriya Abhipratārin in the same Saṃvarga-vidyā indicates his own Kṣatriya status;
for generally, mentions occur among those who are similar.
Furthermore, from the sending of the steward and other indications of his possession of sovereignty, Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya is understood;
therefore, a Śūdra has no qualification [for this knowledge].

Because of the reference to purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and the expression of the desire for that state [of being initiated], [the Śūdra has no eligibility]. In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, it is stated: "For this reason also, the Śūdra has no eligibility: because in the sections concerning knowledge (*vidyā*), purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*) are referred to—such as 'He initiated him,' 'He approached him, saying, "Teach me, O Venerable One!'"', and 'Devoted to Brahman, established in Brahman, seeking the Supreme Brahman, they approached the venerable Pippalāda with fuel in their hands, thinking, "He indeed will tell us all that.
Furthermore, by the phrase 'without having initiated them,' the very necessity of initiation is demonstrated."
Furthermore, the absence of sacramental rites for the Śūdra is declared, because of the traditional teaching that he is "of a single birth" as the fourth caste (*caturtho varṇa ekajātiḥ*),
and because of such statements as, "There is no sin in a Śūdra, nor does he deserve sacramental rites."
And because activity proceeds toward the determination of the non-existence of that [object].
For this reason as well, there is no eligibility for a Śūdra:

because, when Jābāla’s lack of Śūdra-status was determined by his speaking the truth, Gautama proceeded to initiate and instruct him, as indicated by the scriptural sign: "A Brāhmaṇa ought not to speak thus; bring the fuel, my dear; I will lead you [to the teacher]; you have not departed from the truth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
Because the Smṛti prohibits [them] from hearing, studying, and understanding the meaning [of the Veda].
For this reason as well, the Śūdra has no entitlement:
because there is a prohibition against his hearing, studying, and understanding the meaning [of the Veda] according to the Smṛti.

It is recorded in the Smṛti that for the Śūdra there is a prohibition against hearing the Veda, a prohibition against studying the Veda, and a prohibition against knowing its meaning and performing its injunctions.
First, there is the prohibition against hearing [the Veda]: "Now, if he should overhear this [Veda] while it is being recited, his ears are to be filled with molten lead and lac";
and also: "A Śūdra is indeed a cemetery; therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."

For this very reason, there is a prohibition against study; for how could one who must not even study in the presence of [such a person] study what has not been heard? Moreover, it is said that in the utterance of the Veda there is the cutting off of the tongue, and in its retention, the breaking up of the body.

For this very reason, there is a prohibition regarding the knowledge of meaning and its practical application for those [lacking qualification], as expressed in the injunctions: "One should not give instruction to a Śūdra," and "Study, sacrifice, and giving belong to the twice-born.

However, in the case of those such as Vidura and Dharmavyādha, for whom the arising of knowledge occurs by virtue of purificatory rites performed in previous lives, their attainment of the fruit cannot be prohibited, because knowledge has an invariable result.

Furthermore, since the Smṛti records the eligibility of all four castes for the acquisition of Itihāsas and Purāṇas in the passage, "One should cause the four castes to hear [them]," [the attainment of knowledge by others is not barred].
It is established, however, that there is no entitlement for Śūdras preceded by the Vedas.
Because of trembling.
The incidental discussion regarding the scope of the subject matter is concluded; we shall now proceed with the investigation of the meaning of the sentence under consideration itself:
"Whatever there is in this world, all trembles in fear of Him; from Him, everything that breathes issues forth."
"A great terror, a source of dread;
those who know this raised thunderbolt become immortal"—this statement is characterized by its conformity with the meaning of the verbal root *ej*, "to tremble.

In this passage, it is heard that this entire world vibrates resting upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that there is a certain great cause of fear designated by the word "thunderbolt" which is raised, and that through the knowledge of that, one attains immortality.

In this regard, since there is a lack of understanding as to what that *prāṇa* is and what that terrifying *vajra* is, when an inquiry is undertaken, it is first suggested— on account of common usage— that the *prāṇa* is the fivefold-functioning wind (*vāyu*), and by common usage alone, the *vajra* would be the thunderbolt (*aśani*). Furthermore, this greatness of the wind is being proclaimed here.
How so? This entire world, being established upon the fivefold wind designated as "prāṇa," vibrates;
and it is solely on account of the wind that the great, terrifying thunderbolt is raised up.
For they declare that when the wind transforms itself into the form of Parjanya (the rain-god), lightning, thunder, rain, and thunderbolts likewise transform.

If it be argued that this immortality results from the air alone—since another scriptural passage states, "Air indeed is the individual, air is the collective; he who knows this conquers recurrent death"—and therefore it must be understood here as air, we reply: it is Brahman alone that is to be understood here.
Why? Because of the consideration of what precedes and follows;
for in the preceding and following portions of the text, we perceive that Brahman alone is being pointed out.
How then could we suddenly understand Vāyu to be pointed out here in the middle? First, in the preceding passage: "That indeed is the Bright, that is Brahman, that is called the Immortal."
In that [passage], Brahman is indicated by the words: "Upon it all worlds are supported; no one transcends it.

It is understood that this very same [Brahman] is indicated here as well, because of its proximity and because of the recognition of its being the support of the worlds in the phrase, "The whole world trembles in breath" (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, this word *prāṇa* is used for the Supreme Self alone, as in the Sūtra: "The breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*). This is the first chapter.
Because it is seen [in scripture]. This quality of being the impeller also belongs only to the Supreme Self, not to the mere air (vāyu);
and thus it has been said: "No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna)."
"But by the other they live, on whom these two depend";
and later as well, "From fear of Him the fire burns, from fear the sun shines;

from fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run on"—here Brahman alone will be indicated, not Vāyu, because it is stated that the entire world, including Vāyu, has Brahman as the cause of its fear.

Therefore, it is understood that here too, by virtue of proximity and because the quality of being a cause of fear is recognized in the phrase "a great terror, a raised thunderbolt," that very same [Brahman] is indicated;
furthermore, this word "thunderbolt" (vajra) is employed on account of the commonality of being a cause of fear.

Just as people invariably comply with the commands of a king or similar authority out of fear, thinking, "May this raised thunderbolt not fall upon my very head if I do not carry out his instruction," so too this world—consisting of fire, wind, the sun, and so forth—proceeds in its respective functions according to fixed law, fearing this very Brahman. Thus, Brahman is described as being like a terrifying thunderbolt. Accordingly, there is another scriptural passage concerning Brahman: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows;
out of fear the sun rises."
"From fear of him, fire and Indra,
and death as the fifth, run away.
From the hearing of the fruit of immortality as well, it is understood that this is Brahman.

Immortality is attained through the knowledge of Brahman, according to the scriptural verse: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. As for the mention of immortality in some instances arising from the knowledge of Vāyu, that is merely relative;

for in that very context, after defining the Supreme Self by introducing a different topic, it is stated, "Everything else is perishable," thereby declaring that Vāyu and the rest are subject to destruction.
The determination that the Supreme Self is the subject here is also established by the context,

because the Supreme Self was the one questioned in the passage: "Tell me that which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, and other than the past and the future."
Because of the perception of light.
It is heard in scripture: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form.
Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the word "light" refers to the physical light that is the object of the eye and dispels darkness, or whether it refers to the supreme Brahman.
What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That the word "light" (jyotis) refers to physical light alone. Why? Because the word "light" is conventionally established (rūḍha) in that sense.
For in the case of the sūtra "Light [is Brahman] because of the mention of feet," the word "light" abandons its own primary meaning and refers to Brahman only due to the context.
And here, unlike that [other case], no reason for abandoning its own primary meaning is observed.

Thus, in the section on the channels (nāḍī-khaṇḍa), it is stated regarding the seeker of liberation: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays," thereby declaring the attainment of the sun.
Therefore, it is well-established that the word *jyotis* denotes light. This being the position reached, we reply: the word *jyotis* refers to the Supreme Brahman alone.
Why?
Because it is observed that [the subject] continues as something to be discussed within the context of the *darśana* (vision/insight) in the first chapter.

Because at the beginning of the section, the Self characterized by qualities such as "having evil shaken off" (*apahatapāpmatva*) is declared as that which is to be sought and that which is to be known through inquiry;
because of the subsequent connection [in the text] stating, "I shall explain this very same one to you further";
and because the attainment of light is described here for the sake of bodilessness (*aśarīratā*), as in the passage: "Verily, when one exists as bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him."
Furthermore, a state other than that of Brahman is impossible for one who is bodiless;
this is also indicated by the qualification, "That highest light, that supreme person.
As for the claim that the seeker of liberation is said to reach the sun, that is not ultimate liberation, because it involves movement and departure from the body.
For we shall explain that in absolute liberation there is neither going nor departure.
Space [is distinct from the Self], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth.
It is heard in scripture: "That which is called space (ākāśa) is the revealer of name and form; that within which these two are contained is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the word *ākāśa* refers to Brahman—which is distinct from other things—or to the well-known elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), it is appropriate to accept the latter [in this context]. This is the section concerning Ether (*Ākāśādhikaraṇa*).

Because the word "ether" (ākāśa) is conventionally established in that sense [of elemental ether], because the carrying out of names and forms can be attributed to it by way of providing space, and because no clear mark of Brahman—such as being the creator—is heard here; such being the position reached, this is said: the supreme Brahman alone must be the one denoted by the word "ether" here. Why? Because of the designation of its being something other than that [elemental ether] and so forth.
"That which is between them is Brahman"—thus the text designates space as something distinct from name and form;
yet nothing other than Brahman can possibly exist as something distinct from name and form, since the entire aggregate of effects is manifested solely through name and form.

Furthermore, the unrestricted manifestation of name and form cannot belong to anyone other than Brahman, for scripture declares that Brahman is the agent: "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms."
But surely the individual soul (jīva) also possesses the perceptible capacity for directing name and form?
Certainly it does;
however, what is intended here is non-difference.
And by the very mention of "conducting name-and-form" (nāmarūpa-nirvahaṇa), the marks of Brahman such as being the creator and so forth are thereby expressed.
Furthermore, the phrases "That is Brahman," "That is the Immortal," and "That is the Self" are marks of the doctrine of Brahman.
This [present discussion] is an elaboration of the very same point made in the sūtra: "Ether [is Brahman], because of its marks."
On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure.
The phrase "on account of designation" (vyapadeśāt) is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].

In the sixth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with "Which is the Self? It is that which consists of cognition among the vital breaths, the light within the heart, the person who is the lord of deep sleep," an extensive section concerning the Self is composed.
Is this passage intended merely to describe the nature of the transmigrating self (*saṃsārin*), or is it intended to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating self?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it concerns only the nature of the transmigrating self.
Why? Because of the opening and the conclusion; for in the opening [it says], "He who... (First Chapter).
Because of the characteristic mark of the embodied soul in the passage, "consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths" (vijñānamaya prāṇeṣu);
because that [mark] is not abandoned in the conclusion, "He indeed is this great unborn Self who is this one consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths";

and because even in the middle [of the text], it is that very same [Self] which is elaborated upon by the presentation of states such as waking and so forth—this being the position reached, we reply: this passage has the Supreme Lord alone as its subject of instruction, and does not have the mere description of the embodied soul as its purpose.
Why? Because the Supreme Lord is designated as distinct from the embodied soul (śārīra) both in deep sleep and at the time of departure.

First, regarding deep sleep, [the text] designates the Supreme Lord as distinct from the embodied soul, stating: "This person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman), knows nothing external nor internal.
In this context, the "person" is the embodied soul, because it possesses the quality of being a knower.
Because when there is the possibility of external and internal experience, there is the possibility of its negation;
the "Prājña" is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), because he is eternally inseparable from the wisdom characterized by omniscience.

Likewise, even regarding departure [from the body], the text designates the Supreme Lord as distinct from the individual soul (jīva): "This embodied self, mounted by the Prājña Self, goes forth uttering [the sound]."
Even in that case, the embodied one would be the individual soul (jīva) because of its ownership of the body;
however, the "wise one" (prājña) is none other than the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, it is understood from the designation of difference during deep sleep and departure that the Supreme Lord alone is intended here.

As for what was stated—that because of the characteristic marks of the embodied soul at the beginning, middle, and end, this passage refers to that [embodied soul]—to this we reply: First, regarding the introduction, in the words "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths," it is not the nature of the transmigrating soul that is intended to be expressed.
Rather, having referred back to the nature of the transmigrating soul, it intends to express its identity with the Supreme Brahman;
for the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "It thinks, as it were; it moves, as it were" is seen to be intent upon the negation of the attributes of the transmigrating soul.
Likewise, in the conclusion as well, [the text] concludes exactly as it began: "That indeed is this great unborn Self, which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths.

The meaning is that he who is perceived here as the transmigrating being consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths—that very one is the great unborn Self, the Supreme Lord himself, as has been established by us.

As for one who, because of the presentation of states such as waking and dreaming in the middle [of the passage], thinks that the nature of the transmigrating being is intended to be taught, he, having been set out toward the eastern direction, would end up heading toward the western direction.

For the Teacher does not intend to describe the state of possessing conditions or being subject to transmigratory existence by introducing states such as those of other Buddhas; rather, he intends to show the absence of conditions and the state of being free from transmigratory existence.

How is this understood? Because at every step the disciple asks, "Tell me further for the sake of liberation alone," and at every step the Teacher replies, "He becomes untouched by that, for this Person is unattached."
And [it is said]: "Not followed by merit, not followed by evil, for then one has crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart.
Therefore, it must be understood that this statement is solely intended to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self.
From words such as "husband" (pati) and others.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this passage is intended solely to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self;

for in this passage, words such as "Lord" (pati) and so forth serve to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self and to negate the nature of the transmigrating Self— expressions such as "the controller of all, the ruler of all, the lord of all," which are of this kind, are intended to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self.
"He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by bad action"—passages of this kind negate the nature of one who is subject to transmigratory existence.
Therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Lord, who is not subject to transmigratory existence, is the one spoken of here.

Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas. Composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.

In the fourth quarter of the first chapter, having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the definition of Brahman was stated: "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]. Anticipating the objection that this definition applies equally to the Pradhāna (the primordial material cause), it was refuted on the grounds of its lack of scriptural authority in the sūtra: "Because of the absence of scriptural authority, [the Pradhāna is] not [Brahman]. Furthermore, it has been elaborated upon in the preceding section that the Vedānta texts possess a uniform purport (*gatisāmānya*) regarding the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, and not regarding the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause.

Now, however, this remaining doubt is raised: as for what was stated—that the Pradhāna is not based on the Word (aśabda)—that is unproven, because in certain Vedic branches words that appear to designate the Pradhāna are indeed heard.
Consequently, it would follow that the causality of the Pradhāna is established by the Veda itself and has been accepted by great supreme sages such as Kapila and others.

Therefore, until it is demonstrated that those words have another referent, the doctrine that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world, even though it has been established, would become confused.
Therefore, the subsequent section proceeds in order to demonstrate that those [scriptural passages] have another purpose.
Oṃ, the fourth quarter.

In the *Sūtrabhāṣya* on the *Gauḍapādakārikās*, under the section beginning with "Even that which is inferential for some," [the author] shows that even the *pradhāna*—which is determined by inference—is perceived as having a verbal designation among certain followers of the Veda. For it is recited in the *Kāṭhaka*: "Higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. In this regard, those very entities named the Great One (*mahat*), the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the Puruṣa, which are well-known in the Smṛtis, appear here in the same names and in the same order. This constitutes the topic of discussion.
These very same [entities] are recognized here;

for there, it is established by tradition as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and because it is devoid of sound and other qualities, the etymological derivation "that which is not manifest" (*na vyaktam avyaktam*) is possible. Thus, what is designated is the *pradhāna* well-known from tradition;
therefore, since that possesses sound, its being "devoid of sound" (*aśabda*) is untenable.

If it be argued that this very [unmanifest] is the cause of the world on account of its being well-known from Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning, we reply: this is not so. For this passage from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad does not aim at establishing the existence of the "Great" (mahat) and the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) as they are known in Smṛti. Indeed, the independent cause consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), namely the Pradhāna as established in Smṛti, is not recognized here;
for what is recognized here is merely the word "unmanifest."

And that word, because it is etymological (*yaugika*), is applied to anything manifest or unmanifest, as well as to other things that are subtle and difficult to perceive; nor is this word restricted by conventional usage (*rūḍha*) to any single object.

As for the conventional usage among those who maintain the doctrine of *pradhāna*, since that is merely their own technical terminology (*pāribhāṣikī*), it does not serve as a basis for determining the meaning of the Veda.
Nor does the cognition of an identical object arise merely from the similarity of sequence, as in the case of "bhāpā" and "cecca."
MESTRON sū: Thus begins the first chapter.
[The cognition arises] when there is recognition of that form;
for one who sees a cow in the place of a horse does not, being undeluded, determine "this is a horse."
Furthermore, in the investigation of this context, the *pradhāna* imagined by others is not perceived, because it is understood as being presented through the metaphor of the body;
for here, the body—presented in the metaphor of a chariot—is what is grasped by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
Why? Because of the context and because of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

For indeed, the immediately preceding passage demonstrates the metaphorical construction of the self, the body, and so forth, as the chariot-owner, the chariot, and so on: "Know the Self as the owner of the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins."
"The senses, they say, are the horses; their objects are the paths. The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer."

Having shown that one goes to *saṃsāra* by means of those unrestrained senses and so forth, whereas by means of them restrained one attains the further shore of the path—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—in response to the inquiry, "What is that further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu?", the text shows the Supreme Self as the further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, as being superior to those very senses and other factors under discussion: "The objects are indeed superior to the senses; the mind is superior to the objects; the intellect is superior to the mind; and the Great Self is superior to the intellect. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10)
"Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.

In this context, those very same things—the senses and so forth—which were previously introduced in the allegory of the chariot as the horses and other parts, are here also taken up, in order to avoid abandoning what was already introduced and introducing what was not.
In this regard, in the Sūtra and its commentary, the senses (*indriya*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*) are indeed the same terms as those used previously and here;

however, as for the objects—namely sound and the rest—which were designated as the range of the horses that are the senses, their superiority to the senses is well-known from scripture, as is the fact that the senses are "graspers" (*graha*) while the objects are "over-graspers" (*atigraha*);
furthermore, the mind is superior to the objects, because the functioning of both objects and senses is rooted in the mind.
The intellect (*buddhi*) is higher than the mind (*manas*), for having mounted upon the intellect, the host of objects to be enjoyed approaches the enjoyer.
The Self (*ātman*) which is higher than the intellect is that which was introduced as the charioteer in the passage, "Know the Self as the lord of the chariot.
Why? Because of the use of the word "Self," and because it is logical that the enjoyer should be superior to the instruments of enjoyment.
Its greatness is appropriate because of its lordship;

or else, as stated in the Smṛti: "The Great One (Mahān), Intellect (Manas), Thought (Mati), Brahmā, the Ancient One (Pūḥ), Intelligence (Buddhi), Renown (Khyāti), the Lord (Īśvara), Wisdom (Prajñā), Consciousness (Saṃvit), Cognition (Citi), and Memory (Smṛti) are thus enumerated," and as stated in the Śruti: "He who first creates Brahmā and who indeed bestows the Vedas upon him."
That intellect which belongs to Hiraṇyagarbha, the first-born, is the supreme foundation of all intellects;
it is here called the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā).
Although it was already included previously by the mention of "intellect," it is taught separately here because it is logically possible for it to be superior even to our own intellects.

But in this view, the mention of the "Person" (puruṣa) as the Supreme Self must be understood as including the Self who is the rider of the chariot, because in the ultimate sense there is no difference between the Supreme Self and the cognitional self (vijñānātman). Thus, in this way, the body alone remains as the one subject remaining among those [entities] under discussion—the senses and so forth—intended here for the purpose of demonstrating the supreme state. This concludes the first chapter.

It is understood that, as it proceeds through the various objects of sense, [the text] indicates by means of the final term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) which remains—that the body under discussion is what is left over.

For here, the intended purpose is the realization of the inner Self as Brahman, achieved by describing the journey from transmigratory existence to liberation for the ignorant enjoyer who is bound to the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations, through the metaphorical representation of the body and so forth as a chariot and its parts.
And thus [it is said]: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."

Having stated that the supreme state of Viṣṇu is difficult to comprehend—saying, "But it is seen by those of subtle vision with a subtle and foremost intellect"—the text shows the means (*yoga*) for its comprehension: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self consisting of knowledge;

he should restrain knowledge in the great self; he should restrain that [great self] in the peaceful self. This is what is meant: one should restrain speech in the mind, and having abandoned the activity of the external senses such as speech, one should abide in the mind alone.

One should also restrain the mind—which is oriented toward the conceptualization of objects—by perceiving the defects of such conceptualization, within the intellect (*buddhi*) designated by the term "knowledge," which has the nature of ascertainment;

one should further fix that intellect within the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*), the enjoyer, or within the foremost intellect (*agryā buddhiḥ*) by bringing it to a state of subtlety; and one should establish that Great Self within the Peaceful Self (*śānta ātmā*), which is the subject of this context, the Supreme Person, the ultimate goal.
Thus, when considering the preceding and following [arguments] together, there is no room here for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by others.

"But it is subtle, because it is fit for that term. This has been stated [in the Sūtra-bhāṣya]: "By means of the context and the remainder of the passage, the body is denoted by the word 'the Unmanifest' (avyakta), not the Pradhāna.

Now, this objection is raised: how is the body fit for the word "Unmanifest," since this body, being gross, is more clearly manifest and thus more fit for the word "Manifest" (vyakta), whereas the word "Unmanifest" denotes that which is indistinct?
To this, the answer is given: "But it is subtle"; for here the body is intended in its causal state, and the subtle is indeed fit for the word "Unmanifest."
Although this gross body does not itself deserve to be designated by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta), nevertheless, its constituent subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) do deserve that designation;
and the word "prakṛti" (material cause) is seen to be applied to the modification (vikāra), as in the passage, "Let him mix the intoxicating drink with milk.

Furthermore, the Śruti text, "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest," indicates that this very world—differentiated by manifest names and forms—is, in its prior state, fit for the term "unmanifest" when it has abandoned manifest names and forms and exists in the state of a seed-potency.

If it were admitted that this world, in its prior state, exists in the form of a seed with name and form unmanifested and is thus fit to be designated by the term "unmanifested" (*avyakta*), and if, on that basis, the body were also asserted to be fit for the designation "unmanifested" by virtue of having that [prior state] as its essence, then it would follow that this is precisely the doctrine of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause;

for you would be admitting that the prior state of this very world is the *pradhāna*. To this, it is replied: if we were to admit some independent prior state of the world as its cause, then we would indeed be open to this objection. But [we do not]. First Adhyāya.
Then [it would follow that we accept] the doctrine of primordial matter as the cause;
however, we maintain that this prior state of the world is dependent upon the Supreme Lord, not independent,
and it must necessarily be accepted as such.
For she is indeed purposeful;
for without her, the Supreme Lord’s status as creator is not established, since activity is impossible for one devoid of power;
and [she ensures] the non-rebirth of those who are liberated.
Why? Because of that seed-potency which is destroyed by knowledge.

For that seed-potency, consisting of ignorance, designated by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*), resting upon the Supreme Lord, composed of *māyā*, is the great deep sleep in which transmigrating individual souls lie, devoid of the awakening to their true nature.
This very unmanifest is in some places indicated by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), according to the scriptural text: "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof."

In some places it is designated by the word "syllable" (akṣara), according to the Vedic revelation: "Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme"; in other places it is indicated as "Māyā," from the wording of a mantra: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā.
For that Māyā is indeed unmanifest (avyakta), because it is impossible to define it either as being identical to or different from the [other] principles (tattva).
This very thing is called "the Unmanifested is beyond the Great" because the Great arises from the Unmanifested; for when the Great is the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha,
and when it is the individual soul (jīva), even then, since the state of being an individual soul depends upon the Unmanifested, it is said that "the Unmanifested is beyond the Great."
Ignorance is the unmanifest;
it is precisely through its possession of ignorance that the entire continuity of the individual soul's worldly activity proceeds.
And that state of being beyond the Great (mahat), which resides in the unmanifest, is figuratively attributed to the body—its modification—by means of a metaphorical identification.

Even though, according to the Sūkhavibhāṣya, there is no difference between the body and the sense organs and so forth insofar as they are all modifications of that [unmanifest], it is the body alone that is grasped by the term "the unmanifest" through a metaphorical identification; for the sense organs and the rest have already been grasped by their own specific terms, and the body remains as the only thing left over.
Others, however, describe it thus: the body is indeed twofold, gross and subtle. The gross is that which is perceived here;
the subtle is that which will be described later [in the passage]: "In the transition to another body, he goes enveloped [by the subtle elements]," as determined by the questions and answers.

Both of these bodies were previously mentioned without distinction as being the chariot; however, here it is the subtle body that is grasped by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta), because the subtle is worthy of the designation "unmanifest.
Furthermore, since the worldly transactions of bondage and liberation depend upon it, that [subtle body] is superior to the individual soul (jīva).
Since the operation of the sense organs is dependent upon their objects, the objects are superior to the sense organs.

To this, however, they must reply: since both bodies were previously mentioned without distinction as being the chariot, and since both possess the same status of being the subject matter under discussion and being what remains to be accounted for, why is only the subtle body grasped here, and not the gross body as well?

We are able to comprehend the meaning of what has been handed down in scripture, but we cannot subject that which is handed down to critical questioning. And if it is argued that the handed-down text, being composed of indistinct words, is capable of conveying only the subtle [reality] and nothing else because of its manifest nature, we say no;
for the comprehension of meaning depends upon syntactical unity.
Indeed, these two [sections], the preceding and the following, do not convey any meaning at all without attaining syntactical unity.
There would be an abandonment of the subject at hand and an introduction of what is not the subject at hand;
furthermore, there is no comprehension of a single syntactical unity without a mutual expectancy [between the parts]. Thus ends the first chapter.

In that case, since there is no distinction between the two bodies regarding their status as objects of perception, if a connection [between them] is not admitted according to the requirement, the unity of the sentence itself is contradicted; how then could the meaning of what has been revealed be understood? Nor should it be thought that only the subtle body is grasped here because it is difficult to purify, while the gross body is not grasped because it is easily purified due to its visible loathsomeness;
for here no purification of anything is intended to be expressed, as there is no verb here that prescribes a process of purification.
Because it was mentioned immediately before, one might ask: "Is this which is intended here [the answer to] 'What is that highest step of Viṣṇu?
For, having stated "this is beyond this" and "this is beyond this," the text concludes by saying, "There is nothing whatsoever higher than the Puruṣa.
Nevertheless, since the refutation of the inferential [Sāṅkhya] doctrine is established in every way, let it be so named.
Nothing of ours is being cut away.
And because [the scripture] does not state that [Brahman] is an object of knowledge.

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the *pradhāna* is to be known, as they say, "Liberation results from the knowledge of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*"; for it is not possible to know the distinction of the *puruṣa* from the *guṇas* without first knowing the nature of the *guṇas*.
Moreover, some remember that the *pradhāna* is to be known as the means to attaining specific powers (*vibhūti*).
However, this *avyakta* is not mentioned here as being something to be known.
For the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) is merely a single term; there is no sentence here stating that the unmanifest is to be known or meditated upon.
Nor can it be maintained that knowledge of a thing not so enjoined constitutes a human goal.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the Pradhāna is not denoted by the word "unmanifest."

For us, however, since this presentation follows the body and other features fashioned in the form of a chariot in the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, it is faultless, as it aims to reveal Viṣṇu’s own supreme abode.
If it is argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one [is meant], according to the context.
To this, the Sāṃkhya proponent says: "Because its being an object of knowledge is not mentioned, [the claim] is unestablished.

How so? For later on, there is indeed a statement regarding the Pradhāna—denoted by the word "unmanifest"—that it is an object of knowledge: "Having perceived that which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless; which is without beginning or end, beyond the Great (Mahat), and constant—one is released from the jaws of death."

For here, that very same Pradhāna which is described in Smṛti as being devoid of sound and other qualities and as being beyond the Mahat is indicated as the object to be perceived; therefore, this is indeed the Pradhāna, and it is that which is designated by the word "Unmanifest" (avyakta).

To this we reply: here the Pradhāna is not indicated as the object to be perceived; rather, it is understood that the wise Supreme Self (paramātman) alone is indicated here as the object to be perceived. Why? Because of the context.

For the context of the "wise one" (prājña) extends extensively, as indicated by such passages as, "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal," and because, by stating its difficulty of knowledge in the words, "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth," there is a desire to know that very Self. Furthermore, in the passage, "The wise one should restrain speech and mind," the restraint of speech and other faculties is prescribed specifically for the sake of knowing that [Self], and because its fruit is liberation from the jaws of death.
Indeed, it is not accepted by the Sāṃkhyas that one is liberated from the jaws of death merely by contemplating the Pradhāna alone.
For it is their accepted doctrine that one is indeed released from the jaws of death through consciousness of the Self consisting of volition (cetanā); moreover,
in all the Vedāntas, the quality of being beyond sound and other [sensory objects] is predicated of the very Self that is conscious (prājña),
or its being so designated.
First Chapter.
Therefore, the Pradhāna is not the object of knowledge here; for in this manner, there is both an introduction and a question regarding only the three things denoted by the term "the Unmanifest."
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna cannot be denoted by the word "Unmanifest" (avyakta), nor can it be the object of knowledge;

because in this text, the Kaṭhavallīs, only three categories— the fire, the individual soul, and the supreme Self— are seen to be introduced as subjects to be explained due to the power of the granting of boons, and the questions likewise concern only those objects.

Thereafter, no other question or introduction exists; first, there is the question concerning Agni: "O Death, you know that fire which leads to heaven; tell it to me, who am full of faith. Then, there is the question concerning the individual soul (jīva): "This doubt regarding a human being after death—that some say he exists and others say he does not—may I be instructed by you in this; of the boons, this is the third boon."

"Other than dharma and other than adharma, other than what is done and what is not done, other than what has been and what is to be— that which you see, tell me that"— this refers to the Supreme Self; and the reply, "He told him about that Agni who is the source of the worlds, and [described] what bricks [are used], how many there are, and how [they are arranged]," refers to Agni.
"Come, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman,
and how the self becomes [otherwise] upon reaching death, O Gautama. Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of acquiring a body."
In the passage, "Some follow the post according to their karma and according to their learning," the subject is the individual soul (*jīva*), though it is mentioned in a remote context;
whereas the extensive elaboration beginning with "The wise one is neither born nor dies" concerns the supreme self (*paramātman*).
There is no such question concerning the primal matter (*pradhāna*) in this manner.
And because it was not asked, it is not to be introduced [as a topic].

Here the opponent says: Is this question concerning the Self—namely, "There is this doubt regarding a man who has died"—the very same as that which is drawn back again in the words "Other than dharma, other than adharma"? Or is a different, entirely new question being raised?

What follows from this? If it is said that this is the same question being drawn back, then because two questions concerning the Self would become one, there would be only two questions—namely, the one concerning fire and the one concerning the Self—and thus it should not be stated that there is a presentation of three questions.
If it were argued that this is another entirely new question being raised, then just as there would be no fault in postulating a question even apart from the granting of the boons,
so too there would be no fault in postulating the introduction of the Pradhāna even apart from a question.

To this it is replied: We do not here assume any question other than the granting of the boons, because of the force of the opening of the discourse. For the entire course of the dialogue in the Kaṭha Upaniṣads, from its beginning until its conclusion, is observed to have the granting of boons as its starting point. It is reported that Death granted three boons to Naciketas, who had been sent by his father.

It is said that Naciketas chose his father’s goodwill as the first of those boons, the knowledge of the fire-sacrifice (*agnividyā*) as the second, and the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) as the third, based on the indicative mark [in the text]: "This which concerns the deceased" and "Of boons, this is the third boon.
[Objection: No;

for if, in that context, another entirely new question were raised by the words "other than dharma," then the integrity of the statement would be violated, because one would be assuming a question even though no boon had been granted.
But surely, this question must be considered unprecedented because of the difference in the subject matter of the inquiry;

for this question is indeed unprecedented, as it concerns the individual soul (jīva), given that it expresses doubt regarding the deceased person with the words, "There is this doubt concerning a man when he has died: does he exist or not? And since the individual soul is the object of religious merit and so forth, it cannot be the subject of the question, "Other than dharma... etc.

But the wise man, because he has transcended dharma and the rest, is worthy of the question, "Other than dharma. Furthermore, the character of the two questions is not seen to be identical: for the former has existence and non-existence as its subject matter, whereas the latter has as its subject matter a reality that transcends dharma and the rest.
Therefore, due to the absence of recognition, there is a difference between the two questions.

If it is argued that there is no carrying forward of what was stated previously into what follows, we reply: because the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme intelligent self (prājña) is accepted.
This distinction might exist due to a difference in the questions asked, provided that the individual soul were different from the supreme intelligent self;
however, no such difference exists, on account of other scriptural passages such as "That thou art" (Tattvamasi).

Furthermore, here the answer to the question "other than dharma" is "the wise one is neither born nor dies," which, by negating birth and death, demonstrates the non-difference between the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord;
for a negation occurs only when there is a possibility [of the thing being negated],
and the possibility of birth and death belongs to the embodied soul because of its connection with a body, not to the Supreme Lord.

Likewise, in the *Svapnasūtra-bhāṣya* [Brahmasūtra 3.2.1], it is shown that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not other than the *prājña*, by demonstrating that the cessation of grief occurs through the contemplation of the very soul who perceives both the state of dreaming and the state of waking—characterized as "great" and "all-pervading"—according to the text: "The wise one, having realized the great, all-pervading Self, by which he perceives both the end of sleep and the end of waking, does not grieve.
For it is the established doctrine of Vedānta that the cessation of grief results from the realization of the *prājña*.
Likewise, the passage, "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here.
He goes from death to death who perceives any difference here," refutes the view of a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme conscious self (prājña).

Likewise, immediately after the question concerning the existence or non-existence of the soul, when Naciketas did not waver even though Death tempted him with various desires—beginning with "Choose another boon, Naciketas"—Death praised him for desiring knowledge, saying, "I consider Naciketas to be one who seeks knowledge; many desires did not distract you," and further praising his question, he spoke as follows: "Him who is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret place, situated in the cave, dwelling in the abyss, the ancient..."

"Having realized the Divine through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow"—by this also, it is understood that the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Intellect (prājña) alone is intended here. Furthermore, since Naciketas received great praise from Death on account of his question, if he were to set that aside and introduce an entirely different question immediately after the praise, that entire praise would have been extended out of place.
Therefore, "other than dharma" is merely a restatement of the very same question, "that which there is when one has died."
As for the objection regarding the difference in the character of the questions, that is not a fault, because it is precisely that specific distinction which is being questioned again.

For in the first instance, the existence of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth was asked about; whereas in the subsequent instance, its state of being beyond transmigratory existence (*asaṃsāritva*) is questioned.

As long as ignorance does not cease, so long do the soul's state of being an object of the sphere of dharma and the like, as well as its status as a *jīva*, not cease; but upon the cessation of that [ignorance], it is realized through the scriptural text "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) that it is indeed the *prājña* (the intelligent Self).
Furthermore, there is no difference whatsoever in the reality itself between its state of possessing ignorance and its state when that [ignorance] has been removed.

Just as someone, perceiving a rope fallen in deep darkness to be a snake, flees in fear and trembling, and another says to him, "Do not fear; this is not a snake, it is only a rope," and upon hearing that, he abandons the fear caused by the snake, as well as his trembling and flight—yet there is no difference in the object itself between the time of the cognition of a snake and the time of its removal—so too should this matter be viewed.
Consequently, such statements as "It is neither born nor does it die" also serve as a response to the question regarding existence and non-existence.
