The Sūtra, however, must be interpreted with reference to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the conscious Lord (prājña), which is imagined through ignorance; for although the subject of the question regarding the Self is one and the same, the first part is inferred to concern the individual soul because, at the time of death, there is a lack of doubt as to its existence apart from the body, and because the nature of transmigratory existence—such as agency—is not yet discarded. The latter part, on the other hand, concerns the conscious Lord because it mentions the transcendence of merit and demerit. Consequently, the conceptualization of fire, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self is appropriate.
But in the case of the postulation of Pradhāna, there is a discrepancy: there is neither the granting of a boon, nor a question, nor an answer.
The Great Word.

In the Sūtra-bhāṣya (pāda 1), it is stated: Just as the word *mahat* is employed by the Sāṃkhyas for the first-born [principle] which is mere existence (*sattāmātra*), yet it does not denote that very thing even in Vedic usage—due to reasons such as the employment of the word *ātman* in passages like "The Self greater than the intellect" (*buddherātmā mahān paraḥ*) and "I know this great Person" (*vedāhametaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam*)—so too the word *avyakta* cannot denote the *pradhāna* in Vedic usage. Therefore, that which is based on inference lacks the quality of being supported by scripture (*śabdavat*).
It is like the cup, because there is no distinction.
Furthermore, the proponent of *pradhāna* states that the lack of scriptural authority for *pradhāna* is unproven;

why? Because of the wording of a mantra: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, who produces many offspring of similar form upon her single seat; for there is indeed one unborn male. This refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*).
"The other, the unborn, having enjoyed her, lies with her and leaves her once her enjoyment has been experienced";
for in this mantra, the qualities of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* are denoted by the words "red," "white," and "black" respectively—
the red being *rajas* because its nature is to color (or passion), and the white being *sattva* because its nature is luminosity.
Darkness is black because its nature is that of concealment;
their state of equilibrium is designated by the qualities of red, white, and black.
And she may be called "unborn" (ajā) because she is not born, according to the accepted principle that "the root-primal matter (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification."
Surely the word *ajā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a she-goat;
certainly it is so.
However, that conventional meaning cannot be accepted here, because this is a context concerning knowledge (*vidyā*).

And she (Prakṛti) gives birth to many offspring endowed with the three qualities (guṇas). A single Puruṣa, taking pleasure in—that is, being fond of or serving—that Prakṛti, lies along with her. Having approached her through ignorance as his own self, he transmigrates due to a lack of discrimination, thinking "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded."

But another person, a soul who has produced discriminative knowledge and is dispassionate, abandons this Prakṛti—having experienced its enjoyments and having accomplished both enjoyment and liberation—and leaves it behind; that is to say, he is liberated.

Therefore, since the Kapila school’s conception of Pradhāna and so forth is thus based on scripture, such being the position reached, we reply: the Sāṃkhya doctrine cannot be supported as being rooted in scripture on the basis of this mantra.

For this mantra is not capable of supporting any particular doctrine independently, since it is possible to establish "unborn-ness" and so forth through any conceptual construction whatsoever; furthermore, there is no reason for a specific determination that the Sāṃkhya doctrine alone is intended here.

Just as in the mantra, "The sacrificial cup has its mouth below and its bottom above," it cannot be determined with certainty that this refers specifically to a particular cup, because the description of having a downward-turned mouth and so forth can be applied in some way or another to any vessel; likewise here, there is no distinction in the mantra "the one unborn female" (ajāmekām), and it cannot be determined that the Pradhāna alone is intended by the term "unborn."
In that case, however, the understanding of a specific cup arises from the supplementary passage: "This is that head; for this is a cup with its mouth below and its bottom above.
But here, as to what this "unborn" (aja) is to be understood as, we reply: "But [the one] beginning with light, for thus it is studied by some. (Sūtra 1.4.9).

This unborn one (ajā), produced from the Supreme Lord, consisting of light and characterized by fire, water, and food, is to be understood as the primordial material cause of the fourfold collection of beings.
The word "but" (tu) serves to emphasize that this unborn one is to be known as characterized solely by the three elements, not as characterized by the three qualities (guṇas).

Why? Because certain followers of other Vedic schools, having recorded the origin of fire, water, and food from the Supreme Lord, further declare their respective forms as red and so forth: "That which is the red form of the fire is the form of fire; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food."

These very same elements—fire, water, and food—are recognized here [in this passage] because of the commonality of the words "red" and so forth. For the words "red" and so on have their primary application to specific colors, whereas their application to qualities is secondary.
And it is considered a logical principle that the resolution of what is doubtful should be made by means of what is certain.
Thus, in this case as well, it says: "The exponents of Brahman say..."

Having begun with "What is the cause, Brahman?", the text continues: "Following the path of meditation and yoga, they beheld the divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities. Since this introduces the supreme power of the Lord that ordains the entire universe, and since in the remainder of the passage it is understood to be that very same power—through the statements, "Know Māyā as Prakṛti (Nature), and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā," and "He who alone presides over each and every womb"—it cannot be asserted that some independent Prakṛti called Pradhāna is what is taught by the term *ajā* (the Unborn) in this mantra.
However, on account of the context, it is said that this very divine power— the state prior to name and form, which is unmanifest—
also is recorded by this mantra;
and its threefold nature has been described through the threefold nature of its own modifications.

But how can it be understood that the unborn (ajā) possesses a threefold nature through the three forms of fire, water, and food? For, on the one hand, the form of a goat does not exist in fire, water, and food; and on the other hand, since fire, water, and food are heard of as having specific genera, the word "unborn" cannot possibly be based on the absence of birth (ajāti).
To this, the author reads the reply: "And because of the teaching of a metaphorical conception, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth."
This word "ajā" (goat) is not based on the mark of having the form of a goat, nor is it etymological;

what then? This is a teaching by means of a metaphorical representation; this designation as a "goat" is taught as a figurative depiction of the source of the moving and unmoving world, characterized by fire, water, and earth.

For just as in the world there might be some heifer, red, white, and black in color, with many calves and of uniform appearance, and a certain bull might lie with her out of desire, while another might abandon her once she has been enjoyed; even so this primordial nature of the elements, characterized by fire, water, and earth, possessing the three colors, produces a vast variety of similar modifications consisting of the moving and the unmoving, which is experienced by the ignorant knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and abandoned by the wise one.
Nor should it be suspected that because one *kṣetrajña* lies dormant while another abandons [the body], a real plurality of *kṣetrajñas*— which is desired by our opponents— is thereby established;
for this is not an intention to propound a plurality of *kṣetrajñas*, but rather an intention to establish the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation.

Having restated the well-known distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman], the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation is established; however, this distinction is caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is constructed by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), not ultimate.
This is because of such scriptural passages as: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."

The meaning is that just as in the case of honey and so forth—where the nature of honey is attributed to the sun which is not honey, the nature of a cow to speech which is not a cow, and the nature of fires to the heavenly world and so forth which are not fires—such a figurative conception is formed; in the same way, the nature of being unborn is attributed to this [Prakṛti] which is not unborn.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the application of the word "ajā" (unborn) to fire, water, and earth.
Nor [is the number five established] even by the inclusion of a number, because of the diversity [of the elements] and because of the excess [of qualities].

Even when the *ajā* mantra has been thus refuted, the Sāṃkhya again objects on the basis of another mantra: "In whom the five groups of five (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) and the ether (*ākāśa*) are established—knowing that very Self as the one who encompasses the number, I, being immortal, am immortal" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). This is the section concerning the [Sāṃkhya] doctrine.
In this mantra, another number five is heard in relation to the number five in the phrase "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*), because two words "five" (*pañca*) are seen there;
these five fives amount to twenty-five.
And by that number twenty-five, exactly as many principles as are required to be numbered are enumerated by the Sāṃkhyas, beginning with primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
"The seven, beginning with Mahat, are both evolvents and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is only an evolute; and the Puruṣa is neither an evolvent nor an evolute.

Thus, because these twenty-five principles well-known in Smṛti are subsumed under the number twenty-five established in Śruti, it follows that Pradhāna and the others indeed possess scriptural authority.
To this we reply: one should not entertain the hope that even because of the mention of a number, the Pradhāna and other principles possess scriptural authority;
why? Because of their diversity;
for these twenty-five principles are indeed diverse.

There is no common property belonging to each group of five among these by which further groups of five could be established within the interval of twenty-five; for numbers such as "two" and so forth do not apply to distinct entities without a single unifying basis.

Now, it might be argued that this very number "twenty-five" is indicated through its constituent parts, just as when they say, "Indra did not rain for five and seven years," they are speaking of a twelve-year drought. To this we reply: [this is not so].
That too is not tenable;
this very point is the defect in this position, namely, that one would have to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, the word "five" here is compounded with the word "persons" as *pañcajanāḥ*, because the accentuation according to the Bhāṣika rules determines it to be a single word.

Furthermore, in another application [of the mantra], because it is understood as a single compound word with a single accent and a single case-ending in the phrase "pañcānāṃ tvā pañcajanānām," and because it is a collective whole, there is no distributive repetition such as "five-five.
Therefore, the expression "five five" does not denote the grasping of two groups of five.
Nor can the number five, being itself a single entity, be qualified by another number five—as in "five pentads" (pañca-pañcakāḥ)—because a subordinate term cannot be connected with a qualifier.

[Objection: But surely, people who have already attained the number five, when further qualified by the number five, will be understood as twenty-five, just as in the expression "five groups of five," twenty-five bundles are understood;
we say: no.

It is appropriate that for the word *pañcapūlī*, because it intends a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), there should be the qualification "five" as in "five five-bunches" when there is an expectation of distinction regarding the number;

however, in the case of "five persons" (*pañca janāḥ*) and so forth, since the distinction is already grasped from the outset, there is no expectation of a number, and thus the qualification "five" would not apply to "five persons.
Even if this qualification were to occur, it would pertain only to the number five itself.
And the fault has already been stated in that regard;
therefore, the expression "five fivefold people" does not intend to refer to twenty-five principles.
Furthermore, because there is an excess [of elements], it does not intend to refer to twenty-five principles.
For there is an excess over the number twenty-five due to the self (ātman) and space (ākāśa);

first, the self is indicated here as the support and substratum, because that which was pointed out by the locative case in the word "in whom" is drawn back as the self in the phrase "him alone I consider to be the self";
and the self is the conscious person (puruṣa).
And since that [space] is already included within the twenty-five principles, it would be illogical for it to possess both the status of being a substratum and the status of being a superstratum;
or, if one were to accept it as a distinct entity, it would entail an excess in the number of principles, which contradicts the established doctrine.
Likewise, in the statement "and space is established," it is not logical to mention space separately when it is already included within the twenty-five principles.
Furthermore, the refutation has already been stated regarding the acceptance of a different meaning.

And how, in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, Chapter One, could the inclusion of the twenty-five principles—which are not explicitly mentioned—be understood merely from hearing the word "five"? For the word *jana* is not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "principles" (*tattva*), and the number remains logically consistent even if a different meaning were included.

How then is the expression "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) to be understood? It is said: because of the specific grammatical rule "Directional words and numerals [form a compound] when they constitute a name" (*diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*), the word *pañca* forms a compound with the word *jana* only when it denotes a name. Consequently, with the intention of referring to a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), certain individuals named "the Five Peoples" (*pañcajanāḥ*) are intended to be expressed, not with the intention of referring to the categories (*tattva*) of the Sāṃkhya system. When the question arises as to how many these are, the word "five" is used once again.
The term *pañcajanāḥ* means whoever they may be, they are exactly five in number, just as in the expression "the seven seers" (*saptarṣayaḥ*) refers to seven.
Who, then, are these so-called "five people"? To this it is replied: they are prāṇa and the others, because of the complementary passage.

In the mantra following "In whom the five [groups of] five persons," namely, "They who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind"— the five [groups of] five persons mentioned there for the purpose of defining the nature of Brahman are intended here as the "five persons" (pañcajanāḥ) because of their proximity within the remainder of the passage.

But how, then, is the word "people" (jana) applied to the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth? Or how is the word "people" applied to the [five] principles (tattva)? Since the departure from the conventional usage is equal in both cases, the vital breaths and so forth must be understood [as the referents] on account of the remainder of the sentence; furthermore, the vital breaths and so forth come to possess the designation "people" because of their connection with people; and the word "person" (puruṣa), which denotes people, is used for the vital breaths in the passage: "These indeed are the five persons of Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.6). In the commentary on the Sūtra: "te vā ete pañca brahmapuruṣāḥ. (Sūtra Bhāṣya).

And there is the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the father, the vital breath is indeed the mother," and so forth. Furthermore, due to the force of the compound, the conventional meaning (rūḍhatva) of the whole is not contradictory. But how can a conventional meaning be resorted to when there has been no prior usage? [The author] says: it can be, as in the case of the word *udbhid* and others. For when a word of unknown meaning is used in proximity to a word of well-known meaning, its referent is restricted through syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*).

Just as in the cases of "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "he cuts the sacrificial post," and "he prepares the altar," so too this word *pañcajana*, its status as a technical name being understood from its grammatical derivation as a compound, requires a named object and will therefore refer to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth mentioned in the context of the supplementary passage.
However, some have explained the five *pañcajanas* as the gods, ancestors, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rakṣases;
while others have adopted the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth.

Furthermore, the word *pañcajana* is seen used in the sense of "progeny" in the passage, "Whatever [is done] with the *pāñcajanya* people"; even if that meaning were accepted here, there would be no contradiction whatsoever.
However, the Teacher (Bādarāyaṇa) stated, "The vital breaths and so forth, because of the complementary passage," with the intention that there is no cognition of twenty-five principles here.
Let it be granted that for the Mādhyandinas, the five *pañcajanas* are indeed the breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, since they mention food (*anna*) among the breath and the rest;

but how can the breath and so forth be the *pañcajanas* for the Kāṇvas, who do not mention food among the breath and the rest? To this, the author reads the following reply: "On account of light (*jyotis*), for some, even though food is absent. (Sūtra 1.4.12)
Even if food were not present among the Kāṇvas, their number five would still be completed by means of light;

for they too, in the mantra preceding "In whom the five groups of five persons," study light precisely for the purpose of defining the nature of Brahman: "That is the light of lights, which the gods worship."

But how is it that this light, though recited identically for both [recensions], is accepted by some and not by others despite being contained within the same mantra? He says: it is due to a difference in requirement (*apekṣā*). For the Mādhyandinas, having obtained the "five people" (*pañcajana*) consisting of prāṇa and so forth already recited in that same mantra, have no further requirement for the light recited in another mantra; however, because they do not obtain it, the Kāṇvas do have such a requirement.
And thus, due to this difference in requirement, there is the inclusion or non-inclusion of the light even within the same mantra.
Just as, although the Atirātra sacrifice is the same, there is the taking up or not taking up of the Ṣoḍaśin cup due to a difference in scriptural injunctions, so it is here.
Thus, in this way, there is no scriptural authority whatsoever regarding the Pradhāna; as for the authorities of Smṛti and reasoning, they will be refuted later.
And because, in the case of ether and so forth, that which has been designated [as Brahman] is taught as being the cause.
The definition of Brahman has been established;
the uniformity of the purport of the Vedānta passages concerning Brahman has been established;
and it has been established that Pradhāna lacks scriptural authority as a cause.
In this regard, another objection is raised:

it is not possible to establish that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, nor that there is a uniformity of purport (*gati-sāmānya*) among the Vedānta passages concerning Brahman. Why? Because contradictions are observed.
For in each Vedānta text, a different creation is observed due to the diversity of sequence and other factors.
To illustrate: in some places, a creation beginning with ether is recorded, as in "From the Self, ether was produced"; in others, it begins with fire, as in "It created fire."

In some places, the creation begins with the vital breath (prāṇa), as in: "He created the vital breath; from the vital breath, faith"; in other places, the origin of the worlds is recorded without any specific order, as in: "He created these worlds:
water, light-rays, death, and the waters."

Likewise, in some places, a creation preceded by the non-existent (asat) is recorded: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent (sat) was born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), and "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; that became existent; that developed. In other places, however, after introducing the theory of the non-existent with the words, "On this point, some say that in the beginning this was indeed non-existent," the process is asserted as being preceded by the existent by means of a refutation of the doctrine of the non-existent: "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? He said: 'How could the existent be born from the non-existent? In the beginning, my dear, this was only the existent'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1–2).
In some places, the manifestation of the world is said to be caused by itself, as in: "This was then undeveloped; it became developed by means of name and form.

Because there are such diverse contradictions and because a conceptual alternative regarding a real entity is logically untenable, it is not reasonable to hold that the Vedānta texts have as their primary purpose the determination of the cause of the world;
rather, it is more reasonable to accept another cause based on Smṛti and established reasoning. Such being the position reached, [the Sūtra begins] the first chapter.

We reply: Even though there is a discrepancy regarding the sequence and other details concerning the ether and so forth created in each Vedānta text, there is no discrepancy whatsoever regarding the Creator.

Why? Because He is described exactly as He is taught. For in one Vedānta text, that Lord is described as the cause in His true nature—as omniscient, the Self of all, one and without a second; and in other Vedānta texts, He is described in that very same way, as for example:
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."

In this context, first of all, by the word "knowledge" (jñāna) and by the subsequent statement regarding its desire for its own object, he characterized Brahman as conscious; by the subsequent statement that it is not dependent on another, he declared the Lord to be the cause;

and by the subsequent use of the word "Self" (ātman) with reference to that very same subject, along with the description of the successive layers of sheaths such as the body and so forth, and the entry into their interior, he determined it to be the innermost inward Self within all.

Furthermore, by the expression "May I be many, may I procreate," which praises the becoming manifold with respect to the Self, [the text] declares the non-difference of the created modifications from their Creator; likewise, by the instruction regarding the creation of the entire world in the passage "It created all this,
whatever there is," it teaches that the Creator was without a second prior to creation.

Therefore, that very same characteristic by which Brahman is known as the cause here is known elsewhere as well: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"; "It thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth'; It emitted heat"; and likewise, "In the beginning, the Self alone was all this, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Shall I now create the worlds? Because such a collection of passages, which aim at defining the nature of the Cause, possesses an identical meaning across every Vedānta text.

Regarding the subject matter of the effects, however, a discrepancy is observed in some places, such as that creation begins with ether (*ākāśa*) and in others that it begins with fire (*tejas*), and so forth. Yet, it cannot be argued that because of this discrepancy concerning the effects, Brahman—the cause which is understood without contradiction across all Vedānta texts—should be considered unintended; for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the Teacher will resolve even the discrepancies regarding the effects, beginning with the sūtra: "Not [so] the ether, on account of the absence of scriptural statement" (*na viyadaśruteḥ*).
Furthermore, there might be the objection that the subject matter is censurable because it is not intended to be taught;
for this manifold creation and so forth is not what the author wishes to propound.
Indeed, no human goal (puruṣārtha) is seen or heard of that is connected with such [creation].

Nor can it be imagined [that these passages refer to something other than Brahman], because in various places they are understood to form a single syntactical unity with sentences concerning Brahman through their introductory and concluding sections.

Furthermore, the text demonstrates that the detailed account of creation and so forth is for the purpose of realizing Brahman: "My dear, seek the root of water by means of food as its shoot; my dear, seek the root of fire by means of water as its shoot; my dear, seek the root of Being by means of fire as its shoot.
And it is understood from the analogies of clay and the like that the detailed account of creation and so forth is taught in order to state the non-difference of the effect from its cause.

And thus those who know the tradition say: "The creation described by means of clay, iron, sparks, and so forth, in various ways, is for the purpose of providing an approach; there is no difference whatsoever.

However, the fruit connected with the realization of Brahman is heard in scripture: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death."

And this fruit is directly perceivable: when the realization of one's identity as the non-transmigrating Self occurs through the [instruction] "That thou art," there follows the cessation of the identification with the transmigrating Self.
Furthermore, as for the discrepancy regarding the causal object that was shown in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," that must be resolved;
here it is said: "Because of the drawing together [of the terms]."

In the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is not taught that a non-existent, soulless entity is the cause; for [the scripture continues]: "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent."

Having established that Brahman is characterized by existence through the refutation of the doctrine of non-existence in the passage, "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as existing," and having determined that Brahman—the inner self—is identical with the series of sheaths beginning with the one made of food (*annamaya*), the text draws back to that same subject under discussion with the words, "He desired. It then causes the emanation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) to be heard as proceeding from Him, concludes with, "They call that Truth," and finally, introducing this verse with the words, "On this very point there is also this verse," it cites the following verse regarding that same subject under discussion: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asat*)."

If, however, "non-existent" (asat) were intended here as meaning "devoid of self" (nirātmaka), then, because one thing would be drawn in as an illustration for another, the statement would become incoherent.

Therefore, the word *sat* is generally well-known to refer to an entity differentiated by name and form; thus, with reference to the absence of such differentiation prior to creation, Brahman, though actually existent (*sat*), is figuratively said to have been "non-existent" (*asat*).
This same interpretation applies to the passage, "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent," because of the subsequent drawing in [of the opposite]: "That became existent."

For if an absolute non-existence were accepted in the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, why would [the text] cite "That was Being" (Tat sad āsīt)? Furthermore, even in the passage, "On this point some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent' (Tad vaika āhur asad evedam agre āsīt)," this presentation of the opinion of "some" is not intended to represent the view of another Śruti; for just as with an action, an alternative regarding a real entity is impossible.

Therefore, it should be understood that this is merely a presentation and subsequent refutation of the position of non-existence—which is imagined by those of dull intellect—in order to strengthen the position of Being (Sat) which is upheld by the Śruti.

In the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated," the differentiation of the world is not described as occurring without a presiding agent; for there is a subsequent reference to the presiding agent through the statement, "He entered here even to the tips of the fingernails," which shows that he has entered into the differentiated effects.

For if the assumption of differentiation were without a presiding supervisor, then by which [agent] would that pronoun "he" (saḥ)—which follows immediately and refers back to the subject at hand—be drawn in as participating in the act? Moreover, this entry of the conscious Self into the body is heard of in scripture, because consciousness is attributed to that which has entered: "seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind.

Furthermore, just as this world today undergoes differentiation through name and form under a presiding supervisor, so too must it have been at the beginning of creation; for it is impossible to conceive of a hypothesis contrary to what is observed.
Another scriptural passage also shows that the evolution of the world has a presiding agent: "Entering with this living self (jīva), let me evolve names and forms.

Furthermore, the verbal form "is evolved" (*vyākriyate*)—though it is a reflexive passive (*karmakartari*)—must be understood as referring to the Supreme Lord as the evolver, having regard for His own power, just as one says "the field reaps itself" even when a reaper is present. Thus ends the first chapter.

Alternatively, this *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) should be understood as referring to the object (*karman*) itself, with reference to another agent implied by the sense, just as in the expression "the village is being gone to" (*gamyate grāmaḥ*).
Because it denotes the world.

In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, it is heard: "O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons, or he of whom this is the work—he indeed, O Bālāki, is to be known. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the individual soul (jīva) taught here as the object to be known, or the principal vital breath (mukhya prāṇa), or the Supreme Self (paramātman)?
What, then, is the initial conclusion? That it is the vital breath (prāṇa).
Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "Of whom this is the work," and because action characterized by movement has the vital breath as its substratum;

and because in the supplementary portion of the passage, "Then he becomes one with this very vital breath," the word *prāṇa* is heard, and the word *prāṇa* is well-known to denote the primary vital breath.

Furthermore, regarding those persons previously pointed out by Bālāki—such as "the person in the sun," "the person in the moon," and so forth—it is Prāṇa who is their agent, because the deities such as the sun are particular states of Prāṇa. This is well-established by another scriptural passage: "Which one is the single deity? Prāṇa. He is Brahman; they call him 'That' (tyad). Alternatively, it is the individual soul (jīva) that is taught here as the object to be known;
for its action, characterized by merit and demerit, can also be made known through the statement, "He whose work this is."

He (the Self) is also logically established as the agent of these persons who constitute the instruments of experience, precisely because He is the experiencer. In the remainder of the passage, a characteristic mark of the individual soul (*jīva*) is perceived; for, wishing to instruct Bālāki—who had approached with the desire to know—the agent of the persons presented as the object of knowledge, Ajātaśatru called out to a sleeping man. Since the man did not hear the call, Ajātaśatru demonstrated that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and other such factors are not the experiencers. Then, by rousing him with a blow from his staff, he demonstrated that the individual soul (*jīva*), distinct from the vital breaths and the rest, is the experiencer.

Likewise, further on, the characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva) is perceived: "Just as a master enjoys his own servants, or as his servants enjoy their master, even so this conscious self (prajñātman) enjoys these selves, and even so these selves enjoy this self.

Furthermore, because it possesses vital breaths (prāṇas), it is appropriate for the individual soul to be designated by the word 'prāṇa'. Therefore, either the individual soul or the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) must be understood here, and not the Supreme Lord, because no characteristic mark of Him is perceived. To this we reply: the Supreme Lord alone must be the maker of these persons.
Why? Because of the force of the opening statement (*upakrama*).
For here, Bālāki began a conversation with Ajātaśatru, saying, "I shall tell you about Brahman";
and having mentioned several persons residing in the sun and other spheres who possess the figurative vision (*amukhya-brahma-dṛṣṭi*) of Brahman, he fell silent.

Ajātaśatru rebuked him for his superficial knowledge of Brahman, saying, "Indeed, you have spoken falsely to me; let me tell you the Brahman," and then introduced another as the one to be known, the agent of that [creation].
If that other were also a recipient of the view of Brahman in a secondary sense, the introductory statement would be contradicted;
therefore, this must be the Supreme Lord alone.
Furthermore, the agency of these persons cannot be conceived as belonging to anyone other than the Supreme Lord by virtue of independence.
Regarding the sūtra in the first chapter,

"He whose work this is," this is not a reference to action characterized by physical motion or action characterized by merit and demerit (dharma and adharma), because neither of those two has been introduced in the context nor has either been explicitly mentioned.

Nor is this a designation of the individual souls (puruṣas), because they have already been designated by the words "the maker of these souls," and because there is a discrepancy in gender and number;
nor is this a designation of the act of making pertaining to the souls, or of the fruit of that action, since both of those are already included by the word "maker" itself.
By process of elimination, the world, which is present before the eyes, is designated by the pronoun "this" (etad).
And that which is being done is precisely this world as action;
but is it not the case that the world has neither been introduced nor mentioned?
True, that is so.

Nevertheless, since no specific qualification is mentioned, it is understood that this designation refers to the totality of all things present by virtue of their common proximity, rather than to any particular thing, because there is an absence of any specific proximity;

furthermore, since in the preceding passage persons who constitute a part of the world were specifically mentioned, it is understood here that the world itself is mentioned without such qualification.

This is what is meant: "What is the significance of this distinction regarding the creator of these persons who constitute only a part of the world? Or rather, [the text implies] 'he whose unqualified work is the entire world'—the word 'or' (vā) is for the purpose of excluding the status of being a creator limited to only one part.
The specific qualification is employed to demonstrate that those persons whom Bālāki considered to be Brahman are not actually Brahman.
Thus, according to the maxim of "the Brahmins and the wandering mendicants," the creator of the world is taught as the object to be known by means of both the general and the particular.
And the Supreme Lord is determined in all the Vedāntas to be the creator of the entire world.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the subject of the passage] because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) in the Sūtra and its Commentary, that has already been explained.

Now, as for what was stated—that because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the marks of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) found in the supplementary part of the passage, it is logical that one of those two alone is to be grasped here, and not the Supreme Lord—that must be refuted.

To this it is replied: this has already been settled under the sūtra, "Not so, on account of the threefoldness of meditation, and because it is resorted to, and because of its connection here" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.31).
For if it were so, a threefold meditation would result in this case—namely, meditation on the individual soul, meditation on the chief vital breath, and meditation on Brahman.
And this is not logical;
for it is understood from both the opening and the conclusion that this passage has Brahman as its subject matter.
Among these, the fact that the opening has Brahman as its subject matter has already been demonstrated.

Furthermore, because the hearing of an unsurpassed fruit is also mentioned in the concluding passage, its subject matter is seen to be Brahman: "Having struck down all evils, he who knows this attains supremacy over all beings, sovereignty, and lordship.
Now, one might object that if this were so, this passage would already have been determined by the determination of the Pratardana section;
but it is not so determined, because the status of the phrase "He whose work this is" as referring to Brahman was not established there.
Therefore, the doubt here concerning the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital air (mukhya-prāṇa) is set aside as it arises again;

for the word "prāṇa" is also seen to refer to Brahman in the passage, "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to prāṇa" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2). Furthermore, the characteristic marks of the individual soul must be interpreted with the intention of non-difference, since the introduction and conclusion of the text concern Brahman. (Sūtra 1.1.31) Chapter One.
But Jaimini [holds this view] on account of both questions and explanations; and some [teachers] also [hold it] thus.
Furthermore, one should not dispute here whether this sentence, though having another primary purpose, might have the individual soul as its main subject or Brahman as its main subject;
for the teacher Jaimini considers that the reference to the individual soul in this sentence is for the sake of understanding Brahman.
Why? Because of the question and the explanation.

First, after the individual soul (jīva) has been awakened as distinct from the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth by means of the awakening of the person in deep sleep through a question, there is seen again a question concerning that which is distinct from the individual soul: "O Gārgya, where did this person lie? What did he become then? Whence did he come back?"

The reply is as follows: "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this very breath (prāṇa)," and so forth; and "From this Self, all the vital breaths (prāṇas) proceed to their respective stations; from the breaths, the gods; and from the gods, the worlds. Thus, according to the established principle of the Vedānta, at the time of deep sleep the individual soul (jīva) attains unity with the supreme Brahman, and from the supreme Brahman the world, beginning with the vital breaths, is born.

Therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Self is what is taught here as the object to be known—that wherein this individual soul (jīva) enters its sleep, which consists of a state of non-conscious tranquility, a true nature devoid of the specific cognitions produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and from which it returns to its own form.

Moreover, some followers of a different recension, the Vājasaneyins, clearly teach the Supreme Self as distinct from the individual soul in this very dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru; for, when the question is asked—"Where was this person consisting of cognition (vijñānamaya) then? Whence did he come?"—they answer with a term denoting the Supreme Self. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya).
In the reply as well, it says: "In that which is this space within the heart";
and the word "space" (ākāśa) is used for the Supreme Self in the passage, "This small space within it.

Furthermore, by stating that "all these selves issue forth," the text teaches that the Supreme Self alone is the cause, since it is understood that it is the Selfs possessing limiting adjuncts that issue forth from something else.

Furthermore, by means of raising the person who was in deep sleep, there is the additional teaching that [the Self] is distinct from the vital breaths and so forth, even though the vital breaths have already been refuted.
Because of the syntactical connection of the sentence.

In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is stated: beginning with "Verily, not for the sake of the husband is the husband dear," and continuing until, "Verily, not for the sake of all is all dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that all becomes dear. Verily, the Self, O Maitreyī, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Verily, by the seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing of the Self, all this is known. This constitutes the section.

In this regard, the following doubt arises: is it the individual self (*vijñānātman*) alone that is taught here in the form of being "that which is to be seen," "that which is to be heard," and so forth, or rather the supreme self (*paramātman*)?

From what source does this doubt arise? On one hand, it appears to be an instruction concerning the individual self because the passage begins with the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*), the self indicated by its endearments;
on the other hand, it appears to be an instruction concerning the supreme self because of the teaching that through the knowledge of the Self, there is the knowledge of all.
First Chapter. What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is an instruction concerning the individual self (vijñānātman); why? Because of the force of the opening statement.

For husband, wife, children, wealth, and so forth—all that is an object of enjoyment in the world—is dear because it serves the purpose of the Self. Thus, having introduced the Self as the enjoyer indicated by these "dear" things, what other Self could this [Self] be for whom the subsequent instruction regarding the vision of the Self is intended? Furthermore, in the middle [of the passage], by stating, "This great being, infinite and boundless, consisting of nothing but a mass of consciousness, arising from these elements and perishing after them—after death there is no consciousness," the text shows that this very "great being" under discussion, which is to be seen, arises from the elements in the form of the conscious self (vijñānātman); thus, it demonstrates that this state of being "to be seen" belongs to the conscious self alone.
Likewise, by concluding with the word "knower" in the phrase, "But by what, my dear, should one know the knower?", the text shows that it is indeed the knowing self (vijñānātman) that is taught here.

Therefore, the statement that through the knowledge of the Self everything is known must be regarded as figurative, since the entire range of objects of enjoyment exists for the sake of the enjoyer. This being the position reached, we reply: this is indeed an instruction regarding the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of the consistency of the context of the passage.
Indeed, when this passage is examined in its proper sequence from beginning to end, it is seen that its constituent parts are connected with reference to the Supreme Self.

How so? That is now demonstrated: having heard from Yājñavalkya the statement, "There is no hope for immortality through wealth," Maitreyī, desiring immortality, said, "What should I do with that by which I might not become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows. To her, thus seeking immortality, Yājñavalkya imparts the knowledge of the Self.
Furthermore, scriptural and traditional statements declare that immortality does not exist apart from the knowledge of the Supreme Self (Brahman);
likewise, the claim that through the knowledge of the Self all is known cannot be understood in its primary sense unless it refers to the knowledge of the Supreme Cause.

Nor can this be taken in a figurative sense, because after asserting that "all is known through the knowledge of the Self," the text immediately establishes that very point with the passage beginning, "He who knows Brahman as other than the Self is deprived [of everything]," and so forth.

For one who perceives the world—consisting of the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and so forth—as having its existence independently apart from the Self, that very world perceived falsely through false vision rejects him. Thus, having set aside the view of difference, [the scripture] introduces the non-difference of the entire aggregate of things from the Self by stating, "All this is what this Self is.
Furthermore, it confirms that same non-difference through the analogies of the drum and other instruments.

Furthermore, by stating, "This Rigveda is the breath of this great Being," and so forth, [the text] explains that the Self under discussion is the cause of the manifestation of names, forms, and actions; thus, it leads us to understand that this is indeed the Supreme Self.

Likewise, in the section on the "Single Goal" (ekāyana), by explaining that the goal of the entire manifold world—including its objects, senses, and internal organs—is the one without interior or exterior, the absolute mass of consciousness (prajñānaghana), it leads us to understand that this is indeed the Supreme Self.
Therefore, it is understood that this instruction regarding seeing and so forth refers to the Supreme Self alone.

As for what was further stated—that because the opening [verse] indicates something dear, this instruction regarding seeing and so forth refers only to the individual self (vijñānātman)—to this we reply: "Āśmarathya [says it is] a sign for the fulfillment of the initial proposition."
Thus begins the first chapter.
Here, there is the proposition: "When the Self is known, all this becomes known," and "All this is that which is this Self.
This [subsequent] indication points toward the fulfillment of that proposition, namely, the mention of the Self—intimated by what is dear—as being the object of vision and so forth.

For if the individual self (vijñānātman) were other than the supreme self (paramātman), then even when the supreme self is known, the individual self would not be known; thus, the promise that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be lost.

Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya maintains that the opening statement is made from the standpoint of the non-difference between the individual self and the supreme self in order to fulfill that promise.
Auḍulomi maintains that it is because [the self] will depart from such a state.

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that this introduction [to the subject] by way of non-difference is possible because the individual self (vijñānātman)—which has become turbid through contact with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect—becomes serene through the practice of means such as knowledge and meditation; and as it is about to depart from the aggregate of the body and so forth, its identity with the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established.
To this effect, there is a scriptural passage: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form."

And in another place, [the scripture] indicates that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) has the individual soul (jīva) as its substrate by means of the illustration of rivers: "As rivers flowing toward the ocean lose their names and forms upon reaching it, so the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).

For the meaning understood there is that, just as in the world rivers reach the ocean having abandoned only their own inherent names and forms, so too the individual soul reaches the Supreme Person having abandoned only its own inherent name and form; for such is the equality between the illustration and the thing illustrated.
"Because of the abiding [of the Self in all beings], so says Kāśakṛtsna."
The teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that this introductory statement regarding non-difference is appropriate because this very Supreme Self exists even in the form of the individual self (vijñānātman).

To this effect, the Brāhmaṇa passage—"Entering with this living self (jīva), let me evolve names and forms"—and similar texts show that the Supreme Self itself exists in the state of the individual self. Likewise, there is a Vedic mantra of this kind: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made their names, sits calling them by those names."

Furthermore, in the accounts of the creation of fire and the other elements, no separate creation of the individual soul (jīva) is heard of, by which it could be understood that the soul is a modification distinct from the Supreme Self.

According to the teacher Kāśakṛtsna, the view is that the individual soul is the unmodified Supreme Lord and not something else. However, although the teacher Āśmarathya intends the non-difference of the soul from the Supreme, nevertheless, because he mentions its dependence in the words "on account of the fulfillment of the promise" (*pratijñāsiddheḥ*), it is understood that some degree of the relationship of cause and effect is also intended.
In the view of Auḍulomi, however, difference and non-difference are clearly understood as being dependent upon different states.

Among these, the doctrine of Kāśakṛtsna is understood to be in accordance with the Śruti, because it conforms to the meaning intended to be taught by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*);
and thus [ends] the first chapter of the Sūtras.
Immortality is possible through the knowledge of That [the Self] only if it exists;

for if the individual soul (jīva) were admitted to be of the nature of a modification (vikāra), then upon the dissolution of that modification back into its material cause (prakṛti), the consequence of total destruction would follow, and immortality through such knowledge would not be possible.
Therefore, since names and forms cannot reside in the soul itself, names and forms residing in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are figuratively attributed to the soul.

For this very reason, even the origination of the individual soul (jīva), which is heard of in some places through the illustration of sparks from a fire, must be understood as occurring only by means of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

As for what was also stated—that by showing the emergence of the very great being under discussion from the elements in the form of the knowing self (*vijñānātman*), the text demonstrates that this knowing self alone is the object to be seen—in that case as well, these same three sūtras are to be applied: "The sign [of the truth] is for the sake of fulfilling the initial proposition, according to Āśmarathya. Here, the following has been proposed: "When the Self is known, all this becomes known," and "All this is that which is this Self."

And it has been established that the entire manifold of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and action arises from one source and dissolves into one, because the non-difference between cause and effect is demonstrated through the analogies of the drum and so forth.

The teacher Āśmarathya maintains that this sign indicates the fulfillment of that very proposition (*pratijñā*), namely, that the emergence of the Great Being from the elements is described as being in the form of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*); for only when there is non-difference is the proposition—that by the knowledge of one, all is known—logically possible.

"Because of the state of one who is about to depart," says Auḍulomi. The teacher Auḍulomi considers that this declaration of non-difference is possible because, for the individual self (*vijñānātman*) who is about to depart, there occurs a unification with the Supreme Self through the power of knowledge, meditation, and so forth, once it has become serene. "On account of the persistence," says Kāśakṛtsna. The teacher Kāśakṛtsna considers that this declaration of non-difference is appropriate because this very Supreme Self persists even in this form of the individual self.
But is this not a statement of annihilation, namely: "Having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death"?
How can this be a statement of distinction? This is not a fault;
for this mention of "perishing" is intended to mean the destruction of specific cognitions, not the annihilation of the Self.

Having raised the objection, "In this very matter, the Blessed One has confused me; there is no consciousness after death," the scripture itself shows another meaning: "Verily, I do not speak of delusion; for this Self, O Maitreyī, is indeed indestructible and of a nature that is not subject to annihilation; its association with the elements (mātrās), however, comes to an end.
What is meant by this is that this Self is an immutable and eternal mass of consciousness;
there is no possibility of its destruction.
However, through knowledge, there occurs a non-association with its "measures"—characterized as the elements and the senses—which are produced by ignorance.
And because of the absence of such association, there is an absence of the specific cognition produced thereby; thus it was said, "After departing, there is no consciousness.

As for the argument that this must be understood as referring to the cognizing individual self (vijñānātman) alone, because the concluding statement uses a word denoting an agent—namely, "O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the knower?"—that too must be refuted by the very perspective of Kāśakṛtsna.

Moreover, beginning with the passage, "For when there is duality as it were, then one sees another," the text elaborates upon specific cognition characterized by seeing and so forth within the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Then, in the sphere of knowledge (*vidyā*), it declares the absence of that very same specific cognition characterized by seeing and so forth, through the passage, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?
Furthermore, anticipating the objection that one might still cognize the Self even in the absence of objects, it says, "By what means, O Maitreyi, should one cognize the Cognizer?"

Furthermore, since the sentence is intended to establish the absence of specific cognition (*viśeṣavijñāna*), it is understood that the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) alone is indicated by the agentive suffix *tṛc* (the suffix *-tr*), based on its prior state of existence.
However, it has already been shown previously that the position of Kāśakṛtsna is supported by scriptural authority (*śrutimattva*).

Therefore, this distinction between the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the body fashioned from name and form, which are presented by ignorance (avidyā); it is not ultimate. This meaning must be accepted by all proponents of Vedānta, based on such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"; "The Self alone is all this"; "Brahman alone is all this"; "All this is what this Self is"; and "There is no other seer but He; there is no other seer but Him."

And from such Smṛti passages as, "Vāsudeva is all," "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) in all fields, O Bhārata," and "The Supreme Lord abides equally in all beings"; and from the denial of the perception of difference in texts such as, "He who thinks 'That one is one and I am another' does not know, like a beast," and "He goes from death to death who perceives here any kind of diversity," as well as from the prohibition of all modifications in the Self in the passage, "This indeed is the great unborn Self— undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman."
Otherwise, it would be impossible for those seeking liberation to attain an unassailable cognition, and it would be impossible for that cognition to have a perfectly certain object;

for an unassailable cognition regarding the Self is held to be that which removes all longing, as stated in the Śruti: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedānta" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6), and also:
"What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).
And because of the recollection of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established:

when right vision (samyagdarśana) regarding the identity of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) is established, this insistence on a distinction of selves—such as "this knower of the field is different from the supreme self" or "this supreme self is different from the knower of the field"—is useless, since there is only a difference in name. For this single Self is designated in many ways through a mere difference in names;
indeed, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."

The statement, "He who knows [Him] hidden in the cave," refers to a single cave; and there is nothing other than Brahman hidden in the cave, because scripture declares that the Creator Himself entered [the creation]: "Having created that, He entered into it.
Those, however, who insist otherwise, by contradicting the meaning of the Vedānta, subvert right vision itself—the very gateway to the highest good.
They imagine that liberation is something produced and impermanent,
and this does not accord with logic.
And [Brahman] is the material cause, because this does not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

Just as Dharma is to be inquired into because it is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), so too Brahman is to be inquired into because it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); this has been stated.
And Brahman has been defined by the sūtra: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (1.1.2). This concludes the first chapter: the section on Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*).

In this regard, the characteristic [of being a cause] is common to both the material cause (*prakṛti*)—as clay is to jars, ornaments, and the like, or as gold is to [ornaments]—and the efficient cause (*nimitta*)—as the potter is to the jar, or the goldsmith to the ornament. Therefore, a doubt arises as to what the nature of Brahman’s causality might be. In this context, it first appears that it must be merely an efficient cause;

why? Because its agency is heard to be preceded by reflection (*īkṣā*). For Brahman’s agency is understood to be preceded by reflection from such scriptural passages as, "He reflected," and "He created breath."
Furthermore, agency preceded by deliberation is observed only in efficient causes such as potters and the like;
and in the world, the accomplishment of the fruit of an action is seen to be preceded by multiple causal factors.
This same principle is appropriate to apply to the primal creator as well.
Furthermore, because of the well-known status of [other] lords: for among lords such as kings, Vaivasvata, and others, only the state of being an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) is perceived;
likewise, it is appropriate to understand that the Supreme Lord also possesses only the state of being an efficient cause.

Moreover, this world is observed to be an effect that has parts, is non-conscious, and is impure; therefore, its cause must also be of a similar nature, since a similarity between cause and effect is observed.

Furthermore, Brahman is understood from such scriptural passages as "without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" to possess characteristics other than those [of the material cause].

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), one must accept that there is another material cause for the world, distinct from Brahman, which possesses qualities such as impurity and is well-known from Smṛti; for the scriptural texts stating that Brahman is the cause would otherwise be restricted to its being merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*). This being the position reached, we reply: Brahman must be accepted as both the *prakṛti* (material cause) and the efficient cause, and not merely the efficient cause alone.
Why? Because there is no contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For in this way, both the proposition and the illustrative example remain uncontradicted.
The proposition is as follows: "But indeed, that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known."
And in that context, it is understood that when one thing is known, everything else, even if previously unknown, becomes known;
and this universal knowledge is possible through the knowledge of the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), because the effect is not distinct from its material cause.
However, the effect is not non-distinct from its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), for in the world we observe that a palace is distinct from its architect.

The illustrative example as well—“Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known, for the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the reality is simply ‘clay’”—is recorded in scripture as referring exclusively to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
Likewise: “By a single nugget of gold, all that is made of gold would become known,” and “By a single pair of nail-clippers, all that is made of iron would become known.
Similarly elsewhere, there is the proposition: “Venerable sir, when what is known, does all this become known?”
The illustration is: "Just as herbs grow upon the earth.
Likewise, the proposition is: "Indeed, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known.
And: "As, when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds, but [the sound] of the drum itself... Chapter One.
The illustration is: "By the mention of the beating of the drum, the sound is grasped.

In this way, according to the circumstances, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) in each Vedānta text are to be understood as proving the status of being the material cause (*prakṛtitva*).

Furthermore, this ablative case in the phrase "from which indeed these beings are born" (*yataḥ... imāni bhūtāni jāyante*) is to be seen as denoting the *apādāna* (ablative) characterized as the material cause, because of the specific grammatical rule: "the material cause is the *apādāna* of the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*).
Its status as the efficient cause (nimittatva), however, must be understood from the absence of any other presiding agent;

for just as in the world the material causes such as clay or gold proceed to act by depending on presiding agents such as potters or goldsmiths, there is no other presiding agent required for Brahman, which is the material cause, because of the restrictive declaration [in scripture] that "in the beginning there was only one, without a second."

The absence of another presiding agent should also be understood as being stated precisely through the non-contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For if a presiding agent were admitted who is distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*), then once again, because it would be impossible for the knowledge of all things to result from the knowledge of one thing, there would indeed be a contradiction of the proposition and the illustrative example.

Therefore, due to the absence of another presiding agent, the Self possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*); and due to the absence of any other material cause, it possesses the status of primordial nature (*prakṛtitva*).
And from what [source] do the self's status as agent and material cause [follow]? Also from the teaching of volition.

Furthermore, the teaching of "desire" (abhidhyā) indicates that the Self is both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the material cause (*prakṛti*). This is seen in such passages as, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.
In this context, because there is an independent activity preceded by desire, it is understood that [the Self] is the agent;
and because the desire to become many has the inner Self as its object, it is also understood that [the Self] is the material cause.
Because it is recited directly in the two [Vedic] branches.
This is a further argument for [Brahman] being the material cause.

For this reason as well, Brahman is the material cause: because, with reference to Brahman alone as the cause, both its origin and dissolution are recorded in scripture: "All these beings, indeed, arise from space alone;
they merge back into space."

For it is well known that whatever originates from something and into which it dissolves is the material cause (*upādāna*) of that thing, just as the earth is for rice, barley, and so forth. Furthermore, the word "from space alone" (*ākāśādeva*) indicates that there is no other intervening material cause.
Moreover, the dissolution of an effect is never observed to occur anywhere other than its material cause.
Because of self-activity and transformation.

For this reason also, Brahman is the material cause (*prakṛti*): because in the context of the exposition of Brahman, the text "It made itself by itself" (*tadātmānaṃ svayamakuruta*) shows that the Self possesses both the state of being the object and the state of being the agent—namely, "It [made] itself" indicates the state of being the object, and "It made by itself" indicates the state of being the agent. But how can that which is already established, existing as an agent, be capable of being something produced? We reply: through transformation (*pariṇāma*). For although the Self was already established, it transformed itself into a specific form of modification.
Furthermore, transformation in the form of a modification is observed in primal materials such as clay;
and by the qualification "by itself," independence from any other efficient cause is also understood.
Alternatively, "pariṇāmāt" may be a separate sūtra.

This is its meaning: for this reason also, Brahman is the material cause (prakṛti), because the transformation of Brahman itself into the nature of its modifications is recorded in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) by such passages as, "It became the existent and the non-existent, the defined and the undefined," and so forth.
For it is indeed sung as the source.

For this reason also, Brahman is the *prakṛti* (primordial material cause), because Brahman is also read in the Vedāntas as the "womb" (*yoni*): "the agent, the Lord, the Person, the Brahman-womb," and "that which the wise behold as the womb of all beings. Furthermore, in common usage, the word "womb" is understood to denote the primordial material cause, as in "the earth is the womb of herbs and trees.
Even in the case of a woman's womb, there exists the status of being the material cause for the embryo by way of its constituent parts.
In some instances, the word *yoni* is seen to denote a place, as in "A seat has been prepared for you to sit upon, O Indra.
However, on account of the complementary passage—such as "As a spider emits and retracts [its thread]"—it is understood here to denote the material cause (*prakṛti*).
Thus, Brahman's status as the material cause is well-established.

As for what was further stated—that in the world, agency preceded by deliberation is observed only in efficient causes such as potters and the like, and not in material causes—that is now answered: it cannot be here as it is in the world;
for this matter is not accessible through inference, but since it is accessible through scripture, it must be understood here according to the scripture.
We have already stated that the word "Word" (Śabda) establishes the Lord, the Seer, as the primordial material cause;
furthermore, we shall address this point again later on.
By this, all [cases] have been explained; they have been explained.

Beginning with the sūtra "Because [the word] 'non-sound' [is used] by Īśvara," the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause has been repeatedly raised as an objection and refuted by the sūtras themselves. For certain fallacious marks (liṅgābhāsas) that support that position appear, at first glance, in the Vedānta texts to those whose intellects are not yet mature; this constitutes the subject matter of the present section.

And since it accepts the non-difference of cause and effect, that [doctrine] is closely related to the Vedānta position and has been adopted in their own treatises by Devala and certain other authors of *Dharma-sūtras*; therefore, an effort was made specifically to refute it, rather than to refute the doctrines of atoms and other causes.
Nevertheless, those [other doctrines] must also be refuted because they stand as counter-positions to the doctrine that Brahman is the cause.

**The Section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇam)** A summary of the purport for demonstrating the connection between the two sections characterized by the reconciliation of contradictions regarding the concordance [of the Vedas] (*samanvaya*) and the removal of objections: An objection is raised that the Vedānta texts must be explained in such a way as not to contradict the *smṛtis* (traditional codes) composed by great sages such as Kapila and others—which are accepted by the learned and intended to teach the means to liberation—since these *smṛtis* find no place for themselves if they are left without scope. This prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) relies on the established principle of the previous system (*pūrvatantra*) stated in the aphorism: "But in case of contradiction, there should be no regard; for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference" (*JS 1.3.3*). This objection is refuted on the grounds that it is struck down by its own non-arising. The possibility of the objection being raised again is justified by the fact that those who are dull-witted due to their faith might still harbor doubts regarding the prophetic knowledge (*ārṣajñāna*) of Kapila and others. Since one who stands opposed by the force of *smṛti* will respond with the force of *smṛti*, the author introduces the defect of the lack of scope for other *smṛtis* that maintain God as the cause. He then establishes that when there is a conflict among *smṛtis*, one should accept those that conform to the *śruti*. He refutes the suspicion that the *smṛtis* of Kapila and others possess authority because they are based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and he instructs those who are dull-witted due to their faith. Having determined that this is merely a delusion—whereby an un-Vedic Kapila is mistaken for the Vedic one simply because of a commonality of name—he demonstrates the lack of proof for the supplementary claims found in passages such as "the seer born as Kapila. He shows that Manu and other exponents of Brahman are indeed Vedic. Finally, he concludes by elaborating on how the Sāṃkhya system, which is intent upon the distinction between Pradhāna and Puruṣa, contradicts both *śruti* and *smṛti*. He points out that since the principles beginning with Mahat are neither known in the world nor in the Veda, they are like a sixth sense-organ. **The Section on Yoga (Yogapratyuktyadhikaraṇam):** The rejection of Yoga is extended from the previous section. The reason for starting a separate section despite this extension is to address a specific doubt. It is demonstrated that the very respect shown toward Sāṃkhya and Yoga is the reason for the intense effort to refute them. While Sāṃkhya and Yoga lack authority regarding their object (the nature of reality), their authority regarding their own specific domain—such as the purification of the person, the cessation of activity, and steadfastness—is not undermined. Thus, a partial acceptance of Sāṃkhya and Yoga is granted. **The Section on Non-Dissimilarity (Navilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇam):** To show the internal connection of the section, it is demonstrated that its purpose is to render fallacious arguments contradictory. An objection is raised that there is no conflict between *śruti* and reasoning (*tarka*) because they have different objects; this is resolved by establishing that they do share the same object. Reasoning is introduced as a necessary aid to comprehension and is sanctioned by the injunction to reflect (*manana*). The prima facie view is presented through the inference: "The world is not derived from Brahman as its material cause, because it is dissimilar to Him. The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this argument is established. The dissimilarity of the world to Brahman is proven by observing the impurity and insentience of the world. The insentience of the world is further justified as being an instrument of the sentient. An objection is raised that insentience might deviate from being an instrument of the sentient; this is resolved by imagining the sentience of the entire world through scriptural presumption (*arthāpatti*). The portion of the sūtra "And its being so [is known] from the Word" (*tathātvaṃ ca śabdāt*) is analyzed to demonstrate that a matter established by reasoning must be sublated by the meaning of the *śruti*. The subsequent sūtra is introduced to dispel the objection that the sentience of earth and other elements is not merely a figurative meaning but actually the meaning of the *śruti*. The sūtra's meaning is shown to be that the sentience of the presiding deities is what is intended by the *śruti*. The term "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) in the sūtra is applied in two ways, elaborating on the presence of sentience in the elements and senses both generally and specifically. The prima facie conclusion is reached. Having cited examples such as hair, nails, and scorpions, the author demonstrates that the similarity (*sārūpya*) used to prove the relationship of material cause and effect as claimed by the opponent is inconclusive when analyzed. The opponent’s counter-reason, "dissimilarity," is analyzed in three ways and shown to be fallacious due to being irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), unestablished (*asiddha*), over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*), or contradicted (*bādha*). The author brings forward evidence from sources other than scripture to show that even the perfected Brahman is accessible to other means of knowledge. By showing that the injunction to reflect (*manana*) beyond mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) refers to sound reasoning, and by citing the sūtra "Because of the instability of mere reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*), he leaves no room for dry, speculative logic. Having provided scope for the scriptural division "consciousness and unconsciousness" (*vijñānaṃ cāvijñānaṃ ca*) through the manifestation and non-manifestation of sentience, and having maintained the scriptural presumption regarding the world's sentience, he demonstrates the contradiction of the division-scripture in the opponent's view. In the theory of a sentient cause, he points out the consequence of the doctrine of non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*). He establishes that the denial of the Satkāryavāda (the doctrine that the effect exists in the cause) is not without basis, as it refutes the notion that an indefinable effect becomes real only through the existence of the cause. In the doctrine of the non-difference of cause and effect, he raises four types of inconsistencies: (1) at dissolution, the cause would incur the attributes of impurity and so forth just like the effect; (2) the rule governing the distinction between enjoyers and enjoyed would collapse; (3) even liberated souls might be reborn; and (4) there would be no final dissolution. These are resolved respectively: the first inconsistency is removed by the example of transformation (*pariṇāma*); the first is also removed by the example of illusory appearance (*vivarta*); the third is removed; and the fourth is removed by the fact that it is not admitted by us. He shows that the Upanishadic teachers cannot be questioned regarding dissimilarity and other points, as these are shared by the Sāṃkhyas. Even an object inferred with great effort by skilled logicians... [text ends].

The refutation of the second inconsistency [of the Sāṃkhya argument] is as follows: others, being more proficient, establish the matter quite differently; thus, by means of the examples of deep sleep and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is shown that because the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*) is determinate, there is a necessity regarding origination. Furthermore, the inference proving that [the world] remains with a residue after dissolution is clarified; the reliance on reasoning (*tarka*) is undermined by demonstrating the instability of the arguments of the opponents. By one who attempts to prove the non-establishment of reasoning through the very support of reasoning, it is admitted that reasoning must be established somewhere; thus, the rejoinder based on the pride of skill in following reasoning established in the *Pradhāna* (Sāṃkhya) is addressed by analyzing the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "otherwise it would have to be inferred" (*anyathānumeyam*).
