[Objection: But surely the bodies of humans and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the causes of hair, nails, and so forth, which are also insentient; and the bodies of scorpions and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the effects of cow-dung and the like, which are also insentient.
[Reply: It is said in response: even so, there is indeed a distinction, in that some insentient things become the substratum for the sentient, while others do not.

Furthermore, this transformational disparity in nature is great, due to the difference in form and other qualities between humans and the like on one hand and hair, nails, and the like on the other, as well as between cow-dung and the like on one hand and scorpions and the like on the other.

Moreover, if there were absolute similarity, the very relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) would vanish. If it should be argued that "there exists some nature, such as earthiness (*pārthivatva*), which persists in hair and nails of men and so forth, just as it persists in dung and so forth in relation to scorpions and the like," [we reply: then the same applies to Brahman as well. (Brahma-sūtra, Second Chapter).
The characteristic of existence (*sattālakṣaṇa*), which is the essential nature (*svabhāva*), is observed to persist even in space and other such entities.

Now, by one who seeks to refute the world’s having Brahman as its material cause (*prakṛti*) on the ground of its being "dissimilar" (*vilakṣaṇatva*), it must be stated: is this "dissimilarity" intended to mean the non-persistence of the entire essential nature of Brahman, or of some part of it, or of consciousness (*caitanya*) alone? In the first alternative, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total destruction of the relationship between material cause and its modification (*prakṛtivikārabhāva*);
for the status of being a material cause and its modification does not exist in the absence of some degree of similarity.
In the second case, there is the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhatva*);
for it has been stated that the nature of Brahman, characterized by existence (*sattā*), is observed to persist in ether and the other elements.
In the third case, however, there is an absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*).

For what instance could be cited against the proponent of Brahman as the cause, claiming that whatever is not permeated by consciousness is seen to have a non-Brahman nature, since it is admitted that this entire aggregate of things has Brahman as its material cause?

Furthermore, contradiction with scripture is well-established, because it has been demonstrated that the purport of scripture is that conscious Brahman is both the cause and the material cause of the world.
As for the argument that other means of knowledge might apply to Brahman because it is an already established entity, that too is a mere fantasy.
For, due to the absence of form and other such qualities, this object is not within the range of perception;
and due to the absence of logical marks (liṅga) and so forth, it is not within the range of inference and the like; rather, this object is to be understood solely through scripture, just like dharma.
And so says the Śruti: "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning; it must be declared by another alone for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one.
And these two verses—"Who truly knows? Who here can declare whence this creation arose?"—demonstrate that the cause of the world is difficult to comprehend even for the self-perfected lords.

Smṛti also states in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: "Those entities which are indeed inconceivable—one should not attempt to apply reasoning to them"; and likewise, "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable, this is said to be unchangeable"; and also, "Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin; I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect. As for the argument that the Veda itself, by enjoining reflection (*manana*) in addition to hearing (*śravaṇa*), indicates that reasoning (*tarka*) should be respected—by this pretext, the acquisition of dry reasoning (*śuṣka-tarka*) is not possible here.

For in this context, reasoning (*tarka*) is indeed resorted to as an auxiliary to experience, being supported by scripture (*śruti*). Such reasoning includes: the non-attachment (*ananvāgatatva*) of the Self due to the mutual deviation between the states of dreaming and waking; the nature of the Self as the reality devoid of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañca-sadātmakatva*) because, in the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*), one attains identity with Being through the abandonment of the phenomenal world; and the non-difference of the world from Brahman because the world originates from Brahman, according to the principle that cause and effect are non-different.
Furthermore, the Sūtra "on account of the instability of mere reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*) will demonstrate the deceptive nature of reasoning when it is employed independently.

Even for one who might imagine the entire world to be conscious solely on the strength of hearing that it has a conscious cause, the scriptural statement "consciousness and unconsciousness" can indeed be reconciled with him by means of the manifestation and non-manifestation of consciousness.
However, even this scriptural statement regarding the distinction between the two is not tenable for the supreme [Brahman] alone.
How so? For here, the supreme cause is heard to exist in the form of the entire world, as stated in the words: "It became both consciousness and unconsciousness."
In this regard, just as it is not possible for that which is conscious to have the nature of being unconscious because of their distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇatva*),
so too it is not possible for that which is unconscious to have the nature of being conscious.
However, since the argument regarding distinct characteristics has already been refuted, the conscious [Brahman] must be accepted as the cause in accordance with the scripture itself.
If it is argued that [the self] exists because it is not perceived, we say no, because that is a mere negation.

If Brahman—which is conscious, pure, and devoid of sound and other qualities—were held to be the cause of an effect that is the opposite of it (i.e., unconscious, impure, and possessed of sound and other qualities), then it would follow that the effect was non-existent prior to its production;
and this is undesirable for you, who are a proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavādin*). If [it is argued] "this is not a fault, because it is a mere negation," [we reply]:
indeed, this is a mere negation.
There is no object to be negated by this negation;
for this negation cannot negate the existence of the effect prior to its production.
How so? Because just as this effect exists even now in the form of its cause, it is understood to exist in the same way prior to its production.
For even now this effect does not exist independently, apart from its causal self, as is heard in such scriptural passages as: "All abandon him who knows all as other than the Self";
rather, the existence of the effect prior to its production is non-different from that of the causal self.

Now, one might object: "Surely Brahman, which is devoid of sound and other qualities, is the cause of the world. Certainly so; however, the effect, which possesses sound and other qualities, does not exist—either prior to its production or at present—devoid of its causal self.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the effect was non-existent prior to its production;
we shall explain this in detail in the discussion on the non-difference of cause and effect.
In the commentary on the Sūtras: "If [the world] were merged [into Brahman], it would follow that [Brahman] would likewise [become the world]; therefore, [the doctrine of creation] is inconsistent."

If it were admitted that the effect—characterized by properties such as grossness, having parts, insentience, limitedness, and impurity—is caused by Brahman, then at the time of dissolution (apīti), when the effect is being reabsorbed and attains non-distinction from its cause, it would defile the cause with its own qualities. Consequently, because of the undesirable consequence that even the cause, Brahman, would possess impurity and other such traits just like the effect, this Upaniṣadic view—that omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world—would be untenable.

Moreover, since the entire differentiated world would reach a state of non-differentiation [at dissolution], there would be no cause for its regulated re-emergence; thus, its emergence with the specific distinctions of enjoyers, objects of enjoyment, and so forth, would not be possible, which is inconsistent.

Furthermore, if it is admitted that those enjoyers who have attained non-differentiation from the supreme Brahman are subject to re-emergence even when causes such as karma have dissolved, it follows that even the liberated (muktas) would be subject to re-emergence, which is inconsistent.

Moreover, even during dissolution, this world would remain distinct from the supreme Brahman; thus, dissolution itself would be impossible, and it would follow that the effect cannot be non-different from its cause—therefore, [the doctrine] is indeed inconsistent.
To this it is replied: No, because of the existence of examples.
In our view, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
As for what was stated— that when the effect merges into the cause, it would defile the cause with its own attributes—
that is not a valid objection.
Why? Because there exist illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance, when an effect merges into its cause, it does not defile the cause with its own specific qualities (*dharma*).

To illustrate: objects such as bowls, which have clay as their material cause (*prakṛti*), though they exist in a state of differentiation as high, low, or middling varieties, do not, upon returning to that material cause, contaminate it with their own qualities.
Likewise, ornaments such as necklaces, though they are modifications of gold, do not, upon dissolution, contaminate the gold with their own qualities.
The fourfold collection of beings, which is a modification of earth, does not merge with the earth by means of its own attribute;
however, for your position, there is no illustrative example whatsoever. Indeed, merging itself would be impossible if the effect were to remain in the cause by means of its own attribute alone.

"Even though cause and effect are non-different, it is the effect that has the nature of the cause, and not the cause that has the nature of the effect; this we shall explain under the section beginning with the words 'on account of the word "originating," etc. Furthermore, it is stated too little when one says that the effect, upon dissolution, would merge the cause with its own attributes; for this same undesirable consequence applies even during the state of persistence, since the non-difference of cause and effect is admitted.

For by such scriptural passages as "All this is what this Self is," "The Self alone is all this," "Brahman alone is this immortal one before [us]," and "All this is indeed Brahman," it is taught without distinction that in all three times, the effect is non-different from its cause. In this regard, the solution—that the cause is not affected by the effect or its attributes because they are superimposed through ignorance—is equally applicable here as well.

There is this further illustration: just as a magician is not touched by the illusion he himself has projected at any of the three periods of time because it lacks substantial reality, so too the Supreme Self is not touched by the illusion of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

And just as a single dreamer is not touched by the illusion of the dream-vision, because he remains unaffected during both waking and deep sleep, so too the one unchanging witness of the three states is not touched by the three changing states.
For this manifestation of the Supreme Self in the form of the three states is merely an illusion (*māyāmātra*), like the appearance of a rope as a serpent and so forth;

regarding this, it has been stated by the Teachers who know the tradition of the meaning of Vedānta: "When the individual soul (*jīva*), asleep through beginningless *māyā*, awakens, then it realizes the non-dual (*advaita*) which is unborn, sleepless, dreamless, and free from delusion."
Regarding this, what was said—that upon dissolution, the cause would also incur defects such as grossness just like the effect—is incorrect.

Furthermore, as for the argument that since all differentiation reaches a state of non-differentiation, no regulating cause can be established for its reappearance through differentiation, this too is not a fault; for there exists a supporting illustration: just as in deep sleep, meditative absorption, and so forth, although a natural state of non-differentiation has been reached, differentiation occurs again upon waking just as before because false knowledge has not been dispelled, so it will be here as well.

And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "All these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know that they have merged into Being; whatever they may be here—a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gnat, or a mosquito—that is what they become.

For just as even when there is no actual division, the empirical usage of division—obstructed by false knowledge—is seen to exist unimpeded like a dream, so too, even in the state of absorption (apīti), the power of division is inferred to be obstructed solely by false knowledge.
By this, the objection that those who have been liberated would be subject to rebirth is answered, because false knowledge has been sublated by perfect knowledge.

Furthermore, as for the other alternative imagined at the end—that even after dissolution, this world might remain distinct from the supreme Brahman—that too is refuted simply by the fact that it is not accepted [by us]. Therefore, this Vedantic philosophy is consistent and coherent.
And because of the defect in one's own position.
Moreover, these faults are common to the opponent's own position as well.

How so? It is explained as follows: First, as for what was stated—that "this world cannot have the Unmanifest (avyakta) as its material cause because of its dissimilarity"—that applies equally to the theory that it has Pradhāna as its material cause, since you admit the production from Pradhāna, which is devoid of sound and other qualities, of a world possessing sound and other qualities.

And precisely because you admit the production of an effect dissimilar [to its cause], the consequence of the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect prior to its production (asatkāryavāda) is equally applicable.
Nevertheless, since it is admitted that at the time of dissolution the effect is non-different from its cause, the same objection applies here as well.

Thus, when all modifications whose specific differences have been obliterated have reached a state of non-distinction upon dissolution, those particular distinctions which previously existed prior to the dissolution—such as "this is the material cause for this person" and "this is for that person"—cannot be restricted in the same way during re-creation, because their cause is absent.

Furthermore, if such a restriction were admitted without a cause, then, due to the equality of the absence of a cause, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the re-bondage even of those who are liberated.

If it is argued that some differences attain non-distinction upon dissolution while others do not, then those that do not so attain would fail to be effects of the Pradhāna; thus, these objections—being common to both sides—are not to be raised against either position, as they serve only to confirm their lack of fault, since [the opponent's view] must necessarily be accepted.
If it is argued that, because reasoning is not firmly established, the object must be inferred otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of no liberation.
For this reason as well, one should not oppose [the teachings] regarding a matter inaccessible to scripture by means of mere reasoning alone;
because reasonings that lack scriptural authority and are based solely on human imagination are unstable, since such imagination is unrestrained.
For instance, we observe that reasonings which have been strenuously devised by some experts are seen to be refuted by others who are even more expert.
Since those [reasonings] imagined by one person are themselves countered by others, it is impossible to rely on the stability of reasonings, given the diversity of human intellects.

If it were argued that the reasoning accepted by someone of renowned greatness—such as Kapila or another—is established, even so, there is indeed no stability; for we observe mutual contradictions among the founders of various schools (tīrthakaras), such as Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and others, despite their being regarded as men of renowned greatness.
Now, it might be argued: "We shall infer in another way so that the fault of lack of foundation (apratiṣṭhā) will not occur;
for it cannot be said that there is no reasoning at all that is well-founded."

For even this very lack of foundation of reasonings is established by reasoning itself, because by observing the lack of foundation in some reasonings, one infers the lack of foundation in other reasonings of the same class.
Furthermore, if all reasonings were without foundation, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the destruction of worldly activity;
for the world is seen to act toward the attainment of pleasure and the avoidance of pain in the future as well, based on the analogy with the past and present times.

Furthermore, when there is a conflict regarding the meaning of the scriptures (*śruti*), the determination of the correct meaning by means of refuting apparent meanings is accomplished precisely through reasoning (*tarka*) in the form of an investigation into the function of the sentences;

and Manu also holds this very view: "One who desires purity in dharma should well-understand this triad: perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*śāstra*) consisting of various traditions (*āgama*)."
And by stating, "He who investigates the instruction of the Dharma of the Ṛṣis with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows the Dharma,
and no other," this very lack of finality (apratiṣṭhitatva) is indeed the ornament of reasoning.
If it is argued that, by thus abandoning faulty reasoning (*tarka*), one must instead adopt faultless reasoning—
since there is no proof whatsoever that because one's ancestors were deluded, one must oneself also be deluded,
and therefore the instability of reasoning is not a defect— even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation.

Although in some matters the stability of reasoning (*tarka*) may be observed, nevertheless, with respect to the subject at hand, the fault of instability necessarily follows for reasoning, resulting in its inability to lead to liberation.

For this extremely profound reality of existence, which is the basis for liberation, cannot even be conjectured without the aid of scripture (*āgama*), as we have already stated: because it lacks form and other sensory qualities, this matter is not within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*); and because it lacks logical marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, it is not within the scope of inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge.
Furthermore, it is the consensus of all proponents of liberation that liberation arises from right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*);
and that right knowledge is of a single form, because it is dependent upon the reality of the object.
For that object which exists in a single form is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
In the world, knowledge regarding that [object] is called "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*), just as fire is said to be hot.
This being the case, it is untenable for there to be conflicting views among people regarding right knowledge;
however, conflict among various forms of speculative knowledge (*tarkajñāna*) is well known because they are mutually contradictory.

For it is well known in the world that whatever has been established as "this alone is right knowledge" by one logician is overturned by another, and what has been established by him is in turn overturned by yet another;
how, then, could there be right knowledge arising from reasoning, whose object is not fixed in a single form?
Furthermore, the proponent of Pradhāna is not accepted by all logicians as the best among those who know reasoning, such that we might accept his doctrine as right knowledge;
nor is it possible to assemble all past, future, and present logicians in one place and at one time, so that their consensus on a single subject and in a single form could constitute right cognition.

Since the Veda is eternal and is the cause for the arising of knowledge, it is logical that its subject matter is fixed; therefore, the correctness of the knowledge produced by it cannot be denied by any logicians—past, future, or present.
Thus, it is established that this very knowledge derived from the Upaniṣads is right knowledge.
End of the second chapter.
Otherwise, since right knowledge would be impossible, the consequence would be that there is no liberation from saṃsāra at all.
Therefore, it is established by the authority of scripture and by reasoning consistent with scripture that the conscious Brahman is both the cause and the material source (prakṛti) of the world.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.

Because it is closely related to the Vedic philosophy, because it is endowed with the force of more weighty reasoning, and because it has been accepted in some respects by certain cultured persons who follow the Vedas, the objection raised against the Vedānta texts—based on the grounds that the doctrine of the origination from non-existence (*asad-ārambhavāda*) is not accepted by the instructed—is now refuted. This was done by relying upon the doctrine of the origination from non-existence as a pretext for establishing [the opponent's] own reasoning. That objection which was raised regarding the Vedānta passages has thus been resolved.

Now, since some of dull intellect might again raise objections against the Vedānta texts on the grounds of reasoning by relying on the doctrines of Aṇu and others, [the author] extends the previous argument according to the maxim of "defeating the chief wrestler" (*pradhānamallanibarhaṇanyāya*). "Acceptances" (*parigraha*) means those which are accepted; "non-acceptances" (*aparigraha*) means those which are not accepted;
"non-acceptances by the learned" (*śiṣṭāparigraha*) refers to those views that are not accepted by the learned.
By this aforementioned reason for refuting the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause,

those theories of atoms and other causes which have not been accepted in any respect by the learned authorities such as Manu, Vyāsa, and others, should also be understood as explained— that is, refuted— by the same logic;
since the grounds for refutation are identical, there is nothing further to be doubted here.

In this case as well, the grounds for refutation are of the same nature: that the cause of the world, being supremely profound, is unfathomable by reasoning; that reasoning itself is unstable; and that otherwise, even if one were to infer [the cause] differently, there would be no liberation and a contradiction with scripture. Such are the reasons for the refutation.
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the identity of the enjoyer, [we reply] that it may be so, as in the case of the world.
Otherwise, however, the doctrine that Brahman is the cause is refuted by the force of reasoning alone.

Even though scripture is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own subject matter, it must nevertheless become subordinate to other means of knowledge when its subject matter is sublated by them, as in the case of the section on mantras and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Reasoning (*tarka*) as well would not be established with respect to anything other than its own object, just like *dharma* and *adharma*.
What follows from this? If it were so, then this would be improper: that the Veda should subvert an object already established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

But how can an object established by another means of knowledge be subverted by the Veda? To this it is replied: This distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is indeed well-known in the world—the embodied being is the conscious enjoyer, and sound and the other sense-objects are the things to be enjoyed.

Just as there is the eater, Devadatta, and the food, rice; and the non-existence of that distinction would follow if the eater were to attain the state of the food, or if the food were to attain the state of the eater;
for the mutual transformation of those two would follow from their non-difference from Brahman, the supreme cause.
Nor is it reasonable to subvert this well-established distinction;

for just as the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is observed in the present, so too must it be postulated for the past and the future. Therefore, [this established distinction remains]. (Brahma Sūtra, Second Chapter).

If someone should object that this determination of Brahman as the cause is untenable because it would entail the non-existence of the distinction between the agent and the enjoyer, one should say to him: "It may be as in the world. This distinction is indeed possible even in our view, because it is observed to be so in the world.

For instance, although the foam, waves, ripples, bubbles, and so forth—which are modifications of the ocean—are not different from the water itself, a worldly transaction characterized by their mutual distinction and mutual non-contact is nevertheless perceived.
And although the foam, waves, and other modifications of the ocean are not different from the ocean which consists of water, they do not attain the state of being each other;
nor, even though they do not attain the state of being each other, do they become something other than the ocean which constitutes their self.
In the same way here as well, there is no attainment of the state of being each other by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, nor will they become something other than the supreme Brahman.

Although the enjoyer is not a modification of Brahman—since scripture declares that the Creator himself, remaining unmodified, becomes the enjoyer by entering into his own creation, as in the passage, "Having created that, He entered into it"—nevertheless, for one who has entered into the effect, there exists a division caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as space appears divided due to limiting adjuncts such as jars. Therefore, even though there is non-difference from the Supreme Cause, Brahman, the distinction characterized as enjoyer and enjoyed is established according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves, as has been stated.
The identity of the cause and the effect [is established] from such scriptural terms as "originating" (ārambhaṇa) and others.
Having provisionally accepted this conventional distinction characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the rebuttal "it may be as in the world" was stated;
however, this distinction does not exist in reality according to the Sūtra-bhāṣya on *Ārambhaṇa*, because the non-difference of those two—the cause and the effect—is understood.
The effect is the world, a vast manifold beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
The locus is the Supreme Brahman as the cause;
from that cause, it is understood that the effect is non-different in the ultimate sense— that is, its existence apart [from the cause] is non-existent.
Why? Because of the words concerning "originating" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.

First, regarding the word "originating": having first asserted that by the knowledge of one thing everything is known, the text, in seeking an illustration, says: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known—the modification is a mere matter of words, a name; the reality is simply 'clay'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4–5).

What is meant by this is that when a single clod of clay is known in its ultimate reality as being of the nature of clay, everything made of clay—such as jars, bowls, and water-pots—becomes known, because there is no difference in their essential nature as clay.
"Whatever modification there is, it is a mere verbal handle, a name—merely by speech is it begun as existing, such as 'pot,' 'dish,' or 'water-pot'; but in reality, no modification exists at all;
for this is a mere name, which is untrue."
"‘It is truly only clay,’ thus is this illustration of Brahman handed down in scripture.
From the word *vācārambhaṇa* heard therein, it is understood that even in the case of the thing illustrated (the dārṣṭāntika), the entire aggregate of effects has no existence apart from Brahman.

Furthermore, after stating that fire, water, and food have Brahman as their cause, [the text] declares the non-existence of the effects of fire, water, and food apart from fire, water, and food, beginning with: ‘The fire-nature of fire has departed; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the truth is simply the three forms,’ and so forth."

From the words "from the word concerning the origin" (*ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ*)—this concludes the second chapter of the *Āpā* [commentary]. From the word "etc. (*ādi*), one should also cite that collection of statements intended to establish the oneness of the Self, such as: "All this has that as its essence; that is the Truth; that is the Self; Thou art That"; "All this is what this Self is"; "Brahman alone is all this"; "The Self alone is all this"; and "There is no diversity whatsoever here. Otherwise, the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing would not be possible.

Therefore, just as the spaces within jars, water-pots, and so forth are non-different from the great space, and just as the water of a mirage and the like are non-different from the saline desert and so forth— because they have a nature that appears and vanishes, and because they are indefinable in their own essence— it should be understood that this entire manifold of the world of objects and subjects has no existence apart from Brahman.
But surely Brahman is manifold in nature;
just as a tree has many branches, so too Brahman is endowed with the activity of many powers.
Therefore, both unity and plurality are indeed real—just as there is unity in the sense of "the tree" and plurality in the sense of "the branches."

Just as there is unity in the form of the ocean and multiplicity in the form of foam, waves, and so forth, and just as there is unity in the form of clay and multiplicity in the form of jars, bowls, and so forth; therein, through the aspect of unity, the worldly practice of liberation based on knowledge will be established, while through the aspect of multiplicity, the worldly and Vedic practices based on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) will be established.

And thus, the analogies of clay and so forth will be appropriate. But this cannot be so, because in the analogy, truthfulness is restricted to the material cause alone in the words, "Only clay is true"; because by the phrase "a mere modification originating in speech," the unreality of the entire collection of modifications is declared; because in the case of the subject being illustrated as well, truthfulness is restricted to the one supreme cause alone in the words, "All this has that as its self; that is true"; and because in the words, "That is the Self, That art thou, O Śvetaketu," the identity of the embodied soul with Brahman is taught.
For this identity of the embodied self with Brahman is taught as something already established by itself, not as something to be accomplished through further effort;

therefore, this scriptural identity with Brahman, once accepted, becomes the sublater of the natural identity with the embodied self—just as the cognition of a rope, etc., sublates the cognitions of a snake, etc.;

and when the identity with the embodied self is sublated, the entire natural worldly activity based upon it is likewise sublated, for the sake of whose establishment one might otherwise postulate another aspect of multiplicity in Brahman.

Furthermore, [the scripture] demonstrates the absence of all worldly activity—characterized by action, agent, and result—for one who perceives the identity of Brahman and the Self, through such passages as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?

Nor is it proper to say that this absence of worldly activity is restricted to a particular state, because the identity of Brahman and the Self expressed in "That thou art" is not dependent on any particular state.

Moreover, by means of the illustration of the thieves, [the scripture] shows the bondage of one who intends falsehood and the liberation of one who intends truth, thereby demonstrating that unity alone is the single ultimate reality, while plurality is a manifestation of false knowledge.

For if both were real, how could a living being, even while within the sphere of empirical experience, be called "one who intends falsehood"? Furthermore, by censuring the perception of difference in the passage, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity," [the scripture] demonstrates this very point; thus it is established. (End of Second Chapter)

Furthermore, in this view, it is not tenable that liberation arises from knowledge; for no false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—which must be removed by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) as the cause of transmigratory existence—is admitted [by you]. Indeed, if both [unity and diversity] were real, how could it be said that the cognition of diversity is removed by the cognition of unity?

[Objection: But if one-ness alone is admitted, then because diversity would be non-existent, worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception would be contradicted, as they would lack an object, like the cognitions of a person in a pillar and so forth.
Likewise, the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions (*vidhi-pratiṣedha-śāstra*) would also be contradicted in the absence of such [diversity], since it depends upon difference.
Furthermore, since even the treatise on liberation (mokṣa-śāstra) depends upon distinctions such as the teacher and the disciple, its contradiction would arise in the absence of such distinctions;
and how could the reality of the oneness of the Self (ātmaikatva), as propounded by a treatise on liberation that is itself unreal, be logically established?

To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because all worldly transactions (vyavahāra) are established as real prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self, just as the transactions of a dream are real prior to waking.

For as long as there is no realization of the oneness of the Self with Truth, so long does the notion of unreality not arise in anyone regarding the modifications characterized as the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results;

rather, abandoning its natural state of being the Self that is Brahman, every living being perceives only those modifications through ignorance (avidyā) as "I" and "mine," in the manner of a self and what belongs to the self.

Therefore, prior to the awakening to the Self as Brahman, all worldly and Vedic activity is established, just as for an ordinary person who has fallen asleep and is seeing various high and low objects in a dream, there exists a cognition that is certainly regarded as direct perception until awakening, and at that time he does not have the intention that it is a mere semblance of perception; it is just like that.

But how can the realization of the true identity of Brahman as the Self be effected by the Vedāntic texts, which are themselves unreal? For one does not die from being bitten by a rope-snake seen in a dream.
Nor can the purposes of drinking or bathing be accomplished by the water of a mirage.

This is not a fault, because effects such as death are observed to result from causes like the fear of poison, and because effects such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water are seen for one in the state of dreaming.

If it should be argued that those effects are likewise unreal, we reply: although the effects—such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water—for one in the state of dreaming are unreal, nevertheless the cognition of them is indeed a real fruit, since it remains unsublated even for the person who has awakened.

For indeed, no one who has awakened from a dream, considering the effects seen in the dream—such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water—to be false, considers the cognition of those effects to be false as well.
By this fact—that the cognition of the dreamer is not sublated—it should be understood that the doctrine of the self being merely the body is refuted.
And so says the Śruti: "When, during rites performed for desired ends, one sees a woman in dreams..."

By stating, "One should know prosperity therein in that vision of a dream," [the text] shows the attainment of a real abundance of results through an unreal dream-vision; likewise, after saying regarding certain portents seen directly, "One should know that he will not live much longer," and then stating, "He who sees in a dream a black man with black teeth—that one kills him," and so forth, [the text] shows that even by such an unreal dream-vision, true death is indicated.
And this is well known in the world among those skilled in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*):
by such a vision of one's own [dream] experience, the arrival of a good person is indicated, while by such [a vision], the arrival of an evil person is indicated;
likewise, the comprehension of true syllables such as 'A' and so forth is seen to arise from the comprehension of lines that are not the actual syllables.
Moreover, this final means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishes the oneness of the Self; beyond this, nothing further remains to be desired.

For just as in the world, when it is said "one should sacrifice," there arises an expectation of "what?", "by what?", and "how?", it is not so when it is said "That thou art" or "I am Brahman. In these cases, no other thing remains to be expected, because the realization has the oneness of the universal Self as its sole object.
For there would be a desire for further knowledge only if some other object remained;
however, there is no other object remaining apart from the oneness of the Self that could be desired.

Nor can it be said that this realization does not arise, because of scriptural texts such as "He understood that from him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.3), and because the means of realization—such as hearing, reflecting, and the like, as well as the recitation of the Vedas and so forth—are enjoined.
Nor can it be said that this realization is purposeless or erroneous; for we observe the fruit of it, which is the cessation of ignorance, and there is no subsequent sublating cognition.
Furthermore, as we have already stated, prior to the realization of the oneness of the Self, the entire worldly and Vedic transaction involving both the real and the unreal proceeds unimpeded.

Therefore, since all prior empirical dealings involving duality are sublated once the oneness of the Self has been established by the final means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no room for the postulation of a Brahman that undergoes transformation.
Now, an objection is raised: from the presentation of examples such as clay and so forth, it is understood that the Śāstra intends a Brahman that is subject to modification (*pariṇāmin*);
for in the world, objects such as clay are well-known to be subject to modification.

It is said in reply: "No. For this very Self is the Great, Unborn, the Brahman that is undecaying, immortal, and fearless. This Self is defined as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), because of the scriptural texts that negate all modifications, such as "neither gross nor subtle," from which it is understood that Brahman is immutable.
Indeed, it is impossible to conceive of the one Brahman as both possessing the quality of transformation and being devoid of it.
If it is argued that this could be like the case of standing and moving, we say no.

Because of the qualification "of the immutable" (kūṭasthasya); for it is not possible for the immutable Brahman to be the substratum of manifold attributes such as staying and moving; and we have already stated that the eternal Brahman is immutable because all modifications are precluded from it.

Furthermore, just as the realization of the oneness of Brahman with the Self is the means to liberation, the realization that [Brahman] undergoes transformation into the form of the world is not intended as an independent means for any result whatsoever, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).

For the scripture shows that the fruit [of knowledge] arises solely from the cognition of the oneness of the immutable Brahman and the Self, beginning with "This Self is 'not this, not this'" and concluding with "O Janaka, you have indeed reached fearlessness," and so forth.

In this regard, the following is established: since the attainment of the fruit is accomplished in the context of Brahman simply through the vision of Brahman as devoid of all specific attributes (*viśeṣa*), whatever is heard there that lacks a stated fruit—such as Brahman’s transformation into the form of the world—is employed solely as a means to the vision of Brahman. This is according to the principle that "that which has no fruit, when situated in proximity to that which has a fruit, is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of it";
it is not to be imagined as an independent fruit.

For it is not reasonable to say that from the knowledge of Brahman’s being subject to transformation, the fruit for the Self would be the state of being subject to transformation, because liberation is eternally immutable (*kūṭastha*).

If it be objected that for one who maintains the doctrine of the Self as the immutable Brahman, there is a contradiction with the proposition that God is the cause—since, due to absolute unity, there would be no distinction between the ruler and the ruled—we reply: No;
for omniscience depends upon the manifestation of the seeds of name and form, which consist of ignorance (*avidyā*).

From such statements as, "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced," it has been asserted in the aphorism "from which the birth, etc., of this [world arise" that the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world proceed from the Lord—who is omniscient, omnipotent, and whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—rather than from the non-intelligent *pradhāna* or any other cause.
That assertion remains exactly as it was; no meaning contrary to it is stated here again.

How is it not said [that there is a distinction], by one who asserts the absolute oneness and non-duality of the Self? Listen to how it is not said: name and form, which are as if inherent in the omniscient Lord, yet imagined through ignorance, indefinable as either identical to or different from reality, and serving as the seed for the manifold world of transmigration, are designated in Śruti and Smṛti as the "māyā-śakti" and "prakṛti" of the omniscient Lord.

The Lord is omniscient and distinct from those two, according to the Śruti: "That which is called space is indeed the developer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman"; and from such passages as, "I shall manifest name and form," "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made names, abides calling them forth," and "He who makes the one seed manifold.
Thus, the Lord conforms to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form created by ignorance, just as the ether conforms to limiting adjuncts such as jars and water-pots.

And He (the Lord) accepts as His own those very selves called *jīvas*—who are like the space within a jar, who conform to the aggregate of effects and instruments consisting of name-and-form presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), and who are individual conscious souls (*vijñānātman*)—only for the sake of conventional usage, just as one speaks of the Lord in relation to His domain of activity.

Thus, lordship, omniscience, and omnipotence depend upon the limitation imposed by adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of ignorance; in the absolute sense, however, such conventions as "ruler" and "subject to rule," or "omniscience," are not possible with respect to the Self whose true nature has had all adjuncts removed by knowledge (*vidyā*).
And so it has been said: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman)";
and also by such passages as, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?
Thus, all the Vedāntas declare the absence of all empirical transaction in the state of ultimate reality.

Likewise, in the *Īśvaragītā* as well, it is demonstrated that in the state of ultimate reality (*paramārthāvasthā*), there is an absence of conventional designations such as "ruler" and "subject": "The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is nature (*svabhāva*) that operates. The omnipresent Lord does not take upon Himself the sin or the merit of anyone; knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded."

In the state of worldly convention (*vyavahārāvasthā*), however, even in the revealed scripture (*śruti*), there is the conventional usage of terms such as "Lord" (*īśvara*): "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded.

Likewise, it is said in the *Īśvaragītā*: "The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (*māyā*), as if they were mounted on a machine."
The author of the Sūtras as well, with the ultimate truth (paramārtha) in mind, states "non-difference from that" (tadananyatvam);

however, with the conventional perspective (vyavahāra) in mind, he says "it may be as in the world" (syāllokavat), thereby describing Brahman as being like the great ocean and so forth. Without denying the phenomenal world of effects (kāryaprapañca) and the process of transformation (pariṇāma-prakriyā), he resorts to this [method] in the second chapter, thinking that it will be useful for the meditations on Brahman with attributes (saguṇopāsana).
And because [the self] is perceived when there is existence.
For this reason as well, the effect is non-different from the cause: because the effect is perceived only when the cause exists, and not when it does not exist;
for example, a jar is perceived when clay exists, and a cloth when threads exist;
and it is never observed that one thing is invariably perceived when another thing is absent.

For a horse is not perceived as being of the very nature of a cow, even though it is other than a cow; nor is a jar perceived as being of the very nature of a potter, despite the existence of the relationship between cause and effect, because they are distinct entities.
[Objection: But is it not observed that the perception of one thing is invariably concomitant with the existence of another, as in the case of smoke when fire exists?
This is not so, it is said, because smoke is seen even when the fire has been extinguished, as in the case of smoke held within a cowherd’s horn or similar vessels.
Now, if one were to qualify the smoke by a particular state, saying that "such smoke does not exist without fire," even this would involve no fault;
for we maintain that the cause for the non-difference between cause and effect is the cognition which is colored by the existence of that [cause].
And this [identity] does not exist between fire and smoke.
Or, as the Sūtra states: "Because of the perception of existence.
The meaning is that the non-difference of cause and effect is established not only from scripture, but also because they are perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*).
For there is indeed direct perception of the non-difference between cause and effect;

for example, in the case of a cloth which is a particular arrangement of threads, no effect called "cloth" is perceived apart from the threads themselves. Only the threads, possessing their lengthwise and crosswise extension (*ātānavitānavant*), are directly perceived. Likewise, the threads are [perceived] in the filaments, and the parts of those filaments in their own constituent parts.

By this direct perception, the three colors—red, white, and black—are apprehended; from that, it is to be inferred that there is only air and only space; beyond that, there is Brahman alone, without a second.
Regarding that, we have declared the finality of all means of valid cognition.
And because of the existence of what follows.

For this further reason as well, the effect is non-different from the cause: because it is heard that before its production, the effect exists in the cause in the very form of the cause, as in such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 1.1.1). This is due to the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word "this," which denotes the effect, with the cause.
Furthermore, whatever does not exist in something by way of its own nature cannot be produced from it, just as oil cannot be produced from sand.
Therefore, since the effect is non-different from the cause prior to its production, it is understood that even after being produced, the effect is indeed non-different from the cause.

And just as the cause, Brahman, does not deviate from existence throughout the three periods of time, so too the effect, the world, does not deviate from existence throughout the three periods of time; moreover, existence is one and the same.
For this reason also, the effect is non-different from the cause.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [eternal] because of the designation of its non-existence, we say no; for [this is said] with reference to another state, as is clear from the remainder of the passage.

[Objection: But surely, in some places, scripture even designates the non-existence of the effect prior to its production, as in "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent" (*asadevedamagra āsīt*) and "In the beginning this was verily non-existent" (*asadvā idamagra āsīt*).
Therefore, because of these designations of non-existence, the effect does not exist prior to its production—if you say this, we reply: no.
This designation of the effect as "non-existent" prior to its origination is certainly not intended to mean absolute non-existence.

What then? It is because the state of having unmanifest name and form (*avyākṛta-nāmarūpatva*) is a different property (*dharmāntara*) from the state of having manifest name and form (*vyākṛta-nāmarūpatva*). By means of that different property, this designation of "non-existent" refers to the effect itself—which is existent and non-different from the cause—prior to its origination.
How is this understood? From the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣāt*).

A statement whose meaning is doubtful at its commencement is determined by its concluding portion. Here, that which was indicated at the beginning by the word "non-existent" in the phrase "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent," is again referred to by the word "that" and qualified as "existent" in the words "That became existent. Furthermore, because the non-existent has no connection with prior or subsequent time, the use of the verb "was" (āsīt) would be inappropriate for it.

Even in the passage "In the beginning this was indeed non-existent," there is no absolute non-existence, because of the qualification in the subsequent part of the sentence: "It made itself its own self."

Therefore, this designation of the effect as "non-existent" prior to its origination is due solely to another property [of existence]; for in common worldly usage, a thing that has been differentiated by name and form is well known as the referent of the word "existent.
Consequently, it is figuratively said that "it was as if non-existent" before the differentiation of name and form.
Because it is joined [with the word "fire"] and because there is another word [for fire].

By reasoning as well as by other scriptural statements, it is understood that before its production, the effect exists and is non-different from its cause. First, the reasoning is set forth: in the world, those who desire curds, jars, or golden ornaments are seen to employ specific causes such as milk, clay, or gold respectively;
for those desiring curds do not employ clay, nor do those desiring jars employ milk.
This would not be possible under the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*).

For if everything were equally non-existent everywhere prior to its production, why is it that curd is produced from milk alone and not from clay, or that a jar is produced from clay alone and not from milk? If it is argued that although prior non-existence is equal, there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) in milk for the sake of producing curd, but none in clay; and that there is some excellence in clay for the sake of producing a jar, but none in milk—then, because the prior state possesses such excellence, the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is abandoned, and the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is established.

Furthermore, the causal power (*śakti*) postulated for the sake of restricting the effect to its cause could not restrict the effect if it were either something other than the cause or non-existent, because there would be no distinction in their non-existence or their being "other" respectively.
Therefore, power is the very self of the cause, and the effect is the very self of the power.

Moreover, since there is an absence of any cognition of difference—such as that between a horse and a buffalo—between the effect and the cause, or between substance and its attributes (*guṇa*) and so forth, their identity (*tādātmya*) must be accepted.

Even in the hypothesis of inherence (*samavāya*), if a relation between inherence and its inherent substrates is admitted, then another mutual relation must be postulated for each of those, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, such a relation is not admitted, there would be the consequence of a disconnection. Now, if inherence were to be related without depending on any further relation because it is itself of the nature of a relation, then conjunction (*saṃyoga*) too would be related without depending on inherence, since it is itself of the nature of a relation.
Furthermore, because identity (*tādātmya*) is perceived between substance, quality, and so forth, the postulation of inherence (*samavāya*) is useless.

Moreover, how does the effect—the composite substance—subsist within its causes, the constituent substances? Does it subsist in all the parts collectively, or in each part individually? If it were to subsist in all the parts collectively, then the non-perception of the composite would follow, because it is impossible to have sensory contact with all the parts simultaneously;
for multiplicity, subsisting in all its substrates collectively, is not perceived by the perception of individual substrates.

Furthermore, if it were to exist in its constituent parts within the whole, then one would have to postulate parts of the whole distinct from its constituent parts, by which [parts] the whole would reside part-by-part within the constituent parts;
for a sword pervades its sheath by means of parts distinct from the parts of the sheath itself.
Moreover, this would lead to an infinite regress, because in order for it to reside in each of those various parts, yet other and further parts would have to be postulated.
Now, if it were to exist in each individual part, then while it is operative in one place, it would not be operative in another;
for Devadatta, while being present in Srughna, cannot at that very same time be present in Pāṭaliputra as well.

Furthermore, if it were to exist simultaneously in multiple places, there would be the consequence of its being manifold, like Devadatta and Yajñadatta who reside respectively in Srughna and Pāṭaliputra.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the whole is present in its entirety within each part, like "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, we say no;
for such is not the case in experience.

If the whole were present in its entirety within each part, just as "cowness" is perceived individually in each individual cow, then the whole would likewise be perceived individually in each of its parts.

Nor is it apprehended as being thus restricted; for if the whole were present in its entirety within each part, then— since the whole is one— it would perform the function of the breast even with its horn, and the function of the back with its chest,
yet this is not observed.
Furthermore, if the effect were non-existent prior to its production, then production would be without an agent and devoid of a self-nature;
for production is indeed an action, and like the act of going and so forth, it must necessarily have an agent.
Moreover, it would be a contradiction to claim that something is an action and yet lacks an agent.
Furthermore, if the arising of a jar were being described, it could not have the jar as its agent; rather, it would have to be conceived as having another agent.
Likewise, if the arising of the potsherds and so forth were being described, they too would have to be conceived as having other agents.
And this being the case, when it is said "the jar arises," it would effectively be saying "the causes, such as the potter and so forth, arise."

Furthermore, when it is said that "the production of a jar occurs in the world," the potter and others are not understood to be themselves undergoing production, for they are perceived as already produced.

If it is argued that "production" is simply the connection with the existence of its own cause, and that this is the effect's "acquisition of selfhood," then it must be explained how that which has not yet acquired a self can enter into a connection;
for a connection is possible only between two existing things, not between an existent and a non-existent, nor between two non-existents.
Furthermore, because non-existence is indefinable, it is illogical to establish a temporal limit such as "prior to origination";
for in the world, limits are observed for existing things, such as fields or caves, but not for non-existence.

Indeed, by means of a limitation such as "the son of a barren woman was king prior to the consecration of Pūrṇavarman," the indefinable son of a barren woman cannot be qualified as having been, being, or about to be a king.

And if even the son of a barren woman were to exist after the operation of causal factors (kāraka-vyāpāra), then this too would follow: that the state of being an effect (kārya-bhāva) will also exist after the operation of causal factors.

However, we observe that because there is no distinction between the son of a barren woman and the non-existence of an effect in their commonality as non-existent (abhāvatva), just as the son of a barren woman will not exist after the operation of causal factors, so too the non-existence of an effect will not exist after the operation of causal factors.
But if this were so, it would follow that the activity of the causal agent is purposeless;

for just as no one exerts effort to bring about the nature of the cause because it is already established, so too no one would exert effort to bring about the nature of the effect because it is already established and non-different from the cause.
Yet, people do exert effort.
If it is argued that we must therefore assume the non-existence of the effect prior to its production, so that the activity of the causal agents may have purpose, this is not a fault;
for the purposefulness of the activity of the causal agents is established by defining the cause through the form of the effect.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that even the form of the effect is essentially identical with the cause, since that which is not essentially identical cannot be produced.
Nor does a difference in the substance arise merely from the perception of a particular state;
for Devadatta, though seen with his hands and feet contracted and then with his hands and feet extended, does not undergo a change of substance, because of the recognition that "it is he himself.

Likewise, although fathers and others assume many different postures day after day, there is no change in their substance, because of the recognition that "this is my father," "this is my brother," or "this is my son."
If it is argued that [the term "birth"] is appropriate there because it is immediately preceded by the cessation of birth, but not elsewhere, we say no;
for even in the case of milk and the like, the state of being the precursor to the form of curds and so forth is directly perceived.

Furthermore, even in the case of invisible things such as banyan seeds, when they come within the range of perception in the form of sprouts and the like through the accumulation of other homogeneous parts, this is designated as "birth."
When those very same components reach a state of non-perception due to their gradual diminution, there arises the notion of annihilation.

In that case, because of the interruption caused by such an annihilation of birth, it would follow that what was non-existent becomes existent, and what was existent becomes non-existent. If this were so, it would entail the absurdity of a distinction between the being in the womb and the one lying on its back [after birth];
likewise, it would entail a distinction among the stages of childhood, youth, and old age, and it would result in the collapse of social conventions regarding fathers and other relations.
By this, the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) should be refuted.

Furthermore, for one who holds that the effect is non-existent prior to its production, the operation of causal factors would be devoid of an object, because it is impossible for a non-entity to serve as an object—just like the employment of various weapons such as swords for the purpose of striking at empty space.
If it is argued that the operation of causal factors has the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as its object, we say no.
Because it would lead to the over-extension [of the principle] that one thing could be produced by the operation of a causal factor directed toward a different object;

and if it is argued that the effect is merely a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) itself, we say no, because that would entail the consequence of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatā*).

Therefore, it is substances such as milk themselves that, while persisting in the form of curds and so forth, receive the designation of "effect. Thus, it is impossible—even in a hundred years—to conceive of an effect as something other than its cause. Likewise, the primal cause itself, up to the final effect, assumes the status of being the locus of all worldly transactions through various forms of effects, like an actor. From this reasoning, it is understood that the effect exists prior to its production and is non-different from its cause. [End of] Second Chapter.

This is understood from another scriptural passage as well, because in the preceding sūtra a word designating "non-being" (asat) was cited; therefore, "another word" (śabdāntara) refers to a word designating "being" (sat), such as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. And having introduced the position of non-being with the words, "On this point some say: 'In the beginning this was non-being alone,'" and having refuted it with the words, "How could being be born from non-being?", the text concludes by affirming: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

In this regard, because the effect denoted by the word "this" is heard in scripture to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cause denoted by the word "Being" prior to its origination, its existence and non-difference [from the cause] are established.

If, however, the effect were non-existent prior to its origination and were to subsequently originate and inhere in the cause, it would be something other than the cause; in that case, the proposition—"by which the unheard becomes heard"—would be undermined.
But through the understanding of existence and non-difference, this proposition is validated.
And it is like a sharp arrow.

Just as a rolled-up cloth is not clearly perceived—such that one cannot discern whether it is a cloth or some other substance—the very same cloth, when unrolled, is perceived as manifest through that unrolling, [realizing] that what was the rolled-up substance is indeed a cloth.
And just as at the time of being rolled up, although it is perceived as a "cloth," its specific length and breadth are not perceived; [so too is the case with the Self].

At the time of its expansion, that very same cloth is perceived as having specific length and breadth; it is not something different or distinct from the rolled-up form, such that one could say, "This cloth is another [than before]. In this way, the effect, such as a cloth, which exists in an unmanifest state during the condition of its causes, such as the threads, is perceived in a manifest state when revealed by the operations of the shuttle, the loom, the weaver, and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that the effect is non-different from the cause, according to the analogy of a cloth rolled up and then spread out.
And just as in the case of the vital breaths and so forth.

And just as in the world, when the various vital breaths such as *prāṇa* and *apāna* are restrained by *prāṇāyāma*, they exist in the form of mere causes, and only the effect of mere living (*jīvana-mātra*) is accomplished, but not other effects such as contraction and expansion; yet when those same varieties of vital breaths function again, other effects such as contraction and expansion, in addition to mere living, are accomplished; and there is no difference between the varieties of vital breaths and the vital breath itself, because there is no distinction in their nature as air—so too is the non-difference of the effect from the cause.

And therefore, because the entire world is the effect of Brahman and is non-different from it, this scriptural proposition is established: "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known."
Because of the designation as something else, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth.

Otherwise, however, the doctrine that consciousness is the cause is challenged; for if the process of the world is based on consciousness, defects such as the failure to accomplish what is beneficial would follow.
Why? Because of the designation of the other (itara-vyapadeśāt). This refers to the section concerning the other.
The Śruti declares that the embodied self has Brahman as its Self, as seen in the second chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*:
"That is the Self; 'That art thou,' O Śvetaketu," because of this instruction.

Or alternatively, it declares that the other, namely Brahman, has the embodied self as its Self, because after creating [the world], the very same unmodified Brahman, the creator, entered into that effect, thereby showing that it has the embodied self as its Self.

Furthermore, by stating, "Entering with this living self (jīva), let me manifest names and forms," the Supreme Deity designates the living self by the very word "self" (ātman), thereby showing that the embodied self is not different from Brahman.
Therefore, that which is the creative agency of Brahman belongs to the embodied self alone.

Consequently, being an independent agent, it would produce only what is beneficial and conducive to its own well-being, and not the web of manifold evils such as birth, death, old age, and disease, which are disadvantageous.
For no one who is not dependent on another enters a prison of his own making; nor would anyone who is himself utterly pure ever identify with a body that is utterly impure;
and even if he were to somehow create something painful, he would abandon it by his own will.
And he should take up that which brings happiness; and he should remember: "By me this manifold image of the world has been fashioned.
For everyone in the world, having clearly performed an action, remembers: "This was done by me."
And just as a magician effortlessly withdraws by his own will the illusion he himself has projected, so too the embodied soul (śārīra) would have to withdraw this creation;
yet even his own body the embodied soul is not able to withdraw without effort.
Thus, because we do not observe such purposeful action and the like, it is concluded that the process of the world cannot proceed from a conscious being [in the manner suggested].
In the Bāsarpa-sūtra-bhāṣya: "But [the individual soul is] distinct, because of the designation of difference."
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.

We declare that the creator of the world is that Brahman which is omniscient, omnipotent, and whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free; it is distinct from and superior to the embodied soul.
In that [Brahman], defects such as the failure to perform what is beneficial do not apply.
For there is nothing beneficial that must be done for Him, nor anything harmful to be avoided, because His nature is eternally liberated;
nor is there any obstruction to His knowledge or any limitation to His power anywhere, because He is omniscient and omnipotent. The embodied soul, however, is not of such a nature.
In that case, defects such as being the cause of [the world's] welfare and so forth would follow;

however, we do not say that He is the creator of the world. Why is this? Because of the designation of difference. Passages such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known"; "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the Existent"; and "The embodied self is mounted by the intelligent Self"—this kind of designation of difference between agent, object, and so forth, shows that Brahman is superior to the individual soul (jīva).
But surely, a teaching of non-difference has also been shown in such passages as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

How can both difference and non-difference, which are contradictory, be possible? This is not a fault, because the possibility of both has been established in various places through the analogy of the great ether and the ether within a jar.

Furthermore, when non-difference has been made known by a teaching of non-difference such as "That thou art," then the transmigratory state of the individual soul (*jīva*) ceases to exist. [End of] the Second Chapter.

The agency of Brahman and its status as the creator consist in the fact that the entire empirical usage of difference—which is a manifestation of false knowledge—is sublated by perfect knowledge; for how could there be any creation in that state, or how could defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others] exist? Indeed, the transmigratory existence characterized by the failure to act for one’s own benefit and so forth is an illusion produced by the non-discrimination of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the aggregate of effects and instruments formed by name-and-form presented by ignorance; it does not exist in the ultimate sense. We have already stated that it is non-existent, being like the conceit regarding birth, death, cutting, breaking, and so forth.

But when the conventional usage of difference is not sublated, the superiority of Brahman—comprehended through such designations of difference as "That is to be sought, That is to be desired to be known"—prevents the contingency of defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others].
And like a garden and so forth, that [creation] is untenable.

And just as in the world, among stones which are all equally endowed with the commonality of "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva), one observes a manifold variety: some are precious gems such as diamonds and lapis lazuli; others are of middling potency, such as sun-crystals; and others are base stones fit only to be discarded by dogs and crows.

And just as among seeds that depend upon the same single earth, a great variety of diversity in leaves, flowers, fruits, scents, tastes, and so forth is observed in sandalwood, kiṃpāka, campaka, and other plants.

And just as from a single essence of food there arise diverse effects such as blood and so forth, as well as hair of the head and body and so forth—so too, even from a single Brahman, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the wise one (prājña), as well as the diversity of effects, is logically possible. Therefore, that [objection] is untenable; the meaning is that the defects imagined by the opponent are untenable. Furthermore, this is a supplementary argument based on the authority of scripture, because modification is merely a matter of words (vācārambhaṇamātra), and because it is like the diversity of objects seen in a dream.
If it be argued that [the soul] does not [pervade the body] because we observe its withdrawal [from it], we say no; for it is like milk.
As for the statement that consciousness (*caitanya*) is the one, non-dual Brahman, the cause of the world—that is not tenable.
Why? Because we observe the employment of instruments (*upasaṃhāradarśanāt*).
For in this world, we see that the makers of jars, cloths, and so forth—such as potters and weavers—employ clay, staffs, wheels, and other implements.
It is observed that those who have gathered the means by collecting various factors such as threads, water, and so forth, perform their respective tasks;
however, Brahman is intended by you to be without assistance.
If it does not gather other means, how can its status as a creator be logically established? Therefore, if it is argued that Brahman is not the cause of the world, this is not a valid objection.

Because it is established through a specific nature of the substance itself, like milk. For just as in the world milk or water transforms by itself into the state of curds, ice, crystals, and so forth, without depending on external means, so too will it be here.
[Objection: But even milk and the like, when transforming into the state of curds and so forth, certainly depend on external means such as heat;
how then can it be said, "like milk"? [Reply: This is not a fault.

For even milk itself, to whatever degree it undergoes the process of transformation, is prepared for the state of curd by heat and other factors to that same extent; if it did not possess the inherent nature of becoming curd itself, it would not attain the state of curd even through the force of heat and so forth.
For neither air nor space is forcibly transformed into the state of curd by heat and other such factors;
rather, its fullness is accomplished through the collection of instrumental means (sādhana-sāmagrī);
however, Brahman possesses complete power inherently.
Its fullness is not to be accomplished by anything else; and there is a scriptural passage: "For Him, no effect or instrument exists; neither an equal nor a superior is seen of Him.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent."
Therefore, because even the single Brahman possesses a manifold power, its manifold transformation is possible, just as in the case of milk and other substances.
And also because [the soul] is like the gods and others in the world.
It might be argued as follows: it is observed that non-conscious things such as milk and the like attain the state of curds and so forth even without depending on external means;
however, conscious agents such as potters and others are seen to engage in their respective tasks only by depending on a collection of means.

How can Brahman, being conscious and without a companion, proceed to act? We reply: "Like the gods and others. Just as in the world, gods, ancestors, seers, and others—who possess great power and are conscious—though they do not depend on any external means, are observed to create by mere volition through their possession of special sovereignty many bodies of various forms, such as palaces and chariots, out of themselves alone, according to the authority of the Mantras, Arthavādas, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas;
and just as the spider creates threads from itself alone.

The crane conceives its offspring even without semen, as stated in the *Sūtabhāṣya*; and the lotus plant proceeds from one lake to another without requiring any means of locomotion. In this same way, the conscious Brahman also, without depending on any external instrument, will itself create the world.
If he should say: "These examples of gods and others that have been cited for Brahman are not identical with the subject of the illustration (the dārṣṭāntika), Brahman."

For it is the body itself—which is insentient—that serves as the material cause for the production of the various manifestations, such as other bodies, belonging to gods and others, and not the conscious self;
likewise, in the case of the spider, saliva becomes solidified into a thread through the consumption of very small insects;
and the crane conceives a fetus upon hearing the sound of thunder.

And the lotus plant, being directed by a conscious agent, approaches one lake from another lake by means of its very unconscious body—just as a creeper climbs a tree—but it does not itself, being unconscious, exert effort in approaching another lake.

Therefore, if you say that these [examples] are not illustrations of Brahman, we reply to you: this is no fault, because what is intended to be shown is merely the difference from examples such as the potter. For while the potter and others, as well as the gods and others, are equally conscious, the potter and the like require external instruments for the commencement of their work, whereas the gods and others do not.

Similarly, we intend to show by the example of the gods that Brahman, although conscious, will not require any external means; therefore, the intention is that there is no absolute rule that what is observed as the capacity of one must necessarily belong to all.
