[End of Second Chapter] [The opponent's objection: "There would be the consequence of [Brahman] being entirely consumed, or else there would be a contradiction with scriptural texts concerning its partlessness."
The Section on the Total Transformation (*Kṛtsnaprasakti-adhikaraṇa*).

It has been established that Brahman—the one, non-dual consciousness—is the cause of the world by transforming itself, without depending on any external means, just as milk [turns into curd] or as the gods [manifest their forms].
However, for the sake of purifying the meaning of the scripture, the author now raises an objection.

There would be the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being affected: the entire Brahman would undergo transformation into the form of an effect, because it is partless. For if Brahman were possessed of parts like the earth and other elements, then one part of it would transform while another part would remain as it is.

However, Brahman is understood from the scriptures to be partless—by such texts as: "Without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless"; "For the divine Person is formless, existing both within and without, unborn; this great being is infinite, boundless, and a mass of consciousness alone"; "This Self is 'not this, not this'"; and "neither gross nor subtle"—all of which negate every particular attribute.
Consequently, since a partial modification is impossible, if a total modification were to occur, it would result in the destruction of the very root [of Brahman].

Furthermore, the instruction regarding [Brahman] as something to be seen would become purposeless, because the effect would be seen without effort, and because Brahman, as distinct from that, would be impossible; moreover, there would be a contradiction with scriptural passages concerning its being unborn and so forth. If, on the other hand, one were to accept that Brahman possesses parts in order to avoid these defects, even then those scriptural passages cited in the Sūtras and Bhāṣya which establish its partlessness would be contradicted.
"And if it possesses parts, there follows the consequence of its being non-eternal"—thus he objects that this position cannot be established in any way whatsoever.
But on account of scripture, for [the truth] is rooted in the Word.
The word "tu" (but) removes the objection:
indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in our position;
first of all, there is no possibility of the entire [cause] being consumed.

Why? Because of scripture (śruti). For just as the origin of the world from Brahman is heard in scripture, so too is the subsistence of Brahman apart from its modifications heard, because of the designation of a distinction between the material cause (prakṛti) and its modification (vikāra), such as: "That deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms,'" and "Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that. All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven," and other passages of this kind;
likewise, because of the statement regarding His having the heart as His abode.

Furthermore, because of the statement regarding union with the Existent (*sat-sampatti*): if the entire Brahman were to be exhausted in the form of an effect, then the qualification applied to one who has entered deep sleep—“then, my dear, he becomes united with the Existent” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1)—would be untenable. This is because [the soul] would be eternally united with a modified Brahman, and there would be no unmodified Brahman remaining.
Likewise, because the sense-objects of Brahman are denied, whereas it is logical that a modification of Brahman falls within the range of the senses.
Therefore, there exists an unmodified Brahman.
Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding partlessness (*niravayavatva*), because partlessness itself is indeed accepted precisely because it is heard [in scripture];
and Brahman has the Word as its source and the Word as its authority, not the senses or other means of knowledge. Thus it is according to the scripture. Chapter Two. Second Section. First Sūtra.
This must be accepted;
for the Word (Śabda) establishes both [attributes] of Brahman: the absence of partiality (*akṛtsnaprasakti*) and partlessness (*niravayavatva*).

Even among worldly things such as gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs, powers are observed whose objects are multiple and even contradictory effects, depending on the diversity of place, time, and causal conditions.

Even those [powers] cannot be understood through mere reasoning alone without instruction—such that one could know: "This entity has this many powers, these are its auxiliaries, these are its objects, and these are its purposes";
how much more so, then, would the nature of Brahman, whose essence is inconceivable, not be defined without the Word?
Thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "One should not apply reasoning to those entities which are indeed inconceivable."
"And that which is beyond the primal natures (prakṛtis) is the characteristic of the inconceivable.
Therefore, the comprehension of the true nature of supersensuous objects is rooted solely in the Word (śabda).

Now, it may be objected: even by means of the Word, a contradictory meaning cannot be made known; for instance, that Brahman—which is partless—undergoes transformation, yet does not do so in its entirety.
If Brahman were partless, it could not undergo transformation at all, or else it would have to transform in its entirety.
If, however, it were to transform in one form while remaining as it was in another, then, by the assumption of distinct forms, it would follow that it possesses parts.

For in the realm of ritual action, when a contradiction is perceived—such as in the cases "one takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice" and "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice"—the recourse to an option (*vikalpa*) serves as the means of resolving the contradiction, because the performance [of such acts] depends upon the human agent.
But here, even by resorting to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is not possible to avoid the contradiction, because a real entity (*vastu*) is not dependent upon a person.
Therefore, this [objection] that "this is difficult to establish" is not a valid fault, because we accept a distinction of forms (*rūpabheda*) imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).
For a real entity does not become possessed of parts (*sāvayava*) merely by means of a distinction of forms imagined through ignorance.
For the moon, though appearing as if multiple when seen by one whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts, does not thereby become multiple;

and likewise, through the differentiation of name and form—imagined by ignorance, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, indeterminate as being either identical to or different from the Reality—it is Brahman that becomes the locus of all worldly transactions such as transformation and so forth.

Yet, in its ultimate nature, it remains unchanging and beyond all worldly discourse. Since the differentiation of name and form imagined by ignorance is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), the fact that Brahman is partless is not contradicted.
Furthermore, this scriptural passage concerning transformation is not intended to establish transformation, for no fruit is perceived from such a realization;
rather, its purpose is to establish the identity of the Self with Brahman, which is devoid of all worldly activity, since a fruit is indeed perceived from that realization.
Having begun with, "This Self is 'not this, not this'," the text concludes, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness."
Therefore, in our position, no fault whatsoever follows as a consequence.
And likewise in the self, for [the elements] are indeed manifold.
Moreover, one should not dispute here as to how a manifold creation could arise from a single Brahman without the destruction of its own nature;

for even in the case of a single self that is dreaming, a manifold creation is recorded in scripture without the destruction of its own nature, beginning with the words: "There are no chariots there, no draft-animals, no roads, yet he creates chariots, draft-animals, and roads" (Brhadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.10). This concludes the second chapter.

Even in the world, among gods and others, as well as among magicians and the like, various creations such as elephants, horses, and so forth are observed to occur without any impairment to their own essential nature;
likewise, even within the one Brahman, a manifold creation of diverse forms will come to be without any impairment to its own essential nature.
And because of the faults in one's own position.

This same defect regarding one's own position applies equally to others as well. For even for the proponent of *pradhāna*, the position is that the *pradhāna*—which is partless (*niravayava*), unlimited (*aparicchinna*), and devoid of sound and other qualities—is the cause of an effect that possesses parts, is limited, and is endowed with sound and other qualities.

In that case too, because the *pradhāna* is partless, it follows that either the entire *pradhāna* would be transformed [into the effect], or else there is a contradiction with the very admission that it is partless.
[Objection: But surely they do not admit that the *pradhāna* is partless?
For *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are indeed the three *guṇas*;
their state of equilibrium is *pradhāna*.

Since that [equilibrium] possesses parts by virtue of those very constituents, the fault under discussion cannot be avoided by such a kind of "having parts," because each one of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is equally partless, and each one alone, when assisted by the other two, is the material cause of its own homogeneous manifold; thus, the objection applies equally to your own position.
If it is argued that because reasoning is not firmly established, [the world] must indeed possess parts, then even so, defects such as impermanence and the like would follow.
Or, if the intention is that "parts" are merely powers (śakti) indicated by the diversity of effects, those are no different for the proponent of Brahman either.

Likewise, for the proponent of atoms (aṇuvādin), if an atom, when conjoining with another atom, were to do so in its entirety due to being partless, then, because expansion (prathimā) would be impossible, the consequence would be that it remains a mere atom.

If, on the other hand, it were to join by means of one part, even so, there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of partlessness; thus this same defect applies equally to our own position as well.
And because the defect is equal, it should not be leveled against only one of the two positions. However, the proponent of Brahman has already refuted the defect in his own position.
And she is endowed with everything because of seeing that.
It has been stated that the manifold expansion of transformations is possible for even a single Brahman due to its connection with diverse powers;

however, how is it further understood that the supreme Brahman is endowed with all such diverse powers? To this, the following is said: the section concerning "being endowed with all" (*sarvopeta-adhikaraṇa*).
And that [power] follows from the observation of that [deity];
it must be admitted that the supreme deity is endowed with all powers. Why? Because of the observation of that.

For scripture thus demonstrates the possession of all powers by the supreme deity: "He whose work is all, whose desires are all, whose essence is all; he who has pervaded all this, who is without speech and without regard, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true"; "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"; and "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart"—passages of this kind.
If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the cause] because He is devoid of organs, that has already been answered.
Sūtra 2.1.27.
This might be so: the scripture teaches that the supreme deity is devoid of organs, stating such things as "without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind";

how then, even though it possesses all powers, could it be capable of producing effects? For it is known that beings such as the gods, though conscious and endowed with all powers, are capable of performing their respective functions only when equipped with internal organs and bodies.

If it be asked how the possession of all powers can be possible for a deity from whom all distinctions have been negated by the statement "not this, not this," the answer is that what must be said on this point has already been stated previously:
this exceedingly profound Brahman is to be apprehended through scripture alone, not through logic.
Furthermore, there is no rule that whatever capacity is observed in one thing must necessarily exist in another as well.

It has already been stated that even for Brahman, from which all specific attributes have been negated, the possession of all powers is possible by means of presenting the distinctions of forms imagined through ignorance (avidyā).

Thus, the scripture declares: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears," thereby demonstrating the connection of Brahman—even though devoid of instruments—with the capacity for all activities.
Not so, because it possesses a purpose.
Otherwise, [the opponent] again objects to the world having a conscious creator: "Indeed, the conscious Supreme Self is not capable of fashioning this cosmic image of the world;
why? Because activities in the world are invariably preceded by a purpose. For in the world, a conscious being is observed to act only when there is a motive.

A person acting with prior intelligence, when engaging in activity, is never observed to undertake even a minor undertaking that does not serve his own purpose, much less one involving such great effort.

Indeed, there is a scriptural text echoing common worldly experience: "Verily, it is not for the sake of all that everything becomes dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear.
And this undertaking involves immense effort, in that the entire cosmic form of the world, with its manifold variety of high and low, must be fashioned.
If this activity of the conscious Supreme Self were also imagined to be for the sake of its own purpose, the scriptural teaching of the Supreme Self's perfect contentment would be contradicted;
or, in the absence of a purpose, there would likewise be an absence of activity.

If, on the other hand, it were argued that even though he is conscious, the Supreme Self will act just like a madman who acts without any personal purpose due to a derangement of the intellect, then the scriptural teaching of the Supreme Self's omniscience would be contradicted.
Therefore, creation proceeds from an unattached consciousness.
The world-process is mere sport, being unique in its kind.

With the word "tu" (but), he refutes the objection: just as in the world, the activities of a king or a royal minister who has no desire for gain—undertaken not with any external purpose in mind, but merely in the form of sport—occur during playful diversions;
and just as inhalation, exhalation, and so forth occur by their very nature without aiming at any external purpose; [so too is the case here].
In the same way, the activity of the Lord, being of the nature of mere sport (līlā), will occur solely from His own nature without depending on any other purpose;
for no other purpose of the Lord can be established either by reason or by scripture.
Furthermore, it is impossible to question the intrinsic nature [of the Lord].

Although this creation of the world-image appears to us as if it were an undertaking of great effort, nevertheless, this is merely the sport (*līlā*) of the Supreme Lord, because His power is unlimited.

Even if in the world some subtle purpose might be imagined even for sports, here no purpose whatsoever can be imagined, on account of the scriptural teaching that He has all His desires fulfilled (*āptakāma*).

Nor can it be claimed that there is no activity at all, or that the activity is like that of a madman, because of the scriptural texts concerning creation and the scriptural texts concerning the omniscient one.

Furthermore, it must not be forgotten that this scriptural teaching on creation does not have ultimate reality as its object; rather, it pertains to the sphere of conventional usage involving names and forms imagined through ignorance, and its true purpose is the demonstration of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
There is no partiality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He has regard for [the merit and demerit of souls]; for thus Scripture shows.

Furthermore, the Lord's status as the cause of the birth and so forth of the world is challenged once more, in order to further solidify the matter already proposed, according to the maxim of "driving in a post.

It is not logical that the Lord is the cause of the world's inequality and cruelty. Why? Because of the consequence of His being subject to partiality and ruthlessness: He would be making some beings partakers of extreme happiness [while others suffer].

If God were to fashion such a diverse creation—some, like the gods and others, experiencing extreme suffering; some, like animals and others, experiencing it to a moderate degree; and others, like humans and others, enjoying moderate pleasures—then, just as in the case of an ordinary person, passion and hatred would necessarily arise in Him. Consequently, His divine nature, established by the Śruti and Smṛti as characterized by purity and other such qualities, would be lost. Furthermore, there would follow upon Him mercilessness and excessive cruelty, both loathed even by base people, due to His ordaining the infliction of suffering and His withdrawal of all living beings.

Therefore, since it would follow that [the Lord] is subject to partiality and cruelty, the position is reached that the Lord is not the cause. To this we reply: partiality and cruelty do not attach to the Lord.
Why? Because He is dependent on other factors.
For if the Lord, being independent and alone, were to fashion an unequal creation, these two defects—partiality and cruelty—would indeed ensue.
But there can be no creatorship for one who is independent;
for it is the Lord, being dependent [on other factors], that fashions this unequal creation.
If it is asked "upon what does he depend?", we reply that he depends upon merit and demerit (dharma and adharma).
Therefore, since the diverse creation depends upon the merit and demerit of the living beings being created, this is not the fault of the Lord;

rather, the Lord is to be viewed as being like the rain-cloud. For just as the rain-cloud is the common cause for the production of rice, barley, and so forth, while the specific differences between rice, barley, and the rest are caused by the unique potencies residing in their respective seeds, even so, the Lord is the common cause for the creation of gods, humans, and others, while the specific differences between gods, humans, and others are caused by the unique karmas residing in those respective individual souls.
Thus, because the Lord is dependent [on other factors], He is not tainted by partiality or cruelty.
But how is it known that the Lord fashions the transmigratory world—low, middling, and high—while being dependent? For scripture shows this:

"For it is He alone who makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; and it is He alone who makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8), and also, "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action, and sinful through sinful action" (Brhadāranyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).

Smṛti as well demonstrates that the Lord’s bestowing of grace and His inflicting of punishment depend exclusively upon the specific karma of living beings, as seen in such passages as: "In whatever way people approach Me, in that very same way do I reward them."
If it is argued that there is no such thing as bondage because of the non-differentiation of karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness.

"O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second"—since this determination of non-differentiation prior to creation establishes that there is no karma depending upon which a differentiated creation could occur;

for karma indeed depends on the differentiation of bodies and so forth after creation, while the differentiation of bodies and so forth depends on karma—thus a mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) would result.
Therefore, let the Lord indeed proceed by depending on karma only after differentiation has occurred.
If it be argued that, because prior to the differentiation there is an absence of karma—which is the cause of diversity—the first creation would necessarily be uniform, this is not a fault.

This fault would indeed arise if this transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) had a beginning; but since transmigratory existence is beginningless, the operation of karma and the resulting diversity of creation proceed through the relation of cause and effect, like the seed and the sprout, without contradiction. How, then, is it known that this transmigratory existence is beginningless? To this, the author reads the following reply: "It is both logical and observed. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda).

And the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is established; for if *saṃsāra* had a beginning, it would follow that it arises spontaneously, which would entail the recurrence of *saṃsāra* even for those who are liberated, as well as the fallacies of "attaining what was not earned" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was earned" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*), since there would be no cause for the inequality of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Nor is God the cause of this inequality, as has already been stated;
nor is ignorance alone the cause of inequality, because it is uniform in nature.
However, ignorance (*avidyā*), depending upon karma projected by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*), would cause inequality;
yet, without karma a body cannot come into being, and without a body karma cannot come into being—thus there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
But if [the series] is beginningless, it is established according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout, and thus no fault arises.
Furthermore, the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is perceived in both Śruti and Smṛti.

In the Śruti, for instance, at the commencement of creation, the text "by this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanā*) addresses the embodied self by the word *jīva*, which is based on the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); this demonstrates that *saṃsāra* is beginningless.

For if it had a beginning, how could the self—having previously not possessed the vital breaths—be addressed at the commencement of creation by the word *jīva*, which is based on the maintenance of the vital breaths? Nor can it be addressed on the grounds that it "will maintain" them, because a past relationship is more powerful than a future one, as the former is already established.

And the Vedic mantra, "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before," shows the existence of previous kalpas. Furthermore, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is found in the Smṛti: "Its form is not perceived here in such a way; it has no end, no beginning, and no foundation."
And it is established in the Purāṇa that there is no limit to the number of past and future kalpas.
And because all phenomena arise.

Having established that the conscious Brahman is the cause and material source (*prakṛti*) of the world according to the meaning of the Vedas, the Teacher has refuted the defects such as "heterogeneity" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) and others raised by opponents. Now, desiring to begin a section primarily concerned with the refutation of opposing views, he concludes this section which was primarily concerned with the formal adoption of his own position.

Since, when this Brahman is accepted as the cause, all the attributes of a cause are logically established in the manner demonstrated—namely, that Brahman is omniscient, omnipotent, and possessed of great illusory power (māyā)—therefore, this philosophical view of the Upaniṣads is not to be doubted.

Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the teacher of the wandering mendicants of the supreme order (Paramahaṃsa-Parivrājaka), and the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
This is the second chapter (pāda).

Although this treatise is undertaken to determine the purport of the Vedānta texts, and not—as is the case with the science of logic—to establish or refute any particular doctrine through mere reasoning alone, nevertheless, while explaining the Vedānta texts, the systems such as Sāṅkhya and others, which are opposed to right vision, must be refuted; for that purpose, the subsequent chapter proceeds.

Since the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta serves the purpose of perfect knowledge (*samyagdarśana*), the establishment of one's own position was performed first by means of that determination; for this is more worthy than the refutation of the positions of others.
Now, one might object: "For those seeking liberation, it is proper to perform only the establishment of one's own position in order to define perfect knowledge as the means to liberation;
what is the use of refuting the positions of others, which causes hatred toward others? Certainly, it is so.

Nevertheless, observing that the great systems such as Sāṃkhya and others—which are embraced by the masses—have been presented under the guise of teaching right vision (*samyagdarśana*), some of dull intellect might harbor the expectation that these too should be adopted for the sake of right vision; likewise, they might have faith in them because of the apparent depth of their reasoning and the claim that they were spoken by an omniscient being. Therefore, an effort is made here to demonstrate their lack of essence.

[Objection: But has not the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions already been accomplished previously by such sūtras as "On account of seeing [it is not pradhāna]" (BS 1.1.5), "And on account of desire [it is not pradhāna]" (BS 1.1.8), and "By this all [other theories] are explained" (BS 1.4.27)? What, then, is the purpose of repeating it here? [Reply: It is said in response: The Sāṃkhyas and others, in order to establish their own positions, cite even Vedānta passages and explain them by interpreting them in accordance with their own views. What they offer is a semblance of an explanation (*vyākhyānābhāsa*), not a correct explanation (*samyagvyākhyāna*). This much was established previously. However, here it is shown that those very same passages, when correctly interpreted according to the intention of the scripture, lead to the conclusion that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. Thus, there is no tautology. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others maintain that their own systems are based on reasoning (*tarka*) and do not depend on the Veda; therefore, they claim that the Veda must be interpreted in conformity with their own reasonings. To refute this, it is stated here that the Veda itself possesses the power to negate the Sāṃkhya and other doctrines through its own inherent reasoning, and thus the Sāṃkhya and other systems are shown to be devoid of any basis in the Veda. For this reason, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others, relying on the authority of the Smṛtis, hold that the Veda teaches the doctrine of pradhāna and so forth. To refute this, it is stated here that the Smṛtis which teach the doctrine of pradhāna and so forth are not authoritative because they contradict the Veda. Therefore, there is no tautology. Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "Since the Veda is difficult to understand, we interpret it according to our own reasonings. To show that the Veda is indeed easy to understand for those who follow the tradition of the teachers, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others argue: "If the Veda were to teach that Brahman alone is the cause of the world, then the mention of pradhāna and so forth would be useless. To show that such mentions serve a specific purpose, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is eternal and independent of a personal author; therefore, it cannot be refuted by reasoning. To show that the Veda is indeed subject to reasoning, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who accept its authority; it is not a means of knowledge for those who do not. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for everyone, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Additionally, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*); it is not a means of knowledge for others. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for all human beings, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who possess the capacity for understanding; it is not a means of knowledge for those who lack it. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who possess the capacity for understanding, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Also, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who have cultivated their minds; it is not a means of knowledge for those who have not. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who have cultivated their minds, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who have attained liberation; it is not a means of knowledge for those who have not. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who have attained liberation, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who have realized the Self; it is not a means of knowledge for those who have not. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who have realized the Self, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Also, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who have performed their duties; it is not a means of knowledge for those who have not. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who have performed their duties, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who have faith; it is not a means of knowledge for those who lack faith. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who have faith, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who are devoted; it is not a means of knowledge for those who are not. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who are devoted, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Also, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who are disciplined; it is not a means of knowledge for those who are undisciplined. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who are disciplined, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who are pure; it is not a means of knowledge for those who are impure. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who are pure, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a means of knowledge only for those who are tranquil; it is not a means of knowledge for those who are agitated. To show that the Veda is a means of knowledge for those who are tranquil, it is stated here that the Veda teaches that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. For these reasons, the rejection of the Sāṃkhya and other positions is repeated here. Also, the Sāṃkhyas and others say: "The Veda is a
But here, the refutation of that reasoning is carried out independently, without reliance on the [specific] statement; this is the distinction.
Regarding the word [of scripture]: "And because the arrangement [of the world] is not possible [by means of inference], it is not inference."

In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that just as particular objects such as jars, bowls, and the like, being permeated by the nature of clay, are seen in the world to be preceded by a commonality consisting of clay, so too all external and internal particulars— being permeated by the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion according to their arrangement—
must necessarily be preceded by a commonality consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

That which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion as its common nature is the Pradhāna, composed of the three guṇas; like clay, it is insentient, yet it proceeds by its own diverse inherent nature toward the form of transformations in order to accomplish the purposes of the sentient Puruṣa.
Likewise, they infer that very same Pradhāna through other marks such as finite measurement (parimāṇa) and so forth.

To this we reply: if this were determined solely on the strength of analogies, [the conclusion would not hold]. For in the world, no insentient thing is ever seen to independently fashion modifications capable of accomplishing specific human purposes without being presided over by a sentient being. Indeed, houses, palaces, beds, seats, pleasure-grounds, and so forth, are seen in the world to have been constructed at the proper time by wise artisans as suitable for the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering.

Likewise, how could the insentient *pradhāna* construct this entire world—consisting of the earth and so forth, as well as external and internal things such as bodies—which are fit for the experience of the fruits of various karmas, endowed with diverse species, possessed of specific arrangements of parts, and serve as the substratum for the experience of the fruits of manifold actions; for this world, which is perceived by the most highly intelligent artisans yet remains impossible even for them to conceive in their minds, is never seen to be produced by lumps of clay, stones, or similar insentient materials?

Even in the case of clay and other materials, a specific form and arrangement is seen when they are presided over by a potter and others; likewise, there follows the undesirable consequence that the *pradhāna* must also be presided over by another conscious being.

Nor is there any restrictive rule that the primary cause must be determined solely on the basis of properties inherent in the material cause, such as clay, and not on the basis of external factors like the potter.
This being the case, nothing is contradicted; on the contrary, scripture is supported, since it points toward a conscious cause.
Therefore, for the reason that "the formation [of the world] is impossible," it follows that the cause of the world must be inferred as non-intelligent.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and because of the impossibility of concomitance (*anvaya*)," he combines the lack of proof for the reason.

For indeed, the concomitance of external and internal objects with the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is not tenable; this is because pleasure and so forth are perceived as internal, whereas sound and so forth are perceived as having a different nature, and because they are perceived as being the causes [of those states]. Furthermore, even when there is no difference in the sound and other objects, a specific experience of pleasure and so forth is observed due to a specific mental disposition (*bhāvanā*).

Likewise, having observed that limited differentiated entities such as roots, sprouts, and so forth are preceded by a combination [of causes], one who infers that external and internal differentiated entities must also be preceded by a combination because they are limited, faces the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are preceded by a combination, since there is no difference in their being limited.

Furthermore, since the relationship of cause and effect is seen in things like beds and seats produced with foresight, it is not possible to postulate that the relationship of cause and effect among external and internal differentiated entities implies they are preceded by something insentient.
And because of the commencement of activity.
Let this [evolutionary] arrangement be set aside for a moment;

even that activity directed toward specific effects—which consists in the departure from the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and their assuming the relationship of subordinate and dominant factors—that too is not possible for the insentient *pradhāna* acting independently, because it is not observed in the case of clay and the like, nor in the case of chariots and the like.

For clay and the like, or chariots and the like, being themselves insentient, are never seen to be directed toward specific effects when they are not presided over by sentient agents such as potters or by [sentient beings] such as horses.
Since the unperceived is established through the perceived, the world cannot be inferred to have a non-conscious cause on the ground that activity would otherwise be impossible.

Now, it may be argued that even in the case of a conscious being, activity is not observed in isolation; this is true. Nevertheless, the activity of non-conscious things such as chariots is observed when they are conjoined with a conscious being.
But [this is] not so. In the second chapter: the activity of a conscious being joined with another conscious being is observed.

Now, what is logical here: does that activity belong to the one in whom it is observed, or does it belong to that with which he is joined? Surely it is logical that it belongs to the one in whom the activity is seen, because both are perceptible.
However, a pure conscious being is not perceived as the substratum of activity like a chariot or similar objects;

rather, the existence of consciousness is established only for that which is conjoined with the body and so forth, which serve as the substrata of activity. For it is observed that the living body differs from purely insentient things such as chariots;
and for this very reason, the Lokāyatikas maintain that since consciousness is seen when the body is present and is not seen when it is absent, consciousness belongs to the body alone.
Therefore, it is the insentient alone that possesses activity. To this, it is replied: we do not say that the activity seen in an insentient thing does not belong to it;
let it belong to that very thing.

We say, however, that it arises from consciousness (cetana), because it exists when that [consciousness] is present and is absent when that is absent—just as the transformation characterized by burning and illumination, though dependent on wood and other materials, occurs only from fire even when not perceived in isolation, since it is seen when there is contact with it and not seen when there is separation from it;

likewise, even for the Lokāyatikas, it is observed that the conscious body alone is the activator of unconscious things such as chariots, so the fact that the conscious is the activator is uncontradicted.
If it be objected that, even for your Self which is conjoined with the body and so forth, agency is untenable because activity is impossible apart from the mere nature of consciousness, we say no;
for agency is possible even for that which is devoid of activity, just as in the case of a magnet or as in the case of color and other qualities, as stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya.

Just as a magnet, though itself devoid of motion, becomes the mover of iron, and just as objects such as form and the like, though themselves devoid of motion, become the movers of the eyes and other senses, so too it is logical that the Lord—though himself devoid of activity, yet being omnipresent, the Self of all, omniscient, and omnipotent—should set everything in motion.
If it be argued that because He is one, there is no object to be moved, and thus His status as a mover is untenable, we say no;
for this has been answered more than once by the fact that He enters into the illusion (*māyā*) of name and form presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, activity is possible when there is an omniscient cause, but not when the cause is insentient.
If it is argued that it is like water in a mirage, [we reply] that this is also the case there.

It might be argued: "Just as insentient milk functions by its very nature for the sake of the growth of the calf, and just as insentient water flows by its very nature for the benefit of the world, so too the Pradhāna, though insentient, will function by its very nature for the accomplishment of the purpose of the Puruṣa.

This is not well said, because even in those cases we infer that the activity of milk and water occurs only when they are presided over by a sentient being; for we observe no activity in anything purely insentient, such as a chariot, according to the consensus of both disputants.

Furthermore, the Scripture—in such passages as "He who dwells in the waters," "He who controls the waters from within," and "By the command of this Imperishable One, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward"—declares that all movement in the world is presided over by the Lord.
Therefore, because [the example] is included within the category of things yet to be proven, the comparison "like milk and water" is not a valid objection.
Moreover, it is logical that a conscious cow causes the milk to flow through her desire for affection, and because the milk is drawn out by the sucking of the calf.
Nor is there absolute independence from water on the part of [the flow], since flowing depends upon low ground and other such factors;
however, dependence upon a conscious being has been demonstrated in every case.

As for the statement, "If it be argued that [the Self is not the cause] because we see the withdrawal [of the organs at death], we say no, for it is like milk," therein it was shown from the perspective of worldly observation that an effect can arise within its own substrate even without depending on external instrumental causes.
Furthermore, from the perspective of the scriptures, the fact that everything everywhere depends upon Īśvara is not refuted.
And because there is no stability in their distinction, owing to their independence.

For the Sāṃkhyas, the three *guṇas* abiding in a state of equilibrium constitute the *pradhāna*; yet there exists nothing external to that which, distinct from it, could serve as a cause for its activity or cessation. Furthermore, the *puruṣa* is indifferent, being neither an initiator nor a restrainer; therefore, the *pradhāna* is independent.
Furthermore, because it is independent, the claim that the *pradhāna* sometimes transforms into the forms of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, and sometimes does not transform, is untenable.
For the Lord (*īśvara*), however, both activity and non-activity are not contradictory, owing to his omniscience, omnipotence, and possession of great illusory power (*māyā*).
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the self] is not like grass and so forth.

It might be argued: "Just as grass, sprouts, water, and so forth transform into the form of milk and the like by their very nature (*svabhāva*) without depending on any other cause, so too will the *pradhāna* transform into the forms of the Great Principle (*mahat*), the *sūtra*, the elements (*bhūta*), and so on.
But how is it known that grass and the like transform without depending on another cause? Because no other cause is perceived.
For if we were to perceive some other cause, then we could, at our will, produce milk by taking up grass and such materials with that specific cause.
But we do not establish this; therefore, the transformation of grass and other such things is inherent to them,
and the same would apply to the Pradhāna as well.
To this it is replied: The transformation of the *pradhāna* might indeed be intrinsic, like that of grass and so forth, if the transformation of grass and such were also admitted to be intrinsic;
however, it is not so admitted, because another cause is perceived.
How is another cause perceived? Because of its absence elsewhere.
For it is only grass and the like consumed by a cow that turns into milk, not what has been discarded, nor what is consumed by a bull or other animals;
for if this were without a specific cause, then grass and the like would turn into milk elsewhere as well, simply through connection with the body of a cow.
Nor does something become causeless merely because it cannot be produced at will by human beings.
For there are some effects to be accomplished by human effort and others to be accomplished by fate;
humans are indeed able, by means appropriate to themselves, to produce milk even by gathering grass and other fodder;
for those desiring abundant milk cause the cow to graze on abundant pasture.
Consequently, they obtain abundant milk;
therefore, the transformation of the Pradhāna is not spontaneous in the same manner as grass and other such things.
Even if it were accepted, there would be no object [for the cognition].
It has been established that the activity of the *pradhāna* cannot be inherent (*svābhāvikī*). [End of] the second chapter.
Furthermore, even if we were to concede, out of deference to your faith, that the activity of the *pradhāna* is indeed inherent, the same defect would still necessarily follow.
Why? Because of the absence of a purpose (*arthābhāvāt*).

If it is asserted that the activity of the *pradhāna* is inherent and does not depend on anything else here, then just as it does not depend on any auxiliary cause, it likewise would not depend on any purpose (*prayojana*). Consequently, the proposition that the *pradhāna* proceeds to accomplish the goal of the *puruṣa* would be abandoned.

If he should say: "It depends only on an auxiliary cause, not on a purpose," even so, the purpose of the *pradhāna*'s activity must be distinguished: is it experience (*bhoga*), or liberation (*apavarga*), or both?
If it is enjoyment, what kind of enjoyment could there be for a *puruṣa* to whom no excellence can be imparted? Furthermore, it would follow that liberation is impossible.

If it is liberation, then since liberation is already established even prior to activity, such activity would be purposeless; moreover, it would follow that sound and other objects could not be perceived.

Even if one accepts that both [enjoyment and liberation] are the purposes, since the constituent elements (*pradhāna-mātra*) to be enjoyed are infinite, it would still follow that liberation is impossible.
Nor is activity for the sake of the cessation of longing;
for longing is not possible for the Pradhāna, which is insentient,
nor for the Puruṣa, who is stainless.

If it is argued that the activity [of nature] proceeds out of fear that the power of vision and the power of creation would otherwise be rendered useless, then, just as the power of vision is never severed, the power of creation would also never be severed; consequently, because saṃsāra would not be severed, the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation (anirmokṣa) follows.
Therefore, the claim that the activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of the Puruṣa’s purpose is untenable.
In the Sūtra-bhāṣya it is said: "If it be argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so [the objection remains]."

It might be argued as follows: just as a certain man, endowed with the power of vision but devoid of the power of action, directs an animal—which is devoid of the power of vision but endowed with the power of action—by presiding over it; or just as a magnet, though not moving itself, causes iron to move, so too will the Puruṣa cause the Pradhāna to act. This is a renewed objection based on the support of such examples. To this, it is replied: even so, there is no escape from the defect.

First of all, the fault of abandoning what has been accepted follows [from your position], because you accept the activity of the independent *pradhāna* while not accepting that the *puruṣa* is an instigator.
And how could the indifferent *puruṣa* set the *pradhāna* in motion? For even a lame man sets a blind man in motion by means of speech and so forth;
but the *puruṣa* possesses no such activity of instigation whatsoever, because he is devoid of action and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Nor could [the Pradhāna] cause activity by mere proximity, like a magnet, because that would entail the consequence of perpetual activity due to the permanence of its proximity.

In the case of a magnet, however, its proximity is not constant, as it possesses its own function—proximity—and it requires actions such as rubbing [the iron]; thus, the comparison with the person and the stone is invalid.
Likewise, since the Pradhāna is insentient and the Puruṣa is indifferent, and there is no third entity to connect them, a connection between the two is impossible.
Furthermore, if the relationship were based on fitness (*yogyatā*), then because that fitness would never be severed, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation;
and here too, as before, the absence of an object must be considered.
On the other hand, the Supreme Self possesses indifference (*audāsīnya*) which rests upon its own essential nature. (Brahma-sūtra, Second Chapter).
And since its status as a motivator depends upon illusion (māyā), there is indeed a distinction.
And because the status of being the principal is untenable.

For this reason as well, the activity of the Pradhāna is not tenable: for that state in which Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas exist in equilibrium, having abandoned their mutual relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities and remaining in their own essential nature alone, is the state of the Pradhāna.

In that state, since these qualities have independent natures, a relationship of mutual subserviency (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) is impossible for fear of the destruction of their own nature; and because there is no external agent to cause agitation, the production of Mahat and the other principles—which is caused by the inequality of the qualities—would not occur.
And because, in the case of an inference based on something else, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge.
Now, it might be argued: "We infer otherwise, so that this immediately preceding fault does not apply;
for we do not admit that the qualities (*guṇas*) have an independent nature or are immutable (*kūṭastha*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a claim;
rather, the nature of the qualities is admitted on the basis of their effects."

In whatever manner the production of an effect is logically possible, in that very manner their intrinsic nature must be accepted; and it is their accepted doctrine that the activity of the *guṇas* is mobile.
Therefore, even in the state of equilibrium, the *guṇas* remain as things capable of undergoing disequilibrium.

Even so, the previously mentioned defects—such as the impossibility of construction due to the Pradhāna being devoid of the power of intelligence—remain exactly as they were. Furthermore, one who infers even the power of intelligence in it would cease to be a true opponent, because this would entail the doctrine of Brahman, namely that a single conscious entity is the material cause of the manifold world. Moreover, even if the Guṇas are admitted to be capable of assuming states of inequality, they could not undergo such inequality in their state of equilibrium due to the absence of a cause; or, if they did undergo it, they would remain in a state of inequality forever, since the absence of a cause remains the same. Thus, this immediately following defect also necessarily follows.
And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent.
In some places they enumerate seven sense organs, while in others eleven—thus their Sāṃkhya doctrine is mutually contradictory.
Likewise, in some places they teach that the creation of the subtle elements proceeds from the Great Principle (mahat), while in others from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Similarly, in some places they describe three internal instruments (antakaraṇa), while in others only one.
However, there is indeed a contradiction with the Śruti which teaches that the Lord is the cause, as well as with the Smṛti that follows it;
therefore, for this reason also, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is inconsistent.

Here [the opponent] objects: "The view of the followers of the Upaniṣads is likewise inconsistent, because they do not admit that the sufferer (tapyat) and the causer of suffering (tāpaka) belong to different classes of being.

For those who maintain that Brahman alone, which is the self of all, is the cause of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), they must necessarily admit that the sufferer and the causer of suffering are merely specific states of that one single Self, and not entities belonging to different classes.

And if these two—the sufferer and the causer of suffering—were indeed specific states of the one Self, then that Self could never be liberated from those two, the sufferer and the causer of suffering. (Thus ends the second chapter.)

It might be argued that the scripture teaching right vision for the sake of quelling suffering would be useless, for it is not possible for a lamp—whose nature consists of heat and light—to be liberated from those two while remaining in that very same state.

As for the analogy cited regarding water, waves, ripples, foam, and so forth, there too the specific modifications such as waves and the rest belong to the single essence of water and are eternal in the form of manifestation and disappearance; thus, the impossibility of the water-essence being liberated from the waves and so forth remains the same.
Furthermore, this difference in nature between the sufferer (*tapyamāna*) and the cause of suffering (*tāpaka*) is well-established in the world;
for instance, the seeker (*arthin*) and the object sought (*artha*) are perceived as distinct from one another.

If the object were not inherently different from the seeker, then since the object of a seeker's desire would be eternally established for that seeker, he could have no desire for it. Just as for a lamp, whose nature is light, its so-called "object" (light) is eternally established, and thus it has no desire for it—since a seeker’s desire can only exist for an object not yet attained.
Likewise, even the object-ness of an object would not exist;
if it did exist, it would necessarily be its own object-ness,
and this is not the case.
For these two, "the object" (artha) and "the seeker of the object" (arthin), are correlative terms;
a relationship exists between two correlatives, not with only one.
Therefore, these two—the object and the seeker of the object—are distinct.
Likewise, there are both benefit and non-benefit; "benefit" (artha) is that which is favorable to one who seeks it, while "non-benefit" (anartha) is that which is unfavorable;
the [subject] is connected with both of these alternately.
In that regard, because the good is so slight and the evil so great, both the good and the evil are considered to be nothing but evil—therefore, it is called the "tormentor.

The person, however, is the "tormented," who is connected to both [good and evil] in turn. Thus, if there were identity between these two—the tormented and the tormentor—liberation would be impossible. But if they belong to different categories (jātyantara), then liberation might indeed be possible through the removal of the cause of their conjunction.

It is not said here that liberation is impossible; this defect would indeed arise if, due to oneness alone, the state of the sufferer and the inflictor were untenable—that is, if, within the unity of the Self, the sufferer and the inflictor were to enter into a relationship of object and subject toward one another.

But this is not the case, precisely because of their oneness. For fire, being one, does not burn or illuminate itself, even though it possesses distinct attributes such as heat and light and is subject to transformation.

How could the state of being the sufferer and the causer of suffering possibly exist in the one, immutable Brahman? Where, then, could this state of being the sufferer and the causer of suffering reside? It is replied: Do you not see that the living body, which is the object of action, is the sufferer, and the sun is the causer of suffering? But surely, "suffering" (tapti) is pain;
and that belongs to the conscious being.
[It cannot belong] to the insentient body;

for if the burning belonged to the body alone, it would perish of its own accord upon the destruction of the body, and thus no means would need to be sought for its destruction. It is replied: even in the absence of the body, the burning of the pure sentient principle (cetana) has never been observed.
Furthermore, you do not admit that the modification called "suffering" belongs to the pure consciousness alone;
nor do you admit a conjunction of the body and consciousness, because that would entail defects such as impurity;
nor do you accept that suffering itself possesses suffering.
How can there be the relationship of the afflicted and the afflictor even for you? If it is argued that "sattva is the afflicted and rajas is the afflictor," we say no;
because it is impossible for the conscious principle (cetana) to be conjoined with those two.
[End of] the second chapter on the followers of Sāṃkhya.

If it is argued that even though the conscious self is not subject to obstruction, it nevertheless suffers as if it were, we reply: in that case, it follows from the use of the word "as if" (*iva*) that, in the ultimate sense, it does not suffer at all.
If it does not suffer, the use of the word "as if" is not a fault.

For a *ḍuṇḍubha* (a kind of lizard) does not become venomous simply because it is "like a snake," nor does a snake become non-venomous simply because it is "like a *ḍuṇḍubha*. Therefore, one must admit that this relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering is created by ignorance (*avidyā*) and is not ultimately real. This being so, nothing is wrong with my position either.

Now, if you admit that the capacity to suffer belongs to the conscious self (*cetana*) in an ultimate sense, then for you, liberation would be even more impossible, especially since you also admit the eternity of the suffering agent (*tāpaka*).

Even if the powers of being suffered and of suffering are eternal, if it is argued that—since suffering depends on a conjunction with its cause—the absolute cessation of suffering occurs upon the removal of the non-perception (*adarśana*) which is the cause of that conjunction, and thus absolute liberation is established; we say no, because you admit that *adarśana*, which is darkness (*tamas*), is eternal.

Furthermore, because the emergence and suppression of the *guṇas* are not constant, the cessation of the cause of their conjunction is also not constant; thus, for the Sāṃkhya alone, liberation would be unavoidable and impossible.

For the follower of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada*), however, since he accepts the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) and since it is impossible for a single entity to stand in the relation of subject and object, and because of the scriptural teaching that the diversity of modifications is merely a matter of words (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), even the suspicion of non-liberation does not arise, even in a dream.

In conventional practice, however, in whatever case the relationship between the tormented and the tormentor is observed in a certain way, it remains exactly so; thus, it neither needs to be challenged nor refuted.

In the commentary on the Sūtras, the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause has been refuted; now, the doctrine that atoms are the cause must be refuted. To begin with, the objection which the atomist imagines against the proponent of Brahman is here answered. In this regard, the following is the admission of the Vaiśeṣikas: qualities inherent in the causal substance produce another quality of the same genus in the effect-substance, because we observe that from white threads a white cloth is produced, and because we never observe the opposite.
Therefore, if it is admitted that the conscious Brahman is the cause of the world, then consciousness should also inhere in the world, which is its effect;
however, since that is not observed, the conscious Brahman cannot be the cause of the world.
He refutes this admission by means of the opponent's own method: "Or [the world may be] like the large and the long, from the short and the spherical."

This is their process: it is said that atoms, for a certain period of time, remain without having begun any effect, possessing color and other qualities as appropriate, and having the dimension of sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*);

subsequently, preceded by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, and being accompanied by conjunction, they initiate the entire range of effects beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) in due order, and the qualities of the cause produce another quality in the effect.

When two atoms (paramāṇu) initiate a dyad (dvyaṇuka), then the specific qualities such as color (rūpa) residing in the atoms— such as whiteness and so forth— initiate other [qualities] such as whiteness in the dyad. However, the specific quality of the atom known as spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya) does not initiate another spherical dimension in the dyad, because it is accepted that the dyad possesses a different dimension.
For they describe minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hasvatva*) as dimensions residing in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

Even when two dyads originate a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*), the capacity to originate [qualities] such as whiteness, which reside in the dyads, remains the same; however, minuteness and shortness, though residing in the dyads, do not originate at all, because it is accepted that the tetrad possesses the dimensions of largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*).
Even when many atoms, or many dyads, or an atom together with a dyad initiates an effect, this same application [of reasoning] is identical.
Thus, just as from an atom that is spherical (*parimaṇḍala*), a dyad is produced which is minute and short, while a triad and so forth are large and long, but not spherical;
or just as from a dyad that is minute and short, a triad is produced which is large and long, but neither minute nor short.
If you accept that the insentient universe is produced from a sentient Brahman, what is lost for you?

[Objection: Now, you might think that because the product-substance, such as the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), is occupied by another dimension (*parimāṇa*) which is contradictory [to its own], the sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other qualities residing in the causes do not originate [the dimension]—this is what I admit.

However, there is no other quality occupying the world that is contradictory to consciousness (*cetanā*), by virtue of which the consciousness residing in the cause would not originate another consciousness in the effect.
For there is no quality whatsoever called "non-consciousness" that is contradictory to consciousness, since it is merely the negation of consciousness.

Therefore, if it is argued that consciousness must be the originator [of the body] because of its dissimilarity to spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other such qualities, do not think so; for this point is the same: just as spherical dimension and the like, though existing in the cause, are not originators, so too is consciousness. This aspect is identical in both cases.

Furthermore, the fact that spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other such qualities are already occupied by another dimension is not the reason for their non-productivity; for it is logically possible for spherical dimension and the like to be productive prior to the production of another dimension, since it is admitted that even a produced effect-substance remains momentarily devoid of qualities before the qualities [of that substance] are produced. Nor is it the case that spherical dimension and the like do not produce another dimension of their own kind because they are occupied in producing another dimension, for it is admitted that the production of another dimension has other causes.

"Large [dimension] arises from plurality of causes, from magnitude of causes, and from a particular kind of aggregation; its opposite is minute; by this, longness and shortness are explained"—such are the aphorisms of Kaṇāda.

Nor can it be said that, due to some particularity of proximity, only plurality of causes and the like initiate [a new dimension], while sphericity and the like do not; for when another substance or another quality is being produced, there is no distinction among all the qualities of the causes, since they are all equally inherent in their own substrata.
Therefore, it should be understood that just as sphericality and other such qualities do not originate [other things] due to their very nature, so too is it with consciousness.

Furthermore, because we observe the production of distinct substances and other categories from conjunction, there is no deviation from the rule that things of the same class produce things of the same class. If it is argued that, since substance is the subject under discussion, citing an example of a quality is inappropriate, we say no; [The second chapter continues...]
This is because, by means of the illustration, it is intended merely to show that the production [of an effect] is of a different character [from its cause];
nor is there any reason for a restriction that a substance must be cited as an example for a substance, or a quality for a quality.

The author of the Sūtras also cited a quality of substance (guṇa) on your part: "Because the conjunction [of the elements] is imperceptible, that which consists of five [elements] does not exist," meaning that just as the conjunction inhering in earth and ether—which are respectively perceptible and imperceptible—is itself imperceptible, so too the body inhering in the five elements, both perceptible and imperceptible, would be imperceptible;
yet the body is indeed perceptible, therefore it is not composed of the five elements. What is meant here is that conjunction is a quality (guṇa), while the body is a substance (dravya).
Furthermore, in the passage "But it is seen," the production of something distinct [from its cause] is also elaborated here.
Now, if this is so, is this not already covered by that [previous discussion]? We say: no; that was directed against the Sāṃkhya, whereas this is directed against the Vaiśeṣika.

But is it not the case that an extended application (*atideśa*) was also made on the basis of an identical principle in the sūtra: "By this, those [systems] not accepted by the learned are also explained"?
True, this is so;
however, at the commencement of the examination of the Vaiśeṣika, this detailed exposition (*prapañca*) was provided using an illustration consistent with their own methodology.
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] does not exist.

Now he refutes the doctrine of atoms as the cause. That doctrine arises as follows: in the world, substances such as cloth, which possess parts, are seen to be produced from substances such as threads that are themselves composed of parts, aided by conjunction; this is observed in the case of the world and its constituent atoms.
By analogy with that, whatever possesses parts must have a cause consisting of those very [parts] joined together, aided by conjunction. This is the section [of the argument].

It is understood that [the world] is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*); and that which is the limit of this division of parts and wholes, beyond which it ceases, is the atom reached at the end of the process of diminution.
Furthermore, this entire world, including mountains, oceans, and so forth, possesses parts.

Because they possess parts, they must have a beginning and an end; and since an effect cannot exist without a cause, the intention of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika) is that atoms are the cause of the world.
Having perceived these four elements—known as earth, water, fire, and air—as possessing parts, four kinds of atoms are postulated.

And because it is impossible for those [earth atoms] to be further divided once they have reached the limit of their reduction, the division of the perishing earth and other elements proceeds down to the level of the atom;
that is the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).
Then, at the time of creation, motion arises in the aerial atoms dependent upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
That karma joins its own substrate with another atom;
from that, air is produced through the sequence beginning with dyads;
likewise fire.
Thus water,
thus earth,
and likewise the body with its sense organs— in this way, this entire world arises from atoms.

The followers of Kaṇāda maintain that from the color and other qualities residing in atoms, the color and other qualities residing in dyads and so forth arise, according to the analogy of the thread and the cloth.

To this, it is replied as follows: First of all, the conjunction of atoms existing in a state of separation must be admitted to depend upon action, because we observe the conjunction of threads and other substances that possess action;
and since action is itself an effect, some cause for it must also be admitted.
If [such a cause] is not admitted, then, due to the absence of a cause, there would be no initial motion in the atoms;

even if it were admitted, if some cause of motion such as effort or impact—observed in ordinary experience—were to be admitted, then because of its impossibility, there would still be no initial motion in the atoms;
for in that state, effort, which is a quality of the self, cannot exist, owing to the absence of a body.
For when there is contact between the self and the mind, which is itself established in the body, an effort (prayatna) arises as a quality of the self.
By this, other perceived causes such as impact (abhighāta) and so forth are also to be rejected;
for all those occur only after the time of creation and cannot possibly be the cause of the primordial action.

Now, if it be argued that the unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*) is the cause of the first action, would that [unseen principle] be inherent in the Self (*ātman*) or inherent in the atoms (*aṇu*)? In either case, an action in the atoms could not be accounted for by the unseen principle as its cause, because the unseen principle is insentient (*acetana*). For it was stated in the examination of the Sāṃkhya system that what is insentient does not, being independent and not presided over by a sentient being, either act or cause another to act;
and because the Self, in that state prior to the arising of consciousness, is itself insentient.
Furthermore, because it is admitted that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) inheres in the self, it could not be the cause of motion in the atoms, as there is no connection [between them].

If it is argued that there is a connection between the atoms and the person who possesses the unseen force, then, due to the constancy of that connection, there would follow the consequence of constant activity, since there is no other regulating factor.
Thus, in the absence of any specific cause for action, there could be no initial motion in the atoms. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda)
In the absence of action, conjunction would not occur;
and in the absence of conjunction, the entire class of effects based upon it—such as the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth—would not exist.

Furthermore, would the conjunction of one atom with another occur through its entire self, or by way of a single part? If it were through its entire self, then because an increase in size would be impossible, there would be the undesirable consequence that everything remains merely atomic in magnitude; moreover, this would contradict what is observed, for we observe that the conjunction of one substance possessing spatial parts occurs with another substance possessing spatial parts.
If [the atom] were to combine with another by means of only one part, it would follow that it possesses parts.

If it is argued that these parts of the atoms are merely conceptual constructs, then since conceptual constructs lack reality, the conjunction itself would be unreal; consequently, it could not serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for a real effect.
And in the absence of a non-inherent cause, composite substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth would not be produced.

Just as at the initial creation (*ādisarga*), due to the absence of a cause, no action capable of producing conjunction can arise in atoms, so too at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), no action capable of producing disjunction could possibly arise in atoms.

For even there, no fixed, perceptible cause for such action is observed. Nor can the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) be the cause, since it exists for the purpose of accomplishing experience, not for the purpose of accomplishing dissolution. Therefore, in the absence of a cause, no action can arise in atoms, whether for the purpose of producing conjunction or for the purpose of producing disjunction.
And consequently, due to the absence of conjunction and disjunction, the non-existence of creation and dissolution—which depend upon them—would follow as a logical consequence.
Therefore, this theory of atoms as the cause is untenable.
And because of the admission of inherence (samavāya), there would be an infinite regress due to its being subject to the same [criticism].
The Second Chapter.
"And because of the admission of inherence, there is the non-existence [of the whole]"—this connects with the ongoing refutation of the atomic theory.
For you admit that a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), being produced from two atoms, inheres (*samavāyi*) in those two atoms which are entirely distinct from it.
Nor can the theory that atoms are the cause be established by one who accepts this [view of inherence];

why? Because there would be an infinite regress due to parity. For just as the dyad, being entirely distinct from the two atoms, is connected to them by a relation characterized as inherence, so too inherence itself—being entirely distinct from its correlates (the inherent things)—would have to be connected to those correlates by yet another relation characterized as inherence, since the state of absolute difference is the same in both cases.
Consequently, one would have to postulate a further and further relation for each subsequent one, and thus an infinite regress would necessarily result.

[Objection: But surely, in this case, inherence (samavāya), which is perceptible through cognition, is apprehended as being eternally connected with its substrata (samavāyin); it is not apprehended as unconnected, nor as depending on another relation.
Therefore, one need not postulate another relation for it, by which an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result.
[Reply: This is not so.
This being the case, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as well must be eternally connected with its conjuncts; thus, like inherence (*samavāya*), it would not require another relation.
If it is argued that conjunction requires another relation because it is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then inherence too would require another relation because it is likewise a distinct entity.
Nor is it tenable to say that conjunction requires another relation because it is a quality (*guṇa*), while inherence does not because it is not a quality.
Because the causal condition of dependence is identical [in all cases], and because the technical definition of a "quality" (guṇa) is not a restrictive factor,
it would follow for one who accepts inherence (samavāya) as a distinct entity that there is an infinite regress (anavasthā).
And when such an infinite regress occurs, since nothing would be established, the dyad (dvyaṇuka) could never be produced from two atoms (aṇu), as neither of them would be established.
For this reason as well, the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable.
And because it exists eternally, according to the commentary on the Sūtra.
Moreover, atoms must be accepted as having either the nature of activity, the nature of cessation, the nature of both, or the nature of neither, for there is no other alternative.
Yet none of these four positions is tenable: if they had the nature of activity, activity would exist eternally, leading to the absurd consequence that dissolution could never occur;
if they had the nature of cessation, cessation would exist eternally, leading to the absurd consequence that creation could never occur.
