Furthermore, it is illogical for [the atom] to possess both natures simultaneously due to their mutual contradiction. If, however, it is held that it possesses neither nature, then since the causes for its activity and cessation—such as *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit)—are admitted to exist, and because such a cause as *adṛṣṭa* is eternally present, there would follow the consequence of eternal activity. Even if *adṛṣṭa* and the like were not the governing factors, there would still follow the consequence of eternal non-activity.
Therefore, the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable.
And because they possess form and other qualities, there is a reversal [of the argument], as seen from observation.

Regarding the claim of the Vaiśeṣikas that "atoms (paramāṇus) are of four kinds, possess color and other qualities, and are the eternal originators of the fourfold [elements] consisting of the primary elements (bhūtas) and their derivatives (bhautikas)— these being substances which, when divided part by part, cannot be further divided"—

that assumption of theirs is entirely without foundation; for, because atoms possess color and other qualities, it would follow as a logical consequence that their atomicity and eternity are reversed.
The meaning is that, in relation to the ultimate cause, their grossness and impermanence would result in a state contrary to what is intended.
Why? Because it is observed thus in the world: for whatever object in the world possesses form and other qualities is seen to be gross and impermanent in relation to its own cause;
for example, a cloth, in relation to its threads, is gross and impermanent.
Just as threads are gross and non-eternal in relation to their constituent parts, so too these atoms are accepted by them as possessing color and other qualities;
therefore, they too must have causes, and in relation to those, they necessarily follow as being gross and non-eternal.

Furthermore, the reason they have stated for their eternity—namely, "that which exists and has no cause is eternal"—is untenable in the case of atoms when this is so, because it is established by the aforementioned method that atoms also possess causes.

As for the second reason stated for permanence—namely, that "there is no specific negation of the term 'impermanent'"—that too does not necessarily prove the permanence of atoms; for even in the absence of any particular permanent entity, the formation of a negative compound with the word "permanent" would still be possible;
it does not, however, depend specifically upon the permanence of atoms.
And that supreme cause, Brahman, certainly exists eternally.

Furthermore, the establishment of any object does not occur through the mere usage of words and their meanings, because the application of linguistic usage occurs only when both the word and its referent have been established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for the third reason stated in the commentary on the Sūtra regarding eternity—namely, "and non-perception" (*avidyā ca*)—if this were explained as the non-perception by direct observation (*pratyakṣa*) of the causes of existing, perceptible effects, then it would follow that even the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is eternal.

If, on the other hand, it were qualified by "provided that it is not a substance" (*adravyatve sati*), even so, the very fact of being without a cause would result in being the ground for its eternity; and since that has already been stated [previously], the phrase "and ignorance" (*avidyā ca*) would be redundant.

Furthermore, if it were explained as follows—"Ignorance is the impossibility of a third cause of destruction other than the division of the cause and the destruction of the cause; this [ignorance] demonstrates the eternity of the atoms"—this is not tenable, for there is no rule that a perishing object must necessarily perish due to only two causes.

For this [argument] would hold true only if one were to admit that a substance is produced by another substance when there are multiple substances acting as producers through conjunction as an auxiliary cause.

However, when it is admitted that the cause—which is of the nature of a generality (sāmānya) and devoid of specific qualities—becomes a producer by undergoing a change of state into something possessing specific qualities, then destruction is logically possible even through the dissolution of the state of form (mūrti), just like the melting away of the hardness of ghee.
Therefore, because atoms possess color and other qualities, the opposite of what you intend follows.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the doctrine that atoms are the cause is untenable.
[The Sāṅkhya argument is rejected] because there is a fault in both ways.

Earth, which possesses the qualities of smell, taste, color, and touch, is gross; water, possessing the qualities of color, taste, and touch, is subtle; fire, possessing the qualities of color and touch, is subtler; and air, possessing the quality of touch, is most subtle. Thus, these four elements are observed in the world to be composed of accumulated parts and to possess a gradation of grossness, subtlety, subtler-ness, and most-subtle-ness. Second Chapter. [Furthermore,] they are observed to possess a gradation of qualities such as grossness, subtlety, subtler-ness, and most-subtle-ness.
In the same way, atoms too would have to be conceived as possessing either increased or decreased qualities, or neither;
and in either case, the attachment of defects would be unavoidable.

First, if they were conceived as possessing increased or decreased qualities, then for those with increased qualities, there would follow the consequence of non-atomhood due to the diminution of their form (mūrti).

Nor can it be said that there is an increase in qualities without a corresponding increase in the magnitude of the form (mūrti), for we observe that in the case of elemental effects, an increase in qualities is accompanied by an increase in magnitude.

If, however, one does not admit an increase or decrease in qualities for the sake of establishing the equality of their atomic nature, then if all atoms were postulated as possessing only a single quality each, there would be no perception of touch in fire, nor of both color and touch in water, nor of taste, color, and touch in earth; this is because the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of its cause.

If, on the other hand, all [qualities] were postulated as being present in all four [elements], then there would be the perception of odor even in water, of odor and taste in fire, and of odor, color, and taste in air.
But this is not observed.
Therefore, the doctrine that atoms are the cause is untenable.
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of expectation.

The doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause was even formulated by certain knowers of the Veda, such as Manu and others, with the intention of relying upon aspects such as the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*);

however, this doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the cause has not been accepted by any learned person (*śiṣṭa*) on any point whatsoever, and is therefore utterly unworthy of consideration by those who follow the Veda.

Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas, in their Sūtras and Bhāṣya, accept six categories (*padārtha*)—namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*)—which constitute the subject matter of their system, as being absolutely distinct and possessing distinct characteristics, just like [the distinction between] a man, a horse, and a hare.

Having accepted their being thatness (*tathātva*), they nevertheless accept that the remaining categories depend upon substance (*dravya*), which is contradictory to that [oneness]. That is not tenable.

Why? Just as in the world, things such as a hare, a kuśa-grass blade, and a palāśa-leaf, though existing as absolutely distinct, do not have a relationship of mutual dependence, so too, because substance and the other categories are absolutely distinct, it is impossible for qualities (*guṇa*) and the rest to be dependent upon substance.

Now, if it is argued that qualities and so forth are dependent upon substance—such that they exist when substance exists and do not exist when substance is absent, and thus substance alone, through various distinctions such as configuration and the like, becomes the object of multiple words and cognitions, just as Devadatta, though being one and the same, becomes the object of multiple words and cognitions due to his connection with different states—then, this being the case, both the consequence of the Sāṃkhya doctrine and a contradiction of one's own tenet would result.
[Objection: But is it not observed that smoke, even though it is distinct from fire, is nonetheless dependent upon fire?
It is true that they are perceived;
however, because there is a cognition of difference (*bhedapratīti*), the distinctness of fire and smoke is determined in those cases.

Here, however, in instances such as "the white blanket," "the red cow," or "the blue lotus," since it is that very substance which is perceived through its respective qualifier, there is no cognition of difference between the substance and the quality, as there is between fire and smoke.
Therefore, a quality has the nature of a substance.
By this, the fact that action, generality, particularity, and inherence have the nature of a substance is also explained.
In the *Pāśupata Sūtra*, this is the second chapter.

If it should be argued that qualities are dependent on substance because substance and quality are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), then this so-called inseparability must mean either non-distinctness of location, non-distinctness of time, or non-distinctness of nature.
In no way, however, is this tenable. First, regarding non-distinctness of location, it would contradict your own accepted doctrine.
How so? For it is accepted that a cloth produced from threads occupies the location of the threads, not the location of the cloth;
whereas the qualities of the cloth, such as whiteness and so forth, are accepted as occupying the location of the cloth, not the location of the threads.
And thus they say: "Substances originate another substance, and qualities originate another quality."

For they indeed accept that the causal substances, namely the threads, originate the effect-substance, the cloth, and that the qualities such as whiteness residing in the threads originate another quality, such as whiteness, in the effect-substance, the cloth.
This acceptance would be contradicted if it were admitted that substance and quality do not occupy different locations (*apṛthagdeśatva*).

If, on the other hand, "inseparability" (*ayutasiddhatva*) were said to mean non-difference in time (*apṛthakkālatva*), then the two horns of a cow—the left and the right—would also result in being inseparable.

Likewise, if there is no separate nature—that is, if they are inseparably established—then no distinction in essence between substance and quality is possible, because it is perceived as being identical with that [substance].

The assertion that "conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the relation between two things established separately (*yutasiddha*), whereas inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between two things not established separately (*ayutasiddha*)" is merely false for them, because it is impossible for a cause that is already established prior to its effect to be "not established separately" from that effect.

If, on the other hand, this assertion were intended to depend only on one of the two—namely, that inherence is the relation of an effect not established separately with its cause—even so, a relation with the cause is not possible for an effect that is as yet unestablished and has not yet acquired its own nature, since a relation necessarily depends upon both relata.

If it is argued that [the effect] is connected after having become established (*siddha*), then, since the establishment of the effect prior to its connection with the cause would have to be admitted, the absence of "establishment-in-separation" (*ayutasiddhi*) would follow; consequently, the statement that "conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect" would be wrongly stated.

Furthermore, just as the relation of a produced, inactive effect-substance with other all-pervading substances such as space (*ākāśa*) is admitted to be conjunction alone and not inherence (*samavāya*), so too its relation with the causal substance must be conjunction alone, not inherence.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a relation—whether it be conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)—as something distinct from the related entities themselves.
If it is argued that these two exist because we observe the use of the words and cognitions "conjunction" and "inherence" as distinct from the words and cognitions of the related entities, we say no;
for even in the case of a single entity, we observe multiple words and cognitions depending on whether one considers its own nature or its external form.

Just as Devadatta, though being one, becomes the object of various words and notions in the world depending on his own nature and the nature of his relations—being called a man, a Brahmin, a Vedic scholar, a generous man, a child, a youth, an old man, a father, a son, a grandson, a brother, or a son-in-law—and just as a single line, by being placed in different positions, undergoes a distinction of words and notions such as "one," "ten," "hundred," or "thousand," so too conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are merely fit to be the objects of words and notions of relation apart from the related things themselves; there exists no separate entity [beyond them]. Thus ends the second chapter.
Because there is no non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, there is the absence of another entity;
nor does the consequence of the continuous existence of the word and cognition of the relation follow if they have the related entities as their object,
since this has already been answered by the argument regarding the dependence on the intrinsic form versus the external form.

Likewise, because atoms, the self, and the mind are partless, conjunction is not possible, for conjunction is observed only between a substance possessing parts and another substance possessing parts.
If it is argued that atoms, the self, and the mind will have imagined parts, we say no.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence of establishing all possible objects through the imagination of non-existent things, and because there is no restrictive cause for the rule that "only this much—a non-existent object, whether contradictory or non-contradictory—should be imagined, and nothing more," and because imagination is independent and capable of being abundant, there is no reason to prevent one from imagining hundreds or thousands of objects beyond the six categories imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas. Therefore, whatever anyone finds pleasing would be established.

A certain compassionate person might imagine that the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is so full of suffering for living beings, should simply not exist; or another, being distressed, might imagine the rebirth even of those who are liberated. Who could be the preventer of these two?
Furthermore, it is impossible for a composite dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) to be joined with two partless atoms, just as [it is impossible] for space to be joined [with anything].
For there is no joining of space with earth and the other elements like that of lacquer and wood;

if it is argued that "inherence (*samavāya*) must necessarily be postulated because the relationship of supported and support between cause and effect substances would otherwise be untenable," we say no.

In other cases, as stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya, there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*); for the establishment of the relationship between the supported and the support (*āśritāśrayabhāva*) depends upon the establishment of the difference between cause and effect, and the establishment of their difference depends upon the establishment of the relationship between the supported and the support—just like a bowl and a jujube fruit. Thus, there would be mutual dependence.

However, neither the difference between cause and effect nor the relationship between the supported and the support is accepted by the proponents of Vedānta, because they maintain that the effect is merely a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the cause itself.

Furthermore, because atoms are limited in size, they must possess parts corresponding to the six, eight, or ten directions [in which they are situated]; and since they possess parts, they would be non-eternal—thus, the accepted doctrine of their eternity and partlessness would be contradicted.
If it is argued that those very parts which you postulate as being distinguished by their different directions are themselves the atoms, we say no.

Since destruction is established through a sequence of degrees ranging from grossness to subtlety up to the ultimate cause—just as the earth, though being a substantial entity, perishes when compared to dyads (*dyaṇuka*) and other subtle things, and thereafter the earth-like substances that are more subtle and most subtle perish, and then the dyads perish—in the same way, atoms (*paramāṇu*) must also perish because they belong to the same class as the earth.
If it is argued that even while perishing, they perish only through the disjunction of their parts, this is not a fault.

For we have already stated that destruction is possible even as in the case of the melting of the solidity of clarified butter; for just as in the case of clarified butter, gold, and the like, even though their parts are not being divided, the destruction of their solidity occurs through the attainment of a liquid state due to contact with fire, so too, in the case of atoms, the destruction of their form and other qualities will occur through the attainment of the state of the ultimate cause. Likewise, the commencement of an effect does not occur solely through the conjunction of parts, since we observe the commencement of effects such as curd and ice from milk and water even without a further conjunction of parts.

Thus, because it is constructed from extremely unsubstantial reasoning, because it contradicts the scriptural texts regarding God as the cause, and because it has not been accepted by cultured authorities such as Manu and others who are devoted to the Vedas, this doctrine of atoms as the cause must be completely disregarded by noble seekers of the highest good; this is the completion of the sentence.
Even when both causes are present for the collection, there is no attainment of that.
It has been stated that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is not to be relied upon because of its employment of fallacious reasoning, its contradiction of the Vedas, and its lack of acceptance by the learned.

Since that [Vaiśeṣika] system is "half-destructive" (ardhavaināśika), the doctrine of total destructionism (sarvavaināśika) is even less worthy of reliance due to its commonality with the general class of nihilists;
this we shall now demonstrate.
And that [teaching] is of many kinds, due to differences in practice or differences among those to be trained (*vineya*);
therein, there are these three types of proponents: some are proponents of the existence of all things (*sarvāstitvavādin*);
some are proponents of the mere existence of consciousness (*vijñānāstitvamātravādin*).
Others, however, are proponents of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatvavādin*).

Among them, we shall first address those who maintain that everything exists (*sarvāstitvavādin*), who accept external and internal entities—namely, the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), as well as the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*). In this regard, they consider the primary elements to be the earth-element and so forth, and their derivatives to be form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as the eye and other sense organs. Furthermore, they hold that within the fourfold [classification], the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth and the other elements possess the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion, and that these [atoms] aggregate to constitute the state of earth and the other [elements].

Likewise, in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is held that the five aggregates known as form, consciousness, feeling, perception, and mental formations are also combined internally as the basis for all worldly transactions.

In this regard, the following is stated: This "dual-caused" aggregate (samudāya) intended by the opponents—which is of two kinds, consisting of a collection of atoms and their derivatives (*bhūta-bhautika*), and consisting of the five aggregates (*skandha*)—even when such a dual-caused aggregate is proposed, its attainment would not occur; that is, there would be no attainment of an aggregate, meaning the existence of an aggregate is untenable. Why? Because the constituent members (*samudāyin*) are insentient; because the manifestation of consciousness (*cittābhijvalana*) is dependent upon the establishment of the aggregate; because no other sentient being—whether an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) or a ruler (*praśāsitṛ*)—is admitted as a permanent unifier (*saṃhartṛ*); because if independent activity were admitted, it would entail the consequence of activity never ceasing; because the "intention" (*āśaya*) cannot be defined as either identical to or different from [the constituents]; and because, due to the admission of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), activity is impossible since they are devoid of functional operation (*nirvyāpāra*).
Therefore, the composite whole is untenable;
and if the composite whole is untenable, the worldly course of life which depends upon it would be destroyed.
If it is argued that this is because of their being mutual conditions, we say no, because they are merely the causes for the arising [of the aggregates].

Even though no conscious, permanent agent— whether as an enjoyer or a ruler— is admitted, nevertheless, because ignorance and the other factors stand in a relationship of mutual causality, the course of worldly existence is established; and since that is established,
nothing else need be postulated.

And these factors beginning with ignorance—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*paridevanā*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and dejection (*durmanastā*)—are of such a nature that they are mutually causal. In the Buddhist doctrine, they are taught sometimes in brief and sometimes in detail;
yet this entire collection beginning with ignorance is not to be rejected by anyone.

If it be argued that, since this collection [of the body] is implied by the fact that the complex beginning with ignorance (avidyā) revolves incessantly like a water-wheel through the mutual relationship of cause and effect, such a collection is therefore established—this is not so.
Why? Because it is merely the cause of origination. A collection would be established if some cause for the collection were perceived;
however, no such cause is perceived.

Since, even though ignorance and the rest are mutually dependent, each preceding one may serve merely as the cause for the arising of each succeeding one, yet no cause whatsoever is possible for the arising of the aggregate itself.

Now, it was argued that the aggregate is implied by the very nature of ignorance and the rest; to this it is replied: if your intention is that ignorance and the rest, being unable to establish themselves without an aggregate, require an aggregate, then some cause for that aggregate must be stated.

And it has been stated in the *Vaiśeṣika-parīkṣā* that this [bondage] is not possible even if one accepts eternal atoms and if there exist enjoyers who stand in the relation of substratum and superstratum.

How much less, then, could it be possible when momentary atoms are accepted as being devoid of an enjoyer and empty of the relationship between substratum and superstratum? Now, if the intention is that ignorance and the rest alone are the cause of the aggregate, how can they—being themselves dependent upon that very aggregate for their own existence—be its cause? Or, if you think that aggregates themselves continue in a series throughout beginningless saṃsāra, and that ignorance and the rest depend upon them, even then, an aggregate arising from another aggregate would have to arise either invariably similar to it, or non-invariably, being either similar or dissimilar.

If one accepts the doctrine of necessity (*niyama*), it would follow that a human person could never attain birth as a god, an animal, or a denizen of hell; yet if one accepts the doctrine of non-necessity (*aniyama*), it would follow that a human person might, in a single moment, become an elephant, a god, or again a human—
both of which contradict the accepted tenets.
Moreover, you maintain that whatever aggregate exists for the sake of enjoyment, there is no stable enjoyer who is the soul (*jīva*);
therefore, enjoyment is for the sake of enjoyment alone and should not be sought by anyone else.
Likewise, liberation is for the sake of liberation alone, so one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) should not be anyone other than that [liberation].
If it were argued that both [bondage and liberation] are brought about by something else, then that [cause] would have to endure through the periods of both enjoyment and liberation;
and if it were to endure, there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Therefore, let it be granted—if it must be—that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors are merely causes for the arising of one another.
But the aggregate would not be established, because of the absence of an enjoyer; such is the intended meaning.
And because the subsequent arises when the preceding has ceased.
It has been stated that because ignorance and the other factors are merely the causes for the arising [of the aggregates], there is no establishment of a "collection" [of them]; however,
it is now demonstrated that even this status of being a mere cause for arising is not possible.
This is the position of the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*): that when the subsequent moment arises, the preceding moment ceases.

However, for one who maintains this view, it is impossible to establish a causal relationship between the preceding and succeeding moments; for whether the preceding moment is in the process of ceasing or has already ceased, it is overtaken by non-existence, and thus its status as a cause for the subsequent moment is untenable.

Now, if the intention is that an entity existing as a perfected state (*pariniṣpanna*) in a preceding moment is the cause of a succeeding moment, even so, this is not tenable; for if one further postulates an activity (*vyāpāra*) for that which has already become an entity, it would entail the consequence of its connection with another moment [of existence].

Alternatively, if the intention is that the entity itself is its activity, even so, this is likewise not tenable, because a result cannot arise unless it is permeated by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause.

Furthermore, if one accepts such permeation by the intrinsic nature, then since the causal nature would persist until the time of the result, it would entail the abandonment of the accepted doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Furthermore, for one who accepts the relation of cause and effect even without the coloring of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since that relation would apply everywhere.

Moreover, as for what are called "arising" and "cessation," they must either be the very essence of the entity itself, or another state, or a different entity altogether; in no way whatsoever are these tenable.
If arising and cessation were indeed the very essence of the entity, then the word "entity" and the words "arising" and "cessation" would become synonyms.

If one should think that there is some distinction—namely, that by the two words "arising" (utpāda) and "cessation" (nirodha), the initial and final states of an entity existing in the middle are being designated—even so, because the entity would be connected with three moments (the initial, the middle, and the final), its momentariness would be lost.

Alternatively, if arising and cessation were entirely distinct from the entity, like a horse and a buffalo, then the entity would be untouched by arising and cessation, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the entity being eternal.

Furthermore, if appearance and non-appearance were the arising and ceasing of a thing, even so, those two would be properties of the cognition and not properties of the thing; thus, the consequence would be the eternal nature of the thing.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the Buddhist doctrine is untenable.
If it did not exist, there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity.

In the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, regarding the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), it was stated that because the preceding moment is seized by cessation, it cannot be the cause of the succeeding moment.

Now, if one were to assert the arising of an effect even when the cause is non-existent, there would be a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñoparodha*); this proposition—that "mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon four kinds of causes"—would be abandoned.
Furthermore, if arising were causeless, there would be no restriction, and everything would arise from everything.
If one were to say that the preceding moment persists for as long as the arising of the subsequent moment, then there would be simultaneity of cause and effect;
even so, there would be a contradiction of the thesis, for this thesis—that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary—would be subverted.

"Non-attainment of analytical and non-analytical cessation due to non-interruption. [Sūtra 2.2.21] Furthermore, the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) postulate that whatever is cognizable by the intellect, other than the three, is conditioned (saṃskṛta) and momentary (kṣaṇika);
and they declare those three to be analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), and space (ākāśa).
They consider all three of these to be non-entities (*avastu*), mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*), and indefinable (*nirupākhya*);
for they say that the destruction of entities preceded by conscious effort is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
while its opposite is "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
"Space is merely the absence of obstruction.
They will refute space later on;
now he refutes the two types of cessation—the meaning is that there is no attainment and no possibility of either analytical (pratisaṃkhyā) or non-analytical (apratisaṃkhyā) cessation.

Why? Because there is no interruption. For these two—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—must have either the continuum (*saṃtāna*) or the entities (*bhāva*) as their object.

First, they cannot have the continuum as their object, because in all continua, since the members of the continuum exist in an uninterrupted relationship of cause and effect, the interruption of the continuum is impossible.

Nor can they both have existence as their objective domain; for it is impossible for there to be a destruction of entities that is without continuity or any traceable description, because in all states one observes a continuity through the power of recognition. Even in those states where recognition is not clear, one infers such continuity elsewhere based on the continuity observed in some instances.
Therefore, the two types of cessation postulated by others are untenable.
And because there is a fault in either case.

This cessation of ignorance and so forth, which falls under the category of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and is postulated in the commentary on the subsequent Sūtra—would it arise from right knowledge together with its auxiliaries, or by itself? In the former alternative, there follows the undesirable consequence of admitting a causeless destruction;
in the latter, however, there follows the undesirable consequence of the futility of the instruction on the Path.
Thus, since faults follow in both cases, this view is untenable.
And because there is no distinction in space.

Furthermore, regarding their own intended position that the two types of cessation and space are non-entities (*nirupākhyam*), the non-substantiality of the two cessations has already been refuted previously;
now, space itself is being refuted.

Moreover, the acceptance of space as a non-entity is illogical, because, like the two cessations—both through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā*)—there is no difference in its being established as a real thing (*vastutva*).

First of all, the reality of space is established through the authority of scripture, based on such Vedic texts as, "From the Self, space was produced. However, for those who disagree, it must be stated that space is to be inferred from its quality, sound, because we observe that qualities such as odor have as their substrata real entities like earth and the rest.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that space is merely the absence of obstruction, there would follow the consequence that when one bird is flying, there would be no room for another bird wishing to fly up, since the obstruction already exists [in the space occupied by the first].

If it is argued that "it will fall where there is an absence of obstruction," then that by which the absence of obstruction is qualified must itself be a real entity (*vastubhūta*), namely space (*ākāśa*), and not merely the absence of obstruction.
Furthermore, for the Buddhist who considers space to be merely the absence of obstruction, a contradiction with his own tenets would follow;
for in the *Saṃgītiparyāya-sūtra*, the second chapter of the Buddhist scriptures...

In this series of questions and answers beginning with "O Blessed One, on what is the earth supported?", at the end of the sequence concerning the earth and other elements, there occurs the answer to the question "On what is the wind supported? which is: "The wind is supported by space.
This would not be consistent if space were a non-entity;
therefore, for this reason as well, it is incorrect that space is a non-entity.
Moreover, it is a contradiction to claim that these three—the two kinds of cessation (nirodha) and space (ākāśa)—are both indefinable (nirupākhyam), non-entities (avastu), and eternal (nityam).
For neither eternity nor non-eternity is possible for a non-entity, because the conventional usage of "attribute" (dharma) and "substantive" (dharmin) is dependent upon a real entity (vastu).
Indeed, if there were such a relation of attribute and substantive, they would possess substantiality like a jar or similar objects, and not indefinability.
And because of mindfulness.
Furthermore, O Nihilist, one who accepts the momentariness of every entity must also accept the momentariness of the perceiver;
yet that is not possible,
for *anusmṛti*— recollection— is simply memory arising with respect to a prior experience, which is the perception itself.
Furthermore, that [recollection] occurs only when it has a single cognizer as its agent, because we do not observe recollection in one person regarding an object perceived by another person.
For how could there be the cognition, "I saw that then, and now I see this," if there were not a single person who was both the seer of the prior and the subsequent moments?

Moreover, for every person in the world, there is well-known through direct perception the recognition-cognition regarding the agent of seeing and remembering, namely, "I saw that then, and I see this now."
For if the author of the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya were different persons, then one would perceive it thus: "I remember, but another saw";
yet no one perceives it in this way.
Where such a perception occurs, the whole world understands that there are indeed two distinct agents for the seeing and the remembering, [expressing it] as: "I remember; so-and-so saw that."
In this case, however, even the Nihilist (Vaināśika) understands that the very same single self is the agent of both seeing and remembering, as in the thought "I saw this.
He does not deny that the act of seeing has occurred in the self by saying "it was not I," just as one would not say "fire is cold" or "fire is without light.
This being so, since a single entity is connected with two moments characterized by seeing and remembering, the Nihilist's own admission of momentariness would incur an unavoidable contradiction.

Likewise, recognizing each successive cognition as having the same agent right up until the final breath, and connecting past cognitions from birth onwards as having the self as their sole agent—how could the nihilist who advocates the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) not feel ashamed? If he were to say that this [recognition] is accomplished through similarity, one should reply to him: since similarity depends upon two things, such that "this is similar to that," for the proponent of momentary flux there is no single grasper of two similar entities; therefore, his claim that the connection [of cognitions] is based on similarity is nothing but a false prattle.

If it were argued that there is a single cognizer who grasps the similarity between the preceding and succeeding moments, then, because that one [cognizer] would persist for two moments, the thesis of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would be undermined. If it is claimed that this is merely a distinct cognition—namely, "this is similar to that"—and not caused by the simultaneous grasping of both the preceding and succeeding moments, we say: no.
Because of the employment of distinct word-meanings in the expression "this is that" (*tenedaṃ*);

for if this were a different cognition whose object is similarity alone, then the use of the sentence "this is similar to that" would be redundant, and one would instead have to employ the expression "similarity. Indeed, when a meaning well-established in the world is not accepted by investigators, then neither the establishment of one's own position nor the refutation of another's position—though both may be stated—enters into the stream of consciousness of the investigators or oneself as being in accordance with reality. Only that which is determined as "this is exactly the meaning" should be stated.
To state anything other than this would merely demonstrate one's own prolixity.
Furthermore, this conventional usage based on similarity is not tenable; for there is cognition of that very entity itself, and no cognition of an entity that is merely similar to it.
In the case of external objects, because deception is possible, there might occasionally arise a doubt such as, "This might be that very thing, or it might be similar to it";

however, with regard to the perceiver, even such a doubt never occurs—namely, "I might be that same person, or I might be someone similar"—because one perceives with certainty that identity, thinking, "I who saw this yesterday am the very same I who remember it today.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the doctrine of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) is untenable.
Not from the non-existent, because it has not been observed.
For this reason as well, the doctrine of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) is untenable: for those who do not admit a stable, persisting cause, it would follow that an entity arises from non-existence.
And they indeed demonstrate the arising of an entity from non-existence by saying, "Because there is no manifestation without prior destruction" (*Sūtra-bhāṣya*, pāda 2, sūtra 22).
For, according to them, a sprout arises from a seed that has perished, and likewise curds from milk that has perished, and a jar from a lump of clay [that has perished].
If the effect were to arise from an immutable cause, then, due to the lack of distinction, everything would arise from everything.
Therefore, since sprouts and the like are seen to arise from seeds and the like which have been overtaken by non-existence, they maintain that "an entity arises from non-existence.
To this, it is said: "Not from the non-existent, because it is not observed."
An entity does not arise from non-existence.
If an entity were to arise from non-existence, then because there is no distinction in the nature of non-existence, the postulation of specific causes would be purposeless.

For there is no distinction whatsoever in the state of non-existence between the non-existence of seeds and the like that have been destroyed and the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn, since they are equally devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
In this way, the acceptance of specific causes— such as that a sprout arises from a seed alone and curd from milk alone— would be meaningful; however,
if one were to accept a causeless non-existence (abhāva) as the cause, then sprouts and the like would arise even from things such as a hare's horn,
yet this is not observed.

If, moreover, a specific quality were admitted even for non-existence—just as blueness and so forth are admitted for lotuses and the like—then, precisely because it possesses a specific quality, non-existence would necessarily follow as being an entity, just like a lotus and so forth.
Furthermore, non-existence could not be the cause of the production of anything, precisely because it is non-existence, just like the horn of a hare and the like.
And if an entity were produced from non-existence, every effect would be permeated by non-existence.

But this is not seen to be the case, because every object is perceived as having its own specific form and nature as its very being; nor is it accepted by anyone that objects such as bowls and the like, which are pervaded by clay, are modifications of threads and similar materials. Thus ends the second chapter. [Mādhyamikakārikā 2.1]
However, the world understands that entities endowed with clay as their material cause [arise from it].

As for the claim that "since it is impossible for any immutable entity to function as a cause without the destruction of its own nature, the arising of an existent from a non-existent must be the case," that is poorly argued; for we observe that gold and other substances, which possess a stable nature and are recognized as the same, serve as the causes for things such as earrings and the like.

Even in those cases such as seeds where the destruction of the own-form (*svarūpa*) is observed, it is not accepted that the preceding state, while being destroyed, is the cause of the succeeding state; for it is accepted that the parts of the seed and so forth, which persist without being destroyed, constitute the causal state for the sprout and so forth.

Therefore, since the arising of an existent from non-existent things like a hare’s horn is never observed, whereas the arising of an existent from existent things like gold is observed, this acceptance of the arising of an entity from non-existence is untenable.

Moreover, having accepted that mental states and mental factors arise from the four [great elements], and that a collection characterized by the primary elements and their derivatives arises from atoms, those nihilists—who now deny this very acceptance while imagining the arising of existence from non-existence—throw the entire world into confusion.
And thus, even for those who are indifferent, success is achieved.

If it were admitted that the arising of an entity occurs from non-existence, then in that case, even for people who are indifferent and making no effort, their desired ends would be accomplished, because non-existence is easily available. Thus, a farmer would have the production of grain even without exerting himself in the work of the field; and a potter would have the production of a vessel even without exerting himself in the preparation of the clay.
Even for a weaver, there would be the acquisition of cloth even while not weaving threads, as if he were weaving;
furthermore, no one would ever strive for heaven or liberation in any way whatsoever. And this is neither logical nor accepted by anyone.
Therefore, this acceptance of the arising of an entity from non-existence is untenable.
Not non-existence, because it is perceived.

Now, when objections such as the impossibility of attaining a collective whole have been raised against the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), the Buddhist Proponent of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*) now offers a rebuttal. Indeed, having observed that certain disciples (*vineya*) were attached to external things, this system of the theory of external objects was composed out of deference to them;
it is not the actual intention of the Sugata.
However, his intended position is precisely the doctrine of the single aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-ekaskandhavāda*).

And in that doctrine of consciousness, the entire conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and results (*phala*) is established as being internal, by way of forms mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*); for even if external objects exist, the conventional usage of the means of knowledge and so forth does not occur without their being mounted upon the intellect.
But how is it understood that this entire conventional usage is internal, and that there is no external object distinct from consciousness?
He says that this is impossible because, if an external object is admitted, it must be either atoms or their aggregates such as pillars and the like.
In that regard, atoms cannot be the objects determined by the cognition of pillars and so forth, because a cognition appearing as atoms is logically untenable.

Nor can pillars and the like be their aggregates, because those aggregates cannot be established through the alternatives of being either different from or non-different from the atoms. Thus ends the second chapter.
Because it is impossible to define [the nature of the object], one should likewise reject universals (jāti) and so forth as well.

Furthermore, since cognition arises with a common nature through mere experience, this partiality toward each respective object—such that there is "cognition of a pillar," "cognition of a wall," "cognition of a jar," or "cognition of a cloth"—is not possible without a specific quality residing in the cognition itself; therefore, one must necessarily admit that cognition possesses a form corresponding to its object (viṣayasārūpya).

And once that [simultaneous perception] is accepted, since the form of the object is already encompassed by cognition itself, the postulation of the existence of an external object is useless. Furthermore, because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*), non-difference between the object and its cognition follows;
for there is no apprehension of one of these two when the other is not apprehended.
Nor is this [distinction] tenable when there is a distinction from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viveka*), because of the absence of any obstructing cause;

therefore, too, there is an absence of external objects. And this should be understood as being like dreams and so forth: for just as the cognitions of dreams, illusions, mirages, and cities of the Gandharvas occur in the forms of grasped and grasper even without an external object; [so it is here].

Thus it is understood that even the cognitions of pillars and the like occurring in the waking state must likewise be [mere mental constructs], because there is no difference in their status as cognitions.

But how, in the absence of external objects, is the diversity of cognitions possible? He says: "Due to the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the diversity of cognitions and latent impressions—like seeds and sprouts—is not contradicted by the relationship of mutual cause and effect.

Moreover, it is understood through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the diversity of cognitions is caused solely by mental impressions (*vāsanā*), because we both admit that the diversity of cognitions caused by impressions occurs even in the absence of external objects, as in dreams and the like; whereas I do not admit that the diversity of cognitions caused by external objects occurs in the absence of impressions.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the external object does not exist.
This being the position reached, we reply: "It is not non-existent, because [external objects] are perceived."
Indeed, the non-existence of an external object cannot be determined;
why? Because it is perceived. For in every cognition, an external object is perceived—such as a pillar, a wall, a jar, or a cloth—and that which is being perceived cannot possibly be non-existent.

For just as someone who is eating, while personally experiencing the satisfaction accomplished by that eating, might say, "I am not eating, nor am I satisfied," so too one who is personally perceiving an external object through the contact of the senses, if he were to say, "I do not perceive it, nor does it exist," how could his words be worthy of acceptance?
Now, it may be argued: "I do not say, 'I do not perceive any object at all';
rather, I say, 'I do not perceive anything apart from the perception itself.'"

"Certainly, you speak thus because of the unrestrained nature of your tongue, but you do not speak what is endowed with reason; for the existence of an object distinct from its perception must necessarily be admitted on the basis of that very perception itself.
Indeed, no one perceives perception itself as a pillar or a wall;
rather, all worldly people perceive pillars, walls, and so forth precisely by virtue of their being objects of perception."

And for this very reason, all worldly people perceive things in exactly this way; even those who deny external objects speak thus: "That which is an internal form of the object of cognition appears as if it were external. For they too, while apprehending consciousness—which is well-known to the whole world as appearing externally—and wishing to deny the external object, employ the word "as if" (vat) in the phrase "as if external.
Otherwise, why would they say "as if external"? No one would ever say, "Viṣṇumitra appears like the son of a barren woman."
Therefore, for those who accept reality in accordance with experience, it is logical to accept that [the object] appears as external, and not that it appears as if it were external.
Now, one might argue: "Because an external object is impossible, we have determined that it appears as if it were external.

This determination is not correct, because possibility and impossibility are determined based on whether a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates or does not operate, but the operation or non-operation of a means of valid cognition is not determined based on possibility or impossibility.
For that which is apprehended by even one of the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, is possible;
but that which is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition whatsoever is impossible.

In this case, however, since the external object is apprehended by all the means of valid cognition according to their respective natures, how can it be said—on the basis of mere apprehension—that it is impossible due to dilemmas such as its being distinct or non-distinct [from cognition]? Furthermore, the destruction of the object does not occur simply because the cognition possesses a form similar to the object, for if the object were non-existent, a similarity to it would be untenable, and yet the object is perceived externally.

Therefore, one must accept that even the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) between the cognition and its object is caused by their relationship as means and end (*upāyopeyabhāva*), and not caused by non-difference.
Furthermore, in the cases of "cognition of a jar" and "cognition of a cloth," the difference lies only in the qualifiers—the jar and the cloth—not in the qualified entity, which is cognition.

In the second chapter of the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, it is stated: "In the case of 'black cow,' the difference belongs only to the two qualities of blackness and whiteness; thus, the difference of one from two is established, and the difference of two from one."
Therefore, there is a distinction between the object and its cognition; likewise, this should be understood in the case of "the perception of a jar" and "the recollection of a jar.

For here too, the distinction lies only between the two qualificands—perception and recollection—and not between the qualifier, the jar; just as in the case of "the smell of milk" and "the taste of milk," the distinction lies only between the two qualificands—smell and taste—and not between the qualifier, the milk, so it is here.

Moreover, since two cognitions belonging to earlier and later times are exhausted by their own self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) alone, it is logically impossible for them to stand in the relationship of the grasped and the grasper;

consequently, the propositions found in one's own treatise—such as the distinction between cognitions, the properties of momentariness and so forth, the theory of specific and general characteristics, the relationship between the impressed and the impressioner, and the bondage and liberation resulting from the influence of ignorance regarding existent and non-existent factors—would all be undermined.

Furthermore, it must be explained why one who accepts that consciousness is "consciousness" does not likewise accept external objects such as pillars and walls. If you argue that consciousness is experienced, then it is logical to accept that the external object is also indeed experienced.

If you argue that consciousness, because its nature is luminosity, is experienced by itself like a lamp, whereas the external object is not, then you are accepting an action upon oneself, which is utterly contradictory, like saying "fire burns itself."
However, you do not accept that which is consistent with worldly consensus—that an external object is experienced by a cognition distinct from itself.
Oh, what great scholarship this is! It is like saying, "The cow is white," while maintaining that whiteness is not distinct from the cowness. This is the second chapter. This is indeed astonishing!
Nor is consciousness itself experienced as something distinct from its object, precisely because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
[Objection: If consciousness were to be grasped by something other than its own nature, then that too would have to be grasped by another, and that by yet another, resulting in an infinite regress.

Furthermore, the argument that because cognition is of the nature of illumination like a lamp, the postulation of another cognition is useless—since the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator is untenable due to their equality—is also incorrect for two reasons: first, because the desire to apprehend the witness of cognition does not arise upon the mere apprehension of the cognition itself, the suspicion of an infinite regress is untenable; and second, because the distinction between the witness and the cognition is established by their difference in nature, the relationship of perceiver and perceived is possible, and the self-established witness cannot be denied.

Furthermore, by asserting that consciousness, like a lamp, manifests by itself without depending on another illuminator, you would be saying that consciousness is not accessible through any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇagamya*) and is devoid of a cognizer, like the manifestation of a thousand lamps situated within a solid block of stone.
If you say, "Certainly it is so; however, because consciousness is of the nature of experience (*anubhava*), our position is being accepted by you," we say no;
for we observe that the manifestation of lamps and the like requires another cognizer who employs the eye as an instrument.
Therefore, since consciousness also possesses the common characteristic of being manifest, its manifestation is understood to occur only when there is another cognizer, just like a lamp.

If you argue that by proposing the self-established nature of the cognizing witness (*sākṣin*), you have merely resorted to a different mode of expression for my own position—that "consciousness manifests itself"—we say no;
for you have admitted that consciousness possesses specific attributes such as origination, destruction, and multiplicity.
Therefore, we have established that consciousness, like a lamp, is cognizable as something distinct [from itself].
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams and the like.

As for what was stated by the one who denies external objects—that even the cognitions of waking objects, such as pillars and the like, might occur without an external object, just like the cognitions of dreams and so forth, because there is no difference in their being cognitions—that must be answered. To this it is said: waking cognitions cannot be like the cognitions of dreams.
Why? Because of their dissimilarity; for indeed, there is a dissimilarity between the states of dreaming and waking.

What, then, is the difference? We say it is sublation (*bādha*) and non-sublation. For an object perceived in a dream is sublated by one who has awakened, [thinking]: "I falsely perceived a gathering of a great multitude; indeed, no such gathering of a great multitude exists for me. Rather, my mind was overcome by sleep, and because of that this delusion arose.
In the same way, there is sublation as appropriate in the case of illusions (*māyā*) and so forth.
However, an object perceived in the waking state, such as a pillar and the like, is not sublated in any state whatsoever.
Moreover, that which is the seeing of dreams is memory (smṛti), whereas the seeing of the waking state is perception (upalabdhi);

and the difference between memory and perception is directly experienced by oneself as consisting in the dissociation from or association with the object, as in: "I remember my beloved son, I do not perceive him, I desire to perceive him."

This being the case, it cannot be argued that "the perception of the waking state is false because it is a perception, like the perception of a dream," for one who has personally experienced the difference between the two;
nor is it proper for those who consider themselves wise to deny their own experience.

Moreover, since one who is unable to assert that waking cognitions are inherently without an objective basis—lest it contradict direct experience—seeks to assert it on the grounds of their similarity to dream cognitions;
yet, a property that cannot belong to something by its own nature will not become possible for it merely through its similarity to another thing.
For fire, being experienced as hot, will not become cold simply because of its similarity to water.
But the difference between dreaming and waking has been demonstrated.
There is no existence, because it is not perceived.

As for what was said—that the variety of cognitions can be accounted for solely by the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) even in the absence of an object—that must be refuted. It is considered as follows: the existence of latent impressions is not tenable in your position, because external objects are not perceived;
for it is only due to the perception of objects that latent impressions arise in various forms corresponding to each respective object.

But when objects are not being perceived, what could be the cause for the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? Even if they were beginningless, it would result in a baseless infinite regress according to the maxim of the "blind tradition," which would undermine practical worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), rather than fulfilling one's intended purpose. Furthermore, the arguments from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) put forward by those who deny external objects—namely, that this collection of cognitions has its cause solely in latent impressions and not in objects—are also refuted by this; for latent impressions are impossible without the prior perception of objects.

Moreover, since it is admitted that the apprehension of objects occurs even without mental impressions (*vāsanā*), whereas the arising of mental impressions is not admitted without the apprehension of objects, both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) establish the very existence of external objects.
Furthermore, so-called "mental impressions" are specific types of latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*); and latent dispositions do not subsist without a substratum, as this is observed in the world.
Furthermore, you have no substratum for latent impressions (vāsanā), as it is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And because of momentariness.

Even that which is designated as the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse-consciousness) and postulated as the locus of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) cannot, by virtue of its admitted momentariness, possess a stable nature and thus be incapable of serving as the substratum for latent impressions—just like the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

For, in the absence of a single, continuous entity persisting through the three periods of time, or an immutable, all-seeing principle, the worldly transactions involving the synthesis of memory and so forth—which depend on latent impressions conditioned by place, time, and causes—would be impossible.
However, if the *ālayavijñāna* were to have a stable nature, it would entail the abandonment of your own philosophical tenet.

Moreover, since the acceptance of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is common even in the Vijñānavāda, those objections based on momentariness that were raised against the Bāhyārthavāda—such as "because the preceding has ceased when the succeeding arises," and so forth—are to be applied here as well.
Thus, both these nihilistic positions have been refuted: the position of the Bāhyārthavādin and the position of the Vijñānavādin.
As for the position of the Śūnyavādin, however, it is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, no further effort is made to refute it.

For this worldly convention, established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be denied without first apprehending another reality; for when there is no exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) prevails. Chapter Two: And because it is untenable in every way.

What more need be said? In every way, however this doctrine of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) is examined for its logical consistency, it falls apart like a well dug in sand; we do not perceive any logical justification here at all.
Therefore, the practical application of the Nihilist system is untenable.

Moreover, by teaching these three mutually contradictory doctrines—the existence of external objects, consciousness-only, and emptiness—the Sugata has clearly demonstrated his own tendency toward incoherent prattle, or else his malice toward the people, thinking that they might become deluded by grasping at such contradictory meanings.
The intention is that this system of the Sugata is in every respect to be disregarded by those who desire their own welfare.
Not [is it] in one [substratum], because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes].
The doctrine of the Sugata has been refuted;
now the doctrine of the Vivasanas (Jainas) is being refuted.

They accept seven categories: soul (jīva), non-soul (ajīva), influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa); these are impossible within a single [system].

In brief, however, he [the author] has stated that there are only two categories (*padārtha*), namely those called *jīva* (living beings) and *ajīva* (non-living things), because the others are included within these two as appropriate—so they believe.
They describe another further elaboration of these two, consisting of the five *astikāyas*: the *jīvāstikāya*, the *pudgalāstikāya*, the *dharmāstikāya*, the *adharmāstikāya*, and the *ākāśāstikāya*.
They describe many kinds of intermediate subdivisions of all these [categories] imagined by their own systems in their Sūtras and Bhāṣyas.

And everywhere they introduce this logic called the *saptabhaṅgīnaya*: "perhaps it exists," "perhaps it does not exist," "perhaps it both exists and does not exist," "perhaps it is inexpressible," "perhaps it exists and is inexpressible," "perhaps it does not exist and is inexpressible," and "perhaps it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible";
in this very same way, they apply this *saptabhaṅgīnaya* even to such [attributes] as oneness, eternity, and so forth.
To this we reply: this position is not tenable.
Why? Because of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes] in one [substratum].
For it is not possible for contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to coexist simultaneously in a single substrate, just as cold and heat cannot.
Regarding these seven categories that have been determined to be exactly this many and of such a nature: they must either be exactly so, or they must not be so at all.
For otherwise, knowledge whose form is undetermined—being either thus or not thus—would be invalid, just like doubtful knowledge. [Objection:
But surely, since the object consists of multiple aspects, the knowledge arising in a determined form cannot be invalid, as is the case with doubtful knowledge.

We say no. For one who asserts that non-determinacy (*anekāntatva*) is unrestricted across all things, even the act of determination itself—since it is no different from other things in being a real entity—would, by the application of alternatives such as "it may exist" or "it may not exist," result in being non-determinative in nature.
Thus, for the determiner as well as the fruit of determination, there would be existence in one sense and non-existence in another.

This being the case, how could a teacher who has become an authority (*pramāṇabhūta*) be able to instruct while the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*) remain undetermined? Or else, how could those who follow his intention proceed toward the objects taught by him when their true nature is undetermined? For it is only when there is a determination of the certainty of a result that the whole world proceeds without confusion toward the performance of its means; otherwise, it would not. Therefore, one who composes a scripture whose meaning is undetermined would have speech that is not to be accepted, like that of a drunkard or a madman.

Likewise, when the number five of the five astikāyas is being conceptualized as "it either exists or does not exist," it might indeed hold true according to one position, but according to another position it would not; consequently, the number would result in being either less than five or more than five.
Furthermore, the state of being inexpressible (avaktavyatva) is not possible for these categories;
for if they were inexpressible, they could not be spoken of at all.
To say that they are both expressible and inexpressible is a contradiction;
for if they are being expressed, they are likewise determined to be so, and yet it is said that they are not determined.

Likewise, one who prattles that the fruit of such determination—right vision—either exists or does not exist, and similarly that its opposite—wrong vision—also either exists or does not exist, would belong to the faction of the intoxicated or the insane, not to the faction of those worthy of trust.

Furthermore, there would be the existence of heaven and liberation in one case and their non-existence in another; likewise, there would be permanence in one case and impermanence in another. In such a state of uncertainty, purposeful activity would be impossible.
Moreover, it would follow that the nature of the beginningless soul and other entities, whose natures are determined by their own scriptures, would not be as they have been so determined.

Thus, since it is impossible for two contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to reside in a single substratum like the soul (*jīva*) and other categories; and since, if existence were present in one property, another property such as non-existence could not exist therein, and likewise, if non-existence were present, existence could not exist; this doctrine of the Arhatas is inconsistent.

By this, the various forms of non-absolutism (*anekānta*)—such as being both one and many, or being neither different nor non-different from the cause, and so forth—as accepted [by them], are to be understood as refuted.

As for the claim that aggregates arise from atoms designated as "persons" (pudgala), that has already been refuted by the previous refutation of atomism; therefore, no separate effort is made to refute it here.
And thus, the self is not an agent.

Just as the impossibility of contradictory attributes in a single substratum constitutes a defect in the doctrine of *syādvāda*, so too for the self, that is, the living being (*jīva*), another defect would follow: the state of being bodiless.
How so? For the followers of the Jaina school maintain that the living being has the dimensions of the body.
And if it possesses the dimensions of the body, then the self—being non-atomic, non-omnipresent, and limited—would consequently be subject to impermanence, like a jar or similar objects.

Furthermore, because bodies have unstable dimensions, a human soul, having been of the size of a human body, would not pervade the entire body of an elephant upon attaining birth as an elephant through some ripening of karma; likewise, upon attaining birth as a gnat, it would not be contained within the entire body of a gnat.
This same defect applies even within a single birth during childhood, youth, and old age.
It might be argued that the soul (jīva) has infinite parts;
its very parts would contract in a small body and expand in a large one.
Furthermore, it must be stated whether or not the co-location of those infinite constituent parts of the living being is obstructed;
for if there were obstruction, then infinite parts could not be contained within a limited space.
If there were no obstruction—[the second chapter begins].

Even if one part were destroyed, since it would be possible for [the soul] to occupy the space of only a single part, and because the expansion (prathimā) of all the parts together would be impossible, it would follow that the individual soul (jīva) is merely atomic in size;
moreover, it is impossible even to conceive of an infinity of individual-soul parts that are restricted solely to the dimensions of the body.

Now, if it were argued that, by way of succession, some parts of the living being (jīva) come together upon the acquisition of a large body, while others depart upon the acquisition of a small body—even in that case, it is replied: "And even by way of succession there is no lack of contradiction, because of [the soul's] undergoing modification and so forth."

Nor can this state of the soul having the same dimensions as the body be established without contradiction even by means of the successive addition and subtraction of parts. Why? Because it would entail defects such as being subject to modification. For if the soul were constantly being filled with and depleted of parts through their addition and subtraction, its state of being subject to modification (vikriyāvatva) would be unavoidable.
And if it were subject to modification, it would follow that it is non-eternal, like a piece of leather or similar objects.

Furthermore, the accepted doctrine of bondage and liberation would be contradicted—[the doctrine] that for the *jīva* enveloped by the eightfold karma and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra like a gourd, there occurs an upward movement upon the severing of its bonds.
Moreover, because the parts that come and go possess the properties of arrival and departure, they must be non-self, just like the body and so forth;
consequently, it would follow that some persisting part is the self.

Moreover, it is not possible to specify that "this is it" or "that is it. Furthermore, it must be explained from where these constituent parts of the living being (jīva) emerge when they arrive, and where they dissolve when they depart;
for they could not emerge from the material elements (bhūta), nor could they dissolve into the material elements, since the living being is non-material (abhautika).
Nor can any other substratum for the parts of living beings—whether common or uncommon—be established, due to a lack of evidence.
Furthermore, if this were the case, the Self would possess an indefinite nature, because its dimensions would be unsettled by the coming and going of its parts.
Therefore, since such defects would necessarily follow, it is impossible to maintain that the Self undergoes the accession and departure of parts even in succession.

Alternatively, having raised an objection in the preceding sūtra—that the self, being of the same size as the body, would be subject to impermanence because it would follow that it is incomplete when assuming other bodies that are larger or smaller—there might arise the following doubt: "Even if the size [of the self] does not remain constant through successive states, the self could still be eternal by way of the principle of the eternity of a stream (*srotas-saṃtāna*), just as the Vaiśeṣikas (Raktapaṭas) maintain the eternity of the stream of consciousness even though the individual moments of consciousness do not remain constant; the same would apply to the Digambaras. Anticipating this, the answer is stated in this sūtra: First, if the stream is not a real entity (*avastu*), it follows the doctrine of no-self (*nairātmyavāda*). Even if it were a real entity (*vastu*), this position is untenable because it entails defects such as the self undergoing transformation (*vikāra*). Thus, neither alternative is possible.
And because both are eternal in their final state, there is no distinction.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Furthermore, the Jainas maintain that the size of the soul existing in its final state of liberation is eternal;

by that same logic, it would follow that the sizes of the soul in its prior states—the first and the middle—are also eternal, which would result in the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between them.
There would have to be only the size of a single body, and no attainment of other bodies that are increased or decreased in size.
Alternatively, because the final size of the soul (jīva) is fixed, the soul would have to be of a fixed size even in its two previous states;
consequently, one would have to admit that the soul is always either minute or large without distinction, rather than having the size of the body.
Therefore, like that of the Sugata, the doctrine of the Arhats as well is inconsistent and must be disregarded.
[The doctrine] of the Pradhāna is not tenable, because it leads to inconsistency with the Lord.
Now, the doctrine that the Lord is the cause solely as a superintendent is refuted.

How is this understood? Because the Teacher himself has established that the Lord possesses both natures—as both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the superintendent—by stating: "And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples," and "Because of the teaching concerning the meditation on Him as the Lord. Thus, it is known through these very passages.

If, however, the doctrine of God as a cause were here refuted without distinction, it would follow that the author of the Sūtras has contradicted himself through inconsistent statements due to internal contradiction.
Therefore, this position—that God is not the material cause but merely the presiding instrumental cause—is refuted with effort because it opposes the unity of Brahman established by the Vedānta.

And this conception of a Lord outside the Veda is of many kinds. First, some who rely on Sāṃkhya and Yoga postulate that the Lord is the superintendent of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), being merely the efficient cause; they hold that primordial matter, the individual soul, and the Lord are mutually distinct.

But the Māheśvaras maintain that there are five categories—effect, cause, yoga, ritual injunction, and the end of suffering—which were taught by the Lord Paśupati for the sake of liberating bound souls from their bonds.
"Paśupati is the Lord as the efficient cause";
likewise, certain others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, also maintain in some way that the Lord is the efficient cause according to their own respective systems.
To this objection, the following reply is stated: "On account of the Lord's lack of consistency" (Sūtra 2.2.37).
The Lord’s status as the cause of the world by way of being the presiding controller over primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the individual soul (*puruṣa*) is not tenable.
Why? Because of inconsistency (*asāmañjasyāt*).

What, then, is this inconsistency? For if the Lord were to differentiate living beings according to the states of low, middling, and superior, the consequence would be that He is subject to defects such as attachment and aversion; thus, like ourselves and others, He would be reduced to the status of a non-Lord. If it is argued that there is no fault because He depends upon the karma of living beings, we say no; for if karma and the Lord are respectively the impelled and the impeller, the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would result.

If it is argued that this is not so because [the cycle] is beginningless, we say no; for just as in the present time, even in past times the fault of mutual dependence remains the same, resulting in the fallacy of a "blind tradition.
Furthermore, according to the consensus of those who know the principles of logic (*nyāyavid*), defects are characterized by their capacity to impel action;
indeed, no one is ever observed to act, whether for their own sake or for the sake of others, unless impelled by such defects.
