Furthermore, it is inconsistent that every person, being motivated solely by their own self-interest, should also engage in the welfare of others; for if God were to act thus, He would be subject to the contingency of not being the Lord, because He would possess a self-interest.
Moreover, since you admit that God is a particular kind of person, and since you admit that a person is characterized by indifference (audāsīnya), there is an inconsistency.
And because a relationship [between them] is untenable.
Furthermore, this is indeed inconsistent: for there can be no Lord distinct from Pradhāna and Puruṣa who is the ruler of Pradhāna and Puruṣa without some relation.
A relation characterized by conjunction (saṃyoga) is not possible, because Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and the Lord are all-pervading and partless.
Nor is a relation characterized by inherence (samavāya) possible, because the relationship of substrate and superstrate cannot be established between them.
Nor can any other relation cognizable through an effect be postulated, because the very nature of the causal relation remains unestablished even now.
If it is asked, "How [is this so] for the proponent of Brahman?", we say no; for in his case, a relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) is logically possible.

Moreover, since the proponent of Brahman (brahmavādī) determines the nature of the cause and so forth by the authority of scripture (*āgama*), there is no necessary rule that he must accept everything exactly as it is perceived [in the world].

However, for the opponent who determines the nature of the cause and so forth by the force of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), there exists this distinction: he must accept everything exactly as it is perceived.
If it is argued that the force of scripture is equal for the opponent as well, because of the existence of a scripture composed by an omniscient being, we say no.

Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence: the establishment of omniscience would depend upon the authority of scripture, and the establishment of scripture would depend upon the authority of omniscience.
Therefore, the conception of God by the proponents of Sāṃkhya and Yoga is untenable.
In this same manner, the inconsistency of other conceptions of God held by outsiders should be applied to the relevant passages in the Vedas and the commentaries on the Sūtras, as far as possible.
And because a substratum is untenable.

For this reason as well, the Lord postulated by the logicians is untenable. For, being so postulated, He would have to set the *pradhāna* and other principles in motion by presiding over them, just as a potter works with clay and other materials.
But this is not possible.

It is not possible for the *pradhāna*—which is devoid of color, form, and other sensible qualities—to be an object of the Lord's presiding, because it differs in nature from clay and similar substances.
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of enjoyment and so forth.

It might be argued that just as a person presides over the collection of instruments— the eyes and so forth— which are themselves imperceptible and devoid of form and other qualities, so too will the Lord preside over the Pradhāna;
yet even this is not tenable,
for it is only because we observe [the results of] experience and the like that the presiding over the collection of instruments is inferred.
Furthermore, enjoyment and the like are not observed here [in the Lord];
and if the equality of the collection of instruments were admitted, it would follow that enjoyment and the like would accrue to the Lord just as they do to transmigrating beings.

Or rather, the two Sūtras may be explained otherwise: "And because of the impossibility of a substratum" (2.2.39). For this reason also, the Lord as imagined by the logicians is untenable. In the world, a king who is the lord of a kingdom is seen to possess a substratum—that is, he is embodied—and never without a substratum. Therefore, on the strength of that observed analogy, it is impossible to postulate an unseen Lord [in the manner they do]. Chapter Two. Second Section. Third Sūtra. Fourth Sūtra. Fifth Sūtra. Even for Īśvara, some kind of body as a locus for his instruments would have to be described;
yet that cannot be described, because a body exists only after the creation has occurred, and prior to creation it is impossible.
Furthermore, if he lacked a substratum, his status as a motivator would be untenable, as this is how it is observed in the world.

"Because of the mention of instruments, and because of enjoyment and so forth. Now, even if one were to imagine, in accordance with worldly observation, that the Lord also possesses a body as the locus for certain instruments, this too is not tenable;
for if He possessed a body, there would be the consequence of enjoyment and so forth, just like a transmigrating being (saṃsārī), and thus the status of the Lord as Lord would be compromised.
Either it would have an end, or it would lack omniscience.
For this reason as well, the Lord imagined by the logicians is untenable: for he is accepted by them as both omniscient and infinite;
and the *pradhāna* is accepted as infinite, as are the individual *puruṣas*, which are mutually distinct.
In that case, would the extent of the *pradhāna*, of the *puruṣas*, and of himself be delimited by the omniscient Lord, or would it not be delimited?
In either case, the defect remains attached.

How so? First, in the former alternative, because they are limited by a definite measure, the Pradhāna, the Puruṣas, and the Lord would necessarily be finite, as this is observed in the world; for whatever object in the world is limited by a definite measure, such as a jar or the like, that is seen to be finite; likewise, the triad consisting of the Pradhāna, the Puruṣas, and the Lord, being limited by a definite measure, would also be finite.
To begin with, numerical measure is delimited by the triad consisting of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara;
likewise, even the measure of their essential nature would be delimited by Īśvara, as would the great number pertaining to Puruṣas.

Consequently, among those whose extent is thus delimited, for those who are liberated from saṃsāra, their saṃsāra would have an end, and their state of being subject to saṃsāra (saṃsāritva) would also have an end.
In this way, as the others are also gradually liberated, there would be a finitude of both saṃsāra and those who transmigrate.

Furthermore, primordial matter (pradhāna), along with its modifications, is intended by the Lord as the object of his governance for the sake of the soul (puruṣārtha) and is regarded as saṃsāra; if that were to become empty, what would the Lord govern? Or, in respect to what object would his omniscience and lordship exist? Moreover, if primordial matter, the soul, and the Lord were thus finite, it would follow that they must also have a beginning.
Furthermore, if [the world] were to have a beginning and an end, it would follow that it is empty (śūnyavāda).

Now, if this fault is to be avoided and the latter alternative is accepted—namely, that the Lord does not determine the finite measure of the Pradhāna, the individual souls, and the Self—then another fault would ensue: the abandonment of the accepted doctrine of the Lord's omniscience.
Therefore, the doctrine of God as the cause, as maintained by the logicians, is also inconsistent.
Because of the impossibility of origination.
The position of those for whom God is accepted as the non-material, presiding cause alone—being merely an instrumental cause—has already been refuted.
Now, the position of those for whom God is accepted as the cause consisting of both [aspects], being both the material nature (*prakṛti*) and the presiding agent, is being refuted.
But surely, by relying on the sacred scriptures (*śruti*), such a form of God was already determined previously as having nature as His instrument?
And [the Lord] is the presiding deity;
furthermore, Smṛti that follows Śruti is authoritative. Thus ends the second chapter, beginning with the sūtra "Because of the impossibility of origination."

For what reason is this position intended to be refuted? It is said: although a portion of this kind, being common [to both sides], does not fall within the scope of disagreement, there exists another portion that is a point of contention; therefore, the undertaking [of this work] is for the purpose of refuting that.
In this regard, the Bhāgavatas consider that the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva alone, whose nature is stainless knowledge, is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*);

and he, having divided himself fourfold, is established in the form of the manifestation (*vyūha*) of Vāsudeva, the manifestation of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the manifestation of Pradyumna, and the manifestation of Aniruddha;
for Vāsudeva is called the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
He who is named Saṃkarṣaṇa is the individual soul (jīva); he who is named Pradyumna is the mind (manas); he who is named Aniruddha is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Vāsudeva is their supreme *prakṛti* (material cause), while the others, Saṃkarṣaṇa and the rest, are the effects (*kārya*).

Having worshipped this Supreme Lord, the Blessed One, for a hundred years through the practices of approaching, procuring materials, ritual sacrifice, Vedic study, and yoga, one whose afflictions are exhausted attains the Blessed One himself.

In this regard, as for that which is stated—that Nārāyaṇa, who is well-known as the Supreme Self beyond the Unmanifest, the Self of all, remains having manifested himself in manifold forms through his own self—that is not refuted, because the manifold manifestation of the Supreme Self is understood from such scriptural texts as, "He becomes onefold; He becomes threefold," and so forth. Furthermore, the worship of that Blessed Lord, characterized by approaching him and other such acts, performed incessantly with undivided attention, is also not prohibited, since devotion to the Lord is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.

Regarding what is stated again in the *Bhāṣya* on that Sūtra—that Saṃkarṣaṇa arises from Vāsudeva, Pradyumna from Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Aniruddha from Pradyumna—we reply: it is not possible for the individual soul (jīva), designated as Saṃkarṣaṇa, to originate from the Supreme Self (paramātman) designated as Vāsudeva, because that would entail defects such as impermanence.
For if the individual soul were subject to origination, defects like impermanence would necessarily follow;
consequently, its attainment of the Blessed Lord could never constitute liberation (*mokṣa*), since the effect must dissolve upon the attainment of its cause.

Furthermore, the Teacher will refute the origination of the individual soul (jīva) in the sūtra: "The soul is not [produced], because it is not mentioned [as such] in scripture and because of its eternity according to those [scriptural passages].
Therefore, this conceptualization is inconsistent.
And there can be no instrument for an agent.

For this reason as well, this conception is untenable: for in the world, an instrument such as an axe is never seen to arise from an agent such as Devadatta; yet the Bhāgavatas describe that from the agent, the individual soul (jīva) named Saṃkarṣaṇa, the instrument called the mind (manas) named Pradyumna arises, and from that which is born of the agent, the ego (ahaṃkāra) named Aniruddha arises.
And we are unable to determine this without a supporting illustration.
And we do not find any such scriptural statement.
Or, if consciousness and the rest do exist, there is no negation of them.
Furthermore, it might be argued that these [beings], Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, are not intended to be understood as being of the nature of individual souls (jīva) and so forth;
rather, all of them are accepted as being indeed Lords (īśvara), endowed with the attributes of sovereignty consisting of knowledge,
majesty, power, strength, valor, and splendor, and are thus all Vāsudevas— faultless, without a substratum, and beyond reproach.
"Therefore, this defect of the impossibility of origination as previously described does not apply.

To this it is replied: "Even so, there is no refutation of that"—meaning there is no refutation of the impossibility of origination; the intention is that this defect of the impossibility of origination indeed persists by way of another method.

How so? If, first of all, the intention is that these four Lords, Vāsudeva and the others, are mutually distinct and possess equal attributes, and that they do not possess the nature of a single self—then the postulation of multiple Lords is useless, since the purpose of a Lord is accomplished by a single Lord alone.

Furthermore, there would be an abandonment of your own established tenet (*siddhāntahāni*), because you have accepted that the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*).

Now, if your intention is that these four manifestations (*vyūha*) of the one and the same Blessed Lord possess identical attributes, even so, the impossibility of origination remains exactly as it was;
for the origination of Saṃkarṣaṇa from Vāsudeva is not possible, nor that of Pradyumna from Saṃkarṣaṇa, nor that of Aniruddha from Pradyumna, due to the absence of any distinction [in their nature].
For there must indeed be a distinction between cause and effect, as in the case of clay and a jar;
for if no distinction exists, it is not possible to conceive of one as the effect and the other as the cause.

Furthermore, the proponents of the Pañcarātra system do not admit any difference among Vāsudeva and the others—whether in him alone or among them all—based on a gradation of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth.
For indeed, all these manifestations (*vyūha*) are held to be none other than Vāsudeva himself, without distinction.

Nor do these manifestations of the Blessed One remain restricted to the number four alone, since it is understood that the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is a manifestation of the Blessed One.
And because there is a contradiction with the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya.
Furthermore, various contradictions are found in this scripture, characterized by the conceptualization of qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*),
such as the view that "knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor are qualities, and these venerable Vāsudevas are themselves the Self.

There is also a contradiction with the Vedas, as seen in the disparagement of the Vedas, such as the account that Śāṇḍilya mastered this scripture after failing to attain the highest good through the four Vedas.
Therefore, it is established that this conceptualization is inconsistent.

Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtras composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the wandering ascetic teacher (parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
Composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Śaṅkara-Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.
The third quarter of the second chapter. The third quarter.
In those various [scriptures] concerning the disciplined, scriptural accounts of origination are found to differ in their methods:
some maintain the origination of space, while others do not;
likewise, some maintain the origination of air, while others do not.
The same applies to the soul and the vital breaths;
likewise, a contradiction in sequence is observed in other scriptural passages.
And because of this contradiction, the disregard for the opposing views has been established.

In the same way, one might suspect that even our own position is to be disregarded because of internal contradictions. Therefore, another detailed exposition is undertaken for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the scriptural passages concerning creation found throughout all the Vedāntas;
and the fruit of such clarification is precisely the removal of the aforementioned doubt.
In this regard, first of all, reflection is conducted with reference to ether (*ākāśa*): "Not on account of the scriptural statement."
Does this ether have an origin, or does it not? On this point, it is first established: "Not ether, because it is not heard [in scripture]" (BS 2.3.1).
Indeed, ether is not produced. Why? Because it is not heard [so stated]; for there is no mention of its origin in the context of the account of creation.
Furthermore, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having introduced Brahman denoted by the word "Being" (sat) in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone,

one only without a second," it is taught that the origin of the three— fire, water, and earth— occurs with fire as the first among the five great elements, in the passages, "It thought," and "It emitted heat.
And scripture is our authority for the production of knowledge regarding objects beyond the reach of the senses.
Moreover, there is no scriptural statement here that establishes the origination of space;
therefore, there is no origination of space.
But it does exist.
The word "tu" (but) serves to adopt an alternative position:
let it be that there is no origination of space in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
however, it does exist in another Śruti.
For the followers of the Taittirīya recension record, having introduced [the topic] with "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," [the passage]: "From this very Self, indeed, space was produced.
Consequently, there is a contradiction between two scriptural passages—one describing creation beginning with fire, and another beginning with space.
Now, it might be argued that these two scriptural passages ought to be understood as forming a single coherent statement.
That [argument] is indeed logical, yet it cannot be accepted;

why? Because it is impossible for a single creator, mentioned only once in the phrase "It created fire" (*tat tejo 'sṛjata*), to have a connection with two things to be created, as in "It created fire" and "It created space" (*tad ākāśam asṛjata*).
But surely, even for an agent mentioned only once, a connection with two tasks is observed, just as when one says: "Having cooked the soup, he cooked the rice. (Second Chapter)
"One shall cook"—in this way, I shall connect the passage "having created that space, he created fire.
But it is not so connected; for in the Chāndogya, the fact that fire is the first-born is understood.
And in the *Taittirīyaka*, there is [the mention] of ether;

yet it is not possible for both [ether and fire] to be "first-born. By this, the contradiction with the literal sense of other scriptural passages is also explained. For even in the passage, "From that very Self, ether was produced," it is impossible for the single instance of the origin (saṃbhava) and its material cause (upādāna)—expressed by the word "from that"—to be simultaneously connected to both ether and fire. Furthermore, there is the separate scriptural statement, "From air, fire."
Regarding this very conflict, someone says: "Because a secondary sense is impossible."
There is no origination of space, precisely because it is not mentioned [in the relevant scriptural passages].
As for the other scriptural passage cited which speaks of the origination of space, it must be understood in a figurative sense;
why? Because of impossibility.
For it is not possible to conceive of the origination of space as long as those who follow the view of the venerable Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda) remain alive;
for they deny the origination of space on the grounds that the causal totality is impossible,
since everything that originates indeed originates from inherent, non-inherent, and instrumental causes.
Furthermore, for a substance to arise, multiple substances of the same genus must exist as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*);
however, there exists no such collection of multiple substances of the same genus that could serve as the originator of ether.

For ether would only be produced if there were an inherent cause and a conjunction with it serving as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). But since neither of these is present, ether cannot be produced.

But because that [effect] is absent, the instrumental cause—which functions to favor it—is utterly remote in the case of space. Furthermore, regarding things that possess an origin, such as fire and so forth, a distinction between their prior and subsequent states is conceivable: it is possible to say that before its origin the effect, such as light, did not exist, and after it exists;
however, no such distinction can be conceived for space between its prior and subsequent states.

For how can it be determined that before creation there was something without space, without cavities, and without openings? Furthermore, because of its dissimilarity to earth and other elements—characterized by all-pervasiveness and so forth—the non-produced nature of space is established.

Therefore, just as in common worldly usage expressions such as "make space" or "space has been produced" are figurative, and just as for the single entity that is space there is figurative designation of distinctions such as "the space within a jar," "the space within a water-pot," or "the space within a house," so too in the Veda we find the expression: "They should immolate the wild animals in spaces."
In this same way, the scriptural statement regarding origination is also to be understood as figurative.
And because of the word "how."
Furthermore, the word "indeed" (khalu) in the passage also indicates the non-born nature of space, since it says, "And air and the intermediate region—this is immortal";
for the origination of that which is immortal is not possible.

Moreover, by comparing Brahman with space through the two attributes of omnipresence and eternity in the phrase "and like space, all-pervading and eternal," [the text] implies that those two attributes belong to space as well.

Furthermore, the arising of such a thing is not possible. [This is] from the second chapter of the *Sūtra*: "As this space is infinite, so the Self is to be known as infinite," and also, "Brahman has space as its body; space is the Self."
For if space were something subject to origination, it could not serve as a qualification of Brahman, just as the color blue qualifies a lotus;
therefore, it is understood that Brahman is eternal and common to space.
And it may belong to one [thing] alone, as in the case of the word "Brahman."
This subsequent aphorism is based on reasoning (*tapas*).
It might be argued:

"How is it possible for the single word *saṃbhūta*—occurring within this context beginning with 'From that very Self, space was produced' (*ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*)—to have its primary sense apply to the subsequent elements such as fire (*tejas*) and so forth, while having a secondary sense in the case of space?"
To this, the following is said: Even for a single word such as *saṃbhūta*, there may be both figurative and primary usage depending on the specific context, just like the word *brahman*.

Just as in the case of the single word *brahman*, within the section beginning with "Desire to know Brahman" and "Austerity is Brahman," there is figurative usage with respect to food and so forth, while its usage is primary with respect to bliss.
Just as the word "Brahman" is used figuratively for austerity—the means of attaining the knowledge of Brahman—though it applies directly to the Brahman that is to be known, so it is here.
But how, if the ether is non-originated, is this proposition "one only, without a second" justified? Is it not the case that with the ether as a second entity, Brahman would become "with-a-second"?
And how could everything be known when Brahman alone is known? To this it is replied: first, the term "one only" is appropriate in view of its own effects.

Just as in the world, someone might say after observing on the previous day the clay, staff, wheel, and so forth in a potter’s workshop, and then observing on the following day various kinds of unbaked vessels spread out: "Only the clay alone existed on the previous day. By that restriction, he would intend to imply that the entire collection of effects made of clay did not exist on the previous day, but not that the staff, the wheel, and so forth did not exist; in the same way, the scriptural statement of non-duality excludes another presiding agent. Just as a potter is seen to be the presiding agent of clay, which is the material cause of the vessels, there is no other presiding agent for Brahman, which is the material cause of the universe.
Nor does it follow that Brahman becomes "accompanied by a second" merely because of space;
for diversity is caused by a difference in defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

And prior to creation, there is no difference in defining characteristics between Brahman and space, because they are intermingled like milk and water, owing to the commonality of attributes such as all-pervasiveness and incorporeality.

At the time of creation, however, Brahman strives to produce the world, whereas the ether remains motionless; by this, their difference is determined. Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as "Brahman has the ether for its body," the establishment of the metaphorical identification of Brahman and the ether is achieved.
For this very reason, the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of Brahman is established.

Moreover, every effect that arises does so in a space and time not distinct from space itself, and space exists in a space and time not distinct from Brahman; therefore, when Brahman and its effects are known, space is necessarily known along with them—just as when a few drops of water are poured into a jar filled with milk, they are grasped by the very act of grasping the milk; for once the milk is grasped, no separate grasping of the drops remains.
Thus, because it does not exist in a space or time distinct from Brahman and its effects, the ether is indeed grasped by the grasping of Brahman;
therefore, the scriptural mention of the origin of the ether is established.
This being the case, the following is said: Chapter Two:
There would be a loss of the initial proposition because there is no distinction from the words.

"The unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3); "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6); "O Venerable Sir, when what is known, does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3); and "There is no knowledge greater than this" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1)—such a proposition is recognized in every Vedānta text. For that proposition to be established and not contradicted, there must be non-difference between the entire aggregate of things and Brahman, which is the object to be known.
For if there were indeed a difference [between the cause and its effects], this proposition—that by the knowledge of one, everything is known—would be undermined.
And that non-difference is established only if the entire aggregate of things arises from the one Brahman.
Furthermore, from the words of scripture, the establishment of the proposition is understood precisely through the principle of the non-difference of the effect from its material cause.

For instance: having made the proposition, "By which the unheard becomes heard," this very proposition is supported by examples such as clay, which are intended to demonstrate the non-difference between cause and effect.

And for the very purpose of establishing that [identity], the subsequent portion of the text—beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," "It thought," and "It emitted heat"—first demonstrates the entire range of effects as belonging to Brahman, and then demonstrates their non-difference from it, starting from "All this has that as its self" up until the end of the chapter. Now, if the ether were not an effect of Brahman, then the ether would not be understood when Brahman is understood;
consequently, there would be a failure of the initial proposition.
And it is not proper to render the Veda invalid on account of such a failure of the proposition.

For indeed, in every Vedānta text, various words with their respective illustrations make known that very same proposition: "All this is what this Self is," "Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in front," and so forth;
therefore, like fire and other elements, the ether (ākāśa) also originates.

As for the claim that ether is not produced because it is not mentioned [in the Chāndogya], that is incorrect, because another scriptural passage concerning the production of ether has been shown: "From this very Self, ether was produced.
True, it has been shown; however, it contradicts another scriptural passage, namely, "It created fire.
No, for all the scriptures form a single coherent whole.

Let there be syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) for those things that are not contradictory; but here, contradiction has been stated—because it is impossible for a creator, mentioned only once, to be connected with two things to be created, and because it is impossible for both [fire and air] to be the first-born, and because an alternative (*vikalpa*) is impossible. This is not a fault, because in the Taittirīyaka, the creation of fire is heard as being the third: "From this very Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire.
For this scriptural statement cannot be interpreted otherwise.
However, the *Chāndogya* Śruti can be interpreted as follows: having created space and air, [it] says, "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.3.1).

For this Śruti, being primarily concerned with the production of fire, cannot preclude the origination of space established by another Śruti, since it is impossible for a single sentence to have two distinct functions.

Even though the Creator is one, he may create many things to be created in succession; thus, since the assumption of a single coherent statement is possible, the scriptural texts cannot be rejected on the grounds of contradictory meaning. Nor do we intend to attribute a connection with two different objects of creation to the Creator mentioned only once, for other objects of creation are included by virtue of other scriptural passages.

And just as in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman, for from it [are born], by it [they live], and into it [they enter]" (*tajjalān*), the fact that the entire multitude of things is directly heard to be born from Brahman does not preclude the order of creation beginning with fire (*tejas*) prescribed in another section; so too, the fact that fire is heard to be born from Brahman cannot preclude the order of creation beginning with ether (*nabhas*) prescribed in another scriptural text.
But is it not the case that this sentence is intended to enjoin tranquility, since the scripture says, "Because it is *tajjalān*, one should meditate upon it with a tranquil mind"?
This is not a statement regarding creation.
Therefore, this [text] ought not to conform to the sequence established in another passage; "That [Being] created fire" is a statement regarding creation;
consequently, the sequence must be accepted here exactly as it is heard in the text.
This is not so;

for the entity "ether" (viyat), which is well-established in another scriptural passage, need not be abandoned merely to conform to the priority of fire, since sequence is a property of the entities themselves.
Moreover, in the phrase "It created fire," there is no word here that denotes a sequence.

The sequence, however, is understood from the sense of the context; and that is set aside by the sequence well-known from another scriptural text, namely "From air, fire. As for the alternatives of option or combination regarding ether and fire being produced first, these are refuted by the impossibility [of such a sequence] and by the non-acceptance [of those views].
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the two scriptural passages.

Moreover, in the Chāndogya, in order to support the proposition heard at the beginning of the section—"By which the unheard becomes heard"—the ether (*viyat*), although not explicitly mentioned there, must nevertheless be included among the things that originate;
how much more so, then, should the ether, which is explicitly mentioned in the Taittirīyaka, be accepted?

As for what was said—that because space is not distinct in place or time from anything else, it is already known along with Brahman and its effects, and therefore the initial proposition is not undermined, nor does there arise a contradiction with the scriptural text "one only, without a second," since the non-difference between Brahman and space is established like that of milk and water—[we reply as follows]: This is not so. Because space is eternal and all-pervading, it cannot be produced by Brahman. Furthermore, it is impossible for it to be known through the knowledge of Brahman, since it is distinct from Brahman. Moreover, the scriptural text "one only, without a second" would be contradicted, because space exists as a separate entity. Nor can it be argued that space is non-different from Brahman like milk and water; for while milk and water, being both material (mūrta), may indeed be mixed and thus indistinguishable, space and Brahman cannot be so, as they are of entirely different natures—one being material and the other immaterial (amūrta). Therefore, the objection remains valid. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the "ether within the heart" (*dahara-ākāśa*), which is clearly distinct from the external ether. Thus, the ether is not known through the knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, the initial proposition is indeed abandoned, and the scriptural text "one only, without a second" is contradicted. This is because the ether is eternal, all-pervading, and distinct from Brahman. Therefore, the ether is not included within the knowledge of Brahman. As for the argument regarding milk and water, that is untenable; for although milk and water are both material and thus capable of being mixed, space and Brahman are not, owing to their differing natures. Hence, the ether is not known through the knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, the initial proposition is lost, and the scriptural text "one only, without a second" is contradicted.
