This is because the ether is eternal, all-pervading, and distinct from Brahman. Therefore, the ether is not included within the knowledge of Brahman. As for the argument regarding milk and water, that is untenable; for although milk and water are both material and thus capable of being mixed, space and Brahman are not, owing to their differing natures. Hence, the ether is not known through the knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, the initial proposition is lost, and the scriptural text "one only, without a second" is contradicted. This is because the ether is eternal, all-pervading, and distinct from Brahman. Therefore, the ether is not included within the knowledge of Brahman. As for the argument regarding milk and water, that is untenable; for although milk and water are both material and thus capable of being mixed, space and Brahman are not, owing to their differing natures. Hence, the ether is not known through the knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, the initial proposition is lost, and the scriptural text "one only, without a second" is contradicted. This is because the ether is eternal, all-pervading,
To this it is replied: this "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is not to be understood according to the analogy of milk and water;

for, because of the employment of examples such as clay and so forth, it is understood that this "knowledge of all" is to be understood precisely according to the principle of the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*).
Moreover, if the "knowledge of all" were conceived according to the analogy of milk and water, it would not constitute perfect knowledge.
For water perceived through the cognition of milk does not possess the status of being grasped by correct knowledge;
nor is it possible for the Veda to determine its meaning through illusion, falsehood, deception, and the like, as is the case with human beings;
furthermore, this scriptural statement "one only, without a second," which is definitive in its expression, would be contradicted if it were interpreted according to the analogy of milk and water.

Nor is it logical to maintain that this cognition of the non-duality of all things—which has as its object only a single part of reality—is merely with respect to its own specific effect; for such a possibility exists even in the case of clay and other substances, and thus it would not need to be presented as something unprecedented, as in the passage beginning: "O Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are so conceited, thinking yourself well-versed in the scriptures and arrogant, have you ever asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard? and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that this "all-knowing" is presented as having all things as its object precisely with respect to the fact that everything is an effect of Brahman.

As for what was further stated—that the scriptural mention of the origin of space is figurative because it is impossible—we reply: "But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world."
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of impossibility.
Indeed, no suspicion of impossibility should be raised regarding the origin of space;

because whatever variety of modifications is seen in the world—whether it be jars, pots, and water-pots, or bracelets, armlets, and earrings, or needles, arrows, and swords—all such differentiation is observed to be limited to that very extent.
However, nothing that is unmodified is ever perceived as distinct from anything else;
yet the distinction of space from earth and the other elements is clearly understood. Therefore, space too must be a modification.
By this, the fact that space, time, mind, atoms, and so forth are effects is explained.
Now, one might object: since the Self is also distinct from ether and the other elements, it too must be an effect, like a jar or similar objects.
This is not so, because of the scriptural text: "From the Self, ether was produced."
For if the Self were also an effect, then since nothing else beyond it is heard of in scripture, everything beginning with space would consist of effects, and the Self itself would be an effect;

in that case, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would follow as a consequence. Furthermore, because it is the Self, the suspicion of its being negated is untenable; for the Self is not adventitious to anyone, since it is self-established.
For the self is not established by depending upon a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) directed toward itself;
rather, it is perception and the other means of valid cognition that are employed for the sake of establishing objects of knowledge (prameya) that are themselves unestablished.
Indeed, no one accepts that entities such as space are established in themselves independently of the means of valid cognition.

The self, however, being the substratum for the conventional usage of the means of knowledge and so forth, is established even prior to that conventional usage of the means of knowledge and so forth; and the negation of such a [self] is not possible,
for it is only an adventitious thing that can be negated, not one's own essential nature.
For that which is the negator is itself its own essential nature;
indeed, the heat of fire is not negated by the fire itself.

Likewise, [one thinks]: "I alone know the present object now; I alone have known the past and the more distant past; I alone shall know the future and the more distant future. Thus, although the object of knowledge changes through its states of past, future, and present, there is no change in the knower, because its nature is eternally present.
Likewise, even when the body is reduced to ashes, there is no annihilation of the self;
nor is it possible to conceive of it as having a nature other than its present nature.
Thus, because its nature is irrefutable, the self is non-produced (*akārya*), whereas space (*ākāśa*) is produced (*kārya*).

As for what was stated—that there is no causal substance of the same class as space—that is replied to as follows: there is no such restrictive rule that [an effect] must originate only from a cause of the same class, and not from one of a different class;
for there is no homogeneity between the threads and their conjunctions, since they are admitted to be of the nature of substance and quality respectively.
Furthermore, there is no rule that even non-inherent causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), such as the shuttle and the loom, must belong to the same genus.
It might be argued that the acceptance of being of the same genus applies only to the case of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and not to other types of causes;
however, that too is inconclusive.
It is observed that a single rope is produced from various kinds of materials such as threads and cow-hair;
likewise, they weave variegated blankets from threads, wool, and so forth.

Furthermore, if "being of the same genus" were to be postulated merely with respect to the quality of being a substance (*dravyatva*) or being an entity (*sattva*), then the restrictive rule would be purposeless, because everything would be of the same genus as everything else.

Nor is there a fixed rule that [action] must begin from multiple [causes] alone, nor that it must begin from a single [cause] alone; for it is accepted that atoms and the mind initiate their first action individually.
Indeed, it is maintained that each individual atom and the mind initiates its first action by itself, and not by combining with other substances.
If it is argued that there is a rule that only a substance initiates [another] substance through multiple initiators, we say no;
for we accept the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
This rule would hold if one were to admit that a substance, assisted by conjunction, is the initiator of another distinct substance.

That very substance, however, undergoing a different state characterized by specific qualities, is accepted as being called the "effect"; and that [substance] transforms in some cases as a plurality, such as clay or seeds into the form of sprouts and so forth,
and in other cases it transforms as a unity, such as milk into the form of curd and so forth.
There is no decree from a Lord that a single cause produces only a manifold effect.

Therefore, based on the authority of the Śruti, it is determined that the world was produced from the one Brahman through the sequential emergence of the great elements, beginning with ether; as it has been said: "If it be argued that [the world] is not [produced by Brahman] because we observe the need for preparatory effort, we say no, for it is like milk."
As for what was stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya—that no distinction can be conceived between the prior and subsequent states regarding the origin of space—that is incorrect.
For that very distinction by which space is now determined to have its own nature as something distinct from earth and the other elements did not exist prior to their origin; this is understood.

And just as Brahman does not possess the nature of earth and the other elements such as grossness, on account of scriptural texts like "neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8), so too it is understood from scripture that [Brahman] does not possess the nature of space, being "without space" (anākāśa).

Therefore, it is established that prior to its production there was no space (*ākāśa*). As for the argument that space is unproduced because it differs in nature from earth and the other elements, that too is incorrect; for when there is a contradiction with scripture, an inference regarding the impossibility of production must be considered fallacious, especially since an inference for production has already been demonstrated.
Furthermore, such formal arguments as "space is non-eternal, because it is the substratum of non-eternal qualities, like a jar," and so forth, are possible.
If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to the Self (ātman), we say no;

for, from the perspective of the follower of the Upaniṣads, it is not established that the Self is the substratum of non-eternal qualities; furthermore, properties such as omnipresence (vibhutva) and so forth are unestablished for one who maintains the origination of space (ākāśa).

As for what was said regarding the phrase "and from the word," therein the scriptural mention of immortality (*amṛtatva*) should be understood as being like [the statement] "the gods are immortal" (*amṛtā divaukasaḥ*), since its origination and dissolution have already been established.

Furthermore, the comparison with space in the passage "and it is all-pervading and eternal like space" is made because of its well-known greatness, in order to indicate its unsurpassed magnitude. Thus ends the second chapter.

It is for the sake of reality, not for the sake of equality with space; just as when it is said, "The sun runs like an arrow," this is said for the sake of denoting rapid motion and not for the sake of equality of speed with an arrow, so it is here.
By this, the scriptural comparison regarding infinity is explained.

Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as "Greater than space," the fact that space has a smaller magnitude than Brahman is established; and the passage "There is no likeness of Him" shows that Brahman is beyond all comparison.
And by the statement, "Everything else is afflicted," [the scripture] shows that things other than Brahman, such as ether and the rest, are subject to suffering.

As for the argument that the scriptural mention of the birth of ether must be taken in a figurative sense—just as the word "Brahman" is used figuratively in reference to austerity—that has been refuted by both the direct scriptural statement regarding the origin of ether and by inference.
Therefore, it is established that ether is an effect.
By this, Mātariśvan is explained.
This is an extended application (*atideśa*).
By this same explanation regarding ether (*viyat*), air (*mātariśvan*)—the wind which has ether as its substratum—is also explained.
There too, these same positions should be arranged for air as appropriate: "Air is not produced," according to the section concerning the Chandogas.

One position is that [the origin of air] is not mentioned in the section dealing with origination; however, there is another position that for the Taittirīyas, there is indeed a mention in the section on origination, namely, "From space, air" (*ākāśādvāyuḥ*).
Thus, when there is a contradiction between two scriptural passages, the other intention is that the scriptural statement regarding the origin of air is figurative because of its impossibility.
And this impossibility follows from the prohibition of setting in the text, "This deity, namely air, never sets," and from the hearing of attributes such as immortality.

Because it does not contradict the initial proposition and because it accepts the division [of elements] up to the point of transformation, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "wind is produced.
The denial of its setting is relative, pertaining to the sphere of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), since, like fire and the other elements, wind does not undergo setting.
Furthermore, the scriptural mention of immortality and so forth has already been refuted.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since air and ether are similar in that one is mentioned and the other is not mentioned in the section on their origination, let there be a single adhikaraṇa (topic) for both; what is the need for this extension (atideśa) when there is no difference? To this it is replied: It is true that this is so; nevertheless, this extension is made to remove doubts caused merely by words in those of dull intellect. For in the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other such texts, because air is heard of as being highly exalted as an object of meditation, and because of the prohibition of its setting [into dissolution] and so forth, the doubt might arise in someone that it is eternal.
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is logically untenable.
Having heard of the production of space and air, even though their birth is otherwise inconceivable, someone might think that even Brahman could have an origin from somewhere; likewise,
having heard of the production of subsequent elements from space and the rest— which are themselves modifications despite being impossible [otherwise]—
someone might think that even space has its origin from Brahman, which is itself a modification.
To remove that doubt, this Sūtra states: "But there is no possibility [of origin].
Indeed, one should not suspect the origin—that is, the birth—of Brahman, whose nature is Being, from anything else.
Why? Because it is logically untenable.
Brahman is indeed pure Being (*sanmātra*);

its origination from that very same pure Being is not possible, because if there were no difference (*atiśaya*), the relationship between material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) would be untenable.

Nor can it originate from a particular instance of Being (*sad-viśeṣa*), because that would contradict what is observed: we see particulars, such as jars, originating from a general substance like clay, but never a general substance originating from particulars. *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, Second Chapter.
Nor can it arise from the non-existent, because that would entail being devoid of self-nature;
for there is the scriptural objection: "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?
Furthermore, the passage, "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and of him there is no progenitor nor any lord," precludes the existence of a progenitor for Brahman.
Furthermore, the re-emergence of ether and air has been demonstrated, whereas such re-emergence does not exist for Brahman; this constitutes the difference.

Nor can Brahman be subject to modification simply because one modification is seen to arise from another modification, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if a fundamental material cause (*mūlaprakṛti*) were not admitted.
That which is admitted as the fundamental material cause is precisely what we call Brahman; thus, there is no contradiction.
From that, likewise, fire.
In the Chāndogya, it is taught that fire has Being (sat) as its root; however, in the Taittirīyaka, it is taught that it has air (vāyu) as its root.
Since there is thus a conflict between the scriptural statements regarding the source of fire, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that fire has Brahman as its source.
Why? Because of the [scriptural] evidence.
Because of the teaching beginning with "Existence alone" and continuing with "It created fire," because the promise of universal knowledge is possible only if everything originates from Brahman,
and because of the scriptural statement "That [Brahman] is its origin, its dissolution, and its support" which makes no distinction.

And because another scriptural passage, beginning with "From this [Brahman] is born Prāṇa," teaches that everything without exception is born from Brahman; and also in the Taittirīyaka: "Having performed austerity, he created all this. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda).
Because of the scriptural statement "whatever there is" (*yad idaṃ kiṃca*), which is heard without qualification;

therefore, the instruction regarding the sequence—"from air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*)—should be understood as meaning that fire was produced immediately after air. This being the position reached, it is replied: fire is born from Mātariśvan (the wind).
Why? Because the scripture says, "from air, fire."
If fire were produced directly from Brahman without any intermediate step, or if it were not produced from air, then this scriptural statement, "From air, fire," would be contradicted.
Now, it was argued that this [statement] might be intended to indicate a sequence;

we say: no. Because in the preceding passage, "From this very Self, space was produced," the Self is designated by the fifth case (the ablative) as the source of production (*saṃbhava*), and because that same verb of production (*saṃbhavati*) is the subject under discussion here, and because further on, within that same context, the fifth case is seen as an ablative of source in the phrase "From earth, plants," it is understood that "From air, fire" is likewise the fifth case used in the sense of an ablative of source.

Moreover, while it might be assumed that the connection with the secondary word (upapada) is "fire was produced from above the wind," the established connection between the causal factor and its effect is "fire was produced from the wind.

Therefore, this scriptural passage makes known that fire has the wind as its source. But surely another scriptural passage also makes known that fire has Brahman as its source: "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3)?
No, for there is no contradiction even if it arises through a succession;

for even when it is conceived that, having created ether and air, Brahman—having assumed the state of air—created fire, the fact that fire is born from Brahman is not contradicted, just as in the case of "the curd of that [milk]," "the whey of that [curd]," "the *āmikṣā* of that [whey]," and so forth. (Brahma-sūtra, Second Chapter).
And it shows that Brahman exists in the form of its own modification: "It made itself by itself" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).

Likewise, there is a traditional remembrance (smṛti) concerning the Lord: following the sequence beginning with "Intellect, knowledge, non-delusion," it says, "The various states of beings arise from Me alone.

Although intellect and the other qualities are seen to arise directly from their own respective causes, nevertheless, the entire collection of entities is dependent upon the Lord, either directly or through a mediated succession.

By this, those scriptural passages teaching non-sequential creation are explained, because they are entirely consistent [with the doctrine of simultaneous creation], whereas those teaching sequential creation cannot be otherwise accounted for.
Furthermore, the initial proposition (pratijñā) requires only that the effect be a modification of Being, not that it be produced immediately [after its cause]; thus, there is no contradiction.
The waters.
Therefore, the phrase "for thus it says" continues [from the previous context]: water is born from fire. Why? Because thus it says, "It created water," and "From fire, indeed, water was born."
Since there is no doubt when a statement is present,
having explained the creation of fire, and intending to explain the creation of earth, [the author] composed the aphorism "Water" (*āpaḥ*), thinking that he would include water within it.
The instrument [of perception].
On account of earth, the context, form, and other words.
It is heard in scripture: "Those waters thought, 'May we become many, may we procreate,' and they emitted food.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: by this word "food" (anna), is something edible such as rice, barley, and so forth, or cooked rice and the like, intended; or rather, is it the earth?
On this point, the prima facie view is that either rice, barley, and so on, or cooked rice and the like, should be understood.
For the word "food" (anna) is well-known in common usage to refer to that;

the remainder of the passage also supports this meaning: "Therefore, wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant. Indeed, it is rice, barley, and so forth that become abundant when it rains, not the earth itself.
[The opponent's] argument: This being the case, we reply that it is the earth itself which is intended by the word "food" as that which is produced from water.
Why? Because of the context, because of the form, and because of another scriptural statement.
To begin with, the context concerns the great elements, as seen in the passages, "It emitted heat" and "It emitted water.
In that context, it is not logical to suddenly take up rice and other grains while bypassing the earth, the great element which follows in the sequence.
Furthermore, the description in the complementary passage, "That which is black is of the earth," is seen to be consistent with the earth.
For there is no rule of blackness regarding food such as boiled rice that is to be consumed, nor is there one for rice and the like.
[Objection: But even for earth, there is certainly no rule of blackness, since fields are seen to be white as milk and red as charcoal. [Reply:
This is not a fault, because [the rule] depends on the predominance [of a certain color].

For the color of the earth is predominantly black, not so its white or red aspects; even the authors of the Purāṇas teach that the shadow of the earth is night, and since that has a black appearance, it is concluded that the color of the earth is black.
Another scriptural passage dealing with the same subject also occurs: "The waters became the earth," and "That which was the froth of the waters solidified and became the earth.
Furthermore, it shows the production of rice and other crops from the earth: "From the earth, plants; from plants, food.

Since there are such passages establishing the earth as the subject matter and so forth, how can rice and the like be understood [as the source]? Even common usage is set aside by these very considerations of subject matter and the rest.

It should also be understood that the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*)—by means of the fact that food and the like consist of earth—indicates that the earth alone is the source and origin of water.
Therefore, this "Annamaya" [self] is the earth.
But he [the individual soul] [arises] from that very meditation, on account of its characteristic mark.

Do these elements, beginning with space (*viyat*), create their own modifications by themselves, or does the Supreme Lord alone, abiding in those respective forms and meditating upon them, create each modification through that meditation? This is the section [of inquiry]. When a doubt arises, the initial position is that they create by themselves;
why? Because of the scriptural hearing of their independence, such as: "From space, air; from air, fire," and so forth.

But surely, the independent activity of insentient things has been refuted; this is not a fault, because there is scriptural testimony that even the elements possess sentience, as in the passages: "That fire thought" and "Those waters thought."
This being the position reached, it is replied: It is that very Supreme Lord who, abiding in various forms and intending [to create], emits those respective modifications.
Why? Because of the characteristic marks of Him.

For scripture—such as "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within"—shows the activity of the elements only when they are presided over by a ruler.

Likewise, having introduced the passage, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and then stating, "He became the manifest (san) and the unmanifest (tyat); He made Himself by Himself," the text shows that this very Being possesses the state of being the Self of all.

As for the mention of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) in relation to water and fire, that must be understood as occurring solely through the influence of the entry of the Supreme Lord, because of the prohibition of any other seer in the text, "There is no other seer but He," and because the Being who sees is the subject under discussion in the passage, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"
But by the reverse order, the sequence from this [point] is established as well.
Now, the sequence of the origin of the elements has been considered;
now, the sequence of their dissolution is being considered: does dissolution occur in an indefinite order, or in the same order as their origin, or in the reverse order, that is, contrary to that?
And all three [orders] are subjects for deliberation regarding origin and persistence.
The origin and dissolution of beings are heard in scripture to be dependent upon Brahman: "From which indeed these beings are born;
by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they pass away."

In this regard, the initial position is that there is no fixed rule, because there is no specific distinction [stated in scripture]; or rather, since the order of origination is heard in scripture, that same order should apply to dissolution as well,
for it too stands in need of an order.

This being the case, we reply: "But the order of dissolution is the reverse [of the order of origination]; therefore, it must be so, because of the order of origination. For it is observed in the world that one descends by a sequence opposite to the sequence by which one ascended a staircase;

moreover, it is seen that things such as jars and bowls produced from clay revert to the state of clay at the time of their destruction, and other things such as snow and hail produced from water revert to the state of water.

Therefore, this is logically established: that the earth, having arisen from water, should merge into water upon the passing of its period of duration; and water, having arisen from fire, should merge into fire.

In this manner, by merging successively into causes that are subtler and more subtle, and more immediate and more immediate still, it should be understood that the entire aggregate of effects merges into the ultimate cause, which is Brahman, the supreme and most subtle.
For it is not logical that the dissolution of an effect into its cause’s cause should occur by bypassing its own immediate cause.

Even in the *Smṛti*, the order of dissolution is shown to be precisely the reverse of the order of origination; for instance, in such passages as: "O divine sage, the earth, the support of the world, dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air," and so forth.
The stage of origination (utpatti-krama), however, because it is taught specifically in relation to origination, cannot pertain to dissolution (apyaya);

nor is it required by dissolution, due to its inherent unsuitability. For when the effect is being produced, the dissolution of the cause is not logical, since it is impossible for the effect to persist once the cause has dissolved.
But when the effect has perished, it is logical that the cause remains, because this is observed to be the case with clay and other such substances.

In the *Pasta-mens* commentary on the Sūtra-bhāṣya, [it is argued]: "If it be said that between [the soul, the senses, and the elements] there are consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*) in succession because of their respective indicative marks, we say no, because there is no distinction."
[Objection: An intermediate instrument [is required].
It has been stated that the origination and dissolution of the elements occur through direct and inverse sequences;
it has also been stated that origination begins with the Self and dissolution ends with the Self.

The existence of the mind (*manas*) endowed with the senses and of the intellect (*buddhi*) is well-established by both Śruti and Smṛti through such indicative marks as: "Know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind indeed the reins; they call the senses the horses.

Furthermore, since it is accepted that the entire aggregate of things originates from Brahman, the successive origination and dissolution of those two [the mind and the intellect] must also be understood as occurring within some intermediate stage.

Furthermore, in the Atharvaṇa, within the section on origination, the organs are enumerated between the elements and the Self: "From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses;
[and] space, air, light, water, and the earth, which supports all.
If it be argued that this entails a contradiction of the previously stated order of the origination and dissolution of the elements, we say: no.

Because there is no distinction: if the organs are indeed composed of the elements (*bhautika*), then their origin and dissolution occur precisely through the origin and dissolution of the elements; thus, no other sequence need be sought for them.

Furthermore, there is evidence for the elemental nature of the organs in such scriptural passages as, "For the mind, my dear, consists of food (*annamaya*); breath consists of water (*āpomaya*); speech consists of fire (*tejomayī*)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).

There is also a designation [of the organs] alongside the elements, as in the case of the expression "the Brahmins and the wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇa-parivrājaka-sūtra*). Chapter Two. Second Section.
It must be understood according to reason.

Even if the instruments (karaṇas) are non-material, nevertheless the order of the origin of the elements is not differentiated by the instruments—neither in the sense that the instruments arise first and the elements last, nor that the elements arise first and the instruments last;
for in the Atharvaṇa [text], there is merely a sequence of enumeration regarding the instruments and the elements, but the order of their actual origination is not stated therein.

Likewise, elsewhere as well, the sequence of the instruments (karaṇa) is recorded separately from the sequence of the elements (bhūta), starting with: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this [world]. He looked upon himself; he created mind; that [mind] alone existed. It looked upon itself; it created speech," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no subversion of the sequence of the origination of the elements.
But that designation [of the Self] as dependent on the moving and the non-moving is figurative, because it exists only when those [bodies] exist.

Someone might have the misconception that there is indeed origination and dissolution even for the individual soul (jīva), on account of worldly designations such as "Devadatta was born" and "Devadatta died," and because of the injunctions regarding the moving and non-moving worlds and the performance of sacraments such as the birth-rite (jātakarman).
We dispel this reliance [on such arguments].
There is no origination or dissolution of the individual soul; this is the established position.
[The soul] exists, because the connection between the scripture and its fruit is logically possible;

for if the individual soul were to perish along with the body, then the injunctions and prohibitions intended for the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired in another body would be purposeless.

Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "Verily, this [body] dies when abandoned by the living soul; the living soul does not die. But was it not shown that the worldly designation of birth and death applies to the living soul?
It has been shown that this is true;
however, this designation of birth and death for the individual soul (jīva) is figurative (bhākta).
But what is the basis for this primary [usage], in relation to which this [usage regarding the soul] is figurative? It is said: it rests upon the moving and the unmoving (carācara-vyapāśrayaḥ).
The terms "birth" and "death" refer to the stationary and moving bodies;
for it is stationary and moving beings that are born and die.

Therefore, while the terms "birth" and "death" are primary with respect to those [bodies], they are used figuratively with respect to the individual self (jīvātman) residing therein, because [the self] is affected by the existence of those [bodies]. For the terms "birth" and "death" apply when there is the manifestation and disappearance of the body, not when these do not exist.
For nowhere else than in connection with a body is the individual soul (jīva) observed by anyone to be born or dead;

and the scriptural passage, "This person, indeed, when being born, attains a body; when departing, he dies," shows that the terms "birth" and "death" have as their sole cause the conjunction with and separation from the body.
Furthermore, the injunctions for birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and so forth must be understood as referring only to the manifestation of the body, since there is no manifestation of the soul.
Whether or not the soul has an origin from the Supreme Self, as in the case of ether and the other elements, will be stated in the subsequent sūtra;
by this present sūtra, however, he has declared that the gross birth and dissolution of the soul, which depend upon the body, do not exist.
And because the Self is eternal, it is distinct from those [elements].
There exists a self called the *jīva*, the presiding lord over the cage of the body and senses, who is connected to the fruits of action; regarding this self,
there is a doubt arising from conflicting scriptural statements as to whether it is produced from Brahman like ether and other elements, or whether, like Brahman itself, it is not produced at all.

In some scriptural passages, the origin of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) from the supreme Brahman is recorded through illustrations such as sparks of fire and the like; however, in others, it is understood that the supreme Brahman itself, remaining unmodified, assumes the state of an individual soul by entering into its effects, and no origination is recorded there.
In this regard, it is first established that the individual soul (jīva) arises [from Brahman];
why? Precisely because of the non-contradiction of the initial proposition.

The proposition, "When one is known, all this is known," would not be contradicted if the entire multitude of things has its origin in Brahman; however, if the individual soul were a different entity, this proposition would be contradicted.

Nor can it be understood that the unmodified Supreme Self alone is the individual soul (jīva), because of the difference in their characteristics; for the Supreme Self possesses attributes such as being free from sin and so forth, whereas the individual soul possesses the opposite characteristics.

Furthermore, its nature as a modification is established by the fact of its division; for whatever is divided from space and so forth is all a modification, and the origination of that space and so forth has been established.

The individual soul (*jīvātman*) as well—possessing merit and demerit, joined with pleasure and pain, and distributed within each body—must also have its origin at the time of the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Furthermore, Śruti teaches the separate creation of the enjoyers, the individual souls, in the passage: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths (*prāṇa*), etc., proceed," thus teaching the creation of the entire class of effects beginning with the vital breaths; and [elsewhere]: "All these selves proceed forth. [And: "As from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of the same nature arise..."

In the commentary on that Sūtra, it is stated: "Thus, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also merge. Here, the origination and dissolution of the individual selves (jīvātman) are declared, because of the statement regarding their having a similar nature—for the individual selves indeed possess a nature similar to the Supreme Self due to their connection with consciousness.

Furthermore, the non-mention of something in one place cannot preclude what is heard elsewhere, since additional, non-contradictory matter found in another scriptural passage must be integrated everywhere.

The scriptural mention of "entering" must also, this being the case, be explained as merely the attainment of a state of modification, just like [the statement] "He made himself his own self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1) and others.
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is produced.
This being the case, we reply: the individual soul (jīva) is not produced.
Why? Because it is not so heard;
for there is no mention of its production in numerous passages within the context of [theories concerning] origin.
[Objection: But was it not said that the non-hearing [of something] in one place does not preclude its being heard elsewhere?
[Reply: True, it was so said; however, we maintain that its very origination is impossible.

Why? Because of its eternity, and by the word "and" (*ca*), because of its being unborn (*aja*) and so forth. For its eternity is understood from the scriptures (*śruti*); likewise, its being unborn, its immutability, and the fact that it exists as the individual self (*jīvātman*) while remaining as the unmodified Brahman itself—such a nature does not admit of origination.

Which are those scriptural passages? "The individual soul does not die"; "Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless"; "He is not born, nor does He die, the wise one"; "Unborn, eternal, the ancient One, having created that, entered into it Himself"; "By this living soul, [the Self] which is pure and ancient. Chapter Two.

"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"; "This very one has entered here up to the tips of the nails"; "That thou art"; "I am Brahman"; "This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all"—such passages, proclaiming eternity, refute the production of the individual soul (jīva).
Now, it was argued that because it is divided, it must be a modification (vikāra), and because it is a modification, it is produced;
to this it is replied: its division does not exist inherently, for scripture declares, "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings."
However, its manifestation as divided is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi), just as the manifestation of space is caused by its connection with jars and the like.

And so the scripture—“This very Self is Brahman, consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing,” and so forth—shows that this one, unchanging Brahman itself possesses the nature of consisting of the manifold intellect and so on.

Furthermore, its "consisting of" that [intellect, etc. should be understood as its own nature being colored by them due to the non-manifestation of its true nature as distinct from them, just as in the expression "the fool consists of women."

As for the fact that in some places its origination and dissolution are heard of, that too must be understood as being due solely to connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); its origination is through the origination of the adjunct, and its dissolution through the dissolution of that adjunct.
And thus Scripture shows: "Being a mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, it perishes after them; after death, there is no consciousness."

Likewise, this is merely the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not the dissolution of the Self (*ātman*). This very point is established by means of a question: "In this very matter, the Blessed One has led me into the depths of delusion; I do not understand this, that after death there is no consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13). In response, [Yājñavalkya] says: "Indeed, I speak nothing confusing; for this Self, O Maitreyī, is imperishable and of an indestructible nature; however, it comes into contact with the material elements" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14). Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the initial proposition, because the status of being an individual soul (*jīva*) is accepted as belonging to Brahman itself in its unmodified state.

The difference in characteristics between these two is also caused solely by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), because in the passage, "Speak further for the sake of liberation," it is precisely this self consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) under discussion that is established as having the nature of the supreme self (paramātman) through the rejection of all transmigratory attributes.
Therefore, the self is neither produced nor dissolved.
Therefore, he is indeed a knower.

Is this [Self] inherently insentient with consciousness being adventitious, as the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain; or is it, like the Sāṃkhyas, of the very nature of eternal consciousness? Such is the doubt arising from the conflicting views of those who uphold the doctrine of the knower.

What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is established that the consciousness of the Self is adventitious, produced by the conjunction of the Self and the mind, just as qualities such as redness are produced by the conjunction of fire and a jar.
For if consciousness were eternal, there would have to be consciousness even in those who are asleep, in a swoon, or possessed by a spirit;
yet when questioned, they declare, "We were not conscious of anything at all," and it is observed that they become conscious only when they have recovered their normal state.
Therefore, since consciousness is occasional, the self is consciousness that is adventitious.
This being the position reached, it is replied: This Self is a knower and possesses eternal consciousness.
For this very reason, it is not produced; rather, the supreme Brahman itself, unmodified, exists in the state of a living soul (jīva) due to contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Indeed, the nature of the supreme Brahman as pure consciousness is declared in such scriptural passages as: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "Without interior or exterior, the entire mass of pure intelligence," and so forth.

If that very Supreme Brahman is the individual soul (jīva), then it follows that the soul also possesses the nature of eternal consciousness, just like the heat and light of fire; this is understood from such scriptural passages in the section concerning the "consisting of cognition" (vijñānamaya) as: "Unslumbering, he looks down upon those who slumber," "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous," and "For there is no loss of the knower's cognition. Such are the texts.

Furthermore, from the statement, "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self," and because [the Self] coordinates through all the instruments [of perception] with the cognition "I know this, I know this," its nature as that [cognition] is established.

If it is argued that if its essential nature were eternal consciousness, the sense organs such as the nose would be purposeless, we say no; for they serve the purpose of defining specific objects such as odors.
Thus, scripture shows: "The nose is for the perception of odor," and so forth.

As for the objection that those who are asleep and so forth do not perceive, the refutation of that has been stated by the Scripture itself with reference to deep sleep: "Verily, when there he does not see, yet he is seeing though he does not see;
for there is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of its imperishability;
but there is then no second, nothing else separate from him, that he might see," and so forth.

This is what is meant: because of the absence of objects, this [Self] does not cognize, not because of an absence of consciousness itself; just as the luminosity of the ether (viyat) is unmanifest due to the absence of anything to be illumined, and not due to an absence of its own nature, so it is here.
Furthermore, the reasoning of the Vaiśeṣikas and others becomes fallacious when it contradicts Śruti.
Therefore, we conclude that the Self is indeed of the nature of eternal consciousness.
Of the departing, the going, and the returning.

Now, however, it is considered what the size of the *jīva* is: is it of atomic dimension, or of intermediate dimension, or of great dimension? [Objection: But has it not been stated that the self is not produced and that its consciousness is eternal? And therefore, the supreme self itself is the *jīva*. [Reply: It is the instrument (*karaṇa*). [Objection: But has it not been stated that there is no going out (*utkrānti*)? [Reply: That was said with reference to the supreme self. Here, however, we are considering the *jīva* as an agent of action. Therefore, since it is an agent of action, its size must be determined. For an agent of action cannot occupy the same location as the object of action; otherwise, the act of eating would result in the eater being eaten, and the act of cutting in the cutter being cut. Furthermore, the soul is not omnipresent, because it is an agent of action. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be an agent of action, just like space (*ākāśa*). Nor is it of intermediate size, because it is eternal. For that which is eternal cannot have an intermediate size, just like space. Therefore, the soul is of atomic dimension. Moreover, because of the scriptural texts concerning its departure (*utkrānti*), etc., it is established that the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, there would be no departure, going, or returning. Furthermore, because of the perception of pleasure and pain in specific locations, the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, pleasure and pain would be perceived everywhere simultaneously. Moreover, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "seized" and "bound," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be seized or bound. Furthermore, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "pierced," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be pierced. Moreover, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "departing" and "entering," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, there would be no departing or entering. Furthermore, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "smaller than a grain of millet," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be smaller than a grain of millet. Moreover, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "subtler than a mustard seed," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be subtler than a mustard seed. Furthermore, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "higher than the high," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be higher than the high. Moreover, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "the smallest of the small," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be the smallest of the small. Furthermore, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "the knower of the field," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be the knower of the field. Moreover, because of the scriptural texts concerning its being "the witness," the soul is of atomic dimension. For if it were omnipresent, it could not be a witness. Thus it follows;
and the infinity of the Self (the Supreme) is taught.
In that case, how can there be any occasion for considering the dimensions of the individual soul (jīva)?
It is said: This is true;
however, the scriptural accounts of the soul's departure, going, and returning establish its limited nature, and in some places its atomic dimension is declared by its own specific term.
This undertaking is for the purpose of establishing that all of this is free from contradiction.
In this regard, it is first argued that the individual soul (jīva) is limited and of atomic dimension, because of scriptural statements concerning its departure, movement, and return.
As for departure, [the scripture says]: "When he departs from this body, he departs together with all these."
There is also the going, as stated: "Whoever depart from this world, they all go to the moon";
and there is also the coming back, as stated: "From that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action.
From the hearing of these [scriptural passages] regarding departure, going, and returning, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed limited in size. (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.19–20)
It attains [all things]—for indeed, motion on the part of the omnipresent is not possible;
since spatial limitation exists, and the doctrine that the soul has the same size as the body has been refuted in the "Examination of the Arhat," it is understood that the soul is atomic.
And by its own nature, it is the cause of the two subsequent [moments].

The departure might perhaps be possible even for one who does not move, through the cessation of lordship over the body— just as there is the cessation of lordship over a village— due to the exhaustion of karma; however, the subsequent going and coming are not possible for one who does not move,
for their connection [to the soul] occurs by means of its own self, since going is an action residing in the agent.

Furthermore, coming and going are possible only for that which is of minute size (aṇu), not for that which is of intermediate size; and when coming and going exist, it follows that "departure" (utkrānti) is indeed an exit from the body, for coming and going would not be possible for one who has not departed from the body. Moreover, this is understood from the statement that the points of departure during the departure are the locations of the body: "either from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body."

"Taking these particles of light, he descends into the heart," and "Having taken the light, he returns again to his place"—from these [scriptural passages], the going and coming of the embodied self (śārīra) occur even within the body;
therefore, its atomicity (aṇutva) is established.
If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the scriptural statement regarding its delighting in manifoldness, we say no, because of the context of the other [state].
Moreover, it might be argued: "This self is not atomic;
why? Because it is not so [stated]; that is to say, because a dimension contrary to atomicity is heard in the scripture.

If it be argued that scriptural passages of this kind—such as "This indeed is the great unborn Self, which consists of cognition among the vital breaths," and "Brahman is all-pervading like space, eternal, truth, knowledge, and infinite"—would contradict the atomicity of the Self, we reply: this is not a fault.

Why? Because of the context of the other; for this scriptural mention of a different magnitude occurs within the treatment of the Supreme Self, since the Supreme Self alone is the primary subject to be known in the Vedāntas. Furthermore, because of the specific reference to the Supreme Self in various passages such as, "Stainless and higher than space," it refers to that very Self. An objection may be raised: "But in the passage, 'He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths,' it is the embodied self (the individual soul) that is pointed out by its connection with greatness. To this we reply: this reference must be understood from the perspective of the scripture's vision, just like the case of Vāmadeva.
Therefore, because the hearing of another size refers to the domain of the wise, it does not contradict the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva).
And [the existence of the intermediate state is established] by its own specific term and by measurement.

Furthermore, the soul is atomic, because a word directly expressing its atomicity is heard: "This atomic soul is to be known by the mind, into which the fivefold vital breath has entered" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.9).

And from its connection with the vital breath, it is understood that this atomic being referred to is indeed the individual soul (jīva). Likewise, the measurement [of the soul] also leads to the understanding of the soul's atomic nature: "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9).

"That part, O Jīva, is to be known as the Self"; and "Though the lower [self] is seen to be the size of the tip of an awl"—this is another measurement. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9). Chapter Two. Sūtra. And there is another measurement.
But surely, if [the self] were atomic, it would be contradictory for one situated in a single location to experience sensations throughout the entire body;

yet we observe that those submerged in the waters of the Ganges perceive coolness in all their limbs, and during the summer heat, experience a burning sensation throughout the whole body. To this, he reads the reply: "There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood."

For just as a drop of yellow sandalwood paste, even though it is connected to only one part of the body, produces a pleasure that pervades the entire body, so too the Self, though situated in one part of the body, will bring about a perception that pervades the whole body.
Furthermore, its connection with the skin does not contradict the fact that sensations extend throughout the entire body;
for the connection between the skin and the Self exists throughout the whole of the skin.
"And the skin pervades the entire body.
If it is argued that this is due to a difference in location, we say no, because it is admitted [to be so]; for [the scripture] says, "In the heart indeed..."

Here it is argued: what was stated—that there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood—is incorrect, because the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) are not comparable.

For the illustration of sandalwood would be valid only if it were established that the self resides in one part of the body. However, it is directly perceived that the specific mode of existence of sandalwood consists in its being located in one place while simultaneously providing pleasure to the entire body. In the case of the self, however, what is directly perceived is merely the perception throughout the entire body, not its residence in one part.

If it were stated in the Sūtra or its commentary that "that [self] is the object of inference," and if no inference were possible here—because the doubt would not be resolved as to whether the experience of sensation throughout the entire body belongs to the self while it pervades the whole body like the sense of touch, or like the all-pervading ether, or like a drop of sandalwood paste which is minute and occupies only one spot—then we reply:
this is not a fault.
Why? Because it is accepted [as such].
For it is indeed admitted that even for the Self, there is a specific mode of existence consisting in residing in one part of the body, just as in the case of sandalwood.

How so? It is said: "For this Self is taught in the Vedāntas as being in the heart," from such instructions as, "For this Self is in the heart," "This very Self is in the heart," and "Which is the Self? He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths, the light within the heart, the person" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).
Therefore, since there is no dissimilarity between the illustration and the thing illustrated, this is entirely logical: "And there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood."
Or [the designation is] due to a quality, as in the world.

Alternatively, because its quality of consciousness (caitanya) is all-pervasive, there is no contradiction in the soul (jīva), though it is atomic in size, performing an action that pervades the entire body. This is just as in the world, the light of gems, lamps, and so forth, although situated in only one part of a room, pervades the entire room and performs its function throughout the whole room. One might object: "In the case of sandalwood paste, because it possesses parts, it can refresh the entire body through the spreading of its subtle particles; however, the atomic soul has no parts by which it could spread throughout the entire body. Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "Or [the soul's action is due to its] quality, as in the world" (Guṇādvā lokavat).
The Second Chapter.
But how could a quality exist elsewhere apart from the possessor of that quality? For the white quality of a cloth is never seen existing elsewhere apart from the cloth.
If it is argued that it might be like the light of a lamp, we say no.

Since that [light] is also admitted to be a substance—namely, that the lamp is a substance of light with dense constituent parts, whereas radiance is simply a substance of light with sparse constituent parts—the following sūtra is recited as a reply: "There is a distinction, as in the case of odor."
Just as an odor, though it is a quality, exists apart from the fragrant substance— as the fragrance of flowers is perceived even when those fragrant flowers have not been reached—
so too, although the individual soul (jīva) is atomic, there will be a separation from its quality of consciousness.

Therefore, the argument that "because it is a quality, like color and so forth, its separation from its substratum is impossible" is inconclusive, since we observe the separation of its substratum in the case of odor, which is indeed a quality.
If it is argued that the odor also separates from its coexisting substrate, we say no; because if it were to separate from the original substance, that substance would necessarily undergo decay.
Furthermore, even though it does not decay, it is perceived to be in the same state as before.
Otherwise, it would be deprived of its heaviness and other qualities as they existed in its prior state.
It might be argued: "Because the separated parts that serve as the substrata for the odor are so minute, even though separation exists, it is not perceived;
for subtle odor-atoms, having dispersed in all directions, produce the cognition of odor upon entering the nostrils. If this is said, we reply: no.
Because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses, and because a distinct fragrance is perceived in things such as the *nāgakeśara* flower; furthermore,
there is no common worldly recognition that "the fragrant substance has been smelled," for people in the world understand it rather as "the fragrance itself has been smelled."

If it is argued that, because no separation from a substratum is perceived in the case of visible form and so forth, it is likewise improper for odor to have a separation from its substratum, we say: no;
for since this is a matter of direct perception, inference does not apply.
Therefore, whatever is observed in the world in a certain way must be accepted as such by investigators, and not otherwise.

For it cannot be restricted by the argument that "since the quality of taste is perceived by the tongue, therefore other qualities such as color and so forth must also be perceived by the tongue alone."
And thus he shows:

Having stated that the self has its abode in the heart and possesses an atomic dimension, [the scripture] shows that it pervades the entire body through the quality of consciousness, from the hair to the tips of the nails.
Because of the separate instruction.

Furthermore, because of the separate teaching of the self and wisdom as agent and instrument in the passage, "Having mounted the body with wisdom," it is understood that the self's pervasion of the body occurs solely through its attribute of consciousness. Moreover, the teaching of consciousness as distinct from the embodied agent in the passage, "Taking the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of consciousness," reinforces this very intention.
Therefore, the self is atomic.
This being the case, we reply: [In the second chapter:
"But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that [name], as in the case of the conscious one (prājña)."
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that the self is atomic;

for its origination is not heard [in scripture], whereas the entry of the supreme Brahman itself is heard, and there is instruction regarding identity with it. Thus, it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the supreme Brahman.
If the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the supreme Brahman, then the individual soul must be as extensive as the supreme Brahman;
and since the omnipresence of the supreme Brahman is taught,
therefore the individual soul is omnipresent.

And thus, scriptural and traditional declarations concerning the all-pervasiveness of the individual soul (jīva)—such as "This great unborn Self is indeed this one consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths"—are thereby supported.
Moreover, for an atomic soul, the experience of sensations throughout the entire body would not be possible.
If it is argued that this could occur through connection with the skin, we say no.

Even upon the prick of a thorn, it would follow that the sensation belongs to the entire body, for the conjunction of the skin and the thorn exists in the whole skin, and the skin pervades the entire body;
yet, one experiences the sensation only where the foot is actually pricked by the thorn.
Furthermore, the pervasion of a quality by an atom is not possible, because a quality must reside in the locus of its substratum.
For the very nature of a quality would be lost if it were not dependent upon a substratum possessing that quality;
furthermore, the fact that the light of a lamp is a distinct substance has already been explained.
Even odor, since it is admitted to be a quality, must necessarily move while having a substratum, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of its losing the status of being a quality.

And so it has been stated by the Blessed Lord Dvaipāyana: "If some unskilled persons were to perceive fragrance in water and say [it is there], one should know that it belongs to the earth alone, which has resorted to the water and the air.
Furthermore, if consciousness were to pervade the entire body of the individual soul (jīva), the soul would not be atomic (aṇu).
For consciousness alone is its essential nature, just as heat and light are for fire; here, no distinction between quality and the possessor of the quality exists.
Furthermore, the view that the soul has the same dimensions as the body has been refuted.
By process of elimination, the soul is all-pervading (vibhu).

If so, how then is there the designation [of the Self] as "atomic" (aṇu) and so forth? To this he says: "But that designation [is due] to its having the qualities of that [intellect] as its essence" (tadguṇasāratvāt). The qualities of that intellect are its "qualities" (tadguṇāḥ), such as desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, and so on. That Self for whom these qualities constitute its "essence" (sāra)—that is, its primary factor—in its state of transmigratory existence is "one whose essence consists of those qualities" (tadguṇasāraḥ). The state of being such is "having the qualities of that as its essence" (tadguṇasāratvam).
For without the qualities of the intellect, the transmigratory state of the isolated Self does not exist.

For the state of being a transmigrating soul—characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth—is caused by the superimposition of the attributes of the limiting adjunct, the intellect (*buddhi*), upon the Self which is eternally non-agent, non-enjoyer, and non-transmigrating.

Therefore, because its essence consists of the qualities of that [intellect], there is an attribution of dimension to this [Self] according to the dimension of the intellect; and there is an attribution of departure and so forth to it through the departure and so forth of that [intellect], but not inherently.
And thus: "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts..."
"A portion [of Me], O Jīva, is to be known as that which is fit for infinity"—having thus stated the atomicity of the Jīva, the text then declares its infinity.
And this would be consistent only if the atomicity of the Jīva were figurative, while its infinity were ultimate;
for both cannot be primary simultaneously. (Second Chapter)
Nor can it be understood that this infinity is merely figurative, because in all the Upaniṣads it is intended to be established that Brahman is identical with the Self.

Similarly, in the other measurement as well— where it says, "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the Self, even the inferior [Self] is seen to be the size of the point of an awl"— it teaches that the size of an awl's point is due solely to its connection with the qualities of the intellect, and not by its own nature.

Even in the passage, "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind," the atomic dimension of the individual soul (jīva) is not being taught; for it is the Supreme Self that is the subject under discussion, characterized as being ungraspable by the eyes and other senses and as being accessible through the clarity of knowledge. Furthermore, a primary atomic dimension is logically impossible even for the individual soul. Therefore, this statement regarding its subtlety (aṇutva) should be understood as intended to convey its difficulty of cognition, or else as referring to its limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Likewise, in cases of such teachings of distinction as "having mounted the body by means of wisdom" (prajñā), one should construe it thus: "the individual soul (jīva) has mounted the body by means of the intellect (buddhi) which serves as its limiting adjunct (upādhi)"; or else, it is a mere figurative designation, like the expression "the body of a stone statue.
For it has already been stated that even the distinction between quality and possessor of quality does not exist here.
Furthermore, the statement regarding the heart being its abode refers to the intellect alone, since that is its abode.

Likewise, [the scripture] shows that even departure and so forth depend upon the limiting adjuncts (upādhi): "In whom, when I have departed, shall I have departed? Or in whom, when established, shall I be established? He created the vital breath (prāṇa).
For in the absence of departure, the absence of going and returning is also understood; for one who has not departed from the body, there can be no going or returning.

Thus, because the individual soul (jīva) has the qualities of its limiting adjuncts as its essence, there is the designation of it as atomic and so forth, just as in the case of the Intelligent One (prājña).

Just as for the Intelligent One—the Supreme Self—in meditations upon Him with attributes, there is the designation of minuteness and so on because His nature consists of the qualities of the adjuncts—such as "smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley," "consisting of mind, consisting of breath, having breath as its body, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, having true desires, and having true resolves"—in that same manner [the designations apply to the jīva].

It might be argued as follows: "If the transmigratory state of the Self were imagined to arise because its essence consists of the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), then—since the conjunction between the distinct intellect and the Self must necessarily come to an end—it would follow that upon the separation from the intellect, the Self, being isolated and unperceivable, would either cease to exist or be non-transmigratory. To this, the author reads the following reply: "And because it exists as long as the Self does, there is no fault; for that is seen [in scripture]."
One should not suspect that the defect just mentioned applies here;

why? Because the connection with the intellect persists as long as the self exists: as long as this self remains a transmigrating being, and as long as its state of transmigration is not terminated by right vision (*samyagdarśana*), so long does its connection with the intellect not cease.

And for as long as this connection with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the intellect lasts, for that long alone does its status as a living individual (*jīvatva*) and its state of transmigration persist.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, there is no such thing as a "living soul" (*jīva*) existing apart from the nature imagined through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the intellect. Indeed, in the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta, no second conscious principle is found other than the Lord (*Īśvara*), whose nature is eternally free and omniscient. This is established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "There is no other seer but He... no other hearer... no other thinker... no other knower"; "There is nothing else that sees, hears, thinks, or knows"; "That thou art"; and "I am Brahman."

How, then, is it understood that the conjunction with the intellect (buddhi) persists as long as the self exists? He says: "Because that is seen. For scripture shows this: "This person consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths (prāṇas)—being the same [in both states], he moves through both worlds; he meditates, as it were; he stirs, as it were," and so forth. In this context, "consisting of consciousness" means "consisting of the intellect" (buddhi); for in another passage, the one "consisting of consciousness" is mentioned alongside the mind and other faculties: "Consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing. Thus, it is established that the conjunction with the intellect lasts as long as the self exists.

And its being "consisting of intelligence" (buddhimayatva) is intended precisely as having the qualities of that [intellect] as its essence (tadguṇasāratva); just as in common usage, Devadatta is said to be "consisting of women" when he is characterized primarily by passion for women, so it is here.
Furthermore, the statement, "Being the same, he moves between both worlds," shows that there is no separation from the intellect even during the transition to another world.
With what is he the same? It is understood to be with that very intellect, because of its proximity.
And he shows this with the words, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were";
the meaning is this: it does not meditate by itself, nor does it move; rather, when the intellect (buddhi) meditates, it meditates, as it were, and when the intellect moves, it moves, as it were.
Furthermore, this connection of the Self with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect is preceded by false knowledge (mithyājñāna).

Furthermore, since there is no cessation of false knowledge other than through right knowledge, this connection with the limiting adjunct of the intellect does not subside as long as there is no realization of one's identity with Brahman;
and scripture shows this: "I know this great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness.
Only by knowing Him does one pass over death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).

[Objection: But surely, it cannot be admitted that the Self has a connection with the intellect during deep sleep and at the time of cosmic dissolution, because of the scriptural statement, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own self," and because the dissolution of all modifications is admitted.

How then can the connection with the intellect be said to exist as long as the Self exists? To this, it is replied: "But [the connection] belongs to the existing [Self], because its manifestation is possible, like manhood and so forth."

Just as in the world, qualities such as masculinity, which exist in the form of a seed even though they are not perceived during childhood and are regarded as non-existent, become manifest in youth and so forth— and do not arise as something previously non-existent, for if they did, it would follow that even eunuchs and the like could produce them— so too this connection with the intellect exists only in the form of a potentiality during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, and becomes manifest again upon awakening and creation; for it is thus that this is logically consistent.

For the arising of anything cannot possibly be accidental, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Furthermore, the scripture demonstrates that rising from deep sleep is brought about by the existence of the seed consisting of ignorance, in such passages as: "Having become merged in the Existent, they do not know: 'We have become merged in the Existent,'" and "Whether they were tigers here, or lions," and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the connection with the limiting adjuncts, such as the Buddha-nature and so forth, persists as long as the personal existence (ātmabhāva) endures.
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else the necessity of one or the other being restricted.

And that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the Self, is designated by various names in different contexts—such as *manas*, *buddhi*, *vijñāna*, and *citta*;
and in some instances, it is called *manas* when characterized by functions such as doubt, and *buddhi* when characterized by functions such as ascertainment.

And such an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must necessarily be admitted to exist; for otherwise, if it were not admitted, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception. Since the self, the sense organs, and the objects—the means of perception—are present together, constant perception would result;
or, if despite the presence of the causes there were an absence of the effect, then constant non-perception would result. Yet neither of these is observed.
Alternatively, an obstruction of the power of either the self or the sense organ must be admitted;
yet an obstruction of the power of the self is not possible, because it is changeless,
nor is it possible for the sense organ.
For it is not possible that the power of that [sense-organ], which exists with its capacity unimpeded in the preceding and succeeding moments, should suddenly be obstructed.
Therefore, that by whose attention and non-attention perception and non-perception occur is the mind (*manas*).
And thus says the Śruti: "My mind was elsewhere, I did not see; my mind was elsewhere, I did not hear," and "It is indeed by the mind that one sees, and by the mind that one hears."

And he shows that desire and the rest are its modifications by means of the scriptural text: "Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind.
Therefore, it is correct to say that because the Self has those qualities as its essence, it is designated by their names.
CO. Furthermore, He is the creator, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless.
JUNY: By means of this very section concerning the essence of its qualities (*guṇasāra*), another attribute of the living self (*jīva*) is also elaborated upon:
namely, that this living self must be the agent (*kartṛ*). Why?

Because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless (*śāstrārthavattvāt*). For it is only if there is an agent that scriptural injunctions such as "one should sacrifice," "one should offer oblations," and "one should give" have their purpose fulfilled. This constitutes the reason.
In this way, the scripture of injunctions becomes meaningful;
otherwise, it would be purposeless,
for it teaches a specific duty to one who exists as an agent.
And this would not be possible if there were no agency;
likewise, this scripture also becomes meaningful: "For he is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the agent—the person whose self is consciousness."
Because of the teaching on the [four] abodes.

For this reason as well, the individual soul (jīva) possesses agency: because, in the section concerning the individual soul, the scripture teaches its wandering about in the intermediate state (sandhya-sthāna), stating, "He, being immortal, goes wherever he desires," and, "He moves about at will within his own body.
