[Topic 10] On Account of Appropriating.

Furthermore, its status as an agent is established by the fact that, in the very context concerning the individual soul (jīva), it mentions the taking up of the instruments: "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths through his own consciousness," and "having grasped the vital breaths."
And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action; if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the instruction.

Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) possesses agency, because the scripture designates its agency in both worldly and Vedic actions, stating: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice, and it also performs ritual acts. Now, an objection may be raised: since the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) is understood to refer to the intellect (buddhi), how can the agency of the soul be indicated by this? We reply: no, for this is a designation of the soul itself, not of the intellect.
If it were not the soul's [agency], there would be a reversal of the designation; it would have been stated as "by means of consciousness" (vijñānena).

For elsewhere, when the intention is to denote the intellect (buddhi), the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) is seen used with an instrumental case-ending, as in: "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of consciousness" (vijñānena). But here, in the statement "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," because of the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the agent, the agency of the Self itself—distinct from the intellect—is indicated; thus there is no fault.

Regarding this, an objection is raised here: "If the individual soul (jīva) were an agent distinct from the intellect (buddhi), being independent, it would necessarily accomplish what is pleasant and beneficial for itself, and never the opposite; yet we observe it accomplishing even the opposite. Furthermore, such an irregular activity on the part of an independent self is not logically possible. To this, the author reads the following reply: "The lack of restriction is as in the case of perception. (Sūtra 3.2.19)

Just as this self, although independent with respect to perception, perceives both the desirable and the undesirable without restriction, so too it will bring about the desirable and the undesirable without restriction.

If it is argued that there is a lack of independence even in perception because one observes the employment of the causes of perception, we say no; for the causes of perception have as their sole purpose the mere presentation of objects.
In perception itself, however, the self is independent of anything else, owing to its association with consciousness (*caitanya*).

Moreover, even with regard to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the Self does not possess absolute independence, because it depends upon specific conditions of place, time, and causal factors (*nimitta*);
nor does the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) cease for an agent who requires assistance,
for indeed, one who cooks remains a cook even when depending on fuel, water, and so forth.

Furthermore, due to the variety of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārivaicitrya*), the soul's engagement in purposeful action toward desired or undesired objects without fixed necessity is not contradictory.
Because of the reversal of capacity.
For this reason as well, the individual soul (*jīva*) must be an agent distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If the intellect (*buddhi*), which is denoted by the word "consciousness," were itself the agent, then there would be a reversal of capacities: the capacity to be an instrument would be lost by the intellect, and the capacity to be an agent would accrue to it.
And if the intellect possessed the capacity to be an agent, it alone would become the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). (Second Chapter)
That [Self] must be accepted as such, because in all cases activity is seen to be preceded by the notion of "I," as in: "I go," "I come," "I eat," and "I drink.
Furthermore, for that [Self], which possesses the power of agency and performs all purposes, another instrument (karana) must be postulated;
for even though he is capable, an agent is observed to engage in actions only by employing an instrument.

Consequently, there would be a dispute over mere terminology, for there is no difference in the actual thing, since the status of being an agent is admitted for that which is distinct from the instruments.
And because of the absence of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, this meditative concentration (samādhi), which is taught in the Vedāntas for the purpose of realizing the Self described in the Upaniṣads—characterized by such injunctions as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon; that is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known," and "Meditate on the Self with the syllable Om"—would not be possible if the Self were not an agent.
Therefore, from this also, its agency is established.
And just as a carpenter [acts] in both ways.

Thus, by means of reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures, the agency of the embodied soul has been demonstrated; now, however, it is considered whether that agency is innate, or whether it is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like that of a carpenter.
In this regard, the same arguments—such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures—are employed.
For these reasons, agency is inherent [in the Self], because there is no reason for refuting it as stated in the Sūtra and its commentary.
This being the position, we reply: inherent agency of the Self is not possible, because it would entail the impossibility of liberation;
for if agency were the very nature of the Self, liberation from agency would be impossible, just as heat cannot be removed from fire.

Furthermore, for one who is not liberated from agency, there is no accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because agency is of the nature of suffering. Now, it might be argued: "Even while the capacity for agency remains, the human goal will be accomplished by avoiding the activity of agency; and that avoidance results from the avoidance of its causes, just as fire, though endowed with the power of burning, lacks the effect of burning when separated from wood. This is not so, because it is impossible to completely eliminate the causes when they remain connected to the self through a relationship characterized by their inherent capacity.
Now, it might be argued that liberation will be accomplished through the prescription of the means to liberation; but this is not so, because whatever depends upon a means is impermanent.
Furthermore, the attainment of liberation is intended to result from the teaching of a Self that is eternally pure and free;
and such a teaching of the Self would not be possible if agency were inherent in it.
Therefore, the self’s agency arises solely through the superimposition of the attributes of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and is not innate.

Thus, the Śruti says, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were," and "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. This shows that the attainment of specific states such as being an enjoyer belongs only to the Self when it is associated with its limiting adjuncts. For to the discerning, there exists no other so-called individual soul (*jīva*) distinct from the Supreme who is either an agent or an enjoyer, according to such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer but He."

In that case, it would follow that the transmigrating being is the agent and the enjoyer, and [the Self] would be distinct from the Supreme. For the Scripture, having first shown agency and enjoyership in the state of ignorance with the words, "Where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another," then precludes those very same agency and enjoyership in the state of knowledge with the words, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"

Thus, having made us hear of the exhaustion caused by contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in both the dreaming and waking states—just like that of a hawk flying about in the sky—the text makes us hear of the absence of that [exhaustion] in deep sleep for one who is embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña-ātman*), beginning with: "Now, this is his state in which desires have been attained, which is the self-desiring, desireless form, free from sorrow," and concluding with: "This is his highest goal, this is his highest attainment, this is his highest world, this is his highest bliss."
And thus it is said by the Teacher: "As the carpenter [acts] in both ways. And this particle *ca* is read here in the sense of *tu* (but/rather).
One should not think that the agency of the Self is inherent, like the heat of fire.

Just as in the world a carpenter, having an axe and other tools in his hand, becomes a doer and suffers, but upon reaching his own home, being freed from the axe and other tools, becomes at ease, tranquil, inactive, and happy—so too the Self, when associated with the duality presented by ignorance, becomes a doer and suffers in the states of dreaming and waking; but in order to dispel that weariness, having entered its own Self, the Supreme Brahman, it becomes a non-doer and happy, free from the aggregate of effects and instruments in the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*). Likewise, in the state of liberation as well, having shaken off the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge, the Self alone, being perfectly tranquil, becomes happy.

This analogy is to be understood in this respect: for a carpenter becomes an agent only by depending on specific instruments such as an adze for specialized operations like carving, whereas with his own body he is a non-agent;
even so, this Self becomes an agent in all its activities only by depending on instruments such as the mind, but by its own nature it is indeed a non-agent.

However, the Self does not possess limbs like a carpenter, by means of which it might take up or set aside instruments such as the mind, just as a carpenter takes up or sets aside an adze and other tools with his hands and so forth.

As for what was stated—that the agency of the Self is inherent on the grounds such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures—that is not so. First of all, the scripture of injunctions (vidhi-śāstra) teaches specific duties by taking up an agency that is already established [in experience], but it does not establish the agency of the Self.
Nor does this Self possess inherent agency, as we have already stated based on the teaching that Brahman is the Self.
Therefore, the scripture of injunctions will proceed by taking up an agency created by ignorance (avidyā).

Even scriptural passages of this kind, such as "The agent is the person whose nature is consciousness" (*vijñānātmā puruṣaḥ*), will merely restate the agency created by ignorance exactly as it is found [in common experience], because they are of the nature of restatement (*anuvāda*).
By this, the [scriptural passages concerning] "wandering" (*vihāra*) and "taking up" (*upādāna*) are also refuted, since those two are likewise of the nature of restatement.
But [one might object]: "In the intermediate state (*saṃdhye sthāne*), when the organs have fallen asleep, one wanders at will within one's own body... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18).
When it is taught that "he moves about" (*sa vartate*) in the state of dreaming (*vihāra*), this conveys the agency of the Self alone;

likewise, regarding the act of taking up [the senses], in the passage "having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness" (*tadeṣāṃ prāṇānāṃ vijñānena vijñānamādāya*), the hearing of the accusative and instrumental case-endings in relation to the instruments leads one to understand the agency of the Self alone.

To this, it is replied: first of all, there is no absolute cessation of the instruments for the Self even in the intermediate state (dreaming), because its connection with the intellect (*dhī*) is heard even there in the text, "Becoming one who possesses intellect (*sadhrīc*), having become a dreamer, he transcends this world."
And thus they record in their tradition: "If the mind does not cease even when the senses have ceased, and it continues to enjoy objects, one should know that to be the state of dreaming";
and scripture declares that desire and the like are modifications of the mind.
And these [objects] are seen in a dream;
therefore, that mind alone roams about in this way during sleep.
Furthermore, even the roaming there consists only of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and does not exist in an ultimate sense.
And thus the Śruti describes the activity of dreaming as being connected with the particle "as it were" (iva): "As if rejoicing with women, as if laughing, or even as if seeing terrors.
Worldly people also describe their dreams in the same way: "I climbed, as it were, a mountain peak; I saw, as it were, a row of forests.

Likewise, regarding the taking up [of the body], although there is a designation of the instruments by means of the case-endings for the object and the instrument, nevertheless the agency must be understood as belonging to the Self alone when conjoined with them, since it has been shown that agency is impossible for the isolated [Self].
Furthermore, there are various ways of intending to express things in the world, such as "the warriors fight" or "the king fights by means of the warriors.

Moreover, in this [definition of the agent as] the "appropriator," only the cessation of the activity of the instruments would be intended, not the independence of anyone; for even in sleep, which is not preceded by conscious thought, the cessation of the activity of the instruments is observed.

As for this designation shown—“Consciousness (vijñāna) performs the sacrifice”—it establishes that agency belongs to the intellect (buddhi) alone. This is because the word *vijñāna* is well-known in that sense, because it is mentioned immediately after the mind (*manas*), and because of the statement, “Faith is indeed its head,” which proclaims that faith and the other [limbs] are parts of the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*); furthermore, faith and the rest are well known to be attributes of the intellect. Also, from the supplementary passage, “All the gods worship Consciousness as the eldest Brahman,” and because being "eldest" means being the first-born, a status well known to belong to the intellect; and finally, because another scriptural text, “This sacrifice is the successive progression of speech and thought,” determines that the sacrifice is accomplished by speech and the intellect.

Nor does a reversal of the capacity of the intellect occur when the instruments are admitted to be agents, because agency in their respective functions necessarily belongs to all causal factors alike;
rather, the status of these instruments as instruments is relative to perception,
and that [perception] resides in the Self.
Nor does agency belong to that [Self] when superimposed [upon it], because its nature is eternal perception.
Even agency preceded by the ego-sense cannot belong to the perceiver, since the ego-sense itself is an object of perception.
And this being so, there is no consequence of having to postulate another instrument, because the intellect (buddhi) is admitted to be the instrument.

The absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), however, has already been refuted by the very fact that it possesses the meaning of the scriptures; for the injunctions regarding *samādhi* are based upon agency as it is naturally attained.
Therefore, it is established that the agency of the self is likewise caused solely by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The Second Chapter:
But [the origination of the world] is from the Supreme [Lord], for so scripture declares.

Regarding this agency of the individual soul (jīva) which was stated to be based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) during the state of ignorance: does that occur without depending on the Lord, or does it depend upon the Lord? Thus arises an inquiry into its dependence on another. On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the individual soul does not depend on the Lord for its agency.

Why? Because there is no need for dependence [on another]. For this individual soul (jīva), being itself impelled by defects such as passion and hatred, is capable of experiencing agency when provided with the collection of other causal factors;

what, then, will the Lord do for it? Nor is it established in the world that in actions such as agriculture and the like, another—such as the Lord—is to be depended upon, as one would depend on oxen and so forth.
Furthermore, if God were to create living beings with agency consisting of afflictions (kleśa), the charge of cruelty would attach to Him;
and if He were to ordain their agency as having unequal results, the charge of partiality would likewise follow.

But was it not said that "partiality and cruelty do not apply because [God] has regard for [other factors]"? True, this was said, provided that such dependence on other factors is indeed possible for God.
And dependence on another is possible for God only when merit and demerit exist in living beings;
and the existence of those two depends upon the agency of the individual soul.
If that very agency were dependent upon God, then with reference to what object could God's dependence be said to exist?
Furthermore, in this case, the consequence would follow that the living being (jīva) undergoes the results of actions not performed by itself.
Therefore, having set aside by means of the word "but" (tu) the prima facie view that its agency is intrinsic, the author declares: "from another" (parāt).

This means that in the state of ignorance (avidyā), for the living being who perceives no distinction from the aggregate of the body and the organs, [agency arises] from another—namely, from Ignorance.

In the Sūtra-bhāṣya: For one who is blind [to reality], the accomplishment of transmigratory existence—characterized by agency and enjoyment—occurs through the Supreme Self, the overseer of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious Lord;
and the accomplishment of liberation must likewise occur solely through the knowledge caused by His grace.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement.

Although the individual soul (jīva) is impelled by defects and possesses the necessary causal apparatus, and although in worldly activities such as agriculture the causality of the Lord is not commonly known, nevertheless, it is determined from scripture that the Lord is the causal agent in all undertakings.
For thus says the Scripture: "For He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds."
For there are such passages as: "It is he indeed who makes him perform evil deeds whom he wishes to lead downward," and "He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within."

[Objection: But surely, if God is thus the cause of all actions, there would result partiality and cruelty on His part, and for the individual soul (jīva), there would be the acquisition of what was not earned.
[Reply: No; it is said in response: "But He has regard for the effort made by the soul, because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth."
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of setting aside the objections previously stated.
The Lord causes this [action] to be performed by the individual soul only with reference to that effort made by the soul, characterized as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);
therefore, these aforementioned objections do not apply, because of the inequality [of results] arising from the merit and demerit performed by the individual soul. Chapter Two.

It is precisely with regard to those [individual efforts] that the Lord, like the rain-cloud, distributes their respective fruits unequally by acting merely as a common cause (*nimittatva*). Just as in the world, for various kinds of shrubs, bushes, and so forth, as well as for rice, barley, and the like—which arise from their own specific seeds—the rain-cloud serves as a common cause; for indeed, in the absence of the rain-cloud, the diversity of sap, flowers, fruits, leaves, and so on, would not arise in them, nor would it arise if their own respective seeds were absent. In the same way, it is logical that the Lord, depending upon the efforts made by living beings, ordains their good and evil fortune.
[Objection: But surely, if the soul’s agency depends on another, it cannot be said that it "depends upon its own exertion. [Reply: This is not a fault;
for even though agency depends on another, the soul indeed acts, since the Lord causes it to act while it is acting.

Moreover, He causes it to act now by depending on its previous exertion, and caused it to act previously by depending on an even earlier exertion; thus, because saṃsāra is beginningless, there is no flaw in the argument.
But how is it understood that Īśvara depends upon the effort exerted [by beings]? He says: "Because otherwise the prescribed and the prohibited would be rendered meaningless," and so forth.
For in this way, there is no futility of such things as the prescribed injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and the prohibited rule, "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed";
otherwise, they would be purposeless.
The Lord alone would be subject to injunctions and prohibitions, because the individual soul (jīva) is absolutely dependent [on Him];
likewise, He would bring about misfortune even for one who performs what is enjoined, and prosperity even for one who performs what is prohibited;
and consequently, the authority of the Veda would perish.
Furthermore, if God were absolutely independent, human effort in the worldly sense would be useless, as would the factors of place, time, and causal conditions;
moreover, the previously mentioned defects would follow. By the use of the word "etcetera" (ādi), he indicates this class of defects.
The soul is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of difference, and also because otherwise some record it as having the nature of fishermen, kitavas, and so forth.
The relationship of beneficiary and benefactor between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) has been stated;
and that [relationship] is observed in the world only between things that are connected, such as a master and a servant, or like fire and its sparks (the section on the indicative marks).

Furthermore, since a relationship of mutual benefit between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is admitted, a doubt arises as to whether this relation is like that of a master and a servant, or rather like that of fire and its sparks; in such a state of uncertainty, the conclusion might be that there is no fixed rule.
Alternatively, since the relation of ruler and ruled is well-known only in cases such as those of a master and a servant, the conclusion might be that the relation is of that very kind.
On the other hand, [the Sāṃkhya] says it is a "part" (aṃśa);
the individual soul (jīva) must be a part of the Lord (īśvara), just as a spark is of fire;
it is a "part" in the sense of being like a part.
For a primary part is not possible for that which is without parts.
Why, again, is it not so because of its being without parts? Because of the designation of multiplicity:

"He is to be sought, He is to be understood"; "Only by knowing Him does one become a sage"; and "He who, dwelling in the self, controls the self from within"—such designations of difference as these [are found] in the second chapter.
It is not logical [to speak of difference] when there is no actual distinction.
But surely this designation of multiplicity is even more appropriate when there is a similarity between master and servant; therefore, he says: "And otherwise also.
Nor is the realization of being a part derived from the designation of multiplicity alone.
Rather, there is also another designation that establishes non-difference;

for instance, certain followers of a Vedic school (śākhins), such as the Atharvaṇikas, declare in the *Brahmasūkta* that Brahman exists in the state of the Dāśas, Kitavas, and so forth, saying: "Brahman is the Dāśas, Brahman is the Dāsas, Brahman indeed are these Kitavas," and so on.

"These fishermen who are well-known as *dāśas*, and those slaves who exhaust themselves for their masters, and others who are gamblers and players at dice—all these are Brahman indeed. By means of this illustration of lowly beings, he declares that all individual souls (*jīvas*)—who have entered into the aggregate of effects and instruments produced by name and form—are Brahman.
Likewise, in another passage concerning the nature of Brahman, this same meaning is elaborated: "You are female, you are male, you are a youth, or even a maiden."

"You are old and you speak with a staff; you are born and you become facing in all directions"—thus [it is said]; and also, "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth.

Furthermore, this meaning is established by such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer but He. Moreover, consciousness is common to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), just as heat is common to fire and its sparks.
Therefore, from the cognitions of difference and non-difference, there arises the cognition of being a part.
And from what [source] is the understanding of being a part? From the wording of the mantra, as stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya.
And the coloration of the mantra conveys this meaning: "Such is His greatness;
yet the Puruṣa is greater than that.
All beings constitute but one quarter of Him."

Regarding the passage, "Three-quarters of him are the immortal in heaven," here the word *bhūta* refers to all moving and stationary beings, primarily consisting of individual souls (*jīva*), as seen in the usage, "Not harming any beings except at [sacred] sites.
Furthermore, *aṃśa*, *pāda*, and *bhāga* are synonymous terms.
Therefore, there is also the comprehension of its being a part.
From what is the understanding of being a part derived? Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti.

Furthermore, in the *Īśvaragītās* it is also recorded in Smṛti that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of God: "A portion of My very self, existing as the eternal soul, is in the world of living beings.
From this, too, there is the understanding of its being a part.

As for what was said—that in the world the relationship between ruler and ruled is well known only among masters and servants and the like—even though this is a worldly convention, nevertheless, according to the scripture (*śāstra*), the relationship of part and whole as well as that of ruler and ruled is determined here.
There is nothing contradictory in the claim that the Lord, endowed with unsurpassed adjuncts, governs the individual souls who are endowed with inferior adjuncts.

Here it is objected: "If it is admitted that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of the Lord (*īśvara*), then by the experience of the suffering of transmigratory existence belonging to that [soul], the Lord as the whole (*aṃśin*) would also become subject to suffering—just as in the world Devadatta, the possessor of limbs, suffers from pain occurring in any one of his limbs such as the hand or foot;
and consequently, those who attain Him would incur even greater suffering."
"Therefore, it would follow that right vision (samyagdarśana) is useless, as one might think: 'It is better that saṃsāra remain in its previous state.
To this, it is replied: 'Not so, for the Supreme is like light and other such things.'"
We maintain that the Supreme Lord does not experience the suffering of saṃsāra in the same way that the individual soul (jīva) does.

For the individual soul, under the influence of the onset of ignorance (avidyā), comes to identify with the body and so forth as if they were its self; consequently, through that ignorance, it falsely imagines itself to be suffering, thinking "I am miserable," and thus experiences the suffering produced by ignorance.
The Supreme Lord, however, possesses neither this identification with the body and so forth nor this false conceit of suffering.

For the individual soul (*jīva*) as well, the conceit of suffering is caused solely by the delusion of non-discrimination from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—such as the body and senses—which are produced by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) fashioned by ignorance (*avidyā*); it does not exist in an ultimate sense.

Just as one experiences suffering caused by burning, cutting, and so forth occurring in one’s own body through the delusion of identifying with it, so too does one experience suffering directed toward sons, friends, and others through that very same delusion of identification, becoming attached to sons, friends, and the like under the influence of affection, thinking, "I am the son," or "I am the friend."

From this it is understood with certainty that the experience of suffering is caused solely by the delusion of false identification (*mithyābhimāna*). This is also understood through the observation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); for instance, when many people are seated together—some possessing sons, friends, and so forth, and others not—and it is announced that "a son has died" or "a friend has died," suffering arises only for those who possess the identification with having sons, friends, and so on, and not for those devoid of such identification, such as wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*).

And thus, even for an ordinary worldly person, the efficacy of right vision is observed; how much more so, then, for one who perceives no object other than the Self—which is devoid of external objects and whose nature is solely eternal consciousness?
Therefore, there is no possibility of the contingency that right vision is purposeless.

The presentation of the illustration "like light, etc. is as follows: Light—whether solar or lunar—pervading space remains there; when it comes into contact with limiting adjuncts such as a finger, although it appears to assume their states of being straight, curved, and so forth, it does not in reality assume those states. And just as space, though appearing to move when jars and other objects move, does not in reality move; and just as when a reflection of the sun in a water-bowl trembles due to the shaking of the bowl, the sun itself, which possesses that reflection, does not tremble—even so, although the portion called the individual soul (*jīva*), presented by ignorance and conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*), suffers pain, the Lord who possesses it does not suffer pain.
It has been stated that even the soul’s attainment of suffering is caused solely by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, the Vedānta texts, such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), establish the very nature of Brahman for the soul by removing its state of being a soul which is caused by ignorance.
Therefore, there is no possibility of the Supreme Self becoming subject to suffering through the suffering of the individual soul.
And they remember.
In the Sūtra-bhāṣya, Second Chapter:
Vyāsa and others also record that the Supreme Self does not suffer through the suffering of the individual soul (jīva), as it is said:
"In this regard, that which is indeed the Supreme Self is traditionally held to be eternal and devoid of qualities."
"It is not smeared by fruits [of action], just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
however, that other one which is the *karmātman* (the self of action) is joined with both liberation and bondage.
It is further joined with the aggregate consisting of seventeen."

Because of the word "and" (ca), the remainder of the sentence is "and they recite [the following]": "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other looks on without eating," and also, "In the same way, the one Inner Self of all beings is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external to it."
To this, he says: "If, then, there were only one inner self for all beings, how could there be permissions and prohibitions, whether worldly or Vedic?
But has it not been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of the Lord?
And due to the distinction between them, permissions and prohibitions—which depend upon those [souls]—are logically established as being non-confused."

"What is the objection here? It is replied: this is not so; for the scriptures that teach non-difference also establish the partlessness (*anaṃśatva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), such as: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.6.1); "There is no other seer but He" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.23); "He goes from death to death who perceives here any kind of diversity" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 4.10); "That thou art" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7); and "I am Brahman" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.4.10). Now, it was argued that part-status is established by the cognitions of both difference and non-difference. This might be so, provided that both difference and non-difference were intended to be taught.

However, it is non-difference alone that is intended to be established here, since the human goal is accomplished through the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self; whereas difference, which arises from one's own nature, is merely restated.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that it is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) to be a primary part of the partless Brahman.
Therefore, since the one Supreme Self alone is the inner soul of all beings, existing in the form of the individual soul (jīva), the possibility of both permission and prohibition must be explained.
We shall explain this: permission and prohibition [are possible] due to connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth.
The injunction "one should approach one's wife during her season" is an authorization (anujñā), while the prohibition "one should not approach the wife of a teacher" is a restriction (parihāra);

likewise, the injunction "one should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" is an authorization, while the prohibition "one should not harm any living beings" is a restriction. Similarly, in the world as well, there is the authorization "a friend should be served," and the restriction "an enemy should be avoided"—such are the authorizations and restrictions that occur despite the oneness of the Self, due to its connection with the body. "Connection with the body" means association with the physical body.

What, then, is the connection with the body? It is the arising of a contrary cognition within the Self, such as "I am this very aggregate consisting of the body and so forth. And this is observed in all living beings, taking the form: "I go," "I come," "I am blind," "I am not blind," "I am deluded," "I am not deluded," and so on.
Indeed, there is no other means for its removal than right knowledge (*samyagdarśana*).
Prior to right vision, this delusion extends continuously among all living beings.

Thus, even though the unity of the Self is accepted, permissions and prohibitions are rendered possible due to the distinctions created by the connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the body, which have ignorance as their cause. Chapter Two. PAR. [End]

In that case, it might follow that for one who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśin*), injunctions and prohibitions would be purposeless. This is not so, because such a person has already accomplished their goal and thus cannot be subject to being enjoined. For it is only with respect to things to be avoided or things to be adopted that one who is to be enjoined can be directed by an enjoiner.
But how could one be enjoined when they do not perceive any object—whether to be avoided or to be adopted—as distinct from the Self?
Furthermore, the Self cannot be enjoined by the Self alone.
If it is argued that only one who perceives the self as distinct from the body is subject to injunctions, we say no;
this is because of the conceit of being conjoined with it. It is true that one who perceives distinction is subject to injunctions;
nevertheless, the conceit that the self is subject to injunctions belongs only to one who does not perceive its non-conjunction with the body and so forth, just like space and other such things.
For no injunction is ever observed for anyone who perceives themselves as not being a composite of the body and so forth, much less for one who perceives the absolute oneness of the Self (*ekātmya*).

Nor does the absence of injunction imply that one who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśin*) would be subject to acting according to their own whims; for it is *abhimāna* (egoistic identification) alone that impels action, and such identification is absent in one who possesses right vision.

Therefore, the permissions and prohibitions arise solely from the connection with the body, just as in the case of light and the like: even though light is one, fire is avoided when it is associated with a corpse, but not otherwise.
Just as the light of even a single sun is avoided when it comes into contact with an impure place, while that same light is not rejected when situated on pure ground;
likewise, certain earthly regions such as those containing diamonds and lapis lazuli are accepted, whereas other earthly things such as the corpses in hell are avoided;
and similarly, the urine and dung of cows are accepted because of their purity, yet that very same substance is shunned when found in another species—so it is in this case.
And there is no confusion because there is no continuity [of the self].
It may be granted that the granting of permission and the avoidance of what is forbidden could belong to a single Self due to its connection with specific bodies;

however, if it is argued that this connection between the Self and the fruits of action would become confused under the assumption of a single Self because of the unity of ownership, we reply: this is not so, because there is no such continuity.
For the Self, as both agent and enjoyer, does not have a continuous connection with all bodies.

For it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon its limiting adjuncts (upādhi); and since there is no continuity of the soul when the adjuncts lack continuity, there will consequently be no confusion of actions nor any confusion of their fruits.
And it is merely an appearance.

Moreover, this individual soul (*jīva*) is to be understood as a mere reflection of the Supreme Self, like the sun in water and so forth; it is neither that very Self directly, nor a different entity altogether.

Consequently, just as when one reflected sun in water trembles, another reflected sun does not tremble, so too, when one individual soul is connected with the fruits of karma, another individual soul is not connected with them.
Thus, there is indeed no confusion between actions and their fruits.

And since the appearance (*ābhāsa*) is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), it follows that the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) which has that appearance as its substrate is also produced by ignorance; thus, by the removal of that [appearance], the teaching of the ultimate reality—the identity of Brahman and the Self—is logically established.

However, for those who maintain that there are many selves and that all are omnipresent, this confusion of states necessarily follows. How so? For they hold that the selves are many, all-pervading, consisting solely of the nature of consciousness, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), and without distinction;
and for their sake, there exists a common primordial matter (*pradhāna*), caused by which this [confusion] occurs. This is the second chapter.
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that there is the accomplishment of both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).

According to them, although the selves (*ātman*) are manifold and all-pervading, they are by nature mere substances, like jars or walls, and are inherently insentient. Their instruments—the atomic minds (*manas*)—are likewise insentient. Therein, through the conjunction of the substance of the self and the substance of the mind, the nine specific qualities of the self, beginning with desire, arise; these inhere individually in each self without distinction, and this constitutes *saṃsāra*.
The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) hold that liberation is the absolute non-arising of those nine qualities of the self.

In that regard, for the Sāṃkhyas first, since all selves (ātman) consist of the nature of consciousness and there is no distinction in their proximity [to the primordial matter], it follows that when one self is connected with pleasure and pain, all selves would be connected with pleasure and pain. It might be argued that there will be a fixed order because the activity of the primordial matter (pradhāna) has the purpose of achieving liberation for the individual selves (puruṣa); otherwise, the activity of the primordial matter would be for the sake of manifesting its own power.

And thus, it would follow that liberation is impossible; however, this [objection] lacks substance. For a systematic arrangement based on the attainment of one's desired goal cannot be established [merely by that desire]; rather, an arrangement may be stated through some form of logical justification (*upapatti*). But in the absence of such a justification, let the desired isolation of the person (*puruṣakaivalya*) simply not be attained.
However, due to the absence of a cause for differentiation, there would be a confusion [of experiences].
Even for the followers of Kaṇāda, when the mind is conjoined with one self, it would necessarily be conjoined with other selves as well, since there is no difference in their proximity and so forth;

and consequently, because the cause is not distinct, the result would not be distinct either—thus, when one self is joined with pleasure and pain, it would follow that all selves equally experience pleasure and pain.
It might be argued that this restriction will be caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa); to this he says "no," because there is no restriction regarding the unseen: *adṛṣṭāniyamāt*.

When there are many selves, all-pervading like space and present in every body without distinction between external and internal, [the Sāṃkhyas argue that] having acquired *adṛṣṭa*— characterized as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)— through mind, speech, and body, this *adṛṣṭa* resides in the *pradhāna*, not inhering in the self. Because it is common to the *pradhāna*, it cannot logically serve as the regulator for the individual experience of pleasure and pain for each self.

For the followers of Kaṇāda as well, there is this very same fault: since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is produced by the common conjunction of the self and the mind as previously described, there is no reason for the restriction that "this unseen force belongs to this specific self. Thus, the defect remains.

It might be argued that intentions and the like—such as "I shall attain this fruit," "I shall avoid this," "I shall strive thus," or "I shall do this"—which arise within each individual self, will determine the relationship of owner and owned between the unseen principle (adṛṣṭa) and the selves; to this he says: "And the same applies even to intentions and the like."

Likewise, even in the case of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), since they are produced in the presence of all selves through the common conjunction of the self and the mind alone, it is impossible for them to serve as causes for restriction; thus, the aforementioned defect necessarily follows.

"If it be argued that [the distinction] is due to location, we say no, because [all] are included within [the whole]. (Sūtra 3.2.1) It might be argued: "Even though the self is all-pervading, its conjunction with the mind—which resides in the body—will occur only in that portion of the self delimited by the body;
therefore, the restriction of volition and so forth, as well as of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), pleasure, and pain, will be determined by location. This too is not tenable.
Why? Because of inclusion; for, due to the lack of distinction in their omnipresence, all selves indeed include all bodies within themselves.
In that case, it is not possible for the Vaiśeṣikas to postulate even a spatial part of the self as delimited by the body.
Even if this [body] were to be postulated, it could not, by virtue of being merely a conceptual construct, restrict the effects of a partless self to a specific location;

for even a body, arising in the proximity of all selves, could not be restricted as belonging to this one self alone and not to others. Furthermore, even if a specific location were admitted, there would occasionally be the possibility of experience through a single body for two selves sharing identical pleasure and pain, since it is possible for the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of two selves to occupy the same location.

For instance: when Devadatta’s body has departed from the place where he experienced pleasure and pain, and Yajñadatta’s body has reached that same place, it is observed that the latter also experiences pleasure and pain identical to those of the former;
this would not be possible if there were no unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) common to both Devadatta and Yajñadatta in that location.

Furthermore, for one who maintains the doctrine of localized space (pradeśavāda), there would be the undesirable consequence of never experiencing heaven and the like, because the adṛṣṭa is produced in the specific locations of the bodies of Brāhmaṇas and others, whereas the experience of heaven and so forth occurs in a different location.
In the commentary on the Sūtras, it is stated that there is an absence of supporting examples;
furthermore, the omnipresence of many selves is untenable. Tell me then, how can many things occupy the same location?
If you argue that it is like color and other qualities, we say no.

Even for those [particulars], there is non-difference due to their sharing the same nature (*dharmyaśa*), and because there is no difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*); for there is no difference in the defining characteristics of multiple selves.
If it is argued that the establishment of difference is possible by virtue of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), we say no;
for there would be a circularity between the postulation of difference and the postulation of ultimate particularities.
Furthermore, even the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of ether and the other elements is unestablished for the proponent of Brahman, because they admit that these are effects.
Therefore, it is established that only in the position of the unity of the Self (*ātmaikatvapakṣa*) is there an absence of all defects.

Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka Mīmāṃsā Sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
The venerable Śekharabhagavatpāda’s composition.
The Commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.
The Fourth Pāda of the Second Adhyāya. The Fourth Pāda.
Since the contradiction regarding the subject of ether has been resolved by the third quarter [of the verse],
the contradiction regarding the subject of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is now resolved by the fourth.

In that regard, in the contexts concerning origination such as "It created fire" and "From this very Self, ether was produced," the origination of the vital breaths is not recorded in the sacred texts.

Furthermore, in some places their non-origination itself is taught: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1). Regarding this, they ask: "What was that non-existence? [The answer is: "In the beginning, those very sages were non-existence.
They further ask: "Who are those sages? [The answer is: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the sages. Since here the existence of the vital breaths prior to origination is heard;

In other places, however, the origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is also taught, as in: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a blazing fire, even so from this Self all the vital breaths [proceed]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20); "From this [Self] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3); "The seven vital breaths proceed from that" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.1.1); and "He created the vital breath; from the vital breath, faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, the mind, and food" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4). Such are the passages in these and other locations.
In this regard, since there is a contradiction between scriptural passages and because no means for determining one or the other can be discerned, the result would be a lack of comprehension.

Alternatively, since their existence prior to creation is heard [in scripture], it follows that the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is merely figurative. To this, he reads the following reply: "So also the vital breaths."
"Likewise, [the case of] the vital breaths.

But how, in this context, is there a conformity of syllables (anulomya) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*), given that there is no relevant object of comparison? For the refutation of those who maintain the omnipresence and plurality of the Self was the subject under discussion at the end of the preceding section on the origin of the vital breaths; that, therefore, cannot serve as the point of comparison. Nor can it be a point of similarity.
It does not occur, because there is an absence of similarity;
for comparison (*upamāna*) would only exist if there were similarity, as in "Balavarman is like a lion.

If it should be argued that this is for the purpose of demonstrating a similarity with the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)—namely, that just as the unseen, arising in proximity to all selves, is unrestricted, so too the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are unrestricted with respect to all selves—that too would be a mere repetition, since this has already been stated by means of the non-restriction of the body itself.

Nor can the vital breaths (prāṇas) be compared with the individual soul (jīva), because that would contradict the established doctrine; for the non-origination of the soul has been declared, whereas the origination of the vital breaths is intended to be explained. Therefore, [the objection] that "thus" [the comparison] appears incoherent is not correct, because a comparison is possible even by means of an illustration provided as an example. In this context, the collection of passages asserting the origination of the vital breaths—such as "From this Self all vital breaths, all worlds, all gods, and all beings issue forth"—serves as the illustration. Thus ends the second chapter of the Sūtras.
The meaning is that just as the worlds and so forth arise from the supreme Brahman, so too do the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Likewise, in such passages as, "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;
ether, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe," it should be understood that the origin of the vital breaths is like that of ether and the other elements.

Alternatively, since even a connection with a remote object of comparison is accepted in such cases as "And [the case of] the mishap with the drinking is like that" (PMS 6.2.19), one should apply the principle as follows: just as ether and the other elements mentioned in the preceding section were established as modifications of the supreme Brahman, so too the vital breaths (prāṇas) are to be understood as modifications of the supreme Brahman.
But what is the reason for the vital breaths being modifications? It is simply because they are so stated in scripture (śruti).
As for the objection that in some places the origination of the vital breaths is not heard of, that is incorrect, because they are heard of in other passages.
For the non-hearing of something in one place does not have the power to preclude its being heard elsewhere;
therefore, since there is no difference in their being mentioned in scripture, it is well said that the vital breaths (prāṇas) also originate, just like ether and the other elements.
Because a figurative sense is impossible.

As for the argument previously stated—that because the existence [of the prāṇas] prior to creation is heard in scripture, the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the prāṇas must be figurative—the Sūtra replies:

"Because a figurative sense is impossible" (gauṇyasaṃbhavāt). "The impossibility of a figurative sense" means that the scriptural statement of the origin of the prāṇas cannot be figurative, as that would entail the abandonment of the initial proposition. For, having proposed the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one—"O Venerable One, when what is known, does all this become known?"—the text "From Him is born the prāṇa," and so forth, is recorded as the means to accomplish that very purpose.

And that proposition is established when the entire world, including the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is an evolution of Brahman, because there can be no modification apart from its material cause (*prakṛti*); however, if the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths were taken in a figurative sense, this proposition would be lost. Accordingly, the text concludes the meaning of the proposition: "The Person alone is all this—action, austerity, Brahman, the supreme immortality," and "Brahman alone is all this, the most excellent."

Likewise, in such scriptural passages as "Verily, my dear, by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing the Self, all this is known," this very same proposition is to be applied. But how can there be a scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths (prāṇas) prior to creation? This does not refer to the Root-Nature (mūlaprakṛti), because the Root-Nature is determined to be devoid of all specific attributes such as the vital breaths, according to the text: "For He is without vital breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable."

However, this determination of the existence of the prāṇas prior to creation—referring to their intermediate material cause and relative to their own modifications—must be understood as such; for it is well known from both Śruti and Smṛti that even among the many states belonging to the realm of the evolved (vyākṛta), there exists the relationship of material cause and modification.

For in the *Viyad-adhikaraṇa*, since the sūtra "gauṇyasaṃbhavāt" (BrahSū 2.3.3) is a sūtra presenting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it was explained that the scriptural mention of birth is figurative because [otherwise] it would be impossible;
and therein the final conclusion (siddhānta) was stated by means of the refutation of the abandonment of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*).

In this case, however, because it is a sūtra of the established doctrine (siddhānta), it has been explained as "because the scriptural mention of birth cannot be taken in a secondary sense. Following that [principle], those who here also explain the scriptural mention of birth as being secondary "because of impossibility" would be disregarding the second chapter's sūtra concerning the "loss of the initial proposition" (pratijñāhāni).
And because of its prior existence.

For this reason as well, the scriptural statement regarding the birth of the vital breaths (prāṇas) must be taken in its primary sense, just like that of ether and the other elements. Since the single word "is born" (*jāyate*), which denotes birth, is heard first in reference to the prāṇas and then recurs in reference to the subsequent elements such as ether— in the passage, "From Him is born the prāṇa"— and since it has been established that the birth of ether and the others is primary,
by parity of reasoning, the birth of the prāṇas must also be primary.

For it is not possible to determine that a single word, uttered once within a single section or a single sentence and connected with many things, is primary in one instance and secondary in another, as this would entail the fallacy of inconsistency (*vairūpya*).

Likewise, in the passage "He created Prāṇa; from Prāṇa, Śraddhā," the verb "created" (*sṛjati*), heard in relation to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is also applied by extension (*anuṣajyate*) to the subsequent entities such as Śraddhā that possess an origin.

Even where a word expressing origination is heard later and is connected with what precedes it, this same principle applies; for example, the word "vyuccaranti" (they issue forth), which is recited at the end in the phrase "all beings issue forth," is connected with the preceding elements such as the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so on.
Because speech is preceded by that.

Although the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is not explicitly mentioned in this section—"It created fire"—since only the origin of the three elements, fire, water, and food, is heard there in the *Sulabhabhāṣya*;

nevertheless, because speech, breath, and mind are declared to be preceded by fire, water, and food which have Brahman as their material cause, and because of the similarity between them, it is established that all the vital breaths indeed originate from Brahman.

For instance, in this very context, it is recorded that speech, breath, and mind have fire, water, and food as their antecedents: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. If, then, their consisting of food and so forth is taken in its primary sense, then their origination from Brahman certainly follows.

Now, even if [the term "consisting of food" (annamaya)] is used figuratively, nevertheless, because it is heard that the differentiation of names and forms has Brahman as its agent, because of the opening statement, "By which the unheard becomes heard," and because of the concluding statement, "All this has that as its self," and because of what is well-known from other scriptural passages, it is understood that the statement regarding the mind and the rest being "consisting of food" and so forth is intended solely to elaborate upon the fact that they are effects of Brahman.
Therefore, for this reason also, the fact that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are modifications of Brahman is established.
And because the destination of the path is specified as being "hundredfold."

The contradiction regarding the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) has been resolved; now the contradiction regarding their number is being resolved. In that regard, the author will later state that there are seven, setting aside the principal *prāṇa*.

Now, however, the present section considers how many other vital breaths (prāṇas) there are. It maintains [the following]. Here, there is a doubt due to conflicting scriptural statements; for in some places seven prāṇas are mentioned, as in: "From him the seven prāṇas arise."

In some places, eight vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are mentioned as "graspers" (*graha*) by way of their quality, as in: "The vital breaths are eight graspers and eight over-graspers" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 2.20.1).
In other places, nine are mentioned, as in: "There are seven vital breaths in the head and two downward ones" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.7.1).
In some places there are nine, as in "Indeed, there are nine vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person, and the navel is the tenth";

in other places there are eleven, as in "These ten are the vital breaths in a person, and the self (ātman) is the eleventh"; and in other places there are twelve, as in the passage: "The skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations."

In some places, thirteen [are mentioned], as in the passage, "The eye and the visible. Thus, indeed, the Śruti texts are in disagreement regarding the number of the prāṇas. What, then, is the prima facie view? That all the prāṇas are [seven].
Why? Because of the going.

For that many [seven] are understood from such scriptural passages as, "From him the seven prāṇas spring forth," and they are specifically designated in the text, "There are indeed seven prāṇas in the head.
Now, an objection is raised: the distributive repetition (vīpsā) is heard in the text, "The prāṇas, dwelling in the cave, are deposited seven by seven";
this implies prāṇas in addition to the seven. This is not a fault; for...
This repetition—"seven, seven vital breaths for each person"—is intended with reference to the distinction between individuals;
it is not intended with reference to a distinction in principles, as if there were different sets of seven vital breaths.
[Objection: But has not the number eight and so forth also been cited in regard to the vital breaths?
How can there be exactly seven? It is true that they have been cited; however, due to contradiction, one of the numbers must be determined as the correct one.
In this case, the number seven is determined in accordance with the principle of assuming the fewer possibilities (*stokakalpanā*).
And he considers that the hearing of different numbers is due to the distinction between the various modes of functioning.
To this it is replied: "But since the hands and so forth exist [only] when [the body] exists, it is not thus."

In the commentary on the Sūtras, however, other prāṇas besides the seven are heard of in scriptural passages such as: "The hand indeed is a grāha (seizer); it is seized by action as the atigraha (over-seizer), for with the two hands one performs action," and so forth. Since the number [of prāṇas] exceeds seven, the number seven can be accounted for through inclusion; for when there is a conflict between a lower and a higher number, the higher number is to be accepted.
For the lesser [number] is included within it, but the greater is not included within the lesser;
therefore, one should not think that there are only seven vital breaths (prāṇas) merely out of deference to a smaller calculation.
Rather, in accordance with the higher number, those vital breaths must be eleven.
And thus a scriptural passage has been cited: "These ten vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person, with the self as the eleventh.
And here, by the word "self" (ātman), the internal organ is intended, because the context concerns the instruments [of perception].
Now, it may be objected that even numbers greater than eleven—namely twelve and thirteen—have also been cited; this is true, they have indeed been cited.
However, there is no class of effects beyond these eleven classes of effects for the sake of which an additional organ would have to be postulated:
there are five distinct types of cognition having sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as their objects, and for those purposes there are five organs of cognition;
there are five distinct types of action—speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure—and for those purposes there are five organs of action.
The mind (*manas*), however, has all objects as its domain and functions throughout the three periods of time; it is single, yet possesses manifold functions.
Due to the distinction of these functions, it is designated by various names in different contexts, such as "mind," "intellect" (*buddhi*), "ego" (*ahaṃkāra*), and "thought" (*citta*).
Accordingly, the Śruti, after enumerating various kinds of functions such as desire and so forth, declares: "All this is indeed the mind."
Furthermore, for one who considers there to be only seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in the head, only four would actually be intended;
for although these are only four, they are counted as seven due to the difference in their locations, as it is said: "two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, and one speech-organ."
Nor can it be said that the other vital breaths (prāṇas) are merely different functions of those [five], because the functions of the hands and so forth are of an entirely different nature.

Likewise, in the passage, "There are indeed nine prāṇas in a person, the navel being the tenth," the ten prāṇas are mentioned with reference only to the different openings of the body, not with reference to different categories of vital breaths, as indicated by the statement "the navel being the tenth";
for there is no well-known vital breath (prāṇa) by the name of "navel."

However, for the principal vital breath (prāṇa), the navel is also one specific abode; therefore, it is said that "the navel is not the tenth. In some places, certain vital breaths are enumerated for the purpose of meditation, while in others, they are mentioned for the sake of illustration. Thus, since there are various scriptural accounts regarding the number of vital breaths, one must discern which among them is the ultimate teaching.
However, it is established that the number eleven is based on the objects of the vital breath (prāṇa), due to the variety of functions to be performed.

This is another way of reconciling the two Sūtras: there would be only seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), because the departure of only seven is heard in the passage: "When he departs, the *prāṇa* departs after him; when the *prāṇa* departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after it. Now, an objection is raised: since the word "all" (*sarva*) is read here, how can it be asserted that only seven depart?

He says [the answer is] "because they have been specified. For it is precisely the seven vital breaths (prāṇas), beginning with the eye and ending with the mind, that are specified here as the subject under discussion through the following sequence: "When the person in the eye turns away, then he becomes one who does not know forms; he becomes unified; they say he does not see," and so forth.
Furthermore, the word "all" (sarva) refers to what has been introduced in the context.

Just as in the expression "all Brāhmaṇas should be fed," it is those Brāhmaṇas who have been invited and are under discussion who are denoted by the word "all," and not others; so too here, it is those seven vital breaths (prāṇas) which are under discussion that are denoted by the word "all," and no others.
[Objection: But surely consciousness (vijñāna) has been mentioned as the eighth here;
how then can there be a mention of only seven? [Reply: This is not a fault.
Because there is no difference in essence between the mind and consciousness, the number seven is established even when there is a difference in their functions.

Therefore, since it has been argued that there are only seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), we reply: other vital breaths, such as the hands and so forth, are perceived in addition to the seven, in scriptural passages such as, "The hand, indeed, is the grasper" (*graha*).
And "grasper-ness" (*grahatva*) is the state of being a bond, for by this bond called a "grasper," the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is grasped—that is, bound.
And that knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is not bound in one body alone, because bondage is equal in other bodies as well;

therefore, it follows by implication that this bondage known as the "graspers" (graha) migrates from one body to another. And so says the Smṛti: "He is joined with the eightfold city [of the subtle body] as his mark, together with the vital breaths and the rest."

"Indeed, for one bound by that there is bondage, and for one liberated from that there is liberation"—by this, [the text] shows non-separation from the bond known as the "grasping" (graha) until final release. Furthermore, in the Atharvaṇa, in the enumeration of the objects and senses, at the point "the eye and the visible," it enumerates the senses such as the hands together with their corresponding objects in an equal manner: "the two hands and the graspable, the organ of generation and the pleasurable, the anus and the excretable, and the two feet and the locomotory."

Likewise, the text, "These ten breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh—when they depart from this mortal body, then they cause one to weep," shows the departure of eleven breaths. Furthermore, the word "all" (sarva), when connected with the word "breaths" (prāṇa) and denoting all breaths without exception, cannot be restricted to only seven by virtue of the context, because the direct word is more powerful than the context. Even in the case of the statement, "All Brāhmaṇas are to be fed," it is logical that all Brāhmaṇas residing on the earth are understood, due to the force of the word "all."
However, because it is impossible for all food to be present there, the application of the word "all" was taken there as referring only to those who had been invited;
here, on the other hand, there is no reason whatsoever to restrict the meaning of the word "all.
Therefore, by the word "all," there is here an inclusion of all vital breaths without exception.
And since the enumeration of seven is for the purpose of illustration, there is no fault.
Therefore, it is established that there are exactly eleven vital breaths (prāṇas), both according to scripture and according to their functions.
And they are atomic.
Now he further establishes another characteristic of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) themselves.
These vital breaths under discussion are to be understood as atomic (*aṇu*);

and their "atomicity" consists in subtlety and limited dimension (*pariccheda*), not in being equal to the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), since they pervade the entire body. This is the topic [of the *adhikaraṇa*].

Because it would otherwise follow that their functioning is impossible, these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are subtle. If they were gross, then at the time of death, as they emerged from the body like a snake from its hole, they would be perceived by those standing beside the dying person.

Furthermore, these *prāṇas* are limited in extent; for if they were all-pervading, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning their departure, going, and returning, and the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) has them as its essential quality (*guṇasāratva*) could not be established.

If it is argued that even though they are all-pervading, their functional activity occurs within the region of the body, we say no; for it is sufficient that the mere function itself constitutes the instrument.

For whatever indeed is the means of apprehension—whether it be the function (*vṛtti*) or something else—it is that alone which possesses instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) for us; the dispute is merely over terminology. Thus, the hypothesis of the pervasiveness of the instruments is useless. Therefore, we conclude that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are subtle and limited in extent.
O Best One!
And he extends this principle to the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), stating that like the other vital breaths, it is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman.

This fact—that all vital breaths without distinction are modifications of Brahman—has been declared [in the scripture]: "From Him is born the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), and all the sense organs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3).

This is because the origin of the vital breath is heard of as being distinct from the senses and the mind, and because of such scriptural statements as, "He created the vital breath" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4).

For what purpose, then, is this extension (atideśa)? It is for the purpose of warding off a further doubt. For in the hymn *Nasadāsīya*, which has Brahman as its primary subject, there occurs a Vedic verse: "There was neither death nor immortality then; there was no sign of night nor of day. That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhā*); other than that, indeed, nothing else existed. [The word] "breathed" (*ānīt*) refers to the second chapter.

Because of the mention of the "appropriation of the vital breath" (prāṇa) prior to its origination, it might occur to someone that the vital breath exists as if already present before birth; therefore, he dispels that notion by means of an extended application (atideśa).

The word "breathless" (ānīc) also does not indicate the existence of the vital breaths prior to creation, because of the qualification "without air" (avātam), and because it has been shown that the primal material cause is devoid of all specific attributes such as the vital breaths, in the passage, "For [He] is without breath, without mind, pure.
Therefore, this word "breathless" is intended solely to demonstrate the existence of the Cause.
Furthermore, the word "best" (śreṣṭha) denotes the principal vital breath, according to the scriptural statement: "The vital breath, indeed, is the eldest and the best."

Furthermore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the eldest, because it acquires its function starting from the moment of the emission of semen; for if it did not acquire its function at that time, the semen emitted into the womb would either putrefy or fail to develop.

The ear and the other senses, however, do not possess this status of being the eldest, as they acquire their functions only upon the completion of the formation of their respective locations, such as the ear-cavity.
Moreover, the vital breath is the best (*śreṣṭha*) due to its superior qualities, according to the Vedic text: "Indeed, we shall not be able to live without you."
Nor [are they] the functions of air, because of their being taught separately.
Now, it is investigated what the nature of that principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is. On this point, it is first established that, according to scripture, the vital breath is air (*vāyu*);
for thus it is heard in scripture: "The vital breath is the function of air; it is air; it is this very air [which has fivefold functions]."
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is fivefold: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*.

Alternatively, according to the view of other systems (*tantrāntara*), it follows that *prāṇa* is the function of the totality of the organs; for those belonging to other systems declare: "The five vital airs, beginning with *prāṇa*, are the common functions of the organs."
To this it is replied: the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is neither air (*vāyu*), nor is it the activity of the organs.
Why? Because of its separate instruction.
For there is a separate instruction of the vital breath from air: "The vital breath alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and glows with air as its light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.4).
For indeed, that which is air itself would not be taught as separate from air.

Likewise, there is a separate teaching of the function of the organs, because after enumerating the organs such as speech and so forth, the prāṇa is enumerated separately in each instance; this is due to the non-difference between the function and the possessor of the function.
For that which is merely the activity of the organs would not be taught as separate from the organs themselves.

Likewise, such passages as "From this [Self] are born breath, mind, and all the sense organs, as well as space and air," which provide separate instruction for the vital breath (prāṇa) from both the elements and the sense organs, must also be followed. Furthermore,
a single function for the entire collection of sense organs is not possible, because each functions individually and a mere aggregate lacks causal agency.

[Objection: "Surely this will occur by the logic of the moving cage: just as eleven birds residing in a single cage, each having its own specific function, together cause the single cage to move; so too, the eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) residing in a single body, each having its own specific activity, together shall obtain a single collective function called 'vital breath' (*prāṇa*).
[Reply: No, it is said. That is correct in that case because there are multiple individuals... [Second Chapter].

Just as birds, endowed with their respective functions and intermediate operations corresponding to the movement of a cage, might together move a single cage— since that is observed to be so— it is not logical that the vital breaths (prāṇas), though endowed with intermediate operations such as hearing and so forth, should breathe together, because there is no evidence for this, and because the act of breathing is of an entirely different nature from hearing and the other senses. Furthermore, the proclamation of the pre-eminence of the prāṇa and the subordination of speech and the other organs toward it would not be possible if the prāṇa were merely the function of the instruments.
Therefore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is distinct from both air (*vāyu*) and its function (*kriyā*).

How then is this scriptural statement to be understood: "That which is *prāṇa* is air"? It is said in reply: This very air, having entered the body (*adhyātma*), assuming a fivefold arrangement and abiding in a specific form, is called by the name *prāṇa*; it is neither a separate ontological principle (*tattvāntara*) nor merely air alone.
Consequently, both scriptural passages—those concerning difference and those concerning non-difference—are not contradictory.

It might be argued that the vital breath (prāṇa), like the individual soul (jīva), would likewise attain independence with respect to this body, because of its preeminence and because the organs such as speech and the rest assume a subordinate status toward it.

For indeed, many kinds of majesty are heard of regarding the vital breath: "While speech and the others are asleep, the vital breath alone remains awake"; "The vital breath alone is not overtaken by death"; "The vital breath is the absorber (saṃvarga), for it absorbs speech and the others"; "The vital breath protects the other vital breaths, just as a mother protects her sons.
Therefore, there arises the contingency that the vital breath also possesses independence like the individual soul.

He refutes that [objection] with the sūtra: "But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them," and so on. The word "but" (tu) excludes the independence of the principal vital breath (prāṇa), just as it does for the individual soul (jīva).
Just as the eye and other organs are instruments for the soul's agency and enjoyment—like ministers to a king—and are not independent;
so too the principal vital breath, like a royal counselor, is an instrument for the soul by performing all its purposes, and is not independent.
Why? Because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons.
In the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and elsewhere, the *prāṇa* is taught together with those [organs] such as the eye;
and it is logical that things possessing common characteristics should be taught together, as in the case of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* chants.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), he indicates the reasons for refuting the independence of the vital breath (prāṇa), such as its being composite and its being insentient.

This might be so if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) were admitted to be an instrument for the living self (*jīva*), as the eye and other organs are; however, it would follow that there must be another object [of its activity], just as there are objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) for the eye and others. For the eye and the rest become instruments for the living self through their respective functions, such as the perception of color-form.
