Furthermore, only eleven classes of effects, beginning with the perception of color-form, have been enumerated for the sake of which the eleven vital breaths are comprised;
no twelfth class of effects is known for the sake of which this twelfth vital breath could be postulated.
To this, he recites the following: "And because it is not an act, there is no fault; for thus [the scripture] shows."
First of all, the objection that it would lead to the consequence of [the prāṇa] having other objects is not a fault, because the prāṇa is not an instrument;
for we do not admit that the prāṇa functions as an instrument through the delimitation of objects, as is the case with the eye and other senses. This is the second chapter.
And yet, it does not follow from this that there is an absolute absence of activity for him.

Why? Because scripture, in the dialogues of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and elsewhere, demonstrates a specific function of the chief vital breath that is impossible for the other breaths. Beginning with "Now indeed the vital breaths disputed as to who was the best," and proposing, "He among you upon whose departure the body appears most wretched—he is the best," the scripture shows that when each of the others, such as speech, departs, life continues just as before, though deprived of their respective functions. Then, showing that at the time of the chief breath's desire to depart there occurs a loosening of speech and the rest and the danger of the body falling, the scripture demonstrates that the stability of the body and the senses is dependent upon the vital breath.

The most excellent Prāṇa said to them: "Do not fall into delusion; it is I alone who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this body. The Śruti declares this very same meaning: "By means of Prāṇa, he protects the lower nest," which shows that while the eyes and other organs are asleep, the protection of the body is due to Prāṇa. Furthermore, "From whichever limb Prāṇa departs, that very limb withers," and "Whatsoever he eats and whatsoever he drinks, by that he sustains the other organs," which shows that the nourishment of the body and the senses is due to Prāṇa.

The texts, "In what, indeed, having departed, shall I depart? Or in what, being established, shall I be established? and "He created the vital breath (prāṇa)," show that the soul's departure and establishment are caused by the vital breath.

It is designated as having five functions, like the mind. For this reason, there exists a specific function of the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa); it is designated in the Śrutis as having five functions: "Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda).

And this differentiation of functions is as follows: the *prāṇa* has a forward-moving function, consisting of actions such as inhalation, depending on its specific effects; the *apāna* has a downward-moving function, consisting of actions such as exhalation; the *vyāna* exists at the junction of those two and is the cause of vigorous actions; the *udāna* has an upward-moving function and is the cause of departure from the body (*utkrānti*) and so forth; and the *samāna* is that which carries the essence of food equally through all the limbs—thus the *prāṇa* has five functions. "Like the mind" means that just as the mind has five functions, so too does the *prāṇa*.
The five functions of the mind are well known, being caused by the ear and other senses and having sound and other objects as their domain.
However, the [mental states] enumerated in the passage beginning with "desire, resolve" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3) should not be included here, because that would exceed the number five.

But one might object: even here, there exists another function of the mind independent of the ears and other organs, having as its objects the past, the future, and so forth; thus, the excess over the number five remains the same. To this we reply: in that case, according to the maxim "the opinion of another, if unrefuted, is accepted," we shall also accept here the five functions of the mind well-known in the Yoga-śāstra, namely: "right cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory."
Or rather, it should be understood that the mind is cited as an illustration for the vital breath merely because of its possession of multiple functions.
Alternatively, one may connect the argument thus: the vital breath is also an instrument of the individual soul because it possesses five functions, just like the mind.
And [the chief vital breath] is atomic. (Sūtra 2.4.13) This chief vital breath is to be understood as atomic, like the other vital breaths.
And here too, "atomicity" refers to subtlety and limitedness, not to being equal in size to an atom; for, due to its pre-eminence and its fivefold functions, it pervades the entire body.
Topic:

The subtle vital breath (prāṇa) is atomic, because it is not perceived by a person standing nearby at the time of departure; and it is limited, on account of scriptural texts concerning its departure, movement, and return.

But is it not also taught that the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses omnipresence in such passages as, "He is equal to a fly, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, equal to all this"?

To this it is replied: this omnipresence is recorded with reference to the cosmic vital breath (hairaṇyagarbha) itself, which exists in the form of both the collective totality (samaṣṭi) and the individual manifestations (vyaṣṭi) within the divine realm (ādhidaivika), and not with reference to the vital breath within the body (ādhyātmika).
Moreover, by the statement of equality in "equal to a fly" and so forth, the very limitation of the vital breath residing in each individual living being is demonstrated.
Therefore, there is no fault.
But the presiding over fire and the other elements belongs to Him, because of the scriptural teaching to that effect.

Furthermore, it is now considered whether these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) under discussion are capable of performing their respective functions by their own power alone, or whether they are capable of doing so only when presided over by deities; this is examined starting with light (*jyotis*). On this point, the initial position is as follows: the vital breaths would proceed by their own power alone, because they possess the capacity for their respective effects.

Moreover, if it were understood that the vital breaths proceed under the superintendence of deities, it would follow that those presiding deities themselves are the enjoyers, whereby the individual soul's status as the enjoyer would be lost;
therefore, their activity must proceed by its own power.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "But there is superintendence by light and the rest."
By the word "tu" (but), the prima facie view is set aside.

He asserts that the collection of instruments, such as speech and so forth, presided over by deities who identify themselves with fire and the rest—namely Jyotis and others—proceeds toward their respective functions.
And he explains the reason for this: "Because of the scriptural teaching of that" (*tadāmananāt*).

For they declare: "Having become speech, [the breaths] entered the mouth," and so forth; and this state of fire as speech and its entry into the mouth is stated by accepting that it presides over them in the form of a deity, for apart from a connection with a deity, no specific relationship of fire with speech or the mouth is observed.

In the same way, passages such as "Air, having become breath, entered the nostrils" should also be applied accordingly. Furthermore, elsewhere, by stating that speech and the other organs possess the nature of light through their association with fire and the like—as in "Speech indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and glows with fire as its light"—the text confirms this very point.

Moreover, by stating that speech and the others attain the state of fire and the rest—as in "He carried speech across first; when it was released from death, it became fire"—the text illuminates this same meaning.

And everywhere, through this very proximity, there occurs a sequential enumeration of speech and the other [senses] with fire and the other [deities], according to the division between the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata).
Even in the Smṛti it is said:
"The Brahmins who perceive the truth declare that speech is the internal [aspect]. (Brahmasūtra 2.4.15)

By the passage beginning with "But the *adhibhūta* is to be declared as fire, and therein the *adhidaivata* is [fire]," the fact that speech and the other organs are presided over by deities such as Agni has been demonstrated in detail.

As for the claim that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) would function by their own majesty alone through the possession of power for their respective functions—that is incorrect; for we observe that even capable things like carts function only when presided over by oxen and the like.
Since both explanations are possible, it is on the basis of scripture (*āgama*) that the presiding of deities over speech and the others is established.

As for what was said—that it would follow that the presiding deities themselves are the enjoyers, and not the embodied soul—that is refuted by the statement: "By one who possesses vital breaths, on account of the scriptural word."

Even though there exist presiding deities for the vital breaths, it is understood from scripture that the connection of these vital breaths is with the embodied self alone—the possessor of the vital breaths and the master of the aggregate of causes and effects. For thus says the scripture: "Now, where this eye is directed toward space, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing. And he who knows, 'Let me smell this,' he is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling. Scriptural passages of this kind declare the connection of the vital breaths with the embodied self alone.
Moreover, because there would be a plurality of presiding deities for each individual organ, their status as the enjoyer in this body is not tenable;
for it is understood that there is only one embodied enjoyer in this body, since such functions as the synthesis of experiences are possible only for a single subject.
And because that [self] is eternal.

And that embodied self possesses permanence within this body by virtue of being the experiencer, because it is possible for it to be smeared by merit and demerit and because the experience of pleasure and pain is possible for it; this is not the case for the deities.
For they, abiding in a state of supreme sovereignty, are not entitled to assume the status of an experiencer in this inferior body.
And there is a scriptural text to this effect: "Merit alone goes to him [the deceased]; indeed, evil does not go to the gods."

Furthermore, the connection of the vital breaths with the embodied soul is constant, as their persistence is observed during the processes of departure from the body and so forth—according to such scriptural texts as: "When he departs, the vital breath departs after him; when the vital breath departs, all the other breaths depart after it. Therefore, even though there exist deities who govern the organs, the status of the embodied soul as the enjoyer does not disappear;
for the deities belong to the category of instruments (karaṇa), not to the category of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ).
Those are the organs, because they are designated as such [in scripture], except for the best one.

The principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) and the other eleven vital breaths have been enumerated; regarding this, another doubt arises: are the other sense-vital breaths merely different functions of the principal vital breath itself, or are they distinct entities?
What, then, is the initial position? That the others are indeed different functions of the principal vital breath.
Why? Because of scripture (*śruti*).

For scripture, having brought together both the principal breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) and the other breaths, declares that the others have the principal as their self: "Come, let us all assume his very form.
This is the section [concerning] the second chapter.
"All became form," it says;
and because the word "prāṇa" is used in the singular, there is a determination of oneness.

Otherwise, it would result in the improper consequence of the word "prāṇa" having multiple meanings, or else its primary sense would have to be restricted to one instance while being figurative in the other.
[Otherwise] it would result in [the organs] being merely derivative characteristics (*lākṣaṇikatva*).
Therefore, just as there are five functions (*vṛtti*)—namely prāṇa and so forth—of the single prāṇa itself, so too there are eleven [functions] beginning with speech (*vāk*);
this being the position reached, we reply: speech and the others are indeed distinct principles (*tattvāntara*) from the prāṇa.
Why? Because of the difference in designation (*vyapadeśabheda*).

What is this difference in designation? Those aforementioned vital breaths (*prāṇa*), excluding the "best" one, are called the remaining eleven organs (*indriya*), because such a difference in designation is seen in the Scripture itself. For in passages of this kind, such as "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the organs," the vital breath is designated separately and the organs are designated separately.
[Objection: If this is so, then the mind also, like the vital breath, should be excluded from being an organ, since it is seen to be designated separately in the phrase "the mind and all the organs."
This is true; however, according to the Smṛti, there are eleven organs, and thus the mind (manas) is also included as an organ along with the ear and the others.
But the status of the vital breath (prāṇa) as an organ is not established either in Śruti or in Smṛti.
Furthermore, this distinction in designation is appropriate only if there is a difference in their essential natures (tattva).
But if they were identical in essence, it would be contradictory to say that the one and same Prāṇa, while being one, both receives and does not receive the designation of "sense-organ.
Therefore, the others are distinct entities from the principal Prāṇa.
And for what reason are they distinct entities? In the Sūtra-bhāṣya: "Because of the scriptural teaching of their difference."

Furthermore, the vital breath (prāṇa) is heard of everywhere as distinct from speech and the other organs; for instance, beginning with "They said to Speech," and after presenting Speech and the others as being struck down by the evil of the Asuras, the section concerning Speech and the rest is concluded, and then the chief vital breath, which destroys the Asuras, is introduced separately: "Then they said to this breath in the mouth. Likewise, other scriptural texts that teach distinction, such as "He made mind, speech, and breath for himself," should also be cited. Therefore, the others are indeed different entities from the chief vital breath.
And for what further reason are they distinct entities? Because of their difference in characteristics.
There is also a distinction: while the others, such as speech and so forth, are asleep, the principal one alone remains awake;
and while he alone is untouched by death, the others are subject to it;
furthermore, it is his staying and departing that cause the maintenance and falling of the body, not those of the senses.

Furthermore, there is a manifold difference in characteristics between the vital breath (prāṇa) and the sense organs (indriyas), such as that the sense organs serve as the cause for the perception of objects, whereas the vital breath does not.
Therefore, their status as distinct principles is established.

As for the argument that "the sense organs are indeed the vital breath" based on the scriptural statement, "All these became its very form," that is incorrect; for even in that passage, a distinction is perceived upon examining the preceding and following context.

For instance, after enumerating the organs beginning with speech—starting with "I shall indeed speak" and "I have taken hold of speech"—and having stated that speech and the others were seized by Death in the form of exhaustion, as in "Death, becoming weariness, overtook them; therefore speech indeed becomes weary," the text then proceeds to enumerate the central breath separately as one not overcome by Death: "But he did not reach this one, which is the middle breath."

And by saying, "He is indeed the best among us," one determines his preeminence; therefore, it must be understood that the speech and other organs' acquisition of movement and their becoming of his form are dependent upon the Prāṇa in a manner consistent with that preeminence, but not through identity.
For this very reason, it is established that the word "Prāṇa" is used for the sense-organs in a figurative sense;
and thus says the Śruti: "All of them became his very form."

Therefore, they are designated by this term "prāṇas"; thus [the author] shows that the word *prāṇa*, which primarily refers to the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), has a figurative application (*lākṣaṇikavṛtti*) to the sense organs.
Consequently, speech and the others are distinct entities from the vital breath; they are the sense organs.
But that fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who performs the tripartition, because of the scriptural instruction.

In the section concerning the sixfold process (*satprakriyā*), after describing the creation of fire, water, and food, it is taught: "This deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva*) whose nature is name and form, and let me manifest names and forms.

[And] having determined their arrangement, [she thought]: 'Let me make each one of them threefold. Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is this manifestation of names and forms performed by the individual soul (*jīva*), or is it performed by the Supreme Lord? On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: this manifestation of names and forms is indeed performed by the individual soul.

Why? Because of the qualification "by this living self" (anena jīvenātmanā). Just as in common worldly usage, for example in the expression, "Having entered the enemy's army by means of a spy, I shall enumerate it," the king—who is the causal agent—superimposes upon himself the enumeration of the army, which is actually performed by the spy, by using the first person verb "I shall enumerate" (saṃkalayāni); even so, the deity—who is the causal agent—superimposes upon itself the differentiation of names and forms, which is actually performed by the individual soul (jīva), by using the first person verb "I shall differentiate" (vyākaravāṇi).
Moreover, in names such as "Ḍittha" and "Ḍavittha," and in forms such as "jar" and "bowl," it is observed that the soul alone is the agent of manifestation.
Therefore, when the prima facie view is reached that this manifestation of name and form has the individual soul as its agent, the author states: "But [it is] the fashioning of names and forms...
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
"The fashioning of names and forms" means the differentiation of name and form.

The phrase "making tripartite" indicates the Supreme Lord, because he is designated as the undisputed agent of the tripartition. This fashioning of names—such as fire, sun, moon, and lightning—and this fashioning of forms—such as those found in grass, reeds, leaves, and so on, as well as in cattle, wild animals, humans, and so forth, which occurs in manifold ways according to each species and each individual—all this must indeed be the work of the Supreme Lord alone, who fashions fire, water, and food.
Why? Because of the scriptural teaching.

For instance—beginning with "That divinity," and continuing in the second chapter with the use of the first-person pronoun in "Let me evolve [the names and forms]," it is taught here that the agency of evolution belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone. Now, one might object: because of the qualification "by means of the living self" (jīvena), it is determined that the act of evolution has the individual soul as its agent. This is not so; for...
The word "by the individual soul" (*jīvena*) is connected with the phrase "having entered," due to their immediate proximity;
it is not connected with "I shall manifest," for if it were so connected, the first-person verb "I shall manifest" would have to be interpreted figuratively as referring to the Deity.
Furthermore, the individual soul, which is not the Lord, lacks the power to manifest the various names and forms found in mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth.
Furthermore, even in those cases where there is capacity [for action], that too is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Lord.

Nor is the so-called individual soul (jīva) absolutely different from the Supreme Lord, like a servant is from a king, because of the qualification "by the Self" and because the state of being a jīva is based solely on limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Therefore, even the differentiation of names and forms performed by him is indeed performed by the Supreme Lord; and that the Supreme Lord alone is the differentiator of names and forms is the established doctrine of all the Upaniṣads, according to such scriptural texts as, "Ether, verily, is the bringer-out of name and form."
Therefore, the differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Lord alone as he performs the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).

It is precisely this differentiation of names and forms preceded by tripartition that is intended here, because the differentiation of each individual name and form has already been stated by the mention of the production of fire, water, and food;

and Śruti demonstrates that tripartition in the case of fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning, beginning with the passage: "That which is the red color of fire is the color of fire, that which is white is the color of water, and that which is black is the color of food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1).
In that context, "fire" is this form that is manifested; and when the form is manifested, because of the acquisition of its object, "fire" is this name that is manifested.
The same should be understood regarding the sun, the moon, and lightning as well.

By this illustration of fire, the threefold combination (trivṛtkaraṇa) is stated without distinction for all three substances—earthly, aqueous, and luminous—since the introduction and the conclusion are common to all.

For thus, the introduction is made without distinction: "These three deities become each one threefold"; and likewise, the conclusion is made without distinction, beginning with "That which appeared as if red was the form of fire," and ending with "That which appeared as if unknown was a combination of these very same deities."

Regarding those three deities which have already been made tripartite externally, another internal tripartition has been stated: "These three deities, having reached the person, each become tripartite.

Now the Teacher demonstrates this exactly according to the scripture, while intending to remove certain suspected defects, [stating]: "The flesh and so forth are from the earth, according to the word; and so it is for the other two."
From the threefold earth being consumed by a person, its effects such as flesh and so forth are produced according to the scriptural texts;
for thus says the Śruti: "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts.
Of it, that which is the grossest constituent becomes feces; that which is the middle one becomes flesh; that which is the subtlest becomes mind. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.1)
The meaning is that this very earth, once differentiated, is eaten in the form of food such as rice and barley;
and of that [earth], its coarsest form goes outwards in the state of excrement,
while its middling form nourishes the flesh within the body.
The mind, however, is the subtlest.

In this same manner, the effects of the other two—water and fire—should be understood according to the scriptural statements: urine, blood, and breath are the effects of water; bone, marrow, and speech are the effects of fire.

The opponent (Mistī) says here: If all elements and elemental products are indeed made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*), as stated without distinction in the scripture, "He made each of these threefold," then for what reason is this specific designation used, namely, "this is fire, these are waters, this is food"? Likewise, regarding the internal body (*adhyātma*): why is it said that the flesh and so forth are the effects of the food eaten, the blood and so forth are the effects of the water drunk, and the bones and so forth are the effects of the fire consumed? To this, it is replied: "But on account of the predominance (*vaiśeṣya*) [of one element], there is that designation; that designation."
The word "but" (tu) removes the objection raised.

"Vaiśeṣyam" means the state of being specific, that is to say, abundance. Even though there is a threefold combination (trivṛtkaraṇa), an abundance of a particular elemental constituent is observed in certain cases: fire has an abundance of heat (tejas), water has an abundance of moisture (ap), and earth has an abundance of food (anna).

Furthermore, this triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) is for the sake of common worldly usage (vyavahāra). And such usage regarding the three elements would not be established by the world through their distinction once they have attained oneness, like a rope made of three strands.

Therefore, even though triplication exists, the designation of the specific distinctions among fire, water, and food with respect to the elements and elemental objects is justified precisely because of their predominance (vaiśeṣya).
The repetition of the words "That discourse, that discourse" indicates the completion of the chapter.

Thus ends the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa-Parivrājaka-Ācārya).
The Third Chapter.

In the second chapter, the contradiction with Smṛti and reasoning regarding the realization of Brahman as ordained by the Vedānta has been resolved; the lack of authority of rival doctrines has been demonstrated, and the contradictions among the Śrutis have been refuted;
and therein it was stated that the principles distinct from the individual soul (jīva), which serve as its instruments, are born from Brahman.

Now, in this third [section], the following group of topics will be investigated: the manner in which the individual soul (*jīva*), when endowed with its instruments (*upakaraṇa*), undergoes the various states of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-gati*); the intermediate states of that [soul]; the true nature of Brahman (*brahma-tattva*); the distinction and non-distinction of various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*); the combination and non-combination of qualities (*guṇa*); the attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) through perfect realization (*samyag-darśana*); the different types of injunctions regarding the means to perfect realization; and the lack of uniformity regarding the fruit of liberation (*mukti*).
Furthermore, certain other matters will be discussed as they arise in connection with these topics.

In that regard, first of all, in the first chapter, the various paths of transmigratory existence are demonstrated by relying on the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), because at the end it is heard [in the text]: "Therefore, one should feel aversion."

It has been understood from scriptural passages situated within the context of transmigratory existence—beginning with "Now these vital breaths (prāṇas) gather around him" and ending with "He creates for himself another newer and more beautiful form"—as well as from the possibility of experiencing the fruits of merit and demerit, that the individual soul (jīva), accompanied by the chief vital breath, the sense organs, and the mind, and taking along with it ignorance, karma, and the impressions of past experience (pūrvaprajñā), leaves its former body and attains another body.
Now, it is considered whether it goes enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), which are the seeds of the body, or whether it goes unenveloped.
What, then, is the prima facie view in the commentary on the Sūtra? That he is not enveloped by the elements.

Why? Because there is no scriptural mention of his taking up the elements, as there is of his taking up the organs. For in the passage, "He, taking these subtle essences of light," the term "subtle essences of light" denotes the taking up of the organs, since the eyes and other organs are mentioned in the remainder of the sentence;
whereas there is no such mention of his taking up the subtle elements.
Furthermore, the elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are easily available everywhere; they exist right where the body is to be commenced.

Therefore, their being led [from one body to another] would be purposeless. Consequently, when the prima facie view is reached that "he goes unenclosed," the Teacher [Bādarāyaṇa] reads: "In the attainment of another [body], he moves along, enclosed";
this is known from both the question and the explanation.
"At the transition to that other state, he goes enveloped.
This means that at the transition to another body—that is, at the attainment of a new body—he goes, meaning he departs, enveloped by the subtle elements which are the seeds of the body.
Why? Because of the repetition of the question and its explanation [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]. Chapter Three.

Indeed, for this reason, the question is: "Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be designated as a person? And the determination is the answer given through the process of understanding, concerning the sequence of the rain-cloud, the earth, the man, and the woman as the substrata.

Having shown the five oblations in the form of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen within the five fires, [the Chāndogya Upaniṣad] states: "Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'.
Therefore, it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) departs, moving along, enveloped by water.
But is it not the case that another scriptural passage, "like a caterpillar," shows that [the soul] does not abandon the previous body until it has stepped into another body?

Even in that case, there is no contradiction, because it is merely the prolongation of the cultivation of the object—the body to be attained—which is projected by karma, that is compared to a leech, provided that [the soul] remains unenveloped.

Since the manner of attaining another body has been thus declared by Śruti, all those conceptualizations originating from human intellect—which suggest that upon attaining another body, there is either the acquisition of functioning for the pervasive organs and the Self under the influence of karma; or that only the isolated Self acquires functioning there while the sense organs are produced anew at each place of experience just like the body; or that the mind alone proceeds toward the place of experience; or that the individual soul (jīva) itself, having leaped out of one body, attains another body like a parrot moving from one tree to another—all these are to be disregarded, because they contradict Śruti.

In the commentary on the Sūtra: [Objection]—Surely, from the question and answer cited above, it follows that [the soul] departs enveloped by water alone, because of the force of the mention of the word "water" (apa);

how then can it be asserted in general that it departs enveloped by the subtle elements of all [three] states of being? To this, he reads the reply: "But because of its consisting of the three [elements], and because of their predominance."
With the word "tu" (but), he cuts away the doubt that has been raised:

for water is threefold in nature, according to the scriptural teaching on triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*); and when those [waters] are accepted as the constituent causes, the other two elements must necessarily also be accepted.
Furthermore, the body consists of three constituents, because the effects of all three—fire, water, and food—are perceived therein.
Moreover, it is tripartite by virtue of having three humors (dhātus), namely wind, bile, and phlegm;
it cannot be produced by water alone, setting aside the other elements.
Therefore, this word "water" (*āpas*) in the question and the answer—"Water, having assumed a human form"—refers to the predominance [of water], not to its absolute isolation;
for in all bodies, a predominance of liquid substances such as lymph and blood is observed.
But surely, the earth-element (*pārthiva-dhātu*) is perceived as the most abundant in bodies?
This is not a fault, for there will be an abundance of water in relation to the other [elements];
and an abundance of fluidity is observed even in the seed of the body, characterized by semen and blood.
Furthermore, karma is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) in the commencement of another body.

Furthermore, rituals such as the Agnihotra depend upon liquid substances like Soma, clarified butter, and milk; and the waters inherent in those rituals, denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā), are offered together with the rituals into the fire called the world of the moon (Soma-loka),
as will be stated in the third chapter.
Therefore, the abundance of water is established;
and because of this abundance, it is faultless to conclude that by the word "water" (āpaḥ), all the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which are the seeds of the body are intended.
And because of the movement of the vital breaths.

Furthermore, the movement of the vital breaths (prāṇas) at the time of attaining another body is declared by scriptural texts such as: "When he departs, the prāṇa departs after him; when the prāṇa departs, all the other prāṇas depart after it.

Since this movement of the prāṇas is not possible without a substratum, it follows by implication that the waters—which serve as their substratum and are conjoined with the other elements—also possess movement, being impelled by the movement of the prāṇas.
For the prāṇas never move or remain anywhere without a substratum, as is observed in the case of a living being.
If it be argued that [the soul does not go to Brahman] because of the scriptural mention of its going to Agni and others, we say no, because that is figurative.

It might be argued: "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not indeed depart together with the individual soul (*jīva*) upon the attainment of another body, because of the scriptural texts concerning their departure into fire and so forth.

For scripture shows that at the time of death the vital breaths such as speech go to the deities such as fire, in the passage beginning: 'When this person has died, his speech goes into fire, his breath into wind,' and so on. To this we say: No, because that is figurative.

The scriptural statement regarding the transition of speech and the other organs into fire and the other elements is figurative, because it is not observed that the body hairs and head hairs go [there]; for it is recorded in the scripture: "The body hairs go to the herbs, the head hairs to the trees" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.6). Indeed, it is not possible that the body hairs and head hairs, having departed, go to the herbs and trees;
nor is movement conceivable for the individual soul if its limiting adjunct, the vital breaths, were rejected;
nor is experience in another body possible without the vital breaths.
Moreover, the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) along with the individual soul (jīva) to another place is clearly proclaimed in scripture;

therefore, it is only figuratively stated that speech and the other organs go to Agni and the other deities—who are their presiding deities and benefactors—at the time of death, based merely on the cessation of their assistance.

If it be argued that [the intermediate state] does not exist because it is not mentioned in the first [sūtra], we say no; for it is indeed those very [beings] who are referred to, as this is logically consistent.

It might be argued: "How can it be determined that 'in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called man,' when there is no mention of water at all in the first fire? For here, the five fires beginning with the world are taught as the substrata for the five oblations;

and at their head, having introduced them with the words, 'That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire,' it is stated, 'In that very fire, the gods offer faith (śraddhā),' whereby faith is presented as the substance to be offered.
Water is not heard of there as the substance to be offered."

If, indeed, water were to be imagined as the substance to be offered (*homya-dravya*) in the four subsequent fires beginning with Parjanya—let it be so imagined, for in those cases it is logical that Soma and the other substances, which are presented as things to be offered, are abundant;
however, in the first fire, to abandon the "faith" (*śraddhā*) explicitly mentioned in the scripture and instead imagine unmentioned water is sheer rashness. This concludes the third chapter.
This is indeed reckless.
If it is argued that faith (*śraddhā*) is indeed a specific kind of mental state (a *pratyaya-viśeṣa*), by virtue of its conventional usage,
and therefore it is incorrect to say that water attains the state of a person at the fifth oblation— this is not a fault;
for even there, in the first fire, those very waters are intended by the word "faith."
Why? Because of the logical consistency (*upapatti*).
For in this way, through the connection of the beginning, middle, and end, this constitutes a single coherent sentence without confusion.

Otherwise, however, when it is asked how water comes to be called "man" at the fifth oblation, if one were to introduce "faith" (*śraddhā*) as the substance to be offered at the place of the first oblation during the response, then the question would be of one nature and the answer of another, and there would be no unity of the discourse.
And by concluding with the words, "Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters become the essence of man," [the text] demonstrates this very point.

Furthermore, the effects of faith—such as Soma, rain, and so forth—are observed to consist predominantly of water as they become grossified; and that is the logical reason for faith being of the nature of water.
For the effect must correspond to its cause.

Furthermore, that which is called "faith" (śraddhā)—being a quality of either the mind or the individual soul (jīva)—cannot be extracted from its substrate and employed for the oblation, as one might extract the heart and other organs from a sacrificial animal. Therefore, it must be water itself that is denoted by the word "faith.
Moreover, the word "faith" is appropriately applied to water, as seen in Vedic usage: "Water, indeed, is faith" (śraddhā vā āpaḥ).

The waters, which constitute the seed of the body, attain a state of subtlety and acquire a resemblance to faith; therefore, they may be designated by the word "faith," just as a man possessing the prowess of a lion is called a "lion.

Furthermore, because of their association with actions preceded by faith, the term "faith" appropriately applies to the waters, just as the word "chariot" is applied to men [who are parts of a chariot].

Moreover, the designation "faith" is justified because the waters are the cause of faith, according to the Vedic scripture: "The waters indeed bow down to him for the sake of meritorious action, providing faith."
If it be argued that this is not so because [the path] is not mentioned in scripture, we say no, because those who perform sacrifices and other works are known [to travel by it].

Now, it might be argued: "Indeed, by means of the question and answer, it is established that the waters, through the sequence beginning with faith, assume the form of a person upon the fifth oblation;

however, the individual souls (jīvas) cannot depart enveloped by those [waters], because this is not heard in scripture. For here there is no word that makes known the souls in the same way as it does the waters.
Therefore, the statement that 'he departs enveloped' is incorrect. If this is the objection, it is not a valid fault.

Why? Because those who perform sacrifices and other works are recognized [in this context]. Starting with the passage, "Now, those here in the village who worship by means of sacrifice, works of public utility, and charity—they pass into smoke," the text describes how those who perform sacrifices and other works reach the moon by way of the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) via smoke and so forth, saying, "From space they go to the moon; that is King Soma.
These very same persons are understood here as well, because of the similarity of the scriptural statement: "In this very fire the gods offer faith; from that oblation King Soma arises."

Furthermore, for those [performers of rites], substances such as curd and milk—which serve as the means for performing rituals like the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa—are visibly water due to their preponderance of liquid substance.

When these are offered into the Āhavanīya fire, they become subtle oblations in the form of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which take hold of those who perform sacrifices and other such works. And their body, according to the ritual procedure for cremation, the officiating priests offer it into the final fire with the mantra:
"To that world of heaven, Svāhā! Thus ends the third chapter.

Therefore, that which is expressed here by the verb "to offer" (*juhoti*) in the phrase "they offer faith" (*śraddhāṃ juhvatīti*) is as follows: the waters, which are associated with ritual acts preceded by faith and consist of the nature of the oblation, having assumed the form of the *apūrva* (unseen potential), envelop the individual souls (*jīvas*) who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭāpūrta*, and lead them to that world for the purpose of bestowing the fruit.

Thus, in the Agnihotra section, through the supplementary passage consisting of the explanation of the six questions—beginning with "These two oblations, once offered, depart"—the attainment of another world for the commencement of the fruit of the Agnihotra oblations is demonstrated.
Therefore, those living beings, embraced by the waters consisting of the oblations, depart for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their own karma.

But how can this departure of those who perform sacrifices and pious works for the sake of enjoying the fruits of their own karma be maintained, when another scriptural passage concerning the same subject—namely, that those who have ascended to the moon by way of the path characterized by smoke are shown to become food, stating: "This is King Soma; that is the food of the gods; the gods eat it"—and another scriptural passage with the same scope states: "Having reached the moon, they become food; there the gods eat them, just as they consume King Soma with the words, 'Swell up! Wane away!'? Furthermore, it is argued that enjoyment is not possible for those being eaten by the gods, as if they were being devoured by tigers and other beasts.

To this, he reads the following: "Or [it is] figurative, because of the lack of knowledge of the Self; for thus the scripture shows. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda 3, section 1). The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to set aside the objection previously raised.
Their status as food is figurative, not primary;
for if their being food were primary, scriptural injunctions regarding qualification—such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice"—would be contradicted.
If, in the lunar orb, the performers of sacrifices and other rites were the enjoyers, for what purpose would those entitled to the results perform such laborious acts as sacrifices and the like?

Furthermore, the word "food" (anna) is seen to be used figuratively even for that which is not food, on account of the commonality of being a cause of enjoyment; for example, it is said, "The Vaiśyas are the food of kings," and "Cattle are the food of the Vaiśyas.

Therefore, the "eating" intended here refers to the gods' pleasure and recreation by means of those who have performed sacrifices and other rites—who have entered into a subordinate status—just as one enjoys the company of beloved wives, sons, friends, and servants; it does not mean chewing or swallowing them like sweetmeats and the like.
Furthermore, the passage, "The gods indeed neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar," precludes any activity such as chewing on the part of the gods.
And for those performers of sacrifices and other rites who have entered into a subordinate state toward the gods, enjoyment is possible—just as it is for the attendants who live off a king.
Moreover, because the performers of sacrifices and other rites do not possess self-knowledge (*anātmavit*), their status as objects of enjoyment for the gods is logically established.

For thus the Śruti shows that those who do not know the Self are objects of enjoyment for the gods: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like a beast to the gods.

It is understood that in this world, by pleasing the gods with sacrifices and other rites, he serves them like a beast; and in the other world as well, subsisting upon them and enjoying the fruits prescribed by them, he serves the gods just like a beast.
The Third Chapter.

An alternative explanation of the aphorism *anātmavittvāt tathā hi darśayati* (Because they do not know the Self, for so [the scripture] shows) is as follows: These performers of sacrifices and the like are indeed non-knowers of the Self (*anātmavid*) who are mere ritualists (*kevalakarmin*), not practitioners of the combined performance of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*). Here, the "knowledge of the five fires" (*pañcāgnividyā*) is figuratively designated as "knowledge of the Self" (*ātmavidyā*) because of the context. Furthermore, because these performers of sacrifices lack the knowledge of the five fires, their status as food is presented through figurative description (*guṇavāda*) in order to praise the knowledge of the five fires.
The practice of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) is intended [to apply] here, because this is understood from the purport of the passage.
For another scriptural text (*śruti*) shows the existence of enjoyment in the lunar sphere: "Having experienced greatness in the world of Soma, he returns again.

Likewise, another scriptural text also shows that those who perform sacrifices and the like attain enjoyment while dwelling together with the gods: "Now, a hundred joys of the ancestors who have won their worlds constitute one joy of the 'gods by action' (*karmadeva*), who attain the state of divinity through their ritual acts. Thus, it is shown that those who perform sacrifices and the like attain enjoyment while living together with the gods.
Thus, because the statement regarding the state of being food is used figuratively, it is understood that the living selves of those who perform sacrifices and other rites proceed here.
Therefore, it is rightly said that "he proceeds enveloped."
Upon the exhaustion of the performed [work], one who possesses residual karma returns by the same way and not by that way, according to what is seen and what is remembered in scripture.

Regarding those performers of sacrifices and other rites who have ascended to the lunar orb by the path of smoke and so forth, and having experienced their enjoyment, their descent from there is recorded in scripture, beginning with: "Having dwelt there until their [merit] is exhausted, they then return again by that very same path as they came" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5), up to: "Those whose conduct was virtuous attain the womb of a Brāhmaṇa or others;
those whose conduct was base attain the womb of a dog or others.
This must now be investigated: do they descend without any remainder of karma (*niranuśaya*), having exhausted all their actions, or rather, with a remainder (*sānuśaya*)?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are "without residual karma" (niranuśaya).

Why? Because of the qualification "as far as the falling together" (yāvatsampātam); by the word *sampāta*, the store of karma (*karmāśaya*) is meant, since it is by means of this that [beings] fall from this world to that world for the sake of experiencing the fruits.
Furthermore, the phrase "having dwelt as far as the falling together" shows that the entirety of that performed [karma] has been exhausted right there.
And this very same point is demonstrated by another scriptural passage: "When that [merit] of theirs comes to an end.

One might argue: "I shall assume that he enjoys only as much karma as is to be experienced in that world. But it is not possible to assume this, because of the reference elsewhere in the phrase "whatever [he does]" (yatkiñca): "Having reached the end of that karma, whatever he does here..."

"From that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action"—thus says another Śruti passage. By means of the non-specific reference "whatever [he has done]," it shows the exhaustion there of all the karma performed here without exception. Moreover, death is the manifestor of karma whose fruit has not yet begun;
for manifestation is impossible for that which has been obstructed by karma whose fruit has already begun prior to death.
And that [destruction], being without distinction, is the manifestor of everything whatsoever whose fruit has not yet begun;
for when the cause is common, the effect cannot be uncommon. (Sūtra, Third Chapter)
For it is not tenable that, when the proximity of a lamp is equal for both, a jar is manifested but a cloth is not.

Therefore, when it has been argued that those who descend do so without any residual karma (*anushaya*), we reply: "Upon the exhaustion of [the results of] what was done, he descends possessing a residual karma."

By whatever mass of karma they have ascended to the moon for the enjoyment of its fruits, when that [karma] is exhausted through such enjoyment, their watery body—which was commenced for the sake of enjoyment on the moon—melts away due to contact with the fire of grief at the sight of the exhaustion of enjoyment, just as hailstones melt from contact with the rays of the sun, or as the hardness of ghee melts from contact with the flames of fire.

Then, "when the performed [karma] has passed away"—that is, when the fruit of the performed karma, such as sacrifices and the like, has been consumed through enjoyment—they descend to this world still possessing a remainder of karma (*sānuśayā*).
For what reason? He says: "On account of perception and scripture."

For indeed, direct scriptural revelation shows the descent of those with residual karma (*sānuśaya*): "Now, those here whose conduct has been pleasant, it is likely they will attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya; but those here whose conduct has been foul, it is likely they will attain a foul womb—the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla.
He will later explain that by the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*), residual karma is indicated.

Moreover, this experience, which is observed to be distributed among individual living beings in various high and low forms from the very moment of birth, indicates the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), since its occurrence cannot be accidental; for it is understood through scripture in general that prosperity and adversity have good and evil deeds as their causes.

Furthermore, the *Smṛti* in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* also shows that the descent occurs only for those with residual karma (*sānuśaya*), stating: "The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after dying and experiencing the fruit of their actions, then—by means of the remainder—obtain birth characterized by distinguished place, caste, family, form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence."

What, then, is this so-called *anuśaya* (latent tendency)? Some say that it is a certain remainder of the karma performed for the sake of heaven after its fruit has been experienced, like the oil adhering to a vessel. For just as a vessel of oil, when being emptied, is not emptied in its entirety, but some residue of oil remains adhering to the vessel, so too is the *anuśaya*.
[Objection: But since what is seen is opposed to its effect, it is not logical for a remainder to persist once the fruit has been experienced.
[Response: This is not a fault.
For we do not assert that the fruit of karma has been fully enjoyed in its entirety.
[Objection: But surely they have ascended to the lunar sphere for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of their karma without remainder.
[Reply: Certainly; nevertheless, even with only a small residue of karma remaining, staying there is no longer possible.

Just as it is said that a certain servant, having approached the royal court with all his service implements, is unable to remain at the royal court once, due to long absence, he has become depleted of many implements and possesses only a few remaining such as a parasol and sandals; even so, one who possesses only the remainder of their karma (*anuśaya*) is unable to remain in the lunar orb.
But this is not reasonable.

For it has been stated that the persistence of a remainder of a ritual action performed for the sake of heaven—once its fruit has been experienced—is not possible, because such a remainder would contradict the very nature of the result.
Now, it might be argued that this too has been addressed: namely, that it is not the case that the entire ritual action whose fruit is heaven will have its fruit fully experienced.

This is not plausible: namely, that an action performed for the sake of heaven does not produce its entire heavenly fruit for one who remains in heaven, but rather produces some small portion of that fruit even for one who has fallen from heaven. Such a conception is not tenable for those for whom the Vedic word is the sole authority.
In the case of an oil-vessel, however, the persistence of a trace of oil is logical because it is observed;
likewise, the persistence of a trace of implements is seen in the case of a servant;
but here, no such persistence of a trace of karma that has heaven as its fruit is observed.
Nor can it be conceived [that the remainder consists of the fruits of works], because that would contradict the scriptural teaching that heaven is the fruit [of those works].

This must necessarily be understood in this way: the *anuśaya* (remainder) is not a portion of the work such as sacrifice (*iṣṭādi*) which has heaven as its fruit, persisting like the oil that remains in a vessel.

For if one were to imagine that some single portion of that very same well-performed work—such as sacrifice—by which they experienced heaven constitutes the *anuśaya*, then the *anuśaya* would be exclusively pleasant and never the opposite.

In that case, this scriptural passage concerning the classification of residual karma (*anuśaya*) would be contradicted: "Now, those here whose conduct was pleasant, and those here whose conduct was foul.

Therefore, when the collection of karmas whose fruits are to be experienced in the next world has been exhausted, the remainder—the collection of other karmas whose fruits are to be experienced in this world—is the *anuśaya*; it is those possessing this who descend.

As for what was stated—that because of the reference to "whatever" without qualification, one reaches the end of all karma performed here by experiencing its results and descends without any residual karma (*niranuśaya*)—this is not so; for the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*) has been established. It is understood that "whatever karma performed here has a result in the next world and has begun to be experienced, having exhausted all of that by the experience of its results. Furthermore, as it was said in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*: "Because there is no distinction, [the fire] manifests the entire karma whose results have not yet begun."

In that regard, the claim that a distinction cannot be made—such that by some karma the fruit is commenced in the next world, while by others it is commenced in this one—is already refuted by the very demonstration of the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, it must be explained by what cause death (*prāyaṇa*) is asserted to be the manifestor of karma whose fruit has not yet been commenced.

If it should be argued that because the manifestation of another [karma] is impossible while one whose fruit has already begun is obstructing it, its manifestation occurs at the time of death due to the subsidence of that obstruction—then it must be said: just as before death there is no manifestation of another [karma] because it is obstructed by the karma whose fruit has begun, so too at the time of death, since it is impossible for multiple karmas with contradictory fruits to produce their results simultaneously, there can be no manifestation of a weaker karma when it is obstructed by a stronger one.

For it cannot be said that multiple karmas, whose fruits are to be experienced in different births, become manifest simultaneously at a single death simply because they share the commonality of having results not yet begun, and thus initiate a single birth; this would contradict the principle that each karma has its own specific fruit.
Nor can it be said that at death some karma becomes manifest while another is destroyed, for this would contradict the certainty of their fruition;
indeed, the destruction of karmas is not possible except through causes such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).

Smṛti also shows that another action, being obstructed by an action with a contrary result, persists for a long time; for instance, [it says]: "Sometimes a well-performed action remains here fixed, until one who is sinking in saṃsāra is liberated from evil" (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.21). Such is the nature of these passages.

Furthermore, if all karma whose fruits have not yet begun were manifested at a single death and initiated only one birth, then—since no further qualification for rebirth would be perceived in the realms of heaven, hell, or animal wombs—there would be no production of further merit or demerit due to the absence of a cause, and thus no subsequent birth could occur. Moreover, this would contradict the traditional Smṛti teachings that each individual act, such as the killing of a Brahmin, serves as the cause for multiple births.
Nor can any cause other than the scripture (śāstra) be conceived for the comprehension of the essential nature, fruits, and means of merit and demerit.
Furthermore, since death cannot be the manifestor of actions that yield visible results—such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice—this assumption that death is a universal manifestor is too narrow in scope;
even the illustration of the lamp has been refuted by demonstrating the relative strength and weakness of karmic forces.

This should be understood as being like the manifestation of gross and subtle forms. For just as a lamp, despite being equally present [to all objects], manifests a gross form and not a subtle one, so too death, although it provides an equal opportunity for the entire collection of uncommenced fruits of action, brings about the operation of a powerful karma and not that of a weak one. Therefore, this admission of the manifestation of all karma without exception is untenable, as it contradicts scripture, tradition, and logic.

The objection that "if residual karma remains, there would be the consequence of non-liberation" is also a misplaced anxiety, because scripture declares the destruction of all karma through right vision (*samyagdarśana*). Therefore, it is established that those who descend do so while possessing residual karma.
And as they descend, they do so both in the same manner and in a different manner as they ascended.
"Yathetam" means "as it was come";
"anevam" means "in the opposite manner.

Because smoke and space are mentioned as having been traversed on the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) during the descent, and because of the word "yathetam," it is understood that [the soul returns] "as it was come."
From the mention of "kingdom" (*rājya*) and so forth, as well as from the supplementary rule regarding "clouds" (*abhra*) and so forth, the opposite [of the primary meaning] is also understood.
If it be argued that [the term] refers to the feet, Kāṣrṇājini says it is for the purpose of indication.

Moreover, it might be argued that the scriptural passage cited to establish the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)—namely, "Those here whose conduct was pleasant"—indeed shows the attainment of a new birth resulting from conduct (*caraṇa*), not from latent dispositions.

"Conduct" (*caraṇa*) is one thing, while "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is another; conduct, character, and behavior are synonymous. Latent tendency, however, is intended to mean action (*karman*) remaining over from that which has already borne its fruit. Furthermore, scripture designates action and conduct as distinct: "As one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes"; and "Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, not others"; and "Those well-performed deeds of ours should be emulated by you."

If it be argued that, because of the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of other births based on one's conduct (*caraṇa*), the existence of residual karma (*anuśaya*) is not established, this is not a valid objection; for the teacher Kārṣṇājini considers that this scriptural mention of conduct is intended merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the residual karma.

"If it be argued that [the passage] is meaningless, we say no, because it depends on that. (Sūtra 3.1.9) It might be asked: why, discarding the directly stated (*śrauta*) conduct (*śīla*), is the latent disposition (*anuśaya*)—which is indicated only figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*)—understood by the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*)? Surely the result of birth in auspicious or inauspicious wombs will belong to the directly stated conduct itself, whether enjoined or prohibited, and consisting of good or evil forms. Furthermore, one must necessarily admit some fruit for conduct as well; otherwise, the futility of conduct would indeed follow. If this is the objection, it is not a valid fault. [The Sūtra continues: "Because it depends on that. It is not the case that conduct has no fruit at all. However, its fruit is subordinate to the fruit of the latent dispositions. For it is the latent dispositions that are the primary cause for attaining a particular state of existence; conduct merely serves as an auxiliary factor. Therefore, the word "conduct" refers to the latent dispositions by way of their accompaniment. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding conduct—namely, "By conduct one becomes a virtuous Brahmin, by conduct one becomes a Kṣatriya, by conduct one becomes a Vaiśya, and by conduct one becomes a Śūdra"—is also seen to refer to the latent dispositions. Why? Because of its dependence on that;
for the entire collection of rites such as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice depends upon conduct (*caraṇa*).
Indeed, no one devoid of good conduct (*sadācāra*) can be qualified [for these rites], according to such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as: "The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of conduct."
Even though conduct has human purpose as its goal, it is not purposeless;
for when a collection of rites such as sacrifices begins to produce its fruit, conduct—being dependent upon that very [rite]—will initiate some excellence therein.
And it is well known from Śruti and Smṛti that ritual action accomplishes all goals.
Therefore, according to the opinion of Kārṣṇājini, it is karma alone— characterized by conduct and existing as a latent disposition— that is the cause for entering a new birth;
for when karma is present, it is not logical that entry into a birth should result from conduct alone,
just as one who is able to flee on his feet ought not to run on his knees.
But Bāri [says] that it is indeed good and evil deeds.
The teacher Bādari, however, maintains that "good and evil deeds" alone are denoted by the word *caraṇa*;
for "conduct" (*caraṇa*), "performance" (*anuṣṭhāna*), and "action" (*karman*) are synonymous.

For it is observed that the verb *carati* is used without distinction for action in general; indeed, when a person performs meritorious action characterized by sacrifices and the like, worldly people say of him, "This great soul practices virtue" (*dharmaṃ carati*).
Conduct (*ācāra*) is also indeed a specific kind of dharma.

Furthermore, the designation of a distinction between "action" (*karman*) and "conduct" (*caraṇa*) is justifiable by the analogy of the "Brāhmaṇas and wandering mendicants" (*brāhmaṇa-parivrājaka*). Therefore, the conclusion is that those of "pleasant conduct" are those whose actions are praiseworthy, while those of "wicked conduct" are those whose actions are censurable.
And it is also heard in scripture regarding those who perform undesirable deeds and the like.
It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds go to the moon.
Now, it is considered whether those others who do not perform such deeds also go to the moon, or whether they do not.
Regarding this, he first states the section concerning those who perform sacrifices and so forth (*iṣṭādy-adhikaraṇa*).
It is not the case that only those who perform meritorious deeds go to the moon;
why? Because it is heard in scripture that even those who perform undesirable acts must go to the lunar orb.
For thus the Kauṣītakins record without distinction: "Whoever indeed depart from this world, they all go to the moon."

Furthermore, the commencement of a body for those being reborn is not possible without reaching the moon, because of the fixed rule regarding the number of oblations stated as "in the fifth oblation. Therefore, all must ascend to the moon. If it is argued that it is not logical for those who perform sacrifices and others to have the same destination, we say no; for others lack any experience of enjoyment in the lunar sphere. — Third Chapter —
But for others, after experiencing [the results] in Saṃyamaṇa, there is ascent and descent, because their course is seen to be such.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that all go to the moon;
why? Because the ascent to the moon is solely for the sake of enjoyment, not without purpose.
Nor is it for the sake of descending alone, as when someone climbs a tree for the purpose of gathering flowers and fruit, neither without purpose nor merely to fall back down;

furthermore, it has been stated that there is no enjoyment for those who perform undesirable acts (aniṣṭādikārin) in the moon. Therefore, only those who perform desirable acts (iṣṭādikārin) ascend to the moon, not others.
But having entered the world of Yama, Saṃyamana, and having experienced the torments of Yama corresponding to their own evil deeds, they descend again to this very world;
such are their ascent and descent.
Why? Because their destination is seen [in scripture].

For indeed, scripture, in words similar to those of Yama, shows that those who perform what is undesirable and so forth fall under Yama's control: "The path to the hereafter does not reveal itself to the fool, who is deluded by the infatuation for wealth and is heedless;
thinking 'this world exists, there is no other,' he again and again falls under my power.
And there are many such indications of falling under Yama's control, such as "the son of Vivasvat, the gathering place of people."
And they remember.
Moreover, cultured authorities such as Manu and Vyāsa record in the Nāciketa narrative and elsewhere that in the city of Saṃyamana, the ripening of evil deeds is subject to Yama.
Moreover, there are seven.
Moreover, the authors of the Purāṇas record that there are seven hells, headed by Raurava, which serve as the ground for experiencing the fruits of evil deeds;
those who perform undesirable acts and so forth reach these, so how could they possibly reach the moon? This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: Is this not contradictory, that those who have committed evil deeds experience torments dependent upon Yama, given that in those places such as Raurava, other presiding authorities like Citragupta and others are recorded in tradition? [Reply: No; for even there, there is no contradiction with his (Yama's) activity.
Even regarding those seven hells, there is no contradiction in accepting that Yama himself performs the function of presiding over them;
for Citragupta and the others are recorded in tradition as presiding authorities acting solely under the direction of Yama.
"But [the reference is] to knowledge and action, because they are the subjects under discussion."

In the *Pañcāgnividyā*, at the time of answering the question, "Do you know why that world is not filled?", it is heard: "Now, those beings who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small, repeatedly returning creatures;
'Be born and die'—this is the third station. By this [path], that world is not filled. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8) This is the third chapter.
In this context, "of these two paths" refers to knowledge and action.
Why? Because they are the subjects under discussion.

For knowledge and action are presented as the means for entering upon the path of the gods and the path of the fathers; by the words "those who know thus," knowledge is mentioned, and by that [knowledge], the path of the gods to be reached is proclaimed.

The path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) is proclaimed in that context as being attainable through ritual action (*karman*), such as "sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts" (*iṣṭāpūrte dattam*). It is heard in scripture: "Now, by neither of these two paths...

This is what is meant: for those who are not qualified for the path of the gods (*devayāna*) by means of the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*), nor for the path of the fathers by means of ritual action, this third path—characterized by small creatures and involving repeated return—exists.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the moon is not reached by those who perform undesirable acts and so forth.

It might be argued that they too, having ascended to the lunar orb and then descended from it, will attain the state of small creatures; but even that is not the case, because such an ascent would be purposeless.

Furthermore, if all those who strive were to reach the world of the moon, that world would become overcrowded by those striving for it; consequently, the reply given would be inconsistent with the question.
For an answer must be given such that this world is not filled.
If it is argued that its non-filling is established by the admission of descent [from the moon], we say no, because it is not so stated in scripture.
It is true that even through descent, non-filling would be possible; however...
Scripture, moreover, shows the non-filling [of the world] by mentioning it as the third place: "This is the third place; therefore that world is not filled.
Thus, it is logical that the non-filling results precisely from the failure to ascend.
Furthermore, since descending would be common to those who perform sacrifices and the like as well, it would follow that the mention of the third place would be purposeless.
The word "tu" (but), however, cuts off the suspicion that there might be a lack of completeness arising from the statements belonging to other recensions;

this being so, the word "all" in the statement belonging to another recension remains dependent on those qualified [for the rite], meaning: "Whosoever indeed depart from this world, all of them go to the moon."

Regarding what was further stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya—that all must go to the moon for the sake of obtaining a body, because of the restriction on the number of oblations in the passage beginning with "at the fifth oblation"—that is answered: "Not so, because it is not perceived as such in the third [case]."
In the case of the third place, the restriction of the number of oblations to five need not be observed for the sake of attaining that state.
Why? Because it is perceived to be so;
for, even without a fixed number of oblations, the attainment of the third place is perceived in the manner described: "Be born and die—this is the third place."

Moreover, the number of oblations is mentioned as the cause for a human body in the passage, "In the fifth oblation, the waters become human speech" (*pañcamyām āhutāv āpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavanti*), and not as the cause for the bodies of insects, moths, and so forth, because the word *puruṣa* denotes the human species. Furthermore, it is taught that the waters attain the state of human speech in the fifth oblation; it is not prohibited that they attain the state of human speech in any oblation other than the fifth, for that would entail the fault of the statement being purposeless. Therefore, for those for whom ascent and descent are possible, their body will arise in the fifth oblation. (Third Adhyāya)
But for others, however, the body will be commenced by means of waters infused with other elements, even without a specific count of oblations.
And it is also recorded in common worldly usage.
Moreover, it is recorded in the world that Droṇa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others, as well as Sītā, Draupadī, and others, were not born from a womb.
In those cases, for Droṇa and the others, there was no single oblation pertaining to a woman;
but for Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the others, there were neither of the two oblations pertaining to both woman and man.
And just as there is no regard for a fixed number of oblations in that case, so it will be elsewhere as well;
it is a worldly convention that even the crane conceives a fetus without the emission of semen.
And because it is seen [in scripture].

Moreover, since it is observed that among the fourfold collection of living beings—namely those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from a sprout—the latter two, those born from sweat and from a sprout, arise even without sexual intercourse (*grāmyadharma*), there is no regard for the number of oblations (*āhuti*).
The same will be the case elsewhere as well.
[Objection: But surely, in the passage, "Of these beings, there are indeed only three origins—the egg-born, the living-born, and the soil-born"—only a threefold collection of beings is heard;
how then is a fourfold nature of the collection of beings asserted? To this it is replied: "The third term includes those born from moisture."

In the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya*, regarding the passage "born from an egg, born from a living being, and born from a sprout" (*āṇḍajaṃ jīvajamudbhijjam*), it should be understood that the inclusion of those born from sweat (*svedaja*) is accomplished by the very third term, "born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*). This is because both the sweat-born and the sprout-born are equally characterized by their origin from the breaking forth [of life] from earth and water.

However, since the breaking forth of mobile beings is distinct from that of stationary beings, there is no contradiction in other contexts where a distinction is made between the sweat-born and the sprout-born.
The attainment of that very nature [occurs] because of the logical possibility [of it].

It has been stated that those who perform sacrifices and other rites, having ascended to the moon and dwelt there for as long as their karma lasts, descend from there with a remainder of their residual karma (sānuśaya).
Now, the manner of this descent will be examined through the principle of attaining similarity of nature (sārūpyāpatti).
In this regard, the scriptural text concerning descent is as follows: "Now begins the section [on descent]."

"They return again by that same path as they came—[passing] through space; from space they go to air; having become air, they become smoke; having become smoke, they become mist; having become mist, they become a cloud; having become a cloud, they rain down. Regarding this, a doubt arises: do those descending attain the very nature of space and the other elements, or rather a similarity to space and the others?
On this point, the initial position (pūrvapakṣa) is that they attain the very nature of space and so forth.
Why? Because such is the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*);
otherwise, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And when there is a conflict between direct scriptural statement and figurative indication, the direct scriptural statement is the proper course, not figurative indication.

And thus, scriptural passages such as "having become air, he becomes smoke" and so forth are directly applicable to the assumption of those respective forms; therefore, there is the attainment of the nature of ether and the rest. This being the position reached, we reply: [this is not so] regarding ether and the others. Chapter Three. Third Section. Fourth Sūtra. Fifth Sūtra. Sixth Sūtra. Seventh Sūtra. Eighth Sūtra.
