"They attain uniformity with the quarters":
that watery body which was commenced in the lunar orb for the sake of experience, upon the exhaustion of that experience, dissolves and becomes subtle like space;
therefrom it comes under the power of the wind.

Then it becomes united with smoke and so forth; this is expressed by the passage beginning, "As he came, [he goes] to space, from space to air," and so on. Why is this so? Because it is logically consistent.
For it is thus that this is logically consistent;
indeed, the primary existence of one thing as another is not logically possible;
and furthermore, if the nature of space were being attained, a descent through the sequence beginning with air would not be logical.

Furthermore, because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) and its eternal connection with space (*ākāśa*), no other relation to that [space] is possible than the attainment of similarity to it. And when a direct primary sense (*śruti*) is impossible, it is indeed proper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, here the "attainment of the state of space and so forth" is figuratively designated as the "attainment of equality with space and so forth."
Not long after, due to a specific distinction.

In that regard, concerning the attainment of ether and so forth prior to reaching the state of rice and other grains, there arises a doubt as to the duration: do they remain for a long time, persisting through similarity with each preceding stage, and only after a very short interval attain similarity with each succeeding stage, or is it for a brief period? This is the point of discussion. Since there is no scriptural rule to establish a specific limit, the initial position is that there is no fixed rule. To this, the author says: "not for a very long time" (nāticireṇa).
Having remained in the state of space and so forth for a very short time, they descend upon this earth along with showers of rain;
why is this so? Because of the observation of specific characteristics; for it is thus stated in the commentary on the Sūtra concerning rice and other grains.
Immediately after the attainment of that state, [the text] qualifies it by saying, "From this, indeed, it is more difficult to emerge" (*ato vai khalu durniṣprapataram*).
One *t* sound must be understood as elided according to Vedic grammatical rules;
the meaning is that the emergence from this state of being rice and so forth is more difficult, that is, more painful, than the departure from it.

In this context, by demonstrating that there is suffering in the descent (*niṣprapatana*) here, [the author] shows that there was happiness in the previous [stages]. Furthermore, the distinction between happiness and suffering in the descent is caused by the shortness or length of time; for during that interval, because the body has not yet been produced, experience is impossible.
Therefore, prior to reaching the state of rice and so forth, the descent would occur in a very short time.
In the case of those [bodies] presided over by others, it is as before, because of the expression [of the soul].

In that very same descent (*avaroha*), immediately after the description of the raining down [of the rain], it is recited in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "From this, rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans are born.

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether, during this interval, those with a remainder of karma (*anuśayin*) become partakers of the pleasure and pain of the stationary species (*sthāvara-jāti*), or whether they merely undergo contact with the bodies of stationary beings presided over by other conscious subjects (*kṣetrajña*).

What, then, is the prima facie view? That those possessed of residual karma (*anuśayin*) who have entered the genus of stationary beings (*sthāvara-jāti*) become partakers of the pleasure and pain associated with that state.

Why is this so? Because it is appropriate to take the word "birth" (*janman*) in its primary sense; because the state of being a stationary being is well-known in Śruti and Smṛti as a place for experiencing [the results of karma]; and because it is possible for a class of actions such as sacrifices—which involve the injury of animals and the like—to yield undesirable fruits.
Therefore, this birth of those possessed of residual karma as rice and other plants is indeed to be taken in its primary sense. (Third Adhyāya, Sūtra).

Just as in the case of birth as a dog and so forth—where it is said, "or into the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Cāṇḍāla"—the actual birth as a dog or the like, accompanied by its own pleasure and pain, occurs for those who have fallen [from their state] due to a curse; so too would it be with birth as rice and so forth. This being the position reached, we reply: in the rice and so forth presided over by other living beings, those who have fallen [due to their karma] undergo mere contact; they do not become partakers of the pleasure and pain belonging to that [state]. Just as in the previous case, the state of being wind, smoke, and so forth, for those who have fallen, is merely contact with them, so too the state of being rice and so forth is merely contact with stationary beings (plants) belonging to a particular species.
Whence is this [known]? Because here too there is a mention [of the soul] in the same manner as in those cases.

What is this "being in the same manner" regarding the mention? It is the mere enumeration [of the soul] without reference to any activity of action (*karma-vyāpāra*). Just as in the case of ether and the others ending with rain, [the text] does not refer to any activity of action, so it is also in the case of birth as rice and other grains.
Therefore, there is no participation in pleasure and pain for the souls accompanied by residual karma (*anuśayin*) in this state.
But where one intends to convey the experience of pleasure and pain, there one refers to the operation of karma, as in the passages: "Those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct.

Moreover, if the birth of those with residual karma (*anuśayin*) in rice and so forth were taken in its primary sense, then while the rice and other grains are being reaped, threshed, cooked, and eaten, the residual selves identifying with them would have to depart;
for it is well known that whatever body a living soul identifies with, it departs when that body is afflicted.
In that case, the state of being a seed-sower would not be predicated of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) by virtue of their becoming rice and so forth;
rather, for those possessing residual karma, there occurs merely a conjunction with the rice and other plants presided over by other [souls].
This is stated in the commentary on the sūtra beginning with "ataḥ" (Brahmasūtra 3.1.24).
One might reply that birth has its primary meaning and that the state of being stationary is a locus of experience;
nor do we deny that the state of being stationary is a locus of experience;
let it be a locus of experience for other beings who have reached the state of being stationary through the power of their demerit.
But we maintain that those possessed of residual karma (anuśayin), descending from the moon, do not experience the state of stationary beings (sthāvara).
If it is argued that [the Veda] is impure because it is composed by a person, we say no, because it is established by the Word (Śabda).

As for the argument that sacrificial ritual action is impure due to its connection with the injury of animals and so forth, and that therefore an undesirable fruit is also possible for it— consequently, let the birth of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) as rice and other plants be taken as primary rather than figurative, making the figurative interpretation useless— that is not so, because the knowledge of dharma and adharma is based on scripture.
Scripture alone is the cause for the cognition that "this is dharma" and "this is adharma," since these two are beyond the reach of the senses.

Furthermore, because place, time, and occasion are not fixed, whatever action is performed as *dharma* in a particular place, at a particular time, and on a particular occasion becomes *adharma* under different places, times, and occasions;
therefore, no one possesses knowledge regarding the subject of *dharma* and *adharma* except through the scripture (*śāstra*).
Since the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, consisting of acts such as injury and favor, has been determined by the scripture to be *dharma*, how can it be said to be impure?

But surely the scripture itself, in the injunction "One should not harm any living beings," makes it known that violence toward living beings is unrighteousness; quite so, but that is a general rule (utsarga),
whereas this— "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma"— is an exception (apavāda).
In the third chapter on renunciation,
it has been established that [the rules] beginning with *pava* have a restricted scope of application;
therefore, action is pure because it is performed by the learned and is not censured.
Therefore, being stationary as a plant is not a fitting fruit for that [action];
nor can birth as rice and so forth be like birth as a dog and so forth,
for the latter is spoken of with reference to those of foul conduct (*kapūyacaraṇa*).
There is no such specific qualification here for the Vaiśe�ṣikas.

Therefore, for those who have fallen from the lunar station and are in the state of being "anuśayins," the mere contact with rice and other grains is figuratively designated as "becoming that" (tadbhāva).
Now, the union with the emitter of semen.

Moreover, their becoming rice and so forth consists merely in their being conjoined with them, for this reason: immediately after the state of being rice and so forth, the state of being one who emits semen is taught for those possessing residual karma (anuśayin) in the passage, "For whoever eats the food and whoever emits the semen, he becomes that very thing again.
And here, the state of being one who emits semen cannot be taken in its primary sense, for one becomes an emitter of semen only after being born for some time and reaching youth.

How, indeed, can that state be understood in its primary, non-figurative sense as something followed by a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) while being consumed? In that case, one must necessarily admit that the state of being a man who has emitted semen consists simply in the conjunction with such a man;
likewise, the state of being rice and so forth consists simply in the conjunction with rice and so forth—thus there is no contradiction.
From the womb, the body.

Then, immediately after the state of being the shedder of semen, when the semen has been poured into the womb, the scripture states that a body for those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) is born from the womb for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of their residual karma, in the passage beginning with, "But those whose conduct here has been pleasant," and so forth. From this also, it is understood that at the stage of becoming rice and so on during the descent, that very body becomes endowed with pleasure and pain. Therefore, it is established that the birth of those possessing residual karma as rice and so on consists merely in contact with them.

Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
