This being the case, even the distinction between the conditions for staying and moving must be admitted as a mere deception.
Furthermore, there is a discrepancy regarding time in dreams: one who has fallen asleep at night during the land of Bhārata perceives it as being day;
likewise, in a dream lasting only a moment, one sometimes passes through many series of years. Moreover, even the signs [of dreams] are not suitable for either cognition or action.
For, due to the withdrawal of his instruments, he possesses no eyes or other senses for the purpose of grasping horses, chariots, and so forth;
[Māṇḍūkya Sūtra, Third Chapter].
Furthermore, how could he have the capacity to produce chariots and such in the mere twinkling of an eye, or even wood?

Furthermore, these chariots, horses, and so forth seen in a dream are sublated upon waking; indeed, within the dream itself, they are easily sublated, because their deviation is observed at the beginning and the end. For that which was determined in a dream as "this is a chariot" becomes in an instant a human being, and that which was determined as "this is a human being" becomes in an instant a tree.
Moreover, the scripture clearly declares the non-existence of chariots and the like in a dream, stating: "There are no chariots there, no yoked horses, and no roads," and so forth.
Therefore, the vision of one's own dreams is merely an illusion.
For the scripture indicates this, and those who know it declare so.

If it is argued that because dreams are mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), there is not even a trace of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) in them, we say: no, for a dream is indicative (*sūcaka*) of future good and evil.

Thus it is heard in scripture: "When, in the course of rites performed for desired ends, one sees a woman in one's dreams, one should know that there will be success in accordance with that dream-vision."
Likewise, [the scripture] makes it known that one's life is not long by means of such sounds as, "He sees a black man with black teeth; he kills him.
And those who know the treatises on dreams declare: "Riding an elephant and the like in a dream are auspicious, while riding a donkey and the like are inauspicious.
Furthermore, some hold that certain dreams, caused by specific mantras, deities, or substances, possess a scent of truth.
Even in that case, let it be granted that the object being indicated possesses reality;

however, the indicator—such as the sight of a woman and so forth—is indeed false, because it is sublated. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, it is logically established that a dream is mere illusion (māyāmātra).

Regarding what was stated as "for it says," since this is so, that [statement] must be explained in a figurative sense. Just as one says, "The plough draws up the oxen and so forth," because it is merely the instrumental cause, and yet the plough does not actually draw them up in a literal sense; in the same way, because he is merely the instrumental cause, it is said that the sleeper creates chariots and so forth, and that "he is the agent," but the sleeper does not literally create chariots and so forth.

However, it must be stated that its being the "cause" (nimittatva) consists in its being the agent of the good and evil deeds which are the causes of the chariots and other objects, since joy, fear, and so forth are observed to have those [objects] as their cause.

Furthermore, because the soul's self-luminosity (svayañjyotiṣṭva) is difficult to discern while awake due to the contact of the senses with objects and the interference of external lights such as the sun, the state of dreaming is introduced for the purpose of discerning it;
if, in that context, the scriptural statement regarding the creation of chariots and so forth were taken literally, then the self-luminosity would not be definitively established.

Therefore, the statement regarding the absence of chariots and so forth must be explained according to the direct scriptural text (*śruti*), whereas the statement regarding the creation of chariots and so forth must be explained as being figurative (*bhakti*). By this, the mention of "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) is also explained.

As for what was said—that "they declare this one to be the wise creator"—that too is incorrect, because another scriptural passage states that it is the activity of the individual soul (*jīva*): "Having himself struck down [the body], having himself created [the world], he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light."
Here too, because of the restatement of what is well-known in the passage, "He who is awake among those who sleep," this very Jīva is proclaimed as the creator of desires;

however, by the remainder of that sentence, "That indeed is the Bright, That is Brahman," his state as a Jīva is set aside and his state as Brahman is taught— just as in passages such as "That art thou"— and thus there is no contradiction with the context of Brahman.

Nor do we deny the activity of the Wise One even in a dream, for since He is the Lord of all, it is logical that He presides over all states of existence. However, what is being established here is merely this: that this creation based on the intermediate state (saṃdhyā) is not ultimately real, unlike the creation of ether and the other elements.
Furthermore, even the creation of ether and the rest does not possess absolute reality;
for it has been demonstrated in the sūtra, "Its non-difference [from Brahman] follows from such terms as 'originating' and so forth," that the entire phenomenal world is mere illusion (māyāmātra).
Prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self, however, the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of ether and the rest exists in a stable form;

whereas the phenomenal world based on the intermediate state (saṃdhyā) is sublated every day. Therefore, this specific nature of the intermediate state as being mere illusion (māyāmātra) has been stated.
But it is concealed by the meditation upon another; for from that arise its bondage and its opposite.
Now, it might be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a mere part of the Supreme Self, like a spark from a fire;
this being the case, just as fire and its spark possess equal powers of burning and illuminating, so too do the individual soul and the Lord possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty.
Consequently, by virtue of its own knowledge and sovereignty, the individual soul will bring about the creation of chariots and other things through its mere volition (*saṃkalpa*).

It is observed that even though there exists a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), the individual soul’s possession of qualities contrary to those of the Lord is directly perceived.
But is it the case that the individual soul possesses no qualities at all identical to those of the Lord? No, it is not that they do not exist;
although they do exist, they are concealed by the intervention of ignorance (avidyā) and other such factors.

Furthermore, that [Self], though hidden, becomes manifest only to some perfected person who, having meditated upon the Supreme Lord and exerted effort, has shaken off darkness; it is like the power of vision restored by the efficacy of medicine when it had been obscured by cataracts. It does not manifest by its own nature to all living beings. Why? Because from Him—from the Lord as the cause—the bondage and liberation of this individual soul (jīva) occur: bondage arises from the non-recognition of the Lord’s true nature, while liberation arises from the full recognition of His true nature.
And thus says the Śruti: "Having known the God, there is the falling away of all bonds; with afflictions destroyed, there is the abandonment of birth and death.
Through meditation upon Him, at the dissolution of the body, one attains the third state—sovereignty over all, absolute, with all desires fulfilled"—and so forth.
Or, that [knowledge] also [arises] from the conjunction with a body.

But why is it that the individual soul (*jīva*), being indeed a portion of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), has its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would be more logical for knowledge and sovereignty to remain unobscured, just as the burning and illuminating powers of a spark remain unobscured.
To this it is replied: This is indeed true;

however, that obscuration of the individual soul’s knowledge and sovereignty occurs due to its connection with a body—that is, due to its connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, sensations, and so forth.
And there is an illustration for this in the *Upadeśasūtra*, Chapter Three:

Just as the powers of burning and illuminating, though possessed by fire, become hidden when it is situated within the fire-drill wood (*araṇi*), or as they are hidden when the fire is covered by ashes; even so, due to its connection with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the body—which is produced by name and form presented by ignorance—the concealment of the individual soul’s (*jīva*) knowledge and sovereignty occurs through the delusion of non-discrimination from that [Supreme Self].
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to exclude the doubt that the individual soul is something other than the Lord.

[Objection: Let the individual soul (jīva) indeed be something other than the Lord (īśvara), because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; what is the use of imagining a connection with a body? [Reply: No, it is said in response— for the distinctness of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. This is because, having begun with "That divinity thought," the text refers to the soul by the word "Self" in the passage "having entered by means of this living Self";
and furthermore, in the words "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou, O Śvetaketu," it teaches the soul that its very nature is the Lord.
Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed non-different from the Lord (*īśvara*), though its knowledge and sovereignty become concealed due to its connection with a body.
Consequently, it is not possible for the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream to be produced by the will of the individual soul;
for if the creation of chariots and so forth in a dream were produced by will, no one would ever experience an undesirable dream, since no one wills what is undesirable.

As for the further argument that the scriptural mention of the waking state's location indicates the reality of the dream state—that statement of similarity does not intend to assert actual reality, because it would contradict the self-luminosity [of the Self] and because scripture itself has shown the absence of chariots and other such things in dreams.
Rather, since the dream is constructed from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) originating in the waking state, that statement intends to convey that the dream appears as if identical to the waking state.
Therefore, it is established that the dream is merely illusion (*māyāmātra*).
In the commentary on the Sūtra: "The absence [of that state] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements to that effect."
The state of dream has been examined;
now the state of deep sleep is being examined.
In this regard, there are these scriptural passages concerning the subject of deep sleep:

In one place it is heard: "Where [this state occurs], because of the absence of that [waking state], he who is asleep, fully composed and serene, does not know anything; at that time he has entered into these channels (nāḍīs)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3). In another place, however, after enumerating the channels themselves, it is heard: "Having descended by means of them, he rests in the pericardium (purītat)" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19).

Likewise, elsewhere, after enumerating the channels (nāḍīs), it is said: "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this prāṇa alone. Similarly, elsewhere: "He rests in that space which is within the heart.
And likewise, elsewhere: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has gone to his own self."
And likewise: "Embraced by the non-intelligent Self, one knows nothing external nor internal."

In this regard, there is a doubt: are these channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth distinct places for deep sleep (*suṣupti*), independent of one another, or are they, through mutual dependence, a single place for deep sleep?

What, then, is the initial position? That they are distinct. Why? Because they serve a single purpose; for it is never observed that things serving a single purpose—such as rice and barley—are mutually dependent.

Furthermore, the identity of purpose among the channels (nāḍīs) and the others is observed in deep sleep, as it is stated in various places: "He has entered into the channels" and "He lies in the pericardium.
This is because the use of the locative case is identical in those instances.
But is it not the case that when this is so, the locative designation is not actually seen in the passage: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being (sat)"?

This is not a fault, because even there the sense of the locative case is understood. For the supplementary part of that passage states: "The individual soul, seeking a dwelling-place, approaches Being," and "Not finding a dwelling-place elsewhere, it takes refuge in Prāṇa alone"; for in that context, Being (sat), which is the subject under discussion, is taken up by the word.

Furthermore, a dwelling-place is the meaning of the locative case, and the use of the locative is also seen in the supplementary portion of that passage: "Having merged into Being, they do not know; we have merged into Being."
And in all cases, deep sleep—characterized by the cessation of specific cognition—is not differentiated.
Therefore, because they share a single purpose, one resorts to any one of the locations, such as the channels and so forth, alternatively for the sake of sleep.
When the state of being in the vital breath (prāṇa) has thus been reached as a prima facie view, it is now established that its absence occurs in the channels (nāḍīs) and in the Self (ātman).
"Its absence" means the absence of that which is under discussion—the seeing of dreams—which is deep sleep;
and by the conjunction "in the channels and in the Self," the meaning is that these—the channels and so forth—approach [the soul] for the sake of sleep collectively, not optionally.

Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect; for thus, in various places, all the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth are heard of as being the locus of deep sleep, and this is consistent only if they are combined.
For if there were an option between them, there would be a contradiction in one of the alternatives.
But has it not been stated that, because they serve a single purpose, there must be an option (*vikalpa*) between the channels (*nāḍīs*) and so forth, just as with rice and barley?

No, it is replied. For a single grammatical case-ending (*ekavibhakti-nirdeśa*) alone does not necessarily entail a single purpose or an option, since we observe the use of a single case-ending even where there is a plurality of purposes and a combination (*samuccaya*), as in "he sleeps on the palace" and "he sleeps on the couch. Likewise here, in the passage "he sleeps in the channels, in the pericardium, and in Brahman," a combination is appropriate.

And thus the Śruti declares their conjunction in deep sleep: "When he is asleep and sees no dream whatsoever, then he becomes one with this prāṇa alone"—this scripture proclaims the combination of the channels and the prāṇa in deep sleep because they are mentioned in a single sentence; and that the prāṇa is Brahman has been established in the sūtra, "The prāṇa [is Brahman], because of the subsequent agreement."

Even where the scripture speaks of the channels as if they were independent, presenting them as the locus of deep sleep—stating, "At that time, he has entered into these channels"—there too, since Brahman, which is well-known from other passages, is not excluded, it is understood that he abides in Brahman itself by means of the channels.

Nor is the locative case used for the channels contradicted even in this view; for one who reaches Brahman by way of the channels has indeed "entered" the channels. Just as when someone goes to the ocean by way of the Ganges, he has already reached the Ganges.

And in this regard, since the path to the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) consisting of the network of rays is intended [to be described], the mention of "creeping" is for the purpose of praising the channels. Having stated, "He creeps into the channels," the text praises the channels by saying, "No evil whatsoever touches him.

Furthermore, it states the reason for the absence of contact with evil: "For then he becomes united with light. This means that, being pervaded by the light known as bile residing in the channels, his vision is not directed toward external objects. Thus ends the third chapter.
Alternatively, "by light" (*tejasā*) is a designation for Brahman itself, because in another scriptural passage—namely, "Brahman indeed is light indeed"—the word "light" is used for Brahman;

for he then becomes united with Brahman by means of the channels, and therefore no evil touches him. And this union with Brahman is established as the cause for the absence of contact with evil, based on such scriptural texts as: "All evils turn back from there, for that world of Brahman is free from evil."

This being the case, it is established that there is a combination of the channels (nāḍīs) with Brahman, which is well-known from other passages as the locus of deep sleep. Likewise, since the pericardium (purītat) is also mentioned in the context of Brahman, its status as a locus of deep sleep is understood to be consistent with that: "He rests in that space which is within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17). Since the space within the heart is presented here as the locus of deep sleep, it is stated: "He rests in the pericardium. By "pericardium" (purītat), the membrane surrounding the heart is meant.

Even though [the soul] is within that [space], while lying in the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*), it can be said that "it lies in the pericardium" (*apurītati śete*); for even one who resides in a city surrounded by a rampart is said to reside in the rampart.

Furthermore, the nature of the space of the heart as Brahman has been established in the section beginning with "The small [space], because of the subsequent [scriptural reasons]" (*dahara uttarebhyaḥ*).

Likewise, the conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the pericardium (*purītat*) is understood from their inclusion in a single sentence: "Having descended through them, it lies in the pericardium. (*tābhiḥ pratyavasṛpya purītati śete*)
And the status of being Brahman is well-established for both "the True" (sat) and "the Wise" (prājña).

Thus, in these scriptural passages, only three places of deep sleep are mentioned: the channels (nāḍyaḥ), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman. Among these, the channels and the pericardium are merely gateways; Brahman alone is the one, infallible place of deep sleep.
Moreover, the channels (nāḍīs) or the pericardium (purītat) serve merely as the support for the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva)—in them its instruments (karaṇas) abide.

Indeed, apart from its connection with limiting adjuncts, no support whatsoever is possible for the soul in its own right, because it is non-different from Brahman and is established in its own majesty. Even its state of having Brahman as its support during deep sleep is not stated with the intention of implying a distinction between support and the supported; how then? It is stated with the intention of identity (tādātmya).

For it says, "O dear one, then he becomes united [with Being], he has gone to his own (svam apīto bhavati). By the word *sva* (own), the Self (*ātman*) is denoted; the meaning is that the sleeper has attained his true nature.
Furthermore, there is never a time when the individual soul (*jīva*) is not united with Brahman, because its true nature is never lost.

However, with reference to the states of dreaming and waking—where, due to contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is as if an assumption of another form—the attainment of its true nature in deep sleep is intended by the statement, "he has gone to his own. This is because those adjuncts have subsided.
Therefore, it is untenable to claim that in the state of deep sleep one sometimes becomes united with the Existent (sat) and sometimes does not.
Moreover, even if one were to admit a distinction of locations, deep sleep—characterized by the cessation of specific cognitions—is in no way differentiated therein.

In that state, it is logical that one who has become united with the Existent does not cognize because of oneness, as the scripture states: "Then by what and whom should he cognize? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

For one lying in the channels (nāḍīs) or in the pericardium (purītat), no cause for non-perception can be discerned, because non-perception pertains to distinct objects, according to the scriptural text: "Or where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another.
Now, one might argue that even for an object within the domain of distinction, a cause such as excessive distance could be the reason for non-perception.
This would indeed be so if the individual soul (*jīva*) were admitted to be limited by its own nature, as when Viṣṇumitra, being away from home, does not see his own house;
however, no limitation exists for the soul apart from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

If it be argued that the cause of non-cognition—such as extreme distance—is actually located in the adjuncts, even then, since the adjunct has ceased to exist, it is logical that one who has become one with Being (*sat*) does not cognize.
Nor do we here intend to establish a combination of the channels and so forth as being equally [valid];
for there is no purpose served by the cognition that "the channels and the pericardium are the place of sleep," since no fruit dependent upon such a cognition is heard in scripture.
Nor is this consciousness taught as a subordinate member of anything that possesses a fruit;
rather, we establish that Brahman is the imperishable locus of deep sleep.

However, there is a purpose for this consciousness: namely, the ascertainment by the individual soul (jīva) of its identity with Brahman, and the ascertainment of its freedom from the empirical dealings of the dreaming and waking states.
Therefore, the Self alone is the locus of sleep.
Therefore, awakening arises from this.

And because the Self alone is the place of sleep, for that very reason, awakening from this Self is taught as if it were constant within the context of sleep; at the time of answering the question, "Whence did he come? [it is said] in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a fire, even so all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) issue forth from this Self," and so on, as well as: "Having come from Being, they do not know that they have come from Being."

If, however, these states were subject to conceptual differentiation, he would have taught that one awakens from the channels at one time, from the pericardium at another, and from the Self at yet another;
therefore, for this reason as well, the Self alone is the locus of deep sleep.
But he [is the same], on account of the recollection of past actions, the scriptural texts, and the injunctions.

Regarding this re-union with Being (*sat-sampatti*) mentioned in the scripture, it must be considered whether the one who awakens is the very same person who had become united with Being, or whether it might be that person or someone else.
In this regard, the initial position is that there is no fixed rule.
Why? Because when a certain drop of water is cast into a mass of water, [it becomes indistinguishable].

It is thrown [into the ocean], and at that time it becomes merely a mass of water; yet upon being drawn out again, it becomes that very same drop of water—thus it is difficult to accomplish. In the same way, one who has fallen asleep and attained oneness with the Supreme becomes serene; therefore, that very same person ought not to be able to rise again.
Consequently, it is either that Lord Himself or another individual soul (jīva) who awakens.
This being the case, the following is said: That very same living soul (*jīva*), having slept and attained its natural state, rises again, and not another.
Why? Because of action, recollection, scriptural texts, and injunctions.
I shall demonstrate the reason by dividing it: first, because we observe the performance of the remainder of actions, that same soul must be the one who rises, and not another.
For instance, it is observed that one who has performed a ritual action on the previous day continues to perform its remainder on the following day;
moreover, one person is not able to proceed with the performance of the remainder of a ritual action commenced by another, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it is understood that there is only one agent of a single action on both the previous and the subsequent day.

For this reason as well, it is that very same person who rises [from deep sleep], because the subsequent recollection of a previous experience—expressed as "I saw that on the past day"—would not be possible if someone else had risen;
for one person is not able to remember what was seen by another.
Furthermore, the recollection of the Self in the form "I am he" is not possible if it were to arise from another Self;
moreover, it is understood from the sacred texts that its arising is from that very [Self].

For indeed, such scriptural passages as, "Again, according to the rule and according to its place of origin, it rushes forth toward the state of waking," and "All these creatures go day after day into this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it; they become here again what they were—whether tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gnat, or mosquito"—which are read in the context of sleep and waking, would not attain consistency if there were an arising from a different Self.
This is likewise understood from the injunctions regarding ritual action and knowledge.
Otherwise, the injunctions regarding ritual action and knowledge would be purposeless;
for on the view that [the self] arises from something other [than itself], it would follow that one is liberated merely by falling asleep.
If this were the case, what would be accomplished by ritual action or knowledge, which have their fruits at a later time?

Moreover, regarding the position that [the soul] rises from something else: if the individual soul (*jīva*) were to rise while engaged in worldly activity in another body, it would follow that the activity occurring there would be interrupted.

If, on the other hand, it were to rise while sleeping there, the assumption would be purposeless; for what benefit is there in this assumption that he who was asleep in one body does not rise in that same body, but rather, having been asleep in one body, rises in another? Furthermore, if it were to rise as a liberated soul (*mukta*), liberation would become finite;
moreover, a rising again is impossible for one whose ignorance (*avidyā*) has ceased.
By this, the arising of a Lord (Īśvara) has been refuted, because he would be eternally free from ignorance.

Furthermore, under the view that one person arises [as another], the faults of "attaining what was not earned" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was earned" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) would be unavoidable.
Therefore, it is that very same person who arises, and not another.

As for the objection that was raised—that just as a drop of water thrown into a mass of water cannot be extracted, so too a soul that has become merged [in Brahman] ought not to emerge—this is refuted: it is logical that the drop of water cannot be extracted there because of the absence of any cause for differentiation; but here, however, there exists a cause for differentiation, namely *karman* and *avidyā*, and thus there is a difference.
Furthermore, we observe that even milk and water, when mixed and difficult for those of our kind to distinguish, are separated by a swan.
Moreover, there exists no such thing as a "living soul" (jīva) distinct from the Supreme, which could be separated from it like a drop of water from a body of water;
rather, it has been explained more than once that it is the very Reality itself that is metaphorically designated as the "living soul" due to its contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
This being so, as long as the persistence of bondage continues within a single limiting adjunct, so long does the conventional usage of "one living soul" persist.
But when the persistence of bondage resides within a different limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is the designation of another soul;

that very same limiting adjunct [persists] through the analogy of the seed and the sprout during sleep and waking. Therefore, it is logical that this very soul awakens. Thus ends the third chapter. It is thus established that this very soul awakens.
O charming one, the attainment of the half [of the body] follows by elimination.
There is that which is called "the fainting" (mugdha), which worldly people refer to as "swooning" (mūrchita).
Regarding the investigation into what state that is, it is said: first of all, three states of the living soul (jīva) residing in the body are well known—namely, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
the fourth is the departure from the body.
However, no fifth state of the individual soul (jīva) is well-known in either Śruti or Smṛti;
therefore, fainting must be one of these four states! This concludes the section on the "Fainting" (mugdha-adhikaraṇa).

This being the case, we reply: first of all, the one in a swoon cannot be in the waking state, for he does not perceive objects through the senses. It might be argued that the swooning person will be like the "arrow-maker" analogy: just as an arrow-maker, though awake, perceives no other objects because his mind is absorbed in the arrow, so too the swooning person, though awake, perceives no other objects because his mind is preoccupied with experiencing the pain produced by the blow of a club or similar cause.
No, because of the absence of conscious thought.

For an arrow-maker, with his mind fully absorbed, says: "I have been perceiving only the arrow for all this time"; whereas one who has fainted, upon regaining consciousness, says: "I was cast into blind darkness for all this time; nothing was consciously perceived by me.
Furthermore, even when the mind of a waking person is attached to a single object, the body is maintained [in its functions].
But the body of one who has fainted falls to the earth;
therefore, he does not wake up,
nor does he see dreams, because he is devoid of consciousness.

Nor is he dead, because of the presence of breath and warmth. For when a person has fainted, those who are in doubt as to whether "this one is dead or not dead" feel the region of the heart to determine whether warmth exists or not, and they feel the region of the nose to determine whether breath exists or not.
If they do not perceive the existence of breath and warmth, then concluding "this one is dead," they carry him to the forest for cremation.
But if they perceive either breath or warmth, then concluding "this one is not dead," they treat him with medicine to restore consciousness.
Nor has he gone to the realm of destiny (diṣṭa), because of his subsequent rising;
for one who has gone to Yama does not return from the kingdom of Yama.
Let it be, then, that he is in deep sleep, because of the absence of consciousness and because of immortality.
No, because of their distinct characteristics: one who is fainting sometimes does not breathe for even a long time, his body trembles, his face is terrifying, and his eyes are wide open;
whereas one in deep sleep has a serene face, breathes repeatedly at regular intervals, his eyes are closed, and his body does not tremble;
moreover, they awaken a person in deep sleep by a mere touch of the hand, but not one who is fainting even with the blow of a mallet.
Furthermore, there is a difference in the causes [of these states]: delusion (moha) has as its cause the striking of a club and so forth, whereas sleep (svāpa) has fatigue as its cause.
Moreover, in common worldly usage, there is no established convention that one who is "deluded" is "asleep.

By process of elimination, we understand that the state of being deluded is a half-attainment [of death]: it is "attained" because of the absence of consciousness, and it is "unattained" because of its distinctness from the other [states].

Thus ends the third chapter. But how can it be said that "half-attainment" constitutes the state of being "stupefied" (mugdha)? For regarding one who is asleep, the Śruti has stated: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1); and further: "In this state, a thief is no longer a thief; day and night do not cross this bridge, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds," and so forth.
Indeed, the connection of the individual soul (jīva) with good and evil deeds occurs through the production of the notions of happiness and suffering.
Furthermore, neither the cognition of happiness nor the cognition of suffering exists in deep sleep;
those two cognitions do not exist in the state of being swooned either.
Therefore, due to the cessation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as in deep sleep, there must be the attainment of the whole in the state of swoon as well, and not the attainment of only half.

To this it is replied: O deluded one, we do not say that there is a "half-attainment" of Brahman by the individual soul (jīva); rather, we say that fainting (mugdhatva) consists of one half of the state of deep sleep (suṣupta) and the other half of the state of another condition [death]. And the similarity and difference between fainting and sleep have already been demonstrated.
And this is the gateway to death:
when his karma remains with a residue, then speech and mind return [to him];
but when the karma is without residue, then the vital breath and the out-breath depart.
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman desire the perfection of the offering.
As for what was said—that no fifth state is well-known—this is not a fault;
it may simply not be well-known because this state occurs only occasionally.
Moreover, this is well-known in the world and in Ayurveda;
and because it is accepted as being included within the "accomplishment of half," it is not counted as a fifth [cause], which is therefore faultless.
In the Sūtra-bhāṣya [it is stated]: "The Supreme [Self] does not possess both characteristics even from the standpoint of its location, for [it is described as such] everywhere."

That Brahman by which the individual soul (jīva) attains union through the cessation of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in states such as deep sleep—the nature of that Brahman is now determined on the basis of scripture.

There exist scriptural passages concerning Brahman that possess both types of characteristics (ubhayaliṅga); for instance, there are those with specific attributes (saviśeṣaliṅga), such as: "He whose work is all, whose abode is all... desire, all odors, all tastes."
Furthermore, there are scriptural indications of the absence of attributes, such as "neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long," and so forth.
Regarding these scriptures, the inquiry is whether Brahman is to be understood as possessing both sets of characteristics, or as possessing only one set;
and if it possesses only one set, whether it is with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) or without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*). Thus the matter is deliberated.

In this regard, since both types of scriptural indications are supported, it might be concluded that Brahman possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅga). To this we reply: first of all, it is not possible for the supreme Brahman to possess both characteristics by its own nature; for it is impossible to determine that a single entity is by its very nature endowed with specific qualities such as form and the like, and yet the opposite as well, because of the contradiction. Let it be, then, that [Brahman appears so] "from its location" (sthānataḥ), due to connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the earth.
That too is not tenable; for even through association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is impossible for a thing of one nature to possess a different nature.

Indeed, a crystal, though naturally transparent, does not become non-transparent through association with limiting adjuncts such as lac-dye, because the conviction that it is non-transparent is merely an illusion;
furthermore, these limiting adjuncts are themselves presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).
And for this reason,

even when a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is accepted [as a means of cognition], Brahman must be understood as being devoid of all distinctions and free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*), and not its opposite; for in all those passages intended to establish the true nature of Brahman— such as "without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying"— Brahman is taught precisely as that which has all distinctions cast aside.
If it is argued that [the whole] does not exist because of its difference [from the parts], we say no, because it is perceived in each individual part.

Now, it might be argued: "What was stated—that Brahman is indeed without conceptual differentiation (nirvikalpa) and possesses only one characteristic (ekaliṅga), and that it does not possess both characteristics either by its own nature or from the standpoint of its locations—that is untenable.

Why? Because of difference (bheda). For distinct forms of Brahman are taught in each respective meditation (vidyā): Brahman as four-footed, Brahman as sixteen-fold, Brahman characterized by being 'the dwarf' (vāmanī) and so forth, and Brahman designated by the word Vaiśvānara whose body is the three worlds; such are the types [of forms]."
Therefore, it must also be admitted that Brahman possesses specific qualities.
Now, it was argued that it is impossible for Brahman to possess both characteristics;
however, this too is not a contradiction, because the difference in forms is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

If it be argued that otherwise the scripture concerning difference would result in being entirely without a subject matter, we say: no; why? Because of the statement of non-difference with respect to each [limiting adjunct].

For the scripture makes known the non-difference of Brahman with respect to each individual limiting adjunct, as in: "That person consisting of light and immortal who is in this earth, and that person consisting of light and immortal who is within the body (adhyātma) — he indeed is this Self," and so forth.

Therefore, it cannot be said that the association of diverse forms with Brahman is scriptural, because difference exists for the purpose of meditation, while the ultimate purport lies in non-difference.
Moreover, some hold this view as well.

Moreover, some recensions of the Veda, after first censuring the perception of difference, teach the perception of non-difference alone: "By the mind alone this is to be attained; there is not the slightest diversity here.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity.

Likewise, others also study that the entire phenomenal world—characterized by the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller—is of the single nature of Brahman: "Having understood the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller, all that has been declared is the threefold Brahman for me. Thus, they maintain that the whole universe possesses the single essence of Brahman.

But how is it that, when there exist Vedic texts concerning Brahman that teach it as having form and others that teach it as being without form, Brahman is determined to be only formless and not the opposite? To this, the author reads the reply: "For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because that is its primary nature."
Indeed, Brahman is to be understood as being devoid of forms such as color and so forth, and not as possessing form and so forth.
Why? Because that [absence of form] is its primary characteristic.

For it is said: "Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long"; "Without sound, without touch, without form, immutable"; "That which is called space is the revealer of name and form; that within which these two exist is Brahman"; and "For it is divine, formless... (Third Chapter).

Sentences such as "The Person is indeed without interior or exterior, for He is unborn; this very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior; this Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all"—these have been established in the sūtra *But that [is so] because of the harmony* (*tattu samanvayāt*) as having the reality of Brahman as the Self, which is free from phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), as their primary subject matter, and not as having any other subject matter as their primary focus.
Therefore, in sentences of this kind, Brahman must be understood exactly as heard in the text as being formless (*nirākāra*).
Other sentences, however, which concern Brahman as possessing form, do not have that [form] as their primary subject matter.
For those [scriptural passages] primarily concern the rules for meditative worship; therefore,
in the absence of contradiction, they must be accepted exactly as they are heard in the text.

But when there is a contradiction, those [scriptural passages] whose primary focus is that [Brahman] are stronger than those whose primary focus is not; this is the reason for the definitive conclusion, by which, even though both types of scriptural statements exist, Brahman is determined to be indeed formless, and not the opposite.
What, then, is the status of those scriptural passages whose objects appear to be non-existent? To this he says: "And [the texts] are like light, for otherwise they would be purposeless."

Just as the light of the sun or the moon, pervading the sky, remains there and—due to its connection with limiting adjuncts such as a finger—appears to assume the qualities of those [adjuncts], such as straightness and so forth, even though it does not actually do so; in the same way, Brahman also, through its connection with limiting adjuncts such as the earth and so on, appears to assume their form.
Therefore, the teaching of specific forms for Brahman based upon those [adjuncts] for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory.
In this manner, the scriptural passages concerning Brahman as possessing form will likewise not be rendered meaningless.

For it is not reasonable to maintain that some Vedic statements possess meaningfulness while others lack it, since there is no difference in their status as authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: Even so, this contradicts what was previously asserted—that Brahman does not possess both characteristics even through connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). [Reply:
We say no; for it is impossible for that which is caused by a limiting adjunct to be an inherent property of the reality itself.
Furthermore, since limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*),
we have stated in various places that the engagement in worldly and Vedic transactions occurs only when innate ignorance is present.
And in the Sūtra-bhāṣya it says: "only that."

And the Śruti says: "Brahman is pure consciousness alone, devoid of any other distinct form, and without attributes; 'Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a solid mass of taste, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a solid mass of consciousness.'"

This is what is meant: there is no form of this Self other than consciousness, either internally or externally; rather, consciousness alone is its uninterrupted essential nature. Just as in a mass of rock salt there is only the salty taste, uninterrupted both inside and out, and no other taste, so it is exactly thus.
Moreover, it is shown [in scripture] and is also recorded in traditional memory (smṛti).
Moreover, Scripture demonstrates that Brahman is devoid of attributes precisely by negating all other forms;

for instance: "Therefore, the instruction is: not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6); "It is indeed other than the known and above the unknown" (Kevala Upaniṣad 1.4); and "From whence words return, together with the mind, failing to reach it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).

Furthermore, it is heard in the scriptures that when Bādhva was questioned by Bāṣkali, he declared Brahman through silence alone: "He said, 'Teach me, sir! He remained silent. When [Bāṣkali] asked him a second and even a third time, he said, 'I am indeed speaking, but you do not understand.'"
"This self is tranquil.

Likewise, in the Smṛtis as well, it is taught solely by means of the negation of the other, in such passages as: "I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality—the beginningless supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither existent nor non-existent," and so forth.
Likewise, it is recorded in the Smṛti that Nārāyaṇa, assuming a universal form, said to Nārada: "O Nārada, this which you see me as is indeed a māyā created by me;
endowed with the qualities of all beings, you ought not to know me in this way.
For this very reason, there is the comparison [of the Self] to the reflection of the sun and so forth.

And precisely because this Self is of the nature of consciousness, devoid of distinctions, transcending speech and mind, and teachable only through the negation of the other, it is for this very reason that the scriptures on liberation employ analogies such as "like the sun in water" with reference to its non-ultimate possession of distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). As it is said: "For just as this luminous self, the sun, though one, enters into many different waters and appears divided by the limiting adjuncts, so does this unborn Self appear divided among the various fields (*kṣetra*). And: "The one alone, indeed, is the elemental Self (*bhūtātman*), residing in every single being."
And in such passages as, "It is seen like the moon in water," and so forth.
To this, it is objected: "Though [the Self] is one and yet manifold, because it is perceived like water, it is not so [as the opponent claims]."
The comparison with the sun in water and the like is not applicable here, because it is not perceived in that manner;

for water, which is a material entity distinct from and located at a distance from material objects such as the sun, is perceived, and thus the arising of reflections of the sun and so forth is logical in that case.
But the Self is not material, nor are its limiting adjuncts (upādhis) separate from it or situated at a distance, because [the Self] is all-pervading and non-different from everything.
Therefore, this illustration is inappropriate.
To this, it is replied: "There is participation in increase and decrease because of being included within both; thus, there is consistency."
This illustration, however, is indeed appropriate, because the intended aspect is present;
for it is not possible for anyone to demonstrate complete similarity between an illustration and the subject illustrated by excluding some intended aspect;
for if there were complete similarity, the very relationship between the illustration and the subject illustrated would be destroyed.
Nor is this formulation of analogies, such as the sun in water and so forth, based on one's own imagination; rather,
it is the purpose of this [analogy] already established in the scripture that is here set forth.
What, then, is intended here by "similarity"? It is stated: it is the participation in increase and decrease.

For the reflection of the sun in water increases when the water increases, decreases when the water decreases, moves when the water moves, and is divided when the water is divided; thus, it conforms to the properties of the water. However, in reality, the sun does not possess such qualities.

In the same way, although Brahman is in reality unchanging and of a single nature, it appears, as it were, to partake of the properties of its limiting adjuncts—such as increase and decrease—due to its inclusion within adjuncts like the body.
Thus, because there is consistency between both the illustration and the illustrated subject, there is no contradiction.
And because it is seen [in scripture].
And scripture demonstrates the entry of the supreme Brahman alone into the limiting adjuncts such as the body, in passages such as: "In the city he made bipeds, in the city he made quadrupeds;
having become a bird, he entered the city as the Person" (RV 10.90.3), and "Having entered by means of this living self" (ChU 6.3.2).
Therefore, this is correct: "And for this very reason, the comparison is like that of the sun's reflection and so forth.
Consequently, it is established that Brahman possesses only one characteristic—that of being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa)—and not both characteristics or a contrary characteristic.

In this regard, some propose two distinct topics: first, whether Brahman is of a single form with all manifoldness entirely subsided, or whether it is endowed with multiple forms like the manifoldness itself;
second, if it is that in which manifoldness has subsided, whether Brahman is characterized by existence (*sat*), or by consciousness (*bodha*), or by both characteristics.
To this we reply: in every case, the commencement of a separate topic is entirely purposeless.

If this effort is intended to refute the multiplicity of attributes in the supreme Brahman, then since that has already been refuted by the preceding section, "Not even on account of place," the subsequent section, "And like light," would be entirely redundant.

Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that Brahman is characterized solely by existence (*sallakṣaṇa*) and not by consciousness (*bodhalakṣaṇa*), for that would result in the scriptural passages such as "He is a mass of pure consciousness" becoming meaningless.

Or how could Brahman, from which consciousness has been excluded, be taught as the Self of the conscious individual soul (jīva)? Nor can it be said that Brahman is characterized solely by consciousness and not by existence, for that would result in the absurdity of rendering such scriptural passages as "It is to be apprehended only as 'it is'" meaningless. Furthermore, how could consciousness be admitted to exist if its very being (sattā) has been excluded?
Nor can it be said that Brahman possesses both characteristics, for that would result in a contradiction with the previously accepted position.

For one who asserts that Brahman is endowed with both consciousness (bodha) excluded from existence (sattā) and existence (sattā) excluded from consciousness, the very same state of possessing manifoldness (saprapañcatva)—which was refuted in the preceding section—would necessarily follow. If it is argued that this is not a fault because it is so stated in scripture, we say no; for it is logically impossible for a single entity to possess multiple distinct natures. If it were further argued that existence itself is consciousness and consciousness itself is existence, such that there is no mutual exclusion between the two, even then the following dilemma would remain without resolution: Is Brahman characterized by existence, or by consciousness, or by both? This alternative would thus be rendered entirely groundless.
However, we have treated these sūtras as forming a distinct section (adhikaraṇa).

Furthermore, since there are conflicting scriptural statements regarding Brahman— some presenting it as having form and others as being formless— once the formless Brahman has been accepted, the interpretation of the other scriptural passages must necessarily be explained.
Thus, the sūtras beginning with "And like light" (aprakāśavacca) become more meaningful.

Furthermore, as for what they say—that even those scriptural passages which speak of forms (ākāra) are intended solely for the realization of the formless (anākāra) by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca), and do not have a separate meaning—this also does not appear to be correct.

Why? For those few phenomena that are mentioned in the context of the higher knowledge (paravidyā), such as "For his bay horses are yoked, ten times a hundred," or "He indeed is the bays, he indeed is the tens, the thousands, the many, and the infinite," let these be for the purpose of dissolution.
This is because of the concluding statement: "This is that Brahman, without interior, without exterior, without beyond, and without within.

Furthermore, as for the elaborations mentioned in the context of injunctions for meditation—such as "consisting of mind, having prāṇa as its body, and having light as its form"—it is not logical to hold that their purpose is dissolution (into Brahman), since they are connected with the very injunctions for meditation under discussion, such as "He should form a resolve" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*).

Moreover, since it is possible for qualities of this kind to serve the purpose of meditation according to the direct statement (śruti), it is not tenable to assume through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) that they serve the purpose of dissolution.

Furthermore, if all [qualities] were equally intended for dissolution, the statement providing the reason for determination—namely, "For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is the principal"—would be rendered meaningless. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda).

It is indeed understood that their fruits, according to the instruction, consist in some cases of the destruction of evil, in some cases of the attainment of sovereignty, and in some cases of gradual liberation; therefore, it is logical that the meditative passages (*upāsanā-vākya*) and the passages concerning Brahman (*brahma-vākya*) possess distinct purposes, and not that they form a single syntactical unity.

[The opponent] asks: "How is it to be explained that these [texts] possess a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*)? If you say it is because a single injunction (*niyoga*) is perceived, as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, we reply: No, because there is no injunction in the texts concerning Brahman. For the texts concerning Brahman culminate in the mere reality (*vastumātra*) itself; they do not teach an injunction. This has been established in detail in the sūtra, 'But that [Brahman is known] through the harmony [of the texts]' (*tattu samanvayāt*). Furthermore, it must be stated what the object of the injunction here is intended to be; for a person being enjoined is enjoined to some activity of his own, such as 'Do this!'"

Objection: The dissolution of the manifold world of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*) will indeed be the object of the injunction (*niyoga*). For as long as the manifold world of duality has not been dissolved, the realization of the reality of Brahman does not occur; therefore, the manifold world of duality, which stands as an obstacle to the realization of the reality of Brahman, must be dissolved. Just as a sacrifice is taught to be performed by one desiring heaven, so too is the dissolution of the manifold world taught for one desiring liberation (*apavarga*).

And just as one who desires to perceive the true nature of a jar or similar object situated in darkness must dissolve that darkness which stands in opposition to it, so too must one who desires to perceive the reality of Brahman dissolve the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which stands in opposition to it; for the phenomenal world has the nature of Brahman, whereas Brahman does not have the nature of the phenomenal world.
Thus, through the dissolution of the phenomenal world of names and forms, the realization of the reality of Brahman occurs. This concludes the third chapter. MARTINA.

In this regard, we ask: what is this so-called dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? Is the dissolution of the phenomenal world to be effected like the melting away of the solidity of ghee through contact with the heat of fire; or rather, is the phenomenal world of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) within Brahman to be dissolved by knowledge (*vidyā*), just as the manifold moons created by a visual disorder (*timira*) are dissolved when there is only one moon?

In that regard, if it were said that this existing phenomenal world—consisting of the internal body and so forth, as well as the external earth and so forth—is to be dissolved, then since it is impossible for a mere human being to dissolve it, the instruction for its dissolution would have an unattainable object;
furthermore, if the dissolution of the earth and so forth were accomplished by a single person who was liberated from the beginning, the world would now be devoid of earth and the other elements.

Now, if this world-phenomenon (prapañca), which is superimposed upon the one Brahman by ignorance (avidyā), is dissolved through knowledge (vidyā), then Brahman alone—by the negation of the world-phenomenon superimposed by ignorance—must be made known [through the scriptures] by such statements as: "Brahman is indeed one without a second," and "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou. When that has been made known, knowledge arises of its own accord.

And by that [knowledge], ignorance is sublated; consequently, this entire phenomenal world of name and form, superimposed by ignorance, dissolves like the phenomena of a dream. However, if Brahman has not been made known, then even if one were told a hundred times, "Produce the knowledge of Brahman and effect the dissolution of the phenomenal world," neither the knowledge of Brahman nor the dissolution of the phenomenal world would occur. Now, it might be argued that once Brahman has been made known, there could be an injunction regarding its knowledge or regarding the dissolution of the phenomenal world which is its object, since both [Brahman and the world] are established [by perception]. [To this we reply: No, because of the commentary on the *Rajjusūtra*.

No; for by the very knowledge that Brahman is the Self free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), and by the manifestation of its own true nature alone, there occurs both the realization of its true nature and the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca) such as the snake superimposed through ignorance;
nor is that which has already been accomplished performed again.

Furthermore, as for that which is understood as the so-called *jīva* during the state of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), it must belong either to the side of the phenomenal world or to the side of Brahman. In the first alternative, since the *jīva*—like the earth and other elements—is dissolved by the teaching of the non-phenomenal reality of Brahman, to whom could an injunction regarding the dissolution of the phenomenal world be addressed? Or to whom could liberation be said to be attained through adherence to an injunction? In the second case as well, once it is established that Brahman alone—which is by nature not subject to injunction—is the true nature of the *jīva*, and that its status as a *jīva* is merely produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), there is an absence of an injunction due to the absence of any person to be enjoined within Brahman.

Words such as "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), though read in the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), are primarily intended to direct one's attention toward reality (*tattva*); they do not have the primary purpose of enjoining the act of knowing reality itself.

Even in common worldly usage, in instructions of this kind—such as "look at this" or "listen to this"—one is told merely to apply one's attention (*praṇidhāna*), not that one should produce knowledge directly.
Even for one who is directed toward the object of knowledge, knowledge sometimes arises and sometimes does not.

Therefore, one who wishes to make something known must show it as an object of knowledge to that person; when that object is shown, knowledge arises spontaneously according to the object and according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even for one who is instructed, it is not possible for a contrary cognition to arise regarding an object already established otherwise by another means of valid cognition.
If, while among the wise, one were to form a contrary cognition—thinking, for instance, "I have been appointed again"—that would not be true knowledge; rather, it is a mental activity.
If such a cognition were to arise spontaneously as something contrary, it would simply be an error.
Knowledge, however, is produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and has as its object things as they truly are;
it cannot be brought about even by a hundred injunctions, nor can it be prevented even by a hundred prohibitions;
for it is not dependent on the person, but is indeed dependent solely on the thing itself.
For this reason as well, there is an absence of *niyoga* (an injunction).

Furthermore, if the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) were to culminate solely in being centered on *niyoga*, then that which has been accepted—the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self, which is not subject to an injunction—would be rendered without any means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇaka*).

If, on the other hand, the scripture itself were to declare that the soul has Brahman as its non-subject-to-injunction self and yet also enjoin a person toward the realization of that, then it would follow that the single scripture concerning Brahman would have both a futile purpose and a contradictory purpose.

Furthermore, if there were a focus on injunction (*niyoga*), there would be the abandonment of what is heard in scripture (*śrutahāni*) and the assumption of what is not heard (*aśrutakalpanā*); moreover, liberation would have the status of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭaphalatva*) like the fruits of ritual action, as well as the consequence of being non-eternal (*anityatva*). Such defects could not be resolved by anyone.
Therefore, the sentences concerning Brahman culminate in comprehension alone, and do not culminate in injunction.
Consequently, the claim that they constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) because of the cognition of a single injunction is incorrect.

Moreover, even if the existence of an injunction (*niyoga*) were admitted in the statements concerning Brahman, their unity—both in those teachings that deny the world of plurality (*niṣprapañca*) and those that teach it with plurality (*saprapañca*)—would remain unestablished.

For when a difference in injunctions is understood through means of knowledge such as the "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*), it is impossible to maintain that there is one single injunction everywhere.

However, in the case of the sentences regarding the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, unity is appropriate because of the non-difference in the aspect of the qualification (*adhikāra*).
But here, in the injunctions concerning the qualified and the unqualified, there is no part that effects their identity;

for qualities such as consisting of light do not assist in the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca), nor does the dissolution of the phenomenal world assist qualities such as consisting of light, because they are mutually contradictory.
Indeed, it is not possible to reconcile within a single substrate both the total dissolution of the phenomenal world and the dependence upon a portion of that very world.
Therefore, the distinction we have stated regarding the teachings on those with form and those without form is indeed more logical.
For [the scripture] negates only that which has been previously stated; thereafter, it speaks further.
The Adhikaraṇa concerning the Discourse (Vākya).

Having begun with, "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless," and having divided the five great elements into two groups, and having shown the colors such as saffron and so forth belonging to the formless essence—which is designated by the term "this" (*etat*) as previously described—it is further recited: "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this' (neti neti); for there is nothing else higher than this 'not this'.
Regarding this, we desire to know: what is the object of this negation?
For here nothing specific is perceived that could be negated as "this is that";
rather, by the word *iti*, something to be negated is presented here, because the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) follows the phrase "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
This word *iti* has a proximate object as its referent and functions in the same manner as the word *evam* (thus), when it is employed [in such contexts]. Thus ends the third chapter.
[This occurs] in passages such as, "It is seen," and "Thus indeed the teacher used to say.
And here, by the force of the context, two forms of Brahman together with their manifold expansion are present; and that is Brahman, to which those two forms belong.
In this regard, a doubt arises in us: does this negation negate both the forms and the possessor of forms, or only one of the two?
Even when it is one or the other, does it negate Brahman and leave the forms remaining, or does it negate the forms and leave Brahman remaining?

In this regard, one might raise the doubt that since there is no distinction in their being the subject under discussion, both [negations] negate [Brahman]; for there are two such negations, as evidenced by the employment of the word "not" twice.
Of these, by one the form of Brahman together with its phenomenal expansion (saprapañca) is negated, while by the other it is thought that Brahman possessing form is negated;
or else, Brahman itself as possessing form is negated.
For that [Brahman], because it transcends speech and mind, its existence is not easily conceived and thus it is fit for negation;

however, the manifold of forms (rūpa-prapañca) is not fit for negation, as it falls within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge. Since the repetition [of the negation] is for the sake of showing reverence, such being the position reached, we reply: first of all, the negation of both is not tenable, because it would lead to the doctrine of nihilism (śūnyavāda). For something unreal is negated only by taking recourse to some ultimate reality, just as snakes and the like are negated in relation to ropes and so forth.

And that [negation] is possible only when some entity remains; but if there were a total negation of everything, what other entity would remain? Furthermore, if nothing else remained while another entity was being attempted to be negated, that negation would be impossible because the very thing being negated would, by default, attain the status of ultimate reality. Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable, because it contradicts the opening statement, "I shall tell you of Brahman," and because of the passage: "He becomes non-existent indeed."

Because this would contradict condemnations such as "If one knows Brahman as non-existent," because it would contradict definitive declarations such as "It is to be apprehended as indeed existing," and because it would entail the subversion of all the Vedāntas;
furthermore, the fact that Brahman transcends speech and mind is not stated with the intention of implying its non-existence—

for having established Brahman in the Vedāntas with great elaboration through such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," its non-existence could certainly not be asserted thereafter.
For there is the maxim: "Indeed, it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
The method of exposition, however, is this: "From whence words return, together with the mind, having failed to reach it."

This is what is meant: Brahman is that which transcends speech and mind, does not fall within the range of any object, is the innermost self (pratyagātman), and is by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free.
Therefore, it should be understood that [the scripture] negates the manifold expansion of forms belonging to Brahman and leaves Brahman alone as the remainder.
This is what is stated: "For it negates the extent of that which has been presented.
This word negates that form of Brahman which has been presented—that is, that which is limited by such a measure, characterized as both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta).
For that [form] was indeed presented and elaborated in the preceding text, both with respect to the divine (adhidaivata) and the corporeal (adhyātma).

And another form produced by that very [Brahman], characterized as *vāsanā* (latent impression), consisting of the essence of the incorporeal, denoted by the word "Person" (*puruṣa*), and residing in the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), is shown through similes such as saffron-dyed cloth and the like. This is because it is impossible for the Person, who is the essence of the incorporeal, to possess a form perceivable by the eye.
It is understood that this manifold form of Brahman is presented to the negative particle (*nañ*)—which functions as a negator with respect to what is proximate—by means of the particle "iti."
In the preceding text, Brahman was indicated by the genitive case as a qualifier of form, not as a primary subject.
And when its two forms have been elaborated, this inquiry into the true nature of the possessor of those forms is commenced with the words: "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'.
In that context, it is determined that the revelation of Brahman’s own nature occurs through the negation of its superimposed forms.
For this entire effect, which has that [Brahman] as its substratum, is negated by the words "not this, not this.

And it is logical that the non-existence of the effect is established through such means as the scriptural statement "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*); thus there is the negation "not this, not this," but this does not apply to Brahman, because Brahman is the root of all conceptualization.

Nor should this doubt be raised here: "How is it that the scripture itself, having shown two forms of Brahman, then negates them again—as the saying goes, 'It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off'? For this scripture does not point out these two forms of Brahman as things to be established; rather, it refers to these two forms, well-known in the world and superposed upon Brahman, for the purpose of negating them and for the purpose of establishing the nature of pure Brahman. Thus, there is no fault.
These two negations, according to the principle of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhyanyāya*), negate both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*).
Alternatively, the former negation negates the aggregate of elements (*bhūtarāśi*), while the latter negates the aggregate of latent impressions (*vāsanārāśi*).

Or else, this is a repetition (*vīpsā*)—"not this, not this"—meaning that whatever may be imagined, all that is not Brahman. For if the negation were applied only to a limited enumeration, there might arise the inquiry: "If this is not Brahman, what else could be Brahman?"

But when there is distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), because the entire range of objects is negated, the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—which is Brahman—is not an object [of cognition], and thus the desire to know ceases.
Therefore, the conclusion is that [the text] negates only the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) imagined upon Brahman, while leaving Brahman itself remaining.

For this reason also, this alone is the definitive conclusion: because after the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the text further declares "there is another, higher [than that]" regarding Brahman.
For if the negation were intended to terminate in non-existence (*abhāva*), why would it say "there is another, higher"?

In this regard, the construction of the words is as follows: having pointed out Brahman with "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), it then explains that very instruction: what is the meaning of "not this, not this"? It is not that there exists anything distinct from this Brahman; therefore it is said "not this, not this," but not that Brahman itself does not exist.

And he shows that [the opponent's view]: "There is another, supreme Brahman, which is not denied. But when the syllables are construed thus—"Indeed, there is no other, supreme instruction regarding Brahman than this instruction consisting of the negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in the form 'not this, not this'"—then the statement, "And it speaks further than that," must be understood as referring to the name. For it says: "Now follows the name: 'The Truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth; He is their truth. Thus it speaks.
And that [negation] is appropriate when it culminates in Brahman;
for if the negation culminated in non-existence, why would it be said, "the Truth of truth"? Therefore, we conclude that this negation culminates in Brahman, not in non-existence.
For that indeed states it explicitly.

AMALĪYA: If that Supreme Brahman, which is other than the prohibited multitude of phenomenal manifestations, exists, why is it not perceived? It is said in reply: it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), not graspable by the senses, because it is the witness of all that is visible.

Indeed, the Śruti declares thus: "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other gods, nor by austerity or ritual action"; "This very Self is 'not this, not this'—ungraspable, for it is not grasped"; "That which is invisible, ungraspable"; and "When indeed he [the seeker] reaches that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and supportless," and so forth.
Smṛti as well [confirms this], beginning with: "This is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable."
Moreover, [the existence of the Lord] is established through perception and inference during the process of propitiation.
Moreover, yogins perceive this Self—which is unmanifest and devoid of all phenomenal expansion—at the time of *saṃrādhana*;
and *saṃrādhana* consists in the practice of devotion, meditative concentration (*vyāna*), focused application (*praṇidhāna*), and so forth.
But how is it known that they perceive it at the time of *saṃrādhana*? By means of perception and inference; that is to say, by means of Śruti and Smṛti.
For thus says the Śruti: "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self.

But some wise man, desiring immortality, looked within himself with his vision turned back. And likewise: "With the clarity of knowledge, one whose being is purified beholds Him, the partless, through meditation. And so forth. Smṛti also says: "Those who are sleepless, who have conquered their breath, who are contented, and whose senses are restrained..."
Salutations to that Self of Yoga, whom those who practice yoga perceive as light.
"Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One"—and so forth.
[Objection: "But surely, from the admission of the relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator, there would be a difference between the higher and lower selves.
[Reply: No; it is said: "And as in the case of light and so forth, there is non-distinctness; and light [is manifested] through practice in action."

Just as light, space, the sun, and so forth appear as if they possess distinctions when associated with limiting adjuncts such as a finger, a hand, or water, yet do not abandon their own inherent nature of non-distinction;
even so, this differentiation of the Self is caused solely by limiting adjuncts, whereas in its own right, there is only oneness of Self.
For it is thus that in the Vedānta texts, the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Intellect (prājña) is established repeatedly through constant repetition.
The Third Chapter:
"Therefore [the soul is] with the Infinite; for thus there is an indicative mark."

And therefore, because non-difference is innate and difference is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), the individual soul (*jīva*), having dispelled ignorance through knowledge (*vidyā*), attains oneness with the supreme, infinite, and wise Self (*ātman*).
For thus says the indicative scriptural text: "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "Being Brahman, he goes to Brahman," and so forth.
But [the case is] like that of a serpent and its coils, because of the designation of both.
Having established [the identity] in that very state of the one who propitiates and the one being propitiated, he introduces another view for the sake of clarifying his own position:

in some places, a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Intelligence (prājña) is designated—as in "Then, meditating, he beholds Him who is partless," where they exist as the meditator and the object of meditation, or the seer and the object seen;
and as in "He goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high," where they exist as the goer and the goal.
"Who controls all beings from within"—thus [they are distinguished] by the relationship of controller and controlled.

However, in some places their non-difference is also designated, as in: "That thou art, that thou art," "I am Brahman," "This is thy Self, the innermost of all," and "This is thy Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
Since both types of designation occur there, if non-difference alone were grasped exclusively, the designation of difference would be entirely without foundation.

Therefore, because both designations are observed, the reality here must be like that of a snake and its coils: just as there is non-difference in saying "it is a snake," yet there is difference in the qualities such as being coiled, expanded, or long, so it is in this case as well.
In the commentary on the Sūtra, it is stated: "Or rather, it is like light and its substratum, because of its nature as fire."

Alternatively, this should be understood as being like light and its substrate: just as the solar light and its substrate, the sun, are not absolutely distinct—since there is no difference between the two in their nature as fire—and yet they both admit of a designation of distinction, so it is here as well.
The syllable *pā* is as before.
Or, just as it was previously proposed that "there is no distinction [between the two], like light and so forth," so too must this be the case;
for since bondage is produced by ignorance, liberation through knowledge is logically possible.

If, however, some self were admitted to be bound in the ultimate sense—existing as a particular configuration of the supreme Self according to the analogy of a snake and its coils, or as a part of it according to the analogy of light and its substrate—[then liberation would be impossible].
Consequently, since an ultimately real bondage cannot be set aside, the futility of the scriptures on liberation would follow.
