Furthermore, the Śruti does not here designate both difference and non-difference as being equally authoritative;

rather, it points to non-difference alone as that which is to be established, while it merely restates difference—which is already well-known from prior experience—with the intention of conveying a different meaning.
Therefore, the established conclusion is precisely this: "And like light and so forth, there is no difference [in nature]."
And because of the prohibition.

For this reason as well, this alone is the established conclusion (siddhānta): because the scripture negates any conscious being other than the Supreme Self, stating, "There is no seer other than He," and so forth; and because, by negating the phenomenal world (prapañca) apart from Brahman through the teaching, "Now follows the instruction: not this, not this," and "This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior," it is understood that this alone is the established conclusion, since nothing remains but Brahman.

Regarding this Brahman which has been determined as that in which all manifoldness (*prapañca*) is cast aside, there arises a doubt due to conflicting scriptural statements as to whether there exists some other reality beyond it or not.
For certain passages, appearing at first glance, seem to establish a reality even higher than Brahman;

it is for the purpose of refuting these that this undertaking is commenced, [beginning with the Sūtra]: "On account of the designation of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference, [there is something] beyond."
Therefore, there must exist another reality beyond this Brahman.
Why? Because of the designation of a bridge, the designation of measurement, the designation of relation, and the designation of difference.
First, regarding the designation of a bridge: "Now, that which is the Self is a bridge and a support"—this declares that Brahman, denoted by the word "Self," possesses the nature of a bridge.
For in common worldly usage, the word "bridge" (setu) is well known to denote a collection of earth, wood, and so forth that interrupts the flow of water;

and since the word "bridge" is applied here to the Self, it implies the existence of something other than the bridge-like Self, just as in the case of a worldly bridge. Furthermore, because of the use of the verb "to cross over" in the phrase "having crossed the bridge," it is understood that just as one crosses a worldly bridge and reaches a dry land that is not a bridge, so too, having crossed the Self which is the bridge, one reaches the non-Self which is not a bridge.
Furthermore, there is a designation of measurement: "This Brahman has four feet, eight hooves, and sixteen parts.
Now, it is well known in the world that whatever is measured—such as a kārṣāpaṇa coin or the like, defined as "this much"—there exists another thing beyond it.
Similarly, because Brahman is measured, it is understood that there must exist something other than it.

Likewise, there is a designation of a relationship [between them], as in: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), and "The embodied self is completely embraced by the conscious Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21). Furthermore, a relationship between limited things and a limit is observed, as for example, that of men with a city;
and the scripture designates a relationship between individual souls and Brahman during deep sleep.
Therefore, it is understood that there exists something else, different and immeasurable beyond this.
Furthermore, the designation of difference leads to this conclusion;

for instance, having designated the Lord as residing in the sun in the passage, "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun," the text then designates the Lord as residing in the eye as distinct from him: "Now, this person who is seen in the eye."

Furthermore, he extends [the attributes] of this [Self] to those [elements] such as form and so on, saying: "The form of this one is the very same as the form of that one, up to its strides (geṣṇau) are those strides, and its name is that name";

and he designates the lordship of both as being limited: "He rules over the worlds that are beyond that [sun], and over the desires of the gods," thus for one; and "He rules over the worlds that are below this [breath], and over the desires of men," thus for the other—just as one says, "This is the kingdom of the Magadha king, and this is the kingdom of the Videha king."
Thus, from these designations such as "bridge" and so forth, it follows that there exists something higher than Brahman.
This being the case, it is now established that these are indeed general [injunctions].
The word "but" (tu) negates the attainment [of duality] that was previously indicated.
Nothing other than Brahman can exist, because there is a lack of evidence; for we do not perceive any proof whatsoever for the existence of anything else.
Indeed, it has been determined that for the entire multitude of born things, birth and so forth proceed from Brahman, and that the effect is non-different from its cause.

Furthermore, nothing unborn (*aja*) is possible apart from Brahman, because of the restrictive determination in the passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second";
and because the promise of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is made, the existence of any entity distinct from Brahman cannot be conceived.
Now, it was argued that designations such as "bridge" and so forth indicate a reality distinct from Brahman.

To this it is replied: the designation of a "bridge" (setu) is not capable of establishing the existence of something external to Brahman; for the text says, "The Self is the bridge," and does not say, "There is nothing beyond this.
In that case, if there were nothing beyond, the nature of being a bridge would not be possible, and thus some further entity beyond it would have to be postulated.
And this is not logical;

for it would be a mere dogmatic assumption to postulate something unestablished. Furthermore, by using the worldly bridge as an illustration, one who attributes the status of being an external object to the Self on the basis of its designation as a "bridge" would also be led to the conclusion that it is made of clay or wood;
and this is not logical, because it contradicts scriptural texts concerning the Self's birthlessness and other such qualities.
However, it is accepted that the word "bridge" (setu) is applied to the Self because of a commonality with a bridge;
the commonality with a bridge in the Self consists in its being the upholder of the world and its boundaries.
Therefore, the Self under discussion is praised as "a bridge, as it were, a bridge."

In the expression "having crossed the bridge" (*setuṃ tīrkhā*), the root *tṛ* (to cross) functions only in the sense of "reaching," because crossing over [the bridge] is impossible; just as when one says "he has crossed grammar" (*vyākaraṇaṃ tīrṇaḥ*), it means he has mastered it, not that he has passed beyond it. It is the same here.
Until the purpose of awakening is fulfilled.

As for what was said—that there exists something beyond [Brahman] because of the mention of its measurement—it is replied to this: even the mention of measurement is not intended to establish the existence of an entity distinct from Brahman.
What, then, is its purpose? It is for the sake of the intellect (*buddhy-artha*), that is to say, for the sake of meditation (*upāsanā*).

The thought, "How indeed might a firm conception of Brahman as having four feet, eight hooves, and sixteen parts arise?"—it is precisely for this reason that a measurement of Brahman is conceptually constructed by means of its modifications (*vikāra*).
For it is not possible for all men to fix their intellect upon the changeless and infinite Brahman, because of the inferiority, mediocrity, and superiority of men's intellects.

It is like the case of the "feet": just as in the case of the mind and the ether—which are taught as symbols (*pratīka*) of Brahman with respect to the self (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaivata*) respectively—four "feet" consisting of speech and so forth are imagined as related to the mind, and four others consisting of fire and so forth are imagined as related to the ether for the purpose of meditation (*ādhyāna*), so it is here.

Alternatively, "like a quarter" means that just as a division into quarters is conceived for a kārṣāpaṇa for the sake of facilitating common transactions—since not all people are always able to transact using the entire kārṣāpaṇa due to the lack of fixed rules regarding the quantities in buying and selling—it is the same in this case.
The soul is not limited by a particular location, just as light and other such things are not.
In this Sūtra, a refutation of both the designation of relation and the designation of difference is stated.
As for what was said—that because of the designation of relation and the designation of difference, there must be another [entity]—that too is incorrect;
for even in the case of a single entity, these two designations are possible with respect to its particular location.

Regarding the designation of "relation" (*saṃbandha*), the meaning is as follows: when specific cognition has arisen due to connection with particular limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and their respective locations, the cessation of that [cognition] upon the withdrawal of the adjuncts is figuratively designated as "relation with the Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) in relation to those adjuncts, not in relation to any limitation [of the Self].

Likewise, even the designation of "difference" (*bheda*) regarding Brahman is figuratively applied only in relation to the difference of its limiting adjuncts, not in relation to any difference in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The phrase "like light, etc. is employed as an illustration: just as in the case of a single light—whether solar or lunar—which acquires particular distinctions through association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there occurs a designation of relation upon the cessation of those adjuncts, and a designation of difference due to the diversity of the adjuncts;

or just as in the cases of the space within a needle's eye, a water-jar, and so forth, these two designations of relation and difference occur solely in dependence on limiting adjuncts, so it is here.

And on account of the logical possibility. In this context, such a relationship alone is logically possible, and not any other. For the scripture declares this to be a relationship of essential nature in the passage, "He becomes merged in his own [Self]" (*svam apīto bhavati*).
Since the essential nature is indestructible, a relationship in the manner of a man and his city is not tenable.
However, because the essential nature is concealed by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the statement "He becomes merged in his own" is logically consistent.
Likewise, a difference of any other kind is not possible, because it would contradict the oneness of the Lord well-established by numerous scriptural texts;

and thus scripture explains the designation of a difference in the single ether based on its locations: "That which is the ether outside the person, that which is the ether within the person, and that which is the ether within the heart."
Likewise, because of the negation of others.
Having thus refuted the arguments of the opposing side regarding designations such as "bridge" and so forth, he now concludes his own position with another reason:
likewise, it is understood from the negation of anything else that there is no other entity superior to Brahman.

For instance, such statements as "He alone is below; I alone am below," "The Self alone is below," "Everything would desert him who knows everything as other than the Self," "Brahman alone is all this," "The Self alone is all this," "There is not the slightest diversity here," and "Than whom there is nothing higher, nothing further—this is that Brahman, without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior"—these and other passages situated within their own respective contexts cannot be interpreted as having any other meaning, and they exclude any entity distinct from Brahman.
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the "innermost," it is understood that there is no Self other than the Supreme Self;
there exists no inner self distinct from it.
By this [sūtra], its omnipresence is established on account of the words "extent" (āyāma) and so forth.
By this refutation of designations such as "bridge" and by resorting to the negation of anything else, the all-pervasiveness of the Self is also established;
otherwise, it would not be established.
For if the designations of "bridge" and so forth were accepted in their primary sense, limitation would result for the Self, since bridges and the like possess such a nature.
Likewise, even when there is no negation of another, if a thing were not excluded from other things, it would follow that the self is merely limited [in its cognition].
Furthermore, its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) is understood from words such as "extent" (*āyāma*); the word "extent" is a term denoting pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For scriptural texts, traditional codes, and logical arguments—such as "As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart; like space, it is all-pervading and eternal," "Greater than heaven, greater than space, eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient"—demonstrate that the Self is omnipresent.
The fruit [proceeds] from Him, because that is logical.
In this very Brahman, during its empirical state characterized by the distinction between the ruler and the ruled, another nature is described.

Regarding that which is well known among living beings as the threefold fruit of action—consisting of the desirable, the undesirable, and the mixed—which falls within the sphere of *saṃsāra*: does this fruit have action as its locus, or does it come from the Lord? Such is the inquiry. In this regard, it is first established that the fruit must indeed proceed from the Lord.
Why? Because it is logical.

For he, as the presiding lord of all, ordaining the diverse processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, brings about fruits corresponding to the actions of the agents because he is cognizant of the specific details of place and time; this is logical.
However, it is illogical that an action which perishes moment by moment should have a fruit occurring at a later time, because an entity cannot arise from non-existence.

It might be argued that an action, while perishing, produces its own corresponding fruit at its very time of destruction, and that this fruit will be experienced by the agent at a later time. This too is not tenable, because it cannot be established as a "fruit" prior to its connection with an experiencer. For in the world, only that pleasure or pain which is actually experienced by the self at a given time is recognized as a "fruit.
Indeed, worldly people do not acknowledge the status of being a fruit for a pleasure or pain that is not connected to the self.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let there not be the production of the fruit immediately after the action; rather, the fruit will arise from the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is the effect of the action. That too is untenable, because it is impossible for the *apūrva*—which is insentient, equivalent to a piece of wood or a clod of earth, and not impelled by a conscious agent—to engage in activity. Moreover, there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. If it is claimed that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the means of valid cognition, we say no; for once the existence of God (*Īśvara*) is established, the need for *arthāpatti* is exhausted.
And because it is so stated in scripture.

We do not postulate God as the cause of the fruit solely on the basis of logical reasoning; rather, we consider God alone to be the cause of the fruit because He is so stated in scripture. And there is a scriptural passage of this kind: "He indeed is that great unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.24). Thus ends the third chapter.
Jaimini [holds that] Dharma [is the subject matter], for this very reason.

The teacher Jaimini, however, considers the ritual action itself to be the giver of the fruit of dharma; for this very reason—namely, on account of scripture (*śruti*) and logical reasoning (*upapatti*).
First, this meaning is heard in such scriptural passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*);
and since the injunction (*vidhi-śruti*) therein functions as the subject matter, it is understood that the sacrifice is the producer of heaven.
Otherwise, the sacrifice would result in being without an agent of performance, and in that case, its instruction would be purposeless.
Now, it may be argued that since an action perishes moment by moment, a fruit [arising from it] is not possible; however, this position has already been abandoned.

This is not a fault, because the Veda is authoritative. If the Veda is authoritative, then this connection between action and its fruit, as it is heard in scripture, must be understood in such a way that it becomes logically consistent.
Furthermore, an action, having perished without first producing some unseen principle (*apūrva*), cannot bestow a fruit at a later time.
Therefore, it is inferred that there exists either a certain subtle subsequent state of the action, or a prior state of the fruit, which is called *apūrva*.
And this meaning is established by the manner already stated.

However, the claim that Īśvara bestows the fruit is untenable, because it is impossible for a non-diverse cause to produce diverse effects, which would entail the faults of partiality and cruelty, and would result in the futility of performing religious duties.
Therefore, the fruit arises from dharma alone.

"But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the former view, because of the designation of a cause. (Sūtra-bhāṣya) The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, considers the previously mentioned Lord alone to be the cause of the fruit. The position that the fruit arises from action alone or from the *apūrva* alone is set aside by the word "but" (*tu*).
Whether it be through dependence on action or dependence on the *apūrva*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fruit comes from the Lord.
Why? Because of the designation of a cause;

for even in the case of merit and demerit, the Lord is designated as the cause by virtue of being their instigator, and as the giver of the fruit, as it is said: "For he alone makes him perform good action whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds;
and he indeed makes him perform evil action whom he wishes to lead down."
And this meaning is recorded in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "Whatever form of deity a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his firm."
"Endowed with that faith, he attains through its propitiation the great [state], and from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone for his welfare.
Furthermore, in all the Vedāntas, it is declared that creations have God alone as their cause.
And this indeed is the Lord's causality regarding the fruit: that he creates progeny in accordance with their own karma.
Furthermore, defects such as the impossibility of diverse effects and so forth do not apply to the Lord, because he takes into account the efforts already exerted [by beings].

Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya). Composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.
The Third Pāda of the Third Chapter. The Third Pāda.
The true nature of Brahman, the object of knowledge, has been explained.
Now, however, it is investigated whether the cognitions [of Brahman] differ according to each Vedānta text or not.

But surely, Brahman, the object of knowledge, has been determined to be devoid of distinctions such as prior or posterior, to be of a single essence, like a mass of salt; [how then can there be differences in cognition]?

In that case, what occasion is there for considering the difference or non-difference of cognitions? For it cannot be said that, like the multiplicity of actions, the multiplicity of Brahmas is intended to be taught in the Vedāntas; because Brahman is one and of a single nature.
Furthermore, multiple forms of cognition are not possible regarding a Brahman that is of a single form;
for knowledge that is otherwise than the object cannot be non-erroneous.

If, however, many cognitions regarding a single Brahman were intended to be taught in the Vedāntas, then there would follow the consequence of a lack of confidence in the Vedāntas, since one among them would be non-erroneous while the others would be erroneous.
Therefore, it is not possible to suspect a difference in the cognition of Brahman for each respective Vedānta.
Nor can its non-difference be asserted on the grounds of the non-distinction of injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth, because the cognition of Brahman does not have the nature of an injunction.

The Teacher stated in the commentary on the Sūtra "But that [Brahman is known] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*) that the knowledge of Brahman is produced by Vedic statements which primarily concern the nature of reality and culminate in the object itself.
How then does he now undertake this investigation into difference and non-difference?
To this it is replied: there is no fault here, for this inquiry into the difference or non-difference of cognitions concerns both the qualified Brahman and the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth.
For in this case, as with ritual actions (*karma*), both difference and non-difference of meditations (*upāsanā*) are possible;

and just like ritual actions, these meditations are said to have visible results, invisible results, and some have the result of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) by way of the arising of perfect knowledge (*samyagdarśana*).
Regarding these, the following consideration arises: is there a difference in the cognitions in each Vedānta text, or rather not?

In this regard, the arguments for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) are first set forth: it is well known that a difference in name is a cause for the cognition of difference, as seen in the case of [the sacrifices] called *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others.

Furthermore, here there exist various distinct names for the cognitions enjoined in different Vedāntas, such as the *Taittirīyaka*, the *Vājasaneyaka*, the *Kauthumaka*, the *Kauṣītaka*, the *Śāṭyāyanaka*, and so forth.

Likewise, a difference in form (*rūpa*) is also well known to establish a difference in ritual action (*karma*), as in the cases of "the curd (*āmikṣā*) belongs to the Viśvedevas" and "the whey (*vājina*) belongs to the Vājins," and so on.
Moreover, there is a difference in form here:
for instance, some followers of certain Vedic schools mention a sixth additional fire in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), while others read of only five;
likewise, in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so forth, some mention fewer [organs] such as speech, while others mention more.

Likewise, a specific feature of the ritual (*dharmaviśeṣa*) has also been suspected as an indicator of a difference in action (*karmabheda*) in the case of the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others; and such a specific feature of the ritual exists here [in the *Agnihotra*], as stated in the third chapter of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*.
"The vow of the head for the Vāṇikas"—thus, repetitions and other such factors should also be applied as appropriate to the differences among the various Vedāntas.

Therefore, when it is thus argued that there is a difference in the cognitions (vijñāna) according to each Vedānta, we reply: "The cognition [of Brahman] is the same in all Vedāntas, because there is no difference in the injunctions (codanā) and so forth."
The means of proof: The cognitions taught in all the Vedāntas must be identical in each respective Vedānta;
why? Because there is no difference in the injunctions and other such factors.

By the inclusion of "all Vedāntas" and so forth, the reasons for non-difference set forth in the sūtra of the *Śākhāntara-adhikaraṇa*—namely, "because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name"—are drawn into this context; this is the meaning.

Just as in the case of the single Agnihotra sacrifice, even though the Vedic branches differ, the same human effort is enjoined by the injunction "one should offer oblations," so too in the case of the statement, "He who knows the eldest and the best," the injunction is identical for both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas.
Furthermore, the connection with the purpose is likewise undifferentiated, as it is stated: "He becomes the eldest and the best among his own people."

The form (*rūpa*) of that very consciousness is also the same in both cases; namely, the principle of *prāṇa* endowed with such qualifiers as "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and "best" (*śreṣṭha*). And just as the substance and the deity constitute the form of a sacrifice, so too the object to be known constitutes the form of consciousness, for by means of that [object], it is made manifest (*rūpyate*). Its designation (*samākhyā*) is also the same: "the knowledge of *prāṇa*" (*prāṇavidyā*).
Therefore, there is a single cognition of the meditations taught in all the Vedāntas.
In this same way, this principle should also be applied to the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*), the Vaiśvānara-knowledge, the Śāṇḍilya-knowledge, and so forth.

As for those apparent reasons for difference, such as name, form, and the like, they have already been refuted in the first section (the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya*) beginning with the sūtra: "It cannot be [determined] by name, because it is not a designation of an injunction" (*na nāmnā syādacodanābhidhānatvāt*).

Here too, having raised a certain objection regarding a distinction, he refutes it: "If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because of the difference [in number], no; for even in the case of a single [vow]."

It might be argued that the uniformity of all Vedāntic cognitions is not tenable due to differences in their qualities; for instance, the Vājasaneyins, having introduced the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), mention a sixth fire as something additional in the passage beginning with, "For him, fire itself becomes the fire," and so forth;
whereas the Chandogas do not mention that [sixth fire], but conclude with the number five alone, saying, "Now, he who knows these five fires thus."

How could one and the same knowledge be possible for both those who possess that quality and those who do not? Furthermore, the inclusion of these qualities cannot be accepted here, because it would contradict the number five.

Likewise, in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the Chandogas mention four other vital breaths besides the chief one—namely speech, sight, hearing, and mind—whereas the Vājasaneyins mention a fifth: "Semen indeed is Prajāpati; he who knows this is procreated with offspring and cattle."

If it be argued that "there is a difference in the object of knowledge (vedya) due to the difference in insertion and omission, and from the difference in the object of knowledge there follows a difference in the knowledge (vidyā), just as there is a difference in the sacrifice due to the difference in the substance and the deity," this is not a valid objection;
because such a difference in qualities is possible even within a single knowledge,
as in the case of the inclusion of the sixth fire in the third chapter of the Sūtras.
This is not possible; nevertheless, because the five fires beginning with *dyu* (heaven) are recognized in both [texts], a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) cannot exist.
For the *atirātra* sacrifice does not differ merely by the inclusion or exclusion of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
Moreover, the sixth fire is also recited by the Chandogas: "When he has departed from here, they carry him, as one destined, to the fires."

The Vājasaneyins, however, record in their text "His fire indeed becomes fire, the fuel becomes fuel," and so forth, in order to terminate the conceptualization of fuel, smoke, and so on, which persists in the case of the five fires that are merely figurative.
This is a constant restatement (nityānuvāda);
yet, even if this statement were for the purpose of meditation (upāsanā), even so, that quality can be combined by the Chandogas as well.
Nor should one fear a contradiction with the number five here;
for this number five, referring to the fires as they are meditated upon (sāṃpādika), is a constant restatement (nityānuvāda) and does not belong to the injunction itself—thus there is no fault.
In the same way, in the dialogues of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda) and so forth, the inclusion of an additional quality elsewhere is not contradictory.

Nor should one suspect that there is a difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) or a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) itself due to the addition or subtraction of certain elements; for even when some portion of the object of knowledge is added or subtracted, the non-difference of the vast majority of the aggregate of objects of knowledge is understood.
Therefore, it is indeed a single knowledge.

For, because of the nature of the private recitation (svādhyāya), and because of the qualification for the Samācāra [section], there is a restriction regarding that [recitation], just as in the case of the Sava sacrifice.

As for the argument that because the followers of the Atharva Veda require the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) and so forth for their knowledge (*vidyā*), while others do not, there must be a difference in the knowledge itself—that is refuted [in the following]. It is stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya:
"This is a duty (*dharma*) of the sacred study (*svādhyāya*), not of the knowledge.

How is this understood? Because, as a duty of the sacred study, the followers of the Atharva Veda record in their *Samācāra*—a text devoted to the instruction of Vedic vows—"This too has been explained as a Vedic vow. Thus, it is established that it is a duty of the sacred study.

Furthermore, from the statement, "One who has not performed the vow does not study this," it is determined—by means of the word "this" (etad) referring to the subject under discussion and by the word "study" (adhyayana)—that this is indeed a duty pertaining specifically to the study of one's own Upaniṣad.

Now, an objection might be raised: since the text, "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow (śirovrata) has been performed according to rule," mentions a connection with the "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā), and since there is only one single knowledge of Brahman everywhere, this duty would therefore apply universally. This is because the word "this" (etām) in that passage refers back to the very same subject previously introduced.

Furthermore, since the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is dependent upon a specific text, this rule [of study] is connected specifically to that particular text. The phrase "and like the *sava* sacrifices" is an illustrative reference; for just as the seven *sava* sacrifices, beginning with the *saurya* and ending with the *śataudana*, are restricted to the followers of the Atharva Veda alone—because they have no connection with the three fires mentioned in other Vedas, but rather a connection with the single fire mentioned in the Atharva Veda—so too is this rule of conduct restricted to that same [text] due to its connection with that specific recension of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).
Therefore, the threefold nature [of the Veda] is also beyond reproach.
And it demonstrates [this].

The Veda also demonstrates the unity of knowledge, because all the Vedāntas teach that the object of knowledge is one, as in the passage: "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim"; likewise: "For the Bahvṛcas investigate this very one in the Great Hymn (Mahad-uktha), the Adhvaryus in the Fire-altar, and the Chandogas in the Mahāvrata. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1)

Likewise, there is seen in the *Taittirīyaka* a reference to the quality of being a cause of fear—which was stated in the *Kāṭhaka* as "A great terror, a raised thunderbolt"—for the purpose of censuring the perception of difference: "For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear comes upon him;
it is precisely from that [perception] that fear arises for the one who knows [the distinction] but does not reflect."

Likewise, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, there is the reference to Vaiśvānara—as established in the Vājasaneyaka—where he has been described as being "span-long," in the passage: "But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Ātman, the span-long, the all-measuring.

Similarly, because meditations such as the Uktha and others enjoined elsewhere are referred to in other places for the purpose of enjoining their meditation, it is established by the principle of "observation of the majority" (prāyadarśananyāya) that these meditations also possess the character of being recognized across all Vedāntas.
And in the case of what is common [to both], there is a bringing together [of the details] because there is no difference in the purpose, as in the case of the supplementary injunctions.
This is the sūtra concerning the purpose.

And since it is thus established that all cognitions of the Vedānta texts have a single purport, there occurs a synthesis of the qualities of a cognition mentioned in one place even in another cognition, provided the cognition is the same;
this is the section concerning the object (*arthādhikaraṇa*).
Because of their non-difference: for whatever purpose those qualities serve toward a specific cognition in one place, that same purpose serves them in another as well;
since in both cases it is indeed that same single cognition, therefore there is a combination [of the qualities].

As in the case of the supplementary elements of an injunction, as stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: "Just as in the case of the duties of the Agnihotra and other rites which are supplementary to an injunction—since that very same single rite such as the Agnihotra exists everywhere, there is a combination [of its details] because there is no difference in purpose;
so it is here as well.

For if there were a difference in the cognitions, then, because the qualities would be bound to a different cognition and because there would be no relationship of original and modification, there would be no combination."
But in the case of the unity of consciousness (*vijñānaikatva*), it is not thus.
An elaboration of this very *prayojana-sūtra* will follow, beginning with the words "because of the non-difference of all" (*sarvābhedāt*).
If it is argued that there is a change [in the object] because of the word, we say no, because there is no distinction.

In the Vājasaneyaka, having introduced the passage, "The gods said, 'Come, let us overcome the Asuras by means of the Udgītha in the sacrifice,'" and "They said to Speech, 'Sing the Udgītha for us,'" and after rejecting Speech and the other vital breaths because they were pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the adoption of the principal breath (mukhya prāṇa) is recorded: "Then they said to this breath in the mouth, 'Sing the Udgītha for us'; 'So be it,' said he; then this breath sang the Udgītha for them. Similarly, there is a different presentation in the Chāndogya.

"Then the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, 'By this we shall overcome them. Having begun thus and having censured the other vital breaths (*prāṇas*) as being pierced by the evil of the Asuras, the adoption of the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is recorded in the same way: 'Then they meditated upon that which is this chief vital breath as the Udgītha.
In both cases, by means of the praise of the vital breath, the injunction for the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is determined.
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this a single knowledge? [End of Third Chapter]
There would be a difference [between the two], or rather, is there unity of knowledge?
What, then, is the initial position? That there is unity of knowledge according to the previous reasoning.
But is it not improper to maintain the unity of knowledge, because of the difference in the introductory context?

For the Vājasaneyins proceed in one way and the Chandogas in another: the Vājasaneyins enjoin the vital breath (prāṇa) as the agent of the Udgītha in the words, "Do thou sing out for me"; whereas the Chandogas enjoin it as the Udgītha itself in the words, "They meditated upon that as the Udgītha.
If it be asked how there can be identity of knowledge in such a case, we reply that this is no fault;
for the identity of knowledge does not disappear on account of such a difference, since a much greater degree of non-difference is also perceived.

For instance, the following many points are perceived without distinction in both places: the commencement of the battle between the gods and the Asuras; the intention regarding the destruction of the Asuras; the introduction of the Udgītha; the mention of speech and the other organs; the recourse to the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) through the censure of those [other organs]; and the destruction of the Asuras by its power, illustrated by the example of the clod of earth and the stone.

Furthermore, in the Vājasaneyaka as well, the co-referentiality of the vital breath with the Udgītha is heard in the text: "This, indeed, is the Udgītha. Therefore, even in the Chāndogya, the status of being the agent must be understood as implied.
And therefore, there is multiplicity.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" and other such passages.
Nor is it logical that there is identity of knowledge here; rather, a difference in knowledge alone is logical here.
Why? Because of the difference in context—that is to say, because of the difference in the introductory passage.

Likewise, in the Sūtra-bhāṣya [Pāda 3, Adhikaraṇa 3], a difference in the introductory context is observed: in the Chāndogya, having first introduced the object of meditation as the syllable *oṃ*—a part of the *udgītha*—in the words, "One should meditate on this syllable *oṃ* as the *udgītha*," and having then provided an explanatory exposition of its qualities such as being the "most essential essence" (*rasatama*) and so forth, the text subsequently returns once more to that very same *oṃ* syllable, which is a part of the *udgītha*, by means of the narrative of the gods and the Asuras, and states: "The gods meditated upon the *udgītha* as breath" (*prāṇamudgīthamupāsāṃcakrire*).

In this regard, if by the word "udgītha" the entire chant-portion (bhakti) were intended, and its performer the priest called the Udgātṛ, then the initial statement would be contradicted and a figurative interpretation (lakṣaṇā) would result;
moreover, within a single sentence, the conclusion must be in accordance with the opening.

Therefore, in this context, the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) is taught with respect to the syllable "Om," which is a part of the udgītha; however, in the Vājasaneyaka, because there is no reason for taking the word "udgītha" to refer to a mere part, the entire chant-portion is indicated.
The statement, "Do thou sing for us," likewise identifies the officiating priest, the Udgātṛ, as Prāṇa; thus, this constitutes a different method of exposition (*prasthānāntaram*).

Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of Prāṇa with the *udgītha* there is intended solely to demonstrate that Prāṇa—which is sought to be presented as the Udgātṛ—is the Self of all; therefore, it does not bring about the identity of the two meditations (*vidyaikatvam*).
Moreover, even in that case, the word *udgītha* refers only to the entire *bhakti* (chanting portion), which is another point of distinction.

Nor is the status of the Udgātṛ abandoned on the ground of impossibility, because, just like the nature of the Udgītha, the status of the Udgātṛ is also taught for the purpose of meditation; and since the Udgātṛ performs his office of the Udgātṛ solely by means of the power of Prāṇa,
there is no impossibility.
And thus it has been declared in that very same place: "For with speech and with breath he sang the udgītha.
Nor is it proper to determine identity of meaning merely on the basis of a similarity in the phrasing of the sentences when a difference in the intended meaning is clearly perceived.

For instance, although there is a similarity in the instructional formulations between the *Abhyudaya* passage and the *Paśukāma* passage—such as "One should divide the rice grains into three parts; those which are middling, one should make them into a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ"—nevertheless, due to the difference in their introductory contexts (*upakrama*), the displacement of deities is determined in the *Abhyudaya* passage, whereas in the *Paśukāma* passage, it is an injunction for a sacrifice. Likewise here, due to the difference in introductory contexts, there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*).

It is like the case of "being higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) and so forth. Just as, despite the similarity in the superimposition of the vision of the Supreme Self, the meditation on the *udgītha* characterized by the quality of being "higher than the high"—in the passages, "For space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort," and "This is that *udgītha* which is higher than the high; this is infinite"—is distinct from the meditation on the *udgītha* characterized by qualities such as having golden hair and beard located in the eye or the sun;
and just as there is no mutual combination of qualities even within a single recensional school (*śākhā*), so it is with regard to meditations of this kind situated in other recensional schools.
If it is argued that it exists as a designation, it has already been stated that even that [designation] exists.

Now, it might be argued that because the name is the same, it is logical that the knowledge (*vidyā*) is one here, since the name "Udgītha-vidyā" is identical in both places. That too is not tenable; for this has already been stated: "Or rather [the vidyās are different], because of the difference in context, as in the case of the 'higher than the high' (*parovarīyas*) and so forth. (Sūtra 3.3.7). And that alone is more reasonable here, as it follows the literal words of the scripture (*śruti*).
As for the identity of the name, however, it lies outside the literal words of the scripture; it is merely a conventional usage by worldly people based on the employment of the word "Udgītha" alone.
Moreover, there exists this unity of name, "Udgītha-vidyā," even for those meditations on the "higher and lower" (parovarīyas) and so forth whose differences are well-established.

Likewise, we observe that even for the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites whose differences are well-established, there is a unity of name, "Kāṭhaka," because they are recited in the single text of the Kaṭhas; so it will be here as well.
However, where no such cause for difference exists, let there be unity of the vidyā due to the unity of name, as in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā and others.
And the pervasiveness [of the Self] is perfectly logical.

Regarding the passage, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," since the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words 'syllable' (*akṣara*) and 'Udgītha' is heard, there arise the four possible positions of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), negation (*apavāda*), qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), and substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The inquiry is: which of these positions is the appropriate one here? Among them, "superimposition" (*adhyāsa*) means that while the cognition of one of two things has not yet been withdrawn, the cognition of the other is superimposed upon it.

In that wherein the cognition of another is superimposed, the cognition of that [original object] continues even when the cognition of the other has been superimposed; just as when the cognition of Brahman is superimposed upon a name, the cognition of the name continues and is not removed by the cognition of Brahman, or as the cognition of Viṣṇu and others is superimposed upon images and so forth—so too here, either the cognition of the Udgītha might be superimposed upon the Imperishable (akṣara), or the cognition of the Imperishable upon the Udgītha.

Sublation (*apavāda*) occurs when, regarding some object, a previously established false cognition has become certain, and a subsequently arising cognition of the thing as it truly is serves to remove that previously established false cognition. For example, the notion of a self with respect to the aggregate of the body and senses is removed by the subsequent true cognition "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), which concerns the Self itself; or again, the erroneous cognition of direction is removed by the cognition of the true nature of direction. In the same way here, the cognition of the *udgītha* would be removed by the cognition of the Imperishable (*akṣara*), or the cognition of the Imperishable would be removed by the cognition of the *udgītha*.

Identity (*ekatva*), however, consists in the two words "syllable" (*akṣara*) and "Udgītha" having no distinct referents, just as in the case of "best of the twice-born," "Brāhmaṇa," or "god of the earth.

Qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), on the other hand, serves to specify that particular portion of the Udgātṛ's office which pertains to the syllable "Om" that pervades all the Vedas, amidst the context of grasping that syllable—just as one says, "Bring that lotus which is blue. Likewise here, it means: "One should meditate upon that Udgītha which is the syllable Om.
When this sentence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is thus examined, these alternative views present themselves.

In this context, since there is no cause for determining any one [of the three alternatives] specifically, and because the state of non-determination would otherwise result, it is said: "And because of pervasion, [the view of] Samajasam is appropriate.

This word "ca" (and) is placed in the position of the word "tu" (but), with the purpose of excluding the other three positions. Thus, here the three faulty positions are set aside by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Only the position that [the word] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is accepted as being irreproachable.

In that regard, first concerning superimposition (*adhyāsa*): if the cognition that is superimposed upon another were [the meaning of] the word, it would follow that the word functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and its fruit would have to be postulated.
If it is argued that the fruit is indeed heard in such passages as, "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires," etc., we say no, because that has a different fruit.
For that is the fruit of the view of identity (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), not the fruit of superimposing [the Self] upon the *udgītha*.
Even in the case of sublation (*apavāda*), there is no such fruit;
if it is argued that the fruit is the cessation of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna-nivṛtti*), we say no.
Because no utility for human goals is perceived [in such a case];
nor would the cognition of "oṃ" ever cease from the syllable "oṃ," nor the cognition of the "udgītha" from the udgītha;
furthermore, this sentence does not aim at establishing the true nature of reality, because its purpose is the injunction of meditation (upāsanā).
Nor is the position of identity tenable;
for in that case, the utterance of two words would be purposeless, since the intended meaning would be conveyed by one alone.

Furthermore, there is no established usage of the word *udgītha* for the syllable *oṃ* as it occurs in the domain of the *hautra* or the *ādhvaryava*, nor is there any established usage of the word *oṃ* for the second part of the *sāman* known as the *udgītha*, such that they would have non-distinct meanings.
By process of elimination, the view that it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is adopted, because [the syllable *akṣara*] as the pervader would otherwise be common to all the Vedas;

lest the syllable *akṣara*—which is the pervader of everything—be erroneously understood here, the syllable is qualified by the word "Udgītha," so that the *oṃkāra* which constitutes a part of the Udgītha may be grasped.
But even in this view, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is equally present, since the word "Udgītha" must indicate its own constituent part.
This is indeed true;
however, even in the case of subtle things, proximity and remoteness do indeed exist, for [this is so] under the view of superimposition (adhyāsa). Thus ends the third chapter.

The figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is remote when the cognition of one object is applied to another object; however, in the case of the view that it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), a part is presented by a word denoting the whole, and thus it is proximate.
For words that function for wholes are seen to apply to parts as well, as in the cases of "cloth" or "village.
Therefore, because of this pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is logical that "this syllable *oṃ*" is the qualifier of "the *udgītha*"; the meaning is that this is faultless.
These others [are included] because there is no difference from all [of them].

The Topic: In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) of the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas, it is stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), endowed with the quality of preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*), is the object of meditation;
for there, speech and the other organs are also described as being endowed with qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth, which are non-different from all [the others].
And those qualities are further attributed to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by such passages as, "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent," and so forth.

However, in the dialogues concerning the vital breath among other Vedic schools, such as the Kauṣītaki, in passages of this kind beginning with, "Now, therefore, follows the acquisition of the highest good; these deities, indeed, were disputing as to who was the best," the superiority of the vital breath is stated, but these qualities such as being the most excellent are not mentioned there either.
In this regard, a doubt arises: should these qualities such as being the most excellent, which are mentioned in one place, be applied elsewhere as well, or should they not be applied?
In this regard, it is first established that they would not go [to the sun];
why? Because of the connection with the word "thus" (*evaṃ*).
For in various places in the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, such as "Now, he who, knowing thus, having understood the highest good in Prāṇa," the object to be known is indicated by the word "thus."
In this way, the word [“thus”] refers to what is proximate; it cannot indicate a collection of qualities of this kind that is recited in another branch.

Therefore, when it is argued that the soul’s fullness (*pūrṇatva*) is accomplished by the qualities residing in its own context alone, the Sūtra replies: these qualities—such as being the best (*vasiṣṭhatva*), and so on—which are mentioned in one place, should be admitted elsewhere as well.

Why? Because of the non-difference of all [the meditations]; everywhere, that same single knowledge of Breath (*prāṇavijñāna*) is recognized as non-different due to the similarity of the dialogue with Breath and other such features.
And if consciousness were non-different [in all cases], how could these qualities mentioned in one place not be admitted elsewhere?
But has it not already been stated that the word, in each respective instance, presents such a collection of qualities as belonging to a distinct [entity] for the sake of being known?

To this it is replied: although the collection of qualities found in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa is not mentioned by the word "thus" (*evam*) in the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa because it is not proximate there, nevertheless, since that same knowledge (*vijñāna*) is mentioned by the word "thus" in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa, the collection of qualities belonging to another recension (branch), being bound to that non-differentiated knowledge, does not differ from that which belongs to one's own recension.
And this being so, there is neither the abandonment of what is heard in scripture nor the assumption of what is not heard.

For even in the case of a single recensional branch (*śākhā*), qualities heard in one are indeed heard everywhere, because there is no difference in the possessor of those qualities; for Devadatta, who is well-known in his own country for qualities such as heroism, does not cease to possess those qualities when he goes to another country, even if those qualities are not yet recognized by the inhabitants of that other land. And as in that case, so it is here. (End of the third chapter.)

Just as the qualities of Devadatta are recognized even in another place due to his specific identity, so too, by virtue of a specific application (*abhiyoga*), the qualities to be meditated upon in one recensional branch (*śākhā*) should be applied even in another branch.
Therefore, those attributes connected to a single primary subject, even when mentioned in only one place, must be integrated everywhere.
Bliss and the other qualities belong to the Principal.

In the Śrutis dedicated to establishing the nature of Brahman, certain attributes of Brahman—such as being of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpatva*), being a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*), being all-pervading (*sarvagatatva*), and being the self of all (*sarvātmatva*)—are heard in various places. Regarding these, there arises a point of doubt: are the attributes such as bliss and the rest to be understood only insofar as they are heard in a particular passage, or are they all to be understood everywhere?

In this regard, when the practice of the Dharma has been established according to the distribution of the scriptural texts, the following is stated: The attributes of the primary Brahman, such as bliss and so forth, are to be understood everywhere.

Why? Because of the non-difference of that [Brahman] everywhere. For in all cases, that one primary Brahman, which is the substantive, does not differ. Therefore, the attributes of Brahman are universal, by virtue of the very same illustration of Devadatta’s bravery and so forth mentioned in the preceding section.
[Objection: But if this were so, then all attributes such as "having joy as its head" would also be intermingled everywhere.
For instance, in the Taittirīyaka, having introduced the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is taught: "Joy indeed is its head; delight is its right wing. [Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya, pāda ...]
"Bliss is its head; joy is its right wing; delight is its left wing; the Self is its trunk; Brahman is its tail, the foundation."
To this, he recites the following: "There is no attainment of having 'the beloved as the head' and so forth, for increase and decrease exist only where there is difference."

The attributes such as "having pleasure as its head" (priyaśiras), which are recorded in the Taittirīyaka, have no application elsewhere, because pleasure, joy, delight, and bliss are perceived as being of varying degrees—more or less intense—relative to one another and relative to different enjoyers;
and such increase and decrease are possible only where there is difference.
However, Brahman is without difference, according to scriptural passages such as "One only, without a second."
Furthermore, these qualities such as having bliss as the head and so forth are not attributes of Brahman;
rather, we have taught in the section beginning with "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition" that these are attributes of the sheaths (kośa).
Moreover, these are postulated merely as a means for directing the mind toward the supreme Brahman, and not as objects to be perceived [as Brahman itself].
Even so, there is all the more non-attainment of the "having pleasure as its head" and other such qualities elsewhere.
However, having established these as attributes of Brahman, the Teacher has merely demonstrated this principle—that there is no attainment of the "having pleasure as its head" and so forth.
And that same principle is to be applied to other well-established attributes of Brahman taught for the purpose of meditation, such as "being the center of all blessings" and "having true desires."

For even though the Brahman to be meditated upon is one in all those cases, since there is a distinction between the meditations due to the difference in the introductory context (*prakrama*), there is no transfer of the attributes of one to the other;

just as in the third chapter of the *Vedāntasūtras*, when two women serve a single king— one with an umbrella and the other with a fly-whisk— there is a distinction in their service and a fixed arrangement of their respective duties despite the oneness of the object served, so it is here as well.

For the quality of being augmented or diminished is possible only in the case of Brahman possessing qualities (saguṇa) when there is the conventional usage of distinction; it is not possible in the case of the supreme Brahman which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Therefore, the meaning is that qualities such as having true desires, though heard in one place, do not apply everywhere.
But the others [are included] because of the commonality of their meaning.

But other attributes, such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, are mentioned solely for the purpose of establishing the nature of Brahman; because the subject to be established—Brahman—is one and the same in all cases due to the identity of its essential meaning, all [attributes] should be understood everywhere. This constitutes the distinction, for their purpose is merely to bring about comprehension.
Because there is no purpose for meditation upon [the individual soul].
For it is recited in the *Kāṭhaka*: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind (*manas*);

higher than the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*)," and so on, up to: "There is nothing higher than the Person (*puruṣa*), who is to be meditated upon; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal. (The section on the Supreme Goal).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: are all these—beginning with the objects (*artha*)—taught as being superior one after another, or is it that the *puruṣa* alone is taught as being superior to all of them?
On this point, the initial view is that all of these are indeed taught as being superior;
for thus it is heard in scripture: "This is superior to that," "This is superior to that."
Objection: If many objects are intended to be taught as being supreme, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Response: This is not a fault, because a plurality of sentences is appropriate;
for these very many sentences are capable of teaching many objects endowed with supremacy.

Therefore, when it is thus proposed that the state of being "higher" is not to be established for each of these individually, we reply: it is logical that the Person alone is established as higher than all these, and not that the state of being higher is established for each of them individually.
Why? Because there is no purpose [in doing so];
for indeed, when the others are understood as being higher, no purpose whatsoever is seen or heard of.
But when the Puruṣa—who is beyond the senses and so forth, and who transcends the entire multitude of misfortunes—is realized, a purpose is seen: namely, the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Thus says the Śruti: "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death.

Moreover, by employing the word *kāṣṭhā* (the limit) and by negating what is beyond, [the text] demonstrates its regard for the Puruṣa as the subject matter, showing that the discourse concerning the preceding and succeeding stages is intended solely for the realization of the Puruṣa.
"For the sake of meditation" means for the sake of right vision preceded by meditation;
for it is right vision alone that is taught here as the purpose of meditation, and not meditation itself as the primary goal.
And because of the word "self."

Moreover, this discourse on the stream of the senses and so forth is intended solely for the purpose of realizing the Puruṣa; for the Sūtra [Brahma-sūtra 3.2.5] states the reason: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
but it is seen by subtle seers through the sharp and subtle intellect," thus referring to the Puruṣa under discussion as the "Self" (ātman).

And from this it is understood that the lack of selfhood (*anātmatva*) of the others is what is intended to be expressed; moreover, [the text] demonstrates that very [self] to be difficult to know and accessible only to a refined intellect, and for the sake of knowing it, it prescribes meditation in the words: "The wise man should restrain speech and mind."
This has already been explained under the sūtra, "And for some, [the Self] is inferential" (1.4.1).
Thus, a manifold excellence of intention is observed in the Śruti regarding the Puruṣa, and not regarding the others.

Furthermore, it is said: "He reaches the end of the path, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. When there arises the inquiry as to what that end of the path—the supreme abode of Viṣṇu—is, it is determined from the sequential enumeration of the senses and so forth that this traditional teaching is intended solely for the realization of the supreme abode.
The grasping of the Self [is taught] as in other cases, because of what follows.

In the *Aitareyaka*, it is heard: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds. Having grasped these worlds by means of Himself, He created them: water, light-rays, death, and the waters. This constitutes the subject matter. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the Supreme Self alone denoted here by the word "Self," or is it some other [self]?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the Supreme Self cannot be what is denoted here by the word "Self.
Why? Because we observe the connection of the passage [with something else].

But surely, the connection of the passage is seen to concern the Supreme Self even more clearly, because it establishes the oneness of the Self prior to creation and because it speaks of a creator who acts preceded by reflection.

No, it is said in reply, because of the mention of the creation of the worlds. For if the Supreme Self were intended as the creator, the creation of the great elements would have to be mentioned first; however, here the creation of the worlds is mentioned at the beginning, and the worlds are specific arrangements of the great elements.
And likewise, [the text] declares Ambhas and the others to be worlds themselves, in the passage beginning, "Beyond the sky was Ambhas," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is observed in both Śruti and Smṛti that the creation of the worlds is performed by a certain other Lord presided over by the Supreme Lord;
for instance, there is the Śruti passage beginning, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self, in the form of a Person."
Smṛti also states: "He is the first embodied one; he is indeed called Puruṣa;

as the original creator of beings, Brahmā came into existence. Furthermore, the Aitareyins, in the preceding section of the passage beginning, "Now, therefore, follows the creation from semen; the semen of Prajāpati is the gods," record a manifold creation having Prajāpati as its agent.
Furthermore, the word "ātman" is seen to be applied to that [Brahman] in the passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person.
The determination of its oneness prior to creation is also appropriate with respect to its own effects.
Its power of seeing (īkṣaṇa) is likewise appropriate, since its nature as a conscious being is admitted.

Furthermore, a great many specific activities of this kind—such as "He brought a cow for them," "He brought a horse for them," "He brought a man for them," and "They said"—are well known in the case of individual worldly selves possessing specific characteristics, and they are here followed [in the text].
Therefore, when it is argued that there must be some individualized self here, we reply: the Supreme Self alone is grasped here by the word "self."

As in other cases, just as in other scriptural passages concerning creation—such as "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced"—the Supreme Self is understood, and just as in other worldly usage of the word "Self" the inner self (pratyagātman) alone is primarily grasped by the term "Self," so too should it be here.

However, where in passages such as "In the beginning, this was the Self alone," further qualifications like "having the form of a person" are heard, there the Self possessing those specific attributes may be understood.

Furthermore, in this context, a subsequent qualification is found that is indeed consistent with the grasping of the Supreme Self: "He thought, 'Shall I create the worlds? He created these worlds," and so forth;
therefore, it is logical that it is He alone who is being grasped.
And because of the statement "from positive concomitance," it is determined by the restrictive particle "eva."

Regarding what was stated again—that the Supreme Self is not to be understood because the syntactical connection of the sentence [suggests otherwise]—that must now be refuted. To this it is replied: "Because of the restriction" (*khāvadhāraṇāt*).
It would be logical for the Supreme Self to be understood;
why? Because of the restriction.
For if the Supreme Self is understood [as the subject], then the determination of the oneness of the Self prior to creation is appropriately established as direct;
otherwise, it would have to be conceived in an indirect manner.
As for the mention of the creation of the world, however, I shall interpret it as occurring after the creation of the great elements, which is well-known from other scriptural passages.
Just as we have connected the statement "It created fire" with the creation of ether and air as established by other scriptural passages, so it is here as well;
for a specific detail concerning the same subject matter, though established in one scriptural passage, must be integrated into other scriptural passages.

Furthermore, this sequence of specific activities, such as "From them He brought forth a cow," is also to be understood only insofar as it is consistent with the determination of the intended meaning.
For it cannot be said that this entire narrative sequence is intended [as the primary subject], because there is no human purpose (puruṣārtha) in its comprehension;
rather, the identity of Brahman and the Self is what is intended here.

For thus [the text] shows: after teaching the creation of the worlds beginning with water and their guardians beginning with Agni, as well as the organs and the body which is the abode of the organs, that very Creator, having reflected, "How indeed might this [body] become fit for me? entered this body, as shown by the passage: "He, having pierced this very aperture, entered through this door."

Furthermore, by means of the passage beginning with "If it is uttered by speech, if it is breathed forth by breath," and so on, [the text] first analyzes the operations of the instruments; then, having investigated "Who am I?", it establishes the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self in the statement: "He saw this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman."

Likewise, later on, after enumerating the entire range of differentiated things along with the great elements in the passage beginning "This is Brahman, this is Indra," the text concludes: "All that has consciousness as its leader, is established in consciousness; consciousness is the leader of the world, consciousness is the foundation; consciousness is Brahman. Thus, it establishes the vision of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
Therefore, the inclusion of the Self here is beyond dispute.
Another interpretation: "The grasping of the Self [is Brahman], as in the other cases, because of what follows.

In the Vājasaneyaka, having begun with the word "Self" in the passage, "Which is the Self? He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths, the light within the heart, the person," it establishes the identity of the Self with Brahman by demonstrating that very Self's freedom from all attachments;
for it concludes thus: "This indeed is the great unborn Self—undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman."

In the Chāndogya, however, having commenced with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"—without even using the word "Self"—it teaches identity in the conclusion with "That is the Self; thou art That.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: are these two scriptural accounts of equal meaning, or of unequal meaning?
First, it is argued that they are of unequal meaning, because the scriptural accounts are dissimilar.
For it is not reasonable to assume identity of meaning when there is a discrepancy in the scriptural texts, since the determination of meaning is dependent upon the specific wording of the text;
moreover, in the Vājasaneyaka, because it begins with the word "Self," it is understood that the instruction concerns the reality of the Self,
whereas in the Chāndogya, due to the reversal of the opening statement, there is a reversal of the instruction.

But was it not stated that even for the Chandogas there is an instruction regarding identity in the concluding part? True, this was stated; however, because the conclusion is dependent on the introduction, [the opponent] considers that it refers to the attainment of identity.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the grasping of the Self must also occur for the Chandogas in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

The term *māva* is as in other cases, just as there is a grasping of the Self (*ātman*) among the Vājasaneyins in the passage "Which is the Self?"; why? because of the teaching of identity in what follows. If it is argued that this is not so because of the context—specifically, that there is no grasping of the Self because the word "Self" is not heard in the opening section—then the reply is given: "It would be so, because of the restriction. This means: if you ask what the rebuttal is to the claim that there is no grasping of the Self due to the context and the absence of the word "Self" at the beginning, that is now stated: "It would be so, because of the restriction."
The apprehension of the Self would be justified here, because of the restrictive emphasis;

for thus, having restricted the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one in the passage, "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known," the text says, "Being alone [was this]," with the desire to accomplish that [knowledge]; and that is accomplished only when there is the apprehension of the Self.
For otherwise, if this primary Self were not known, the knowledge of all would certainly not be accomplished.

Likewise, the determination of oneness prior to creation, the reference to the individual soul (jīva) by means of the word "Self," the statement regarding its attainment of that very nature during the state of deep sleep, and the repeated determination "That thou art" following an inquiry—all of this is possible only for the purpose of establishing identity, not for the purpose of bringing about identity.
Nor is it proper here to introduce the argument concerning the dependence on the opening statement (upakrama).

For there is no mention of "selfhood" or "non-selfhood" in the opening statement; moreover, a general opening is not contradicted by a specific qualification found in a subsequent part of the sentence,
because a generality requires specification.

Furthermore, when the meaning of the word "sat" (Being) is carefully examined, nothing other than the primary Self can possibly exist; for it is established that all other categories of things are unreal, on account of scriptural passages such as those concerning "originating from speech" (*ārambhaṇa*).

Nor does a difference in grammatical form necessarily entail a difference in meaning, since we observe that in expressions such as "bring the vessel" and "the vessel, bring it," the meaning remains the same despite the variation in wording.
Therefore, it is proven that in sentences of this kind, even though there is a difference in the mode of presentation, there is no difference in the object to be presented.
Because it explains a result, it is not something previously unknown.
The Chandogas and Vājasaneyins, having recorded in the dialogue of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda) that the food of the prāṇa extends from dogs downward, further record that water is its clothing.

Immediately thereafter, on account of the description of an action, the Chandogas record: "Therefore, indeed, those who are about to eat surround it with water both before and after. This is the section [of the sūtra].

The Vājasaneyins also recite: "Knowing this, learned scholars who are about to eat sip water, and having eaten they sip water; thus they think that they are making this very [breath] non-naked. And: "Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and should sip water after eating; thus he makes this very [breath] non-naked. In this context, both the sipping of water and the contemplation of the breath as being non-naked are perceived. Therefore, it is deliberated whether both are enjoined, or only the sipping of water, or only the contemplation of non-nakedness.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That both are enjoined.
Why? Because both are understood from the sūtra and its commentary (bhāṣya);
and both of these, being unprecedented (apūrva), are worthy of being enjoined.

Alternatively, it might be argued that the sipping of water (*ācamana*) itself is what is being enjoined; for in that case, there is a clearly expressed injunctive suffix: "Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating, and having eaten, he should sip water. The mention of non-eating is merely for the purpose of praising that very act. This being the position reached, we reply: the injunction of the sipping of water is not tenable, because it is a description of an existing practice (*kāryākhyāna*). For this sipping of water, which serves the purpose of purification (*prāyatya*), is already established as a duty through the Smṛtis and is here merely restated.
Now, it might be argued that this Śruti passage must be the source for that Smṛti;
we say no, because their subject matters are different.
For the Smṛti, having a general scope, prescribes rinsing of the mouth for the sake of purification as something connected to every person.

The Śruti passage, however, being recited within the context of the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā), would enjoin the act of sipping water (ācamana) as pertaining specifically to that subject;
moreover, the relationship of root and derivative cannot be established between a Śruti and a Smṛti that have different subjects.

Nor can it be maintained that this Śruti enjoins a previously unknown sipping of water connected with the knowledge of the vital breath, because here we recognize the very same sipping of water already known as being connected with all persons in general.
For this very reason, there is no injunction for both [actions];
for if both were enjoined, the sentence would be split.

Therefore, having merely referred to the rinsing of the mouth that is already established for those who are hungry and those who have eaten, this sentence—“Thinking ‘this indeed makes him not eat’”—enjoins the mental resolve to make the breath ‘not-eating’ (anamna) with respect to the water used for rinsing. This concludes the third chapter.
It is taught as something new by virtue of its connection with the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Nor is it reasonable to claim that this statement regarding "not being naked" is for the purpose of praising the sipping of water (*ācamana*), because the sipping of water is not itself something to be enjoined;
rather, the intention to remain "not naked" is clearly perceived as what is to be enjoined.

And this being the case, it does not follow that a single act of sipping water (ācamana) is admitted to have two purposes—namely, the purpose of purification (prāyatya) and the purpose of clothing (paridhāna)—because they are admitted to be distinct actions. For the act called *ācamana* is admitted to be a distinct action for the purpose of a person's purification, whereas the mental conception (*saṃkalpana*) of those waters as a garment for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is admitted to be another distinct action for the purpose of clothing; thus, there is no fault.

Moreover, regarding the passage, "Whatever there is here, from dogs down to worms, insects, and moths—that is your food," it cannot be said that the consumption of all such food is enjoined, because it is neither scripturally stated nor practically possible.
Rather, what is enjoined here is the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) upon everything as the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
And by virtue of its association with that [meditation], in the passage "Water is your clothing" (*āpo vāsaḥ*), the sipping of water (*ācamana*) is not enjoined.
It is more reasonable, however, that the meditation on the act of wearing [a garment] is enjoined with reference to the very water used for sipping (ācamanīya), which is already well-known;

for a partial contradiction [of scriptural injunctions] is not possible. Furthermore, because the word "they sip" (*ācāmanti*) expresses a present state, this term is incapable of being an injunction.
But is it not the case that the status of being a statement in the present tense is the same for the phrase "they think" as well?
True, indeed;

however, since one of the two must necessarily be enjoined, and because of the description of an action (kārya), it is the very volition of the waters' dwelling that is enjoined as something previously unestablished (apūrva).
There is no rinsing of the mouth [to be understood here],
for it has already been established that such is the case as before.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that there is a clearly expressed injunctive suffix regarding the rinsing of the mouth— that too has been refuted by the very same reasoning applied previously.
