For this very reason, since the sipping of water (ācamana) is not intended to be enjoined, the Kāṇvas conclude at the passage, "They think that they are thus eating and breathing," and do not recite the words "Therefore, one who knows this," etc.

Therefore, even in the text of the Mādhyandinas, it must be understood that, by restating the sipping of water, the state of being "one who knows this" is enjoined as the knowledge of the cloth of the aforementioned Prāṇa.

Furthermore, the position that one should sometimes enjoin the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and sometimes the cognition of the garment (vāsovijñāna) is also not tenable, because the application of the scriptural passage beginning with "Water is the garment" (āpo vāsaḥ) is uniform in all instances.
Therefore, it is logical that here only the cognition of the garment is enjoined, not the rinsing of the mouth.
And it is the same because there is no difference.
In the *Abhirahasya* of the Vājasaneyi Śākhā, the knowledge marked by the name of Śāṇḍilya is known;
and there, qualities are heard: "He should meditate upon the Self as consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose form is light, and which is without organs," and so forth.

In that very same branch, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, it is further recited: "This person consists of mind (*manomaya*), has light as his essence, and is truth; within the heart, he is like a grain of rice or a grain of barley. He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, who governs all this, whatever exists.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is this one single meditation (*vidyā*) in the *Agnirahasya* and the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, with a combination of their qualities, or are these two separate meditations, with no combination of qualities?

What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That there is a difference between the meditations (*vidyā*) and a restriction of their qualities (*guṇavyavasthā*). Why? Because of the consequence of redundancy (*paunaruktya*). For it has been stated that in the case of different recensional branches (*śākhā*), since there is a difference among the students and knowers, one avoids redundancy by determining the unity of the meditation and then importing the qualities that are in excess in one place into the other—as in the case of the "Dialogue of the Vital Breaths" (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so on. However, in the case of a single recensional branch, since there is no difference among the students and knowers, redundancy cannot be avoided; therefore, a single meditation cannot exist in two locations widely separated from one another.
Furthermore, in this case, no such distinction is possible that one recitation is for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge and the other is for the purpose of enjoining qualities;
for if that were so, only additional qualities would be mentioned in one place and the other, rather than identical ones.
Yet, qualities such as "consisting of mind" and so forth are mentioned identically in both places.

Therefore, when it is argued that there is no mutual inclusion of qualities, we reply: just as there is unity of knowledge and inclusion of qualities across different recensions (śākhās), so too should it be the case within a single recension, because the object of meditation is non-different.

For we recognize that very same Brahman, characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (manomaya) and so forth, as the identical object of meditation in both places; and the form of the object of meditation constitutes the identity of the knowledge.
Furthermore, since there is no difference in the nature of the object (rūpa), we cannot determine a difference in the meditations (vidyā);
nor can there be a restriction of qualities when there is a difference in meditation.
But surely, a difference in meditation has been determined due to the consequence of redundancy?

This is not so, because the distinction in meaning is logically consistent. For it is not at all untenable that one recitation in the Sūtra and Bhāṣya is for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge (*vidyā*), while the other is not.

[Objection: If this were the case, then only that which is not read in the *Agnirahasya* should be read in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, such as "He is the lord of all" and so forth; whereas that which is already read there, such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, should not be read here. [Reply: This is no fault, because by means of those very words, there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the knowledge as being the same as that read in another section.
For, by means of the mention of identical qualities, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā located at a distant place is recognized, and within it, attributes such as "lordship" (īśānatva) and so forth are taught;

otherwise, how could this injunction of qualities be said to apply to it? Moreover, since the sentence becomes purposeful through the teaching of an unestablished portion, and since the reference to an already established portion can be justified as a constant restatement (nityānuvāda), recognition cannot be disregarded on that basis.
Therefore, even though the branch (śākhā) is the same, it is logical that there is oneness of knowledge and the combination of qualities.
The word "pā" is for the purpose of enjoining a quality; thus it is also elsewhere because of the connection.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, beginning with "Truth is Brahman," it is taught that "That which is Truth is yonder Āditya—the person who is in this orb—and also this person in the right eye. Having thus instructed upon the specific abodes of that very Truth-Brahman, both with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*) and the self (*adhyātma*), and having established its nature as having the *vyāhṛtis* for its body, two secret names (*upaniṣads*) are assigned: "Its secret name is *Aha*" with respect to the deities, and "Its secret name is *Aham*" with respect to the self. (Third Adhyāya)

In this regard, there is a doubt: whether both Upaniṣads are to be combined in both places without distinction, or whether they are to be applied separately—one with reference to the deities (adhidaivata) and the other with reference to the self (adhyātma).

On this point, the Sūtra begins its discussion: Just as in the case of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, where it was stated that even though the meditation is studied separately, there is a combination of qualities, so it must also be in other cases of this kind; for these two belong to a single vidyā, since this Satya-vidyā is studied both with reference to the deities and with reference to the self, owing to the non-difference of the introductory statement and the interconnected manner of the textual recitation.
How could that which is taught as the Dharma in one [text] not exist in that very same [text]?
For whatever practice, such as following behind, is enjoined regarding a teacher, it remains exactly the same whether he has gone to the village or to the forest.
Therefore, both Upaniṣads are applicable in both places.
This being the case, it is replied: "Or rather, because there is a distinction."
There is no application of both [meditations] in both places;
why? Because of a distinction—meaning because of the connection with specific locations for meditation.

How is there a connection with specific locations? It is said: for, having introduced the cosmic person (ādhidaivika-puruṣa) with the words, "This person who is in this orb," the scripture declares, "His secret name (upaniṣad) is Aha."

And with reference to the internal person (ādhyātmika-puruṣa) introduced by the words, "This person who is in the right eye," it is said, "His secret name (upaniṣad) is 'Aham'. Here, the pronoun "his" (tasya) refers back to that which is proximate; therefore, these two secret names are taught specifically in relation to particular abodes.
How can there be the attainment of both [attributes] in both places?

Is it not the case that this is one and the same person, both with respect to the divine and with respect to the self, since it is the single, true Brahman that is being presented as having two abodes?
True, this is so.
However, because a specific secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) is taught only by taking into account a particular state of the teacher, that doctrine must belong to the teacher in that very state.

There is indeed this illustrative example: even though the essential nature of the teacher does not change, it is said that one should follow the teacher when he is seated, but that does not apply when he is standing; and what is said regarding him when he is standing does not apply when he is seated.

However, because the essential nature of the teacher does not depart whether in the village or in the forest, and because the duty (dharma) connected to that essential nature lacks any distinction based on being in a village or a forest, these two states are equal; thus, that [comparison] is an inappropriate illustration.
Therefore, there is a fixed rule regarding these two Upaniṣads.
And [the scripture] also shows this.

Moreover, there is an indication of the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of such qualities [in the following passage]: "Of this one, that very form is what the other's form is; whatever his joints are, those are his joints; whatever his name is, that is his name.

How is this an indication? That is explained: observing that the qualities distinguished by the difference of locations—such as the eye and the sun—are not to be combined with one another, the text here, by means of transference (*atideśa*), combines the form and other attributes residing in the person in the sun with the person in the eye, through the words "Of this one, that very form," and so forth.
Therefore, the conclusion is that these two Upaniṣads indeed remain distinct.
And for this reason, there is also the accumulation and pervasion.

"Virtues for which Brahman is the eldest have been gathered together; Brahman, the eldest, has stretched out the heaven"—thus, in the *Khilas* (supplementary texts) of the Rāṇāyanīyas, the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of Brahman, beginning with the gathering of virtues and their placement, are recited;
and of these very [manifestations], there is a description in their own Upaniṣad, where the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and other such knowledges of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) are taught.

In the investigation of whether those manifestations of Brahman (*brahmavibhūti*)—such as being "collected" (*saṃbhṛti*), "pervading" (*dyubhyāpti*), and so forth—should be combined within those various knowledges of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) or not, the following is stated: since they are connected with Brahman, their combination might initially seem appropriate; however, [the Sūtra] declares that manifestations such as being "collected" and "pervading" are not to be combined in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, precisely because of their connection with specific abodes (*āyatanaviśeṣa*).
For instance, in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, Brahman is said to have the heart as its abode in the passage: "This is my Self within the heart. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3)
In the same way, in the Dahara-vidyā as well, there is the statement: "The lotus of the heart is a small dwelling; within it is the small ether" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).
In the Upakośala-vidyā, however, there is the abode of the eye: "This person who is seen in the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1).
Thus, in each of these various meditations, a respective internal abode is perceived.
But these manifestations, such as the gathering together, pervading, and so forth, belong to the divine sphere (*ādhidaivika*);
how, then, could they be attained in these [human] bodies?

Is it not the case that even in these [bodies], divine manifestations are heard of in the Sūtra-bhāṣya? For instance: "Greater than heaven, greater than these worlds; he indeed is the light-bringer (*bhāmanī*), for he shines in all worlds"; or, "As large as this space here is, so large is this space within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it"—and so forth.
There are indeed other Brahma-vidyās here that lack specific distinctions, such as those consisting of sixteen parts and so forth; this is true.

Nevertheless, there exists a distinction here regarding the reason for not combining [certain qualities], namely, the recitation of common qualities. For it is logical that when even distant vidyās are presented through the mention of common qualities, the qualities belonging to the distant location should be combined.

However, qualities such as "being collected" (*saṃbhṛti*) and others, which fall within the scope of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and similar passages, are incapable of presenting a vidyā located in another place, because their essential natures are mutually exclusive.
Nor can it be said that the presence of a knowledge taught in another location is established merely by the connection with Brahman, for this is possible even when the knowledges are distinct;

for it is an established principle that even the one Brahman is meditated upon in many ways through various manifestations, as seen in the Veda in cases such as the "higher than the high" (parovarīyas).
Therefore, there is no inclusion of the "accumulation of vigor" and other attributes within the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and similar meditations.
[The answer is: No, because the others are not mentioned, as they are in the Puruṣavidyā.
In the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa* of the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅgins, there is a "knowledge of the person" (*puruṣavidyā*);
therein, the person is conceived as a sacrifice, and his lifespan is divided into three parts for the sake of the sacrificial sessions. This is the third chapter.
This triad is imagined;
furthermore, hunger and so forth are assigned the status of initiation and the rest within the Puruṣavidyā,
and other attributes are likewise superimposed there.
The application of benedictions, formulas, and so forth has been concluded.

The Taittirīyakas also postulate a certain "human sacrifice" (puruṣayajña) in this section: "Of that sacrifice of one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife," and so on, according to this Anuvāka.
In this regard, a doubt arises: should the characteristics of the human sacrifice mentioned elsewhere be incorporated into the Taittirīyaka text, or should they not be incorporated?

Since there is no distinction in the fact that both are "sacrifices of the person" (*puruṣayajña*), the question arises as to whether the details of one should be combined with the other. We reply: they are not to be combined. Why? Because there is no recognition of their identical form. To this effect, the Teacher says: "As in the case of the Puruṣavidyā"—that is, just as there is a specific scriptural recitation for the Puruṣavidyā among certain followers of the *Tāṇḍins* and *Paiṅgins*, there is no such recitation for the others, namely the Taittirīyas.

For their performance of the sacrifice is seen to be entirely distinct from others, due to the enumeration of the wife, the sacrificer, the altar, the sacrificial grass, the stake, the clarified butter, the animal victim, the officiating priests, and so forth.
Even that which is the performance of the *savana* (pressing) is likewise distinct from others, as in the passage: "That which [occurs] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.

As for any slight similarity, such as the fact that death serves as the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), even that is overwhelmed by the greater dissimilarity because of its insignificance, and is thus incapable of effecting recognition.
Furthermore, the identity of the person with the sacrifice is not heard in the Taittirīyaka;

for in the phrase "of the wise man's sacrifice," these two genitives are not in apposition as in "he who is the sacrifice, of him [the wise man]," because the person cannot possess the status of a sacrifice in its primary sense.
But these two genitives are in different grammatical cases (vyadhikaraṇa), meaning "the sacrifice which belongs to the wise man";
for the connection of the sacrifice with the person is primary.
And when a primary sense is possible, one must resort to that very primary meaning, not a figurative one.

Furthermore, by explaining the sacrificer-hood of the person in the passage "The self is the sacrificer," the text shows his connection to the sacrifice precisely through a grammatical distinction (vaiyadhikaraṇya).

Moreover, since there is the scriptural restatement of an established fact in the words "of him who knows thus," if one were to seek to establish both the state of being a sacrifice for the person and the state of being a sacrificer and so forth for the self and the others, there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda).

Moreover, having previously taught the knowledge of the Self together with renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), we observe that the subsequent sequence beginning with "of him who knows thus" (*tasyaivaṃvidaḥ*) is a continuation of that very [teaching]; thus we understand that this scriptural passage is a supplement to what precedes, not an independent one.
Furthermore, we perceive a single fruit for both these sections, namely: "He attains the greatness of Brahman.
On the other hand, the teaching concerning the "knowledge of man" (*puruṣavidyā*) is not a supplement to anything else.

For this [meditation] has the increase of longevity as its fruit, as indicated by the statement: "He who knows thus lives for a hundred and sixteen years. Therefore, there is no application in the Taittirīyaka of the attributes of the Puruṣavidyā—such as the benedictory mantras and so forth—which are studied in other recensions.
Because of the difference in meaning, such as piercing and so forth.

At the beginning of the Upaniṣads for the followers of the Atharvaveda, there is a recitation of mantras beginning with: "Piercing all, piercing the heart, cutting through the vessels, cutting through the head, [piercing] the three-fold thread...
and so forth;
for the Tāṇḍins, it begins: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice, O Ordainer," and so forth.
The *karaṇa* of the Śāṭyāyanins begins with "O white-horsed one,
you are greenish-blue," and so forth;
that of the Kaṭhas and Taittirīyas begins with "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious," and so forth.

However, at the beginning of the Upaniṣad of the Vājasaneyins, the Pravargya-Brāhmaṇa is recited, starting with "The gods, indeed, sat down for a sacrificial session" (devā ha vai satraṃ niṣeduḥ) and so forth;

and among the Kauṣītakins as well, there is the Agniṣṭoma-Brāhmaṇa: "The Agniṣṭoma is indeed Brahman; that day is Brahman; by means of Brahman they approach Brahman; those who perform this day attain immortality.
We now investigate whether all these mantras, such as the Pravidhya, and rituals such as the Pravargya, should be combined with the meditations (vidyās), or whether they should not be so combined.

What, then, appears to us? That these [meditations] belong to the *vidyās* (knowledge-instructions) themselves. Why? Because they are recited in proximity to the Upaniṣadic texts, which have the *vidyās* as their primary subject matter.

[Objection: But we do not perceive an injunction for these as being for the sake of the *vidyās*. [Reply: Quite true; even though we do not perceive it, we shall infer it on the strength of their proximity (*saṃnidhi*).
For when it is possible for them to have a purpose through proximity, it is not right to assume they are purposeless without cause.

Now, one might object: "We do not perceive any capacity of these mantras with respect to the subject matter of knowledge (vidyā); and how can we accept that rites such as the Pravargya, which are enjoined for other purposes, also serve the purpose of knowledge? This is not a valid objection; for it is possible to conceive some capacity of the mantras with respect to the subject matter of knowledge as well, since they mention the heart and other such parts.
For the heart and other organs are generally taught in meditations as the abodes and so forth;
and by that fact, the status of mantras such as "piercing the heart" as auxiliary elements of meditation is established;
moreover, the application of mantras is observed even in meditations, such as "I take refuge in Bhū with this, with that, and with that," and so on.

Thus, when it is argued that rites such as the Pravargya—which have been employed elsewhere—may also be employed in connection with the meditations (vidyās) without contradiction, just as the Bṛhaspatisava is employed in the Vājapeya sacrifice, we reply: there is no inclusion of these [rites] within the meditations.

Why? Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing the heart. For the purposes of those mantras of that kind, such as "piercing the heart," namely the piercing of the heart and so forth, are different from and unconnected with the meditations taught in the Upaniṣads;
they have no capacity to be joined with them.
Now, it might be argued that since the heart is also employed in meditations (*upāsana*), its connection to meditation is presented by way of that [mention]; to this we reply:
such an application could perhaps be imagined for the mere mention of the "heart" itself.
However, the "heart" alone is not the meaning of the mantra here; for the entire meaning of the mantra—such as "piercing the heart, cutting the arteries"—is not connected with the meditations.
For this subject matter pertains to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*); therefore, this mantra, "piercing everything," is connected with a rite of malevolent magic.
Likewise, [the mantra] "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice. Thus ends the third chapter.
Since this [mantra] possesses the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of generating a sacrifice, it is connected with the ritual action of sacrifice;
however, its connection with specific details must be followed from other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, in the case of other mantras—some of which are applied to different purposes through their characteristic mark (*liṅga*), some through direct statement (*vacana*), and some through other means of knowledge—even though they are recited in the secret portion (*rahasya*), it is not possible for them to be subordinate to the meditations (*vidyā*) merely by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhi*).

For it has been stated in the first system (Mīmāṃsā) that "proximity is weaker than direct statement and the rest," in the passage: "In the case of a conflict between direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the purpose.
Likewise, it is not possible for ritual acts such as the Pravargya—which are enjoined elsewhere—to be subordinate parts of knowledge (vidyā);
for there is no commonality of purpose whatsoever between these acts and the knowledges.
In the case of the Vājapeya, however, there is a clear alternative application for the Bṛhaspatisava, namely: "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava.

Moreover, this Pravargya rite, having been produced once, has been applied elsewhere by a stronger means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and cannot deserve application elsewhere by a weaker means of knowledge;
for such would only be the case if there were no perceived distinction between the two means of knowledge.

But it is not possible for there to be a lack of perceived distinction between two means of knowledge, one strong and the other weak, precisely because of the distinction between their strength and weakness.

Therefore, in the case of such mantras or ritual acts, one should not suspect that they are subordinate to a meditation (vidyā) merely on account of their proximity in the text; rather, one should be content with the fact that they are recited in proximity due to common characteristics such as the duty of reciting them in the forest (araṇyānuvacana). In the case of the "leaving" (hāni), however, [the reference to the soul's departure] is subordinate to the word "taking up" (upāyana), like the kuśa grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing; this has already been stated. (Sūtra-bhāṣya)

There is a scriptural text of the Tāṇḍins: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I, with a perfected self, attain the uncreated world of Brahman. Likewise, there is a text of the Ātharvaṇikas: "Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high."
Likewise, the Śāṭyāyanins read: "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds.
Similarly, the Kauṣītakins read: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen take over his good deeds, and those who are not dear take over his evil deeds.
Thus, in some places, the non-transference of good and evil deeds is heard.

In some cases, there is the bringing forward of both [the prāṇas] separately by means of pleasant and unpleasant things; in other cases, however, there is both abandonment and bringing forward. Regarding that case where both are heard, there is nothing at all to be said.

Even where only the taking over (*upāyana*) is heard and not the casting off (*hāna*), the casting off is nevertheless implied by the very sense of the matter; for when the good and evil deeds of another are being taken over by someone else, the casting off of those deeds on the part of that other person is necessarily involved. However, where only the casting off is heard and not the taking over, there arises a doubt as to whether the taking over should be supplied or not. In such a case, it is not supplied because it is not explicitly heard, and because the scriptural mention in one branch belongs to the scope of a different knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, [this is established] in the third chapter of the *Sūtras* under the section "The Self" (*ātma-pāda*).
The relinquishing of good and evil deeds has the [deceased] as its agent, whereas the taking up has another as its agent.

Since the existence of these two [acts] is not necessarily simultaneous, how could the taking up be implied by the relinquishing? Therefore, there is no conjunction of the taking up with the relinquishing.
Regarding this attainment, the author reads the word "in the case of loss" (hānau).
For even when this "loss" is heard of alone, the "attainment" (upāyana) must be understood as necessarily accompanying it;
because it is supplementary to that, for the word "attainment" has been established in the Kauṣītaki-rahasya as being supplementary to the word "loss."
Therefore, even where there is only the mention of "abandoning" (hāna), there is the inclusion of "taking up" (upāyana).

As for what was said—that there is no conjunction because it is not mentioned, because it pertains to a different knowledge, and because it is not necessary—that is now answered: this restrictive rule might hold if something heard in one place were intended to be transferred to another as something to be performed; however, in this case, neither abandoning nor taking up is proclaimed as something to be performed.

The mention of these two, however, is for the purpose of praising the knowledge: "So great is this knowledge that by its power the good and evil deeds of this knower—which constitute the cause of transmigratory existence—are shaken off, and they enter into his friends and enemies.

Since this mention is for the sake of praise, and because the "attainment" (upāyana) is heard in some places as occurring immediately after the "shaking off" (hāna), one infers the recurrence of the attainment even where only the shaking off is mentioned, in order to achieve the excellence of the praise.

Moreover, dependence on other explanatory passages (arthavādas) for the occurrence of other explanatory passages is well known in cases such as, "This sun over there is indeed the twenty-first," and so forth; for how else could the number twenty-one of the sun be stated here, if another explanatory passage—namely, "Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun make the twenty-first"—were not taken into account? Likewise, in statements such as, "There are two Triṣṭubh verses for the sake of possessing the senses," dependence on other explanatory passages such as, "The Triṣṭubh is indeed the senses," is observed.

Furthermore, since this statement regarding the "taking up" (upāyana) is for the purpose of praising knowledge (vidyā), one should not be overly insistent on how the good and evil deeds belonging to one person could be taken up by others.

By pronouncing the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra phrase "because it is supplementary to the word 'taking up' (*upāyanaśabdaśeṣatvāt*)," [Bādarāyaṇa] indicates that the reference to "taking up" in the context of "forsaking" (*hāni*) is solely for the sake of praise.

For if he had intended to prescribe the inclusion of subordinate qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*), he would have stated that the very meaning of "taking up" is to be carried over into the context of "forsaking."

Therefore, this Sūtra is intended to demonstrate the inclusion of praise (stuti) by way of the discussion on the inclusion of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra). This is illustrated by the analogy: "As in the case of the Kuśa grass, the meters, the praise, and the chanting. Regarding the invocation used by the Bhāllavins, "O Kuśa grasses, you are of the nature of trees; protect me," although the origin of the Kuśa grass from trees is heard there without qualification, the Audumbara Kuśa grasses are adopted because of the specific statement of the Śāṭyāyanins: "They are made of Udumbara wood."

Just as in some cases, when there is no distinction between the meters of the gods and the Asuras and a question arises regarding their sequence, it is understood from the *Paingī* tradition that "the meters of the gods come first";
and just as in the case of the *Ṣoḍaśin-stotra*, where some might otherwise obtain no specific time, a specific time is established by the Vedic text of the *Ṛgveda*: "when the sun has half-risen";

and just as some transmit the singing of accompaniment (*upagāna*) without distinction while the followers of the *Bhāllavins* transmit it with a specific distinction—just as in these instances of the *kuśa*-grass and so forth, there is a connection with specific details found in other scriptural texts, so too in the case of the "taking away" (*hāni*), there is a connection with the "taking up" (*upāyana*). This is the meaning.
of the feet; as follows: thus ends the third chapter.
For if one were not to accept the distinction established by one scriptural passage in another scriptural passage, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) in every case.
And that [interpretation] is unjustified when another way is possible;

as it has been stated in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*: "But rather, because it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), there should be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the other; for if it were a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*)."

Alternatively, with reference to these very scriptural passages concerning "shaking" (vidhūnana), this Sūtra should be considered as follows: what is denoted by this expression "shaking"—is it the casting off of good and evil deeds, or is it something else? In this regard, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) should be established thus: "shaking" does not denote abandonment, because of the traditional rule (smaraṇa) that *dhū* means "to shake," and because we observe the usage of the word in expressions such as "the tips of the banners are shaken" (*dodhūyante dhvajāgrāṇi*) when the banner-tips are being moved by the wind;
therefore, "shaking" denotes movement.

Having first established that "shaking off" (cālana) means the temporary obstruction of the fruits of good and evil deeds for some time, one must reply: this term "shaking off" (vidhūnana) must apply only to the act of abandoning (hāna), because it is supplementary to the term "appropriation" (upāyana);
for it is not possible for others to appropriate good and evil deeds that have become the property of another without those deeds having been abandoned.

Although this "taking over" (*upāyana*) of the good and evil deeds belonging to others by others cannot be conceived as literal, nevertheless, because it is mentioned in that context, it can be determined that—in accordance with that—what is called "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) actually means "abandonment.

Furthermore, where this "taking over" is heard in proximity to "shaking off," like the case of the *kuśa* grass, meters, hymns, and chanting, it serves as a universal cause for determination, being required everywhere by the scriptural mention of "shaking off. (Śaṅkara Bhāṣya on the Sūtra)
Furthermore, a primary shaking of good and evil deeds, like that of the tip of a banner, is not possible because they are not material substances.

And when a horse shakes its hair, it casts off the dust along with the hair itself, thereby shedding even the worn-out hairs—this is supported by the Brāhmaṇa text: "As a horse shakes its hair, so shaking off evil.
Moreover, since verbal roots are admitted to have multiple meanings, there is no contradiction with traditional usage.
"That has been stated" has thus been explained.
Because there is nothing further to be crossed in the hereafter; for thus it is with others as well.

The Kauṣītakins, in their Paryaṅka-vidyā, declare the separation from good and evil deeds at the midpoint of the journey for one who has set out toward Brahman seated upon the couch by way of the path of the gods. Beginning with, "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni," they continue: "He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it by mind alone, and thereby shakes off his good and evil deeds. (KauṣU 1.3–4) This refers to the section concerning the intermediate state (*sāmparāya*).

Now, in considering whether this statement regarding the separation of the soul from the works of merit and demerit is to be understood as occurring only on the way (during the intermediate state), or rather at the very beginning upon departing from the body, it might follow—given the authority of scripture—that it should be understood exactly as stated. To this, the Sūtra replies: "At the time of departure" (*sāṃparāye*). This means that at the very moment of going forth, upon departing from the body, this abandonment of good and evil deeds occurs through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*); thus he asserts the proposition. And he states the reason: "Because there is nothing further to be crossed" (*tartavyābhāvāt*). This implies that since all that remains to be traversed has already been accomplished by the time of death, the abandonment takes place then.

For one who is wise and has departed, who seeks to attain Brahman through knowledge, there is nothing else to be reached in the interval that would require those two [good and evil deeds] to remain unexhausted for some moments;
moreover, because their fruits are contrary to knowledge, they are destroyed by the power of that very knowledge.
And that [destruction] must occur at the very moment knowledge becomes directed toward its fruit.
Therefore, although this destruction of good and evil deeds exists previously, it is mentioned later.

For likewise, other followers of different recensions—the Tāṇḍins and the Śāṭyāyanins—declare the casting off of good and evil deeds precisely in the prior state: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair," and "His sons inherit his property; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds."
According to one's preference, because there is no contradiction between the two.

Furthermore, if it were admitted that the destruction of good and evil deeds occurs halfway along the path of the gods for one who has departed from the body, then—since the body has already fallen—it would be impossible to perform at will the human effort consisting of the practice of restraints, observances, and knowledge, which is the cause of the destruction of good and evil deeds; consequently, the destruction of good and evil deeds caused by that effort would be impossible.

Therefore, it should be understood that the performance of that effort must take place previously, while one is still in the state of a seeker, and the abandonment of good and evil deeds follows as a result of that.
Thus, the logical connection between the sign (nimitta) and that which is signified (naimittika), as well as the consistency with the *Tāṇḍi* and *Śāṭyāyani* Śrutis, is established.
The meaningfulness of the transition [from one state to another] exists in both ways; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.

In the commentary on the Sūtras (Sūtrabhāṣya), the path of the gods (devayānaḥ panthāḥ) is mentioned in some instances in proximity to the casting off of merit and demerit (puṇyapāpāpahāna), while in others it is not.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: does the path of the gods apply to the casting off of [karmic results] without distinction in all cases, or is there a division such that it applies in some cases and not in others?
As for the casting off, the following is the established position.

Since it has been stated that the following of the path of approach (*upāyana*) occurs specifically [in certain cases], one might conclude that the following of the path of the gods (*devayāna*) must likewise occur [specifically]. To this position, we reply: The purposefulness of the path of the gods must exist through a distinction between two cases; in some instances the journey is purposeful, while in others it is not—it cannot be so without distinction. For otherwise, if this journey were admitted to apply universally, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural text: "Having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, he attains the highest equality," for in that case, a journey leading to another location would contradict this teaching.
For how could one who is devoid of activity go to another place?
Moreover, since the goal to be reached is supreme identity, which does not depend upon reaching another location, we consider that movement here is entirely purposeless.
It is established [as real] because its characteristic object is perceived, like a lamp.
And this "being born" occurs in two ways: in some cases it has a purposeful destination, while in others it does not.
An object that serves as the cause for such a destination is perceived in the meditations on the qualified Brahman, such as those concerning the couch and so forth;
for there, one mounts the couch, converses with the Brahman seated upon the couch, and perceives specific fragrances and other qualities. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.7)
Furthermore, results such as "attainment" and so forth are heard in scripture as being dependent upon reaching various distant locations;
in those cases, movement is purposeful.
However, in the case of perfect realization (samyagdarśana), there is no perception of any object characterized by such [spatial] movement.

For those who have realized the oneness of the Self, whose desires are fulfilled, and for whom the seeds of all afflictions have been burnt away even here, there remains nothing further to be expected except for the exhaustion of the residual impressions of karma that have already begun to bear fruit; therefore, the journey to another world is useless for them.

This distinction should be understood as being like the worldly usage: just as in the world a path leading to another country is required for reaching a village, but not for attaining health, so it is in this case as well.
Furthermore, we shall explain this division more precisely in the fourth chapter.
There is no restriction regarding all [the faculties], for there is no contradiction with either scripture or inference.
It has been stated that the journey is purposeful in the case of meditations with attributes (*saguṇa-vidyā*), but not in the case of the meditation on the Supreme Self (*nirguṇa-paramātma-vidyā*).
However, even among the meditations with attributes, it is heard in some instances that the journey is not mandatory, as in the case of the Paryaṅka-vidyā (the meditation on the couch),
the Upakośala-section, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Pañcāgni-vidyā, and the Dahara-vidyā.
It is not as it is in other cases, such as the Madhu-vidyā, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Ṣoḍaśakala-vidyā, and the Vaiśvānara-vidyā.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is this path restricted only to those specific vidyās in which it is heard? Or is it connected, without restriction, with all vidyās of this kind?
What, then, is the prima facie view? It is that there is a restriction; for the path must apply only where it is explicitly heard, because the context (prakaraṇa) acts as a restrictor.

If the path, though not heard in another place, were to apply to other meditations, the authority of scripture and the other means of proof would be undermined, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence that everything could serve every purpose.
Moreover, the single path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) is taught identically both in the Upakośala-vidyā and in the Pañcāgni-vidyā;
if it were intended for all [paths], this repetition would be purposeless.
Therefore, when the prima facie view is that there is a restriction [to specific vidyās], the author of the Sūtras states: "There is no restriction."

This path known as the "way of the gods" (devayāna) ought to belong without distinction to all qualified sciences (*vidyā*) that have the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) as their fruit.

[Objection: But if non-restriction is accepted, does this not contradict the context? [Reply: There is no such contradiction, because of both scripture and inference—that is to say, according to *śruti* and *smṛti*.

For thus the Śruti, introducing the path of the gods for those possessing the knowledge of the five fires with the words, "Those who know this thus," and then stating, "And those who in the forest worship through faith and austerity," indicates that even those devoted to other forms of knowledge share the same path as the knowers of the five-fire-vidyā. But how is it understood that this destination belongs to those devoted to other forms of knowledge? Is it not the case that it should belong only to those dedicated to faith and austerity, since only those are mentioned? This is not a valid objection; [The full argument continues: For the word "faith" (śraddhā) here denotes the meditation on Brahman, because it is preceded by the word "Brahma-world" (brahmaloka); and the word "austerity" (tapas) denotes the means [to that end], because it is mentioned alongside "faith. Furthermore, the word "forest" (araṇya) signifies solitude, which is common to all meditations. Moreover, the mention of "those who do not perform sacrifices" (akṛta-yajña) implies others who do perform sacrifices, and thus includes those devoted to other meditations. Therefore, it is established that those who possess the knowledge of the five fires and those who follow other meditations both attain the path of the gods. Thus, there is no contradiction with the Smṛti. And so it is said: "The path of the gods, which leads upward, is different from the path of the fathers; by that [former] go the knowers of Brahman, the performers of sacrifices, and those who practice austerity in the forest. Therefore, it is concluded that the knowers of the five fires and those devoted to other meditations alike proceed by the path of the gods. ||| 1.2.14 || [End of Section 14] ||| 1.2.15 || [End of For this goal is not attained by faith and austerity alone without the power of knowledge, as stated in the conclusion of the Śruti: "By means of ignorance they ascend to that place where desires have vanished;
neither those who give sacrificial gifts nor ignorant ascetics go there. Thus ends the third chapter of the Sūtra.
Therefore, in this context, "faith" (śraddhā) and "austerity" (tapas) serve as indicators for other forms of knowledge.
However, the Vājasaneyins study in the section on the knowledge of the five fires: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, worship faith as the Truth (satya).
There, it should be explained that "those faithful ones who worship the Truth, which is Brahman," because the word "Truth" is used repeatedly in reference to Brahman.

Furthermore, since those who know the science of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā) are already included by virtue of their specific knowledge, it is logical that this passage refers only to those devoted to other sciences. Moreover, the Śruti—by stating, "But those who do not know these two paths become worms, birds, and whatever is biting"—indicates a miserable downward destiny for those who have strayed from both paths, thereby including them within either the Devayāna or the Pitṛyāna. Even in that case, due to the excellence of their particular knowledge, they attain the Devayāna path.
Smṛti also states: "These two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered to be eternal for the world;
by one a person goes to non-return, by the other he returns again.
As for the fact that the path of the gods (devayāna) is mentioned twice—in the Upakośala-vidyā and in the Pañcāgni-vidyā—that is for the purpose of meditation in both instances.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule.
The continued existence of those entrusted with authority lasts as long as their office.

It is considered whether or not another body arises for the wise man immediately after the fall of his current body. Now, one might object: "When the means of knowledge have been perfected, it is not appropriate to consider whether or not liberation will occur; for it is not as if one considers whether or not rice will be produced when the means for cooking it have been fully prepared. To this we reply: [this objection does not hold].

A doubt arises: one might wonder whether even while eating, one would be satisfied or not. However, this doubt is indeed appropriate, for we observe from the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* that even some knowers of Brahman undergo rebirth in another body.
For instance, tradition records that the ancient seer and teacher of the Vedas named Apāntaratamas was born as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali ages by the command of Viṣṇu.
Vasiṣṭha, who was a mind-born son of Brahmā, having lost his former body due to the curse of Nimi, was born again from Mitrāvaruṇa by the command of Brahmā;
likewise, the rebirth of Bhṛgu and others—who were also mind-born sons of Brahmā—at the sacrifice of Varuṇa is recorded in the Smṛti;
and Sanatkumāra, who was also a mind-born son of Brahmā, manifested as Skanda through the granting of a boon to Rudra.
In this very way, the repeated production of other bodies for Dakṣa, Nārada, and others is recounted in the Smṛti for various reasons;
it is also frequently observed in the Śruti, within the mantras and arthavādas.

Some of them assume another body after their previous body has fallen away, while others, by virtue of their mastery over yoga (yogaiśvarya), assume multiple bodies even while that [previous] body remains, according to the principle of taking on many forms.
And all these [sages] are remembered as having mastered the entire meaning of the Vedas.
Therefore, since the arising of new bodies is observed for them, it follows that the knowledge of Brahman has either only an occasional cause for liberation or is not a cause for it at all.
Thus ends the third chapter.

To this, the following reply is given: No, because for those such as Apāntaratamas and others who have been appointed to offices that cause the stability of the world—such as the promulgation of the Vedas—their continued existence is dependent upon their office. Just as the blessed Sun, having performed his office for the world until the end of a thousand yugas, at its conclusion experiences absolute liberation (kaivalya) free from rising and setting, according to the Śruti: "Then, having risen from there upwards, he neither rises nor sets; he remains alone in the center."

And just as the knowers of Brahman existing in the present experience isolation (*kaivalya*) upon the exhaustion of the karma already begun, according to the Śruti: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]," so too the lords such as Apāntaratamas and others, though appointed by the Supreme Lord to various offices, remain in their positions for as long as their office lasts—even though they possess perfect insight, which is the cause of isolation—because their karma has not yet been exhausted. And at the conclusion of that period, they attain liberation; thus, there is no contradiction.

For they, having exhausted their store of karma (karmāśaya) which was set in motion only once for the sake of yielding its fruit, move from one body to another—just as one moves freely from one house to another—in order to fulfill their respective offices. With their memory unimpaired, they create bodies either simultaneously or in succession through their mastery over the body, the senses, and primordial nature (prakṛti), and preside over them.

Nor are these called "rememberers of former births" (jātismara) merely on the basis of the common usage of memory; for it is recorded in tradition that the female exponent of Brahman named Sulabhā, desiring to debate with Janaka, cast off her own body, entered the body of Janaka, debated with him, and afterwards re-entered her own body.

For if, once the [present] action has been exhausted, another action—which is the cause for the commencement of another body—were to manifest, then other actions whose seeds have not yet been burnt would likewise necessarily follow, and one might suspect that the knowledge of Brahman is either only an occasional cause of liberation or not a cause at all.
However, this suspicion is not tenable, because the burning away of the seed of action through knowledge is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.
Thus says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is broken, and all doubts are cut asunder."

"His actions are exhausted when He, the High and the Low, is seen," and "Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the loosening of all knots"—such passages as these [attest this]. Smṛti also says: "Just as a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes; just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again."
And likewise: "The self does not come into being again when the afflictions have been burnt by knowledge," and so forth.

Furthermore, once the afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest have been consumed, it is not logically possible for there to be both partial burning and partial sprouting of the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*), which is the seed of the afflictions;
for a partial sprouting of a rice seed that has been burnt by fire is never observed.

However, the cessation of the store of karma whose fruit has already begun is due to the exhaustion of its momentum, like that of a released arrow, because the scripture—specifically the passage "for him there is delay only so long"—specifies the falling of the body as the limit.
Therefore, it is logical that those who hold office remain in their positions as long as their term of office lasts.
Nor is there any uncertainty regarding the fruit of knowledge.

And thus, scripture shows that liberation results from knowledge for all without distinction: "Among the gods, whoever awakened to That, he indeed became That; likewise among the seers, and likewise among human beings.
Furthermore, the great seers might have been attached to other forms of knowledge whose fruits are sovereignty and the like.

It is logical that they, becoming disillusioned upon subsequently observing the decay of their sovereignty, became firmly established in the knowledge of the Supreme Self and attained liberation (*kaivalya*), according to the traditional scripture: "When the dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected themselves at the end of the highest [Brahmā] enter the supreme state.
Furthermore, because knowledge has direct perception as its fruit, any doubt regarding the absence of a result is untenable.
For regarding the fruit of action, such as heaven and the like, since it has not yet ascended to direct experience, there may be doubt as to whether it exists or not;

but the fruit of knowledge has indeed ascended to direct experience, because of the scriptural text, "Brahman is immediate," and because of the instruction "That thou art" given as an established fact.
Indeed, the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" cannot be transformed into the sense that "you will become That after death."

Furthermore, the passage, "Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and I was the Sun,'" shows that the fruit of knowledge—namely, the state of being the Self of all—occurs at the very time of perfect realization.
Therefore, the attainment of absolute liberation for the knower is certain.

"But there is an inclusion of those meditations on the Imperishable that are directly stated, on account of the commonality [of the object] and the existence [of the meditation], as in the case of the *aupasada* [offerings]; so it has been said."

In the Vājasaneyaka it is heard: "This, indeed, O Gārgī, is that imperishable (akṣara) which the Brāhmaṇas declare as neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily," and so forth.

Likewise, in the Atharvaṇa it is heard: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that imperishable is realized—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, and without color," and so forth. This constitutes the section [on the Imperishable].
In the same way, elsewhere as well, the supreme Brahman is taught as the Imperishable by means of the negation of specific attributes;
and in those instances, certain additional attributes are negated in some places.

Regarding these cognitions of specific negations, there arises a doubt as to whether they apply everywhere to all [texts] or whether their application is restricted. Since a restriction might be inferred from the division of the scriptural passages, it is replied: however, all cognitions of specific negations concerning the Imperishable (akṣara) must be included everywhere, because of the commonality and the existence of that [object]. For the method of teaching Brahman—consisting in the exclusion of specific attributes—is the same everywhere;
and that very same Brahman, which is to be taught, is recognized as non-different in all places.
In that case, why should cognitions formed regarding one thing not apply to another?
This has already been explained under the sūtra "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal" (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.11).
There, the qualifying attributes were considered in their positive form; here, however, they are considered in their negative form—this is the distinction.
This distinction in reflection is for the sake of detailed exposition;
the example is that of the *aupasada* sacrifice.

Just as in the *jāmadagnya-ahīna* sacrifice, when the *upasads* involving sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are enjoined, the mantras for offering the cake—such as "O Agni, you are the Hotṛ, you are the Adhvaryu" and so forth—which originate in the Udgātṛ-veda, are nevertheless connected with the Adhvaryus, because the offering of the cake is performed by the Adhvaryu, and because subordinate elements depend on the principal action. So it is here as well. [End of] the third chapter of the Akṣara-tattva.
Because they are subordinate, the meaning is that the qualifiers produced in any particular context are connected with the syllable everywhere;

as it was stated in the first section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "In the case of a conflict between a subordinate and a primary element, the Vedic connection belongs to the primary, because it is for its sake."
On account of this much being taught.
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.

One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. This mantra, concerning the supreme self (*adhyātma*), the Ātharvaṇikas read with the addition of "so much," and the Tāṇḍins recite it as well.

Likewise, the Kaṭhas [read]: "The two who drink the reward of good deeds in the world, having entered the cave in the highest supreme heaven—those who know Brahman call them shade and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and the three *Nāciketa* sacrifices.
Here, a doubt arises: is there identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikatva*), or is there a plurality of knowledges (*vidyānānātva*)?

What, then, is the prima facie position? That there is a plurality of knowledges. Why? Because of the observation of distinctions. For in the passage "Two birds," one is seen to be an enjoyer and the other is seen to be a non-enjoyer;
whereas in the passage "Drinking the [fruits of] Ṛta," both are seen to be enjoyers.

When it is argued that the object of knowledge (*vedyarūpa*), being differentiated, must cause a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*), we reply: there is oneness of knowledge. Why? Because in both these mantras they enjoin the same undifferentiated form of the object of knowledge, which is defined by its limited measure as being "two.
But was not a difference in form pointed out? No, it is said in reply.
In the commentary on the *Ubhaya-sūtra*, these two mantras also establish that there is a second [entity] which is subordinate (*avara*), and not some other meaning.
Regarding the verse "Two birds," first, in the phrase "the other, not eating, looks on," the Supreme Self, who transcends hunger and other such states, is established;
furthermore, in the remainder of the passage, that very same [Self] is seen to be established: "When he sees the other, the Lord, beloved, and His greatness."

In the passage "drinking the ṛta," however, while the individual soul (jīva) drinks, the Supreme Self—which transcends hunger and other such needs—is also figuratively said to drink due to its association with the former, according to the maxim of the "men with umbrellas.
For this is a context concerning the Supreme Self, as indicated by the opening statement, "Other than dharma, other than adharma";
and the remainder of the sentence here also refers to that very subject: "That which is the bridge for those who sacrifice, the imperishable Brahman which is supreme."
And this has been explained in detail in the passage, "The two selves have entered the cave" (KaU 1.3.1).
Therefore, there is no difference in the object of knowledge; and from that, there is oneness of the meditation.
Moreover, upon examining the preceding and following passages in all three of these Vedānta texts, it is understood that only the knowledge of the Supreme Self (paramātma-vidyā) is intended;
the mention of the individual soul (jīva) is solely for the purpose of expressing identity with It, not for the purpose of implying a different entity.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no occasion for an inquiry into difference or non-difference within the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
Therefore, this application is solely for the purpose of elaboration;
and from that, there is the inclusion of additional attributes.
Like the collection of living beings within, [the self is] of its own nature.

The Vājasaneyins record twice in succession, in the questions of Uṣasta and Kahola, the passage: "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1;
3.5.1). Regarding this, a doubt arises: is there a single knowledge (vidyā) or are there multiple knowledges?
First, it is established that there is a difference between the two [recensions] because they are distinct; this is due to the principle of repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*).
For otherwise, if the meaning were neither deficient nor redundant, the twofold recitation would be entirely purposeless.

Therefore, since it might be argued that just as there is a difference of ritual acts due to repetition, so too there is a difference of knowledge (vidyā) due to repetition—this being the position reached—the Sūtra replies: "On account of the non-distinction of the scriptural mention of the Inner One, there is oneness of the knowledge of the Self.
For the Self, which is the innermost of all, is questioned and answered without distinction in both places;
indeed, two selves cannot both be the innermost of all within a single body.

For in that case, the state of being the innermost of all would be possible for only one [of the two]; however, for the other, there could not be the state of being the innermost of all, just as in the case of the collection of elements.

And just as in the body, which is a composite of the five elements, earth has water as its interior, and fire has water as its interior—so that even though there is a relative "interiority," it is by no means the primary state of being the innermost of all—so it is here as well; such is the meaning.
Alternatively, the phrase "like the collection of elements" points to another scriptural passage as an illustration.

Just as in this mantra, "The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings," it is taught that there is only one inner Self in the entire collection of beings, so it is with these two Brāhmaṇas as well—this is the meaning.
Therefore, because the object of knowledge is one, the knowledge is one.
If it is argued that otherwise the distinction [between the two] would be untenable, we say no, for it is like other types of instruction.

In the commentary on the Sūtras (Sūtrabhāṣya), regarding the objection that if a difference between the cognitions is not admitted, the difference in scriptural accounts would be untenable—that must be refuted. To this it is replied: this fault does not apply, because it is as tenable as other instances of instruction.

Just as in the sixth chapter of the *Tāṇḍinām Upaniṣad*, despite the instruction being given nine times in the words "That is the Self; thou art That, O Śvetaketu," there is no difference in the knowledge [conveyed], so it will be here as well.

And how is it that there is no difference in the knowledge despite the instruction being given nine times? Because a single meaning is understood from both the introduction and the conclusion; because the request, "Please, venerable sir, inform me further," introduces the very same subject matter with the intention of explaining it again and again; and because the repeated instruction is justified by the removal of successive doubts.

Likewise here too, because there is no difference in the form of the questions and because there is no distinction in the conclusion with the words "everything else is perishable" (*ato 'nyad ārtaṃ*), the introduction and the conclusion are seen to have a single subject matter.

By employing the particle *eva* in the second question—"That which is immediate and direct" (*yad eva sākṣād aparokṣād brahma*)—the text shows that the very same subject matter contained in the previous question is being carried over into the subsequent one.
Furthermore, in the preceding Brāhmaṇa, the existence of the Self as distinct from the body and the organs is stated.

In the latter [text], however, the specific distinction is stated as that very same [Self] being beyond the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and so forth; thus, the identity of meaning is established.
Therefore, there is but one *vidyā*.
The new vyatihāra [is established], for they distinguish it just as in the other cases.

Just as the Aitareyins, with reference to the person in the sun, recite in the third chapter, "He who is I, that is he; he who is he, that am I," so too do the Jābālas [recite]: "O venerable deity, I am indeed you, and you are indeed I. This is the section concerning the exchange (vyatihāra).
In this regard, there arises a doubt: should the meditation here be performed in both forms by means of the exchange [of attributes], or is it to be of only one form?
First, he says that it is of only one form;
for here, nothing else whatsoever is to be meditated upon except the oneness of the Self with the Lord.

And if one were to imagine a distinction in the object of contemplation such that the transmigrating soul possesses the nature of the Lord, or the Lord possesses the nature of the transmigrating soul—then, in the case of the transmigrating soul having the nature of the Lord, there would be an elevation [of status]; however, if the Lord were to have the nature of the transmigrating soul, a degradation would be incurred.
Therefore, the form of the meditation must be uniform.

When it is thus argued that the traditional teaching of the exchange (vyatihāra) is intended merely to strengthen the realization of oneness, the Sūtra replies: This exchange is taught for the purpose of meditation (ādhyāna);
"as in other cases," meaning just as other attributes such as being the Self of all and so forth are taught for the purpose of meditation, so it is here.
For the teachers who transmit the text distinguish [the two] by uttering both: "I am thou, and thou art I."
And that [instruction] becomes meaningful when it is intended as a cognition of both forms;
otherwise, this specific mention of both would be purposeless, since the purpose would already have been accomplished by one alone.

Now, it was argued that if a specific meaning is postulated for the mention of both, it would result in the degradation of the deity by making her out to be the self of a transmigrating being; but this is not a fault.

Because it is precisely the single Self that is to be meditated upon in this manner, according to the Sūtra and its Commentary. Now, one might object: "If this is so, does it not follow that there would be a mere reinforcement of the idea of oneness? We do not deny the reinforcement of the idea of oneness; rather, we establish only this much: that by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, the cognition here must be formed in two ways through mutual exchange, and not in a single form alone.
As a result, even oneness becomes firmly established;

just as, for instance, although the teaching of qualities such as "having true desires" is intended for the purpose of meditation, the Lord endowed with those qualities is thereby established, so it is here.
Therefore, this reciprocal exchange (vyatihāra) is to be meditated upon and should be combined when the subject matter is the same.
For that very [meditation] consists of truth and the other [virtues].
The Reconciliation (Upadeśa):

In the Vājasaneyaka, after prescribing the meditation on the name-syllables as part of the "Knowledge of Truth" (*satyavidyā*) with the words, "He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa, the Truth, Brahman," and so forth, there is subsequently recorded the passage: "That which is the Truth is yonder sun; he who is the person in that orb, and he who is the person in the right eye," and so on.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: are these two separate knowledges of Truth, or are they one and the same?

To begin with, it might be argued that there are two [vidyās], because the connection with the fruit occurs separately: "He conquers these worlds" is stated earlier, while "He slays evil and leaves it behind" is stated later. Furthermore, the reference back to the subject matter is due to the identity of the object of meditation. This being the position reached, we reply: this is indeed one single Satya-vidyā.
Why? Because of the reference back to the subject matter under discussion in the words, "That which is that Truth.
Now, it was argued that even when there is a difference between two meditations (*vidyā*), a reference back to the subject matter is possible because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is one;
but this is not so.

However, where a distinction between the meditations (*vidyā*) is perceived from a clearly stated different cause, there this [distinction] would indeed apply. But in the present case, since both possibilities exist, the fact that "that which is the True" (*satya*) is drawn forward from the context of the preceding meditation implies that the very same "True" connected to the prior meditation is what is drawn forward in the subsequent passage; thus, the certainty of it being a single meditation is established. As for the argument that it must be a different meditation because another fruit is heard, it is replied here: this hearing of another fruit is merely a commendation of the instruction regarding another auxiliary (*aṅga*), namely, "His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is 'Ahaṃ' (I)," and therefore there is no fault.

Moreover, since the fruit must be inferred from the explanatory passages (arthavāda) themselves, and since the knowledge is one, even the many fruits mentioned in relation to its constituent parts are to be combined within the knowledge as a whole.

Therefore, this very same single knowledge of the True (Satyavidyā), being handed down with various specific attributes, requires that all the qualities beginning with "Truth" (satya) be combined in a single performance.

Some, moreover, citing this passage from the Vājasaneyaka concerning the person in the eye and the sun—namely, the Chāndogya passages, "Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun" and "That person who is seen in the eye"—and considering that this very same knowledge concerning the person in the eye and the sun is one and the same in both places, maintain that qualities such as truthfulness and so forth are to be combined by the Chāndogyas from the Vājasaneyins.
That does not appear correct;
for in the Chāndogya, the knowledge is understood to be connected with ritual action and dependent upon the *udgītha* chant.

For in that [Bṛhadāraṇyaka] Upaniṣad, there are signs connected with ritual action at the beginning, middle, and end: at the beginning, "This very [earth] is Ṛc, and this [fire] is Sāman"; in the middle, "The Ṛc and the Sāman are its two joints, therefore it is the Udgītha"; and in the conclusion, "He who, knowing thus, sings the Sāman. In the Vājasaneyaka, however, there is no such sign connected with ritual action. Since there is a difference in the introductory statements (prakrama), resulting in a difference between the two meditations (vidyā), it is proper that the distribution of qualities (guṇavyavasthā) should remain distinct.
Desire and so forth [are abandoned] elsewhere and there, from the sense-bases and so on.

Now, having introduced the subject with the words, "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether," the Chandogas study [the following]: "This Self, free from sin, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1–3), and so forth.

Likewise, the Vājasaneyins [study]: "The great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, who is the ether within the heart; in him dwells the ruler of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether there is identity of the knowledge (vidyā) and a mutual connection of qualities, or not; the conclusion is that there is identity of the knowledge.

On this point it is said: "Because of [the mention of] desire and so forth," meaning because of [the mention of] qualities such as having true desires and so forth—just as Devadatta is called Datta, or Satyabhāmā is called Bhāmā.

This collection of qualities, such as having true desires and so forth, which is perceived in the Chāndogya with respect to the ether within the heart, should be connected elsewhere in the Vājasaneyaka at the passage: "He indeed is that great unborn Self."
And that which is perceived in the Vājasaneyaka as lordship and so forth—that too should be connected with the other [text], namely the Chāndogya passage, "This Self is free from evil" (Chānd.
Up. 8.7.1). Why? Because of the commonality of the abode and other such factors.

For in both cases, the heart is equally the abode, the Lord to be known is equally the object of knowledge, and His nature as a bridge—whose purpose is the non-confusion of the worlds—is equally established; thus, many such commonalities are observed. But is not a difference also observed, in that the *Chāndogya* connects the qualities to the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*), whereas the *Vājasaneyaka* connects them to Brahman residing in space? No, for by the sūtra "The small [space] is Brahman, on account of the subsequent [arguments]" (1.3.14), it has been established even in the *Chāndogya* that the word "space" refers to Brahman itself.

However, there is this distinction here: for in the Chāndogya, Brahman-knowledge is taught as being endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*), since [the text] declares that both the Self and the objects of desire are to be known—"Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires... (Chānd. Up. 8.7.1). In the Vājasaneyaka, on the other hand, Brahman is seen to be taught as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), because of the consistency between the question and the answer beginning with, "Speak further for the sake of liberation; for this person is unattached" (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.14–15). The collection of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka is intended solely for the purpose of praise.
And likewise, later on, [the scripture] concludes that Brahman is indeed devoid of qualities with the passage beginning, "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6).

It should be understood that this compendium of qualities is formulated in the Sūtra for the purpose of demonstrating the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the qualified Brahman due to its unity, and not for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*).
There is no omission [of the rite] due to respect.

In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, concerning the Vaiśvānara-vidyā in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is heard: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as a sacrifice. That first oblation which he should offer, let him offer with respect, saying: 'To Prāṇa, Svāhā! and so forth. Therein, a modification is made: five oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are prescribed.

And in those [sections], the term *agnihotra* is used later on, as in: "He who, knowing this thus, offers the *agnihotra*," and "Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother, so do all beings wait upon the *agnihotra*.
In this regard, the following is considered: Is there a suspension of the *prāṇāgnihotra* when eating is suspended, or is there no suspension?

Since there is a scriptural mention of the conjunction with the arrival of guests in the passage, "That which is the guest-offering," and since the arrival of guests is for the purpose of eating, it follows that when eating is omitted, the Prāṇāgnihotra is also omitted. This being the prima facie view, the author says that it should not be omitted.
Why? Because of reverence.
For thus, in the very Vaiśvānara-vidyā, the Śruti of the Jābālas states: "One should eat before the guests."

"Just as if one were to offer the Agnihotra for another without having offered it for oneself, so it is"—thus, by censuring the priority of feeding guests and establishing that the master's own meal must come first, the text shows its regard for the Prāṇāgnihotra.
For if [the text] does not tolerate the omission of priority, it certainly cannot tolerate the omission of the Agnihotra, which possesses that very priority.

But is it not the case that because of the connection with the arrival of the rice-portion intended for eating, its omission would follow upon the omission of the meal? No, for that [connection] is intended for the purpose of prescribing a specific material.

Third Adhyāya, Sūtra 1. Since the materials such as milk and so forth are fixed when the Agnihotra has been established, and since here too the word "Agnihotra" brings about the application of those same characteristics—just as in the case of the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana—this statement, "That which is food (bhakta)," is intended to enjoin a specific quality, namely that the material consists of cooked rice. Therefore, the prima facie conclusion is that according to the principle "when a subordinate element is omitted, the primary act remains," [the Agnihotra should be performed with rice].
Even in the absence of food, the Prāṇāgnihotra is to be performed by means of water or any other non-conflicting substance, according to the principle of substitution.
To this, he recites the following: "Because it is stated [in the scripture] that [the result] occurs when [the time] has arrived."

When food is present, the Prāṇāgnihotra is to be performed from that very food-substance which first arrives. Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect. For it says: "Whatever food comes first, that is to be offered as an oblation. By referring to the arrival of food as an established fact, this passage teaches that the oblations to the vital breaths are to be accomplished by means of a substance intended for another purpose.
Since these [acts] have acquired the characteristic of being non-obligatory, how could they cause another substance to be substituted in the event of the omission of the food?
Furthermore, there is no extension here of the properties of the archetypal *agnihotra*;

for in the case of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*, where it is said "He performs the *agnihotra* for a month," the word *agnihotra* occurring in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) would rightly cause the extension of those properties by enjoining a state of similarity (*tadvadbhāva*). But this is not the case here.

Furthermore, the word *agnihotra* occurring here as part of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) cannot enjoin the state of being "like that" (i.e., like the original Agnihotra sacrifice); and if the assumption were made that its specific characteristics (*taddharma*) are to be extended [to this new rite], then even acts such as the formal taking out of the sacred fires (*agnyuddharaṇa*) would have to be performed, which is impossible.
Thus, it is not possible [for the characteristics of the original to apply].
First of all, the taking out of the fire (*agnyuddharaṇa*) is for the purpose of providing a locus for the oblation (*homa*);
yet this is not an oblation into the [sacrificial] fire, because that would entail the contradiction of its being for the purpose of eating;
and since it is connected with substances brought forth for the sake of eating, this oblation occurs only in the stomach.
And likewise, the Jābāla Śruti—"One should eat before the guests"—shows that this accomplishment of the oblation has the mouth as its locus.

For this very reason, it also shows here that the members of the Agnihotra are merely figurative (sāṃpādika): "The chest is the altar, the body hair is the sacrificial grass, the heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire.

Furthermore, the mention of the "altar" (vedi) here should be understood as indicating the mere leveled ground (sthaṇḍila), because there is no actual altar in the primary Agnihotra, and it is those [figurative] members that are intended to be established here.
Furthermore, because of the conjunction with the very time for eating, there is no possibility of obstructing the time for the Agnihotra;
