likewise, other duties such as the Upasthāna and so forth are also in some way or another contradicted.
Therefore, these five oblations must be performed according to the eating-pakṣa (the view that the rite is part of the meal), due to the connection with the mantras, the materials, and the deities.
As for the statement regarding the observation of respect, that is intended to prescribe priority in the case of eating; it is not an excessive burden,
nor can the obligatory nature of this [act] be demonstrated by it.
Therefore, when the eating [of food] is omitted, the Prāṇāgnihotra itself is necessarily omitted.

For there is no fixed rule for the determination of that [result] by means of the scriptural statement, because its connection is seen to be distinct; for the fruit is separate. (Sūtra, Third Chapter). There exist meditations based on the constituent parts of ritual acts, such as: "One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," and so forth.
Are these [meditations] necessarily permanent members of the rituals, like the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood and the like? Or are they optional?
Furthermore, we shall investigate whether these [rites] have a fixed locus, like the *godohana* vessel and so forth.
What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are obligatory (*nitya*).

Why? Because they are encompassed by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*). For even though these [meditations] are studied as unattached (*anārabhya-adhīta*), they are connected to the sacrifice through the *udgītha* and other such elements; thus, like other subsidiaries, they are touched upon by the very injunction of the sacrificial performance.

As for the mention of fruits in their own respective passages—such as "he indeed becomes a fulfiller of desires"—that is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because it takes the form of a statement of present fact, like the hearing of the world being free from evil, and is not primarily intended to enjoin a fruit.

Therefore, just as in the case of such passages as "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," which, though read outside of a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇa*), are nevertheless permanent because they enter the sacrifice through the medium of the *juhū* and so forth—just like those read within a context—we might initially conclude that the meditations on the *udgītha* and other elements are likewise permanent. To this we reply: "The determinations thereof are not mandatory" (*tannirdhāraṇāniyama*). Those determinations of the true nature of the qualities of the ritual acts, such as the *udgītha*, namely: "the most excellent essence," "attainment," "prosperity," "the chief vital breath" (*mukhyaprāṇa*), "the sun," and so forth—these are not to be restricted as permanent parts of the rituals.
Why? Because that is seen;

for scripture shows the non-eternality of things of this kind by permitting action even for the ignorant, stating: "Therefore both perform [the rite], he who knows this thus and he who does not know" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10). Furthermore, we observe that even those such as the *prastotṛ* priests—who lack knowledge of the deities presiding over the *prastāva* and other parts—persist in their sacrificial duties, as evidenced by the texts: "O *prastotṛ*, if you shall chant the *prastāva* without knowing the deity that is connected with the *prastāva*," "if you shall sing the *udgītha* without knowing it," and "if you shall respond with the *pratihāra* without knowing it."

Moreover, for consciousness that relies upon such action, a fruit of action is perceived as distinct from the action itself; there is no obstruction to the accomplishment of the fruit of action, and there is a certain excellence and distinction in its fulfillment. As it is said: "Both perform [the rite], he who knows this thus and he who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are different; what one performs with knowledge, faith, and the Upanishad (inner realization), that alone becomes more powerful."

In this regard, because of the distinction made between the performance of the learned and the unlearned in the phrase "but it is different," and because of the use of the comparative suffix "-tara" in the expression "more powerful," it is understood that even an action devoid of knowledge is powerful;
and that is possible only if knowledge is non-eternal.
But if it were eternal, how could an action devoid of it ever be authorized as being powerful?

For it is an established principle that an action is "possessed of vigor" (vīryavat) only when all its constituent parts are combined. Likewise, in the case of the *loka-sāman* and other meditations, specific fruits are taught for each individual meditation, such as: "The worlds above and below are fit for him," and so forth.
Nor is it appropriate to regard this mention of fruit as being merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
For otherwise, it would result in a mere figurative statement (guṇavāda);

however, when there is an instruction regarding a fruit, the interpretation as a primary statement (mukhyavāda) is appropriate. But in the case of the Prayāja offerings and so forth, since the sacrifice has a requirement for its procedure (itikartavyatā), and because they are mentioned in connection with that [sacrifice] which is under discussion, it is logical that the mention of the fruit is an explanatory praise (arthavāda). Thus ends the third chapter.

Likewise, even in the case of qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood, which are taught without reference to a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), a connection with a fruit is not possible for these non-actional qualities without a substratum.

For while injunctions regarding fruits are appropriate in the case of the *godohana* vessel and the like because they obtain a substratum in the form of the *praṇayana* (water-carrying) and other rites already under discussion,

so too is an injunction regarding a fruit appropriate for the *bilva*-wood and the like because they obtain a substratum in the form of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and other elements already under discussion.
But in the case of [the quality of] being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth, there is no such substrate (*prakṛta*) under discussion;

for if one intended to enjoin the *juhū* and other implements as the substrate by means of a single sentence, while also intending to enjoin them toward a fruit, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

However, since meditations (*upāsanā*) are of the nature of action (*kriyātmaka*), the injunction of those based on the *udgītha* and so forth toward a fruit is not contradictory, because the injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*) is possible.

Therefore, just as the *godohana* vessel and other such items, although dependent on a ritual (*ṛtu*), are non-permanent due to their connection with specific results, so too should it be understood that meditations (*upāsanā*) on the *udgītha* and others are likewise non-permanent.
For this very reason, the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* did not prescribe such meditations within the rituals.
That has been stated as being like the giving [of a gift].

In the Vājasaneyaka, in the passage "I shall surely speak," speech and the others determined that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the best among the internal organs (adhyātma); and among the deities (adhidaivata), air (vāyu) is the best among fire and the others.

Likewise, in the Chāndogya, in the section concerning the absorber (saṃvarga), it is determined that among the deities air is the absorber of fire and the others ("Vāyu, indeed, is the absorber"); and in the section where it says "The vital breath, indeed, is the absorber," the vital breath is determined to be the absorber of speech and the others among the internal organs. Thus, in the Sūtra-bhāṣya, [the comparison] is established.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: should these two, the wind (*vāyu*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), be understood as distinct, or rather as non-distinct?
For now, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are non-distinct, because there is no difference in their essential nature (*tattva*);
for it is not logical to contemplate a non-different reality as being separate.

Moreover, Scripture demonstrates the non-difference of reality (*tattvābheda*) with respect to both the internal (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaivata*), beginning with the passage: "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth.

Likewise, in the text: "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite," it shows that the divine manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) constitute the very self (*ātman*) of the internal ones.
Similarly, in various other places as well, there are numerous demonstrations of the non-difference of reality between the internal and the divine.
And in some places, it makes the wind and the vital breath (prāṇa) clearly one, as in the statement, "That which is prāṇa is indeed wind.

Likewise, even in the cited Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa passage, in the concluding verse beginning with "From whom the sun rises," the text concludes by means of the vital breath itself, saying, "Verily, he rises from prāṇa and sets in prāṇa," thereby demonstrating their identity. Furthermore, by concluding with the single observance of prāṇa alone—stating, "Therefore, one should observe only one vow: one should breathe in and breathe out"—it confirms this very point.

Similarly, in the Chāndogya as well, further on, the text leads to one and the same Saṃvarga with the words: "The one God, the protector of the world, has swallowed the four great ones—Who is He? It does not state that one among these four is the Saṃvarga, while another is the Saṃvarga of others.
Therefore, the approach [to Brahman] is non-distinct. This being the position reached, the third chapter of the Sūtras begins.
We say that Vāyu and Prāṇa are to be understood as distinct; why? Because of their separate instruction;
for this instruction concerning the division between the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva) is intended for the purpose of meditation.

In that case, the meditation on them as distinct would be entirely purposeless. [Objection: But was it not stated that there is no separate meditation because of the non-difference of their essential nature (*tattva*)? [Reply: This is not a fault; for even though the essential nature is non-different, a distinction in meditation is possible due to the distinction in states (*avasthā*), by virtue of the difference in instruction. Furthermore, the citation of the world (*loka*)—which can be justified even with the intention of showing non-difference of essential nature—lacks the power to refute the previously mentioned distinction between objects of meditation (*dhyeya*). This is also evident from the employment of a comparison and its subject in the passage: "As the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities."
By this, the introduction of the vow is explained.
Furthermore, in the phrase "the one vow alone," the particle *eva* (alone) is intended to establish the vow of Prāṇa by excluding the vows of speech and the other organs;
for speech and the others have been described as having broken their vows, according to the Vedic text: "Death, having become weariness, seized them."

Nor is it for the purpose of withdrawing from the vow of Vāyu, because, having introduced the subject with "Now, therefore, the investigation of the vow," the fact that both Vāyu and Prāṇa possess an unbroken vow is determined as being equal; and furthermore, after stating, "One should observe only one single vow," the text, by declaring the attainment of Vāyu as the fruit—"By this he wins union with and residence in the same world as this deity"—indicates that the vow of Vāyu is not to be withdrawn from when one resorts to Prāṇa.

In this context, the deity must be Vāyu, because his nature as the undivided self is celebrated, and because of the preceding application: "This is that non-setting deity, namely Vāyu" (Sūtra-bhāṣya).
Likewise, he designates them separately: "These two are the two absorbers—Vāyu among the gods and Prāṇa among the vital breaths.
And he concludes with a distinction: "These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the Kṛta [dice]."

Therefore, the approach [to the deity] is indeed separate, just like the offering (*pradāna*). For instance, in this sacrifice of three cakes (*tripuroḍāśinī iṣṭi*)—namely, "To Indra the King, a cake on eleven potsherds; to Indra the Overlord; to Indra the Self-Ruler"—there might be a suspicion that the offerings are made together because of the scriptural statement, "He cuts off [the portions] while making them reach all [deities], so as not to cause a failure," and because there is no distinction between the Indras. However, due to the difference in qualities such as "King" and so forth, and because of the injunction to transpose the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, the offerings are made separately according to their respective order, since the deities are distinct.

Thus, even though there is no difference in the reality (*tattva*), the meaning is that there is a distinction in the meditations (*ādhyāna*) because of the distinctness of the portions to be meditated upon (*ādhyeyāṃśa*).
This has been stated in the *Saṃkarṣa*: "Or rather, the deities are manifold, because they are known separately.
In that case, however, a distinction in sacrifice (*yāga*) exists due to the difference between the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*).

In this case, there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā), because from both the opening and the conclusion, it is understood that a single form of knowledge is being enjoined throughout the teachings concerning the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva).

Even though the knowledge is one, however, a difference in practice arises due to the distinction between the internal and the divine, just as in the case of the Agnihotra sacrifice there is a difference in practice due to the distinction between evening and morning times; it is with this intention that the phrase "like the offering" (pradānavat) was stated.
On account of the abundance of inferential marks, for that indeed is more powerful; and that too [is established].

In the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyins, in the third chapter [beginning with] "Verily, this was not non-existent in the beginning," there is the section concerning the *Bandi*. In that Brāhmaṇa, with reference to the mind (*manas*), it is studied: "He beheld thirty-six thousand Agnis, his own selves, which were Arka hymns, consisting of mind, built of mind," and so forth.
In the same way, they mention separate fires consisting of mind, breath, sight, hearing, action, and fire, as being of a symbolic nature (*sāṃpādika*).

Regarding these, a doubt arises: are these fires, such as that consisting of mind and the rest, subordinate to ritual action and part of it, or are they independent and purely of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*)?

In this regard, although the context suggests their subordination to ritual action, the author first asserts their independence on the ground of "the abundance of indicatory marks" (*liṅgabhūyastvāt*).

For indeed, many indicative marks (*liṅga*) are seen in this Brāhmaṇa that strengthen the view that these [fires] consist solely of knowledge (*vidyā*); for example: "Whatever these beings conceive with their mind, that is the very work of those [fires]," and "All beings always build these [fires] for one who knows thus, even while he sleeps. Such are the types of marks found there. And a mark is more powerful than the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This has also been stated in the previous section (*kāṇḍa*): "In the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker because of its remoteness from the meaning."
COMI: The previous alternative should apply because of the context, as the action is mental, like [the meditation on] Mānasa.
This is not correct: that these fires are independent and do not constitute a subordinate part of anything else.

Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the preceding fire consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*), this instruction regarding the specific alternative must refer to that very subject and cannot be independent. [Objection:
But surely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than context; [Response: True, it is so.
Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this kind is not stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*);
for this is a "perception of another purpose," since it consists in the praise of the fires as they are mentally constructed (*sāṃpādika*).

And a perception of another purpose, being capable of being explained even as a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*) in the absence of any other established application, is not able to subvert the context.

Therefore, these fires, being of a symbolic nature (*sāṃpādika*), must enter into the ritual action because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). This is like the "Mental" (*mānasa*) [rite]: on the tenth day of the ten-night sacrifice, the *Avivākya*, when the Soma of the ocean is being taken for the deity Prajāpati with the earth as a vessel, the taking, placing, offering, bringing back, invitation, and consuming are all prescribed as purely mental; and although that ritual procedure of the mental cup is mental, it remains a supplement to the ritual action because of the context of action. The meaning is that this ritual procedure of the fires is likewise so. Furthermore, because of the extended application (*atideśa*).

Furthermore, this extension (*atideśa*) supports the entry of these fires into ritual action: "There are thirty-six thousand fires, each one of them being as large as that former one. For an extension operates only when there is a commonality;

therefore, by extending the fires consisting of bricks—which entered into ritual action—to the fires consisting of mental identification (*sāṃpādika*), it indicates that these [fires] likewise enter into ritual action.
"But it is knowledge alone, because of the determination. (Sūtra, Third Adhyāya).
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
These fires, such as the mind-fire (*manaścita*) and others, must consist of knowledge alone and be independent; they are not subordinate elements of ritual action.
For it determines thus: "These are indeed built of knowledge alone," and "By knowledge alone these are built for those who know thus."
And because it is seen [in scripture].
And an indicative mark for their independence is indeed seen;
that was shown previously in the section beginning with "Because of the abundance of indicative marks."

But surely, since an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not a means of establishing any object when there is no other [means] available, one might discard it and determine that [the mantra] is a supplement to the ritual action by virtue of the power of the context (*prakaraṇa*). To this, he recites the reply: "And because of the greater strength of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, there is no sublation."

One should not, on the strength of the context (*prakaraṇa*), determine that [the passages] are subordinate to an action and thereby refute the position of their independence; for direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof are more powerful.
Indeed, it is established in the *Śrutiliṅga* Sūtra that direct statement, indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are more powerful than context;
and these very means are seen here to establish the position of independence.

How so? First, there is the scriptural statement (śruti): "These [fires] are indeed piled up by knowledge alone" (*te haite vidyācita eva*). Likewise, there is an indicative mark (liṅga): "Even while one sleeps, all beings pile them up at all times. Similarly, there is also a syntactical connection (vākya): "By knowledge alone these fires become piled up for those who know thus. For this scriptural statement, "They are indeed piled up by knowledge alone," which contains a restrictive particle (*eva*), would be contradicted if their entry into ritual action were admitted.

Now, it might be argued that this restriction (avadhāraṇa) is intended to mean that [the fires] have no external means of accomplishment; but we say "no. For if that were the intention, the restriction would be redundant, since the very mention of their essential nature in the words "built of knowledge" (*vidyācita*) would already suffice, as their very nature consists in having no external means of accomplishment. However, even though they have no external means of accomplishment, there might still be a suspicion that they enter into the performance of ritual action like the mental cups (*mānasagraha*); it is for the purpose of removing that suspicion that the restriction becomes meaningful.

Likewise, the observation of their continuity—expressed in the passage, "For one who knows this, all beings always gather around these [fires] while he sleeps and while he is awake"—is possible only if they are independent. This is just as in the case of the ritual fire-sacrifice (agnihotra) consisting of speech and breath, where after stating, "Then he offers breath into speech, and then he offers speech into breath," it is further said, "These two endless, immortal oblations he offers continuously, both waking and sleeping.
If, however, they were subordinate to a ritual action, their performance could not be conceived as continuous, because the performance of a ritual action occupies only a short duration of time.
Nor is it reasonable to maintain that this is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*);
for where a clear injunctive suffix such as the optative (*liṅ*) is perceived, it is appropriate that a mere mention should be considered an explanatory statement.
But here, since no other clear injunction is found, the injunction of these cognitions must be inferred from the very fact of their being mentioned.

And since that [agency] can only be postulated in accordance with what has been mentioned, it is postulated as being exactly of that nature because of the observation of continuity; and therefore, by the force of the context, their independence is established. (Sūtra, Third Chapter) *bhū*... [The text continues: ...by the force of the capacity [of the evidence].
By this, the passage beginning with "Whatever these [beings] here conceive with the mind, that is their very act" is explained.
Likewise, the statement "to one who knows thus" (evaṃvide), by declaring a connection specifically with a particular person, does not tolerate a connection with the ritual sacrifice (ṛtu).
Therefore, the position of independence alone is superior.
On account of the connection and other reasons, it is seen that there is a distinction between the various forms of knowledge, as has been stated.

For this reason as well, one must understand that the mental fires (*manaścit*) and so forth are independent, setting aside the context of the ritual action, because [the text] connects the constituent parts of the ritual to the operations of the mind and other faculties: "They were acquired by the mind alone, they were piled up by the mind alone; by the mind alone the cups were drawn, by the mind they chanted, by the mind they recited; whatever rite is performed at the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that is performed as consisting of mind alone, in those which consist of mind, the mental fires.
For this connection has the attainment of identity (*saṃpat*) as its fruit.
Furthermore, the perceptible constituent parts of the ritual action do not exist as such that they ought to be sought through meditative identification (*saṃpad*).

Nor should it be suspected here—on the grounds of their connection with the members of the ritual action—that these [names] enter into the action in the same manner as the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth, because of the dissimilarity of the scriptural statement;
for the scripture does not say here that one should take some member of the ritual action and superimpose the name "A-da" upon it.

Taking up thirty-six thousand varieties of mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti-bheda*), it conceives of them as the fires, the cups (*graha*), and so forth—just as in the case of the "Sacrifice of the Person" (*puruṣayajña*) and other such rites.

Furthermore, this number, being observed in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* in relation to the days of a person's lifespan, should be understood as being superimposed upon the mental fluctuations associated with that lifespan.
Thus, due to these connections, the independence of the mind and the others is established.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), extension (*atideśa*) and other such principles are also to be applied as far as possible;

for instance, by extending the greatness of the fire consisting of action to each one of those consisting of knowledge—stating, "Each one of them is indeed as great as that former one"—the text shows a disregard for mere ritual action.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the former and the latter only while the connection to action remains actually present.
For it is not the case that by the same function—such as maintaining the Āhavanīya fire—that which assisted in the prior rite can assist in the subsequent ones.

As for the argument that the extension (*atideśa*) [of rites] even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) serves as a supporting reason because extension operates only when there is a commonality, that has already been refuted; for even in our position, extension is possible through the commonality of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*), since even the fires that are merely meditative constructs (*sāṃpādika*) possess the nature of fire. Furthermore, the grounds such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth have already been demonstrated.
Thus, due to reasons such as their specific adjuncts (*anubandha*), the fires consisting of mind (*manascit*) and so forth possess independence.

This is like the distinctness of other meditations (*prajñāntara-pṛthaktva*): just as other meditations, such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, being connected with their own respective adjuncts, become independent from ritual acts and from other meditations; so it is here.
Furthermore, it is observed that the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice, though recited within the context of the Rājasūya, is extracted from that context because it is connected with the three castes.

And because the Rājasūya is a royal sacrifice (rājayajña); as it was stated in the first section (kāṇḍa): "If it be argued that [the prohibition] applies to what is for the sake of the ritual (ṛtvartha), we say no, because of its connection with the three castes."
The Third Chapter: [Objection:
It is not so, because perception occurs even through similarity, as in the case of death; for there is no actual transition to another world.
As for what was said regarding the analogy with the mental [sacrifices], that is now answered:

even on account of their commonality with the mental cup-offerings (*mānasagraha*), the mental fires (*manaścidādi*) cannot be conceived as being subordinate to ritual action, because it is perceived from the previously mentioned reasons—such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth—that they serve solely the purpose of the person;
for indeed, nothing whatsoever shares some commonality with something else.
And yet, by that much alone, their respective specific natures do not cease to exist.

This is like the case of "death": just as in the passages, "Now, this person who is in this orb is indeed death" and "Fire is indeed death," although the term "death" is applied equally to the person in the sun and to fire, there is no attainment of absolute identity between them;

and just as in the passage, "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; its fuel is the sun," the world does not actually become fire merely because of the commonality of the fuel and other attributes, so it is here as well.
And the same nature applies to the subsequent sound; however, there is a connection [of the suffix] due to its frequency.

Furthermore, in the immediately following Brāhmaṇa passage, "This world indeed is this piled fire-altar," the purpose of the word is observed to be the injunction of pure knowledge (*kevalavidyāvidhitva*), not the injunction of mere ritual accessories (*śuddhakarmāṅgavidhitva*). For therein, by censuring mere ritual action and praising knowledge with the verse, "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have vanished; neither sacrificial fees go there, nor do the ignorant who practice austerities," it leads to this conclusion.

Likewise, in the preceding section as well—in the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "That orb which shines"—it is observed that knowledge alone is the primary subject, because the conclusion is made solely through the fruit of knowledge: "He becomes immortal; death becomes his self. There is no predominance of ritual action there.
By virtue of that similarity, the same applies here as well.

However, because many components of the fire-altar must be mentally constructed within this meditation, the meditation is connected with the fire-altar for that reason, and not because it is a subordinate part of the ritual.
Therefore, it is established that the mind-altars (manaścita) and the others consist solely of knowledge (vidyā).
[The self is] one, because of its existence in the body.
Here, the existence of a self distinct from the body is established for the sake of proving the qualification for bondage and liberation;

for if there were no self distinct from the body, the injunctions concerning rewards in another world resulting from the state of the body would not be tenable, nor would there be anyone for whom such a qualification could exist.
The identity of Brahman and the Self would thus be taught.

But, one might object, at the very beginning of the scripture, in the first quarter (pāda), the existence of a Self distinct from the body—one capable of enjoying the fruits of the scripture—was already stated; it is true that this was stated by the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra), yet there is no actual Sūtra regarding the existence of the Self there.
But here, the author of the Sūtras himself has established its existence by means of an objection;
and having drawn [the argument] from this very source, the teacher Śabarasvāmin described it in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*; and for this very reason, it is treated in the third chapter of the Bhāṣya.
The venerable Upavarṣa, when the occasion arose for stating the existence of the Self in the first *tantra*, made the following reservation: "We shall explain this in the *Śārīraka*.

And here, while meditations characterized by injunctions (*codanā*) are being investigated, the existence of the Self is examined in order to demonstrate that [this topic] is supplementary to the entire scripture. Furthermore, in the preceding section, by accepting a departure from the immediate context, it was described how the mental fires (*manaścit* etc. serve the purpose of man.

In response to the inquiry, "Who is this person for whose sake these [fires] such as the mind-made (*manaścita*) and others exist?", the existence of the Self as distinct from the body is stated here.

This first Sūtra is intended to raise that question; for an answer preceded by an objection produces a firm conviction regarding the intended subject, according to the maxim of "digging in a pillar" (*sthūṇānikhanana*).

PSA: Here, some Lokāyatikas, who perceive the self as consisting of the body alone and who maintain that there is no self distinct from the body, speculate that consciousness—though not observed in the external elements such as earth and the rest, whether taken collectively or individually—might nevertheless exist in those elements when they have transformed into the shape of a body; and they assert that consciousness arises from them, like the power of intoxication, and that the "person" (puruṣa) is the body characterized by consciousness. They hold that there is no self distinct from the body capable of going to heaven or attaining liberation, by whose agency consciousness would reside in the body.
However, they assert that the body itself is both conscious and the Self, and they state the reason for this: "Because [consciousness] exists when the body exists.

For whatever exists when something else exists, and does not exist when that thing is absent, is determined to be an attribute of that thing—just as heat and light are attributes of fire. (Sūtra-bhāṣya)

Furthermore, those things such as vital breath, movement, consciousness, and memory—which are asserted by proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) to be attributes of the self—are perceived only within the body and not outside of it; therefore, since a substratum distinct from the body is unestablished, they must necessarily be attributes of the body alone.
Consequently, there is no difference between the self and the body.

This being the case, we reply: there is a distinction [between the self and the body], because [the qualities of the self] exist only when that [self] exists, and not merely through perception, as in the case of [perceptual objects].
But this which was stated— that there is no distinction between the self and the body— is not the case;
rather, there must indeed be a distinction of this [self] from the body,
because [the self] does not exist when that [body] is absent.

If it is thought that because [the qualities] exist when the body exists, they are attributes of the body, then why not consider them to be non-attributes of the body precisely because they do not exist even when the body exists? This is because they differ from the attributes of the body;

for those which are the attributes of the body, such as form and so forth, persist as long as the body lasts, whereas vital functions, movement, and so forth do not exist during the state of death, even though the body is present.
Furthermore, bodily attributes such as form and so forth are perceived by others as well, but the attributes of the self—such as consciousness, memory, and so on—are not.

Moreover, while the body exists in its living state, it is possible to ascertain the presence of these [attributes]; however, their absence when the body is no longer present cannot be so ascertained.
For even after this body has fallen, the attributes of the self might continue through a transition into another body.
Even by mere doubt, the opposing position is refuted.

Furthermore, the opponent must be questioned as to what kind of consciousness (*caitanya*) he considers this to be, of which he desires origination from the elements; for the Materialist (*Lokāyatika*) does not admit any reality apart from the four elements.

If it is argued that consciousness (*caitanya*) is the experience of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), then, because they are its objects, consciousness could not be an attribute of them, since it is contradictory for an action to operate upon itself.

Indeed, fire, being hot, does not burn itself; nor will an actor, though well-trained, ever mount his own shoulders. Furthermore, the primary elements and their derivatives cannot be made into objects by a consciousness that is itself an attribute of those very elements and derivatives.
For neither its own nature nor the nature of another is made an object by form and the like;
rather, external and internal elements and elemental products are made objects by consciousness.
Therefore, just as the existence of this perception—which has the elements and elemental products as its objects—is admitted, so too must its distinction from them be admitted.
Furthermore, since the self is not of the very nature of cognition (*upalabdhi*), it is distinct from the body.

Cognition is eternal because of its uniformity, and because there is recognition as the cognizer even when associated with different states, such as "I saw this," as well as because memory and other such functions are otherwise inexplicable.
As for the argument that cognition is a property of the body because it exists when the body exists, that has been refuted by the manner already described.

Moreover, although perception occurs when instruments such as a lamp are present and does not occur when they are absent, perception does not thereby become a property of the lamp and so forth; likewise,
even though perception occurs when the body is present and does not occur when it is absent, it cannot be a property of the body,
because its utility for the body is established merely by its being an instrument, just like a lamp.
Furthermore, the utility of the body for perception is not seen to be absolute, since various kinds of perceptions are observed even while this body is motionless during dreams;
therefore, the existence of the self as distinct from the body is beyond reproach.
But those [rites] connected with the bodily limbs are not restricted to specific branches, for they belong to every Veda.
The incidental discussion is concluded; we shall now proceed with the subject at hand.

"One should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha"; "One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds"; "People say 'Hymn, hymn,' but it is this very [earth] that is the hymn"; "This earth indeed..."—this is the section.

There arises a doubt as to whether those meditations (pratyayas) connected with the constituent parts of rituals such as the *udgītha*, which are enjoined in each Veda across various recensions (*śākhābhedas*)—beginning with the text, "This very world is this piled fire-altar" (*vāva loka eṣo 'gniścitaḥ*)—should apply only to the *udgītha* and other parts belonging to their own respective recensions, or rather to those belonging to all recensions.
This discussion is undertaken by taking into account the difference between the *udgītha* and other parts, which arises from differences in accent and so forth in each recension.
What, then, is the prima facie view? That they should be enjoined only with respect to the *udgītha* and other parts belonging to one's own recension.

Why? Because of proximity. For when there is a requirement for specification regarding those things generally enjoined by the rule "one should meditate on the Udgītha," that requirement is satisfied by the specific [details] belonging to one's own Vedic branch (śākhā) which are in close proximity; thus, there is no reason to bypass that and adopt specifications enjoined in other branches. Therefore, the conclusion being reached that there is a restriction to each respective branch, the author says: "But those connected with the members [of the sacrifice]."
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.

These [meditations] do not remain restricted to their own branches within each Veda; rather, they should recur in all branches. Why? Because there is no distinction in the scriptural mention of the *udgītha* and so forth.

For, within the restriction to one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), the general scriptural statement "one should meditate on the *udgītha*"— which applies without distinction— would be strained if it were restricted to a particular instance by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*); and this is not right,
for scripture (*śruti*) is stronger than proximity.
Nor is it the case that a cognition based on a universal (sāmānya) is untenable;

therefore, even though there are differences such as the specific tones (svarādi), because there is no distinction in their being the *udgītha* and so forth, such cognitions should indeed apply to all instances of the *udgītha* and other elements found across all Vedic branches (*śākhā*).
B. Or rather, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of mantras and the like.

Or rather, one should not suspect any contradiction here, such as: "How can meditations prescribed in one Vedic branch apply to the *udgītha* and other elements found in another branch? For there is no contradiction, as is established by the case of mantras and so forth. To explain: it is observed that mantras, ritual acts, and subsidiary qualities, even when originating in a different branch, are incorporated into another branch. For instance, although the mantra for taking up the stone, "Thou art a *kuṭaru*," is not recited in the text of certain followers of a branch, its application is nevertheless seen among them: "He takes up the stone with [the mantra] 'Thou art a *kukkuṭa*' or 'Thou art a *kuṭaru*.'"

Even for those [schools] in whose Sūtra-commentary the *samit* and other *prayāja* offerings are not explicitly mentioned, an injunction regarding their qualities is recorded: "The *prayājas* are indeed the seasons; they are to be offered together.

Likewise, even for those for whom there is no instruction regarding a specific genus—such as "the *agnīṣomīya* animal is a goat"—a mantra-text concerning that subject is found: "Recite for the omentum and fat of the goat.
Similarly, the inclusion of mantras originating in one Veda within another Veda is observed, such as "O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ; advance the sacrifice," and so forth.

Likewise, in the case of the hymn frequently recited by the Bahvṛcas, "He who was born as the first, the wise one" (*yo jāta ekaḥ prathamo manasvān*), its inclusion is seen in the injunction, "The *sajanīya* [hymn] is to be recited for the Adhvaryu.

Therefore, just as there is a universal application of the ritual acts that serve as the substrata, so too is there such an application of the suffixes that depend upon them; thus, there is no contradiction.
The preeminence of the abundant belongs to the ritual act, for scripture shows it to be so.

In this narrative beginning with "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava," the meditation upon Vaiśvānara both in his distributed and his unified forms is heard. First, regarding the meditation on him in his distributed form: "Aupamanyava, whom do you meditate upon as the Self? [He replied,] "The sky alone, O venerable King. [The teacher said,] "This indeed is the Self Vaiśvānara called 'the Splendidly Radiant' (Sutejas), which you meditate upon as the Self," and so forth; likewise, there is the performance of the meditation upon him in his unified form. Chapter Three.

"Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head is indeed *sutejas* (the well-shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (the multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (the manifold-pathed), the trunk is *bahula* (the extensive), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), and the feet are the earth," and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is there here worship in both ways—of the distributed [parts] and of the aggregate—or only of the aggregate?

What, then, is the prima facie position? Since the verbal action "you meditate" (*upāsse*) is heard in connection with each individual member, such as Sutejas and the others, and since distinct fruits are heard, such as "therefore, Soma-pressing, continuous pressing, and constant pressing are seen in your family," it follows that the meditations are indeed separate. This is the initial conclusion.

Therefore, it is stated that in this passage, what is intended to be expressed primarily is the superiority of the entire meditation on Vaiśvānara—which consists of an accumulation of constituent elements—not the meditations on each individual limb;

just as in the case of the *ṛtus*, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, where the performance of the principal rite together with all its auxiliary parts is intended as a single whole, and not the separate performance of the auxiliaries like the *prayājas*, nor the principal rite joined with only a portion of its auxiliaries, so it is here.
Whence is it known that "the Infinite (bhūman) alone is greater"? For thus the scripture shows the superiority of the Infinite, because a single unified statement is understood;
for this entire discourse concerning the Vaiśvānara-knowledge is perceived as a single unit upon consideration of its preceding and succeeding parts.
To illustrate: [it begins with] Prācīnaśāla and others, ending with Uddālaka.

Six Ṛṣis, not attaining full perfection in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, approached King Aśvapati Kaikeya. Beginning with the words "They went to King Aśvapati Kaikeya" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.6), [the text] causes each Ṛṣi to hear one by one of the objects of meditation, such as the sky and so forth, and then establishes their status as the head and other limbs through the passage beginning, "He said, 'This is indeed the head of the Self,'" and so on.
Furthermore, it refutes meditation on the parts separately through the passage beginning, "'Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me,'" and so forth.

Furthermore, having set aside the meditation on the parts individually and continuing instead with the meditation on the whole, the text shows that the fruit rests solely upon the "Bhūman" (the Infinite), stating: "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.

As for the mention of distinct fruits for each individual part beginning with Sutejas, this should be understood as follows: when such is the case, the fruits of the subordinate members are subsumed within the principal [meditation] itself. Likewise, the repeated hearing of the verb "you meditate" (*upāsse*) for each limb is intended merely to restate the intention of others, not to enjoin the meditation on the parts separately.
Therefore, the position that the meditation is performed as a whole is indeed superior.

However, some here, having established the view that meditating on the whole is superior, assume that the author of the Sūtras must also approve of the view of meditating on the parts, precisely because of the statement regarding its superiority.

That is incorrect, because when a single unified meaning is understood, it is improper to assume a split in the sentence; because it contradicts such censures as "your head would have fallen off"; because when the concluding portion clearly reveals that all [meditations] are to be combined, it is impossible to maintain their absence in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa); and because the Sūtra’s statement regarding "superiority" (jyāyastva) is also justifiable on the grounds that it intends to refer to the possession of authoritative means of knowledge. [End of] Third Chapter. [Topic: They are distinct, because of the difference in words and so forth.
In the preceding section, it was stated that even though there is a scriptural mention of different fruits for those beginning with Sutejas, meditation on the whole is superior;
therefore, the notion arises that other meditations mentioned in different scriptural passages—on account of differences in words and so forth—should also be combined and practiced together.
Moreover, this is not at all a matter of the identity of the object of knowledge (vedya).

A difference between the two knowledges can be recognized, for the object of knowledge constitutes the essence of a knowledge, just as the material and the deity constitute the essence of a sacrifice.

And yet, even though there is a plurality of scriptural passages, the Lord who is to be known is understood to be one and the same in such texts as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body, Brahma, the ether-Brahma" and "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true," and so forth. Likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa) is one and the same in such texts as "Breath indeed is the absorber; breath indeed is the eldest, the best; breath is the father, breath is the mother," and so forth.

And because the object of knowledge is one, the knowledge itself is one. Even the multiplicity of scriptural texts in this view is not purposeless, as it serves to introduce other subordinate qualities (*guṇa*).

Therefore, the collection of qualities prescribed in one's own and other Vedic branches, which rest upon a single object of knowledge, must be combined for the sake of the meditation—this being the position reached, the following is established: "They are manifold."
Even though the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is non-different, a meditative knowledge (*vidyā*) of this kind must nevertheless be distinct.
Why? Because of the difference in words and so forth.
For there is a difference in words such as "one should know," "one should meditate," and "he should form a resolve," and so on.

It was established previously that a difference in words is a cause for a difference in ritual acts, as stated [in the *Śābarabhāṣya*]: "When there is another word, there is a difference in the act, because of the connection with what has been performed.
By the inclusion of the term "etcetera" (*ādi*), other causes of difference such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth should also be applied according to their possibility.

Now, an objection is raised: in cases such as "veda" (he knows) and so on, only a difference in words is perceived, not a difference in meaning as in the case of "yajati" (he sacrifices) and so on; for all these [words] are non-different insofar as they have mental activity as their object, and no other meaning is possible.

How then can there be a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to a difference in words? This is not a fault, because even though there is no difference in the object of the mental activity (*manovṛtti*), a difference in knowledge is established when there is a difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) resulting from a difference in the adjuncts (*anubandha*).
Although the Lord, who is the object of meditation, is one, distinct qualities are taught for Him in each respective section.

Likewise, although Prāṇa, who is the object of meditation, is one and the same in various places, He is to be meditated upon with one set of qualities in one instance and with another set of qualities in another; thus, when there is a difference in injunctions (*vidhi*) due to a difference in adjuncts, a difference in knowledge is understood.

Nor can it be said that in this case there is one injunction for knowledge while the others are injunctions of qualities, because there is no reason for such a determination (*vinigamanā*), and because it is impossible to enjoin multiple qualities within each section by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a knowledge already established. Furthermore, on this view, qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāma*), being common to all, would have to be repeated more than once. Moreover, since in each section one understands a state of self-sufficiency through the realization that "one desiring this should meditate on this," and "one desiring that should meditate on that," there is no resulting unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*).

Moreover, in this case, there is no other overarching injunction—as there is in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā—by the force of which the meditations on the individual parts, occurring within their respective contexts, would become unified into a single coherent whole.
Third Chapter [of the Sūtras].

And if the unity of the meditation were asserted everywhere without restriction on the grounds of the identity of the object of knowledge (vedya), then the impossible task of combining all the attributes [from different sources] would have to be asserted.
Therefore, it is rightly said: "On account of the difference of words and so forth.
And this section being established, the principle that "the cognition [of Brahman] is the same in all Vedānta texts," and so on, is to be understood.
The option is not applicable because the result is indistinguishable.

The distinction between the Vidyās having been established, it is now considered whether there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) among them according to one's wish, or whether there is a restrictive rule for option alone. Since the distinction between the Vidyās has already been established, there is no reason for a restrictive rule of combination. [Objection: But surely there is a difference in the instruments (*karaṇa*).

Even in the case of various rites such as the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and so forth, a rule of simultaneous performance (samuccaya) is observed; this is not a fault, for in those cases the scriptural statement regarding their obligatory nature (nityatā) is the reason. However, there is no such scriptural statement regarding the obligatory nature of the meditations (vidyās).

Therefore, there is no rule of combination, nor is there a rule of option, because there is no prohibition against one who is qualified for one knowledge undertaking another. By process of elimination, it follows that there is freedom of choice (*yāthākāmyam*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that an option (*vikalpa*) between these meditations is logical because their fruits are indistinguishable?

For instance, such passages as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body" (*manomayaḥ prāṇaśarīraḥ*), "Brahman is Ka, Brahman is Kha," and "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true"—all of which appear to have the attainment of lordship (*īśvaratva*) as their equal fruit. [Response: This is not a fault, because even among ritual acts (*karma*) that have the same result, such as those leading to heaven and so forth, we observe the freedom to choose according to one's desire (*yāthākāmya*).

Therefore, since the freedom to choose would otherwise apply, it is said: an option alone must prevail between these meditations, not a combination (*samuccaya*). This is stated in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*.

Why? Because their fruit is non-distinct. For the fruit of these [meditations] is the direct realization of the object of worship; and once the object of worship, such as the Lord, has been realized through one meditation, a second one is purposeless.
Moreover, realization is simply impossible under the view of combination (*samuccaya*), because that would be a cause for mental distraction;

yet the scriptures show that the fruit of knowledge is to be accomplished through realization—for instance, "He for whom this is so, there is no doubt," and "Having become a god, he goes to the gods," and so forth.
And the traditional texts (*smṛti*) likewise state, "Always permeated by that state," and so on.

Therefore, having taken up any one of those knowledges which yield indistinguishable results, one should be devoted to it until that result is attained through the direct realization of the object of meditation.
But these optional rites may be combined according to one's desire, or not, because of the absence of the previously mentioned reason.
This is the counter-example to the statement "because there is no difference in the fruit.

However, in those optional meditations (*vidyā*) such as, "He who knows this Vāyu, the calf of the quarters, does not weep for the loss of a son through desire," and "He who meditates on Name as Brahman—so far as Name extends, he has free movement therein"—and so forth, which accomplish their own fruit by means of an unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*) through action, there is no requirement for direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). Chapter Three.

Therefore, they may either be combined according to one's desire, or they may not be combined; for there is an absence of the reason for such an option, namely, the absence of a prior cause and the fact that the prior [action] does not have a distinct result.
Just as there is the state of being a support among the limbs.

Regarding the meditations (*pratyaya*) based on the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), such as the *udgītha* and others, which are prescribed according to their respective bases in the three Vedas: in the doubt as to whether these should be combined or may be practiced according to one's preference, [the author] states that they exist according to their bases.
Just as their bases—the hymns (*stotra*) and so forth—exist collectively, so too do the meditations, because the meditations are dependent upon their bases.
In what remains.

Just as the bases, such as the *stotra* and others, are prescribed in the three Vedas, so too are the dependent *pratyayas*; the meaning is that there is no distinction whatsoever between the auxiliary elements (*aṅgas*) and the *pratyayas* that depend upon them, even with respect to their instruction.
Because of their combination.

Furthermore, the statement, "He indeed rectifies even a badly sung [chant] from the seat of the Hotṛ," indicates that by the greatness of the knowledge of the identity of the *praṇava* and the *udgītha*, the Udgātṛ priest repairs a defect arising in his own ritual action through the action of the Hotṛ. By thus speaking, it suggests the synthesis of meditative realizations (*pratyaya*) taught in all Vedas, on the basis of the commonality of the relationship between the meditative realization taught in one Veda and the ritual object (*padārtha*) taught in another; this is the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities.

And it makes known the syllable *oṃ*, which is common to the three Vedas, as being the locus of knowledge and possessing the quality of knowledge—through such passages as: "By that this triple science proceeds; [the Adhvaryu] causes [the Hotṛ] to announce with 'Om', [the Hotṛ] recites with 'Om', and [the Udgātṛ] chants the Udgītha with 'Om'.
Thus, because the locus is common, the thing located is also common; this is indeed a scriptural indication (*liṅga*).
Alternatively, it is because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the qualities.

If these qualities of action, such as the *udgītha* and so forth, were not common to all ritual performances, then there would be no coexistence of the meditative reflections (*pratyaya*) that depend upon them.

However, those *udgītha* elements and others are heard through the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which encompasses all constituent parts, and are thus common to all ritual performances.
Consequently, due to the coexistence of their substrates, there is a coexistence of the meditative reflections.
Or rather, it is not so, because their coexistence is not heard of.
The phrase "or rather" serves to exclude the aforementioned position.
It is not possible for the meditations (*upāsanā*) that depend [on the body] to exist in the same manner as the locus itself.
Why? Because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture].

For whereas the coexistence of the subordinate elements (aṅga) such as the hymns (stotra), which are prescribed in the three Vedas, is indeed heard—through such passages as, "Having taken the cup (graha) or having lifted the bowl (camasa), he begins the hymn; having praised, the Acchāvāka recites the response; O Prastotṛ, sing the Sāman; O Hotṛ, sacrifice this"—[such coexistence is not mentioned for the meditations].
There is no such scriptural statement regarding the simultaneous performance of these meditations (*upāsana*).

Now, one might argue that the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) would necessitate their simultaneity; we reply: no, because these meditations have the person as their purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
For the injunction of performance would necessitate the simultaneity of those elements like the *udgītha* which serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*).

We have already stated in the section "For the fruit is separate and unobstructed" that the meditations on the *udgītha*, although resting upon elements that serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), nevertheless serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), just like the *godohana* vessel and similar things.

This very distinction based on the scriptural instruction—that some auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) and the meditations resting upon them serve the purpose of the sacrifice, while others serve the purpose of the person—is the difference.

Furthermore, the two previously mentioned indicative marks (*liṅga*) are not grounds for the simultaneous performance of the meditations, because there is neither scriptural statement (*śruti*) nor logical reasoning (*nyāya*) to support such a requirement.

Nor can it be understood that because the substratum is withdrawn in every individual application, those things dependent upon it must likewise be so withdrawn; for meditations are not prompted by their substrata. Indeed, although meditations are dependent on their substrata, they may well cease to exist in the absence of a substratum;
however, they do not merit a rule of coexistence based on the coexistence of the substratum, precisely because there is no scriptural statement regarding such coexistence.
Therefore, the meditations should be performed according to one's own desire.
And because it is seen [in scripture].

Moreover, scripture demonstrates the non-simultaneity of these meditative states (*pratyaya*), stating: "The Brahman priest who knows this indeed protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests.

For if there were a combination of all meditative states, it would follow that everyone is an omniscient knower; consequently, the fact that others are to be protected by the wise Brahman priest would become confused.
Therefore, the meditations may be combined or chosen optionally according to one's desire.

Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
Composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.
The Fourth Pāda of the Third Adhyāya: Love Shines. The Fourth Pāda.

Now, investigating whether this knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads enters into ritual action by way of a specific qualification, or whether it is an independent means for achieving the goal of man, [the author] begins with the established conclusion: "The goal of man [is attained] from this [knowledge], because of the scriptural word; thus says Bādarāyaṇa. (Sūtra 3.4.1)
"Puruṣārtha [is attained] from this.

The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the human goal (puruṣārtha) is accomplished from this independent knowledge of the Self prescribed by the Vedāntas. On what basis is this understood? He says: "From the Word (śabda)."

Likewise: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"; "He who knows that supreme Brahman indeed becomes Brahman itself"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "The person who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]"; and beginning with "That Self which is free from evil," it continues: "He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires."

Beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," and concluding with "In truth, in the knowledge of the Self is immortality," scripture of this kind declares that pure knowledge alone is the cause of the human goal.
Now, an objection is raised here: "Because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement of human purpose, as in other cases," so says Jaimini.

Since the self is subordinate to ritual action by virtue of being its agent, the knowledge of that self is likewise connected to ritual action through its object, just like the sprinkling of rice grains and similar rites; therefore, the teacher Jaimini maintains that any scriptural mention of a fruit regarding that knowledge of the self—which has already served its purpose [as a subordinate factor]—is merely an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or commendatory statement).

Just as in the case of other material preparations and ritual acts—such as "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," "When he marks [the animal], he indeed blinds his rival's eye," and "When the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are performed, a shield is created for the sacrifice and a shield for the sacrificer for the sake of overcoming his rival"—in such instances, the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), so it is here as well.

But how can it be suspected that this knowledge of the Self, which is taught outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), enters into connection with a ritual sacrifice (*kratu*) in the absence of any reason such as the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth? If it is argued that its connection with the sacrifice is established through the sentence (*vākya*) by way of the agent (*kartṛ*), we say no; for a connection with the sacrifice based on a sentence is not possible here. For even in the case of things taught outside of a context, a connection with the sacrifice caused by a sentence is only plausible when there is some non-deviating medium;
however, the agent is a deviating medium, because he is common to both worldly and Vedic actions. (Chapter 3)

Therefore, it is not established that self-knowledge is connected to ritual action by means of the *tā* suffix—no, because the cognition of the soul's distinction [from the body] is of no use elsewhere than in Vedic rituals.
For the knowledge of a soul distinct from the body is not useful in worldly activities, since such activities can be undertaken in every way based on visible purposes;

however, in the case of Vedic rituals, whose fruits occur after the fall of the body, activity is not possible without the knowledge of a soul distinct from the body. Thus, the cognition of distinction is indeed useful.

[Objection: But surely, because of such qualifiers as "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*), the Upanishadic vision must concern a non-transmigrating Self and thus cannot be a factor for [worldly] activity. [Reply: No, because it is taught that the very transmigrating Self, indicated by its "beloveds" and so forth, is that which is to be seen; the qualifiers such as "freedom from evil," however, will serve the purpose of praise (*stuti*). [Objection: But this has been established in various places—that there is a non-transmigrating Brahman, superior [to the individual self], which is the cause of the world.
And it has been truly established that this very [nature] is taught in the Upaniṣads as the ultimate, real nature of the transmigrating self;
however, regarding that very [nature], an objection and its resolution are now being presented by way of the result, like the firming of a pillar by repeated hammering.
Because of the observation of [their] conduct.

In passages such as "Janaka, the King of Videha, performed a sacrifice with many gifts" and "I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice, O venerable ones," we observe a connection with ritual action even in the case of those who know Brahman, despite these statements being intended for another purpose.
Likewise, from the observation of Uddālaka and others giving instructions to their sons and so forth, their connection with the householder's life is understood. (Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya, p. 450)

If the fulfillment of human goals were to occur through knowledge alone, why would they perform rituals involving manifold exertions? This follows the maxim: "If one finds honey in the hollow of a tree, why should one go to the mountain?"
Because of that scriptural statement.

Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that knowledge is subordinate to action—namely, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful"—knowledge by itself is not the cause of the human goal.
Because of the act of supporting one another.
And because the text, "Knowledge and action follow him," shows that knowledge and action act together in the commencement of their fruit, knowledge does not possess independence.
Because it follows from that injunction.

"Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the rule, and having returned home at the conclusion of the duties for the teacher, one should apply oneself to the private recitation of the Veda in a pure place within the family"—this and other such scriptural passages show that the qualification for ritual action belongs to one who possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda;
therefore, even for this reason, knowledge is not the cause of the fruit independently.
Now, an objection is raised: here, by the word "having studied," only the mere study of the Veda is heard, not the knowledge of its meaning. This is not a valid objection.
It is established that the study of the Veda, because it has a perceptible purpose, extends as far as the comprehension of its meaning.
The third chapter:
And because of the restrictive rule.
"Only performing actions here, one should desire to live a hundred years;

thus it is for you, there is no other way than this, for action does not cling to a man"—and likewise, "This Agnihotra is indeed a rite pertaining to old age, for by old age or by death one is released from it"—from such injunctions as well, it follows that knowledge is merely a subordinate part of ritual action.
This being the case, [the author] provides the following rebuttal: "But because of the additional teaching of Bādarāyaṇa, it is thus, for that is seen."
By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed.
What was stated—that "it is a statement of human purpose because it is a subsidiary"—is not tenable; why? Because of the teaching of something additional.

If the transmigrating self alone—the embodied one who is both agent and enjoyer—were taught in the Vedāntas as distinct from the body, then, in the manner described, the mention of results would be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

However, in addition to the embodied self, the non-transmigrating Lord, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—who is devoid of transmigratory attributes such as agency and is characterized by qualities such as being "free from sin"—is taught in the Vedāntas as the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, the knowledge of that [Supreme Self] does not incite one to action; on the contrary, it destroys actions, as will be stated in the section beginning with "And [there is] sublation" (*upamarda ca*).

Therefore, that opinion of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa which stands in the Sūtra and its Commentary—namely, "The human goal [is attained] from this [Self], because of the scriptural word"—remains exactly so;
it cannot be shaken by fallacious reasons such as being a mere subordinate element (*śeṣatva*).

For indeed, the Śrutis reveal that Lord, the Self who is superior to the embodied soul (the *śārīra*), in passages such as: "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving"; "From fear of Him the wind blows"; "A great terror, a raised thunderbolt"; "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī"; and "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It created fire," and so forth.

As for the fact that the transmigrating self alone, as indicated by "the beloved" and so forth, is drawn forward as the object to be known, [it is said]: "But it is for the sake of the self that everything becomes dear."

The passages beginning with "Verily, the Self (ātman) is to be seen," "That which breathes by means of the vital breath (prāṇa)—that is your Self, the innermost of all; that person who is seen in the eye"—and further, "I shall explain this very [Self] to you again," are likewise intended to teach something additional, as evidenced by the concluding statements: "This Rigveda is the breath of this great Being," "He who transcends hunger and thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death," and "Having attained the highest light, he appears in his own form; he is the Supreme Person. Thus, there is no contradiction, as these passages intend to express absolute non-difference [between the individual self and Brahman] once the desire to instruct regarding the higher reality has been established.
For the supreme Lord alone is the ultimate, real nature of the embodied soul;
its state as an embodied being, however, is produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). This is known from such scriptural texts as "That thou art" and "There is no other seer but He.
All of this has been explained by us at length in various places previously.
The Third Chapter:
But the scriptural vision is equal.

As for what was said—that knowledge is a supplement to ritual action because of the observation of certain practices—we reply: the observation of such practices is equally applicable even when knowledge is not a supplement to ritual action.
For there is a scriptural text to this effect: "Knowing this, indeed, the Ṛṣis, the descendants of Kavaṣa, said: 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices?'"

"Indeed, the ancients who knew this did not perform the Agnihotra sacrifice. Having known that Self, the Brāhmaṇas, rising above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lead the life of mendicants"—such is the nature of these [scriptural passages].

Furthermore, the lack of engagement in ritual action among knowers of Brahman such as Yājñavalkya is observed from scriptural texts such as: "Having said, 'O, this much indeed is immortality,' Yājñavalkya departed."
Furthermore, the scriptural indication, "O venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice," pertains specifically to the Vaiśvānara-vidyā;
and while it is possible for a knowledge of Brahman associated with limiting adjuncts (sopādhika) to be seen as compatible with ritual action,
this [knowledge] does not constitute an auxiliary part of ritual action either, because there is an absence of context (prakaraṇa) and other such indicators.
As for what was further stated, namely, "Because of that scriptural statement, because of that scriptural statement," we reply: it is not universal.

The scriptural passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge," does not have all forms of knowledge as its subject matter; rather, in the Sūtra-bhāṣya, it refers specifically to the Udgītha-knowledge under discussion, because of its connection with that specific knowledge in the statement, "One should meditate upon that syllable as the Udgītha. "Om" thus refers to the Udgītha.
The distribution is like that of a hundred [coins].

Regarding the statement that "knowledge and action both accompany him," which was cited as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the non-independence of knowledge—this is answered as follows: here a distinction (*vibhāga*) must be observed; knowledge accompanies one person, while action accompanies another.
It is just like when it is said, "Let a hundred be given"; it is given by dividing it, fifty to one and fifty to the other. Similarly, it is here.

Furthermore, this statement regarding "commencement" (samanvārambha) does not refer to one who desires liberation, because it concludes with reference to the transmigrating soul in the passage, "But he who desires thus," and because the seeker of liberation is introduced separately in the passage, "Now, he who does not desire.
In that context concerning the transmigrating soul, both knowledge—whether enjoined or prohibited—is included, as there is no distinction made;
likewise, action—both enjoined and prohibited—is included, since the text merely restates what has already come into being.
This being so, this statement regarding simultaneous undertaking is also intelligible even without distinction.
And as for this [objection] that "it is because of the injunction for one who possesses that," he reads the following reply: "[The qualification applies] to one who possesses merely the study."

In the passage, "Having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher," since mere study is what is heard, we conclude that the injunction for ritual action applies only to one who possesses mere study. But if this were so, would it not follow that there is no qualification for rituals due to a lack of knowledge? This is not a fault; for...

We do not deny that the understanding of ritual action resulting from Vedic study is a cause for qualification [for rites]; rather, we establish this: that the knowledge of the Self derived from the Upaniṣads, being perceived as having its own independent purpose, does not serve as a cause for qualification for ritual action.
And just as the knowledge of one sacrifice is not required for qualification for another sacrifice, so too should this be understood.
As for what was also stated, "And because of the restriction," it is replied here: No, because there is no distinction.

In such scriptural injunctions as "One should desire to live performing works here," there is no distinction made that they apply only to the knower, because the rule is prescribed without qualification.
Or it may be for the sake of praise, or it may be an approval.
In the passage beginning "performing actions here," another distinction is stated.

Although, by the force of the context, the word "performing" should be connected only with "the knower," nevertheless, this permission for action must be seen as intended for the purpose of praising knowledge;
for it will later state, "action does not cling to the man."

This is what is meant: even while performing actions throughout his entire life, no action adheres to you, the wise person, because of the power of knowledge; thus, in this way, knowledge is being praised.
And some [hold that it occurs] by one's own will.

Moreover, certain wise men, having directly realized the fruit of knowledge, reflect—by virtue of that realization—that there is no further purpose in offspring and other means for attaining other fruits, acting according to their own will; as the Śruti of the Vājasaneyins states: "Indeed, the ancient wise men did not desire offspring, thinking, 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world?
And we have stated more than once that the fruit of knowledge is established in immediate experience, and does not belong to a future time like the fruit of ritual action.

For this reason as well, it is impossible to maintain either that knowledge is a subordinate part of ritual action, or that the scriptural declarations of fruit concerning its subject matter are not true to fact.
And suppression.

Moreover, they teach that through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), there occurs the destruction of the essential nature of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—characterized by action, agent, and fruit—which is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), as in such passages as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he smell? For one who hopes for the establishment of eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) based on the knowledge of the Self taught in the Vedānta, the very subversion of that eligibility for action would result.
Therefore, knowledge possesses independence.
And [the rule applies] to those who have drawn up their vital seed, for there is a scriptural statement to that effect.
Now begins the third chapter.
Knowledge is heard of even in the stages of life (āśramas) characterized by perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas),
and in those cases, it is not possible for knowledge to be subordinate to ritual action, because of the absence of such action.

For those [ascetics] do not possess Vedic rituals such as the Agnihotra and so forth.
