It might be argued that the stages of life (āśramas) for those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) are not heard of in the Veda; but even that is not the case, for they too are understood from Vedic texts, such as: "There are three branches of dharma," "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," "Those who dwell in the forest with austerity and faith," "Desiring this world alone, wandering mendicants go forth," and "One should go forth from the state of studenthood (brahmacarya)"—and so on.

The state of being an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose vital energy is drawn upward) is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti for those householders who have either entered or not yet entered [the stage of renunciation], and who have either discharged or not yet discharged their three debts;
therefore, knowledge is independent [of the stages of life].
Jaimini [holds that] it is mere mental reflection, for there is no injunction [to that effect], and scripture indeed prohibits it.

As for those words such as "the three groups of dharma" which have been cited to establish the existence of the stages of life (*āśrama*) for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), they are not capable of establishing them,
because Master Jaimini considers that in these words there is a reference (*parāmarśa*) to other stages of life, not an injunction (*vidhi*).
Why? Because there is no word of injunction (*codanā*) here, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) or others;
moreover, each of these is observed to have a different purpose.

Regarding the passage, "There are three branches of duty," it first refers to the stages of life (*āśrama*)—beginning with the statement, "Sacrifice, study, and charity constitute the first; austerity alone is the second; and the third is the student who dwells in the teacher's house for his entire life, exhausting himself there"—and having thus proclaimed that these stages have non-final results, it then praises being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) as having the final result in the words, "One who is established in Brahman attains immortality.
Now, one might object: even in this reference, the stages of life are indeed understood. True, they are understood.
The establishment of these [orders] is through tradition and custom, not through direct Vedic revelation;
therefore, when there is a contradiction with direct Vedic revelation, they will either be disregarded or will concern those who are not qualified [for them].
But is it not the case that even the householder’s life is mentioned together with those of perpetual chastity, as in: "Sacrifice, study, and giving—this is the first"? True, this is so.
Nevertheless, since the rites such as the *agnihotra* are prescribed specifically for the householder, their existence is indeed well-established by the Śruti;

therefore, this reference is solely for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), not for the purpose of an injunction (*codanā*). Moreover, direct Śruti passages explicitly deprecate the other stages of life (*āśrama*), such as: "He who lets the sacred fire go out is a slayer of the heroes of the gods"; "Having brought dear wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny"; and "There is no world for one who has no son—all animals know this," and so forth.

Likewise, the passages "And those who in the forest worship with faith, [saying] 'Austerity'" and "Those who dwell in the forest, practicing austerity and faith," are instructions regarding the path of the gods (*devayāna*), not instructions regarding other stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, the mention of other stages of life in such texts as "Austerity alone is the second" is ambiguous.
Thus ends the third chapter.
"The world-seekers go forth as wanderers"—this is merely praise of the world, not an injunction for the life of wandering.
But is it not the case that "one should go forth from the stage of studentship itself" is a clear and direct injunction for the life of wandering found among the Jābālas? True, this is so;
however, it should be understood that this present inquiry is conducted without taking that scriptural passage into account.
Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that it] is to be performed, because of its equality.

The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that another stage of life (āśrama) must be practiced. He rejects the view that—because it is not heard of in the Veda and because rites such as the Agnihotra must necessarily be performed—a different stage of life is to be practiced only by those who are ineligible for those rites; rather, he considers that just like the householder's stage, the other stages of life must also be entered even by one who has no desire for them.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement of equality;
for a scriptural reference to the other stages of life is seen to be equal to that of the householder's stage, in passages such as, "There are three branches of duty," and so forth.

Just as the householder’s stage of life (*gārhasthya*), which is enjoined in another Vedic text, is here referred to, so too must it be understood that the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are likewise referred to. And just as in a passage whose purpose is to enjoin the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), there is a reference to the *nivīta* and *prācīnāvīta* postures already established by other scriptures;
therefore, the status of being something to be practiced is equal for the other stages of life as it is for the householder’s stage.
Likewise, there is the co-mention [of renunciation] with the study of the Vedas and so forth in the passage: "Desiring this world alone, mendicants go forth into homelessness."
And [the phrase] "those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" is connected with the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
As for what was stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya— that the mention of another stage of life (*āśrama*) in passages such as "austerity alone is the second," etc., is ambiguous—
this is not a fault, because there exists a basis for certainty.
For it has been asserted that "there are three divisions of dharma" (*dharmaskandha*);
and since numerous other duties such as sacrifices (*yajña*) exist with distinct origins, they cannot be included within the number three except by their connection to the stages of life (*āśrama*).

In this context, the householder's stage, characterized by sacrifices and so forth, is indicated as one division of dharma; the term "student" (*brahmacārī*) is a clear designation of a stage of life; and as for "austerity" (*tapas*), what other division of dharma could be accepted than the stage of life in which austerity is predominant?
And because of the indicative mark of the "forest" (araṇya) in the passage, "And those who in the forest," the stages of life are understood through faith and austerity;
therefore, even though they are mentioned [in the context of the other stages], the other stage of life must also be practiced.
Or rather, it is an injunction, like the rule regarding the holding [of the sacrificial ladle].
This is indeed an injunction regarding another stage of life (āśrama), not a mere reference (parāmarśa). [Objection:

But if it is accepted as an injunction, the perception of syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) would be obstructed; yet here syntactical unity is indeed perceived: "The three branches of dharma have the worlds of merit as their fruit, but being established in Brahman has immortality as its fruit. [Reply: This is true.

However, even though there is the perception of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), one must rather accept that this is an injunction (*vidhi*), because it conveys something not previously known (*apūrvatva*), because no other injunction is observed, and because it is impossible to construe it as a single sentence by assuming it to be a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*) due to the clear cognition of a different stage of life (*āśrama*). This is like the case of "holding [the fuel-stick] below": in the passage, "He should run after holding the fuel-stick below; for he holds it above for the gods," although there is the perception of a single syntactical unity with the holding below, the holding above is indeed enjoined, because it conveys something not previously known.

And so it has been stated in the *Śeṣalakṣaṇa*: "But there is an injunction regarding the wearing [of the sacred thread], because it is something not previously established"; likewise here too, the scriptural text referring to the stages of life (*āśrama*) is to be understood as an injunction itself.

Even if this is merely a reference (*parāmarśa*) to the other stages of life (*āśrama*), nevertheless, "being grounded in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) must necessarily be accepted as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) by the force of that praise.
Furthermore, it must be determined whether this applies to anyone among the four stages of life, or only to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

If, while the stages of life beginning with studentship are being referred to, the wandering mendicant is also included therein, then—since there is no distinction in the fact that all four stages are being referred to, and since it is impossible for one to exist without belonging to a stage of life—it would follow that anyone among those in the four stages of life could be "grounded in Brahman."

If, however, he is not included [among those previously mentioned], then it will be established that the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) alone, being the one remaining [by elimination], is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*). Regarding this, some maintain that the wandering mendicant is also included by the word "austerity" (*tapas*), which refers to the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*).
That is incorrect; for...
For when another possibility exists, it is not appropriate to include the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) by means of the qualification "forest-dweller" (vānaprastha);

just as the student (brahmacārin) and the householder (gṛhamedhin) are each qualified by their own unique, specific attributes, so too should the mendicant (bhikṣu) and the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) be understood.

Furthermore, austerity (tapas) is the unique characteristic of forest-dwellers, since their practice primarily consists of bodily mortification, and the word "austerity" is conventionally established in that sense.
Furthermore, the duty of a monk, characterized by the restraint of the senses and so forth, would have to be designated by the word "austerity" only through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*).
Moreover, it is improper that the stages of life (*āśrama*), which are well-known to be four, should be referred to as three.
Furthermore, there is a declaration of distinction here: "These three partake of the worlds of merit; one partakes of immortality."
And the designation of difference is appropriate only when there is separateness;

for it does not happen that "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted, but one of these two is highly intelligent"; rather, it happens thus: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted, but Viṣṇumitra is highly intelligent."
Therefore, the first three stages of life (*āśramins*) partake of the worlds of merit, while the remaining one, the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), partakes of immortality.

But how can the term *brahmasaṃstha*—which, being applicable through its etymological connection (*yoga*), could potentially apply to all [stages]—be restricted to the wandering mendicant alone? Furthermore, if its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) were accepted, it would follow that immortality is attained merely by the stage of life itself, rendering knowledge useless. To this it is replied: the expression *brahmasaṃstha* indeed denotes completion in Brahman, which is to say, being established in that as a state of having no other activity.

And that [state] is not possible for the three other stages of life (*āśrama*), because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from the non-performance of the duties prescribed for one's own stage;

however, in the case of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), since all actions have been renounced, no transgression can arise on account of non-performance. Furthermore, his specific duties such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*) serve to strengthen the state of being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthā*), rather than contradicting it.
For his prescribed duty according to his own stage of life consists precisely in being devoted to Brahman, augmented by tranquility, self-control, and so forth;
whereas for others, it consists in sacrifices and the like.
And upon the transgression of that duty, there is sin for him.
And likewise, the Śrutis and Smṛtis such as "Renunciation is Brahman; for Brahman is supreme, and the supreme is indeed Brahman";

"These other austerities, O Sūta, renunciation alone excelled them" (Mahābhārata); and "The ascetics whose nature is purified through the yoga of renunciation, having well-ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of Vedānta" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad), as well as "Those whose intellect is fixed on That, whose self is That, who are established in That, and for whom That is the supreme goal" (Gītā)—all these demonstrate the absence of ritual action for one who is firmly established in Brahman.

Therefore, the objection that knowledge would become useless because one attains immortality merely by entering the stage of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) does not apply here either. Thus, even when considering the other stages of life, the state of being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is indeed obtained as the characteristic of the wandering mendicant.
It was with this in mind that the Teacher initiated this inquiry, without taking into account the *Jābāla* scripture which prescribes the other stages of life.

But there certainly exists a scriptural injunction for other stages of life (*āśrama*), which is directly perceived: "Having completed the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); having been a forest-dweller, one should go forth (*pravrajeta*).
Or otherwise, one may go forth from studentship itself, or from the home, or from the forest.

Nor can it be said that this scripture refers to those who are ineligible [for the Vedic path], because it is heard without distinction and because there is a separate injunction for those who are ineligible, beginning with: "Whether he be one who has taken vows or one who has not, whether he be a graduate (*snātaka*) or one who is not, whether his sacred fires have been extinguished or he is without fires," and so forth.

Furthermore, because the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) is an auxiliary factor for the maturation of the knowledge of Brahman, it does not have as its object those who are ineligible [for such knowledge]. This is shown by the text: "Now, the wandering mendicant, clothed in the ochre robe, shaven-headed, without possessions, pure, non-injurious, subsisting on alms, becomes one with Brahman. Therefore, the stages of life (*āśrama*) for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) are established;
and since they are prescribed for those of perpetual chastity, it is established that knowledge possesses independence.

If it be argued that in the commentary on the Sūtra [1.1.4] the passage is merely a eulogy because it is based on something already known, we say no, because it conveys what is not previously established.

"Of all essences, this is the essence, the highest, the supreme, the eighth, namely the *udgītha*"; "The *ṛc* is this [earth], the *sāman* is that [heaven]"; "This world indeed is this fire-altar, the *stoma* is its measure, and this very thing is the *uktha*; this earth is the foundation. Regarding such scriptural passages, there arises the doubt: do they serve the purpose of praising the *udgītha* and so forth, or do they enjoin meditations (*upāsana*)? It is more reasonable that they serve the purpose of praise, because they are heard in connection with the *udgītha* and other such auxiliary elements of ritual action.

If it is argued that these [passages] are like the statement, "This very *juhū* ladle is the sun, the tortoise is the heavenly world, the *āhavanīya* fire is [the sky]," which serves for the purpose of praising the *juhū* and so forth, we say: no.

For it is not appropriate that the mere purpose of these scriptural texts (*śruti*) should be praise; rather, because they convey something unprecedented (*apūrva*), when they serve the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), an unprecedented matter is enjoined.
If, however, they were intended for the purpose of praise (stuti), they would be entirely purposeless;

for it has been stated in the sūtra, "But because of their being part of a single sentence with the injunction, they serve as praise for the injunctions" (*vidhinā tvekavākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ*), that praise is useful only when it attains the status of a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) to an injunctive word.

But in this case, since the Udgītha and other elements are enjoined in one location while this praise is recited in another, this praise—failing to attain the status of a supplementary part to those injunctions—would indeed be useless.
"But passages such as 'This indeed is the juhū-ladle' are recorded only in proximity to an injunction; thus there is a difference [between them and other texts].
Therefore, scriptural statements of this kind have injunctions as their sole purpose."
This is the third chapter.
And because of words denoting states of being.
Furthermore, clearly expressed injunctive words are heard, such as "One should meditate on the Udgītha," "One should meditate on the Sāman," and "One should know: 'I am the hymn'";
and these would be contradicted if their purpose were merely for the sake of praise.

Accordingly, there is the traditional teaching of those who know the system of logic: "One should do (kuryāt), it should be done (kriyeta), it is to be done (kartavyam), it will be (bhavet), and 'it may be' (syāt) as the fifth."

"This would be the fixed characteristic of injunction (*vidhi*) in all the Vedas"; for those who consider that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is injunction remember this. Furthermore, in each respective section (*prakaraṇa*), results are proclaimed: "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of desires," "For he alone rules over the attainment of desires," "The worlds above and below are prepared for him," and so on.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the scriptural passages concerning the *udgītha* and so forth are intended to enjoin meditative worship (*upāsana*).
If it is argued that they are for the sake of protection, we say no, because of the specific qualification.

Now, there arises a doubt regarding those narratives recited in the Vedānta texts, such as: "Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī"; "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, went to the beloved abode of Indra"; and "Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, a liberal giver of faith, was a great donor and a provider of much food. Are these intended for use in the *pāriplava* (the ritual circumambulation), or rather for the purpose of introducing the proximate meditations (*vidyā*)?

[Objection: These scriptural narratives (*ākhyāna-śruti*) serve the purpose of the *pāriplava* [recitation], because they are common to all narratives, and because the performance of narrative recitation is enjoined in the *pāriplava*;

consequently, the Vedāntas would not have knowledge (*vidyā*) as their primary subject matter, since—like mantras—they would be subordinate to ritual performance. [Reply: This is not so. Why? Because of the specification (*viśeṣitatvāt*). For, having introduced the topic with "He should recount the *pāriplava*," certain specific narratives such as "Manu Vaivasvata was king" and so forth are specified therein.
If, on account of the commonality of being "narratives" (ākhyāna), there were to be a grasping of all [narratives], then this qualification would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, these scriptural mentions of narratives are not for the sake of the Pāriplava ceremony.
And likewise, because they are connected as a single syntactical unit.

And since the narratives do not serve the purpose of mere diversion, it is logical that they should serve the purpose of elucidating the proximate meditations (vidyās), because they are connected as parts of a single syntactical whole.

For in various instances, a connection with the proximate meditations is observed, both for the sake of generating interest and for the sake of facilitating comprehension. In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, for instance, a connection with the meditation beginning "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" is observed; and in the Prātardana-vidyā as well, a connection is seen with the meditation beginning "I am Prāṇa, the conscious Self."

In the case of the passage "Jānaśruti," as in the case of "Vāyu is indeed the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1) and so forth, just as the narratives found within the ritual scriptures—such as "He cut out his own omentum"—serve the purpose of praising the proximate injunctions, so it is here as well.
Therefore, they do not have the purpose of being mere incidental stories (pāriplava).
Thus ends the third chapter.
And for this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of fire and so forth.

The phrase "The human goal [arises] from this, on account of scripture" (Puruṣārtho'taḥ śabdāt), although separated by distance, is referred to by the word "from this" (ataḥ) because it is possible; it is for the sake of fueling the fire.
And for this very reason, there is this section (adhikaraṇa).

Since knowledge is the cause of the human goal, the duties of the stages of life (āśramakarmāṇi), such as fueling the fire and so forth, need not be depended upon for the accomplishment of its own purpose. Thus, with the intention of saying more, he concludes the result of the very first section.
And there is a dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse-sacrifice.
The instrument [of knowledge] has been established.
Now this is considered: Is there an absolute lack of dependence on the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) for knowledge, or is there some dependence?
In this regard, it is concluded that the duties of the stages of life, such as kindling the sacred fires and so forth, are not required by knowledge for the accomplishment of its own purpose.
When it might thus follow that there is absolute disregard [for ritual action], this is said: "and [knowledge] requires all.
Knowledge requires all the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*); it is not entirely independent of them.
But is this statement not contradictory—to say that knowledge requires the duties of the stages of life, and yet does not require them?
We say: no;
for once knowledge has arisen, it requires nothing else for the accomplishment of its fruit, but it does require something for its own arising.
Why? Because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth.

For thus the Śruti says: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," thereby showing that sacrifice and the rest are means for knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, because of their connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), they are determined to be means for its origination. And in the passage, "Now, what people call sacrifice is really just celibacy (*brahmacarya*)," since celibacy—which is a means for knowledge—is praised along with sacrifice and the rest, the status of sacrifice and the others as means is likewise indicated in the Sūtra.

The Śruti passage beginning with, "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim, and which all austerities declare; desiring which they lead a life of celibacy—that goal I tell you briefly," indicates that the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi) are means for attaining knowledge (vidyā-sādhana). Smṛti also states: "Ritual actions serve to cook away the impurities (kaṣāya-pakti), but knowledge is the supreme goal."
"When the impurity has been cooked away by actions, knowledge then arises"—such passages as these [are relevant].

The phrase "like a horse" is an illustration of fitness (*yogyatā*); just as a horse is not employed for pulling a plough due to its specific fitness, but is employed for the movement of a chariot, so too the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*) are not required for the accomplishment of the fruit through knowledge, yet they are required for its origination.
Even if one were endowed with tranquility, self-control, and other such qualities, nevertheless, because they are auxiliary parts of that [knowledge], they must necessarily be practiced.

If someone should think that it is not logical for sacrifices and the like to be means for the attainment of knowledge because there is no injunction—on the grounds that scriptural passages such as "They desire to know through sacrifice" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) are merely explanatory restatements (anuvāda) intended to praise knowledge, and do not intend to enjoin sacrifices and so forth, meaning "Knowledge is so highly esteemed that people desire to attain it through sacrifices"—nevertheless, one who seeks knowledge should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and other virtues. Therefore... [Third Chapter]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

"Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, he beholds the Self in the very Self"—since this passage enjoins tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth as means for knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*), and because what is enjoined must necessarily be performed.

Now, one might object: "Even here, the expression 'having become endowed with tranquility and so forth, he beholds' is found as a statement in the present tense (*vartamānāpadeśa*); it is not an injunction. To this we reply: No, because the injunctive nature is understood from the inclusion of the praise of the subject under discussion by the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*);
furthermore, the Mādhyandinas clearly read the injunction itself as "he should behold" (*paśyet*).
Therefore, even when there is no requirement for sacrifices and the like, tranquility (śama) and other qualities must be required;
however, sacrifices and the like must also be required, precisely because of the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifices and so forth.
Now, it was argued that in the passage "they desire to know through sacrifices and the like," no injunction is perceived; this is true.
Nevertheless, because this connection is something not previously established (*apūrva*), it is construed as an injunction (*vidhi*);
for this connection of sacrifices and so forth with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) was not previously obtained, such that it could be merely restated (*anūdyeta*).

Furthermore, even in sentences where no injunction is explicitly heard—such as "Therefore Pūṣan has a portion of ground flour, for he is toothless"—an injunction is construed on account of its being *apūrva*, and an investigation was initiated in the first section of the Mīmāṃsā system (the *Tantra*) beginning with: "The grinding for Pūṣan should be understood as applying to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)."
And thus it has been said: "Or [it is] an injunction, like the wearing [of the sacred thread].

Even in the Smṛtis, such as the Bhagavadgītā and others, it is explained in detail that sacrifices and other rites performed by one seeking liberation without aiming for their fruits become means for the attainment of knowledge.

Therefore, all the duties of the stages of life (āśramakarma), including sacrifices and so forth, as well as tranquility, self-restraint, and the rest, according to each respective stage, must be relied upon for the arising of knowledge.

In that regard as well, because of the connection with knowledge in the phrase "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvit*), tranquility (*śama*) and the other means of knowledge are proximate; however, because of their connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), sacrifices and the like are more external—this distinction must be made.
And there is permission to eat all food in the event of danger to life, for that is so seen in scripture.

In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is heard among the Chandogas: "Indeed, for one who knows thus, there is nothing whatsoever that is not food. Likewise, among the Vājasaneyins: "Indeed, by the permission of all food, nothing that is eaten becomes uneaten, nor does anything taken as food become uneaten."
The meaning is that everything becomes fit to be eaten by him.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this permission to eat all food is enjoined as a limb of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) like tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, or is mentioned merely for the sake of praise (*stuti*), the initial position is that it is an injunction;
for in that way, the instruction serves to produce a specific inclination toward action.
Therefore, because of the proximity of the knowledge of the vital breaths (*prāṇavidyā*), this cessation of restraint is taught as being subordinate to that [knowledge].

But if this were so, would there not be a contradiction with the scripture that distinguishes between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit? This is not a fault, because sublation is logically established through the relationship of the general and the particular.

Just as the prohibition against injuring living beings is set aside by the injunction for the ritual slaughter of animals, and just as the general scriptural rule distinguishing between permissible and impermissible women is set aside by the statement "one should not avoid any woman" found in the context of the Vāmadevya-vidyā, so too might the scriptural rule distinguishing between edible and inedible food be set aside by this statement regarding the consumption of all food within the context of the Prāṇa-vidyā. To this we reply: this is not an injunction permitting the consumption of all food. *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, Third Chapter, Section 14.1–6: "Then, when he is about to eat, let him make an offering with the first morsel, saying: 'To Prāṇa, svāhā! Let him make an offering with the second morsel, saying: 'To Apāna, svāhā! Let him make an offering with the third morsel, saying: 'To Vyāna, svāhā! Let him make an offering with the fourth morsel, saying: 'To Udāna, svāhā! Let him make an offering with the fifth morsel, saying: 'To Samāna, svāhā! He indeed offers the sacrifice to these [breaths] alone, and they become satisfied. When they are satisfied, the organs (prāṇas) become satisfied; when the organs are satisfied, the vital breaths (prāṇas) become satisfied; when the vital breaths are satisfied, the self becomes satisfied; when the self is satisfied, the organ of sight becomes satisfied; when the organ of sight is satisfied, the sun becomes satisfied; when the sun is satisfied, heaven becomes satisfied; when heaven is satisfied, whatever is under heaven becomes satisfied. Through that satisfaction, one becomes satisfied; one's offspring becomes satisfied; one's cattle become satisfied; one's Brahman-study becomes satisfied; one's merit becomes satisfied; and through the satisfaction of that merit, the whole world becomes satisfied. Whatever he eats from then on, he eats as an oblation; whatever he drinks, he drinks as an oblation; whatever he chews, he chews as an oblation. He indeed becomes a sacrificer of the five fires. [The Sūtra continues: "But there is no such permission, because of the non-abrogation of the scriptures concerning what is to be eaten and what is not to be eaten. (3.4.28) This means: this is not an injunction permitting the eating of all food. Why? Because there is no abrogation of the scriptures that distinguish between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten. Just as the general rule regarding the avoidance of certain women is not set aside by the specific statement in the Vāmadevya-vidyā, but rather applies to other contexts, so too the rule regarding the division of edible and inedible food remains authoritative even in the presence of this passage on the Prāṇa-vidyā. Furthermore, the text itself indicates a limitation: "Whatever he eats from then on, he eats as an oblation"—this shows that the permission is restricted to food consumed during the performance of the sacrifice to the five fires, and does not extend to ordinary daily life. Therefore, the scriptural rules concerning what is edible and inedible are not sublated. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

For no injunctive word is perceived here, because the statement "Indeed, for one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever remains uneaten" is a mere description of an existing state (*vartamānāpadeśa*). Nor can an injunction be assumed merely out of a desire for it to produce a particular activity, even in the absence of the perception of an injunction.
Furthermore, having stated that everything down to dogs constitutes food for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is said: "for one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever remains uneaten."
Furthermore, food as far as dogs and other such creatures cannot be consumed by means of a human body;

however, it is possible to contemplate that "all this is food for the vital breaths" (prāṇas). Therefore, this explanatory passage (arthavāda) is intended to praise the knowledge of the vital breaths as food, and is not an injunction permitting the consumption of all kinds of food.
He shows this with the words: "And all [is permitted], except for what is forbidden, in a life-threatening emergency.
This is what is meant: only in a life-threatening emergency—that is, in the most extreme adversity—is all food permitted as something to be eaten, because that is what is seen in scripture.

For instance, the Śruti shows the sage Cākrāyaṇa engaging in the eating of what is not to be eaten when he was in a state of distress, in the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning, "When the Kurus were destroyed by hailstones": it is said that the sage Cākrāyaṇa, having fallen into calamity, ate half-chewed kulmāṣa beans from an elephant-driver.
He, however, refused the accompanying drink on the grounds that it was leftover from his meal,
and gave the reason for this, saying, "I would not have lived if I had not eaten these," and "Water is my desire.
Furthermore, on the following day, he ate those very same kulmāṣas, which were stale and leftover from both himself and others.

This very fact—that the consumption of leavings, food left over from others, and stale food is permitted—reveals the profound intention of the Śruti as seen in the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*: that in the event of a life-threatening emergency, even what is normally unfit to be eaten may be consumed for the sake of sustaining life;
however, in a state of health, this must not be done even by one possessed of knowledge, as is understood from the rejection of the accompanying drink.
Therefore, the passage beginning with "For indeed, for one who knows thus... is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
And because there is no contradiction.
And this being so, the scriptural injunctions concerning the distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten—such as "When food is pure, the mind becomes pure"—will remain uncontradicted.
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti:

Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛtis that even the eating of all kinds of food is permitted for both the learned and the unlearned alike in times of distress: "One who has fallen into a life-threatening situation and eats food from any source whatsoever is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. Likewise, the avoidance of non-food is recorded: "A Brāhmaṇa [should avoid] liquor constantly," and "For a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, [the gods] should pour hot [liquor] upon him because of his eating what is unfit to be eaten," and "Those who drink liquor become worms. Thus, the avoidance of forbidden food is enjoined.
And from this very reason, there is the scriptural statement regarding the non-performance of what one desires.

Furthermore, in the *Kaṭha Saṃhitā*, there is heard a scriptural statement prohibiting the eating of meat and having its purpose being the cessation of acting according to one's own desires: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not drink liquor.
This [prohibition] also becomes consistent because the passage "Indeed, for one who knows thus... is an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or corroborative statement).
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, explanatory passages (arthavādas) of this kind are not injunctions (vidhis).
And because it is prescribed, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed.
In the sūtra "And there is dependence on all," it was established that the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karmāṇi) are means for the attainment of knowledge (vidyā-sādhana).

Now, however, it is considered whether these duties must be performed even by one who does not desire liberation, who is intent merely upon his stage of life, and who does not desire knowledge—or whether they need not be. This is the topic of the present section.

In this regard, since the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) have been prescribed as means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*) by such passages as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas," it follows that for one who does not desire knowledge but desires some other fruit, the obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) are not to be performed. Alternatively, if they are indeed to be performed even by him, then they cannot be means for attaining knowledge, because of the contradiction between the connection with what is obligatory and what is non-obligatory. To this prima facie view, the author replies: the obligatory rites must certainly be performed even by one who abides merely in his stage of life and does not seek liberation, because they are enjoined by such texts as, "As long as one lives, one should offer the Agnihotra."
For there is indeed no such thing as an excessive burden for a statement.
Now, as for what was said—that if this were so, these [rites] could not be means for the attainment of knowledge—the author reads the following reply: "And by being auxiliaries. (Sūtra 3.4.15)
And these [works] are auxiliaries to knowledge precisely because they are enjoined by such passages as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacana*).
As it has been stated in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*: "There is a requirement for all [works], on account of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse.

Nor should this statement regarding the auxiliary nature of works to knowledge be understood as referring to the fruit of knowledge—like the *prayāja* offerings and the like—with respect to the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*), because knowledge is not characterized by an injunction and because the fruit of knowledge is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*).
For a means characterized by injunction, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, requires another auxiliary means due to the desire to accomplish the fruit of heaven; knowledge is not like this.
Thus it has been said: "And for this very reason, there is no dependence on the Ānandamaya and so forth.
Therefore, the expression regarding their being "auxiliaries" applies only to their being means for the origination [of knowledge].

Nor should one suspect here a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the permanent and the impermanent, because even though the action is the same, the conjunctions are different. For one conjunction is permanent, established by such scriptural injunctions as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), and that does not have knowledge (*vidyā*) as its fruit; but another conjunction is impermanent, established by such scriptural injunctions as "him [one approaches] through the recitation of the Vedas" (*tametam vedānuvacanena*), and that has knowledge as its fruit. Just as for the single quality of being made of *khadira* wood, there is a connection with the ritual (*kratvarthatva*) due to a permanent conjunction, while there is a connection with human purpose (*puruṣārthatva*) due to an impermanent conjunction, so it is here.
In every way, they alone [are the subject], because of the dual characteristic.

In every respect—both in the view that they are duties belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) and in the view that they are auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā-sahakāritva*)—those very same duties such as the *agnihotra* and others are to be performed.
By using the restrictive phrase "those very same," what does the Teacher exclude? We say: he excludes the suspicion that there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karma-bheda*).

The meaning is that, unlike in the case of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice where the statement "they offer the *agnihotra* for a month" teaches a different act from the obligatory (*nitya*) *agnihotra*, no such difference in the ritual act exists here.
MAKsū, Third Chapter. Why [is this so]? Because of the marks of both: from the mark of Śruti and from the mark of Smṛti.

First, regarding the mark of Śruti: the text, "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas," enjoins sacrifices and other rites—which already exist in a completed form—for the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); it does not, however, produce their form as something previously non-existent (*apūrva*), as is the case with the injunction "they offer oblations" (*juhvati*).

The indicative mark of Smṛti as well—namely, "He who performs the required action without depending on the fruit of action"—shows that it is precisely action whose duty is already known that serves for the arising of knowledge.

Furthermore, the well-known status of Vedic rites as "purifications" (saṃskāra), expressed in such passages as "For whom these forty-eight purifications [exist]," occurs in Smṛti with the intention that knowledge arises for one who has been purified by them.
Therefore, this determination of non-difference is correct.
And he demonstrates non-overpowering.
This observation of indicative marks (liṅga) serves as a corroborator for the very fact of [the works'] being cooperative factors.

Furthermore, the Śruti demonstrates their non-overpowering nature in the case of one who is endowed with the means such as celibacy (brahmacarya), stating: "For this Self does not perish, which one finds through celibacy," and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that sacrifices and other duties belonging to the stages of life (āśrama-karma) are indeed cooperative factors for knowledge.
But even in the interval, because that is seen.

A doubt arises as to whether those such as Vidhura—who are destitute of the wealth required for the various stages of life (*āśrama*) and who stand between them, having failed to enter any particular stage—are qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*), or whether they are not. On this point, the initial position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that they are not qualified; for it has been determined that the duties of the stages of life are the cause of knowledge, and these individuals are incapable of performing the duties of the stages of life. To this, the following is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "But even one who stands in the interval," that is, even one who exists as a non-ascetic (*anāśramin*), is qualified for knowledge.
Why? Because we observe from scripture that even such persons as Raikva, Vācaknavī, and others were knowers of Brahman despite having such [defects].
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti.

In the Itihāsas, it is recorded that even for those such as Māhapā and Saṃvarta, who disregarded the duties of their respective stages of life (āśrama) through practices such as naked asceticism, the status of great yogis (mahāyogitva) is remembered.

Now, it may be objected that this indicative mark consisting of the observation of Śruti and Smṛti has been presented; what then is the prima facie argument? That is now stated: "And there is the favoring of the specific."

Furthermore, even for those such as Vidura and others who were unable to perform the duties of the stages of life, the favoring of knowledge is possible through specific dharmas—such as recitation (japa), fasting, and the propitiation of deities—which are not contradictory [to their status] and are common to all human beings.
Accordingly, the Smṛti states: "A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.

Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa. This shows that eligibility for recitation exists even for one who cannot perform the duties of the [specific] stages of life.

Furthermore, even through the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) performed in other births, there certainly occurs a favor toward knowledge; for thus the Smṛti says, "Perfected through many births, he thereafter attains the supreme goal," which shows that specific purificatory impressions (saṃskāra-viśeṣa) accumulated in other births are also benefactors toward knowledge.
Furthermore, knowledge that has a visible result qualifies a seeker for hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices even by the mere absence of prohibitions;
therefore, the eligibility of widowers and others is not contradicted.
Therefore, however, the other is superior, also because of an indicative mark.

Therefore, because it occupies an intermediate position, the other state of life (the householder's stage) is a superior means for the attainment of knowledge, as it is firmly established by both Śruti and Smṛti;

and from the indicative mark of the Śruti: "By this [path] goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of meritorious deeds, and the man of light"; and: "A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an āśrama."
And because of the indicative mark in the Smṛti: "Having remained for a year without belonging to any stage of life (āśrama), one should perform one Kṛcchra penance."
But for one who has become that [liberated], there is no becoming otherwise, even according to Jaimini, because of the restrictive rule, the absence of such a nature, and the absence of that form.
It has been established that there are stages of life (*āśrama*) for those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*).
However, a doubt arises as to whether there is a falling away from those stages once they have been attained, or not.
This discussion [is undertaken] because, previously, one might desire to perform duties belonging to a former stage, or due to the influence of passion and other such factors.

Or perhaps he might fall away from it because there is no specific distinction [between the stages]. This being the position reached, it is said in reply: For one who has become that—that is, for one who has attained the state of an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose vital energy is drawn upward)—there can never be a non-becoming of that state; he cannot fall away from it. Why? Because of the restrictive rules (*niyama*), the absence of such a form [in the other stages], and [the scriptural] indications. For instance: "Wearing himself out completely in the family of the teacher," "He should go to the forest; from that place he should not return—this is the secret teaching (*upaniṣad*"); and "Permitted by the teacher, [he should enter] one of the four stages of life."
Furthermore, a rule of this kind—“He should practice according to the injunction until the liberation of the body”—shows that there is no falling away.

Moreover, while we find statements of the nature of an ascent, such as “Having completed the student life, one should become a householder” and “One may renounce even from the student life,” we do not find any such statements regarding a descent.
Nor are there any cultured people (śiṣṭas) who follow such a practice.

As for the claim that there is a "descent" (to a lower stage) out of a desire to perform the duties of a previous [status], that is incorrect; for it is remembered in the Smṛti: "One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed," and because of logical reasoning as well. For that which is enjoined for someone is his duty, and not that which can merely be performed by him; this is because duty is defined by scriptural injunction (*codanā*).
Nor does a fall from one's status occur through the force of passion and the like, because the scripture of restrictive rules (*niyama-śāstra*) is more powerful.

Regarding the phrase "of Jaimini also," the word "also" (api) teaches that there is agreement between Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa on this point; for it is not the case that [the sin] belongs to one holding an office, because of the inference of falling [from grace] due to the connection with that [office].

If a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*) should, through negligence, break his vow of chastity, should the penance prescribed in the text—"An unchaste student who has broken his vow shall sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti"—apply to him, or not?
It is said: it does not apply.

Furthermore, as for the expiation determined in the section concerning eligibility (*adhikāralakṣaṇa*)—namely, "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow (*kīrṇi*), like that [other penance], because the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived"—that too cannot apply to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). What is the reason? "But he who, having ascended to the duty of a lifelong student, falls away again..."

"I see no expiation by which that self-killer might be purified," because of this traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding a downfall that cannot be remedied; for just as a remedy is impossible for one whose head has been severed, so too is it here.
However, in the case of the student (upakurvāṇa), such an expiation is possible, since there is no traditional teaching of a downfall of that nature for him.
However, some maintain that even when preceded by the prefix *upa*, it denotes a state of being (*bhāva*), just like the word for "eating" (*aśana*); this has already been explained.

However, some teachers consider this to be merely a minor offense (*upapātaka*); namely, that if the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) should fail in his vow of celibacy with anyone other than the wife of his teacher and so forth, that does not constitute a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), because it is not enumerated among the mortal sins such as violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*).

Therefore, they maintain that just like the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*), the lifelong student also has a penance, since there is no difference in their status as celibates and no difference in their having broken their vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*).

It is like the case of eating food: just as for a religious student (*brahmacārin*), the consumption of honey or meat constitutes a breach of his vow (*vratalopa*) and requires a rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*), so it is here.

For those who maintain that there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*), no scriptural basis (*mūla*) is found; whereas for those who maintain that there is expiation, the basis is the unqualified scriptural statement in the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* [of Śaṅkara]: "And the one who has broken his vow of chastity (*cāryavakīrṇī*)."
Therefore, existence is more logical;
as it was stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "There would be an unequal conflict of views, or rather [the view] established by the scriptures [prevails], because that is the cause.
Furthermore, the traditional teaching regarding the absence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be explained as being intended to produce a sense of great effort [toward avoiding such acts].

In the same way, for the mendicant (bhikṣu) and the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) as well, one should follow the traditional legal codes (smṛti) regarding penance, such as: "A forest-dweller, upon a breach of initiation, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, should increase the great thicket [of his hair and beard]," and "A mendicant, like a forest-dweller, except for the growth of the Soma-plant, shall undergo the purificatory rites prescribed by his own scripture," and so forth.
But outside [the village], it is in both ways, according to Smṛti and established custom.

Whether the falling away from their own stages of life by those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) constitutes a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or a minor offense (*upapātaka*), in either case they must be excluded by the learned. As it is said: "For one who has ascended to the duty of a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and then falls away again, I see no expiation by which that person might purify his soul. And: "A Brahmin who has fallen from his vows and been cast out from the assembly..."

And from such Smṛti texts expressing extreme condemnation as, "Having touched one who has cut his nails, one who has eaten garlic, one who is afflicted by a disease, one who is bound, one who is swollen with dropsy, one who is afflicted by worms, or one who has been bitten by a worm, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance," and from the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas)—for the learned do not perform sacrifices, Vedic study, marriage, and so forth together with them.
Ātreya [maintains] that the fruit belongs to the master, because of the scriptural declaration of the fruit.
Regarding the meditations on the constituent parts [of the sacrifice], there arises a doubt: are they the duties of the sacrificer, or are they the duties of the officiating priests?
What, then, is the initial position? They are the duties of the sacrificer, because he is the master.
Why? Because of the mention of a fruit;
"fruit" refers to the section [of the text].
It is heard [in scripture]: "It rains for him, and he causes it to rain, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the rain," and so forth.

And it is logical that this [result] should accrue to the master (svāmin), because he is the one authorized for the performance of the rite along with its constituent parts, and because such a category of action involves the authority of the authorized person;
moreover, the fruit of meditations is heard in scripture as belonging to the agent, in passages such as, "It rains for him who meditates upon it.

But is it not seen that the fruit also belongs to the officiating priest (ṛtvij), as in, "Whatever desire he may have, either for himself or for the sacrificer, that he brings about by singing"?—No, because that is based on a specific scriptural statement (vācanika).
Therefore, the teacher Ātreya maintains that the master alone possesses the status of agent in those meditations that yield results.
"Auḍulomi says it is the office of the officiating priest (ārtvijya), for that is what is hired for."
This is not so—that these meditations are the duties of the patron (svāmin);
rather, these must be the duties of the officiating priests (ṛtvij), according to the teacher Auḍulomi.
For what reason? Because the officiating priest is hired by the patron for that ritual action together with its constituent parts (sāṅga).
Furthermore, the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth fall within the conclusion of those ritual applications, because they are subordinate to the qualified person [the officiant].
Therefore, like the rule regarding the *godohana* vessel, they must be performed by the officiants (*ṛtvij*).
Accordingly, the text "Baka Dālbhya knew this; he became the *udgātṛ* priest for the residents of Naimiṣa" shows that the knowledge has the *udgātṛ* as its agent.

As for the statement that "the fruit is heard to reside in the agent," this is not a fault; because the officiating priests (ṛtvij) exist for the sake of another, and since there is no scriptural statement to the contrary, it is impossible for them to have a connection with the fruit.
And because of scripture.

"Whatever blessing the officiating priests (ṛtvij) invoke during the sacrifice, they invoke it for the sake of the sacrificer (yajamāna)"—thus he said. Furthermore, by stating, "Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows thus should say: 'What desire shall I sing forth for you? [the text] shows that the fruit of the knowledge performed by the officiating priests accrues to the sacrificer.
Therefore, it is established that the meditations on the subordinate members (aṅga-upāsanā) are the work of the officiating priests.
The injunction of another auxiliary occurs in the third [chapter], by way of an alternative, just like the beginning of an injunction.

"Therefore, a Brahmin, having discarded scholarship, should remain as one possessed of childlike innocence; and having discarded both childlike innocence and scholarship, he becomes a sage; and having discarded both non-sagehood and sagehood, he becomes a Brahmin who has completed his task. Thus it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. In this regard, there arises the doubt: is sagehood (*mauna*) enjoined here, or not? The initial position is that it is not enjoined, because it is merely mentioned as an instrument alongside "childlike innocence" (*bālya*).

Because the injunction is concluded right here with the words "he should remain [a silent sage]," and because no injunctive suffix is perceived in the phrase "then he is a silent sage" (*atha muniḥ*), this is therefore a restatement (*anuvāda*). Thus ends the third chapter.
It is appropriate.

If it is asked why this conclusion is reached, it is because the words *muni* and *paṇḍita* both signify knowledge; therefore, silence (*mauna*) is already implied by the phrase "having become proficient" (*pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*).
Furthermore, in the passage "Having become proficient in both non-silence and silence, one is then a Brāhmaṇa," Brāhmaṇahood itself is not being enjoined, as it has already been attained previously.

Therefore, just as the statement "Now, a Brāhmaṇa" is a commendatory declaration (praśaṃsāvāda), so too must the statement "Now, a sage (muni)" be understood; for the reference is identical. This being the position reached, we reply: it is an injunction of another auxiliary means (sahakāryantara-vidhi).

An injunction must indeed be accepted for *mauna* (sagehood) as an auxiliary to knowledge, just as there are injunctions for *bālya* (childlike behavior) and *pāṇḍitya* (scholarship), because it is something not previously established (*apūrvatvāt*).

[Objection: But has it not already been stated that silence (*mauna*) is understood by the very word "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*)? [Reply: This is not a fault, because the word *muni* signifies an excellence of knowledge, and because the etymological derivation "a *muni* is so called because of reflection" (*mananāt muniḥ*) is possible, and because we observe its usage in such passages as "Of munis too, I am Vyāsa.

[Objection: But the word *muni* is also heard used to denote the highest stage of life (*uttamāśrama*), as in the passage "The householder's state, the teacher's family, silence (*mauna*), and forest-dwelling"; for in such cases as "the bull among munis" (*munipuṅgavaḥ*), we see its deviation from the primary sense.

However, because of the proximity of the other stages of life (*āśrama*), the highest stage of life is understood there by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), since the highest stage of life has knowledge as its primary characteristic.
Therefore, in relation to childhood (*bālya*) and proficiency (*pāṇḍitya*), this third stage, characterized by the excellence of knowledge, is enjoined as "mauna" (sagehood).

As for the claim that the injunction terminates with childhood itself, even so, because sagehood (*munitva*) is something not previously established, it is accepted as being subject to an injunction, namely: "one should be a sage."

Furthermore, from the teaching on the state of being "not to be felt" (*nirvedanīyatva*) in the *Māṇḍūkya-sūtra-bhāṣya*, the status of the one who possesses that [knowledge] as being subject to discipline—by way of the terms "childhood" and "panditya"—is established for the renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*) who possesses knowledge.

How is it understood that this refers to the renunciant who possesses knowledge? Because of the context of that [section]: "Having known the Self, having risen above the desires for sons and so forth, they then lead the life of a mendicant."

[Objection: But surely, if one possesses knowledge (*vidyā*), excellence (*atiśaya*) necessarily follows; so what is the purpose of an injunction for silence (*mauna-vidhi*)? To this he replies: "In one case" (*pakṣeṇa*). This is what is meant: in that case where [excellence] does not follow due to the predominance of the perception of difference (*bhedadarśana*), this injunction applies.

Just as in the case of an injunction and the like—such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—the collection of subsidiary elements such as the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*) is enjoined as auxiliary factors, so too in this statement concerning knowledge, which primarily concerns what is not an injunction, there is an injunction for silence. This is the meaning.

Since the stage of life characterized by celibacy and so forth, which is supported by scripture, exists even within the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalya), why is there a conclusion in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad with the householder, in the passage "having returned home, [he should dwell] in his family"? For by concluding with that, the text shows a special regard for that stage. To this, the author reads the answer: "But the conclusion is made with the householder because of the presence of all [stages] in him."
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of qualification;
its state of being "entire" (kṛtsna) is qualified.

For many duties of the stages of life, such as sacrifices and so forth, which involve great effort, are taught as obligations toward him, and the duties of other stages of life—such as non-violence, restraint of the senses, and so forth—are also present for him as far as possible.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the inclusion of the householder.
The Third Chapter:
[The rule of] silence applies to others as well, because they too are instructed [to observe it].

Just as the stages of silence (the forest-dweller) and the householder possess scriptural authority, so too do the other two—the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the student dwelling in the teacher’s household (*gurukulāvāsa*).
For scripture was shown previously in such passages as: "Austerity is the second; the student dwelling in the teacher’s household is the third," and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no distinction in the instruction regarding all four stages of life, they are to be understood as equal, through either option or combination.

Regarding the phrase "of the others," it should be understood that the plural number refers to two stages of life (āśrama), either with respect to the diversity of their modes of livelihood (vṛtti) or with respect to the diversity of those who practice them (anuṣṭhātṛ).
Because it does not manifest itself, following from the logical sequence.

Therefore, [the text] says, "Having renounced scholarship, O Brāhmaṇa, one should remain in a state of childlikeness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1), where childlikeness (*bālya*) is heard as something to be practiced.

In this regard, when the secondary derivative suffix is applied in the sense of "the state or action of a child," there arises a doubt: since the specific physical condition of childhood—characterized by the involuntary discharge of urine and excrement as it happens, and so forth—is impossible to achieve intentionally, does "childlikeness" refer to such childish behavior, or rather to an internal purity of being, the non-development of the senses, or the absence of hypocrisy and the like?

What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that "childhood" (*bālya*) is well-known in the world as consisting of acting, speaking, and eating according to one's desire, and voiding urine and excrement as it occurs; therefore, its adoption [as the meaning here] is appropriate. Objection: This is not appropriate, because it would entail faults such as moral corruption (*patitatva*). Reply: No; for in the case of one who possesses knowledge and has renounced the world (*saṃnyāsin*), the fault is removed by the power of the scriptural injunction, just as in the case of animal sacrifice and similar acts. To this, we reply: No, because the injunction admits of another interpretation.
For when another [meaning] denoted by the word "childhood" (bālya) is available that is not contradictory, it is not proper to assume a sublation of other injunctions;
moreover, a subsidiary (aṅga) is prescribed for the sake of assisting the principal (pradhāna),
and here, for ascetics, the practice of knowledge is the principal duty to be performed.
Furthermore, if the entire conduct of a child were accepted [as the requirement], the practice of knowledge would not be possible;
therefore, "childhood" here refers to a specific internal disposition of the child, such as the non-development of the senses and so forth.
Thus he says: "without manifesting."

One should be free from hypocrisy, pride, and the like, not proclaiming oneself on account of one's knowledge, learning, piety, and so forth—just as a child, because its senses are not yet fully developed, does not strive to reveal itself to others;
for in this way, the conformity of this statement with its primary purpose is established.
And thus it has been said by the authors of the Smṛtis: "Him who is neither existent nor non-existent, neither unlearned nor deeply learned..."
No one knows him as either well-conducted or ill-conducted; he is a Brāhmaṇa.
"The wise man, relying on the hidden Dharma, should conduct himself with unknown behavior;
he should traverse the earth like one who is blind, like one who is dull-witted, and like one who is mute. And likewise: "With unmanifest signs and unmanifest conduct," and so forth.
(End of the third chapter.)
Even that which pertains to this life [occurs], provided there is no obstruction of what is currently underway; for that is observed.

Beginning from the sūtra, "And there is need for all [works], on account of the scriptural statement regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse," the various means of knowledge (*vidyā*) have been determined.

Now, it is considered whether that fruit, namely knowledge, when it is being accomplished, is accomplished here in this very life, or sometimes also in the next world. This is the topic of discussion.
What, then, is the prima facie view? That [liberation] occurs right here.
What is the reason? For knowledge is preceded by hearing and so forth;
and no one engages in hearing and so forth with the intention, "May knowledge arise for me in the hereafter."
However, it is observed that one engages in these [sacrifices and so forth] with the intention of producing knowledge in this very life;
for even sacrifices and the like produce knowledge only by way of hearing and so forth, since knowledge is produced by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that the birth of knowledge occurs only in this life, we state the following: the birth of knowledge occurs in this life, provided there is no obstruction to what has been undertaken.

This is what is meant: when no obstacle is placed against the practice of the science (*vidyā*) that has been undertaken by another karma whose fruition is imminent, then the science arises right here;
but when an obstacle is indeed placed against it, then [it arises] there.
And the imminence of the fruition of a karma occurs through the encounter with the appropriate place, time, and causal conditions.
Furthermore, it cannot be determined that the same places, times, and causal conditions which ripen the fruit of one action must necessarily apply to another as well;
for actions may have even contradictory results.
Moreover, the scripture concludes merely by stating that "this is the fruit of this action," and does not specify particularities of place, time, or causal conditions.
However, due to the excellence of the effort in spiritual practice (*sādhana-vīrya*), a supersensory power manifests for someone, while for another it remains bound by that very obstacle.
Furthermore, the intention regarding knowledge does not arise indiscriminately as "may my knowledge arise either here or there," because such an intention is unrestricted.
Even when knowledge arises through the means of hearing and so forth, it arises only in dependence upon the destruction of obstacles.
And thus, scripture demonstrates the difficulty of realizing the Self: "Though many seek to hear it, he is not found by them; though many hear it, they do not know him.
A wonder is its speaker, a wonder is its attainer; a wonder is the knower who has been well-instructed.
Furthermore, by stating that Vāmadeva attained the state of Brahman while still in the womb, [scripture] shows the arising of knowledge in one birth from means accumulated in a previous birth.
For indeed, no means for achieving anything pertaining to this world is possible for one who is still in the womb.

Even in the *Smṛti*, when Arjuna asked, "O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does he go to who has not attained perfection in Yoga? Lord Vāsudeva replied, "No doer of good, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state. Having thus spoken, and having further described his attainment of the worlds of merit and rebirth in a virtuous family, He immediately followed with the words, "There he regains the mental disposition belonging to his former body," and so forth, up to, "Perfected through many births, he then goes to the Supreme Goal" (Gītā 6.45). This concludes the third chapter.
By the words ending with "gatim," he demonstrates this very point:
therefore, it is established that the arising of knowledge—whether pertaining to this world or the next—depends upon the destruction of its obstacles.
Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state [of liberation] is determined to be of that very nature.

Just as for one seeking liberation who relies on the means of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is a fixed determination of specific distinctions regarding whether the fruit characterized as knowledge is to be realized in this life or the next—based on the particular intensity of the power of those means—and yet no such distinction is observed in the fruit that is liberation itself; likewise, one might suspect that even in the fruit characterized as liberation, there could be some fixed determination of specific distinctions based on superiority or inferiority. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "There is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation. Indeed, one should not suspect any such fixed determination of specific distinctions in the fruit of liberation.
Why? Because the state of liberation, as determined in all the Vedāntas, is indeed of one and the same form.

For the state of liberation is Brahman itself; and Brahman cannot possess a manifold nature, since it is determined to have a single characteristic (liṅga) by such scriptural passages as: "Neither coarse nor fine," "This Self is 'not this, not this'," "Where one sees nothing else," "Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in front," "All this is what this Self is," "He is indeed that great unborn Self—undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman," and "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? and so forth.

Moreover, the means of knowledge (*vidyāsādhana*), by virtue of its own specific potency, might bring about some excellence within the knowledge itself—which is its own fruit—but not within liberation, which is the fruit of knowledge;

for we have stated more than once that liberation is unattainable through effort, being of an eternally established nature, and is merely realized through knowledge (as explained in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*).
Furthermore, even in that [knowledge], an excellence consisting of increase or decrease is not possible, because that which is deficient cannot possess the status of true knowledge.
For knowledge alone is indeed superior; therefore, while an excellence consisting in the rapid or slow arising [of results] may exist in that [knowledge],
no possibility of any excellence whatsoever exists in liberation.

Furthermore, because there is no difference in the knowledge [of Brahman], there is likewise no necessity for a difference in its fruit, as is the case with the fruits of ritual actions (karma). For there is no difference in the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation, in the way that there is a difference among ritual actions. However, in the case of the meditations on the qualified Brahman (saguṇavidyā)—such as "consisting of mind, having breath for a body" and so forth—since a difference is possible due to the addition or subtraction of qualities, a corresponding necessity for a difference in their respective fruits is justified, just like the fruits of ritual actions. And there is a scriptural indication (liṅga) to this effect: "In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become."
This is not so in the case of the qualityless (nirguṇa) knowledge, because of the absence of qualities;
and thus the Smṛti says: "For there is no higher goal for anyone; indeed, when a quality exists, they proclaim inequality.
The repetition of the words "because of the determination of that state" at the end of the chapter indicates the completion of the book.

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya* (Commentary on the Aphorisms of the Enquiry into the Body), composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda. The Fourth Chapter.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.
Composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma Sūtras.
We shall proceed with the first quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter.
The Fourth Chapter.

In the third chapter, the discussion concerning the means (*sādhana*) in relation to the higher and lower forms of knowledge has for the most part been completed; now, in this fourth chapter, the discussion concerning the fruits (*phala*) will follow,
and certain other matters arising from the context will also be considered.

First, by means of several topics, we shall continue the investigation into the basis of the means [of knowledge], beginning with the point: "There is repetition because of the instruction being given more than once."

"Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"; "The wise man, having known Him alone, should practice wisdom"; and "He is to be sought after and He is to be understood"—in these and other such scriptural passages, a doubt arises: should the cognition be performed only once, or by repetition? What, then, is the initial position? It should be a single cognition, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, because the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by that much; for if repetition were performed when it is not expressly enjoined, one would be doing what is not the meaning of the scripture.

[Objection: But have not repeated instructions been cited, such as "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), and so forth? Even so, one should repeat [the practice] only as many times as the words [prescribe], namely once for hearing, once for reflection, and once for meditation, and no more. However, in cases of single instruction, such as "One should know" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.3) or "One should meditate" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1), there is no repetition. This being the position reached, we reply: the repetition of the mental realization (pratyaya) must be performed. Why? Because of the repeated instruction. For an instruction of this kind, such as "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon," indicates the repetition of the mental realization.
Is it not said that one should repeat [the practice] only as long as the word [indicates], and no further? No; for these [practices] culminate in direct perception (*darśana*).

Indeed, hearing and the other [means] become purposeful through repetition only when they culminate in direct perception, just as threshing and so forth culminate in the production of rice grains and the like.
Moreover, the terms "meditation" (*upāsana*) and "contemplation" (*nididhyāsana*) denote actions that inherently include the quality of repetition.
For instance, in common usage, one who follows a teacher or a king with total devotion is said to "worship the teacher" (*gurum upāste*) or "worship the king" (*rājānam upāste*);
likewise, a woman whose husband is away from home and who longs for him with constant remembrance is described as "meditating on her husband" (*patim dhyāyati*).
Furthermore, in the Upanishads, the terms *vid* (to know) and *upās* (to worship) are used interchangeably. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3–4)
Mere mention is seen here:

in some places, having begun with "knowing" (vid), it concludes with "meditating" (upāsin); as for example, in the passage "He who knows what he [the teacher] knows—this has been told by me to you"—[Naciketas replies] "Venerable sir, teach me that deity which you meditate upon.

And in other places, having begun with "meditating," it concludes with "knowing"; as for example, in the passage "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman"—[it continues] "He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge."
Therefore, even when the instruction is given only once, the necessity of repetition is established;
however, an instruction given more than once is an indicator of that repetition.
And because of the indicative mark (liṅga).
An indicative mark (liṅga) also demonstrates the repetition of meditation.

For instance, having introduced the knowledge of the Udgītha, the text sets aside the notion that "the sun is the Udgītha" due to the defect of having only one son, and then, by enjoining the knowledge of the multiplicity of rays with the words "you should turn back the rays" for the sake of having many sons, it shows the repetition of meditation as an established fact.
By analogy with this case, the necessity of repetition is established for all meditations.

Here it is objected: Let it be granted that there is repetition (*āvṛtti*) in the case of meditations whose fruits are things to be accomplished, since an excellence produced by such repetition is possible in those cases;

but as for the meditation concerning the Supreme Brahman, which presents the Supreme Brahman—whose very nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—as one's own self, what is the purpose of repetition there?
