If it is argued that repetition must be admitted because the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self is not possible from hearing [the scripture] only once, we say no, because even with repetition that [realization] remains impossible.

For if a sentence of this kind, such as "That thou art," being heard even with great effort, were not to produce the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self, then what hope could there be that it would produce it when merely repeated?

Furthermore, since a sentence alone cannot effect the direct intuition of any object, one might argue that the sentence, supported by reasoning, will bring about the experience of the identity of Brahman and the Self; even so, repetition remains entirely useless.
For that reasoning, once set in motion, will indeed manifest its own object.
Nevertheless, it might be argued that through reasoning and verbal testimony, only a cognition with respect to a generality is produced, not one with respect to a particular;

just as from the statement "I have a pain in my heart" and from signs such as trembling of the limbs, another person understands only the general existence of the pain, but does not experience the particularity as the sufferer himself does.

If it is argued that the experience of distinction is what removes ignorance, and therefore repetition is for that purpose—this is not so; for even if that much [repetition] were performed many times, the arising of a specific cognition is impossible.
Indeed, a distinction not apprehended by scripture and reasoning when applied once cannot be apprehended even if those two are applied a hundred times.

Therefore, whether a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) is established by means of scripture and reasoning, or whether it is only a general feature (*sāmānya*), in either case, those two (scripture and reasoning) perform their own function as soon as they have once operated; thus, there is no utility for repetition (*āvṛtti*).

Nor can it be restricted that scripture and reasoning, when employed but once, do not produce an experience for anyone, because the understandings of those who receive instruction vary. Furthermore, in the case of a worldly object consisting of many parts and possessing both general and specific features, [it is understood] through a single act of attention. [End of Chapter Four] *Note: The text fragment "MANOR BUR WEEsū caturtho'dhyāyaḥ" appears to be a corrupted or non-standard marker indicating the end of the fourth chapter.*
One might hold that practice is useful when one part [of an object] is grasped by one [act of cognition] and another part by another, as in the case of learning long recitations and the like;

however, it is not logical to require practice for the arising of valid knowledge regarding Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions, free from generalities and particulars, and consists solely of pure consciousness.
To this it is replied: Repetition would indeed be useless for one who is able to realize the identity of Brahman and the Self from what has been stated only once;
however, for one who is not so able, repetition is certainly useful.

For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, after the instruction "That thou art, Śvetaketu," when he is questioned again and again with the words "Please, revered sir, instruct me further," the teacher, having removed each respective cause for doubt, repeatedly instructs him with the very same words, "That thou art."

And thus it has been shown in such passages as, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (*śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavya*). Now, an objection is raised: "If the sentence *tat tvam asi* (That thou art), even when heard once, is unable to bring about the experience of its own meaning, then it will certainly not be able to do so even when repeated. This is not a fault; for indeed, there is no such thing as the impossible in what is actually observed.

For indeed, those of duller intellect, having heard the sentence only once, repeat the meaning of the sentence and attain a correct understanding by means of the exclusion of various fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*).
Furthermore, this sentence "That thou art" declares that the referent of the term *tvam* (thou) possesses the nature of the referent of the term *tat* (that).

And by the word "That" (tat), the subject under discussion—Being, Brahman, the seer, and the cause of the birth and so forth of the world—is denoted. This is established by such scriptural passages as: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"; "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss"; "The unseen seer"; "The unknown knower"; "Unborn, undecaying, immortal"; and "Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long. In this context, by words such as "unborn" (aja), the modifications of being such as birth and so forth are excluded;
and by words such as "not gross" (asthūla), qualities of substance such as grossness and so forth are excluded.
Furthermore, words such as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and so forth have expressed the nature of being the light of sentience (*caitanya-prakāśātmakatva*).

This, which is free from all transmigratory attributes (*saṃsāra-dharma*), consisting of pure experience (*anubhavātmaka*), and designated as Brahman, is the meaning of the term *tat* well-known among those devoted to the Vedānta.

Likewise, the meaning of the term *tvam*—the inner self (*pratyagātman*) who is the listener—is determined to extend inwardly from the body up to the limit of sentience, conceived as the innermost self.

In this regard, for those whose understanding of these two categories [of subject and object] is obstructed by ignorance, doubt, or misconception, the sentence "That thou art" is unable to produce valid knowledge regarding its own meaning, because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words. Therefore, for their sake, the practice of the scriptures and reasoning aimed at the discrimination of the categories must be undertaken. And although the Self to be realized is partless (*niraṃśa*), nevertheless, manifoldness—characterized by the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations—is superimposed upon it.
In that case, it is appropriate that there be a gradual realization, wherein one removes one part by means of one act of attention and another part by means of another;
however, that [gradual process] is merely a preliminary stage for the realization of the Self.

On the other hand, those of subtle intellect, for whom there exists no obstruction regarding the subject matter consisting of ignorance, doubt, or error, are able to experience the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" at the very moment it is uttered. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.3) Chapter Four.
Regarding those [who hold such a view], the futility of repetition is indeed accepted;
for the realization of the Self, once arisen, removes ignorance, and no sequence whatsoever is admitted here.
This would indeed be logical if such a realization were to occur for anyone.

If it is argued that the perception of one's own suffering and so forth is indeed powerful, and therefore no one can perceive the absence of suffering and the like—[we reply: no, for just as the conceit of being the body and so on is a false conceit, so too the conceit of suffering and the like is established as a false conceit.
For it is observed through direct perception that when the body is being cut or burned, there arises the false conceit, "I am being cut," "I am being burned."
Likewise, even when external things such as sons and friends are suffering, the superimposition "I myself am suffering" is observed;

similarly, there may be the conceit of being a sufferer and so forth, because suffering and its like are perceived as external to consciousness, just like the body and other such objects, and because they do not persist in states such as deep sleep.
Indeed, they declare the persistence of consciousness even in deep sleep through such passages as: "Verily, when there he does not see, he is indeed seeing, though he does not see."
Therefore, this experience of the Self is: "I am the one conscious Self, entirely liberated from all suffering.
For one who thus experiences the Self, no further duty remains.

Accordingly, the Śruti demonstrates the absence of anything to be done for the knower of the Self: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

Smṛti also states: "But for that man who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who is content in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be performed. However, for one in whom this realization does not arise immediately, the acceptance of repetition is intended solely for the sake of attaining that realization.
Even in that case, one should not cause [the person] to deviate from the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" and engage them in repetition;
for they do not marry off a bride in order to kill the groom.
Furthermore, in one who is enjoined, there necessarily arises a cognition contrary to the realization of Brahman, such as: "I am authorized in this," "I am the agent," and "this must be done by me."

However, for one who, being dull-witted by nature, would wish to abandon that meaning of the statement due to a lack of confidence, stabilization regarding that very meaning of the statement is accepted through the method of repetition and so forth.
Therefore, even with respect to the cognition of the Supreme Brahman, the accomplishment of repetition is established in the instructions on its means.
But they indeed approach [the view] that there is a self, and they cause others to grasp it as such.
One reflects on this: whether that Supreme Self, characterized by the attributes mentioned in the scriptures, is to be grasped as "I" or as distinct from me.

But how can there be doubt when the word *ātman*, which primarily refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is being used? It is said in reply: this word *ātman* can be accepted as having its primary meaning [in both senses] when the possibility of non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) exists.
Otherwise, however, one considers that this [usage] must be accepted as figurative.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That "I" is not to be grasped [as the Self];

for one whose qualities are such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) cannot be grasped as having contrary qualities, nor can one with contrary qualities be grasped as having freedom from sin and so forth.
Furthermore, the Supreme Lord possesses qualities such as being free from sin, whereas the embodied soul possesses qualities contrary to those;
for if the Lord were the self of the transmigrating soul, it would follow that there is no Lord at all. Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Consequently, the scriptures would be rendered purposeless;

even if the transmigrating soul were identical with the Lord, the scriptures would still be purposeless due to the absence of any person eligible for their practice, and there would also be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge.
If it is argued that—even though they are different—the identity must be realized through the scriptures, just as Viṣṇu and others are perceived in images and the like, let it be so.
But it must not be brought about by us that the transmigrating soul is the primary Ātman, namely, the Lord (Īśvara).
This being the position reached, we reply: the Supreme Lord alone is to be understood as the Self.
For, within the context of the Supreme Lord, the Jābālas approach Him precisely as the Self, saying: "I am indeed you, O Venerable Deity; you indeed are I, O Deity.
Likewise, other approaches identifying [the Self] with the Self, such as "I am Brahman," are to be seen in the same way.

Furthermore, the Vedānta texts—such as "This is your Self, which is within all," "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," "That is the True, That is the Self, That art thou"—cause one to grasp Īśvara as the very Self.

As for the claim that this is a meditation on a symbol (pratīka-darśana) according to the analogy of an image of Viṣṇu, that is incorrect; for it would entail the consequence of [the teaching] being figurative (gauṇa), and because of the uniformity of the statements. For where a meditation on a symbol is intended, the statement occurs only once, as in "The mind is Brahman" or "The sun is Brahman. But here, the repetition of "That art thou" shows that the identity of the Self with Brahman is what is intended.

Furthermore, here [in the text], you say, "I am you" and "You are I"; therefore, because of this difference in the form of the scriptural statements (*pratīka-śrutivairūpyāt*), there is no realization of non-difference.

Moreover, there is a refutation of the perception of difference (*bhedadṛṣṭyapavādāt*). For instance, numerous scriptural passages refute the perception of difference, such as: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10); "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.1.10); and "Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6). Thus, and so forth, the scripture extensively refutes the perception of difference.

As for what was said—that there is no possibility of two things with contradictory qualities being identical to one another—that is not a fault, because the contradiction in their qualities is established as being illusory (*mithyātva*).

Furthermore, as for what was said—that this would result in the non-existence of God—that is incorrect, because of the authority of the scripture (*śāstra*) and because we do not accept such a consequence.
For we do not admit that the scripture teaches that God is identical in nature to the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*).
Rather, what is intended to be established is that the transmigrating being, through the removal of its state of transmigration, possesses the nature of the Lord.
This being so, it is settled that the non-dual Lord possesses qualities such as freedom from sin, while the contrary qualities of the other [the individual soul] are false.

As for the objection that there would be no qualified person for the teaching and that this contradicts perception and other means of knowledge—that too is incorrect, because the state of being a transmigrator is admitted prior to awakening, and because the operation of perception and the rest has that very state as its object.

For by the passage beginning, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? [the text] demonstrates the absence of perception and other means of knowledge upon awakening.
If it is argued that in the absence of perception and so forth, there would follow the non-existence of the Śruti as well, we say no; for this is precisely what is accepted.
Starting with the words, "The father becomes a non-father," the text continues, "The Vedas become non-Vedas"; thus, we indeed accept the non-existence of even the Śruti upon awakening.
If it is asked, "Whose is this lack of awakening? we reply: "It belongs to you who ask," as stated in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, Chapter Four.
Now, if it is argued that "I am indeed the Lord" according to the Śruti, and if you are thus awakened, there is no lack of awakening for anyone.
Furthermore, the objection raised by some—that because the Self possesses a second [entity] through ignorance (*avidyā*), non-duality (*advaita*) is untenable—is also refuted by this very [point].
Therefore, one should fix the mind on the Lord as "the Self" alone.
Not in a symbol, for he is not that.

The reason is as follows: regarding meditations on symbols (pratīkopāsana) such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman"—which refers to the internal self—and "Space is Brahman," which refers to the divine; and likewise, "The sun is Brahman—this is the instruction"—and "He who meditates on Name as Brahman," and so forth, a doubt arises: should the grasping of the Self (ātma-graha) be performed in these cases as well, or not?
What, then, is the initial position? It is argued that even in those cases, it is proper to perform the grasping of the Self.

Why? Because Brahman is well-known in the Śrutis as the Self, and because even the symbols (pratīkas), being modifications of Brahman, possess Brahman-hood and thus the status of being the Self is logically established. This being the position reached, we reply: one should not fix the notion of the Self upon the symbols. For that worshiper would not conceive of the symbols as separate things as being the Self. As for the argument that the symbols possess Brahman-hood—and consequently the status of the Self—because they are modifications of Brahman, that is incorrect, because it would entail the non-existence of the symbols themselves.
For, by the sublation of the nature of the modifications, it is precisely the Brahman-nature of the entire class beginning with Name that is resorted to;

and when their own nature is sublated, how could there be either the status of being a symbol (*pratīka*) or the grasping [of them] as the Self (*ātma-graha*) for Name and the rest? Nor, because Brahman is the Self, should the view of the Self be assumed in those teachings where the view of Brahman is instructed; for agency and so forth are not thereby set aside.
Indeed, the teaching that Brahman is the Self occurs through the setting aside of all transmigratory attributes such as agency.
And because that [distinction] is not set aside, there is the injunction for meditation.
Consequently, since the meditator is identical with the symbols (*pratīka*), the apprehension of them as the Self is not tenable;
for indeed, there is no mutual identity between a gold necklace (*rucaka*) and a svastika.
We have already stated that if there were identity with the Self of Brahman as if with the nature of gold, it would follow that no meditative image (*pratīka*) could exist;
therefore, the vision of the Self is not to be applied to meditative images.
Because of the excellence of the view of Brahman.

The means [of meditation]. Regarding those very examples, there arises another doubt: should the meditations on the sun and so forth be superimposed upon Brahman, or should the meditation on Brahman be superimposed upon the sun and so forth? Why does this doubt arise concerning the superimposition of the meditation on Brahman? Because the specific cause for the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is not determined.

For here, the word *brahman* is observed to be in grammatical apposition with words such as *āditya*, as seen in the use of identical case-endings in expressions such as "The sun is Brahman," "Breath is Brahman," and "Lightning is Brahman.
Moreover, a literal apposition is not possible here, because the words *brahman*, *āditya*, and so forth, denote different things;
for there can be no apposition between "cow" and "horse."

Now, one might object that because of the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), there should be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between Brahman and the sun and so forth, just as between clay and a jar; to this we reply: no, for in such a case, the modification would necessarily be dissolved into its material cause.
And we have already stated that this would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the meditation] becoming a mere symbolic representation (*pratīka*).

If this were a statement concerning the Supreme Self (paramātman), then the qualification for meditative worship (upāsanā) would be sublated, and the assumption of a limited modification (parimita-vikāra) would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, as in the case of "The Brāhmaṇa is Agni Vaiśvānara," when there is a superimposition of the vision of one upon the other, a doubt arises as to which vision should be superimposed upon which. On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is no fixed rule, because there is no scriptural injunction (śāstra) to establish such a rule.
Alternatively, the conclusion reached is that one should indeed perform the meditations on the sun and so forth as being Brahman;
for in this way, Brahman becomes worshipped through the meditations on the sun and so forth,
and it is the established rule of the scriptures that the worship of Brahman is fruitful.
Therefore, when it is argued that the vision of Brahman does not apply to the sun and so forth, we reply: the vision of Brahman alone should indeed be applied to the sun and so forth.
Why? Because of superiority (*utkarṣāt*).
In this way, the sun and others become viewed with superiority, since the vision of the superior is superimposed upon them.
And thus the worldly principle is followed;
for it is a worldly principle that a superior vision is to be superimposed upon an inferior object, as the vision of a king is [superimposed] upon a charioteer;
and that principle must be followed, because in its reversal there would be the consequence of sin.
For a king who is under the influence of the perspective of a charioteer would not be led toward his own welfare when being brought into subjection.

[Objection: But surely, on account of the authority of the scriptures, the possibility of sin (pratyavāya) in this matter is not to be suspected; nor is it proper to restrict a scriptural view by means of worldly reasoning. To this it is replied: This would indeed be so if the meaning of the scripture were already determined;
but while that meaning is still doubtful, worldly reasoning is not contradicted when it is employed for the purpose of determining it. (Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya 1.3.34).

And when the meaning of the scripture is being determined as the superimposition of the vision of the superior upon [the inferior], it follows that one would incur sin by superimposing the vision of the inferior.
Furthermore, because they appear first and there is no contradiction, the words "Āditya" and so forth must be understood in their primary sense.

Since the word "Brahman," which enters later, cannot be in grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with them through its primary sense once the intellect has been occupied by those words functioning in their own primary meanings, it remains that its purpose is solely to enjoin the meditation on [Āditya, etc. as Brahman.
Thus, because of its priority [in the text], this alone is the logical meaning of the word "Brahman";

for in all such instances—"the instruction is 'Brahman'," "one should meditate on it as Brahman," and "he meditates on it as Brahman"—it always utters the word "Brahman" followed by the particle *iti*, whereas it uses the pure words "Āditya" and so forth without it.

And therefore, just as in the case where one perceives mother-of-pearl as silver—where the word "mother-of-pearl" (śuktikā) denotes the mother-of-pearl itself, while the word "silver" (rajata) has the purpose of indicating the perception of silver, for one merely perceives "this is silver," yet there is no silver there—in the same way, it is understood here as well that one should perceive the sun and so forth as Brahman.

Moreover, the supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa), by means of the accusative case-ending, show that it is Āditya and the others who are pervaded by the act of meditation: "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman," "He who meditates upon Speech as Brahman," and "He who meditates upon Will as Brahman.

As for the argument that the meditation on Brahman alone is to be respected here because it yields fruit, that is incorrect; for, according to the reasoning already stated, it is understood that Āditya and the others themselves are the objects of meditation.

As for the fruit, however, just as in the meditation on guests and so forth, in the meditation on Āditya and the others as well, it is Brahman alone that is indicated [as the source of the result]. Chapter Four.
It will grant [the fruit], because it is the presiding lord of all;
and this has been explained in the sūtra "The fruit [comes] from that, because it is logical" (Brahmasūtra 3.2.38).

And such is the nature of Brahman's being an object of meditation here: namely, the superimposition of the vision of That upon the symbols, just as Viṣṇu and others are superimposed upon images and the like.
And the meditations on the limbs [of the sacrifice] as being the sun and so forth are appropriate because of the logical possibility.

[The opponent says: "One should meditate on that which shines as the *udgītha*"; "One should meditate on the fivefold *sāman* in the worlds"; "One should meditate on the sevenfold *sāman* in speech"; "This earth is the *ṛc*, the fire is the *sāman*," and so forth. Regarding these meditations connected with the [Vedic] limbs (*aṅga*), a doubt arises: are the perceptions (*dṛṣṭi*) of the *udgītha* and so on enjoined upon the sun and so forth, or rather, are the perceptions of the sun and so forth enjoined upon the *udgītha* and so forth?
On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there is no fixed rule, because there is no cause for such a restriction.
For here, no specific superiority of anyone is determined as is the case with Brahman;
for Brahman can indeed be determined to be superior to the sun and other deities because it is the cause of the entire world and because it possesses qualities such as being free from evil,
whereas there is no reason to determine any specific superiority among the sun, the udgītha, and so forth, since they are all equally mere effects (vikāras).
Alternatively, the conceptions of the *udgītha* and so forth might be superimposed upon the sun and other objects by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Why? Because the *udgītha* and so forth consist of action (*karma*), and because it is well known that action leads to the attainment of results.
Thus, the sun and other objects, when meditated upon through the conceptions of the *udgītha* and so forth, will become causes of results by virtue of being of the nature of action.

And likewise, in this very *Sūtra-bhāṣya* regarding the passage "This [earth] is the *ṛc*, fire is the *sāman*," it says: "Therefore, this *sāman* is superimposed upon these two *ṛcs*"; here, the word *ṛc* refers to the earth, and the word *sāman* refers to fire.

And that is possible only if one intends to effect the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) on the earth and fire as being the *ṛc* and *sāman*, not if one intends to effect the meditation on the *ṛc* and *sāman* as being the earth and fire.
For the word "king" is applied metaphorically to a doorkeeper by virtue of effecting the meditation on him as a king, but the word "doorkeeper" is not applied to the king.
Moreover, from the designation of the locus in the passage, "One should meditate on the Sāman as fivefold in the worlds," it is understood that the Sāman is to be superimposed upon the worlds;
and the statement, "This Gāyatra is woven upon the vital breaths," shows exactly this.
Furthermore, in cases such as "The sun is Brahman—this is the instruction," where Brahman is superimposed upon the sun and so forth mentioned last, while they were mentioned first.

Earth and the others are mentioned first, while the *hiṃkāra* and so forth are mentioned last in such scriptural passages as "The earth is the *hiṃkāra*" and so on. Therefore, since the superimposition of the members [of the sacrifice] onto non-members such as the sun and so forth would be appropriate, this being the prima facie view, we reply: the conceptions of the sun and so forth should indeed be superimposed upon the members, such as the *udgītha*. Why? Because it is logical (*upapatteḥ*). For in this way, through proximity to the unseen potency (*apūrva*), the success of the ritual action is accomplished when the *udgītha* and other members are consecrated by the conceptions of the sun and so forth.

And by stating, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful," it shows that knowledge is a cause for the success of ritual action. Let this be so regarding those results which consist in the success of ritual action; but how is it with regard to those results which are independent [of ritual]? [As it is said: "He who, knowing this thus, [sings] the fivefold Sāman in the worlds... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3). Fourth Chapter.

In passages such as "He who meditates on [the Sāman] as food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.6) and so forth, even there, because they concern those already qualified for ritual action, it is proper to assume a fruit through proximity to the primary apūrva (unseen potency), just like the rule regarding the *godohana* vessel and others.
Furthermore, since the Sun and other deities are of the nature of fruits, their superiority over the *udgītha* and other elements—which consist of ritual action—is logical;
for the attainment of the Sun and other deities is taught in the Śrutis as the fruit of ritual action.

Moreover, having introduced the *udgītha* itself as the object of meditation in the passages, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*" and "This indeed is the further explanation of that very syllable," the text enjoins the meditations on the Sun and so forth. As for the claim that the Sun and others, when meditated upon through the forms of the *udgītha* and so forth, will become the ritual action (*karman*) and thereby produce a fruit—that is incorrect; for it is the meditation itself that constitutes the action, and thus its fruitfulness is logically established. Furthermore, even when the *udgītha* and other elements are perceived in the form of the Sun and so forth, they do not lose their essential nature as ritual action.
"But as for the statement, 'This Sāman is superimposed upon this Ṛc,' the application of the words 'Ṛc' and 'Sāman' to the earth and fire is indeed figurative (lākṣaṇika).
And figurative usage proceeds according to possibility, either through a proximate or a remote connection with its own primary meaning.

In this case, although there is a desire to effect the perception of the earth and fire as the Ṛc and Sāman, nevertheless, because of the mention of the well-known Ṛc and Sāman as distinct entities and because of the proximity of the earth and fire, it is determined that this application of the words 'Ṛc' and 'Sāman' refers to those two [the earth and fire] themselves by virtue of their connection with the Ṛc and Sāman."
For even the word "steward" (kṣattṛ), when applied to a king for some particular reason, cannot be prevented from doing so.
Furthermore, the phrase "this very [earth] is the Ṛg-verse" determines that the earth is the Ṛg-verse according to the literal arrangement of the words;
for if it were being determined that the Ṛg-verse is the earth, the literal arrangement of the words would have been "this Ṛg-verse is indeed [the earth]."

Furthermore, the statement, "He who, knowing thus, sings the Sāman," concludes that the cognition is based solely on the subordinate members (the limbs of the Sāman), and not on the earth and so forth.

Likewise, although the worlds are indicated by the locative case in the passage, "One should meditate upon the sixfold Sāman in the worlds," nevertheless, those worlds must be superimposed upon the Sāman itself; for this is understood from the use of the accusative case, which indicates that the Sāman is the object of meditation.

For when the worlds are superimposed upon the Sāman, the Sāman becomes meditated upon as having the nature of the worlds; otherwise, the worlds would instead be meditated upon as having the nature of the Sāman.
By this, passages such as "This Gāyatra is woven upon the vital breaths" are explained.

Even where there is an identical use of the accusative case, as in "Now, one should meditate on that sun as the sevenfold Sāman," there too—because the meditation begins with the Sāman itself, as in "The meditation on the Sāman in its entirety is indeed good," "Thus for the fivefold [Sāman]," and "Now for the sevenfold [Sāman]"—the superimposition of the sun and so forth occurs upon that very Sāman.

And because it is understood from this very [text] that the *sāman* itself is the object of meditation, even though there is a reversal in the designation—such as "the earth is the *hiṃkāra*" and so forth—the contemplation of the earth and the rest is to be applied precisely to the *hiṃkāra* and the other parts.

Therefore, it is established that the conceptions of Āditya and the rest, which do not have the subordinate members themselves as their basis, are to be superimposed upon the subordinate members such as the *udgītha*.
He is seated because of the possibility [of it].

First, in the case of meditations connected with the constituent parts of ritual action (*karma*), there is no consideration of posture and so forth, because they are dependent on the ritual action itself.
Nor is there such consideration in the case of perfect knowledge (*samyagdarśana*), because realization is dependent on the nature of the reality (*vastu*) itself.
But as for the other [meditations]... [Chapter Four].
[The topic of] the means [of performance].

Regarding meditations (*upāsana*), one considers whether one may proceed without restriction—standing, sitting, or lying down—or whether there is a restriction such that one must sit alone. On this point, the prima facie view being that because meditation is mental in nature, there is no restriction on the posture of the body, [the author] declares: "One should meditate while sitting alone."
Why? Because it is possible.
Meditation (upāsana) consists in the production of a continuous flow of identical cognitions;
and that is not possible for one who is walking or running, because movement and the like cause distraction of the mind.
Even for one who stands, the mind is occupied with maintaining the body and thus becomes incapable of perceiving subtle objects;
even for one who lies down, he is suddenly overcome by sleep; but for one who sits, such defects are easily avoided, and therefore his practice of meditation is possible.
And because of meditation.
Moreover, this is the meaning of "meditates" (*dhyāyati*): namely, the production of a continuous flow of identical cognitions.

And the verb "to meditate" is seen to be used metaphorically for those whose bodily movements are relaxed, whose gaze is steady, and whose minds are fixed on a single object—such as when one says, "The crane meditates," or "He whose kinsmen are away meditates.
Furthermore, one who is seated becomes free from exertion.
For this reason also, the meditation on the acts [is to be performed] while seated.
And with reference to immovability.
Moreover, in the passage "The earth, as it were, meditates" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.6.1), the expression "meditates" is used with reference to the immobility of the earth and other such things;
and that is an indicative mark (liṅga) that meditation is an act performed while sitting.
And they remember.
Moreover, the learned (śiṣṭas) also remember that posture is an ancillary to meditation, as in the passage beginning, "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place.
For this very reason, specific postures such as the lotus-posture (padmaka) and others are taught in the Yoga-śāstra.
Regarding the focus on the tip of the nose, there is no distinction [in its application] therein.
Regarding the question of whether there is any rule concerning direction, place, and time—namely, whether such a rule exists or not—the opponent’s view is as follows:

since a rule regarding direction and so forth is generally observed in the commencement of Vedic undertakings, one might think that here too there is some rule, such as the requirement for one-pointedness of mind; this is the subject of the discussion (*adhikaraṇa*).
To this, he replies: in matters of direction, place, and time, the rule is determined solely by the purpose (*artha-lakṣaṇa*).

In whatever direction, place, or time one’s mind attains ease and one-pointedness, there alone should one practice meditation; for no specific rule is heard regarding the eastward direction, the forenoon, or a slope facing east, etc., since the desired one-pointedness is equally possible everywhere. Now, it may be argued that some indeed prescribe a specific rule: "One should apply oneself to a place that is level, clean, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, devoid of noise and water-sources, agreeable to the mind but not distressing to the eyes, and sheltered in a cave or a windless spot. To this it is replied: [The full response follows: ... [as the text continues] ... Therefore, because of the absence of a restrictive scriptural injunction, one should meditate wherever one-pointedness of mind occurs. Furthermore, even where a specific rule is prescribed, it is intended only for those whose minds are not easily concentrated elsewhere. Thus, the rule regarding a level and clean place and so forth is merely illustrative; it does not preclude other locations where one-pointedness is achieved. Moreover, the scripture itself shows that meditation is not restricted to a single mode: "He should meditate on the Self as 'I am Brahman'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), and "He should meditate on the Self as 'I am Brahman'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1). Since the object of meditation is the same in all cases, the location is immaterial. Consequently, one should meditate wherever the mind becomes steady. This concludes the discussion.
It is true that there is such a rule; however,
even this being the case, the Teacher, acting as a friend, declares in the fourth chapter that regarding the specific details contained therein, there is no fixed rule.
And this scriptural statement, "in what is agreeable to the mind," demonstrates precisely this: that [meditation] occurs only where there is one-pointedness.
For it is seen even there [in the case of those who have attained knowledge] until the time of departure from the body.

It was established in the first section (adhikaraṇa) that repetition must be observed in all meditations (upāsana). Among those, it is already known from the section [on the meditation on the "I am Brahman"] that those meditations which aim at perfect knowledge terminate with their effect—like the act of threshing grain until the husk is removed—and thus their measure of repetition is determined. As for the others:

For once the goal has been accomplished through right vision, it is impossible to enjoin any further effort; this is because the scripture has no jurisdiction over one who has realized the identity with Brahman, which is not something to be enjoined.

However, regarding those [meditations] that have prosperity as their fruit, this consideration arises: should one desist after repeating the mental representation for some time, or should one repeat it throughout one's entire life?

What, then, is the prima facie position? One should abandon the meditative practice after practicing the mental representation for some time, because the purpose of the term "meditation" (upāsana), which is characterized by repetition, has been fulfilled. To this we reply: one should repeat the mental representation until the moment of death, because the attainment of the unseen fruit depends upon the final mental representation.

For even karmas, when initiating a fruit to be experienced in another birth, project at the time of death a corresponding consciousness consisting of latent impressions (bhāvanā-vijñāna), according to such scriptural passages as: "He becomes possessed of consciousness; it is with consciousness that he descends"; "With whatever mind he comes to the vital breath"; and "The vital breath, united with heat, together with the self, leads him to the world as he has willed. This is also supported by the illustration of the caterpillar on the blade of grass.

But these meditations (*pratyaya*), apart from the persistence of their own nature, what else could they require except for the cognition resulting from mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-vijñāna*) occurring at the time of death?
Therefore, those meditations whose essence consists in the cultivation of the fruit to be attained must be repeated until the moment of death.
Thus, scripture also shows the persistence of the meditation at the time of death: "As long as he has this resolve, so long does he go from this world" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).

Smṛti also states: "Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly permeated by that thought"; and "with an unshaken mind at the time of departure.
Furthermore, the passage "At the time of death, he should take recourse to these three" declares that there remains a duty to be performed even at the moment of dying.
For one who has attained that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of future and past sins respectively, because of the designation thereof.
The third section is concluded;
now, an inquiry is undertaken regarding the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
A doubt arises as to whether, when Brahman is realized, evil (*durita*)—which has a result contrary to that realization—is destroyed, or whether it is not destroyed by such realization.
What, then, is the primary topic? It is this: since action exists for the sake of its fruit, its destruction is not possible without having bestowed that fruit;
for its power to bestow a fruit is established by scripture.
If that [karma] were to be exhausted even without the experience of its fruit, the scripture would be contradicted;
and they also remember in the Smṛti: "Indeed, karma does not perish.
[End of the Fourth Chapter].

[Objection: But if this were so, the instruction regarding expiations (prāyaścitta) would result in being purposeless. [Reply: This is not a fault, because it is logical that expiations are occasional (naimittika), like the sacrifice performed when one's house is burned (gṛhadāheṣṭi) and so forth.
Moreover, since expiations are enjoined in connection with a fault, they might indeed have the purpose of destroying that fault;
however, there is no such injunction for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).

[Objection: "If the destruction of karma is not admitted for the knower of Brahman, then since the fruit of that karma must necessarily be experienced, there would be no liberation. [Reply: This is not so; liberation will occur in dependence upon place, time, and cause, just like the fruit of karma. Therefore, upon the realization of Brahman, there is no cessation of evil deeds. To this position, we reply: Upon the realization of that—namely, upon the realization of Brahman—there occur the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and the destruction (*vināśa*) of subsequent and prior evils respectively: non-clinging of the subsequent and destruction of the prior.
Why? Because of the designation of that [non-attachment].

For, in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the scripture designates for the knower—who is connected with future evil—that there is no connection with it: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus.
Likewise, it also designates the destruction of previously accumulated evil: "Just as tuft of cotton placed in a fire would be consumed, even so all his evils are consumed."

This is another scriptural declaration regarding the exhaustion of karma: "The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas waste away when that which is both high and low has been seen. As for the objection that the scripture would be undermined if one were to postulate the destruction of karma whose fruit has not yet been experienced, this is not a fault.
For we do not deny that action possesses the power to yield its fruit; indeed, that power exists. However, we maintain that it is obstructed by other causes such as knowledge (vidyā) and the like.

The scripture operates merely with regard to the existence of the capacity [for fruition], and not with regard to whether there is an obstruction or lack of obstruction to that capacity. Even the traditional rule that "karma is not exhausted" is a general principle; for karma is indeed not exhausted except through experience, since that is its purpose.

However, its exhaustion through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like is certainly accepted, based on such scriptural and traditional texts as: "He overcomes all evil," "He overcomes the murder of a Brahmin, who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and he who knows this thus."

As for the claim that these will be occasional expiations (*naimittika-prāyaścitta*), that is incorrect; for since these [acts] are enjoined in connection with a fault, it is illogical to assume another result when the result of the removal of that fault is already possible.

As for what was stated previously—that there is no injunction for knowledge (*vidyā*) with the specific aim of destroying defects for one who possesses expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—to this we reply: In the case of meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavidyā*), an injunction certainly exists; and in the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) of those texts, the attainment of lordly power (*aiśvarya*) and the cessation of evil (*pāpanivṛtti*) are declared for the possessor of such knowledge. Since there is no reason to disregard these two, it is determined that their fruit is the attainment of lordly power preceded by the abandonment of evil.

However, although there is no injunction in the case of the meditation on the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇavidyā*), nevertheless, the destruction of karma is established through the realization of the Self as a non-agent (*akartrātmatva*).
By the term "non-attachment" (*aśleṣa*), he shows that the knower of Brahman does not assume the status of an agent with respect to future actions.

As for past actions, although one may have seemingly assumed the status of an agent due to false knowledge, nevertheless, through the power of knowledge, those very actions are dissolved once false knowledge has ceased; thus he says "destruction" (*vināśa*).

Indeed, the knower of Brahman realizes: "I am that Brahman whose nature is non-agency and non-enjoyment throughout the three periods of time, which is the opposite of the previously established states of being an agent and an enjoyer; I was not an agent or an enjoyer even in the past, nor am I so now, nor shall I be so in the future.
And it is only in this way that liberation is possible;
otherwise, if there were no exhaustion of the karmas that have been operating since beginningless time, there would be no liberation.
Furthermore, liberation cannot be dependent on place, time, or causal conditions like the fruit of ritual action,
for that would entail the consequence of impermanence, and because it is impossible for the fruit of knowledge to be something beyond perception.
Therefore, it is established that upon the realization of Brahman, there is the destruction of evil.
In the other case as well, there is likewise no connection; but at the time of falling away, however...

In the preceding section, it was established on the basis of scriptural teaching that the non-clinging and destruction of sin (*agha*), which is the cause of bondage and is innate, are brought about by knowledge;

however, since merit (*dharma*) is of a different nature due to its being based on scripture, there was a doubt regarding its contradiction with knowledge. To dispel that doubt, the principle of the preceding section is extended here: for one who possesses knowledge, even the other—meritorious action—likewise undergoes non-clinging and destruction, just like sin.

Why? Because that [merit] also, by being the cause of its own fruit, would entail the consequence of obstructing the fruit of knowledge; because in such scriptural passages as "He indeed crosses over both," there is the designation of the destruction of good deeds just like evil deeds; because the destruction of karma caused by the realization of the non-agent self is equal for both good and evil deeds; and because of the scriptural statement without qualification, "And his works are exhausted."
Even where the word *pāpman* (evil) alone is recited, it should be understood that merit (*puṇya*) is also included therein, because [merit] yields an inferior fruit when compared with knowledge.

Furthermore, the word *pāpman* is used for merit as well in the Śruti; in the passage "Day and night do not cross this bridge," after mentioning both evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*) and good deeds (*sukṛta*) together, the text says, "All evils (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from here," employing the word *pāpman* without distinction for the merit under discussion.
In the phrase "But at the fall" (*pāte tu*), the word *tu* (but) serves to emphasize.

Thus, since the destruction of the stains of merit and demerment—the causes of bondage—is established through the power of knowledge, he concludes that liberation is inevitable for the wise man upon the fall of the body.
But first, those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed by that limit.
In the two preceding sections, it was established that the destruction of good and evil deeds is caused by knowledge;

however, it must now be considered whether this occurs without distinction—applying to both those deeds whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*) and those whose effects have not yet begun (*anārabdhakārya*)—or whether it applies specifically only to those whose effects have not yet begun. This is the point under investigation.

In this regard, since scriptural passages such as "He indeed transcends both of these" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.13.1) mention this without distinction, the prima facie view is that the destruction of karma occurs without exception. To this, the author replies: "But only those whose effects have not yet begun.

Only those good and evil deeds whose fruits have not yet commenced—those accumulated in previous lives and those accumulated in this very life prior to the arising of knowledge—are destroyed by the attainment of knowledge; however, those whose effects have already begun—that is, those whose fruits have been partially enjoyed, by which this birth serving as the locus for the knowledge of Brahman was indicated—are not destroyed. Chapter Four.
It is not, however, non-emanated.

Why is this? Because the attainment of security has as its temporal limit the falling away of the body, according to the text: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute].
For otherwise, if all karma were destroyed by knowledge, then in the absence of any cause for continued existence, one would attain security immediately upon the acquisition of knowledge.
In this regard, one should not say that there is a waiting for the fall of the body.

[Objection: Surely, by the power of the reality itself, this realization of the non-agent Self, while exhausting all karmas, how could it exhaust some and yet remain indifferent toward others? For it cannot be admitted that when fire and seeds are equally in contact, the seed-potency of some is destroyed while that of others is not.
To this it is replied: the arising of knowledge is possible only by depending upon the *karmāśaya* (store of karma) whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*).

And once that [knowledge] has taken hold, just as in the case of a potter’s wheel, because there is no possibility of obstruction in the midst of the momentum already set in motion, there remains the maintenance of that momentum until its exhaustion.
For even the realization of the non-agent self cuts off karmas by subverting false knowledge;
yet, even though false knowledge has been subverted, it continues for some time due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), just like the cognition of two moons.
Moreover, one should not dispute here whether the body is maintained for some time or not by one who knows Brahman;

for how could another possibly refute the knowledge of Brahman—which is realized within one's own heart—as well as the maintenance of the body by such a person? This very point is explained through the description of the characteristics of the "one of steady wisdom" (sthitaprajña) in the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
Therefore, the conclusion is that only those good and evil deeds whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed by the power of knowledge.
But the Agnihotra and other such rites are for that very purpose [of the sacrifice], because it is so seen in scripture.
In the commentary on the Sūtras (Sūtrabhāṣya), the principle applicable to sin has been extended by analogy to merit as well, concerning its non-clinging and destruction;
anticipating the objection that this extension applies to all merit whatsoever, he replies with the words "But the Agnihotra, etc. Here, the word "but" (tu) dispels that doubt.

The obligatory rite (*nitya-karma*) refers to Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra* and the like; it serves precisely for that purpose [of knowledge]. The meaning is that whatever is the effect of knowledge is indeed the effect of this [obligatory rite] as well.
Why? Because of such scriptural indications as: "Brahmins desire to know Him through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth. [Objection:

But since knowledge and action have different effects, the unity of their effect is untenable. [Reply: This is not a fault, because we observe that even curd and poison—which have the effects of fever and death respectively—when combined with molasses and mantras, produce the effects of satisfaction and nourishment; likewise, action joined with knowledge can logically have liberation as its effect.

[Objection: But liberation is something that is not produced (anārabhya); how then can it be said to be the effect of action? [Reply: This is not a fault, because action serves as a remote auxiliary (ārādupakāraka).
For it is only knowledge that brings about liberation; action is figuratively described as a cause of liberation by way of being its indirect means.
For this very reason, this statement regarding the unity of their effects refers to a subject matter already transcended.

Indeed, for one who knows Brahman, future duties such as the Agnihotra are no longer possible, because the realization of the Self as Brahman—which is not subject to injunctions—lies outside the scope of the scriptures.
In the case of meditations accompanied by qualities (*saguṇa-vidyās*), however, since the state of being an agent has not been transcended, even future rites such as the *agnihotra* are possible.
Even for that [future rite], because it is performed without desire for rewards (*nirabhisaṃdhi*) and lacks any other purpose, its connection with knowledge (*vidyā*) is logically established.

But what is the subject matter of this statement regarding non-clinging and destruction? Or what is the subject matter of this statement regarding the distribution [of works] by certain reciters of the Veda: "His sons obtain his inheritance; his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds"? To this, he reads the following reply: "For according to some, there is something else besides these two for both."

Therefore, apart from the obligatory rite of the Agnihotra and others, there is indeed another "good deed" (sādhukṛtyā) which is performed with a view toward its fruit; regarding that, the application has been stated by some reciters of the Veda: "His friends take over his good deeds. And this description of the non-clinging and destruction of that very [deed]—namely, that it is accompanied by evil—is likewise [applicable] to the other [kind of deed], such that there is no clinging for it either. Thus, both teachers, Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa, are in agreement regarding the fact that such optional (kāmya) action does not assist knowledge.
For it is said: "By knowledge alone."

This has been established in the immediately preceding section: the obligatory *agnihotra* and other such rites, when performed by one seeking liberation with liberation as their intended purpose, serve as the cause for the destruction of accumulated sins. By acting as a means to the purification of the internal organ (*sattvaśuddhi*) through the gateway of knowledge and realization (*vidyājñāna*), they function as instruments for the attainment of Brahman, which is the ultimate purpose of liberation; thus, they belong to the section concerning Brahman. It is held that they achieve a single result together with spiritual knowledge (*vidyā*).

In this regard, there exists both knowledge conjoined with the constituent parts of rituals such as the Agnihotra and knowledge that is independent [of ritual action]. This is known from such scriptural statements as: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices," "He who, knowing thus, offers oblations," "He who, knowing thus, recites," "He who, knowing thus, sings," "Therefore, one should make him who knows thus the Brahman-priest," and "Both perform [the rite]—he who knows this thus and he who does not know. Thus, there is knowledge conjoined [with action], and there is also that which is independent.

In this regard, the following is considered: Is it only the Agnihotra and other such rites conjoined with knowledge that, for one seeking liberation, serve as a cause for knowledge and thus attain the status of having a single purpose (ekakāryatva) together with it; or are they both—those conjoined with knowledge and those performed independently—equally so?

Why is there this doubt? Because of the scriptural statement, "They desire to know this very Self through sacrifice," which declares that sacrifices and the like are, without distinction, auxiliary means (*aṅga*) to the realization of the Self; and because it is understood that the Agnihotra and other rites conjoined with knowledge possess a superior status.

What, then, is the initial position? Ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* when conjoined with knowledge attain the status of being subsidiary to the knowledge of the Self, but not when devoid of knowledge; for it is understood that what is conjoined with knowledge is superior to what is devoid of knowledge, based on scriptural texts such as, "On whatever day he offers [the oblation], on that very day the knower thus overcomes death," and from traditional texts (*smṛti*) such as, "Endowed with wisdom, O Pārtha, you shall cast off the bond of action," and "For action is far inferior, O Dhanañjaya, to the yoga of wisdom. This being the position reached, it is replied: "Verily, by knowledge alone" (*yadeva vidyayā*).

This is true: ritual action such as the *agnihotra*, when conjoined with knowledge, is superior to ritual action devoid of knowledge—just as a learned Brāhmaṇa is superior to a Brāhmaṇa who lacks learning.
Nevertheless, ritual action such as the *agnihotra* that is devoid of knowledge is not entirely disregarded.

Why? Because it is heard in scripture without distinction that the *agnihotra* and other rites are causes of knowledge, in the passage: "They desire to know this very Self by means of sacrifice" (*yajñena*).

Now, it might be argued that since it is understood that the Agnihotra and other rites conjoined with knowledge are superior to those devoid of knowledge, it is logical that the Agnihotra and so forth lacking knowledge are entirely independent as causes for the knowledge of the Self. This is not so; for it is reasonable to assume that because the Agnihotra and other rites accompanied by knowledge possess an excellence of capacity due to the presence of knowledge, they will have a certain degree of causal superiority toward the knowledge of the Self, whereas that which is devoid of knowledge does not. Thus, it is proper to conclude this.

However, one cannot maintain that the Agnihotra and other rites—mentioned without distinction in the passage "They desire to know through sacrifice" as being auxiliary to the knowledge of the Self—are not auxiliary to it at all.

For the Śruti states: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣad, that alone becomes more powerful. By declaring that actions such as the Agnihotra become more powerful when conjoined with knowledge, this text expresses a certain excellence regarding their own effect and thereby demonstrates that even those same actions, when devoid of knowledge, possess power toward their intended purpose.
And the potency of an action is that which consists in its capacity to accomplish its own purpose.

Therefore, it is established that both the Agnihotra and other rites—whether conjoined with knowledge or devoid of knowledge—which were performed by one seeking liberation (mumukṣu) for the purpose of attaining liberation, either in this life or in another birth prior to the arising of knowledge, serve as causes for the realization of Brahman. This occurs through the channel of destroying the accumulated sins that act as obstacles to the attainment of Brahman according to their respective capacities; thus, depending on internal causes such as hearing, reflection, faith, and intentness, they become co-operative with the knowledge of Brahman to produce a single result. This is the conclusion reached in the Sūtra-bhāṣya.
But having exhausted the others through experience, one attains [the state].
It has been stated that merit and demerit whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed through the power of knowledge.

However, as for the other two—merit and demerit whose effects have already begun—one attains Brahman after exhausting them through experience. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in Brahman]," and "Brahman indeed, becoming Brahman, goes to Brahman," and others of this kind. This constitutes the section [on the exhaustion of karma].

Now, one might object: even when right vision (*samyagdarśana*) has arisen, just as the perception of duality persists after the fall of the body according to the analogy of seeing two moons, so too should it persist thereafter. This is not so, because the cause is absent. For in that case, the cause for persistence is the exhaustion of the remainder of karma to be experienced; and no such thing exists here. One might further object: another residual store of karma (*karmāśaya*) will initiate a new experience. This is not so, because its seed has been burnt.
For another action, supported by false knowledge, would begin another experience upon the fall of the body;

and that false knowledge has been destroyed by right knowledge—therefore, it is correct that for the knower, upon the exhaustion of the effects already commenced, liberation (kaivalya) necessarily occurs.

Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Sūtras of the Śārīraka Mīmāṃsā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas.
·G Composed by the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara-Bhagavatpāda.
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras.
The second quarter of the fourth chapter. The second quarter.
Now, desiring to introduce the path of the gods for the attainment of the fruit in other branches of knowledge, he first describes the sequence of departure according to the scriptures;
for he will state later that "the departure is the same for both the knower and the ignorant," on the grounds of the scriptural statement and the observation that speech merges into the mind.

There is a scriptural passage concerning the time of death: "My dear, when this person departs, his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity.
Here, a doubt arises: does this merging of speech into the mind refer to the organ of speech itself, or to the function of speech? Such is the uncertainty.
In this regard, it follows first that speech itself merges into the mind; for in this way the scriptural statement is upheld,
whereas otherwise there would be a figurative interpretation (lakṣaṇā).
And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), direct statement is authoritative, not indirect indication;
therefore, this dissolution of speech itself is into the mind.
This being the case, we reply: "The function of speech merges into the mind.
How can it be explained as "the function of speech," when the Teacher reads in the commentary on the Sūtra simply "speech into the mind"? This is true;
however, he will state later on: "There is non-division, according to the scriptural statement."
Therefore, it is understood that what is intended here is merely the cessation of activity.
For if the intention were the dissolution of reality, then since there is equality of non-distinction everywhere, why would he specify "non-distinction" only in the subsequent state?
Therefore, the intention here is the withdrawal of activity.
The meaning is that the function of speech is withdrawn first when the function of the mind remains present.
Why? Because it is observed; for the prior withdrawal of the function of speech is indeed seen while the function of the mind exists;
however, the withdrawal of speech itself, as a possessor of function, into the mind cannot be observed by anyone.

[Objection: But was it not stated that, by the force of the scripture, this dissolution of speech into the mind is logical? [Reply: No, he says, because it does not have that as its material cause (*atatprakṛtitvāt*). For when something originates from something else, its dissolution into that source is logical, as in the case of a clay vessel dissolving into clay; however, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to show that speech originates from the mind.
The emergence and suppression of functions, however, are observed even when they do not rely on the primary material cause (*aprakṛti*);
for instance, the function of the fiery element, fire, emerges from fuel consisting of earthly substances, and it subsides in water.
How, then, is the statement "sound merges into speech" to be understood under this view? To this, he says: "And from sound... (*śabdācca*).
The word is also applicable in this view, meaning that it is due to the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between the function and that which possesses the function.
And for this very reason, all [the subsequent rules] follow accordingly.

Regarding the passage, "Therefore, with his vitality stilled, [he goes] to a new birth through the senses merging into the mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6), it is heard here that the merging of all the senses without distinction occurs in the mind.

Even there, for the same reason as in the case of speech—namely, because when the mind remains with its functions suspended, the functions of the eyes and other organs are likewise seen to cease, and because their essential dissolution is impossible—the scriptural statement is justified only by way of the cessation of their functions; thus, all the senses follow after the mind solely through the channel of their functional activity.

Although there is no distinction in the withdrawal of all the organs into the mind, speech is mentioned separately in accordance with the scriptural example: "Speech is merged in the mind" (vāṅ manasi saṃpadyate).
That mind is the vital breath (prāṇa), according to the subsequent [scriptural passage].
It has been established that in the passage "Speech merges into the mind" (*vāṅ manasi saṃpadyate*), what is intended is the merging of the function (*vṛtti*).

Now, regarding the subsequent sentence, "The mind [merges] into breath" (*manaḥ prāṇe*), there arises a doubt: is here too the merging of the function alone intended, or the merging of the organ possessing the function? When this doubt occurs, the initial position is that it is the merging of the organ possessing the function, because this accords with the direct statement of the scripture (*śruti*).
And because it is logical that they have that as their material cause;

for thus [the scripture says]: "The mind, my dear, consists of food, and the vital breath consists of water"—thus the mind is declared to have food as its source and the vital breath to have water as its source; and the Śruti states, "Water created food."
And for this reason, when the mind is dissolved into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is actually food that is dissolved into water;
for the mind is food and the vital breath is water, due to the non-difference between a cause and its modification.

This being the position reached, we reply: it must be understood from the subsequent scriptural passage that even that mind—having withdrawn the functions of the external senses—is dissolved into the vital breath precisely through the medium of its own function.
For instance, in one who is about to fall asleep or about to die, while the vital function (prāṇavṛtti) consisting of movement remains present, no cessation of the other functions is observed;
nor is it possible for the mind to merge into the vital breath in its own essential form, because the vital breath is not the material cause of the mind.
[Objection: But was it not shown that the mind has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its material cause? [Reply: This is not sound.
For the mind cannot be said to merge into the vital breath by such a derivative causal relationship (*prāṇāḍika*);
for in that case, the mind would likewise merge into food, food into water, and the vital breath into water alone.
For even on this view, there is no evidence whatsoever that the mind is produced from water transformed into the state of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
therefore, there is no merging of the mind’s own nature (*svarūpa*) into the vital breath.

However, it has been shown that the word [“merging”] is applicable even to the merging of the function (*vṛtti*), because of the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between the function and the possessor of the function (*vṛttimant*).
But he [the individual soul] is under the supervision [of the Lord], because of such passages as "approaching Him" and others.

This has been established by direct perception: that for whatever there is no origination from something else, its functional activity (vṛtti) merges into that [source], but not its essential nature (svarūpa).

Now, this is being considered regarding the statement "the vital breath [merges] into heat" (prāṇas tejas): does the withdrawal of the function of the vital breath occur into heat alone according to the literal scriptural statement, or rather into the individual soul (jīva), who is the presiding overseer of the cage of the body and senses?

In this regard, since the Vedic text is beyond doubt, the merging of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must occur in fire alone, as it is improper to assume what is not stated in scripture. This being the position reached, the author states:

"He [rests] in the presiding [self]. That aforementioned *prāṇa* rests in the cognitional self (*vijñānātman*), which is conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and prior cognition (*pūrvaprajñā*). (Brahma Sūtra 4.2.4)
The meaning is that the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has that [the Self] as its primary object;

why? Because of the scriptural passages concerning "approaching" that [Self] and so forth. For another Śruti passage, "In this very way, at the time of death, all the vital breaths gather together toward this Self, when one becomes an upward-breather," shows without distinction that all the vital breaths follow the presiding Lord (the Self). And specifically, the passage, "As he departs, the *prāṇa* departs after him," shows that the fivefold *prāṇa* follows the presiding Lord, and that the others follow it, as in: "As the *prāṇa* departs, all the vital breaths depart after it."

And by the statement, "He becomes possessed of consciousness," which demonstrates that the presiding soul (adhyakṣa) possesses internal consciousness, it is made known that the vital breath (prāṇa), whose collection of organs has been absorbed, abides in that soul.
But is it not heard in scripture that "the breath [merges] into heat"?

How then can the addition be made that the breath is in the presiding soul? This is no fault, because the activities such as departure from the body have the presiding soul as their primary agent, and because one must also take into account the specific details found in other scriptural passages.
How then is the scriptural statement "the vital breath [merges] into heat" to be understood? To this, he says: "[The soul merges] into the elements, because that is what the scripture declares."

It should be understood that he [the soul], conjoined with the vital breath (prāṇa), abides in the subtle elements which accompany fire and serve as the seeds of the body, according to the scriptural text: "The vital breath [is merged] in fire. Now, one might object: this scripture shows the abiding of the vital breath in fire, not of the presiding soul (adhyakṣa) conjoined with the vital breath. This is not a fault, because the presiding soul is also included in the intermediate stage by the word "in the presiding soul" (adhyakṣe).
For even one who, having gone from Srughna to Mathurā, then proceeds from Mathurā to Pāṭaliputra, can indeed be said to "go from Srughna to Pāṭaliputra";
therefore, by the statement "the breath [dissolves] into heat," it is the presiding deity (adhyakṣa) conjoined with the breath that abides in the elements accompanied by heat.

How can it be said that [the soul] is associated with the elements accompanied by fire, when it is heard only of fire alone in the passage, "Breath [is merged] in fire"? To this, [the author] replies: "Not in one [element], for [the scriptures] show [it so]."
The individual soul does not abide in fire alone at the time of seeking another body, because we observe that the body, which is its effect, is composed of multiple elements.
Furthermore, this point is demonstrated by the question and answer concerning water being "human-shaped";
this has already been explained under the sūtra, "But on account of the threefold nature [of the elements], and because of their predominance."
Both Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate this point.
The Śruti says: "Consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air, consisting of ether, consisting of fire," and so forth.
Smṛti also says: "The minute, imperishable particles which are known as the fivefold [elements]..."

"By means of them all this [universe] comes into being in due succession," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: when the organs such as speech have been withdrawn at the time of seeking another body, another scriptural passage, beginning with "What does the person then become? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35), determines that action (*karman*) is the substratum, stating: "Whatever those two said, they said it because of action; and whatever they praised, they praised it because of action. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).

To this it is replied: there, it was stated that action is the substratum because the activity of the bondage—consisting of the senses and their objects and designated as "grasps" (graha) and "over-grasps" (atigraha)—is impelled by action;
here, however, the fact that the elements are the substratum is stated because the production of another body results from the appropriation of the elements.
Furthermore, even from the word "praise" (praśaṃsā) used there, only the preeminence of action is indicated, but other substrata are not excluded.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
And they are alike in that they do not attain immortality without having consumed [the fuel of meditation].

Is this departure common to both the knower and the ignorant, or is it characterized by a distinction? For those who are thus in doubt, the initial position is that it is characterized by a distinction; for this departure is indeed distinguished by its dependence on the elements as the means of transition, and the elements serve as the substratum for rebirth.
They are extinguished; moreover, rebirth is not possible for the knower, for it is an established principle that "the knower attains immortality.
Therefore, this departure belongs only to the non-knower.

[Objection: Since these are mentioned in the context of knowledge (*vidyā-prakaraṇa*), would they not pertain only to the knower? [Reply: No, because they are merely restatements of what is already established, just like sleep and so forth. For just as in the passage, "When a person here is said to sleep, is said to hunger, is said to thirst," sleep and the rest are described as common to all living beings—even though they occur within the context of knowledge—they are restated for the sake of elucidating the matter intended to be taught, and are not enjoined as specific attributes of the knower.

Thus, this departure as well is described only with reference to the common people, in order to establish that "That which is the supreme deity into which the light of a person striving for perfection merges is the Self; Thou art That.
Furthermore, this departure is denied for the knower in the text: "His vital breaths do not depart.
Therefore, this [departure] belongs only to the ignorant.

This being the case, we reply: this departure—beginning with "Speech [is merged] in the mind," and so forth—is common to both the knower and the non-knower until the commencement of the path (āsṛtyupakramāt), because there is no distinction heard in the scripture.

The non-knower, having resorted to the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which serve as the seed for the body and being impelled by karma, transmigrates while undergoing the assumption of a body; the knower, however, resorts to the door of the vein of liberation (mokṣanāḍī) revealed by knowledge. This is what is meant by the phrase "until the commencement of the path."

[Objection: Surely immortality is to be attained by the knower, and that does not depend on another place; so how can there be reliance on the elements or the commencement of a path (sṛti) in that case? [Reply: To this it is said: "And without having burned," that is, without having utterly consumed the afflictions such as ignorance and the rest, one who seeks relative immortality through the power of lower knowledge (aparavidyā)—for him, the commencement of a path is possible, as is reliance on the elements; for the movement of the vital breaths (prāṇas), which are without a support, is not logically tenable. Therefore, there is no fault.

"Until then, because of the designation of transmigratory existence. (Sūtra 4.2.7) In the passage, "The fire [is merged] in the highest deity," by virtue of the force of the context, it is stated that this very fire—along with its presiding overseer, its vital breath, its collection of organs, and the other elements—which is designated as transmigratory existence, becomes merged in the highest deity at the time of death for the person departing from the body.
This is what is meant.
Now, it is considered what kind of perfection this might be.
