In this regard, it is first established that there must be an absolute dissolution of one's own nature, because it is logical for that [Supreme Deity] to be the material cause;
for it has been proven that the Supreme Deity is the material cause of the entire multitude of things subject to birth.

Therefore, this attainment of non-distinction is absolute. This being the position reached, we reply: that subtle essence of the elements, such as light and the rest, which serves as the substratum for the instruments of perception like the ear and so forth, persists until the "dissolution" (āpīti)—that is, until liberation from saṃsāra through the cause of perfect knowledge. This is because of the scriptural descriptions of saṃsāra, such as: "Some embodied beings enter other wombs for the sake of a body; others pass into inanimate matter, according to their karma and according to their learning. Thus, [the subtle body] persists.

Otherwise, everyone would attain absolute Brahman at the very moment of death due to the cessation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); in that case, the scripture of injunctions and the scripture of knowledge (*vidyā-śāstra*) would be purposeless.
Furthermore, bondage, which is caused by false knowledge, cannot be dissolved except through right knowledge.

Therefore, even though [the soul] has that [Brahman] as its material cause, this merging into Being (*sat-sampatti*)—like deep sleep or cosmic dissolution—is characterized by the persistence of the state of being a seed.
And it is subtle by measure, because it is perceived as such.

Furthermore, that fire, accompanied by the other elements, must be subtle in its essential nature and in its dimension, serving as the substratum for the individual soul (jīva) when departing from this body. For its subtlety is understood from such scriptural indications as the departure through the channels (nāḍīs). Because of that subtlety, its movement is possible.
And because of its transparency, its lack of resistance is established;
for this very reason, it is not perceived by those standing nearby when it emerges from the body.
Not from comparison.
And for this very reason, because of its subtlety, O Lord, the other subtle body is not destroyed by the destruction of the gross body through such causes as burning and the like.
And it is because of this very reasoning that this is "heat" (ūṣman).

And this heat belongs to this very subtle body, which they perceive as warmth through touch while this living body exists. For indeed, in the state of death, although the body remains and its qualities such as form and so forth persist, no heat is perceived; yet it is perceived only in the state of life. Therefore, it is established that this heat has its basis exclusively in something distinct from the well-known physical body. And thus says the Śruti: "One who is warm shall live; one who is cold shall die."
If it be argued that [the soul is not the agent] because of a prohibition, we say no, because [the prohibition refers only to] the embodied soul.

From the qualification "and without having attained immortality," the absence of both going and departing is accepted in the case of absolute immortality; even there, however, suspecting a departure due to some cause, he prohibits it by means of a refutation. [This concludes] the section.

"One who desires, yet is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, and whose desire is the Self—for him, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart; being Brahman itself, he merges into Brahman.

If it is argued that because of this prohibition concerning the subject of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), there is no departure of the vital breaths from the body for the knower of the Supreme Brahman, we say: "No," because this prohibition regarding the departure of the vital breaths refers to the embodied self (*śārīra-ātman*), not to the body.
How is this known? From the use of the ablative case in another recension: "From him the vital breaths do not depart" (*na tasmāt prāṇā utkrāmanti*).
For the genitive case, whose general scope is relation, is restricted to a specific kind of relation by the ablative case occurring in another branch [of the Veda].
And because of its predominance, the term "from him" (tasmāt) refers to the embodied soul who is the subject of worldly prosperity and the supreme good, not to the body.
The meaning is that the vital breaths do not depart from that living soul when it seeks to rise up; rather, they remain together with it.
And for one who possesses vital breath and is traveling abroad, there occurs an exit from the body.
This being the case, it is replied: "For [the text] is clear for some."
This which was stated—that even for one who knows the Supreme Brahman there is an exit from the body because the prohibition of exit has the body as its point of departure—is not so;
for in the commentary on the Sūtras, it is clearly found among some reciters that the prohibition of exit has the body itself as its point of departure.

For instance, in the question of Ārtabhāga—"When this person dies, do the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart from him, or not?"—Yājñavalkya, having accepted the position that they do not depart by saying "No," then, in response to the doubt that "if the breaths have not departed, this one is not dead," he asserts their dissolution by stating, "Right here they are merged. To establish this, he records the swelling and so forth of the subject under discussion—the limit of departure—which is referred to by the word "he" in the passage: "He swells, he becomes bloated, and being bloated, the dead man lies there."
And these [attributes] belong to the body and not to the embodied soul;

because of that commonality, even in the passage, "Therefore the vital breaths do not depart, they are merged right here," the prohibition of departure must be explained as having the body as its point of departure through figurative identification (abhedopacāra), even though the embodied soul is primary—this being the interpretation for those who read the ablative case (*pañcamī*).

But for those who read the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the departure belonging to the wise man is what is negated; since this statement has the purpose of negating a departure that would otherwise have been expected, that departure is negated as having the body as its point of departure—that is, the departure from the body is negated, not the departure of the embodied one.

Moreover, having first shown in detail the departure and the journey through transmigratory existence regarding the ignorant person—stating: "Whether he departs from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows him out; as the vital breath follows him out, all the vital functions (prāṇas) follow him out"—and having concluded that account of the ignorant with the words "Thus indeed is he who desires," the text then designates the knower with the words "Now, he who does not desire. If, in reference to this knower as well, the text were to imply only departure [from the body], the designation would be utterly inconsistent.

Therefore, it must be explained that while departure and ascent are applicable to the case of the ignorant, they are prohibited for the case of the knower, so as to give meaning to the scriptural designation.

Furthermore, neither departure nor ascent is possible for the knower of Brahman, who has become the all-pervading Self of Brahman and whose desires and karma have been exhausted, because of the absence of any cause.
Scriptural passages of this kind, such as "Here he attains Brahman," indicate the non-existence of both going and departing.
And it is recorded in tradition as well.

Moreover, it is recorded in the *Mahābhārata* that for one who has become the Self of all beings and who perceives all beings correctly, there is an absence of both going and departing: "Even the gods are bewildered regarding the path of him who is trackless, though they seek his tracks. Now, an objection is raised: is it not true that the departure of the knower of Brahman—who has become the omnipresent Brahman-Self—is also recorded? For it is said: "Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, desiring liberation, set out toward the solar orb; having been followed by his father and called out, 'Ho!,' he responded, 'Yes! No; [this is not so].

It should be understood that this is the casting off of the body by one who is still embodied, preceded by the attainment of a specific place through the power of yoga; for this is because of the mention of being visible to all beings.
Indeed, all beings would not be able to see one who is departing while bodiless.
And thus it is concluded in that very same passage: "But Śuka, having attained a swift motion through the wind, traveled through the atmosphere."
"Having displayed his own power in the commentary on the Sūtras, he became one who has entered into all beings, as a knower of the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, there is non-existence [of the soul] at the time of departure and transmigration;
however, we shall explain the scope of the scriptural texts concerning "going" later on.
Furthermore, the sense organs and the elements, which were previously mentioned by the word "prāṇas," merge into that very same Supreme Self for one who knows the Supreme Brahman.

Why? Because the Śruti declares it to be so, just as in the case of speech and the rest: "In this very way, these sixteen parts of this spectator, having reached the Person as their goal, go to their setting."

[Objection: Is it not the case that another scriptural passage, "The fifteen parts have returned to their foundation," teaches the dissolution of the parts elsewhere than in the Supreme Self—that is, with reference to the knower? [Reply: No;
for that [passage], being dependent upon worldly convention, states that the parts consisting of earth and so forth merely return to their own respective primal sources, such as the earth itself.
The other [passage], however, is dependent upon the realization of the knower, stating that for one who knows the Supreme Brahman, the entire collection of parts becomes Brahman alone.
Therefore, there is no fault.
There is no division [of the soul] because of the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, regarding the dissolution of the parts of the wise one, does it occur with a remainder as it does for others, or rather without a remainder?
In this regard, since the general nature of dissolution might suggest the possibility of a residual power remaining, [the author] declares: "It is indeed the attainment of non-distinction."
Why? Because there is no mention of non-distinction.

For, having spoken of the dissolution of the *kalās*, the text says: "Their names and forms are split apart; he is called simply 'the Person' (puruṣa); he becomes partless and immortal. Thus ends the section.
Furthermore, it is not possible for the parts characterized by ignorance to remain as a residue during the dissolution that is characterized by knowledge;
therefore, there is indeed non-distinction.

The flame at the tip of that abode blazes up; its door being illuminated by that [flame], [the soul]—favored by the one dwelling in the heart, through the power of knowledge and through the application of recollection of the path which is its remainder—proceeds by means of the artery that exceeds the hundred.
The reason [for this discussion] is as follows: the incidental investigation concerning the higher knowledge (paravidyā) has been concluded;
now, however, he continues the investigation specifically regarding the subject of the lower knowledge (aparavidyā).
It has been stated that the departure of both the knower and the ignorant is the same up to the commencement of the path (sṛti); he now demonstrates that commencement of the path.

For the conscious self (vijñānātman) who desires to depart and has withdrawn the aggregate of speech and the other organs, the heart is the abode or locus; for the scripture states, "Taking these particles of light with him, he descends into the heart itself. Furthermore, departure is heard of as being preceded by the flaming up of that [heart] and having its point of departure in the locations of the eyes and so forth: "The tip of his heart shines forth; by that light this self departs, either through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body. (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya).

Regarding the doubt as to whether this [departure] occurs without any restriction for both the knower and the ignorant, or if there is some specific restriction for the knower—wherein, since there is no distinction in the scripture, the lack of restriction might initially appear to be established—it is replied: although the illumination of the tip of the heart and the opening of the door illuminated by that light are the same for both the knower and the ignorant, the knower departs only from the location of the crown of the head, whereas others depart from other locations.
Why? Because of the power of knowledge (*vidyā*).

If even a wise person were to depart from some part of the body other than [the crown], he would not attain the exalted world, and in that case, knowledge would be utterly useless. Furthermore, because of the practice of recollecting the path which is subsidiary to that [knowledge], one must cultivate the path connected to the cranial artery (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*), which is prescribed as a subsidiary to specific forms of knowledge; it is logical that by practicing that [path], one departs by means of that very [artery].

Therefore, favored by Brahman who dwells in the heart and has been well-worshipped, the wise man, having attained that state, departs through the hundred-and-first artery—that which exceeds the hundred—specifically through the one at the crown of the head; others depart through the other arteries.

For thus they declare, with reference to the knowledge of the Heart (Hārdavidyā): "There are a hundred and one arteries of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head. Going upwards by that, one attains immortality; the others serve for departing in various directions."
Following the Rays. This is the fourth chapter.
There is the knowledge of the Heart (Hārdavidyā), which was enjoined beginning with the words, "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace";
and in the context of that [knowledge], beginning with the words, "Now, these channels of the heart which extend upwards as rays," the subject is treated in its full setting.

Having stated the connection between the vein and the rays in the passage, "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays," and having further stated, "Going upwards by those two, he attains immortality," it is understood that departing through the vein numbered as the hundred-and-first, he departs following the rays.

Now, when there arises a doubt as to whether the soul's following of the rays occurs without distinction—both by day and by night—or only during the day, we first maintain the thesis that the soul follows the rays without distinction, because the scripture mentions this without making such a distinction.
If it be argued that [the soul] does not exist at night, we say no; for the connection [of the soul with the body] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture also demonstrates this.

If it be argued that because there is a connection between the channels (*nāḍī*) and the rays of light, the deceased would follow the rays only during the day; whereas for one who dies at night, this would not occur due to the severance of the connection between the channels and the rays—[we reply: no, for the connection between the channels and the rays persists as long as the body exists. Indeed, the contact between the vessels and the rays lasts for as long as the body endures.
And scripture demonstrates this point: "From yonder sun they spread out; they enter into these channels; from these channels they spread out; they enter into yonder sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.2).
Furthermore, even during the nights of the summer season, the persistence of rays is perceived through the observation of effects such as heat;
their persistence is merely slight and thus difficult to discern during the nights of other seasons, just as it is on cloudy days in the winter.
And the text, "He places him thus during the night," shows this very point.

For if one who has died at night were to ascend upwards even without following the rays, the instruction regarding the following of the rays would be rendered purposeless; for it is not stated specifically that "he who dies by day ascends upwards by depending on the rays, whereas he who dies at night does so without depending on them."

If, however, even a knower were not to ascend upwards merely because of the fault of dying at night—on the grounds that knowledge has only an occasional fruit—then there would be no engagement in it at all, since there is no fixed rule for the time of death.

Furthermore, if one who has passed away at night were to wait for the arrival of day, even upon the arrival of day his body might somehow lack connection with the rays [of the sun] due to contact with fire or other elements.
Moreover, the scripture, in stating, "As quickly as he might direct his mind, so far does he go to the sun," shows that there is no waiting.
Therefore, this following of the rays occurs day and night without any distinction.
And for this reason, [the same applies] even during the southern course.

For this very reason—because waiting [for a specific time] is illogical, because knowledge has non-exclusive results, and because death occurs at an indefinite time—a wise person who dies even during the southern course of the sun (dakṣiṇāyana) certainly attains the fruit of knowledge. This is because the excellence of dying during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) does not imply that the southern course is ineffective; furthermore, we observe Bhīṣma’s waiting [for the northern course], as established in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras].

Based on the Vedic text, "From the bright fortnight, he goes northward through the months," there arises the doubt that the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) must be awaited; this doubt the author dispels with this Sūtra.
The well-known excellence [of the northern solstice] pertains to those who lack knowledge;
Bhīṣma’s waiting was for the purpose of maintaining established custom and for the purpose of demonstrating his power over death obtained through the grace of his father.
The meaning of the scripture, however, he will state [later] in the sūtra: "The [deities] are conducting [souls], because of the indicative mark thereof."
And these two are taught in the Smṛti with respect to yogins.

Now, it might be objected: since the Smṛti begins by emphasizing the primacy of time—stating, "O bull of the Bharatas, I shall declare that time at which departing yogins go either to non-return or to return"—and specifies particular times such as the day for the sake of non-return, how can one who departs during the night or during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) attain non-return? To this it is replied: This application of specific times such as the day and so forth is prescribed in the Smṛti for the sake of non-return with reference to yogins.
Moreover, these two—Yoga and Sāṅkhya—are based on Smṛti, not on Śruti;

therefore, due to the difference in subject matter and the difference in the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), this application of time from Smṛti has no bearing upon the cognitions derived from Śruti in the Sūtras and Bhāṣya.
Now, [one might object]: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice..."

Since these two paths—the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*)—which are known from Śruti as "smoke, night, and likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern solstice," are recognized even in Smṛti, it is said in response: having raised the objection that there is a contradiction because Smṛti makes a promise regarding time in the words "I shall declare that time," this resolution is stated.
However, when in Smṛti also the deities such as Fire (*agni*) and so forth are understood as the conductors (*ātivāhika*), then there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā Sūtras, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka).
The Commentary on the Brahma-Sūtras composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. Chapter Four, Third Section. Third Section.
It has been stated that the departure [of the soul] is the same for all because it begins with the same path (*sṛti*).

However, that path is heard of in various ways in other scriptural texts: one [path] is by way of the connection between the channels (*nāḍī*) and the rays of light, as in "Then he ascends upwards by these very rays";
another is beginning with light (*arci*), as in "They reach the light, from the light to the day."
"Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni"—this is one [text];
"When a person departs from this world, he comes to Vāyu"—this is another;
and "They go forth, free from passion, through the door of the sun"—this is yet another.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: are these paths mutually distinct, or is there only one path with multiple qualifying attributes?
On this point, the initial position is that these paths are indeed distinct, because they occur in different contexts and because they belong to different meditations (*upāsana*).

Furthermore, the restrictive emphasis in the phrase "then by these very rays" would be contradicted if there were an expectation of the path beginning with light (*arciḥ*), and the statement regarding speed—"as quickly as one could cast one's mind, so quickly does he go to the sun"—would also be undermined.
Therefore, these paths are indeed mutually distinct.
This being the position reached, we reply in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: "By the path beginning with light (arcis), he is led forth."
"By the path beginning with light" means:
we maintain that everyone who desires to attain Brahman departs by the very path beginning with light.
Why? Because of its renown.
For this path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) is well known to all the wise;

thus, for instance, in the section on the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), in the context of the knowledge of the five fires, it is declared that even those who practice other forms of knowledge— namely, "those who in the forest worship faith as the truth"— follow the path beginning with light.

It might be argued: "In those knowledges where no path whatsoever is mentioned, let this path beginning with 'light' (arcis) apply; but in those others where a different path is heard of, why should there be recourse to the path beginning with light? To this we reply: This would be so if these paths were absolutely distinct. However, we maintain that this is one and the same path leading to the world of Brahman, which possesses many attributes and is characterized in various places by different attributes. This is because we recognize identical elements throughout, and because it is logical for the attributes to stand in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified.

For even when there is a difference in the context (*prakaraṇa*), if the knowledge (*vidyā*) is one and the same, there occurs a combination of the specific attributes of one with those of the other, just as there is a combination of the specific attributes of the path; however, even when the knowledge differs, because of the recognition of a portion of the path and because of the non-difference of the goal to be reached, there is indeed no difference in the path. For instance: "In those worlds of Brahman they dwell, supreme over the supreme distances"; "In that [world] they dwell for eternal years"; "Whatever victory and whatever splendor belong to Brahman, that victory he wins and that splendor he attains"; "And those who reach this... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5).
And in various places, such as "He attains the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy," that very same single fruit characterized by the attainment of the world of Brahman is shown.

As for the objection that the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by these alone" would not apply if the path beginning with light (*arcis*) were resorted to—this is not a fault; for this [particle] has the purpose of securing the attainment of the rays, since a single word cannot both secure the rays and exclude the path beginning with light.
Therefore, it should be understood that this refers specifically to the connection with the rays.

Furthermore, the mention of "speed" is not contradicted even when there is a dependence on the stages such as light (arcis) and so forth, because it is intended in relation to other destinations, just as one might say, "He arrives here in the mere twinkling of an eye.

Moreover, by stating that for those who have fallen away from either of these two paths there is a "terrible third place," the text [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8] proclaims a single Devayāna path—distinct from the Pitṛyāṇa—that consists of the stages beginning with light.
The stages of the path are more numerous in the process of creation beginning with light (arcir-ādi), whereas they are fewer elsewhere;
and since it is logical to lead the few in accordance with the many, for this reason also it has been stated that "it is known through that [path] beginning with light."
The air [is merged] after the year, by way of both the non-specific and the specific.

Furthermore, by what specific arrangement do these particular stages of the journey stand in a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified? To answer this, the Teacher, acting as a friend, first explains the stage of Vāyu. In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, the path of the gods (*devayānaḥ panthāḥ*) is recited by the Kauṣītakins as follows: "Having reached this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni, he comes to the world of Vāyu, he comes to the world of Varuṇa, he comes to the world of Indra, he comes to the world of Prajāpati, he comes to the world of Brahmā."
In this regard, since the words "light" (*arcis*) and "day" (*ahaḥ*) both denote fire, they have the same meaning; therefore, no particular order of sequence needs to be sought between them.

However, as for the question of at which point on the path beginning with light the "wind" (*vāyu*) is to be placed, it is said: "They go to the light, from the light to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight, from the waxing fortnight to the six months when the sun moves northward, from those months to the year, and from the year to the sun. From this, it follows that they reach the wind after the year and before the sun.
Why? Because of the general and the specific.

For instance, in the passage "He [reaches] the world of Vāyu," although Vāyu is taught without specification, a specific instruction regarding him is seen in another scriptural text: "When a person departs from this world, he reaches Vāyu; for him, Vāyu makes way there as the hole of a chariot wheel; through that, he ascends upwards and reaches Āditya.
Because of this observation of Vāyu’s precedence over Āditya, Vāyu must be placed specifically in the interval between the rain-cloud (Abda) and Āditya.
But why, since air is seen to come after fire, is it not placed immediately after the flame? We reply that there is no such distinction here.
[Objection: But has not the scripture been cited: "Having reached this path of the gods, he goes to the world of fire, then to the world of air, then to the world of Varuṇa"?
[Reply: It is said in response: In this case, there is merely a sequential enumeration of names; there is no word here expressing a specific order of succession.
For in this [section], the fourth chapter merely presents the subject matter, stating, "He goes to this and that";
whereas in the other [section], the sequence is understood as: "Having ascended upwards through a hole the size of a chariot wheel provided by Vāyu, he reaches the sun."
Therefore, it is well said: "by way of both the non-specific and the specific.
However, the Vājasaneyins record: "From the months to the world of the gods, from the world of the gods to the sun.
In that case, for the sake of immediate succession to the sun, they should pass from the world of the gods to Vāyu.
The statement "from the year to the air" (vāyum abdāt), however, was made with reference to the Chāndogya Śruti.
In the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka, however, the world of the gods (devaloka) is not mentioned in one place, while the year is mentioned in the other;
therefore, based on the authority of both Śrutis, both must be inserted in both places.
Even there, because of the connection with months, one must distinguish that the eastern and western worlds belong to the year [of the gods].
Varuṇa is superior to the lightning, on account of their relationship.

The reason is this: after the passage "from the sun to the moon, from the moon to lightning," this Varuṇa mentioned in the phrase "he [reaches] the world of Varuṇa" would be connected to that lightning;
for there exists a connection between lightning and Varuṇa.

For when vast flashes of lightning, accompanied by the roar of intense thunder, dance within the bellies of the clouds, then the waters fall; and there is a Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "It lightens, it thunders, or it will rain";
furthermore, Varuṇa is well known as the lord of the waters according to both Śruti and Smṛti.
Indra and Prajāpati follow Varuṇa because there is no other place for them and due to the force of the textual sequence;
furthermore, because they are adventitious, Varuṇa and the others are placed at the very end, as there is no specific intermediate position for them;
and lightning is the last in the path beginning with light (arcis).
The subtle bodies are [of this nature] because of the scriptural indication.
Regarding these very [stages] beginning with light (*arcis*), there arises a doubt: are these signs of the path, or stages of enjoyment, or rather leaders who conduct the travelers?

On this point, the initial position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that light and the others are intermediate beings (*ātivāhika*) characterized as such on the path, because the instruction is given in terms of their own nature.

For just as in the world someone setting out for a village or a city is instructed: "Go from here to that mountain, then to the banyan tree, then to the river, then to the village, or then you will reach the city"—so too here [the text] says, "From the flame to the day, to the waxing fortnight," and so forth.
Alternatively, it follows that these are "lands of enjoyment" (bhogabhūmi);
for indeed, by means of the word "world" (loka), it connects them with Agni and the others, as in "He goes to the world of Agni," and so on.
Furthermore, the word "world" (loka) is used to denote the abodes of enjoyment for living beings, as in "the world of men, the world of the fathers, the world of the gods";
likewise, the Brāhmaṇa says, "They become attached to those worlds, namely, days and nights," and so forth.
Therefore, the stages beginning with light (arcis) are not conducting deities.
Furthermore, because they are insentient, it is untenable that they should be conducting deities;
for in the world, it is sentient persons appointed by a king who conduct those to be conducted along difficult paths.
This being the case, we reply: these must indeed be conducting deities.
Why? Because of that characteristic mark (*liṅga*);
for thus [the text] shows the state of being one who leads as an established fact: "From the moon to lightning; there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman."

If it is argued that this statement is exhausted by referring only to those [beings], we say no; for the qualification is intended to exclude the state of being human (mānavatva) which has been previously established.
If the persons who lead through the path of light (arciḥ-ādi) were understood to be human (mānava), then it would be appropriate to use the qualification "non-human" (amānava) to exclude them.
But surely that mere mark is not a means of knowledge, because there is no logical justification;
this is not a fault, since its establishment follows from the mutual delusion of both parties.

Those who travel by the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*) have their collection of organs (*karaṇagrāma*) condensed upon separation from the body; thus they are not independent. Furthermore, since light and the others are insentient, they lack independence. Therefore, it is understood that specific conscious deities presiding over light and the rest are appointed for the journey beyond.
For even in the world, those who are intoxicated or in a swoon, having their organs condensed, proceed according to the direction of others.
Moreover, because light and the others are not permanent, it is not logical for them to constitute the definition of the path.
For it is not possible for a deceased person to encounter the nature of day at night;
nor is there any waiting, as has been stated previously.
However, because the deities are eternal, this defect does not apply to them.
And their designation by terms such as "light" (*arcis*) is appropriate because they identify themselves with light and so forth.

Furthermore, the specific mention in the text—"from light to day," and so on—is not contradicted even if they are conducting deities (*ātivāhika*); for [the meaning is] that one reaches day by means of light as the cause, and reaches the waxing fortnight by means of day as the cause.
Likewise, even in the case of well-known conducting deities in the world, such a mode of instruction is observed: "Go from here to Balavarman, then to Jayasiṃha, then to Kṛṣṇagupta."
Moreover, at the beginning [of the passage], it is merely stated that "they reach the light" (*te 'rcir abhisaṃbhavanti*), without specifying any particular nature of that connection;

however, in the conclusion, it is stated that "he leads them to Brahman" (*sa etān brahma gamayati*), which specifies the particular nature of the connection as being characterized by the relationship between those to be conveyed and the conveyer. Therefore, it is determined that this same relationship holds at the beginning as well.
Furthermore, because their sensory organs are withdrawn into a state of integration (*saṃpiṇḍita-karaṇatva*), no experience of enjoyment is possible for the travelers there.

The word "world" (loka), however, can be applied even to those who do not themselves enjoy [the results], because other inhabitants of that world constitute the ground for enjoyment. Therefore, it should be understood that one who has reached the world presided over by Agni is led across by Agni, and one who has reached the world presided over by Vāyu is led across by Vāyu.

But how, on the view that [the soul] is led by a guide (*ātivāhika*), can such a guide exist in relation to Varuṇa and the others? For Varuṇa and the rest are introduced as being beyond lightning, whereas immediately after lightning, until the attainment of Brahman, the scripture declares that only a non-human person (*amānava*) is the one who leads. To this, the author reads the following reply: "By the one belonging to lightning alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (Sūtra 4.3.6)

Therefore, after emerging from the lightning, being conducted by an amānava (non-human) person who exists immediately beyond the lightning through the worlds of Varuṇa and others, they go to the world of Brahman; this is to be understood from the fourth chapter [of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad], because that very person is heard in scripture to be the conductor: "From the lightning, a non-human person comes and leads them to the world of Brahman. As for Varuṇa and the others, they are to be understood as mere benefactors who assist him by either removing obstacles or performing some form of aid.
Therefore, it has been rightly stated that the deities beginning with *arciḥ* are of a transportative nature (*ātivāhika*).
The body is its instrument, because the occurrence of its movement is thereby established.
The means of proof.
Regarding the passage, "He leads them to Brahman," a doubt arises: does he lead them to the effected (kārya) lower Brahman, or rather to the supreme, unmodified, primary, and non-effected Brahman?
Why is there this doubt? Because of the use of the word "Brahman" and because of the scriptural mention of "going."
Regarding this, the teacher Bādari maintains that it is the effected Brahman itself—the lower Brahman endowed with qualities—that the non-human person leads them to.
Why? Because going is possible for this [effected Brahman]; for it is logical that the effected Brahman is a destination, since it occupies a specific location.

However, in the case of the supreme Brahman, neither the state of being a goer, nor the state of being a destination, nor the act of going is conceivable, because it is all-pervading and because it is the inner self of the goers themselves.
And because of being specified.

Furthermore, because it is specified in another scriptural passage—“He leads them to the worlds of Brahman; they dwell in those worlds of Brahman, in the highest high regions”—it is understood that the journey mentioned in the Sūtra and its commentary has as its object the effected (kārya) Brahman. For a qualification by means of the plural number is not appropriate for the supreme (para) Brahman;
however, in the case of the effected [Brahman], the plural number is possible because of the existence of different states.
Even common worldly usage of the term "world" (loka) applies directly only to a place of experience characterized by a specific arrangement and falling within the sphere of transformation;
in other instances, such as "This world, O Emperor, is Brahman itself," the usage is figurative.
Furthermore, the designation of a locus and a subject would not be direct if applied to the supreme Brahman.
Therefore, this visual perception has only the effect as its object.

But surely, even with respect to the effect, the term "Brahman" is not appropriate; for it has been established in the section on "Coherence" (Samanvaya) that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the entire world. To this, it is replied: "But that designation [of the effect] is due to proximity."
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing a doubt:
because of its proximity to the Supreme Brahman, the application of the term "Brahman" to the lower Brahman is not contradictory even in that case.

For it is the established position that the Supreme Brahman itself, when connected with pure limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and taught for the sake of meditation through certain transformational attributes such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), is designated as the "lower" Brahman.
But surely, if the effect [of liberation] is attained, the scriptural teaching of non-return would not be possible;
for they do not conceive of eternity anywhere other than in the supreme Brahman.

Moreover, scripture shows that those who have set out on the path of the gods do not return: "Those who proceed by this way do not return to this human whirlpool," and "For them there is no return here. Thus ends the fourth chapter.

And [it is said]: "Going upwards from these two, he attains immortality. To this we reply: because it is stated that upon the dissolution of the effect, he goes beyond that [world] together with its presiding deity.
And because of the Smṛti.

When the dissolution of the effected Brahman-world (kāryabrahmaloka) is imminent, those who have attained right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) right there, together with Hiraṇyagarbha—the presiding lord of that world—proceed from there to the supremely pure, highest station of Viṣṇu. Thus, gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) must be accepted on the basis of scriptural declarations such as "non-return" (*anāvṛtti*).
For it has been established that the attainment of the Supreme cannot possibly occur immediately, preceded by a journey.

Smṛti also confirms this meaning: "When the dissolution has arrived, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahman]. Therefore, the established conclusion is that the scriptural texts concerning the journey refer exclusively to the effected (kārya) Brahman.

But what was the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) suspected of being the case, against which this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) beginning with "The effect [is Brahman], according to Bādari" was set forth? That [view] is now presented by means of the sūtras themselves: "The one intent on instruction [is the object], because Jaimini considers him to be primary."
The teacher Jaimini, however, maintains in the *Sūtrabhāṣya* that in the passage "He leads them to Brahman," it is the Supreme Brahman that he causes them to attain;
why? Because of its primacy.
For the Supreme Brahman is the primary referent (*mukhya-ālambana*) of the word "Brahman," whereas the lower [Brahman] is secondary (*gauṇa*).
And between the primary and the secondary meanings, it is the primary meaning that is understood.
And because it is seen [in scripture].

Furthermore, the passage "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality" (KaṭhU 2.3.18) shows that immortality is preceded by a journey; and immortality is possible only in the case of the supreme Brahman, not in the case of a created effect, because a created effect is perishable, as stated in the scriptural teaching: "But where one sees something else, that is the finite, that is mortal" (KaṭhU 2.4.11). Moreover, this journey is taught in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad as having the supreme Brahman as its object; for there is no introduction of another knowledge there, since it is the supreme Brahman itself that has been introduced with the words, "Other than dharma, other than adharma" (KaṭhU 2.14).
And there is no intention to engage with the effect.

Moreover, the intention behind the statement, "O Prajāpati, I enter your assembly-hall and dwelling," does not concern the effected [body], because it is the supreme Brahman itself—distinct from the effected—that is the subject under discussion, as seen in the passage: "That which is within the two, by which the two are sustained, that is Brahman.
Furthermore, the discourse begins with the idea of being the self of all in the words, "I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas";
and it is well known that the name "Glory" (Yaśas) belongs to the supreme Brahman alone, as in the text: "There is no image of Him whose name is Great Glory."
And this attainment of the abode mentioned in the *Hārdavidyā*— "That unconquered city of Brahman, the golden, well-measured palace" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3)— is preceded by a journey;
for since the root *pad* also signifies "going," it is understood that a path is required.
Therefore, there is another position: that the scriptural texts concerning "going" (gati) have as their object the supreme Brahman.
These two positions were set forth by the Teacher [Bādarāyaṇa] in the Sūtras: one based on the possibility of going and so forth, and the other based on primacy and so forth.

In this regard, the arguments for the possibility of going and so forth are capable of casting the arguments for primacy and so forth into the appearance of fallaciousness, but the arguments for primacy and so forth are not capable of casting the arguments for the possibility of going and so forth into the appearance of fallaciousness; thus, the first alone has been explained as the final conclusion (siddhānta), while the second is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
For there exists no one who can issue a command that the primary meaning alone must be accepted even when its occurrence is impossible.

Furthermore, even within the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), the mention of the path belonging to other forms of knowledge is appropriate for the purpose of praising that [higher knowledge], just as in the passage: "The others go in all directions upon departing.

As for the statement, "I enter the assembly hall, the dwelling of Prajāpati," there is no contradiction in the intention to reach the effected [Brahman] (*kārya*) by interpreting it as a separate sentence from the preceding one.

Moreover, even with respect to Brahman as possessing qualities, the proclamation of its being the self of all—as in the passage "possessing all works, possessing all desires," and so forth—is entirely appropriate.
Therefore, the scriptural texts concerning the journey [to Brahman] have only the lower Brahman as their object.

Furthermore, some, adhering to the established rule that the preceding [sūtras] are prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the subsequent ones are conclusive doctrines (*siddhānta*), maintain that the scriptural texts concerning "going" refer exclusively to other objects [than Brahman].
That is untenable, because it is impossible for Brahman to be something to be gone to.

That Supreme Brahman—which is all-pervading, the innermost essence of all, and the self of all, as determined by such scriptural texts as "All-pervading and eternal like space," "The Brahman which is immediate and direct," "The Self that is within all," "This whole world is indeed the Self," and "Brahman alone is this entire universe, the most excellent"—can never logically be an object to be reached. For that which has already been reached cannot itself be the goal of movement;
it is well known in the world that one person goes to another who is different from them.

[Objection: Is it not observed in the world that even for one who has already gone, there remains something yet to be gone to, as distinguished by another location—for example, one who stands on the earth itself goes to the earth by way of another location? Likewise, even though there is non-difference [of the self], old age—which is distinguished by a later time—is seen to be the very thing to be reached by the child, being his own self; similarly, since Brahman is endowed with all powers, it might somehow be something to be reached. [Reply: No, because all distinctions have been denied of Brahman.

From such scriptural passages, traditional texts, and logical arguments as "partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19), "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8), "He is indeed both within and without, unborn; He is this great unborn Self, ageless, deathless, immortal, fearless Brahman; He is this Self defined as 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), it is impossible to conceive of the Supreme Self as being connected with distinctions such as space and time, by virtue of which it could become an object to be reached—according to the analogy of reaching a particular location on earth or a particular stage of life.
For it is only in the case of the earth and age that being an object to be reached characterized by space and time is possible, due to their connection with specific distinctions of place and state.

If it is argued that Brahman possesses manifold powers because the scripture declares it to be the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world, we say no; for the scriptural texts that negate specific distinctions have no other purpose.
If it is argued that the texts concerning origin and so forth likewise have no other purpose, we say no; for those texts are intent upon establishing [Brahman's] oneness.
[Sūtra 4.4] Fourth Chapter.

Indeed, by means of analogies such as clay and the like, the scripture—establishing that the one existent Brahman alone is real while its modification is unreal—cannot have production and so forth as its primary purport.

As for the question of whether the scriptural texts concerning rebirth due to karma are supplementary to those texts that negate distinctions, rather than the other way around, it is said: because the texts negating distinctions have their purpose fully satisfied.

For once there is the realization of the Self’s oneness, eternity, purity, and so forth, no further desire arises, since the conviction that the human goal has been attained has been produced. As it is said: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7); "O Janaka, you have indeed reached fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4); and "The knower fears nothing at all. Truly, this does not afflict him. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).

This is because of scriptural passages such as, "Why did I not do what is good? Why did I commit sin? and because we observe that those who possess knowledge experience contentment and the like; furthermore, there is the censure of the false conception of modifications in the passage, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity.
Therefore, it is impossible to understand that the scriptural texts which negate distinctions are subsidiary to anything else.
The scriptural passages concerning origination and so forth do not possess the capacity to convey a meaning that leaves no further expectancy;
rather, their purpose as having another aim is clearly perceived through direct observation.

For instance, having introduced the subject with the words, "Know this sprout, my dear, that has sprung up here; it will not be without a root," the text shows at the conclusion that the single Existent alone is to be known as the root of the world.
"From which indeed these beings are born;
by which, once born, they live;
into which they enter upon departing."
And [the scripture says], "Seek to know that;
that is Brahman.
Thus, since the scriptural texts concerning origination and so forth have as their ultimate purpose the realization of the identity of the Self, Brahman does not possess multiple powers.
And for this reason, the possibility of going is untenable.

Furthermore, the texts "His vital breaths do not depart" and "Being Brahman, he goes to Brahman" preclude any movement toward the supreme Brahman; this has already been explained under the sūtra "For it is clear to some."

Furthermore, in the conceptualization of motion, the living soul (*jīva*) as the goer must be either a part (*avayava*), a modification (*vikāra*), or something other than Brahman, the goal of the journey; for if there were absolute identity, motion would be impossible.

If this were so, what would follow? To this it is said: if [the soul] were a single part, then because that part is eternally attained by the possessor of the parts, further motion toward Brahman would be untenable.
Moreover, the conceptualization of "part" and "possessor of parts" is untenable in the case of Brahman, since Brahman is well-known to be partless.
This [objection] applies equally even to the view that [the soul] is a modification (*vikāra*), because the modifier (*vikārin*) is eternally attained through its non-modification;
for a jar does not exist having abandoned its nature as clay, nor would it do so if it did abandon it, since that would result in its non-existence.

Furthermore, on the views that [the soul] is either a modification or a part, the soul's transition into transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is impossible, because that which possesses those [modifications or parts]—namely, Brahman—is eternal.
Now, if the individual soul (jīva) were indeed different from Brahman, it would have to be either atomic, all-pervading, or of intermediate size.
If it were all-pervading, its movement [from one body to another] would be impossible;
and if it were of intermediate size, the consequence of non-eternality would follow.
If [the soul] were atomic, the experience of sensation throughout the entire body would be impossible;
and since both atomicity and intermediate magnitude have been refuted in detail previously in the fourth chapter.
Furthermore, if the individual soul were different from [Brahman], there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting such scriptural teachings as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
This same defect applies equally to the views that the soul is either a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) [of Brahman].
If it is argued that there is no fault because a modification or a part is non-different from its substrate, we say no; for in that case, literal oneness (*mukhya-ekatva*) is untenable.

And in all these positions, there follows the consequence of non-liberation, because the transmigrating nature of the self has not ceased; or, if it were to cease, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of its own nature, since the identity with Brahman is not admitted.

As for what some prattle—that obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites are performed to prevent the arising of transgression (*pratyavāya*), optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) acts are avoided to prevent the attainment of heaven or hell, and those actions whose fruits are to be experienced in the present body are exhausted by that very experience; therefore, after the fall of the current body, due to the absence of any cause for the reconnection with another body, liberation (*kaivalya*) characterized as abiding in one's own true nature will be achieved even without the realization of Brahman for one who conducts himself thus—that is incorrect, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
For this has not been established by any scripture that "one seeking liberation should conduct oneself in this manner.
Rather, this was merely conjectured by one's own intellect: "Since transmigratory existence is caused by karma, it will cease to exist due to the absence of its cause.
And this cannot be so conjectured, because the absence of a cause is difficult to ascertain.

For indeed, many actions accumulated over various previous births, which have desirable and undesirable results, are possible for every single living being. Since it is impossible to experience those actions of contradictory fruits simultaneously, some of them—having found their opportunity—fashion this present birth, while others remain awaiting specific place, time, and cause. Therefore, because it is impossible to exhaust those remaining actions through the experience of the present life alone, one cannot conclude with certainty that even for one whose conduct has been as described, there will be an absence of causes for another body upon the fall of the current body.

Furthermore, the existence of a remainder of karma is established by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Those here whose conduct has been pleasant, they [proceed] from there with what remains," and so forth.
It might be argued that the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites will serve as the destroyers of those [karmic residues]; but that is not so, because there is no contradiction.
For the relationship between that which is to be destroyed and its destroyer exists only when a contradiction is present.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction between meritorious deeds accumulated in other births and the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, because they are alike in their nature as being pure (*śuddhi*).
However, since evil deeds (*durita*) are of the nature of impurity (*aśuddhi*), there may indeed be a destruction of them when a contradiction arises;

yet, by that much alone, the absence of a cause for another body is not established, because it is possible for [the body] to have merit as its cause, and because it is not understood that even evil deeds are destroyed without remainder.

Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence to suggest that the performance of obligatory and occasional rites results merely in the non-occurrence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) and not in the production of some other fruit (*phalāntara*), for it is possible that another fruit arises as a byproduct (*anuniṣpādin*).
Indeed, Āpastamba records: "Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as well, so too when dharma is practiced, worldly benefits (*artha*) arise."

Moreover, in the absence of perfect vision (*samyagdarśana*), it is impossible for anyone—between birth and death—to vow to completely avoid all actions that are either desired or prohibited, for even the most skillful are seen to commit subtle transgressions;
indeed, such a matter remains open to doubt.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, Fourth Chapter).
Nevertheless, the non-existence of the causal sign (*nimitta*) is indeed difficult to know.

Furthermore, if the identity of Brahman and the Self—which is accessible through knowledge—is not accepted, it is impossible to desire the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Self whose very nature is that of agent and enjoyer; for its nature, like the heat of fire, cannot be avoided. It might be argued: "The evil consists in the effects of agency and enjoyment, not in their potentiality (*śakti*); therefore, even if the potentiality remains, liberation is possible through the avoidance of the effects. But that is not so.
For when a capacity exists, the production of its effect is unavoidable.
Now, it might be argued that a capacity does not initiate an effect on its own without depending on other causal conditions;

therefore, even though it remains solitary, it is not at fault. But that is not so, because the causal conditions themselves are eternally connected to the capacity through a relationship characterized by that very capacity.

Therefore, as long as the self possesses the nature of being an agent and an enjoyer, and as long as the state of being Brahman—the Self—is not realized through knowledge, there can be no hope whatsoever for liberation.
Furthermore, the Śruti, stating "There is no other path for going," excludes any path to liberation other than knowledge.

If it is argued that even if the individual soul (*jīva*) were non-different from the Supreme, all worldly transaction would necessarily cease because the means of valid cognition such as perception would no longer function, we say: no, for that is possible just as worldly transactions occur in a dream prior to awakening.

Furthermore, the Scripture, having described the operation of perception and other means in the state of the unawakened with passages such as, "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another," subsequently demonstrates the absence of such [dualistic] activity in the state of the awakened with passages such as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15). Thus, the Sūtra-bhāṣya [establishes this].
Thus, since the cognition of a destination and so forth is sublated for one who knows the supreme Brahman, a journey can in no way be established.
To what object, then, do the scriptural texts concerning the journey refer? It is said: they will have as their object the meditations on the qualified Brahman (saguṇavidyā).

For instance—in some places, the journey is described with reference to the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā); in others, with reference to the knowledge of the couch (paryaṅkavidyā); and in others, with reference to the knowledge of Vaiśvānara.

Even where a destination (gati) is mentioned with reference to Brahman—as in "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman" and "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace"—there too, because it is the qualified Brahman alone that is to be meditated upon through attributes such as being the "leader of blessings" (vāmanī) and having "true desires" (satyakāma), a destination is possible.
Nowhere is a destination regarding the supreme Brahman heard of; rather, the denial of a destination is proclaimed: "His vital breaths do not depart."

In passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavidāpnoti param*), however, although the root *āp* has the sense of "going," it must be understood that—given the impossibility of reaching another location according to the reasoning already described—this is merely the realization of one's own true nature, spoken of with reference to the dissolution of name and form superimposed by ignorance, as in the passage "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman" (*brahmava san brahmāpyeti*). Furthermore, if a journey directed toward the Supreme were being explained, it would be either for the sake of providing encouragement or for the sake of meditation.

In this regard, the desire to hear is not produced by statements concerning the departure [of the soul] for those who know Brahman, because that [desire] is accomplished through the very health bestowed by knowledge—which is self-evident, immediate, and uninterrupted. Furthermore, no need for reflection on the path arises for one who has been informed of the eternally established supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), which is a fruit that cannot be further achieved.
Therefore, the departure concerns the lower [Brahman].

In this regard, because of the failure to discern the distinction between the higher and lower Brahman, scriptural passages concerning the state of existence (gati) that apply to the lower Brahman are superimposed upon the higher Brahman.
Are there, then, two Brahmans—the higher and the lower? Certainly; for it is seen in such texts as: "O Satyakāma, this very syllable Om is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman.

What, then, is the higher Brahman and what is the lower? It is said: that Brahman which is taught through words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth, by way of negating the distinctions of name, form, and the like created by ignorance (*avidyā*), is the higher.

That very [Brahman] is "higher" when it is taught for the purpose of meditation as qualified by some particularity such as name and form, through such scriptural expressions as "consisting of mind, having prāṇa for its body, having light for its form," and so forth.

Now, one might object that in this way the scriptural teaching of non-duality would be contradicted; but this is not so, because [the qualification] has been set aside on the grounds that names and forms are created by ignorance (avidyā).

Furthermore, the fruit of that meditation on the lower Brahman—heard in its proximity as "if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," and so forth—is characterized by sovereignty over the world and remains within the sphere of saṃsāra, because ignorance has not yet been dispelled.
And since that [world] is bound to a specific location, travel for the purpose of reaching it is not contradictory.

Furthermore, even though the Self is omnipresent, we have already explained in the section on "The Essence Being Its Qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*) that the conventional designation of "going" occurs when the limiting adjuncts, such as the intellect (*buddhi*), move—just as space is said to "go" when it enters a jar or similar object.
Therefore, the position "the effected [body], according to Bādari" (*kāryaṃ bādari*) remains the established view.
However, the statement "But Jaimini [holds the opposite]" should be understood as merely demonstrating an alternative view for the purpose of expanding one's understanding.
In the Sūtra-bhāṣya, Bādarāyaṇa states: "He leads those who do not rely on symbols," because there is no fault in either case, and because of the nature of their resolve (*tatkratu*).
It has been established that this movement pertains to the realm of effects (*kārya*), and not to the realm of the Supreme (*para*).

Now, the following doubt arises: does the non-human person (*amānavaḥ puruṣaḥ*) lead all those who have meditated upon the modifications (*vikāra*), including those who have meditated upon symbols (*pratīka*), to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) without exception, or only some of them?
What, then, is the initial position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? [The view is that] for all these knowers, except for those who have meditated upon the Supreme... [the non-human person leads them there].
The movement [of the soul] would be with the Brahman;
for indeed, in the rule "there is no restriction for all," this [attainment] has been introduced without distinction into other meditations as well.
This being the position reached, the author replies: "except those who rely on symbols" (apratīkālambanān).
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that, with the exception of those meditations based on symbols (*pratīka*), he leads all others—those based on modifications (*vikāra*)—to the world of Brahman.

For there is no fault whatsoever in accepting this dual status [of being led or not], since the principle of non-restriction (*aniyamanyāya*) applies even to meditations other than those based on symbols.
Furthermore, the scriptural statement "according to his resolve" (*tatkratu*) should be seen as the supporting reason for this dual status.

For it is established that "he who has Brahman as his resolve (brahmakratu) attains the sovereignty of Brahman," according to the scriptural text: "In whatever way they meditate upon it, that alone they become. However, the state of having Brahman as one's resolve does not exist in the case of symbols (pratīka), because meditation upon symbols has the symbol itself as its primary object.
But surely, it is heard in scripture that even one who does not have Brahman as their resolve goes to Brahman;
for example, in the Pañcāgnividyā, it says, "He leads them to Brahman. Let it be so. [End of Chapter Four]

Where such a statement regarding the attainment [of a specific result] is found, that is so; however, in the absence of such a statement, it is understood by the general rule of the "intentionality of the ritual" (*tatkratu-nyāya*) that those whose ritual intention is directed toward Brahman alone attain it, and not others.
And he demonstrates the distinction.

In the case of the meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsana*) such as Name and the rest, the text shows that for each successive meditation there is a superior result compared to the preceding one, through such passages as: "As far as Name extends, so far he has freedom of movement; Speech, indeed, is greater than Name"; "As far as Speech extends, so far he has freedom of movement; Mind, indeed, is greater than Speech," and so forth.
And this distinction of results is appropriate because these meditations are dependent upon the symbols.
However, if they were dependent upon Brahman, since Brahman is without distinction [in all cases], how could there be a distinction of results?
Therefore, those who have the symbols as their support do not possess a fruit equal to that of others.

Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-sūtras composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda, the teacher of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order. The Fourth Quarter of the Fourth Chapter in the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "In this very way, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: does it manifest by means of some adventitious attribute, as occurs in places of enjoyment such as the world of the gods, or rather, by the Self alone?

What, then, is the initial position? It should be that manifestation occurs through some adventitious form, just as in other locations, because liberation is well-known to be a fruit, and because the term "manifests" (abhiniṣpadyate) is a synonym for "arising."
If manifestation were by means of its own nature alone, it would have been perceived even in previous states, since its own nature does not depart [at those times];
therefore, it manifests through some specific attribute.
This being the position reached, we reply: "The manifestation occurs upon attaining [the Self], because of the word 'own'."
It manifests by means of the self alone, and not through any other attribute. Why? Because of the word "own" (*sva*) in the phrase "he is perfected in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*).
This constitutes the section concerning manifestation upon attaining [the Self].
For otherwise, the qualification by the word "own" would be inappropriate.
Now, one might object: "The word 'own' (sva) will mean 'belonging to oneself' (ātmīya). This is not so, because that meaning cannot be maintained.
For in whatever form [the Self] manifests, it is logically possible for that very form to belong to itself; thus, the qualification "by its own" (svena) would be redundant.
However, if it denotes the Self itself, it becomes meaningful: [it shows] that it manifests solely in its own essential nature, and not even in any adventitious or other form.

But what is the distinction between the previous states and this one, given that there is equality in the non-departure from its own nature? To this he says: "The liberated [Self is distinct] because of the scriptural declaration."
He who is said here to "emerge" remains established in his very pure self, entirely liberated from all bonds.

However, in the previous state, he was described as being "blind," "as if weeping," and "having gone to utter destruction"; thus, there is this distinction that in the former case he remained with a self defiled by the substrate of the limiting conditions (*avasthālaya*).
How, then, is it understood that he is now liberated? He says: "Because of the initial proposition."

For instance, having promised to explain the Self—which is free from the defects of the three states—as the subject to be explained by saying, "I shall indeed explain this further to you," and having introduced the topic with, "Verily, when one is bodiless, neither pleasure nor pain touches him," the text concludes with, "He attains his own true form; he is the Supreme Person.
Likewise, at the beginning of the narrative, the promise, "The Self which is free from evil," and so forth, refers exclusively to the liberated Self.
The well-known status of liberation as a fruit also depends solely upon the cessation of bondage, not upon the production of something previously non-existent.

As for the statement that one "becomes manifest" (*abhiniṣpadyate*), which is a synonym for arising—that too does not depend on a new state, just as when a disease ceases, one is said to "become manifest as healthy" (*arogo 'bhiniṣpadyate*).
Therefore, there is no fault.
The Self [is the subject], because of the context.

But how can he be said to be "liberated," given that the text, by stating "having reached the highest light" (*paraṃ jyotir upasaṃpadya*), makes him out to be within the sphere of an effect; for the word "light" (*jyotis*) is conventionally established in the sense of physical light? And one who has not transcended the realm of modifications cannot be liberated, since it is well known that a modification is subject to suffering. This objection is not valid, because here the Self itself is indicated by the word "light," owing to the context.

Since the Supreme Self has been introduced as "the Self which is free from evil, ageless, and deathless," it is not possible to suddenly grasp a material light [as the subject], for that would entail abandoning the context at hand and introducing something not under discussion.

Furthermore, the word "light" (jyotis) is seen to refer even to the Self, as in "That is the light of lights. And this has been explained in detail in the commentary on the sūtra "On account of the perception of light" (Brahmasūtra 1.3.40).
In the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya*: "Because [the soul] is seen as non-distinct [from Brahman]."

Regarding the inquiry as to whether he who, having attained the highest light, manifests in his own true form, remains distinct from the Supreme Self or abides in non-distinction from It: for one who holds the view that he must remain in a state of distinction—on account of the designation of a locus and a subject in the phrase "he moves about there," and on account of the designation of agent and object in the phrase "having attained"—the author explains that the liberated soul abides in non-distinction from the Supreme Self.
Why? Because it is so seen in scripture.

For indeed, such statements as "That thou art," "I am Brahman," "Where one sees nothing else," and "But there is no second, nothing else separate from it that he might see," show the supreme Self precisely as non-differentiated;
and it is logical that the fruit should correspond exactly to such a vision, according to the principle of the "intentionality of the sacrifice" (*tatkratu-nyāya*):
"As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly the same."

Thus, statements such as "The self of the sage who knows thus becomes [Brahman], O Gautama," which are intent on defining the nature of the liberated one, demonstrate non-differentiation; so too do the illustrations of the river and the ocean.

As for the mention of difference, it is used figuratively even where there is no difference, as seen in such passages as, "In what, O Venerable One, is he established? In his own majesty," and "He whose delight is the Self, whose play is the Self."
Jaimini [maintains that the soul is of atomic size], because of the mention [of its departure] and so forth.
Pāṇini Sūtra, Chapter Four.
It has been established in this context—that "in his own form" means he manifests in the form of the Self alone, and not in some adventitious, other form.
Now, however, in response to the desire to know the specific details regarding that Brahman-form, it is stated that his own form consists of the instruments (karaṇa).

The teacher Jaimini maintains that [the soul] manifests in its own nature as consisting of the qualities beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatva), as well as omniscience and omnipotence;
why? Because such a state is understood from the introductory description and other passages.

For instance, by the introductory description beginning with "The Self which is free from sin" and ending with "whose desires are true and whose resolves are true," [the scripture] makes known that the Self has such a nature.

Likewise, the passage "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing" reveals a state of sovereignty; and the statement "He has freedom of movement in all worlds" as well as designations such as "all-knowing" and "lord of all" will thus be appropriately established.
"Audulomi [holds that the soul exists] as mere consciousness, because it has that as its essence."

Although qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are indicated as distinct attributes, nevertheless, these are merely born of verbal conceptualization (*śabdavikalpa*); for in that context, only the cessation of evil and the like is understood.
Consciousness alone, however, is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of this Self; therefore, its manifestation as that nature alone is what is logical.
And thus, scriptural passages of this kind—such as, "In this very way, indeed, my dear, this Self is without interior or exterior, a mass of pure consciousness alone"—will be supported.

As for the qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*), although they are stated as attributes of the essential nature of the thing itself in the sense that "its desires are true," nevertheless, because they depend upon a connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is impossible for them to constitute its essential nature in the same way that consciousness does; for the possession of multiple forms by Brahman has been denied in the passage: "The higher [Self] does not possess both characteristics even on account of its locations" (BS 3.2.11).

For this very reason, even the mention of "eating" (jakṣaṇa) and so forth is intended merely to signify the absence of suffering for the sake of praise, just as in the passage beginning with "rejoicing in the Self" (ātmarati).
Indeed, primary forms of pleasure, play, and sexual union cannot be described as having the Self as their object, because they necessarily involve a second entity.

Therefore, the teacher Auḍulomi maintains that [the liberated soul] becomes manifest as the essence of consciousness—serene, indefinable, and one in whom the entire phenomenal world has been utterly dispelled.
Even on account of such a presentation, Bādarāyaṇa maintains there is no contradiction because of its prior existence.

Even so, although the ultimate nature is admitted to be pure consciousness alone, the teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is no contradiction, because from the perspective of empirical usage, the divine sovereignty—which was previously understood through such means as scriptural declarations—is not denied.
But [the creation of the world occurs] from mere volition alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
In the Hārdavidyā, it is heard: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere will (saṃkalpa) the fathers arise for him," and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the mere will alone the cause for the manifestation of the fathers and others?
Is it that [the manifestation] has a cause, or is it accompanied by other instrumental causes?
Even though there is the scriptural statement for you that "by mere volition alone," it is logical that there is a dependence on other instrumental causes, just as in the world;

for just as in the world, for people like us, the attainment of fathers and so forth occurs through volition as well as causes such as going and so forth, so it would be for the liberated one as well.
In this way, [the view] contrary to what has been seen will not be imagined;

however, the phrase "merely from resolve" (*saṃkalpādeva*) will be appropriate by depending on an easily available collection of other means that accomplish the intended object, as in the case of a king.
Furthermore, fathers and others produced by mere resolve would not be capable of bestowing abundant enjoyment, because of their instability, like the expansion of a mere mental wish.
This being the case, we reply: the emergence of the fathers and others occurs from mere volition alone. Why? Because of the scriptural statement;
for the scriptural passage, "By his mere volition, the fathers arise," and so forth, would be contradicted if there were dependence on any other cause.
Furthermore, if another cause were to conform precisely to one's volition, let it be so;

however, another cause that must be produced by a separate effort is not admitted as such, because that would entail the consequence that volitions prior to the attainment [of the goal] would be fruitless. Moreover, regarding a matter to be understood through scripture, an inference based on general observation—such as "as in the world"—does not apply.

Moreover, by the power of their mere resolve (*saṃkalpa*), these [liberated ones] possess stability for as long as they require, because the resolve of one who is liberated is distinct from that of ordinary beings. For this very reason, they have no other lord (*ananyādhipati*). (Sūtra-bhāṣya)
And for this very reason, because his resolve is never in vain, the wise man becomes one who has no other lord; the meaning is that no other person becomes his master.
