For even an ordinary person, when forming a resolve, does not conceive of himself as being under the dominion of another if a better course is available.
And scripture demonstrates this: "Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds."
For Bāri has indeed stated thus regarding the absence of the self.
From the scriptural text, "By his mere volition (saṃkalpa), his ancestors arise," it is established that the mind is the instrument of volition.

As for the body and the senses, however, [the opponent] maintains that there is an absence of them for the exalted knower, because they have not been attained. That is, he considers there to be an absence of both the body and the senses for the one who is being glorified.
Why? Because the tradition (āmnāya) says: "He rejoices, seeing these desires with the mind, which are in the world of Brahman.
If he were to sport with both the mind and the body and the senses, the qualification "with the mind" would not be necessary.
Therefore, there is an absence of the body and the senses in liberation.
Jaimini [maintains that the soul] exists [after death], because of the mention of various [post-mortem] states.

It is examined whether these belong to the liberated wise one or do not. In this regard, the teacher Bādari holds that they do not exist. However, the teacher Jaimini, like [the teacher] Manu, considers that for the liberated one, there exists the state of a body together with its sense organs.
For [the scriptures] declare the possibility of manifold existence through such passages as, "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold," and so on.
Indeed, this manifoldness could not occur naturally without a difference of bodies.

Although this possibility of manifold existence is recited in the context of the *bhūmavidyā* (the knowledge of the Infinite), which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), nevertheless, this very sovereignty existing in the state with qualities (*saguṇa*) is mentioned for the purpose of praising the *bhūmavidyā*; therefore, it presents itself as the fruit of the knowledge with qualities.
It is said: "Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the meditation] is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice."

But the teacher Bādarāyaṇa, on the other hand, because he observes scriptural texts exhibiting both characteristics, considers it correct that [the liberated soul] possesses a twofold nature: when it wills a state with a body, it becomes embodied; but when it wills a state without a body, it becomes bodiless. This is due to its power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*) and the variety of its resolves.

It is like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which, according to the observation of scriptural texts exhibiting both characteristics, is both a sacrificial session (*sattra*) and a non-session (*ahīna*); so too is this case.
In the absence of a body, [the soul's existence] is established as in the case of the twilight state.

When there is the absence of this body together with its sense organs, then—just as in the state of dream (saṃdhye sthāne), where even though the body, senses, and objects do not exist, there are merely perceptions consisting of desires for fathers and so forth—so too would they be in liberation;
for it is in this way that this [state] becomes logically consistent.
Awake in the state of being.
Furthermore, regarding existence, just as the desires for fathers and so forth exist even while one is awake, so too is it possible for the liberated one.
The entry [of the self into the body] is like that of a lamp; for thus it is shown.
In the sūtra, "Jaimini [holds that the soul] possesses a body because of the mention of manifoldness," the state of having a body for the liberated one was stated;

regarding that, when there is the creation of many bodies in cases such as becoming threefold, a doubt arises: are these bodies created without a soul, like wooden automata, or are they endowed with a soul, like our own bodies? This is the inquiry.

In this regard, since a distinction between the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*) is untenable, and because [the self] is connected with one body, it follows that the other bodies are devoid of a self. To this conclusion, the following is established: "The entry [of the self into all bodies] is like that of a lamp.

Just as a single lamp attains the state of many lamps through its connection with the power of transformation, so too the knower, though being one, attains a manifold state through his connection with sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) and enters all bodies.
Why? Because the scripture shows the manifold state of the one, saying: "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, five-fold, seven-fold, nine-fold," and so forth.
This is not possible under the assumption that the body is like a wooden machine, nor under the theory of the entry of another soul;
furthermore, the activity of bodies devoid of a self is not possible. (From the Fourth Chapter).

As for the objection that because a distinction between the self and the mind is untenable, the connection with multiple bodies is impossible—this is not a fault; for by virtue of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), he can create other bodies that possess minds following after his own single mind.
And once those have been created, the self's status as a controller will be appropriate through a distinction based on the diversity of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

And this very process of the union with multiple bodies is the method for yogins described in the Yoga-shastras. But how can sovereignty characterized by the entry into multiple bodies be admitted for one who is liberated, when such scriptural passages as "Then by what should he know whom? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), "But there is not a second that exists separate from him that he might know" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23), and "He becomes one, a seer, without duality, like water" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32)—passages of this kind—exclude specific cognition? To this, the author reads the following reply: "It refers to either deep sleep or union [with Brahman], for it is so made manifest. (Brahma-sūtra 4.4.16) This means that the scriptural denial of specific cognition applies to the states of deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or union with Brahman (*sampatti*), because in those states all particular consciousness ceases. However, the power of sovereignty consisting in the entry into multiple bodies is not denied for the liberated soul in its own nature; rather, it is established by the scriptures themselves. For instance, the scripture speaks of the liberated soul's power: "He, being one, becomes threefold, fivefold, sevenfold, and ninefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2). Thus, the admission of such sovereignty is consistent with the texts. Furthermore, the term "liberated" (*mukta*) here refers to one who has attained liberation through knowledge while still in the body (*jīvanmukta*), for whom the power of sovereignty is indeed possible. Therefore, there is no contradiction.The final answer is: This very process constitutes the method in the Yoga-śāstras for yogins to achieve union with multiple bodies. As for the objection: "How can sovereignty characterized by entering multiple bodies be accepted for the liberated, since scriptural passages such as 'Then by what should he know whom?', 'But there is nothing else separate from him that he might know', and 'He becomes one, a seer, without duality, like water', exclude specific cognition?", the author reads the reply: "It refers to either deep sleep or union, for it is so made manifest. This means that the exclusion of specific cognition is intended to apply to either the state of deep sleep or the state of union with Brahman, as these are clearly indicated by the context. "Deep sleep" (*svāpyaya*) is *suṣupta*, according to the Śruti: "He has gone to his own (*svam apīta*); therefore they say of him, 'he sleeps' (*svapiti*).
"Attainment" (*saṃpatti*) is *kaivalya*, according to the Śruti: "Being Brahman itself, he goes to Brahman.

With reference to either of these two states, this statement regarding the absence of specific designations is made—sometimes with reference to the state of deep sleep, and sometimes with reference to the state of liberation (*kaivalya*).

How is this understood? Because right there, by virtue of that very context, it is revealed: "Having arisen from these elements, one vanishes again into them; after death, there is no consciousness," and from such scriptural passages as, "But where the Self has become all this," and, "When one is asleep, one desires no desire and sees no dream.
However, this state, wherein this sovereignty is described, is a different condition—like heaven and so forth—that constitutes the place for the ripening of knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā).
Therefore, there is no fault.
[The Lord is] exempt from the activities of the world, because of the context and because of His non-proximity [to such activities].

A doubt arises as to whether those who, through meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahma*), attain union with the Lord (*īśvara-sāyujya*) together with their minds, possess sovereignty that is unrestrained (*niravagraha*), or whether it is restrained (*sāvagraha*). What, then, is the prima facie position? It is without restriction. Their sovereignty must indeed be unrestrained, based on such scriptural texts as: "He attains self-rule" (*āpnoti svārājyam*); "All the gods bring him tribute" (*sarve'smai devā balimāvahanti*); and "For them there is freedom of movement in all worlds" (*teṣāṃ sarveṣu lokeṣu kāmacāro bhavati*). Thus [the prima facie view].
This being the case, the author of the Sūtras states: "Excluding the activity of the world.

Aside from the activity of creating and so forth the world, other forms of sovereignty consisting of powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest may belong to the liberated souls; however, the activity of the world belongs only to the eternally established Lord.
Why? Because He is the subject under discussion in that context.
And because the others are not proximate [to that state];

for the Supreme Lord alone is authorized over the activity of the world, since the teaching of origination and so forth refers specifically to Him, and because He is the basis for eternal scriptural statements;
whereas the sovereignty of the others, such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest, is heard in scripture as being preceded by the search for and the desire to know Him.
Therefore, they are not present in the activity of the world.

Furthermore, because they possess minds, there might even occasionally be a conflict among them due to a lack of unanimity—such that one has the intention to maintain [the world] while another has the intention to destroy it. Thus ends the fourth chapter. And so forth. Because they possess minds, in the event of a disagreement among them, there might even at some time be a contradiction, such as one having the intention for maintenance and another having the intention for destruction.

If, on the other hand, the intention of one were to follow the intention of another, such that there would be no contradiction, then it would be established that the others are entirely dependent upon the will of the Supreme Lord.
If it is argued that this is because of direct instruction, we say no, because [the teaching] refers to those situated in the spheres of authority.

Now, as for what was stated—that because of the direct scriptural instruction, "He attains self-sovereignty" (*svārājyam*), it is logical that those who possess knowledge should enjoy unobstructed lordship—that must be refuted.

To this, it is replied: this is not a fault, because the statement refers to the one who occupies the spheres of authority (*ādhikārika*). The Supreme Lord who resides in specific abodes such as the orb of the sun and so forth is the *ādhikārika* one; it is under His control that this attainment of self-sovereignty is said to occur.
For this reason, he immediately says, "He attains the Lord of the mind" (*manasaspatim*).

What is meant is that he attains that pre-established Lord who is the master of all minds; and in accordance with that very [principle], he immediately [proceeds to say], "The lord of speech, the lord of sight... (*vākpatiś cakṣuṣpatiḥ*).
"He becomes the lord of the ear and the lord of consciousness," so it is said.
Likewise, in other cases as well, the sovereignty of others should be understood as being dependent solely upon the eternally established Lord, according to what is appropriate.
And it does not abide in modification, for thus the scripture declares its state.
Moreover, the supreme form of the Lord, which is eternally free, does not abide only within the realm of modifications—such as the sphere of the sun and other substrates—but transcends them as well.

For the sacred tradition (Āmnāya) declares His twofold state in such passages as: "Such is His greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is greater than that; all beings constitute one quarter of Him, while His three quarters are the immortal in heaven. And so forth.
Nor can it be said that those whose objects of meditation are other than Him attain that changeless form, because they lack the necessary resolve (*atatkratutva*).

Therefore, it should be understood that just as [devotees] remain fixed upon the qualified form alone without attaining the qualityless form of the Supreme Lord who possesses two forms, so too, even regarding the qualified form, they remain fixed upon it with its limitations, without attaining the unbounded sovereignty (*niravagraham aiśvaryam*).
And thus, perception and inference are shown [to be established].

Furthermore, the Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate that the supreme light does not abide within the realm of modifications: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14); and "The sun does not illuminate it, nor the moon, nor fire" (Gītā 15.6).
Thus, the intention is that the fact of the supreme light not abiding within the realm of modifications is well-established.
And because there is a mark [in the scripture] indicating equality only with respect to enjoyment.

For this reason as well, the sovereignty of those who take hold of the transformations is not unrestrained; because it is heard in scripture that their enjoyment alone is equal to that of the eternally established Lord. As stated in the fourth chapter: "They said to him: 'Verily, the waters are measured out; that is the world,'" and "Just as all beings protect these deities, so do all beings protect one who knows thus," and "Therefore, he wins union with and residence in the same world as this deity. These and other such indications of distinction [prove the point].
But if this were so, would not the sovereignty (aiśvarya) be finite because it possesses degrees of excellence?

In that case, the recurrence (āvṛtti) of these [liberated souls] would follow as a consequence. To this, the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa recites the answer: "No return, on account of the scriptural statement; no return, on account of the scriptural statement."

Those who go to the world of Brahman—described with specific attributes in the scriptures—by means of the path of the gods (*devayāna*) consisting of the stages beginning with light and accompanied by the rays of the arteries, do not return after having experienced their enjoyment, as is the case with those who go to the world of the moon. This world of Brahman is that in which, in the third heaven from here, exist the rivers Ara and Nyarū; where there is the lake Airammadīya; where there is the Aśvattha tree called Somasavana; where there is the city of Brahman called Aparājitā; and where there is the golden hall built by the Lord. It is this world, which is elaborately described in many places such as the Mantras and Arthavādas, that they reach, and having reached it, they do not return.

Why? From such scriptural statements as: "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality"; "For them there is no return"; "Those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool"; "They attain the world of Brahman"; and "And he does not return again. Even though their sovereignty is finite, the fact that there is no return has been explained in the passage: "At the dissolution of the effected world, they enter along with the ruler into the highest" (Sūtra-bhāṣya). However, for those whose darkness has been destroyed by perfect knowledge and who are intent upon eternally established liberation, non-return is an established fact.
For it is precisely by taking refuge in Him that even those who have sought refuge in the Saguna Brahman achieve non-return.
The repetition of the words "non-return" (anāvṛtti) in the two sūtras—*anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*, *anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*—indicates the completion of the treatise.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Sūtras of Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Thus ends the venerable commentary on the Sūtras of the Investigation into the Nature of the Self.
May Mitra be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us.
May Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us!
Homage to Brahman!
Homage to you, O Vāyu!
You alone are the perceptible Brahman. To you alone have I spoken of the perceptible Brahman;
I have spoken the Truth.
I have spoken the truth;
may it protect me,
may it protect the speaker.
He has protected me;
he has protected the speaker.
Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! May He protect us both; may He nourish us both;
may we work together with vigor.
May what we have studied not be lost; may we never harbor mutual hatred.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
He who is the bull among the meters, possessing all forms,
who was born from the immortal meters—
may that Indra strengthen me with wisdom.
May I be a sustainer of the nectar of the gods.
May my body be preeminent;
may my tongue be most sweet.
Hearing much with my two ears;
you are the treasury of the Veda, covered by wisdom.
Protect what I have heard.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
I am the line of the tree;
my fame is like the ridge of a mountain.
With my purifier held aloft, I am my own immortal nectar, like a swift steed.
"Obeisance to Draviṇa, the radiant;
obeisance to Sumedhas, sprinkled with immortality.
Thus is the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious;
may we, with firm limbs and bodies, praise you with joyful hearts.
May we attain the life-span ordained by the gods. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being;
may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
The Fullness is that; this is the Fullness. From the Fullness, the fullness is drawn forth. Having taken the fullness of the Fullness, the Fullness alone remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
O Master, may my limbs, speech, breath, sight, hearing, as well as strength and all my senses, be nourished.

May everything that is Brahman and the Upanishads never reject me, and may I never reject Brahman. May there be no rejection; may there be non-rejection for me. May those virtues which reside in the self and are established in the Upanishads abide in me; may they abide in me.
Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! May my speech be established in my mind;
may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest and radiant within me.
Be the axle of my Veda;
do not let what I have heard fall away from me through this study.
I join together the days and nights;
I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me;
may it protect its speaker;
may it protect me.
May it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
May you also direct our minds toward what is auspicious.
Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! I, seeking liberation, go for refuge to that God who illumines the self through the intellect, who created Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace. Table of Contents of the Sūtra.
